seeds.title: あらし
seeds.raw:
Create a horizontal 16:9 full-bleed flat graphic design poster titled "あらし", themed as a nocturnal storm observatory converting wind, rain, pressure, and sound into one editorial graphic system. Use the exact Japanese hiragana title あらし and no additional readable text. Build the poster with the precision of a premium Japanese editorial design, contemporary electronic-music key visual, and gallery-grade silkscreen print. Use flat two-dimensional vector shapes, crisp technical wireframes, weather-chart cartography, geometric collage, torn-paper layers, transparent acetate planes, restrained halftone rain, topographic contour systems, and one controlled glitch event. The result must feel visually rich and professionally art-directed, not like a student poster, anime scene, 3D render, fan wallpaper, or decorative scrapbook.

Hatsune Miku is fixed as the one and only humanoid character. Preserve her canonical identity, aqua eyes, aqua hair, extremely long twin tails, red-and-black hair accessories, futuristic headset, original teal-and-black outfit, and unmistakable silhouette. Render her as a refined cel-shaded 2D graphic with flat color fills, minimal tonal transitions, crisp variable-width contours, and simplified angular hair planes. Do not replace her, add another humanoid character or background person, alter her hairstyle or outfit, use realistic skin, or render her with 3D volume.

Make Hatsune Miku the dominant subject. Place her in the left third at approximately 27 percent of the canvas width and 55 percent of its height, shown from the upper thighs upward at about 62 percent of the canvas height. Turn her body toward the right in a clear three-quarter pose, with her face lifted slightly toward a storm-data current. One hand stays near her shoulder; the other extends toward a broken isobar line. Keep her face, visible aqua eye, mouth, neck, hands, headset, and main silhouette completely unobstructed. Give her a calm, alert expression amid the storm.

Use a full-bleed smoked-silver background with large flat fields of deep ink black, storm blue, warm white, and signal orange. Build an asymmetrical editorial composition with strong clean negative space around Miku's face and shoulders. Do not place her in the central 40–60 percent zone.

Use a flat storm-blue circular radar field as a secondary background structure. Make its diameter approximately 43 percent of the canvas width and place its center near 78 percent of the canvas width and 36 percent of the canvas height, cropped by the right edge. Keep it sharp and screen-printed. Do not blur it, soften it, make it glow, give it 3D volume, or allow it to overlap Miku's torso. Reduce its internal density and integrate only a modest number of concentric grooves, pressure arcs, radial ticks, and calibration gaps.

Place the exact Japanese title あらし horizontally across the upper area, reading from left to right as あ, ら, し. Use oversized contemporary geometric hiragana display typography with high-contrast strokes, sharp terminals, strong curves, and tight professional spacing. It must look like modern Japanese editorial typography, not Chinese calligraphy, Hanzi, brush writing, manga lettering, or faux-Japanese decoration. Use hiragana only. Do not include kanji, Chinese characters, katakana, English, Latin letters, or numbers anywhere in the poster.

Render あ and ら in warm white against the smoked-silver and ink-black fields. Let the final し cross onto the storm-blue circle, switching cleanly to deep ink black while preserving its full contour. Keep all three hiragana characters correctly formed. Do not crop the title at the canvas edge, rotate individual glyphs, substitute another character, duplicate the word, or fracture multiple letters.

Use only one typographic interruption: a narrow horizontal glitch slice across the lower-right terminal of the final し. Confine it to a compact rectangular area and affect less than fifteen percent of the glyph. Preserve the main vertical curve and immediate readability of し. Do not glitch あ or ら, and do not add another glitch anywhere else in the poster.

Do not include birds, feathers, flowers, petals, leaves, botanical imagery, or floral silhouettes. Replace airborne organic forms with exactly fourteen meteorological sounding balloons. Make them compact flat circles, capsules, or rounded instruments with narrow trailing tethers and small geometric instrument triangles. Use three primary balloons with clear warm-white, storm-blue, and signal-orange color blocking. Place one beneath the title, one beside Miku's outer hair, and one near the radar circle. Render the other eleven as distant line silhouettes at multiple depths. Trailing tethers should follow long wind vectors and remain aligned to the technical grid.

Replace floral ground imagery with a layered storm landscape made from topographic contours and rain-data bands. Build the lower third from seven broad contour layers in smoke gray, ink black, storm blue, and thin signal orange. Interrupt the layers with sparse halftone rain fields and straight rain-gauge ticks without readable labels. Let selected contour lines rise behind Miku and connect to the radar system. Do not create clouds shaped like objects, lightning bolts as decoration, or a conventional storm landscape illustration.

Increase material richness with controlled graphic layers: one torn silver-paper strip, one narrow signal-orange pressure band, two flat storm-blue acetate panels with no reflections, one pale warm-white rectangular mask, one sheet of blue-gray halftone rain, one perforated measurement strip containing no readable text, and one small acid-lime registration block. Keep every material flat, cropped, and aligned to the shared grid. Avoid random scrapbook clutter.

Unify all technical decoration on one twelve-column poster grid. Align every vertical rule, collage edge, balloon tether, typography guide, and radar groove to that grid. Center every radial tick on the storm-blue circle. Use only three functional systems:

1. Wind and balloon trajectories represent upward movement. Use long curved arrows without filled arrowheads, parallel flow lines, open nodes, and shallow S-curves.
2. Pressure and rain data represent environmental measurement. Use isobars, short gauge ticks, sparse horizontal bars, and calibrated frequency lines located at grid intersections.
3. Interference is represented solely by the single glitch slice on the final hiragana し.

Do not add random crosses, floating UI panels, fake technical labels, unrelated Japanese symbols, decorative lightning bolts, or marks that do not communicate wind, pressure, rain, or interference.

Construct the geometric collage from seven elements only: one smoked-silver rectangular panel, one ink-black vertical mask, one signal-orange pressure bar, one storm-blue acetate plane, one warm-white circular cutout, one torn-paper halftone strip, and one small chartreuse registration block. Use hard edges, crisp crop lines, and exact grid alignment. Collage may overlap Miku's lower body and the radar circle's edge, but must never cover her face, eye, hands, main hair silhouette, the title, or the three primary sounding balloons.

Use a disciplined palette of smoked silver, deep ink black, storm blue, signal orange, warm white, and a very small amount of acid chartreuse. Keep large fields flat and matte. Use orange only for warning bands, one balloon, and small radial accents. Use acid chartreuse only for tiny registration pieces. Avoid glossy gradients, cobalt neon, realistic glass, volumetric lighting, photographic textures, rainbow noise, and heavy shadows.

Finish with premium silkscreen and risograph qualities: subtle paper grain, dry-ink edges, restrained registration offset, sparse halftone rain, crisp vector contours, and precise line weights. Use hairline strokes for weather systems, medium contours for balloons and topographic layers, and the strongest contour for Miku's silhouette. The title should appear letterpress-printed into the poster rather than pasted above it.

Connect the systems through structure. Let one balloon tether continue directly from the upper loop of ら into the wind grid without touching the character stroke. Let one thin pressure line continue from the lower endpoint of the final し into the contour landscape. Allow one outer strand of Miku's twin tail to pass behind the lower edge of し without changing its outline. Typography, figure, balloons, radar, and storm landscape must interlock while remaining readable.

At a phone-message thumbnail size of approximately 320 by 180 pixels, Miku's face and upper body must read first, the exact hiragana title あらし second, and the storm-blue radar circle third. The signal-orange bands and dark contour landscape should remain visible as supporting graphic masses. Fine balloons, rain marks, topographic details, and paper textures may disappear at thumbnail size, but the main hierarchy must survive.

No additional readable text, kanji, Chinese characters, katakana, English, Latin letters, numbers, captions, subtitles, logos, signatures, watermarks, QR codes, barcodes, fake weather labels, or garbled Japanese typography. Only the exact hiragana word あらし may be readable. No birds, feathers, flowers, petals, leaves, botanical forms, second humanoid character, duplicated face, extra limbs, malformed hands, cropped title, incorrect glyphs, multiple glitch cuts, centered halo, 3D object, painterly rendering, glossy surfaces, decorative lightning, holographic interface, or random visual clutter.

Final quality: horizontal 16:9 full-bleed flat graphic design poster, fixed recognizable Hatsune Miku in the left third, exact horizontal hiragana title あらし, one controlled glitch on the final し, smoked-silver and deep-ink background, smaller storm-blue radar circle on the right, fourteen meteorological sounding balloons, seven topographic contour layers, signal-orange pressure bands, acetate and torn-paper collage, shared technical grid, wind-pressure-rain systems, rich layered visual density, strong thumbnail hierarchy, premium Japanese editorial typography, sophisticated silkscreen finish, contemporary electronic-music poster art direction.

seeds.title: BLACKBOX
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 three-ink data-portrait poster titled "BLACKBOX", printed as a flat graphic sheet. The only figure is Hatsune Miku, shown from the collarbones up at three-quarter profile facing right, her head set left of centre with the crown of her head near the upper third of the frame. Preserve her canonical identity precisely: luminous aqua irises with a fine dark upper lash line, aqua bangs cut as a soft fringe, an extremely long aqua twin tail falling behind each shoulder, a slim silver headset with a thin microphone arm, and clean anime line quality. Hold her left cheek, both eyes, the bridge of her nose and her mouth in one unbroken printed layer; everything behind her right ear may fragment.

Compose on a hard vertical split rather than a centred portrait. The left forty-five percent of the frame is a clean near-black plate carrying her face and the title. The right fifty-five percent is a dense data field that begins exactly at the line behind her right ear and eats outward. The shoulder line stays level, one strip of her collar remains visible, and no shape may cross the vertical split above her jaw.

Use black as the ground and the subject at once: seventy percent of the frame is near-black, with her hair, her collar and the void merging into one dark mass so that only the bright edge describes her. Cold grey-white takes sixteen percent and does the drawing: the contour along her jaw, her lash line, the rim of her headset, the collar edge and the whole type layer. Electric cyan takes eight percent and lives inside the data field only, always as thin scanline and block edges rather than broad fill. Magenta takes three percent and appears once, as a single offset channel line along the far right edge.

Build the right side as printed interference, not as a screen. Stack four systems: a coarse halftone field that thickens toward the right border, horizontal scanlines of three different spacings, rectangular pixel blocks in three sizes that cluster around her right shoulder, and one torn vertical band where the image appears to fold under itself. Let each system stop at a different distance from her ear so the erosion looks layered rather than masked.

Keep the split legible: where the data field meets her right side, her hair must still read as hair for at least two strand groups, then break into squares. Do not let any pixel block cross her cheek, her eye or her mouth. The brightest values belong to her left eye, the rim of her headset and the title, and nothing in the data field may be brighter than her iris.

Set the title as hollow display type running behind her head: "BLACKBOX" in a heavy condensed grotesque, letters three hundred and eighty pixels tall, outlined in cold grey-white with empty interiors, the word starting at the left margin behind her hair and cropped by the right edge, so her head interrupts the middle of it. Print the exact readable text "09 / NO RETURN" once, small, in cold grey, aligned to the bottom-left margin, and the exact readable text "SIGNAL" vertically along the extreme right edge at thumbnail size.

Print the surface as ink. Every shadow is a flat black shape, every light a pasted white shape, no gradients inside the face, no glow around the headset. Apply coarse halftone only in the data field and along the outer hair, fine halftone in the collar shadow. Offset the cyan plate two millimetres sideways in the right half only so the interference slips out of register there while her face stays perfectly registered.

Light it as two flat values: a single cold key raking from the upper left that turns the exposed planes of her face into paper white and the shadowed planes into solid black, plus one thin cyan edge along her right contour where the data field begins. Keep the background unlit, with the deepest black at the top-right corner.

Reserve the upper-left corner as closed negative space: no type, no ticks, no noise, no gradient. Let the title start below it and her hair stay clear of it.

Read the picture in this order: her left eye, the bright contour of her jaw, the hollow title behind her head, the cyan interference eating her right shoulder, the fold at the right edge, the empty upper-left corner.

Keep the sheet honest as printed matter: no readable text beyond the three strings named above, one figure only, no visible hands, no photographic depth of field. Wherever a run of small caption text would naturally sit, replace it with a blank hairline rule, a two-pixel tick band or a non-semantic block, so the margin stays graphic without inventing letterforms.

The final image should read as an identity file that has begun to corrupt from one side only, and it must feel printed rather than rendered: a clean face, a machine half, three inks, absolute black, one offset cyan plate, coarse halftone interference, hard-edged pixel blocks, scanline slicing, hollow display type, torn vertical fold, dark futuristic identity archive, controlled chromatic damage, editorial key visual.

seeds.title: Blooming Frequency
seeds.raw:
Create a vertical 4:5 premium music-festival character poster titled "Blooming Frequency", combining contemporary anime illustration, experimental graphic design, botanical technical drawing, and restrained glitch art. Hatsune Miku is fixed as the one and only humanoid character. Preserve her canonical identity, youthful anime facial structure, aqua eyes, aqua hair, extremely long twin tails, red-and-black hair accessories, futuristic headset, original teal-and-black outfit, and unmistakable silhouette. Do not replace her, create a second character, use a background person, produce a realistic human reinterpretation, or alter her hairstyle or signature clothing design.

Use an asymmetrical circular composition. Place one enormous broken circular field off-center, occupying the upper two-thirds of the poster and extending beyond both the right and top edges. Leave its left side incomplete so it resembles both a botanical radio diagram and an oversized record whose grooves have become rooted plant stems. Do not center the circle, and do not create a perfectly symmetrical halo. Position Hatsune Miku near the lower-left intersection of this circle at approximately 38 percent of the canvas width and 66 percent of its height. Show her from the upper thighs upward in a lively three-quarter pose, leaning slightly backward as if listening to a burst of sound. Her face turns back toward the viewer with a bright, quietly playful expression. One arm sweeps outward along the circular contour; the other rests near her chest. Keep her face, eyes, hands, neck, and main silhouette clearly visible.

Construct the circle from several distinct visual systems. Its outer edge is a thin technical wireframe with calibration ticks, concentric arcs, exposed nodes, small triangular notches, and interrupted geometric panels. Its interior contains broad arcs of warm ivory paper, coral-red risograph texture, mint-green transparent glass, plum shadow, and muted antique-gold linework. Let fine engineering contours bend into the natural curves of leaves and bird wings. Keep the technical elements clean and legible, but avoid a cold blue interface, holographic dashboard, or dense wall of random controls.

Develop a flower sea across the lower third of the poster. The flowers should feel like an immense field growing up toward Miku and the circular structure rather than a bouquet attached to her. Use coral poppies, pale mint cosmos, ivory bell-shaped blossoms, deep plum foliage, and a few gold-edged translucent petals. Make the nearest flowers large, sharply defined, and tactile; reduce the distant field to overlapping graphic silhouettes and soft print textures. A few stems should continue upward into the technical wireframe, turning mechanical arcs into organic branches. Leave selected gaps of pale paper between dense flower clusters so the bottom edge does not become an unreadable mass.

Arrange a flock of approximately thirty birds inside and around the broken circular field. Use elegant long-winged white birds with thin coral-red and graphite contour lines. The birds should fly along layered circular paths rather than in a straight migration line: a dense inner arc near the circle, a looser middle arc crossing behind Miku's twin tails, and a few large foreground birds entering from the right edge. Vary the wing positions and scale while preserving each bird's recognizable silhouette. Keep every bird away from Miku's eyes and facial features. Let several distant birds become simple white paper cutouts partially merged with the ivory negative space.

Add three narrow horizontal glitch zones at different vertical levels, each only a short fraction of the poster width. These zones should resemble controlled digital tears crossing selected wireframe arcs and flower petals. Use small square packets of coral red, mint green, aubergine black, pale yellow, and warm white, with slight RGB channel offset and tiny duplicated contours. Keep the pixels clustered and rhythmic, like fragments of a music signal, rather than covering the whole image or forming random noisy static. At least seventy percent of the poster must remain clean and free of glitch texture.

Build the geometric collage from precision-edged shapes and tactile materials: cropped coral rectangles, translucent mint acrylic chips, narrow ivory paper strips, graphite line fragments, a partial plum-colored grid, and a few gold registration marks. Allow several collage planes to overlap the outer rim of the circle and the lower flowers, but do not place opaque blocks over Hatsune Miku's eyes, mouth, neckline, or hands. Keep the collage spatial and intentional, with clear front, middle, and background layers. Do not create a scrapbook of unrelated panels.

Use a sophisticated palette of warm ivory, aubergine black, coral red, faded apricot, mint green, pale sage, and restrained antique gold. Coral and mint are the principal accent colors. Hatsune Miku's turquoise hair remains slightly cooler than the mint environment so her key features still separate clearly. Avoid cobalt blue, electric cyan, neon magenta, pure black-and-white cyberpunk contrast, and large areas of sodium yellow.

Render the image as a polished mixed-media print: crisp anime facial features and hair, precise vector-like technical contours, soft risograph grain, subtly imperfect screen-print registration, matte paper fiber, restrained translucent glass, fine colored-pencil hatching, and limited gold-ink highlights. Keep Miku's face refined and readable while allowing the surrounding graphic structure to be more experimental. Use varied line weights: almost hair-thin for the botanical diagrams, slightly heavier graphite contours for the main silhouette, and clean geometric edges for the collage panels.

Create strong tonal hierarchy. The brightest ivory remains behind Miku's face and inside the left opening of the circle. Coral flowers and graphic planes carry medium-dark weight. Aubergine and graphite collect in the lower foliage, outer collage fragments, and selected technical lines. Mint-glass and gold highlights create smaller luminous accents. Keep the upper-left quadrant comparatively open so the composition breathes despite its detail.

Lighting should be soft and mostly graphic, with a warm apricot glow entering from the upper-left edge, a pale mint reflection along the translucent collage planes, a delicate silver rim on Miku's hair and shoulders, and shallow colored shadows among the flowers. Avoid heavy volumetric glow or photorealistic lens flare. The atmosphere should feel energetic but elegant, botanical yet technological, playful yet meticulously composed.

Typography must be absent. Do not include readable words, letters, numbers, captions, logos, signatures, watermarks, QR codes, barcodes, subtitles, UI labels, or machine-readable marks. Replace all possible labels with empty rectangles, calibration ticks, open circles, and non-semantic registration marks. Do not add a second character, duplicated face, extra limbs, malformed hands, photorealism, generic cyberpunk city, symmetrical halo, horizontal bird-migration poster, scattered collage clutter, oversized typography, heavy neon glow, or uncontrolled glitch noise.

Final quality: high-end vertical music poster, fixed recognizable Hatsune Miku, off-center circular technical composition, dynamic half-body pose, aerial bird arcs, immense coral-and-mint flower sea, restrained glitch signal slices, refined geometric paper collage, warm ivory print grain, sophisticated botanical wireframes, crisp visual hierarchy, elegant negative space, experimental graphic design, polished anime illustration, premium festival key visual.

seeds.title: DEAD SIGNAL
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 three-ink printed key visual titled "DEAD SIGNAL", built as a flat graphic poster rather than a rendered scene. The only figure is Hatsune Miku, standing as a solid black silhouette at the bottom centre of the frame, about four percent of the canvas height, seen from behind and slightly from her right, chin lifted toward the ring. Preserve her canonical read even at this scale: the two long twin tails must break into clean tapered shapes on either side of her waist, the skirt hem must flare at the knees, and the headset must register as two small blocks. Her silhouette, the ground line and the ring are the only three things allowed to be opaque; everything else is printed mark.

Build the whole image on one colossal structure: a dead orbital relay ring, twelve hundred metres across, its diameter roughly one point three five times the frame width, its axis on the vertical midline a little above centre, so the ring runs off the left and right edges and both its crown and its lower arc are cropped by the frame. Read the ring as a section, not as an object: a thick flat band of black plate seen almost edge-on, three metres deep, carrying a bright cold-grey face only along its inner lip.

Break the ring into twelve unequal segments and let each segment fail differently: three panels have sheared off and left clean angular gaps, two sections carry a fine lattice of cross-bracing reduced to a hairline, one segment is punctured by a single round hole with a raised lip, four segments are intact plate with a hard fold line down the middle, and two are already gone so only the bright inner lip runs across empty black. Hang one service truss from the lower arc with seven antenna fins fanned open at different angles, and let two thin cables swing free from its end.

Set the ground as a black salt-glass plain that stops exactly on a level horizon at thirty-two percent of the frame height. The plain mirrors the ring, but only as line and edge: the reflection is a compressed arc, flattened to about eighteen percent of the ring's height, keeping the bright inner lip and the gaps and losing every surface detail. The horizon itself is the brightest thing in the lower half, a single hard cold-grey rule two pixels high, unbroken from edge to edge.

Print in three inks plus paper. Black covers seventy-two percent of the frame: the sky, the ring plate, the plain and the figure. Cold grey-white covers eighteen percent: the ring's inner lip, the horizon rule, a thin rim along the figure's outline, the ring caps and the entire type layer. Acid signal green takes six percent: one hairline crack of light running along the inner lip for four segments, one small square lamp on the service truss, one measurement tick, and one dot inside the ring's axis. Rust red takes four percent and appears twice only, as a scorched bloom around the punctured hole and as the small numeral "39" printed in the lower-right margin.

Print it, do not render it. Every plane is flat ink with a hard edge, every shadow is a solid black shape rather than a gradient, every highlight is a pasted white shape rather than a glow. Restrict coarse halftone dots to the shadow side of the ring plate and the near edge of the ground, and fine dots only along the outer contour of the figure. Offset the acid-green plate one and a half millimetres up and to the left so it slips out of register along the inner lip, and give the black plate a dry-brush edge wherever it meets the sky.

Light the picture as print values, not as atmosphere. The only source is a low band of acid-white light sitting on the horizon behind the figure, turning the lower inner lip of the ring into a bright cold-grey line and throwing the ring's upper face into flat black. Keep the sky a single unbroken field of near-black with one faint vertical density gradient, carrying no clouds, no stars and no bloom around the lip. Place one hard white highlight only, on the cap of the nearest antenna fin.

Set the title as a hollow display word cut by the frame. "DEAD SIGNAL" sits on the horizon line in a heavy condensed grotesque, two words stacked, each letter four metres tall, outlined in cold grey-white with empty interiors, the left half of "DEAD" cropped by the left edge and the lower third of "SIGNAL" dissolving into the black plain. Add the exact readable text "RELAY // 09" as a single small cold-grey line set tight under the title's right end, and the exact readable text "SIGNAL LOST" running vertically down the far-right margin in the same narrow face, no larger than a thumbnail.

Reserve the upper-left quadrant as a closed empty field. Nothing enters it except one single small cold-grey circle no larger than a coin: no type, no fragment, no tick, no dot field, no gradient. Let the ring's crown pass above it and let the acid-green crack stop well to its right, so the corner stays a clean plate of near-black with only the paper's own tooth and that one island mark visible.

Add a thin measurement language that rewards close reading without ever becoming text: a faint drafting grid of horizontal rules across the sky at irregular intervals, four crosshair registration marks, one circular calibration ring around the axis of the ring, seven short tick marks climbing the left edge, a broken barcode band without numerals along the bottom-right edge, and two short scanline interruptions where the acid plate slips out of register.

Separate four depth layers by edge quality alone: the figure, the acid lip and the horizon rule stay razor sharp; the ring plate and its gaps are sharp with dry edges; the reflection and the service truss soften slightly under halftone; the drafting grid, the scanlines and the title's hollow interiors fade to almost nothing.

Read the picture in this order: the bright inner lip of the ring, the tiny figure on the horizon, the hollow title, the broken segments, the acid-green crack, and the empty upper-left corner.

Keep the sheet honest as printed matter: no readable text beyond the three strings named above, one figure only, no visible hands, and nothing floats — every shard belongs to the ring. Wherever a block of type would naturally sit, replace it with a blank cold-grey rule, a short tick cluster or a non-semantic mark, so the layout still breathes without inventing letterforms.

The final image should feel like a printed warning notice left by a civilisation that no longer transmits, and it must read as a printed poster rather than a rendered scene: monumental dead machinery, one tiny listener, absolute black holding most of the frame, three inks doing the work of a photograph, off-register acid plate, halftone shadow, dry-brush edges, hard horizon rule, hollow display type, controlled negative space, archival warning sheet, dark futuristic key visual, restrained technical poetry.

seeds.title: 羽化
seeds.raw:
Create a horizontal 16:9 full-bleed flat graphic design poster titled "羽化", themed as a contemporary visual interpretation of eclosion, where migrating birds, graphic flowers, radio signals, and botanical sketches emerge from one another. Use the exact Japanese title 羽化 without any additional readable text. Build the artwork with the discipline of a premium Japanese editorial poster, contemporary music key visual, and gallery-grade print design. Work entirely with flat two-dimensional shapes, crisp vector contours, matte color fields, precise technical linework, geometric collage, silkscreen textures, one controlled glitch event, and structurally integrated typography. The result must look professionally art-directed, not like a student project, fan wallpaper, anime scene, 3D render, or decorative collage exercise.

Hatsune Miku is fixed as the one and only humanoid character. Preserve her canonical identity, aqua eyes, aqua hair, extremely long twin tails, red-and-black hair accessories, futuristic headset, original teal-and-black outfit, and unmistakable silhouette. Render her as a refined cel-shaded 2D anime graphic with flat color fills, minimal tonal transitions, crisp variable-width contours, and carefully simplified hair planes. Do not replace her, introduce another character or background person, alter her hairstyle or outfit, use realistic skin, or render her with 3D volume.

Use a new asymmetrical editorial layout. Fill the entire canvas with a warm rice-paper white field, with no black outer border. Place a monumental celadon-green circle in the lower-left quadrant, cropped by the left and bottom edges. This green circle becomes the “eclosion moon” and the dominant circular structure of the poster. Place Hatsune Miku just right of the green circle at approximately 33 percent of the canvas width and 56 percent of its height, shown from the upper thighs upward at around 48 percent of the canvas height.

Turn Miku toward the right in a clear profile-to-three-quarter pose. Lower her chin slightly and let her gaze drift toward the Japanese title on the right. Keep her eyes open, calm, and deliberate. One arm opens outward in a restrained wing-like gesture without becoming theatrical; the other stays close to her chest. Preserve a crisp facial profile, readable aqua eye, nose, mouth, jawline, headset, and continuous hair silhouette. Do not cover her face, eye, neck, hands, or primary outline with birds, typography, wireframes, flowers, or collage.

Place the exact Japanese title 羽化 vertically along the right side of the poster, reading from top to bottom as 羽 first and 化 second. Use oversized contemporary Japanese Mincho-inspired display typography with high-contrast strokes, sharp triangular serifs, and clean vector edges. Do not use brush calligraphy, handwritten lettering, distorted manga lettering, or a fake Japanese aesthetic. The two characters must be correctly formed, easily identifiable, and readable at phone-message thumbnail size.

Set 羽 in deep ink black on the rice-paper field. Let a narrow section of its stroke cross onto a flat vermilion-red collage panel, where the character switches cleanly to rice-paper white while maintaining its complete silhouette. Set 化 in deep ink black, extending slightly into the upper-right edge of the celadon-green circle. Do not crop either character at the canvas edge or fracture its overall form.

Preserve the complete outline of both Japanese characters. No bird, flower, line, hair, or collage shape may cut an additional stroke. Use only one deliberate typographic interruption: a narrow horizontal glitch slice across only the lower-right diagonal stroke of 化. Confine it to a small rectangular region and disrupt less than fifteen percent of that character. Keep the upper stroke, left radical, and main structure intact. Do not glitch 羽. Do not add another glitch anywhere else in the image.

Connect the typography to the rest of the poster through structure. Let one primary white bird pass through the open negative space between the two wings of 羽 without touching the ink strokes. Let one thin celadon technical line continue from the lower edge of 化 and connect to the main orbital grid. Allow one outer strand of Miku's twin tail to approach the lower edge of 化 but remain behind the character's outline. Typography, figure, birds, and technical system must interlock while remaining individually readable.

Build the celadon-green circle as a flat printed field rather than a glowing sphere. Overlay it with rice-paper negative-space cuts, a narrow vermilion arc, sparse ink-black technical lines, small open nodes, and one translucent-look smoke-gray geometric plane with no reflections. Keep most of the green area smooth and quiet. Do not create a dimensional planet, chrome sphere, neon halo, or centered symmetrical composition.

Unify all technical decoration inside one shared grid. Use a twelve-column vertical grid and consistent horizontal baselines across the entire poster. Align every vertical rule, collage edge, bird path, and typography guide to this grid. Center every radial tick and concentric arc on the celadon-green circle. Use only three functional groups:

1. Migration marks represent the route from flowers to birds. Use long interrupted flight arcs, a few parallel trajectories, and open directional points.
2. Growth marks represent botanical structure. Use thin right-angle stems, radial ticks, and node intersections placed only where the grid and circle meet.
3. Interference is represented solely by the single glitch slice on the lower-right stroke of 化.

Do not add arbitrary symbols, random interface panels, unrelated crosses, floating stickers, or technical marks that do not communicate migration, growth, or interference.

Use twelve birds total, approximately twenty percent fewer than a dense flock. Keep only three primary birds with strong rice-paper-white silhouettes and ink contours. Place one inside the open space of 羽, one near Miku's outer hair, and one above the upper arc of the green circle. Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The top flange is rolled steel with its mill scale intact and two polished bands where boots have crossed; the web is darker, dustier and marked by one row of rivet heads and a long weld seam; the lower flange is barely visible and almost black; the sky behind is a flat pale grey with no cloud detail; the distant ground is a single soft band of grey. Build a sequence along the beam's diagonal from the near corner outward. Begin at the lower left with the beam's cut end and its bright burred edge. Use a cold steel-and-sky palette with strict area control. Approximately forty-four percent of the image is pale flat sky. seeds.title: AFTER FIELD

Use a camera at her seated eye level on a slightly wide lens, set back and to her left so she is seen from three quarters and the field's standing weapons recede around her. Place Miku at approximately thirty-four percent of the canvas width, seated on the block with her knees drawn up, occupying about thirty percent of the frame height. Build a stepped sequence from the foreground back. Begin at the bottom edge with the water film and one submerged blade's edge breaking the surface, then Miku on her block, then the nearest weapons standing among their own reflections, then the middle band of leaning shafts, then the far band dissolving into mist, then the horizon. The sequence must read as a field that has already finished, not as a battle in progress.

Keep the middle of the field empty of any weapon for a stretch of several metres, so the gap reads as the only thing that ever happened there.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the water film and one submerged edge. Middle ground: Miku, the block, the nearest weapons. Background: the middle and far bands of weapons, the mist, the horizon. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Let the crystal pass the light rather than return it: one thin saturated magenta line along its thickest edge, and one hard-edged magenta caustic patch thrown onto the water film beside it.

Let the overcast light make her hair the only saturated thing in the frame.

A long dark teal coat heavy with water, hanging open and dragging at its hem, a black shirt beneath, dark trousers, and boots that have been wet for hours. Use a desaturated palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty-two percent of the image is flat water, twenty-six percent is mist and sky, eighteen percent is the weapons, ten percent is mud and the block, eight percent is Miku's coat, four percent is her aqua hair, and two percent is the rust and one pale collar. Add a rectangular dark panel across the far band of weapons as a graphic mask at their height, and let one vertical strip of deep teal run down the frame's right edge from sky to water. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Set the exact readable word “AFTER FIELD” once, in white paint stencilled across the flat water in the empty middle stretch, the strokes broken by the surface's gentle ripple, sized so it spans about a third of the water's visible width and reads clearly at thumbnail size. Fourth: the middle band of leaning shafts. Fifth: the far band, the mist and the horizon. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every blade and shaft, restrained risograph grain in the mist, crisp flat fills in the water, and one clean gradient only along the sky. No second character, no duplicate Miku, no crowd, no bodies, no bones, no blood, no banners, no flags, no birds, no wings, no halo, no standing army, no horses, no glowing crystal, no neon glow, no self-lit weapon, no rainbow dispersion, no stained glass, no plastic, no glass bottle, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no magical effects, no readable text beyond the string named above, no wounds, no armour plates, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no weapon in her hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter.

Use a camera at her waist height on a wide lens, set back and slightly to her left so she is seen from three quarters and the crane's hook line runs up through the frame's upper centre. Place Miku at approximately thirty percent of the canvas width, looking up at the suspended head, occupying about twenty-six percent of the frame height. Let the axe head hang in the upper right quadrant, canted a few degrees off level.

Give Miku exactly one core action: stepping back. Her weight has shifted onto her back leg, both arms are lifted slightly away from her body with the palms open, and her chin is raised toward the hanging mass. Keep her front heel just lifting, her shoulders tight, and put nothing in either hand.

Keep the slab plain — no etched ornament, no runes, no gilding. Let it occupy the upper right quadrant and let the sling's two legs cross the frame's top edge.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. the head is one block of aquamarine, cold blue-green and translucent so the whole mass reads as one saturated stone, its interior holding a scatter of gas voids and one long fracture near the eye, its bevel ground sharp, and it returns no light except where the lamp passes through; the sling is braided wire rope with grease still in its lay; the crane's hook block is orange-painted cast iron, chipped back to bare metal at its horns; the floor is a sand-casting bed, grey-green and uneven, with a mould box still in place; the roof trusses are riveted steel, dark against a skylight. Each behaves differently — cast skin swallows light completely, the ground bevel returns a narrow hard shine, wire rope reads as a spiral of small speculars, painted iron holds a chalky dull flatness, damp sand holds a soft matte shading, trusses read as a hard black scaffold.

Build a stepped sequence from the floor upward. Begin at the bottom edge with the sand bed and the mould box's corner, then Miku's boots and the drag mark her heel has made, then her body and lifted arms, then the axe head and its sling, then the crane block, then the skylight. The sequence must read as a workshop where something too large is being moved, not as a display of a prop.

Leave one deliberate absence. The mould box beside her is empty and open: its cope lifted off and set aside, its cavity holding nothing but a dry imprint of a shape larger than the box should allow. Keep the cavity in shadow, place it at her feet, and let no casting or metal lie inside it.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the sand bed, the mould box, her heel drag. Middle ground: Miku, the hanging head, the sling. Background: the crane block, the trusses, the skylight. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

The work lamp is a small warm secondary at the frame's right edge that puts a low warm rim on her calf and the mould box's corner. Keep the two temperatures separate and let the deep floor beyond the lamp fall to near black. Let the crystal pass the light rather than return it: one thin saturated cyan line where the mass is thickest, and one hard-edged cyan caustic patch thrown onto the sand bed beside it.

Use a cold-on-dark palette with strict area control. Keep the warm note down to that rim alone. The aquamarine's cold blue-green tone is the one saturated colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the foundry's own safety markings rather than from decoration. Let one large rust-red ink bloom spread across the dark upper left, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular pale panel across the trusses at the frame's right as a graphic mask, and let one vertical strip of black run down the frame's left edge from skylight to floor. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “AXE FOUNDRY” once, in white paint stencilled along the main riveted beam above her head, the strokes broken by rivet heads, sized so it spans about three quarters of the beam's visible length and reads clearly at thumbnail size. Put no lettering on the axe head, the sand or her apron, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The axe head's cast skin is pitted with gas bubbles at one corner; its edge bevel is freshly ground and bright; the sling's rope is flattened where it bears on the eye; the sand floor is crusted and cracked in a ring around the mould box; the mould box's frame is warped and its cavity walls are glazed by heat. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where work would put it.

Fourth: the head's upper cheek and the sling. Fifth: the crane block, trusses and skylight. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every rivet and bevel, restrained risograph grain in the dark roof, crisp flat fills in the sand, and one clean gradient only along the ground bevel. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except that bevel and her boot caps.

The final image should feel like the second before something enormous is set down: an axe head hanging from a hook, a girl stepping back with her palms open, and an empty mould box at her feet that is already the wrong size for what it poured.

seeds.title: BACK ALLEY
seeds.raw:

Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the brick.

Use a camera at chest height on a normal lens, set square down the alley so both walls converge and the far opening shows a pale strip of sky. Place Miku at approximately forty-six percent of the canvas width, full body visible from boots to hair ornaments, occupying about thirty-eight percent of the frame height.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Her right hand lifts one corner of a hanging sheet aside at shoulder height, and her left hand holds a wooden peg between two fingers at hip height. Her head is turned toward the far opening, both eyes visible. Keep the pose steady and put nothing else in her hands.

Construct the dominant visual object as the brick wall on her left: a broad face of nineteen-thirties brick about four metres tall, painted cream to shoulder height and bare above, with a blocked-up window and a cast-iron downpipe. Let the wall occupy approximately forty percent of the canvas area on the left and be the brightest large surface in the frame.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The wall is brick, its lower half painted cream and flaking in sheets, its upper half bare and soot-dark; the opposite wall is bare brick in shadow; the ground is wet concrete with a central drain channel; the washing is thin cotton, backlit and translucent; the downpipe is cast iron with rust at every joint; the sky strip is a flat pale blue. Each behaves differently — painted brick reads as a flat cream field with flaking edges, bare brick as dark texture, wet concrete holds a thin sheen, backlit cotton glows at its edges and shadows at its folds.

Build a stepped sequence down the alley. Begin at the bottom edge with wet concrete and the drain, then Miku's boots, then her hand on the sheet, then the washing lines overhead, then the blocked window, then the pale sky strip. The sequence must read as a narrow passage upward, not as a wall.

Leave one deliberate absence. The washing line carries one empty peg gap: about a sheet's width between two hanging pieces where nothing is pinned, and the line itself sags lower there as if a heavy item had just been taken in. Keep the gap just above her head so the line's sag reads as the only interruption in a full row.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: wet concrete, drain, boots. Middle ground: Miku, the sheet, the washing. Background: the blocked window, the alley's far opening. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the sky strip above and behind. The sky is the key: a cool pale light from the alley's far end, backlighting the washing so each sheet glows at its edges and the alley's near half stays in cool shadow. Add one warm bulb above a back door as a small secondary, giving a warm patch on the painted wall. Keep the near wall's cream bright and the opposite wall dark.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the backlight. The nearer tail falls forward and is rimmed cool along its upper edge by the sky; the farther tail drops into the near shadow and reads as a dark mass. Let one strand pass behind the lifted sheet without hiding her eyes.

Dress Miku in an original back-alley costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not workwear. A dark cropped jacket worn open over a pale tee, dark shorts, and ankle boots, with a small canvas bag across her body. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment.

Use a cream-and-shadow palette with one cool accent and strict area control. Approximately forty percent of the image is painted cream brick and pale sky, twenty-four percent is dark brick and shadow, fourteen percent is backlit cotton, ten percent is wet concrete, six percent is Miku's dark jacket, four percent is her aqua hair, and two percent is the rusted downpipe.

Add a rectangular pale panel behind the wall as a graphic mask at the height of the blocked window, and let one vertical strip of deep shadow run from the washing line to the ground, aligned to the downpipe.

Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the wet concrete. The ground carries the pale sky as one long vertical stripe, the washing as soft dark shapes, and Miku's boots as two dark ovals. Let the reflection stop dead at the drain channel.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A cast-iron drain grate with a leaf caught in it, one wooden clothes peg already on the line, a rusted bracket holding the downpipe, and a folded cardboard box against the far wall. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where an alley would actually have it.

Let the sky produce glowing edges on every sheet and a cool rim on Miku's near side. Let the bulb produce one warm patch on the cream wall and a soft pool on the concrete. Keep the near third of the alley in cool shadow.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: concrete, drain, boots. Second: Miku, the lifted sheet, her peg. Third: the washing row and its gap. Fourth: the blocked window and downpipe. Fifth: the far opening and the sky strip. Separate them by value steps of roughly ten percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every brick course and pipe joint, restrained risograph grain in the shadow fields, crisp flat fills in the cream paint, and fine flaking only at the wall's base.

seeds.title: BAKERY

Give Miku exactly one core action. Both hands hold a long wooden peel by its handle at waist height, its blade resting on the counter with one round loaf on it, and her head is turned toward the front window, both eyes visible. Keep the pose still and put nothing else in her hands.

Construct the dominant visual object as the bread rack behind her: three cane-and-steel tiers carrying trays of round and oval loaves, all cooling, with one cloth-lined basket at the lowest tier. Let the rack occupy approximately forty-five percent of the canvas area above the counter line.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The loaves are dark-crusted with flour dust on their tops; the trays are blackened steel sheets; the rack frame is thin steel tube with cane shelves; the counter is worn oak, oiled and pale along its front edge; the floor is dark quarry tile; the window behind is single-glazed with a pale morning sky. Each behaves differently — crust scatters light into small facets, blackened sheet swallows it, cane reads as a fine woven texture, oiled oak holds a soft sheen, tile reflects a dull grid.

Build a stepped sequence from the counter inward. Begin at the bottom edge with the oak's pale front edge and one flour dusting, then the peel's blade and the loaf on it, then Miku's hands, then the lowest tray, then the upper trays with their overlapping rounds, then the window's pale field. The sequence must read as a working counter, not as a still life.

One tray slot on the middle tier is empty and clean: the steel tray is gone, leaving two bare cane runners crossed with a thin dust line, and a hook above it holds nothing. Keep the gap one tray wide, placed just left of her shoulder so the empty runners interrupt the rhythm of rounds.

The window is the key: a low, warm, raking morning light from the left, catching the crusts' upper facets and throwing a long soft shadow of the rack onto the back wall. Add one small warm hanging lamp above the counter as a weak fill on her face and hands. Keep the shadows soft and warm, and let the far corner stay in deep brown shadow.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the morning light. The nearer tail falls forward over her shoulder in one clean aqua mass, its outer edge lit warm; the farther tail drops behind her and is cut by the rack's shadow into a dark vertical. Let two strands rest against the counter's edge.

A pale linen shirt with the sleeves rolled to the elbow over a dark apron tied at the waist, and a thin towel folded on one shoulder. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment, and keep the silhouette simple enough to read at thumbnail size.

Use a warm-brown palette with one cool accent and strict area control. Approximately forty percent of the image is warm crust brown and lamplight, twenty-two percent is deep brown shadow, fourteen percent is the pale oak counter, ten percent is the pale window sky, eight percent is Miku's pale shirt and dark apron, four percent is her aqua hair, and two percent is the blackened steel. Add a rectangular pale panel behind the rack as a graphic mask at the height of the middle tier, and let one vertical strip of deep brown run from the window to the counter, aligned to a rack upright.

Set the exact readable word “BAKERY” once, large, in dark brown paint applied across the full width of the pale oak fascia board above the window, spanning about two thirds of the fascia in heavy capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Chin lifted, eyes fixed on the black core, mouth closed. The disc is the only glossy object she touches and its face turns the light back at the camera.

Build the picture on one dominant structure: a colossal circular cavity opening in a wall of steel, its mouth about sixty percent of the frame width, centred just above the midline, its lip a rolled edge thirty centimetres thick. Behind her the inner wall flares back into a flat, total black, feathered a hair at the lip, so the opening reads as a hole where light ends and the picture continues past the surface.

Read them as a temperature ladder from the lip outward: black, deep indigo, plum, violet, teal, bronze, straw, silver, with the widest rings at the outer edge running off the frame.

Each ring shifts hue with the viewing angle, so one ring reads plum along the left of the frame and teal along its right; the temper lines stay razor sharp where two rings meet; and where a ring passes behind her hair the colour is compressed into a thin bright seam. The whole spectrum lives in a film thinner than a wavelength, sitting on top of black steel.

The flocked panels swallow light with a feathered edge and a fine fibre nap visible where the raking strip skims them; the polished black glass of the floor keeps dust motes, one fingerprint and a thin bright scratch; the steel carries faint grinding marks under its oxide; the rolled lip holds one polished facet that answers the light with a single hard silver line.

It mirrors the twelve rings as one long smeared spectrum, mirrors the cavity as a second black hole sitting inside that spectrum, mirrors her boots and the disc, and takes the disc's band across the whole foreground at a diagonal. The reflection is where the colour runs wrong and beautiful: the ladder reverses, the plum sits under the indigo, and the smeared spectrum is the only place in the frame where the colours touch each other.

Keep her shoulders level, her stance open with feet apart, and put nothing but the string and the nock in her right hand.

Its shaft is one slender rod of the same rose quartz, lit from within along its whole length, so a single hot pink line runs from her knuckles all the way to the point and cuts the pale fog like a drawn stroke. Keep the light confined to the rod, the point and that stained length of string — no rays fanning out, no sparks, no spray and no halo.

seeds.title: BACK DRAW
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “BACK DRAW”, a frame built around one long aquamarine crystal bow held at full anchor, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing half turned away from the camera at the lip of a canyon, her bow arm reaching out toward the frame's left, the string drawn all the way back to her jaw, and her head turned back over her shoulder so her eyes come straight down the lens. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes and twin-tail identity readable against the dark canyon wall behind her.

The weapon is one solid mass of aquamarine glass: translucent, cold blue-green, lit from within, and it throws cyan light onto everything around it.

Use a camera behind her right shoulder on a slightly long lens, set a little above her waist and slightly out to her right, so her back is seen in three-quarter and her bow arm reaches across to the frame's left. Place Miku at approximately sixty-two percent of the canvas width, occupying about sixty-six percent of the frame height. Let the bow's far tip sit just inside the frame's left edge and let the arrow's point stop short of it, so the entire line of the shot stays inside the picture.

Give Miku exactly one core action: holding a full anchor over her shoulder while she looks back. Her left arm is extended straight out ahead of her chest holding the bow's grip, her right hand has drawn the string all the way back until it touches the line of her jaw with the nock under her chin, and her left shoulder is pushed forward into the bow so her back shows the strain. Her head is turned back over her own right shoulder toward the camera, her chin close to her shoulder, so her face comes round into a three-quarter view with her right cheek to the lens and both eyes fully visible. Her legs are straight and she stands upright on both feet a shoulder's width apart, her weight even and her knees unlocked — she is standing, not kneeling and not crouching. Put nothing in her hands but the bow and the string.

Construct the dominant visual object as the fully drawn bow: one stave of aquamarine as tall as she is, recurved at both tips, its grip bound in dark cord, its string a waxed cord with a single red serving at the nocking point, pulled back until its anchor touches her jaw. Because the bow's plane runs almost parallel to the lens, show the stave as one tall arc at the frame's left. There is exactly one arrow in the picture and its shaft is a single unbroken line running from her jaw out past the grip to the haze at the frame's left edge — one straight rod from her face to the edge of the picture, with nothing else in the frame lying parallel to it.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The stave is one length of aquamarine, cold blue-green and translucent so the whole limb reads as one saturated stone, its interior holding long parallel inclusions that follow the recurve, its surface polished to a dull sheen and dark until light crosses it; the grip cord is matte black and furred where her palm has worn it; the string is a waxed cord whose twist catches one dotted line of light; the arrow is a slim shaft of the same crystal with three grey fletchings; the ledge is coarse granite, wet along one seam; the canyon wall behind is stratified sandstone in three bands; the air between them is cold haze. Each behaves differently — the crystal passes light and returns one thin saturated line where it bends hardest, cord absorbs everything, the string breaks into specular dots, granite reads as flat tooth, sandstone as horizontal bands, haze dissolves every edge it crosses.

Build a stepped sequence from the far tip inward. Begin at the frame's left edge with the bow's upper tip and the arrow's point in haze, then along the stave down to the grip and her extended arm, then back along the drawn string to her jaw, then her turned face and the near shoulder, then her back and hips, then the canyon wall behind her. The sequence must read as one line of force running from her back out through her arm to the far tip, not as a figure holding a stick.

Leave one deliberate absence. The bow has no target and the arrow points at nothing: past the frame's left edge there is only the canyon's open air, and no mark, no post and no second figure appears anywhere along the ledge or the wall. Keep the widest quiet area of the frame at the left, past the arrow's point, entirely empty.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: her near shoulder, the back of her jacket and her lifted rear heel. Middle ground: her back, both arms, the drawn string and the bow. Background: her turned face, her twin tails, the bow's far tip, the canyon wall and the haze. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from a low sun out of frame at her right, coming from behind the camera. The sun is the key: a raking warm light that puts a bright rim down the back of her shoulder and neck, one hard line along the top of the stave, and a soft edge on the string where it leaves her jaw. Let the canyon wall beyond her fall into cool shadow and let the haze over the drop go one value lighter than the wall. Keep her front in shade and never light her face from the front, so her turned profile reads as a hard silhouette turned into the light. Let the crystal pass the light rather than return it: one thin saturated cyan line where the recurve is, and one hard-edged cyan caustic patch thrown onto the granite beside her rear boot.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails cross the frame against her turn. The nearer tail is thrown forward over her shoulder and hangs down the frame's right side toward the camera; the far tail sweeps across her back in the opposite direction and lifts at its end where the wall's wind catches it. Keep both tails as clean aqua shapes with hard edges, and route them so neither crosses the string or the arrow, and so her turned cheek, both eyes and the line of her jaw stay completely clear of hair — nothing may fall across her face.

Dress Miku in a tight archer's layer over her canonical palette, not armour. A dark teal sleeveless top with a high collar, a short charcoal jacket cut close at the shoulder with the sleeve pushed to the elbow on her bow arm, dark trousers with a narrow brass belt, and soft-soled boots laced tight at the ankle. Keep every garment matte and unpatterned so the only glossy surfaces are the crystal and the sheath-free line of the string.

Use a warm-on-dark palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty-four percent of the image is stratified canyon wall, twenty-four percent is the cold haze beyond the ledge, sixteen percent is the bow and its string, ten percent is Miku's clothing and her back, six percent is her aqua hair, five percent is the granite ledge, three percent is her skin at the jaw, hands and rear heel, and two percent is the red serving and the grey fletchings. Keep the cool values in the haze, her hair and the crystal. The aquamarine's cold blue-green tone is the one saturated colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the canyon's own stone rather than from decoration. Let one large black ink bloom spread across the wall behind her, breaking along a sandstone band, and let a single pale mineral vein run the width of the frame where the strata change. Keep all printed matter matte and weathered.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “BACK DRAW” once, cut shallow into the flat outer face of the canyon wall behind her at the height of her shoulder and filled with white paint so the letters read as pale grooves following the stone, sized so it spans about a third of the visible wall width and reads clearly at thumbnail size. Put no lettering on the bow, the arrow, her clothing or the ledge, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The stave is chipped in one small spall at its lower tip; the grip cord is furred and greyed under her palm; the string's serving is worn through to bright wire at the nocking point; the arrow's fletchings are split at the tips of two vanes; her jacket's shoulder seam is strained pale where the bow arm pulls against it; the granite is spalled in shallow flakes along its wet seam. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the haze beyond the ledge. The haze carries the bow's far tip as one soft tapering shape, her extended arm as a dark horizontal bar, and the canyon wall as a flat field behind them. Let the haze never mirror the figure and never produce a second silhouette.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One brass ring at her belt, a single grain of grit caught between the string and the nock, one drop of sweat running from her hairline toward her jaw, and a fine crack running down the arrow's shaft from its nock. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where the draw would put it.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: her near shoulder and the back of her jacket. Second: her back, her hips and her lifted rear heel. Third: both arms, the drawn string and her jaw. Fourth: her turned face, the bow's grip and its far limb. Fifth: the bow's tip, the canyon wall and the haze. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each, with the crystal's lit line the brightest small area and the canyon shadow the darkest.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp controlled edges, deliberate value grouping, no airbrush softness, fine grain in the flat fields, every highlight placed rather than suggested, and the whole image composed so it holds at poster scale and again at thumbnail scale.

No second character, no duplicate Miku, no crowd, no birds, no wings, no halo, no arrow in the air, no second arrow, no floating arrow, no duplicate arrow, no arrow below the bow, no second bow, no additional weapon, no quiver on her back, no arrow released, no bow held with both hands, no hand on the string other than her own, no hair across her face, no glowing crystal, no neon glow, no self-lit weapon, no rainbow dispersion, no stained glass, no plastic, no glass bottle, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no magical effects, no readable text beyond the word named above, no blood, no wounds, no armour plates, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no third arm, no third leg, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no motion blur, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like the second before a shot that never comes: a back already carrying the strain, a string pressed into a jaw, a head turned just far enough to find you, and a whole canyon of empty air past the arrow's point.

seeds.title: BROKEN BLADE
seeds.raw:

Keep her face and twin-tail outline readable against the pale concrete wall behind her.

The weapon is one solid mass of amethyst glass: translucent, deep violet, lit from within, and it throws violet light onto everything around it.

Use a camera at her crouching eye level on a normal lens, set square to the blade's flat so the fractured stump faces the viewer and the hall's far wall closes the background. Place Miku at approximately forty-four percent of the canvas width, sitting on the fracture's lower lip, occupying about twenty-two percent of the frame height. Let the broken blade rise from the floor at the frame's centre and stop well below the top edge.

Give Miku exactly one core action: looking down into the fracture. Her body is crouched with both knees drawn up, one hand resting flat on the broken steel beside her boot, the other arm hanging between her knees with the fingers relaxed. Keep her head tilted down, her shoulders rounded, and put nothing in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the broken sword: a colossal blade three metres wide, snapped clean across at chest height so only the lower half stands, with a fracture face of bright torn steel stepped in three ragged planes. Keep the crossguard buried below the floor line so the visible object is only blade and break. Let it occupy the centre third of the frame from floor to just above her head.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. the blade is one mass of amethyst, deep violet and translucent so the whole mass reads as one saturated stone, its fracture face bright and granular where the piece tore away, its interior holding a fine web of cracks that catch the sky, and it casts colour but no glow; the fracture face is bright raw metal, granular and stepped, with one deep tear running down; the floor is poured concrete, dust-grey, cracked in a wide star pattern around the blade's base; the walls are bare concrete with form-board seams and one dark water stain; the ceiling is missing, showing flat overcast sky. Each behaves differently — the flat holds a long dull sheen, the fracture scatters a hard bright broken light, concrete absorbs almost everything and shows only soft value steps, wet stain reads darker and glossier than the wall around it, the sky stays completely matte.

Build a stepped sequence up the frame. Begin at the bottom edge with the cracked floor and the blade's base, then Miku's boots and her hand on the steel, then her crouched body, then the fracture face with its three planes, then the wall behind her, then the strip of sky at the top. The sequence must read as a cross-section of something enormous that has been cut open, not as a prop beside a sitting figure.

On the right side of the fracture, one large piece is missing entirely: a wedge-shaped void where the steel should have continued, its inner faces still bright and sharp. Keep the void about a hand-span wide, place it at her eye level, and let no debris lie beneath it on the floor.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the cracked floor and the blade's base. Middle ground: Miku, the fracture, the missing wedge. Background: the concrete wall, the form-board seams, the strip of sky. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the missing ceiling. The overcast sky is the key: a broad soft light from directly above that lights the fracture's upper plane to near white, leaves the blade's flat in even mid-grey, and drops the wall into a flat darker field. Let the floor hold one pale pool directly under the break and fall off toward the corners. Keep every shadow soft-edged, and never introduce a second source. Let the crystal pass the light rather than return it: one thin saturated violet line along its thickest edge, and one hard-edged violet caustic patch thrown onto the cracked floor beside it.

The nearer tail drops across her knee and disappears into the gap between her boot and the steel; the farther one falls behind her shoulder and pools on the broken surface. Let the sky light run down each tail as one continuous pale streak.

Keep the palette close to teal-and-black with one pale shirt, keep a single brass zipper as the only metal, and keep the silhouette compact enough to read at thumbnail size.

Use a grey-on-grey palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty-two percent of the image is bare concrete wall, twenty-four percent is the blade's flat and base, seventeen percent is the fractured metal, twelve percent is the floor, eight percent is Miku's jacket and trousers, four percent is her aqua hair, two percent is the rust bleed, and one percent is the brass zipper. Keep every warm note down to the crystal and that zipper and the rust. The amethyst's deep violet tone is the one saturated colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the hall's own stencilling rather than from decoration. Let one large rust-red ink bloom spread across the wall in the lower left, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular pale panel across the wall's upper right as a graphic mask at the height of the water stain, and let one vertical strip of black run down the frame's right edge from sky to floor. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “BROKEN BLADE” once, in black paint sprayed across the bare concrete wall directly behind the fracture, the strokes oversprayed at the edges and running slightly where the wall is damp, sized so it spans about two thirds of the wall's visible width and reads clearly at thumbnail size. Put no lettering on the steel, the floor or her clothing, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The blade's flat carries rust weeping from the break in three long stains; the fracture's edges are burred and bright where the metal tore rather than cut; the concrete floor is dusted except in a clean ring where someone swept; the wall's form-board seams are dark and one holds a line of damp; the missing wedge's inner faces are still sharp and unweathered. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the fracture face. The three planes of the break catch the sky at three different values, so the damage reads as a stepped landscape in itself; the missing wedge reads as a clean dark hole against the bright metal; a thin line of dust falls from the lower lip. Never let the fracture read as a second object or a face.
