One brass zipper pull at Miku's collar, a single steel filing caught in the cuff of her glove, a hairline crack running from the blade's base into the floor, and one drop of water hanging from the fracture's lowest edge. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where the damage would put it.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: cracked floor and blade's base. Second: Miku's boots and hand. Third: her crouched body and the fracture's lower plane. Fourth: the fracture's upper planes and the missing wedge. Fifth: the wall and the strip of sky. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every fracture edge and form-board seam, restrained risograph grain in the concrete, crisp flat fills in the sky, and one clean gradient only across the fractured face. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the bright torn metal.

No second character, no duplicate Miku, no crowd, no bodies, no bones, no banners, no birds, no wings, no halo, no second blade, no sword in her hands, no glowing crystal, no neon glow, no self-lit weapon, no rainbow dispersion, no stained glass, no plastic, no glass bottle, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no magical effects, no readable text beyond the string named above, no blood, no wounds, no armour plates, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no rubble pile, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like a room built around a wound: one blade snapped off at chest height, a girl crouched on the break looking into the metal, and one wedge of it simply gone.

seeds.title: BUS STOP
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “BUS STOP”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character sitting on a bench at a roadside bus stop at dusk, with an empty shelter behind her and a wet road in front. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the pale shelter light.

Use a camera at seated eye height on a normal lens, set across the pavement and square to the shelter so its frame runs level and the road recedes to the left. Place Miku at approximately forty-four percent of the canvas width, seated with her knees together and her feet flat, occupying about forty-six percent of the frame height. Let the shelter's glass panel and the road fill the rest, so the composition is one seated figure under a lit roof.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Both hands hold a folded timetable open on her lap, and her head is lifted toward the road, both eyes visible, as if she has just looked up from the paper. One bag strap hangs from her shoulder to the bench. Keep the pose still, the arms close to her body, and put nothing else in her hands.

Construct the dominant visual object as the shelter itself: a steel-framed canopy with a flat roof, two glass side panels, a timber bench with a steel frame, and a backlit advertising panel at one end. Let the shelter occupy approximately forty-five percent of the canvas area in the centre, with its roof cutting the frame above her head.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The canopy frame is powder-coated steel in a municipal grey, scratched at every joint; the roof is translucent polycarbonate with two dirt streaks; the glass side panel is thin and slightly wavy, with a rubber seal that has shrunk; the bench is timber slats on steel brackets, bleached along the front edge; the advertising panel is backlit frosted acrylic; the road is black asphalt with a wet sheen; the pavement is grey block paving. Each behaves differently — coated steel holds a flat cool value, polycarbonate diffuses the sky into a dull field, thin glass returns a faint second image, timber reads as horizontal stripes, acrylic emits a soft rectangle, wet asphalt breaks light into fragments.

Build a stepped sequence across the scene. Begin at the bottom edge with the block paving and one cracked block, then Miku's feet and the bench frame, then her hands and the timetable, then the glass side panel behind her, then the lit advertising panel at the right end, then the road and its wet sheen at the left. The sequence must read as waiting under a roof, not as a portrait on a bench.

Leave one deliberate absence. The timetable frame on the shelter's post stands empty: the cast aluminium frame is there with its scratched glass front, but no printed sheet inside, only a pale backing board with four dried adhesive corners. Keep the empty frame about an arm's width, hung at eye height on the post beside her, so the missing sheet reads as clearly as the one in her hands.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: block paving, cracked block, bench frame. Middle ground: Miku, the timetable, the glass panel. Background: the lit advertising panel, the road and its sheen. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the shelter's own panel and the sky. The advertising panel is the warm key: a soft warm white from her right, laying a warm edge along her cheek, shoulder and the timetable's page edge. The dusk sky is the cool key: a flat blue-grey from above and behind, filling the glass panel with a pale field and lifting the road's sheen. Add one amber street lamp at the far left as a small third source. Keep the warm and cool zones clearly separated at the shelter's frame line.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the shelter light. The nearer tail falls forward over the bench's back edge in one clean aqua mass, its right side warm from the panel and its left side cool from the sky; the farther tail drops behind the bench and is cut by the glass panel into a paler value. Let one strand rest against the bench slats without covering her bag strap.

Dress Miku in an original bus-stop costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not school uniform. A pale trench coat worn open over a dark high-necked top, a narrow skirt, opaque tights and low shoes, with a thin canvas bag across one shoulder. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment, and keep the silhouette simple enough to read at thumbnail size.

Use a cool-grey palette with two warm accents and strict area control. Approximately forty-two percent of the image is dusk blue-grey and shelter glass, twenty percent is municipal grey steel and paving, fourteen percent is the lit panel's warm white, ten percent is the black road and its sheen, eight percent is Miku's pale coat, four percent is her aqua hair, and two percent is the far amber lamp. Keep the amber to a single small pool at the frame edge.

Drive the printed graphic language from the shelter's own fittings rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the lower right of the paving, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular pale panel behind the glass as a graphic mask at the height of the bench's back rail, and let one vertical strip of deep blue run from the roof to the paving, aligned to a shelter post. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “BUS STOP” once, large, in white vinyl lettering applied across the full width of the shelter's canopy fascia band, the last letter lifting slightly at its corner, sized so it reads clearly at thumbnail size across about half the canopy's width. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “ROUTE 12” sit on a small enamel plate bolted to the post above the empty frame. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the wait. The bench's front edge is bleached where hands and legs rest; the glass panel carries one fingerprint cluster at rail height; the paving is darker in a worn path along the kerb; the canopy fascia holds a grey film that is thicker at its lower edge; the empty frame's glass is scratched in two arcs. Keep the wear physical and directional, never a uniform grime.

Build a second composition through the glass. The side panel carries a faint reversed image of the bench, the advertising panel's lit rectangle, and Miku's own silhouette, all at half value and slightly wavy from the glass. Let the reflection stop at the rubber seal and never cross the frame.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A brass bolt cap worn bright on the bench bracket, one steel litter bin at the shelter's far end, a folded newspaper left on the bench arm, and a short length of chain hanging from the canopy's drainage spout. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a bus stop would actually have it.

Illuminate with the advertising panel as the warm key from her right and the dusk sky as the cool key from above. Let the panel produce a warm edge on her cheek, shoulder and page, and a pale pool on the paving beneath it. Let the sky produce a flat cool wash on the glass, the bench and the road's sheen. Let the far lamp produce one small amber pool only.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: paving, cracked block, bench frame. Second: Miku, her hands, the timetable. Third: the glass panel and the empty frame. Fourth: the lit advertising panel. Fifth: the road, its sheen and the far lamp. Separate them by value steps of roughly ten percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every steel joint and paving block, restrained risograph grain in the cool fields, crisp flat fills in the lit areas, and fine scratches only on the empty frame's glass. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the road's sheen.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no waiting passenger, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable advertising copy, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no vehicles, no birds, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like the ten minutes before a bus that may not come: a lit panel warming one side of her face, an empty timetable frame beside her, and a girl looking up from a paper she has already read twice.

seeds.title: CAVERN
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 2:3 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “CAVERN”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing inside a limestone cave chamber, with a single shaft of daylight falling through a roof fissure onto a flat wall face beside her. Use a camera at chest height on a slightly wide lens, set back inside the chamber and angled so the lit wall fills the upper two thirds and the floor pool sits at the bottom. Place Miku at approximately forty-six percent of the canvas width, full body visible from boots to hair ornaments, occupying about thirty-eight percent of the frame height.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Her right hand holds a small head torch pointing at the wall, and her left hand rests flat against the stone at shoulder height. Her head is turned toward the lit face, both eyes visible in profile. Keep the pose steady and put nothing else in her hands.

Construct the dominant visual object as the lit wall face: a broad, flat, pale limestone surface about four metres wide, marked by flowstone streaks, one pale calcite seam, and the smooth water-worn band at its base. Let the wall occupy approximately forty-five percent of the canvas area in the upper half, and let the daylight patch be the brightest large surface in the frame.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The wall is pale limestone with a fine crystalline grain and vertical flowstone streaks; the floor is a shallow pool of clear water over pale silt; the ceiling is dark, hung with short straws; the side walls fall away into black; the daylight is a hard-edged shaft visible only as a bright patch on the stone. Build a stepped sequence from the pool inward. seeds.title: CHAIN FLAIL
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 2:3 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “CHAIN FLAIL”, a frame built around one colossal amethyst weapon, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing in a stone chamber with a long chain flail hanging from her lowered right hand, the chain pulled straight by the weight of the head. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes and twin-tail identity readable against the dark chamber.

The weapon is one solid mass of amethyst glass: translucent, deep violet, lit from within, and it throws violet light onto everything around it.

Use a camera at her knee height on a wide lens, set low and to her left so she is seen from three quarters and the chain runs from her hand down to the frame's lower right corner. Place Miku at approximately forty-four percent of the canvas width, occupying about sixty-six percent of the frame height. Let the flail's head rest on the stone floor with the chain taut, and let her hand be at hip height.

Give Miku exactly one core action: standing under the weight. Her right arm hangs straight down with the handle gripped near its end and the wrist turned so the chain falls clear, her left hand is open at her side, and her head is turned down toward the head on the floor. Keep her shoulders uneven from the pull, her stance wide, and put nothing in her left hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the flail: a haft of dark bound oak two feet long, a swivel of blackened iron, a chain of eight heavy links each as wide as a palm, ending in a spiked iron head the size of a small anvil. Keep it plain — no gilding, no cloth, no engraving on the head. Let the chain read as a straight vertical line of eight links from her hand to the floor.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. the haft, chain and head are all carved from amethyst, deep violet and translucent so the whole mass reads as one saturated stone, the head's interior holding a dense cluster of voids, the links polished at their bearing faces, and the whole thing throws no light of its own; the swivel and chain are blackened iron worn bright on their bearing surfaces; the head is a rough cast iron mass with four stubby spikes and a pitted face; the floor is worn stone flags with a shallow depression where the head rests; the walls are coursed stone blocks with lime mortar; a single narrow slot window admits a blade of light. Each behaves differently — bound oak shows a fine cord grain, blackened iron returns small hard glints at each link's worn face, cast iron swallows light except on its spikes, stone flags hold a soft diffuse sheen and a dark stain, coursed blocks read as regular horizontal bands, the slot's light is a flat hard white.

Build a stepped sequence up the frame. Begin at the lower right with the flail's head and the depression it has worn, then the eight links rising one by one, then her hand and wrist, then her shoulder and turned head, then the stone wall, then the slot window's blade of light. The sequence must read as a weight being held, not as a weapon being displayed.

Leave one deliberate absence. The flail has only seven full links: the eighth position is a single empty ring that has worn through and closed on itself, so the chain is one link shorter than the head's reach suggests. Keep the worn ring at the chain's middle, high enough to notice only when following the links, and let nothing else in the chamber suggest repair.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the head and the worn depression. Middle ground: the chain, her hand and her body. Background: the stone wall, the slot window, the chamber's dark upper volume. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the narrow slot window high at the left. The window is the key: a hard thin blade of light that falls across the wall and just catches the chain's upper three links and the edge of her shoulder. Let the rest of the chamber sit two values lower and let the flail's head hold only a faint reflected gleam on its spikes. Never introduce a second source. Let the crystal pass the light rather than return it: one thin saturated violet line along its thickest edge, and one hard-edged violet caustic patch thrown onto the stone flags beside it.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails hang heavily down her back, pulled slightly to her right by the weight. The nearer tail falls across her ribs as a clean aqua mass with one bright edge from the slot light, the farther one disappears behind her hip. Let a few strands lift and settle with her breathing.

Dress Miku in a heavy harnessed layer over her canonical palette, not armour. A dark teal padded jacket with the sleeves rolled and a padded shoulder on the right, a wide leather belt with two iron rings, dark trousers bound at the knee, and heavy boots with iron toe caps. Keep the palette close to teal-and-black with one pale wrap at her left wrist, and keep the silhouette weighted and compact.

Use a cold low-key palette with strict area control. Approximately forty-two percent of the image is dark stone chamber, twenty-two percent is coursed wall, twelve percent is the chain and haft, nine percent is the flail's head, seven percent is Miku's clothing, four percent is the slot light, three percent is her aqua hair, and one percent is the iron toe caps and the worn link. Keep every warm note out except the crystal. The amethyst's deep violet tone is the one saturated colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the chamber's own mason's marks rather than from decoration. Let one large rust-red ink bloom spread across the wall's upper right, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular pale panel across the wall's lower band as a graphic mask at her hip height, and let one vertical strip of black run down the frame's left edge from the window to the floor. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “CHAIN FLAIL” once, in white paint stencilled across the coursed wall above her head, the strokes interrupted by two mortar joints, sized so it spans about two thirds of the wall's visible width and reads clearly at thumbnail size. Put no lettering on the chain, the head, the floor or her clothing, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The chain's links are worn bright on their inner faces and rusted at their welds; the swivel's bearing is polished from turning; the head's spikes are blunted and its face is pitted with casting voids; the floor's depression is smooth and dark from years of the same contact; her jacket's right shoulder is compressed flat by the strap. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the stone floor. The floor carries the head's shadow as one compact dark mass, the chain as a broken vertical line of eight small shadows, and her boots as two dark shapes at the frame's lower left. Let the depression around the head hold a thin dark ring and never mirror the chain cleanly.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. Two iron rings at her belt, a single link's weld standing slightly proud, one lime-mortar joint crumbling beside the text, and a fine crack running from the head's depression toward the frame's corner. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where use would put it.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the head and its depression. Second: the chain's lower links. Third: the chain's upper links and her hand. Fourth: her body, shoulder and turned head. Fifth: the coursed wall and the slot light. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every link and mortar joint, restrained risograph grain in the dark chamber, crisp flat fills in the slot light, and one clean gradient only along the head's cast face. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the worn iron.

No second character, no duplicate Miku, no crowd, no banners, no flags, no birds, no wings, no halo, no second flail, no additional weapon, no glowing crystal, no neon glow, no self-lit weapon, no rainbow dispersion, no stained glass, no plastic, no glass bottle, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no magical effects, no readable text beyond the string named above, no blood, no wounds, no armour plates, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no chain in her left hand, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no motion blur, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like a weight that has already won: eight links pulled straight down to an anvil of iron, a girl standing over it with her shoulder pulled low, and one link in the middle worn through and closed on itself.

seeds.title: RISING RING
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “RISING RING”, a frame built around one complete ring of light lying flat on a dark stone floor with twelve short straight bars of light rising a hand's height from its twelve radial points, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing at the exact centre of the flat ring with her feet together and both arms held straight at her sides. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her head level so both aqua eyes read clearly against the dark wall behind her.

The ring is one continuous line of light drawn on a single flat plane. The flat ring is complete and bright on the floor, and twelve separate short straight bars rise from its outer ring at even intervals, each one a narrow bright vertical line only a hand's height tall with a flat top and a flat bottom, all twelve the same height and the same width. The inner ring closes without a break, twelve short radial dashes sit between the two rings, and six segmented arcs sit at even intervals along the outer ring. Each short vertical bar rises from the outer end of one radial dash and from one of the six segmented arcs in turn. Nothing inside it is written: no letters, no characters, no symbols, no script of any kind — only geometry. Its light is saturated emerald, the most saturated colour anywhere in the frame, and it reads as a lit tube rather than as white paint. The exact centre of the flat ring sits between her two boots and all twelve short bars stand in a circle around her, so the rising structure reads as built from her stance rather than as a pattern on the floor behind her. It is a magic circle, drawn and lit, and nothing else.

Use a camera at her chest height on a normal lens, perfectly level and set back a few paces, so her full standing figure sits at the frame's centre with both boots on the floor in the lower third and the twelve short bars stay below her knee line. Place Miku at approximately forty-six percent of the canvas width and about forty-six percent of the frame height. Never use a low upward angle, never look down at the floor from above, and never let the bars converge into a cone.

Give Miku exactly one core action: standing still at the exact centre with her feet together, both arms held straight at her sides, her back upright and her head the highest point of her body. She is not kneeling, not crouching, not stepping over a bar and not reaching toward the ring. Put nothing in either hand and no object anywhere between her and the bars.

Construct the dominant visual object as the flat ring and its twelve short bars read as flat lit lines rather than as a solid object. Every line is a thin bright groove of equal width with a crisp lip and no thickness; each short bar has a flat top and a flat bottom and stays below her knee line. Let the dark gaps between the bars be as wide as the bars are tall in the frame and stay completely unlit.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The floor is dark flagstone, matte and dry with pale straight joints; the lit ring and the twelve bars are cut bright lines with hard lips and no thickness; the air above the bars is one flat near-black with no haze; the far wall is one flat dark grey; her working layer is matte dark teal and charcoal. Each behaves differently: stone returns one flat dark value, each lit line one hard bright edge, the air one deep dark, and cloth one dense matte mass. Keep the whole frame matte and let no bar glow or spread.

Build a stepped sequence from her boots outward. Begin at the frame's centre with her two boots together, then the closed inner ring, then the twelve radial dashes, then the six segmented arcs, then the flat outer ring, then the bases of the twelve short bars, and end at their flat tops, her standing figure and the dark far wall. The sequence must read as one measured structure rising a hand's height from one pair of boots.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is no continuous wall of light, no lattice, no grid of lines, no written character, no rune, no glyph, no script, no altar, no candle, no second figure, no beam through the air, no tall light column and no cast shadow of a person. Nothing stands in the frame but her and the ring. Keep the largest quiet area of the picture in the dark wall at the frame's upper right, above the twelve short bars.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the dark flagstone, the stencilled word and the nearest part of the flat ring. Middle ground: her boots, the inner ring, the radial dashes and the twelve short bars. Background: the six segmented arcs, the outer ring, her standing figure and the dark far wall. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the flat ring and the twelve short bars and from nothing else. The lit lines are the only source: a saturated emerald light that sits in each groove, throws one short hard bleed onto the flagstone beside the ring, and lifts the fronts of her boots and the underside of her sleeves from below. The dark air above the bars stays entirely unlit. Never add a second source, never show a beam through the air, never draw a continuous wall of light or a tall column, and never let the light spread as a fog.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails hang quiet down her back without lifting, the nearer one a shade darker than the farther one, so they read as two still vertical lines that answer the twelve short bars. Keep them as clean aqua shapes with hard edges, keep them clear of her hands, and never let a tail tip touch the lit line.

Dress Miku in a plain dark working layer over her canonical palette, not armour and not a costume. A dark teal long-sleeved top with the sleeves pushed to the elbow, a charcoal sleeveless over-vest, dark trousers with a narrow brass belt, and soft boots laced to the ankle. Keep every garment matte and free of ornament, and let the light from the ring pick out the underside of her forearms and the folds where her sleeves are pushed up.

Use a emerald-on-flagstone palette with strict area control. Approximately forty-four percent of the image is the dark flagstone floor and air above the bars, eighteen percent is the flat emerald ring and its twelve dashes, fourteen percent is the twelve short emerald vertical bars, ten percent is her dark teal and charcoal working layer, nine percent is the six segmented arcs and the short bleeds, and five percent is the flat dark grey far wall. Keep the emerald the only saturated colour in the entire frame and make it read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the floor's own wear rather than from decoration. Let one wide dark ink bloom spread across the flagstone at the frame's upper right with its edge following a joint, and let one thin pale scuff band run across the floor where the ring's base sits. Keep all printed matter matte and broken by the joints.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “RISING RING” once, cut shallow into the dry dark flagstone outside the ring at the frame's lower left and filled with pale white paint so the letters read as pale grooves interrupted where the joints cross them, the letters set square to the frame, each letter as tall as her boot, and the whole word spanning about a third of the frame's width so it reads clearly even at thumbnail size. Put no lettering inside the ring, on her clothing or on the wall, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The flagstone under her boots is worn smooth in one small oval; the nearest short bar holds one fine bright lip; one radial dash is a shade dimmer than the rest; and her boots carry a thin rim of stone dust at their soles. Keep the wear directional and small, all of it running with the ground rather than across the ring.

Build a second composition through the far wall. Let the wall read as one flat dark grey field with a single slightly paler strip just above the floor line, banded rather than detailed, with no opening, no fixture and no carving drawn into it. Let that field stay a tone rather than an image, with no hanging object, and let it be broken only where her head cuts into it.

Add only a few working details, all at points of use. One narrow brass keeper at the belt, one fine stitch line along the shoulder seam, one scuffed toe on her rear boot, and one loose thread where a sleeve is pushed up. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where work would put it, and keep no more than four such points in the whole frame.

Maintain five readable depth layers. First: the dark flagstone, the stencilled word and the nearest part of the ring along the bottom edge. Second: her boots and the closed inner ring. Third: the twelve radial dashes and the six segmented arcs. Fourth: the flat outer ring and the twelve short bars. Fifth: her standing figure and the flat dark grey far wall. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each, and let no layer borrow an edge from the one behind it.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp flat dark planes, one hard bright contour on every lit segment, restrained risograph grain only in the shadowed ground, and no gradient anywhere except the short bleed beside the lit line. Keep the whole image matte; no glow around the ring, no beam through the air, no lens flare and no bloom.

Exclude every failure mode explicitly: no written characters inside the circle, no script of any kind, no runes, no glyphs, no lattice, no grid of lines, no continuous wall of light, no beam through the air, no second figure, no extra limb, no extra twin tail, no floating foot, no mirrored duplicate, no readable text beyond the string named above, no continuous wall of light, no tall light column, no lattice, no grid of lines, no rune, no glyph, no beam through the air, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no photographic depth of field, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter, no drop shadow under the figure.

Close on one quiet fact. The whole picture is one dark stone floor, a flat emerald ring with twelve short bars rising a hand's height, one standing figure at its centre and one word cut into the flagstone. Everything else has been removed so the single lit circle can carry the frame alone.

seeds.title: ASH RING
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “ASH RING”, a frame built around one dying ring of light scattered across a field of cold grey ash, with only seven of its twelve arcs still lit, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing just outside its centre with both hands held open at her sides and her boots braced on the ash. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her chin lowered a little toward the ash so the edge of one cheek reads clearly.

The ring is one continuous line of light drawn on a single flat plane. Five of the twelve outer arcs have gone dark and read only as shallow grooves in the ash; the seven that remain burn unevenly, brightest at their leading ends and fading to a dull red at their trailing ends. The inner ring is still closed but holds only a third of its former brightness. The twelve radial dashes are all still visible as dark cuts, the inner ring closes without a break, and a second dimmer arc sits a hand's width outside the outer ring where the light used to arrive. Nothing inside it is written: no letters, no characters, no symbols, no script of any kind — only geometry. Its light is saturated ember orange, the most saturated colour anywhere in the frame, and it reads as a lit tube rather than as white paint. The ring's centre sits directly beneath her two open palms, so the last lit arcs read as answering her hands rather than as a pattern on the ground behind her. It is a magic circle, drawn and lit, and nothing else.

Use a camera at her chest height on a normal lens, perfectly level and set back a few paces, so she stands at the frame's centre at her full standing height with her boots in the lower third and the ash field running out to a dead-level far edge. Place Miku at approximately forty-four percent of the canvas width and about forty-six percent of the frame height. Never use a low upward angle, never look down at the ash from above, and never let the far edge tilt.

Give Miku exactly one core action: standing still with both arms held out and slightly down at about forty-five degrees from her body, elbows nearly straight, palms open and facing the ash at the height of her hips. She stays vertical: feet a shoulder's width apart, knees faintly bent, back upright, head the highest point of her body. She is not kneeling, not crouching, not bending and not touching the ground. Put nothing in either hand and nothing between her palms and the ash.

Construct the dominant visual object as the seven surviving arcs read as a flat drawing on the ash rather than as a solid object. Each lit arc is a thin bright groove of equal width with a crisp lip and no thickness; each dead arc is the same groove holding only a dull dark red. Let the five dead arcs be as clearly drawn as the seven lit ones so the ring reads as one structure slowly going out.

The ash is fine cold grey powder, matte and faintly granular, packed slightly where feet have passed; the lit grooves are cut channels with hard lips lit from inside; the dead grooves hold one dull dark red with no glow; the far wall is one flat near-black; her working layer is matte dark teal and charcoal. Each behaves differently: ash returns one flat grey, a lit groove one hard bright line, a dead groove one dull red, and cloth one dense matte mass. Keep the whole frame matte and let no ember sparkle.

Build a stepped sequence from her palms outward. Begin at the frame's centre with her two open hands held above the ash, then the dim inner ring directly beneath them, then the twelve dark radial cuts, then the seven surviving lit arcs, then the five dead arcs, and end at the second dimmer outer arc and the flat near-black far wall. The sequence must read as one line going out from one pair of hands.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is no flame, no smoke, no spark, no candle, no brazier, no altar, no offering, no debris, no second figure, no cast shadow of a person and no object standing on the ash. Nothing stands in the frame but her and the ring. Keep the largest quiet area of the picture in the cold ash at the frame's upper right, where the last arc has already gone dark.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the cold ash, the stencilled word and the nearest dead arc. Middle ground: her boots, the closed inner ring and the twelve dark radial cuts. Background: the seven lit arcs, the five dead arcs, the dimmer outer arc and the near-black far wall. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the seven surviving arcs and from nothing else. The lit line is the only source: a saturated ember orange light that sits in the groove, throws one short hard bleed onto the cold ash beside it, and lifts the underside of her jaw, her open palms and the fronts of her boots from below. Everything beyond a hand's width of the line falls away to near black. Never add a second source, never show a beam through the air, never draw a flame, and never let the light spread as a fog.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails hang quiet down her back without lifting, the nearer one a shade darker than the farther one, so they read as two still vertical lines against the dark far wall. Keep them as clean aqua shapes with hard edges, keep them clear of her hands, and never let a tail tip touch the lit line.

Dress Miku in a plain dark working layer over her canonical palette, not armour and not a costume. A dark teal long-sleeved top with the sleeves pushed to the elbow, a charcoal sleeveless over-vest, dark trousers with a narrow brass belt, and soft boots laced to the ankle. Keep every garment matte and free of ornament, and let the light from the ring pick out the underside of her forearms and the folds where her sleeves are pushed up.

Use a ember-on-ash palette with strict area control. Approximately forty-six percent of the image is the cold grey ash field, sixteen percent is the seven surviving ember orange arcs, fourteen percent is her dark teal and charcoal working layer, ten percent is the five dead dark red grooves, nine percent is the flat near-black far wall, and five percent is the dim inner ring and short bleeds. Keep the ember orange the only saturated colour in the entire frame and make it read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the ash's own wear rather than from decoration. Let one wide dark ink bloom spread across the ash at the frame's upper right with its edge following a packed footprint, and let one thin pale scuff band run across the field where the dead arcs lie. Keep all printed matter matte and broken by the powder.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “ASH RING” once, cut shallow into the packed cold ash at the frame's lower left and filled with pale grey paint so the letters read as pale grooves softened where powder has drifted into them, the letters set square to the frame, each letter as tall as her boot, and the whole word spanning about a third of the frame's width so it reads clearly even at thumbnail size. Put no lettering inside the ring, on her clothing or on the wall, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The ash under her boots is pressed into one small darker oval; the nearest lit arc holds one fine bright lip; one dead groove is a shade deeper than the rest; and her boots carry a thin rim of ash at their soles. Keep the wear directional and small, all of it running with the ground rather than across the ring.

Build a second composition through the far wall. Let the wall read as one flat near-black field with a single slightly paler strip just above the ash line, banded rather than detailed, with no fixture, no opening and no carving drawn into it. Let that field stay a tone rather than an image, with no hanging object, and let it be broken only where her head cuts into it.

Add only a few working details, all at points of use. One narrow brass keeper at the belt, one fine stitch line along the shoulder seam, one scuffed toe on her rear boot, and one loose thread where a sleeve is pushed up. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where work would put it, and keep no more than four such points in the whole frame.

seeds.title: BINDING RING
seeds.raw:

Keep her face lowered toward her feet and her twin-tail outline readable against the dark floor behind her.

The circle is one continuous line of light drawn on a single flat plane, and part of it has left the plane. Build the flat part from three concentric rings of unequal weight, twelve short radial dashes spaced evenly between the middle and outer ring, and one segmented arc broken into four lengths near the rim; then, from the innermost ring, two narrow hoops of the same light rise and close around her legs, one just below her knee and one across her calf, each fitting the leg like a wide band. Nothing inside any of it is written: no letters, no characters, no symbols, no script of any kind — only geometry. Its light is saturated violet, the most saturated colour anywhere in the frame, and it reads as a lit tube rather than as white paint. It is a magic circle, drawn and lit, and nothing else.

Use a camera at her chest height on a normal lens, set back far enough to show her whole standing figure from boots to head, so the floor rings sit under her boots in the frame's lower third, both hoops read clearly at her ankles, and her head and shoulders are fully inside the picture. Place Miku at approximately fifty percent of the canvas width, occupying about sixty-eight percent of the frame height from her boots to the crown of her head, and let the outer ring's lower arc run out of the frame's bottom edge.

Give Miku exactly one core action: standing still while something closes. Her feet are a short step apart, both planted flat and turned slightly out, her arms hang at her sides with the palms open and facing back, her shoulders are up and her head is lowered, her eyes on the hoops at her ankles. She is not pulling away, not bending down and not stepping out: she is standing in place and letting it finish. Put nothing in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the two hoops around her legs, seen together with her whole standing figure. Each is a narrow band of light of constant width, lying flat and horizontal, one just below her knee and one across her calf, with nothing between the band and her trouser leg — the light touches the cloth. Keep both bands, both knees and her head inside the frame at once. The floor rings below are thin bright grooves of equal width with crisp lips, the radial dashes stop short of both rings, and the segmented arc keeps four equal gaps.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The floor is bare polished concrete, its surface holding a faint mirror sheen and a scatter of fine dust; the grooves are cut channels with hard lips, lit from inside; her trousers are matte dark cloth that the light does not pass through; the wall behind is painted brick gone grey, its courses barely readable in the dark. Each behaves differently — polished concrete returns one long soft reflection of the hoops, a groove holds one hard bright line, cloth absorbs and shows only a rim where the band meets it, and the brick dissolves into shadow.

Build a stepped sequence up her body. Begin at the frame's bottom edge with the floor rings and the outer arc, then up to the lower hoop at her ankle, then the upper hoop, then her knees and hips, then her open hands at her sides, then her lowered head. The sequence must read as one figure held at the feet by one finished drawing, not as a portrait with a pattern around it.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is nothing else on the floor and no one else in the room: no chair, no post, no second figure, no debris anywhere inside or outside the circle. Keep the largest quiet area of the picture in the bare concrete at the frame's upper left, where the light does not reach.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the polished concrete and the floor rings at the bottom edge. Middle ground: her boots, both hoops and her lower legs. The lit line is the only source: a saturated violet light that sits in the bands and channels as lit tubes, throws one short violet bleed onto the polished concrete under her boots so the floor carries the colour, and lifts the underside of her jaw and the fronts of her hands from below. Let the bands touch her trousers so a thin violet rim runs around each ankle. Everything beyond a hand's width of the line falls away to near black. Never add a second source, never show a beam, and never let the light spread as a fog.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails fall forward over her shoulders as her head lowers, both tails dropping past her hips and hanging toward the floor, their ends stopping just short of the lower hoop. Keep them as clean aqua shapes with hard edges, keep them clear of her hands, and never let a tail tip touch the lit band.

Dress Miku in a plain dark layer over her canonical palette, not armour and not a costume. A dark teal long-sleeved top with a high collar, dark trousers cut narrow at the ankle so the hoops sit close to the cloth, and soft boots laced to the ankle. Keep every garment matte and free of ornament so nothing competes with the two bands.

Use a cold low-key palette with one lit element, under strict area control. Approximately forty-two percent of the image is the bare polished concrete, twenty-four percent is the unlit brick and shadow, sixteen percent is the lit hoops and grooves with their bleed, ten percent is Miku's clothing, four percent is her aqua hair, three percent is her skin at the hands and jaw, and one percent is the dust. Keep the violet as the only saturated colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the concrete's own wear rather than from decoration. Let one large black ink bloom spread across the polished floor at the frame's right, its edge following a saw joint, and let a single pale scuff band run across the concrete where boots have turned. Keep all printed matter matte and broken by the joints.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “BINDING RING” once, cut shallow into the bare concrete outside the rings at the frame's upper right and filled with white paint so the letters read as pale grooves, the strokes interrupted where a saw joint crosses them, sized so it spans about a third of the frame width and reads clearly at thumbnail size. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where the pressure would put it.

Fourth: her hips, her open hands and her lowered head. Fifth: the painted brick behind her. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each, with the lit bands the brightest thing in the frame and the brick the darkest.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp controlled edges, deliberate value grouping, no airbrush softness, fine grain in the flat fields, every highlight placed rather than suggested, and the whole image composed so it holds at poster scale and again at thumbnail size.

No second character, no duplicate Miku, no crowd, no chair, no post, no chains, no shackles, no rope, no debris, no birds, no wings, no halo, no second circle, no floating circle, no band around her waist, no band around her wrist, no written characters inside the circle, no letters in the rings, no runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no readable text beyond the word named above, no magic wand, no staff, no floating book, no glowing particles, no sparks, no beam of light, no god rays, no fog glow, no blood, no wounds, no armour plates, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no motion blur, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like a door closing quietly: three thin rings on a polished floor and two narrow violet bands fitted close around a pair of ankles, a girl standing still above them with her hands open and her head down, and not one mark on the concrete to say who set them.

The final image should feel like the instant a decision becomes physical: two open palms held a hand's width above the stone, one thin magenta line already three quarters around the floor and still moving, and a whole dark corner of the frame where it has not arrived yet.

Its line is saturated pale cyan, the most saturated colour anywhere in the frame, and it reads as a lit tube rather than as white paint. It is a magic circle, drawn and lit, and nothing else.

Use a camera at her hip height on a normal lens, set low and to her right, so her kneeling figure fills the frame's upper two thirds and the floor with its rings fills the lower third, and the palm she has pressed down sits at the frame's centre. Place Miku at approximately fifty-six percent of the canvas width, occupying about fifty-four percent of the frame height, and let the outer ring's far arc run out of the frame's right edge. Keep her whole kneeling figure — head, both shoulders and both knees — inside the frame.

Give Miku exactly one core action: pressing one palm flat on the stone. She kneels on her right knee with the shin down and her left foot planted flat ahead of her, her left knee up, and her torso turned down over her left thigh; her right arm reaches across and down with the palm flat on the floor, fingers spread, wrist straight; her left forearm rests across her raised knee. Her head is up and turned toward the camera enough that both eyes are visible. Put nothing in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the ring leaving her palm. Its line is a thin bright groove of equal width everywhere with crisp edges and no thickness; the three rings run without a break, the radial dashes stop short of both rings, and the segmented arc keeps four equal gaps. Let the innermost ring's centre sit exactly under her palm, and let the two nearest radial dashes be the brightest of the twelve so the light visibly begins at her hand and travels outward.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The floor is coarse pale stone, its surface pitted and dusty and its joints wide and dark; the grooves are cut channels with hard lips, lit from inside; her trousers are matte dark cloth pressed flat at the knee; the wall behind is unlit rubble stone, its courses barely readable. Each behaves differently — coarse stone reads as open tooth with pits, a groove holds one hard bright line, her cloth absorbs and shows only a rim, and the rubble reads as soft lumps in the dark.

Build a stepped sequence outward from her hand. Begin at the frame's centre with her flat palm and the innermost ring directly beneath it, then the radial dashes running away, then the bright outer ring sweeping toward the frame's right, then her raised knee and her other forearm, then her lifted face, then the dark rubble behind. The sequence must read as one line being pushed across a floor by one hand, not as a pattern behind a kneeling figure.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is nothing else on the floor: no bowl, no chalk, no tool, no lamp, no debris anywhere inside or outside the rings. Keep the largest quiet area of the picture in the bare stone at the frame's lower left, where the rings have not reached.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the coarse stone and the rings at the bottom edge. Middle ground: her flat palm, her kneeling leg and her raised knee. Background: her torso, her lifted face and the dark rubble wall. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the ring and from nothing else. The groove is the only source: a saturated pale cyan light that sits in the channel as a lit tube, throws one short cyan bleed onto the coarse stone beside it, and comes up onto the underside of her chin, her jaw, her right forearm and the front of her raised knee. Let her face stay one value darker than the floor so her eyes read as dark against lit skin. Everything beyond a hand's width of the line falls away to near black. Never add a second source, never show a beam, and never let the light spread as a fog.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails fall forward over her shoulders and down past her raised knee, the nearer one nearly touching the floor beside her planted foot, the far one disappearing behind her back. Keep them as clean aqua shapes with hard edges, and keep both clear of her pressed palm and of the brightest radial dashes.

Dress Miku in a plain dark working layer over her canonical palette, not armour and not a costume. A dark teal long-sleeved top with the sleeves pushed above the elbow, a charcoal sleeveless over-vest, dark trousers, and soft boots laced to the ankle. Keep every garment matte and free of ornament so the only bright thing in the frame is the line on the floor.

Use a cold low-key palette with one lit element, under strict area control. Approximately forty percent of the image is the coarse pale stone floor, twenty-six percent is the unlit rubble wall and shadow, eighteen percent is the lit groove and its bleed, eight percent is Miku's clothing, four percent is her aqua hair, three percent is her skin at the palm, jaw and forearm, and one percent is her boot's lacing. Keep the pale cyan as the only saturated colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the stone's own wear rather than from decoration. Let one large black ink bloom spread across the coarse stone at the frame's upper left, its edge following a joint, and let a single pale scuff run across the floor in a short arc under her raised knee. Keep all printed matter matte and broken by the joints.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “PRESSING CIRCLE” once, cut shallow into the coarse stone outside the rings at the frame's lower right and filled with white paint so the letters read as pale grooves, the strokes interrupted where the stone's pits break them, sized so it spans about a third of the frame width and reads clearly at thumbnail size. Put no lettering on the floor inside the rings, on her clothing or on the wall, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The coarse stone is pitted across its whole face and holds a scatter of pale grit; the grooves' lips are sharp where the line is bright and dulled at the outer ring's far arc; her trouser cloth is pressed flat and pale at the knee she kneels on; the rubble's mortar is recessed a thumb's depth. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the dusty stone. The stone carries the outer ring as one soft bright arc, her two boots and her kneel as dark shapes standing in it, and the wall as a flat field above. Let the reflection never mirror her face and never extend past the outer ring.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One narrow brass belt, a single grain of grit caught under the edge of her palm, one loose thread at her pushed-up cuff, and a thin crack running from a joint toward the frame's lower right. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where the pressure would put it.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the coarse stone and the rings at the bottom edge. Second: her flat palm and the innermost ring. Third: her kneeling leg and her raised knee. Fourth: her torso, both forearms and her lifted face. Fifth: the rubble wall. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each, with the lit line the brightest thing in the frame and the rubble the darkest.
