No second character, no duplicate Miku, no crowd, no bowl, no chalk, no tool, no lamp, no debris, no birds, no wings, no halo, no second circle, no floating circle, no circle on the wall, no written characters inside the circle, no letters in the rings, no runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no readable text beyond the word named above, no magic wand, no staff, no floating book, no glowing particles, no sparks, no beam of light, no god rays, no fog glow, no blood, no wounds, no armour plates, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no third hand, no both knees down, no sitting, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no motion blur, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like a weight arriving: one palm pressed flat on coarse stone, three thin rings of pale cyan already halfway across the floor and still moving, a girl kneeling over her own hand with her face up, and nothing else in the frame that could have started it.

seeds.title: CIRCLE RIFT
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “CIRCLE RIFT”, a frame built around one colossal ring of light lying on a floor with a single narrow crack torn straight through its centre, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing at the ring's edge with her back to the crack, looking over her shoulder at it. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face and twin-tail outline readable against the light coming up out of the floor.

The circle is one continuous line of light drawn on a single flat plane, and its middle has been torn. Draw three concentric rings of unequal weight, twelve short radial dashes spaced evenly between the middle and outer ring, and one segmented arc broken into four lengths near the rim; then cut one narrow vertical crack straight through all of it, from the outer ring's top edge to its bottom edge, the crack no wider than her hand. Nothing inside it is written: no letters, no characters, no symbols, no script of any kind — only geometry. Its light is saturated white-blue, the most saturated colour anywhere in the frame, and it reads as a lit tube rather than as white paint. It is a magic circle, drawn and lit, and nothing else.

Use a camera at her shoulder height on a normal lens, set behind her and slightly to her left, so she stands at the frame's left with her back three quarters to the lens and the ring's torn centre fills the frame's right half, the crack running from the floor's bottom edge up toward the picture's middle. Place Miku at approximately thirty-two percent of the canvas width, occupying about fifty-eight percent of the frame height from her boots to the crown of her head, and let the outer ring's far arc run out of the frame's right edge.

Give Miku exactly one core action: standing at the edge of it and turning her head back to look. Her feet are a short step apart with her weight on the near foot, her arms hang at her sides with the near hand slightly closed, her shoulders are set, and her head is turned back over her far shoulder so her profile and both eyes come into view. She is not casting, not reaching toward it and not stepping away: the floor is already open and she has turned to look at what she did. Put nothing in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the torn ring. Its line is a thin bright groove of equal width everywhere with crisp edges; the three rings run without a break up to the crack and stop dead at both of its lips; the radial dashes are cut in the same way; and the crack itself is a clean narrow gap with two parallel lit walls, its light coming up out of it rather than lying in it. Let the segmented arc keep its four gaps, and let the crack's lower end run out of the frame's bottom edge.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The floor is dark polished stone, its surface holding a faint sheen away from the light and a scatter of fine dust; the grooves are cut channels with hard lips, lit from inside; the crack's walls are the same stone, cut clean and lit from below with no roughness showing; the far wall is unlit and out of focus in the dark. Each behaves differently — polished stone returns one long soft reflection of the crack, a groove holds one hard bright line, the crack's walls hold the brightest value in the frame at their lower end, and the far wall dissolves completely.

Build a stepped sequence from the crack outward. Begin at the frame's bottom edge with the crack's lit mouth, then up its two parallel walls, then out to the inner ring where it stops at the lips, then the radial dashes, then the outer ring sweeping toward her boots, then her legs and her turned head. The sequence must read as one opening in a drawing on a floor with one figure standing back from it, not as a portrait with a graphic beside it.

Leave one deliberate absence. Nothing comes out of the crack: no smoke, no figure, no shape, no dust falling in from its edges, nothing at all above the floor line except light. Keep the largest quiet area of the picture in the dark polished stone between her boots and the outer ring.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the polished stone and the crack's mouth at the bottom edge. Middle ground: the ring's lines, the radial dashes and her boots. Background: her standing figure, her turned profile and her twin tails, with the dark wall beyond. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the crack and the grooves and from nothing else. Their light is the only source: a saturated white-blue that comes up out of the crack's mouth as a hard-edged column no wider than the crack itself, lies as a lit tube inside every groove, and puts a bright rim along the underside of her jaw, her near arm and the edge of her coat while leaving the back of her head in shadow. Let the polished stone carry one long soft reflection of the crack, and let everything beyond a hand's width of any line fall away to near black. Never add a second source, never let the column spread into a fog, and never let anything rise out of the crack.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails swing with the turn of her head, the far one thrown across her back and lifting slightly at its end, the near one hanging down her front and crossing her collarbone. Keep them as clean aqua shapes with hard edges, and keep both from crossing the crack or the brightest part of the ring.

Dress Miku in a plain dark layer over her canonical palette, not armour and not a costume. A dark teal high-collared top under a charcoal coat cut at mid-thigh, dark trousers with a narrow brass belt, and soft boots laced to the ankle. Keep every garment matte and free of ornament so the only bright thing in the frame is the floor.

Use a cold low-key palette with one lit element, under strict area control. Approximately forty-six percent of the image is the dark polished stone, twenty-two percent is the unlit wall and shadow, eighteen percent is the lit crack and grooves with their bleed, eight percent is Miku's clothing, four percent is her aqua hair, and two percent is her skin at the jaw and hands. Keep the white-blue as the only saturated colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the stone's own wear rather than from decoration. Let one large black ink bloom spread across the floor at the frame's upper left, its edge following a saw joint, and let a single pale scuff run across the stone in a short arc between her boots and the outer ring. Keep all printed matter matte and broken by the joints.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “CIRCLE RIFT” once, cut shallow into the bare stone at the frame's upper left and filled with white paint so the letters read as pale grooves, the strokes interrupted where a joint crosses them, sized so it spans about a quarter of the frame width and reads clearly at thumbnail size. Put no lettering on the floor inside the ring, on her clothing or on the wall, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The stone is scuffed in a broad arc where boots have turned and holds two small chips at a joint; the grooves' lips are sharp up to the crack and dulled where the crack has pulled them; the crack's own lips are clean and show no wear at all because nothing has touched them; her coat's shoulder seam is strained by the turn of her head. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the polished stone. The stone carries the crack as one long hard reflection running toward her boots, the ring's lines as two soft arcs, and her figure as a dark shape standing in the middle of them. Let the reflection never mirror her face and never extend past the crack's own length.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One narrow brass belt, a single grain of dust standing on the crack's near lip, one loose thread at her coat's hem, and a small pale chip of stone lying between two radial dashes. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where the turn of her body would put it.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the polished stone and the crack's mouth. Second: the crack's two walls and the inner ring's lips. Third: her boots and lower legs. Fourth: her torso, her near arm and her coat. Fifth: her turned profile, her twin tails and the dark wall. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each, with the crack's lower mouth the brightest thing in the frame and the far wall the darkest.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp controlled edges, deliberate value grouping, no airbrush softness, fine grain in the flat fields, every highlight placed rather than suggested, and the whole image composed so it holds at poster scale and again at thumbnail size.

No second character, no duplicate Miku, no crowd, no smoke, no dust falling in, no shape rising out of the crack, no birds, no wings, no halo, no second circle, no floating circle, no circle on the wall, no written characters inside the ring, no letters in the rings, no runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no readable text beyond the word named above, no magic wand, no staff, no floating book, no glowing particles, no sparks, no beam through the air, no god rays, no fog glow, no blood, no wounds, no armour plates, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no motion blur, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like something done once and then looked at: one narrow crack of white-blue light standing up out of a floor with a broken ring around it, a girl turned back over her own shoulder to see it, and absolutely nothing coming out.

seeds.title: RIVER GATE
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “RIVER GATE”, a frame built around one tall vertical ring of light standing upright on the cracked bed of a dried river, its lower quarter sunk into the clay, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing a step in front of the gate with one hand raised to its height and her boots planted on the dry clay. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face turned a quarter toward the ring so one cheek reads clearly against the cracked ground.

The ring is one continuous line of light drawn on a single flat plane. The whole ring is complete and upright, but its lower quarter is cut off by the flat line of the clay where the ring meets the ground, so the visible shape reads as a tall bright arch with two straight ends resting on the earth. The inner ring closes above the clay line, twelve short radial dashes point inward from the outer ring and stop short of the inner one, and six segmented arcs sit between the two rings at even intervals along the visible upper curve. Nothing inside it is written: no letters, no characters, no symbols, no script of any kind — only geometry. Its light is saturated amber, the most saturated colour anywhere in the frame, and it reads as a lit tube rather than as white paint. The ring's two cut ends sit exactly at her boot line, one on each side of her, so the gate reads as measured to her stance rather than as a free-standing disc behind her. It is a magic circle, drawn and lit, and nothing else.

Use a camera at her chest height on a normal lens, perfectly level and set back a few paces, so the gate fills the upper two thirds of the frame and her full standing figure sits in the lower third with both boots on the clay. Place Miku at approximately forty-six percent of the canvas width. Never use a low upward angle, never look down at the clay from above, and never let the ring lean into an oval.

Give Miku exactly one core action: standing a step in front of the gate with one hand raised open to the height of her shoulder and the other hanging straight at her side, her head turned a quarter toward the ring. She stays vertical: feet a shoulder's width apart, knees faintly bent, back upright, head the highest point of her body. She is not kneeling, not crouching, not walking through the gate and not touching the lit line. Put nothing in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the upright ring read as a flat drawing of light standing in the air rather than as a solid object. Its line is a thin bright groove of equal width everywhere with a crisp lip and no thickness; the two cut ends are flat, not tapered, and hold the same brightness as the rest of the ring. Let the gate occupy roughly two thirds of the frame's width.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The clay is dry cracked earth, matte and faintly granular, with one flat network of shallow cracks that never forms a grid; the lit groove is a hard bright line with no thickness; the far bank is one flat dark ochre band; the sky beyond is one flat pale grey; her working layer is matte dark teal and charcoal. Each behaves differently: clay returns one flat warm value, the groove one hard bright line, the bank one dark flat, and cloth one dense matte mass. Keep the whole frame matte and let no surface reflect a figure.

Build a stepped sequence from her boots upward. Begin at the frame's lower edge with the cracked clay and the stencilled word, then her boots and the two flat cut ends of the ring, then her standing figure and her raised hand, then the twelve radial dashes, then the six segmented arcs, and end at the crown of the inner ring and the flat pale sky behind it. The sequence must read as one measured gate rising from one pair of boots.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is no water, no puddle, no reflected or mirrored image of her, no fish, no reed, no rock, no bridge, no tree, no second figure, no beam through the air and no cast shadow of a person. Nothing stands in the frame but her and the ring. Keep the largest quiet area of the picture in the cracked clay at the frame's lower right, outside the ring's two cut ends.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the cracked clay, the stencilled word and the near crack pattern. Middle ground: her boots, the two flat cut ends of the ring and her standing figure. Background: the twelve radial dashes, the six segmented arcs, the crown of the gate, the dark far bank and the pale sky. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the upright ring and from nothing else. The lit line is the only source: a saturated amber light that sits in the groove, throws one short hard bleed onto the dry clay beneath its two ends, and lifts the underside of her raised hand, her jaw and the fronts of her boots from below. Everything beyond a hand's width of the line falls away to a warm near black, and the far bank receives only the faintest wash. Never add a second source, never show a beam through the air, never draw a reflection, and never let the light spread as a fog.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails hang quiet down her back without lifting, the nearer one a shade darker than the farther one, so they read as two still vertical lines beside the gate's cut ends. Keep them as clean aqua shapes with hard edges, keep them clear of her hands, and never let a tail tip touch the lit line.

Dress Miku in a plain dark working layer over her canonical palette, not armour and not a costume. A dark teal long-sleeved top with the sleeves pushed to the elbow, a charcoal sleeveless over-vest, dark trousers with a narrow brass belt, and soft boots laced to the ankle. Keep every garment matte and free of ornament, and let the light from the ring pick out the underside of her forearms and the folds where her sleeves are pushed up.

Use a amber-on-clay palette with strict area control. Approximately forty percent of the image is the dry cracked clay bed, twenty percent is the upright amber ring and its twelve dashes, fourteen percent is her dark teal and charcoal working layer, eleven percent is the six segmented arcs and the short bleeds, ten percent is the flat dark ochre far bank, and five percent is the flat pale grey sky. Keep the amber the only saturated colour in the entire frame and make it read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the clay's own wear rather than from decoration. Let one wide dark ink bloom spread across the clay at the frame's lower right with its edge following a crack, and let one thin pale scuff band run beneath the ring's two cut ends. Keep all printed matter matte and broken by the crack pattern.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “RIVER GATE” once, cut shallow into the dry cracked clay at the frame's lower left and filled with dark umber paint so the letters read as dark grooves interrupted where the cracks cross them, the letters set square to the frame, each letter as tall as her boot, and the whole word spanning about a third of the frame's width so it reads clearly even at thumbnail size. Put no lettering inside the ring, on her clothing or on the wall, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The clay under her boots is pressed into one small darker oval; one cut end of the ring holds a fine bright lip; one segmented arc has a slightly uneven end; and her boots carry a thin rim of dry clay at their soles. Keep the wear directional and small, all of it running with the ground rather than across the ring.

Build a second composition through the sky. Let the sky read as one flat pale grey field with a single slightly warmer band just above the far bank, banded rather than graded, with no cloud drawn into it and no sun disc. Let that field stay a tone rather than an image, with no birds, and let it be broken only where the crown of the gate cuts into it.

Add only a few working details, all at points of use. One narrow brass keeper at the belt, one fine stitch line along the shoulder seam, one scuffed toe on her rear boot, and one loose thread where a sleeve is pushed up. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where work would put it, and keep no more than four such points in the whole frame.

Maintain five readable depth layers. First: the cracked clay, the stencilled word and the near crack pattern along the bottom edge. Second: her boots and the two flat cut ends of the ring. Third: her standing figure, her raised hand and the twelve radial dashes. Fourth: the six segmented arcs and the crown of the gate. Fifth: the dark far bank and the flat pale sky. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each, and let no layer borrow an edge from the one behind it.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp flat dark planes, one hard bright contour on every lit segment, restrained risograph grain only in the shadowed ground, and no gradient anywhere except the short bleed beside the lit line. Keep the whole image matte; no glow around the ring, no beam through the air, no lens flare and no bloom.

Exclude every failure mode explicitly: no written characters inside the circle, no script of any kind, no runes, no glyphs, no lattice, no grid of lines, no continuous wall of light, no beam through the air, no second figure, no extra limb, no extra twin tail, no floating foot, no mirrored duplicate, no readable text beyond the string named above, no water, no puddle, no reflected duplicate, no reed, no bridge, no beam through the air, no sun disc, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no photographic depth of field, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter, no drop shadow under the figure.

Close on one quiet fact. The whole picture is one flat bed of cracked clay, a tall amber gate with two cut ends, one small standing figure and one word cut into the dry earth. Everything else has been removed so the single lit circle can carry the frame alone.

seeds.title: ROOF RING
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “ROOF RING”, a frame built around one complete colossal ring of light lying flat across the whole concrete roof of a dark tower, seen from directly above, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing at its exact centre with her feet together and both arms held straight at her sides. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her head lifted a little so the edge of one cheek reads clearly against the pale concrete.

The ring is one continuous line of light drawn on a single flat plane. Every part of it is complete: the inner ring closes without a break, the outer ring closes without a break, and all twelve radial dashes stop short of both rings at the same measured length. Six longer segmented arcs sit between the inner and outer rings at even intervals, each one a short clean segment with two flat ends, and a second dimmer arc sits a hand's width outside the bright outer ring. Nothing inside it is written: no letters, no characters, no symbols, no script of any kind — only geometry. Set the lens wide enough that the complete ring and a narrow strip of dark parapet fit inside the frame. Never angle the camera, never let the parapet lines converge, and never tilt the frame.

Give Miku exactly one core action: standing at the exact centre with her feet together, both arms held straight at her sides and her head lifted a little. She stays vertical from above: her shoulders square to the frame, her boots together directly under her, and her whole figure small inside the enormous ring. She is not kneeling, not sitting, not lying down and not reaching toward the concrete. Put nothing in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the complete ring read as a flat drawing on the concrete rather than as a solid object. Its line is a thin bright groove of equal width everywhere with a crisp lip and no thickness; every radial dash and every segmented arc keeps the same width as the two main rings. Let the ring occupy roughly two thirds of the frame's width so it reads at a glance even at thumbnail size.

The concrete is flat pale grey, matte and slightly granular; the lit grooves are cut channels with hard lips lit from inside; the parapet is one flat near-black band; the sky beyond the roof is not shown; her working layer is matte dark teal and charcoal. Each behaves differently: concrete returns one flat pale value, a groove one hard bright line, the parapet one deep dark, and cloth one dense matte mass. Keep the whole frame matte and let no surface reflect a figure.

Build a stepped sequence from her boots outward. Begin at the frame's centre with her two boots together, then the closed inner ring, then the twelve radial dashes, then the six segmented arcs, then the closed outer ring, then the dimmer arc beyond it, and end at the pale concrete margin and the narrow dark parapet. The sequence must read as one measured structure radiating from one pair of boots.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is no city skyline, no lit window, no antenna, no water tank, no vent, no chair, no table, no railing detail, no second figure, no bird, no aircraft, no reflected or mirrored image of her and no object standing on the roof. Nothing stands in the frame but her and the ring. Keep the largest quiet area of the picture in the pale concrete at the frame's upper right, outside the dimmer arc.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the pale concrete margin, the stencilled word and the nearest part of the outer ring. Middle ground: the twelve radial dashes, the six segmented arcs and the inner ring. Background: her small standing figure at the centre, the far half of the ring and the narrow dark parapet. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the ring and from nothing else. The lit line is the only source: a saturated violet light that sits in the groove, throws one short hard bleed onto the pale concrete beside it, and lifts the edges of her boots and the underside of her sleeves from below. Everything beyond a hand's width of the line falls away to a cool mid grey, and the parapet receives only the faintest wash. Never add a second source, never show a beam through the air, never draw a lit window, and never let the light spread as a fog.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails fall straight down her back without lifting, the nearer one a shade darker than the farther one, so they read as two short vertical lines inside the inner ring. Keep them as clean aqua shapes with hard edges, keep them clear of her hands, and never let a tail tip touch the lit line.

seeds.title: SNOW CIRCLE
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “SNOW CIRCLE”, a frame built around one colossal ring burned through a field of snow, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing at its centre, seen from a high angle so her whole figure sits small inside a ring far wider than she is tall. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face lifted toward the camera and her twin-tail outline readable against the dark ground behind her.

The circle is a trench melted through the snow, not a line of light. Build it from three concentric rings of unequal weight, twelve short radial dashes spaced evenly between the middle and outer ring, and one segmented arc broken into four lengths near the rim. Every part of it is a channel of the same width, cut clean down through the snow to black ground, its walls wet and its floor carrying a low bed of embers. Nothing inside it is written: no letters, no characters, no symbols, no script of any kind — only geometry. The embers are saturated ember-orange, the most saturated colour anywhere in the frame. It is a magic circle, drawn and lit, and nothing else.

Use a camera high above her, looking down at about forty-five degrees off vertical on a wide lens, so the whole ring fits inside the frame with a margin of untouched snow on every side and Miku stands small at its exact centre. Place her at approximately forty-eight percent of the canvas width, occupying about twenty-four percent of the frame height, and let the outer ring's trench run within a hand's width of both side edges.

Give Miku exactly one core action: standing still on ground that is still cooling. Her feet are together inside the innermost ring, her arms hang at her sides with the palms turned slightly out, her shoulders are down and her chin is lifted toward the camera. She is not casting and not reaching: the trench is already burned and she is standing on the ground it exposed. Put nothing in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the burned ring, read as a flat drawing cut into the snow. Its channel is the same width everywhere, with crisp vertical walls and a flat floor of black ground; the three rings run without a break, the radial dashes stop short of both rings, and the segmented arc keeps four equal gaps. Let the snow at the channel's lip be undercut and glossy where it has melted and refrozen, and let the outer ring's lower arc run out of the frame's bottom edge.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The snow is dry wind-packed crust away from the ring, its surface scoured into long shallow ridges and pale blue in shadow; at the channel's lip it turns glassy and clear where it has melted and refrozen; the channel floor is black soil scattered with fine ash and a low bed of embers; the far ground is bare frozen earth showing through in patches. Each behaves differently — dry crust reads as fine granular tooth, glassy lip returns one hard highlight, black soil absorbs everything, the embers hold tiny points of orange that do not spread, and the frozen earth reads as a flat dark field.

Build a stepped sequence from the rim inward. Begin at the frame's edges with the scoured snow and the outer ring's broken arc, then the channel's glassy lip, then the ember bed on its floor, then the radial dashes, then the innermost ring, then the small figure standing on the black ground at the centre. The sequence must read as one continuous cut seen from above, not as a pattern behind a person.

Leave one deliberate absence. The snow field holds nothing else: no footprints leading in or out, no trees, no rock, no second figure, no debris anywhere inside or outside the ring. Keep the largest quiet area of the picture in the untouched crust between the figure and the innermost ring.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the scoured crust and the outer ring's trench at the bottom edge. Middle ground: the glassy lip, the ember bed and the radial dashes. Background: the inner rings, the small figure and the frozen ground beyond. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from a flat overcast sky plus the embers, and let the embers do the colour. The sky gives a diffuse grey light with no direction, so the snow reads as one even pale field and every banked edge stays soft; the ember bed adds the only warm colour in the picture, sitting low in the channel and lifting the black soil and the underside of the snow lip within a hand's width. Never add a sun, never add a cast shadow from a second source, and never let the embers glow upward as a plume.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails hang straight down past her hips and rest on the black ground in two clean aqua shapes, since she is standing still and the air is dead. Keep both tails inside the innermost ring and keep their outlines hard against the dark soil.

Dress Miku in a plain dark winter layer over her canonical palette, not armour and not a costume. A dark teal high-collared top under a charcoal quilted coat cut at mid-thigh, dark trousers tucked into soft boots laced to the ankle, and a narrow brass belt. Keep every garment matte and free of ornament so nothing competes with the ember bed.

Use a cold pale field with one warm element, under strict area control. Approximately fifty percent of the image is scoured snow, eighteen percent is the burned channel and its black soil, twelve percent is the frozen ground beyond the ring, ten percent is Miku's clothing, five percent is her aqua hair, three percent is the ember bed, and two percent is her skin at the face and hands. Keep the ember-orange as the only saturated colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the snow's own weather rather than from decoration. Let one long pale drift line run across the crust at the frame's left where wind has scoured it, and let one dark patch of frozen earth break the snow at the frame's upper right. Keep all printed matter matte and wind-broken.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “SNOW CIRCLE” once, stamped into the untouched crust outside the outer ring at the frame's upper left so the letters read as deep compressions with hard shadows, the strokes softened where fresh snow has begun to drift into them, sized so it spans about a quarter of the frame width and reads clearly at thumbnail size. Put no lettering on the burned ground, inside the rings, or on her clothing, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The crust is scoured into ridges across the wind's direction and holds one shallow sastrugi lip; the channel's lip is undercut and glassy in two runs; the black soil holds fine ash and a scatter of small clinker; the frozen earth beyond the ring is cracked in short straight lines. Keep the wear physical and directional, and keep the crust's ridges all running the same way.

Build a second composition through the snow crust. The crust carries the outer ring as one dark cut, her figure as a small dark shape with two thin tail lines, and the ember bed as a faint warm thread inside the cut. Let the crust never mirror her face and never soften the ring's edge.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One narrow brass belt, a single clinker standing proud of the ash bed, one loose thread at her coat's hem, and a thin skin of clear ice standing in the channel's lip near the frame's right. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where the heat would have left it.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the scoured crust and the outer ring's cut at the bottom edge. Second: the glassy lip and the ember bed. Third: the radial dashes and the middle ring. Fourth: the innermost ring and her boots. Fifth: her figure, her lifted face and the frozen ground beyond. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each, with the snow the brightest and the black soil the darkest.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp controlled edges, deliberate value grouping, no airbrush softness, fine grain in the flat fields, every highlight placed rather than suggested, and the whole image composed so it holds at poster scale and again at thumbnail size.

No second character, no duplicate Miku, no crowd, no footprints, no trees, no rock, no debris, no birds, no wings, no halo, no second circle, no floating circle, no circle of light, no glow above the embers, no written characters in the channel, no letters in the rings, no runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no readable text beyond the word named above, no magic wand, no staff, no floating book, no glowing particles, no sparks, no beam of light, no god rays, no sun, no blood, no wounds, no armour plates, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no motion blur, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like something enormous was done here and then left: three thin channels cut clean through wind-packed snow, a low bed of orange embers still sitting in the black soil, a girl standing small at the middle with her chin up, and not one footprint leading away.

seeds.raw:

She is not casting, not touching it and not stepping through: the ring is already standing there and she has stopped to look at it. Put nothing in either hand.

Build a stepped sequence from the stage floor up. Leave one deliberate absence. The stage is bare: no props, no furniture, no second figure, no audience, no seats in view, no curtain pulled back. Keep the largest quiet area of the picture in the dim cloth at the frame's right, where the ring's light has not reached.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the worn boards at the frame's bottom edge. Middle ground: Miku's profile, her boots and the ring's lit line. Background: the ring's upper arc and the dusty cloth flat. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Everything beyond a hand's width of the line falls away to near black. Never add a stage lamp, never show a beam through the air, and never let the light spread as a fog.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails fall behind her shoulder and down her back, the nearer one crossing her spine as a clean aqua line and the far one dropping out of sight behind her hip. Keep both tails out of the ring's lit line so nothing interrupts its circle.

Dress Miku in a plain dark layer over her canonical palette, not armour and not a costume. A dark teal high-collared top under a charcoal coat cut at mid-thigh, dark trousers, and soft boots laced to the ankle. Use a cold low-key palette with one lit element, under strict area control. Approximately thirty-eight percent of the image is the dusty cloth flat, twenty-two percent is the stage floor's worn boards, twenty percent is the lit ring and its bleed, twelve percent is Miku's clothing and profile, five percent is her aqua hair, two percent is her skin at the jaw and hands, and one percent is the dark wings. Keep the magenta as the only saturated colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the stage's own wear rather than from decoration. Let one large black ink bloom spread across the painted boards at the frame's left, its edge following a seam, and let a single pale scuff oval run across the boards where feet have crossed the stage for years. Keep all printed matter matte and broken by the seams.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “STAGE GATE” once, in worn white paint stencilled across the cloth flat at the height of her shoulder, the strokes broken where the cloth folds, sized so it spans about a fifth of the frame width and reads clearly at thumbnail size. Put no lettering on the ring, on the boards or on her clothing, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The boards are cupped along two seams and their paint is worn through to bare wood in a long oval; the cloth is creased in vertical folds and holds a fine dust film that is thinner where the light stands; the ring's line is perfectly even because it has no substance to wear. Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where the still air would have left it.

Fourth: the ring's lit line and its lower arc. Fifth: the ring's upper arc and the dusty cloth. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each, with the lit line the brightest thing in the frame and the wings the darkest.

No second character, no duplicate Miku, no crowd, no audience, no seats, no props, no furniture, no birds, no wings, no halo, no second ring, no floating ring, no ring lying on the floor, no stage lamp, no spotlight, no written characters inside the ring, no letters in the rings, no runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no readable text beyond the word named above, no magic wand, no staff, no floating book, no glowing particles, no sparks, no beam of light, no god rays, no fog glow, no blood, no wounds, no armour plates, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no motion blur, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like a performance with the house empty: one thin unbroken ring of magenta standing on worn boards, a girl stopped in profile at its side with her chin up, and a dusty cloth flat closing the picture behind it.

seeds.title: TWIN RINGS
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “TWIN RINGS”, a frame built around two overlapping rings of light lying flat on one dark stone floor, one complete and bright and the second dimmer and offset by a third of its own width, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing at the point where the two rings overlap with her boots inside both inner rings. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her chin lowered a little toward the overlap so the edge of one cheek reads clearly.

The ring is one continuous line of light drawn on a single flat plane. The near ring is complete and bright, the far ring is complete but holds only half the near ring's value, and where their lines cross the brighter of the two simply passes over the dimmer one with no spark and no flare. Each ring has its own closed inner ring, twelve short radial dashes, and six segmented arcs at even intervals; the two sets of dashes interleave where the circles overlap without ever forming a lattice or a grid. Nothing inside it is written: no letters, no characters, no symbols, no script of any kind — only geometry. Its light is saturated jade green, the most saturated colour anywhere in the frame, and it reads as a lit tube rather than as white paint. The overlap of the two inner rings sits exactly between her two boots, so both circles read as measured from her stance rather than as two patterns on the floor behind her. It is a magic circle, drawn and lit, and nothing else.

Use a camera at her chest height on a normal lens, perfectly level and set back a few paces, so she stands at the frame's centre at her full standing height with her boots in the lower third and both rings sweeping away across the stone. Place Miku at approximately forty-four percent of the canvas width and about forty-six percent of the frame height. Never use a low upward angle, never look down at the floor from above, and never let either ring lean into an oval.

Give Miku exactly one core action: standing still at the overlap with both arms held slightly out from her sides for balance, her weight even on both boots and her head lowered a little. She stays vertical: feet a shoulder's width apart, knees faintly bent, back upright, head the highest point of her body. She is not kneeling, not crouching, not walking and not reaching toward the stone. Put nothing in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the two overlapping rings read as flat drawings on the stone rather than as solid objects. Every line is a thin bright groove of equal width with a crisp lip and no thickness; where the bright ring crosses the dim one, the bright line simply continues and the dim line stops cleanly at the crossing. Let the two circles occupy roughly two thirds of the frame's width together.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The floor is dark flagstone, matte and dry with pale straight joints; the bright ring is a cut hard line lit from inside; the dim ring is the same cut holding a dull jade with no glow; the far wall is one flat near-black; her working layer is matte dark teal and charcoal. Each behaves differently: stone returns one flat dark value, the bright line one hard edge, the dim line one dull green, and cloth one dense matte mass. Keep the whole frame matte and let no crossing sparkle.

Build a stepped sequence from her boots outward. Begin at the frame's centre with her two boots inside both inner rings, then the two closed inner rings, then the interleaved radial dashes, then the twelve segmented arcs, then the bright outer ring sweeping to the frame's right, and end at the dim outer ring sweeping to the frame's left and the dark far wall. The sequence must read as two lines radiating from one pair of boots.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is no lattice, no grid of lines, no written character, no rune, no glyph, no script, no altar, no candle, no offering, no second figure, no spark at any crossing, no beam through the air and no cast shadow of a person. Nothing stands in the frame but her and the ring. Keep the largest quiet area of the picture in the dark flagstone at the frame's upper right, outside both rings.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the dark flagstone, the stencilled word and the nearest part of the bright outer ring. Middle ground: her boots, the two inner rings and the interleaved radial dashes. Background: the twelve segmented arcs, both outer rings, the clean crossings and the dark far wall. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the two rings and from nothing else. The bright ring is the only strong source: a saturated jade green light that sits in its groove, throws one short hard bleed onto the flagstone beside it, and lifts the underside of her jaw, her sleeves and the fronts of her boots from below. The dim ring lays only a thin skin of the same colour on the stone. Everything beyond a hand's width of either line falls away to near black. Never add a second source, never show a beam through the air, never draw a spark at a crossing, and never let the light spread as a fog.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails hang quiet down her back without lifting, the nearer one a shade darker than the farther one, so they read as two still vertical lines inside the overlap. Keep them as clean aqua shapes with hard edges, keep them clear of her hands, and never let a tail tip touch the lit line.

Dress Miku in a plain dark working layer over her canonical palette, not armour and not a costume. A dark teal long-sleeved top with the sleeves pushed to the elbow, a charcoal sleeveless over-vest, dark trousers with a narrow brass belt, and soft boots laced to the ankle. Keep every garment matte and free of ornament, and let the light from the ring pick out the underside of her forearms and the folds where her sleeves are pushed up.

Use a jade-on-flagstone palette with strict area control. Approximately forty-four percent of the image is the dark flagstone floor, eighteen percent is the bright jade green ring and its dashes, fourteen percent is the dim jade ring and its segmented arcs, ten percent is her dark teal and charcoal working layer, nine percent is the short bleeds beside both rings, and five percent is the flat near-black far wall. Keep the jade green the only saturated colour in the entire frame and make it read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the floor's own wear rather than from decoration. Let one wide dark ink bloom spread across the flagstone at the frame's upper right with its edge following a joint, and let one thin pale scuff band run across the floor where the two rings overlap. Keep all printed matter matte and broken by the joints.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “TWIN RINGS” once, cut shallow into the dark flagstone outside both rings at the frame's lower left and filled with pale white paint so the letters read as pale grooves interrupted where the joints cross them, the letters set square to the frame, each letter as tall as her boot, and the whole word spanning about a third of the frame's width so it reads clearly even at thumbnail size. Put no lettering inside the ring, on her clothing or on the wall, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The flagstone under her boots is worn smooth in one small oval; the bright ring holds one fine white lip; one crossing stops a shade unevenly; and her boots carry a thin rim of stone dust at their soles. Keep the wear directional and small, all of it running with the ground rather than across the ring.

Build a second composition through the far wall. Let the wall read as one flat near-black field with a single slightly paler strip just above the floor line, banded rather than detailed, with no opening, no fixture and no carving drawn into it. Let that field stay a tone rather than an image, with no hanging object, and let it be broken only where her head cuts into it.

Add only a few working details, all at points of use. One narrow brass keeper at the belt, one fine stitch line along the shoulder seam, one scuffed toe on her rear boot, and one loose thread where a sleeve is pushed up. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where work would put it, and keep no more than four such points in the whole frame.

Maintain five readable depth layers. First: the dark flagstone, the stencilled word and the nearest bright outer ring along the bottom edge. Second: her boots and the two closed inner rings. Third: the interleaved radial dashes and her standing figure. Fourth: the twelve segmented arcs and the clean crossings. Fifth: both outer rings and the flat near-black far wall. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each, and let no layer borrow an edge from the one behind it.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp flat dark planes, one hard bright contour on every lit segment, restrained risograph grain only in the shadowed ground, and no gradient anywhere except the short bleed beside the lit line. Keep the whole image matte; no glow around the ring, no beam through the air, no lens flare and no bloom.

Exclude every failure mode explicitly: no written characters inside the circle, no script of any kind, no runes, no glyphs, no lattice, no grid of lines, no continuous wall of light, no beam through the air, no second figure, no extra limb, no extra twin tail, no floating foot, no mirrored duplicate, no readable text beyond the string named above, no lattice, no grid of lines, no rune, no glyph, no spark at any crossing, no beam through the air, no reflected duplicate, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no photographic depth of field, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter, no drop shadow under the figure.

Close on one quiet fact. The whole picture is one dark flagstone floor, two overlapping jade rings with clean crossings, one small standing figure at their overlap and one word cut into the stone. Everything else has been removed so the single lit circle can carry the frame alone.

seeds.title: WELL CIRCLE
seeds.raw:
Create a square 1:1 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “WELL CIRCLE”, a frame built around one bright ring of light lying at the bottom of a dry stone well, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing at its centre, seen from directly above so the well's circular shaft frames the picture. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face lifted straight up toward the camera, fully lit and fully readable.

The circle is one continuous line of light drawn on the single flat plane of the well's floor. Build it from three concentric rings of unequal weight, twelve short radial dashes spaced evenly between the middle and outer ring, and one segmented arc broken into four lengths near the rim of the well. Nothing inside it is written: no letters, no characters, no symbols, no script of any kind — only geometry. Its line is saturated cyan, the most saturated colour anywhere in the frame, and it reads as a lit tube of light rather than as white paint. It is a magic circle, drawn and lit, and nothing else.

Use a camera directly above her, looking straight down the well's axis on a wide lens, so the well's circular wall becomes a ring at the frame's edge and Miku stands small at the exact centre with the lit circle spreading out to the masonry. Place her at approximately fifty percent of both axes, occupying about thirty percent of the frame height, so her whole standing figure and a margin of bare stone floor around her both fit inside the shaft.

Give Miku exactly one core action: standing still and looking straight up. Her feet are together on the stone, her arms hang at her sides with the palms turned slightly out, her shoulders are down, and her chin is lifted so her face is square to the lens. She is not casting and not reaching: the circle is already finished and she is standing inside it, looking up at whoever is above. Put nothing in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the circle, read as a flat drawing on the well's floor. Its line is a thin bright groove of equal width everywhere, cut into the stone and filled with light so both its edges are crisp; the three rings run without a break, the radial dashes stop short of both rings, and the segmented arc keeps its four gaps. Let the outer ring run within a hand's width of the well's wall so the drawing nearly touches the masonry all the way around.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The well's floor is rough flagstone, its joints reading as dark lines and its surface dry and dusty; the well's wall is coursed rubble masonry, its stones rounded and its mortar recessed, running up and out of sight at the frame's edge; the grooves are cut channels with hard lips, lit from inside; the stone mortar carries a pale mineral bloom in one patch. Each behaves differently — flagstone reads as flat tooth with joints, rubble reads as rounded lumps with dark joints between them, a groove holds one hard bright line with no spread, and the mortar bloom reads as a chalky matte that takes no light at all.

Build a stepped sequence from her boots outward. Begin at the centre with her two boots on the flagstone, then up her legs to her lifted face, then out to the innermost ring, then the radial dashes, then the bright outer ring running almost to the wall, then the wall's rubble curving up and out of frame. The sequence must read as one small figure standing in one large drawing inside a closed shaft, not as a portrait with a pattern behind it.

Leave one deliberate absence. The well is empty: no water, no bucket, no rope, no debris, no second figure anywhere on the floor inside or outside the circle. Keep the largest quiet area of the picture in the bare flagstone between the outer ring and the wall.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the dusty flagstone at the frame's left and right edges. Middle ground: the lit rings, the radial dashes and her boots at the centre. Background: her lifted face and figure, and the well's rubble wall rising at the frame's rim. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the circle and from nothing else. The groove is the only source: a saturated cyan light that sits in the channel as a lit tube, throws one short cyan bleed onto the dry flagstone on either side, and comes up onto the underside of her chin and her whole face so her eyes stay readable. Let the well's wall receive only a thin wash that dies inside a hand's width of the floor, so the top of the shaft stays dark. Never add a second source, never show daylight from above, and never let the light spread as a fog.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails fall straight down and pool on the flagstone around her boots in two clean aqua shapes, since she is standing still and nothing is moving them. Keep both tails inside the innermost ring and keep their outlines hard against the stone, so she reads as one bright compact figure at the centre of a very large dark frame.

Dress Miku in a plain dark layer over her canonical palette, not armour and not a costume. A dark teal long-sleeved top with a high collar, a charcoal wrap skirt to just below the knee, dark trousers under it, and soft boots laced to the ankle. Keep every garment matte and free of ornament so nothing competes with the lit line on the floor.

Use a cold low-key palette with one lit element, under strict area control. Approximately forty-four percent of the image is the rough flagstone floor, twenty-six percent is the rubble wall rising at the rim, fourteen percent is the lit groove and its bleed, nine percent is Miku's clothing, four percent is her aqua hair, two percent is her skin at the face and hands, and one percent is the chalky mortar bloom. Keep the cyan as the only saturated colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the well's own masonry rather than from decoration. Let one large black ink bloom spread across the flagstone at the frame's upper left, its edge following a joint, and let a single pale mineral vein run across two stones in the wall where the rubble has cracked. Keep all printed matter matte and broken by the joints.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “WELL CIRCLE” once, cut shallow into the flagstone outside the outer ring at the frame's lower right and filled with white paint so the letters read as pale grooves, the strokes interrupted where the joints cross them, sized so it spans about a quarter of the frame width and reads clearly at thumbnail size. Put no lettering on the floor inside the circle, on her clothing or on the wall, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The flagstone is chipped along two joints; the grooves' lips are worn smooth in one short run; the rubble in the wall is rounded and its mortar recessed by a thumb's depth in places; one stone in the wall is cracked clean across; the floor's dust is thinner in a ring where the light has been standing for a long time. Keep the wear physical and directional, and keep every trace of it outside the lit line.

Build a second composition through the dust on the flagstone. The dust carries the outer ring as one soft bright arc, her two boots as small dark shapes at the centre, and the wall as a dark ring at the frame's edge. Let the dust never mirror her face and never extend past the outer ring.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One thin brass clasp at her collar, a single grain of grit standing upright against the outer ring, one loose thread at her cuff, and a small pale chip of flagstone lying between the radial dashes. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where the still air would have left it.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the dusty flagstone at the frame's edges. Second: the outer ring and its bright arc. Third: the radial dashes and the middle ring. Fourth: the innermost ring, her boots and her pooled twin tails. Fifth: her lifted face and the rubble wall at the rim. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each, with the lit line the brightest thing in the frame and the wall's upper course the darkest.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp controlled edges, deliberate value grouping, no airbrush softness, fine grain in the flat fields, every highlight placed rather than suggested, and the whole image composed so it holds at poster scale and again at thumbnail size.

No second character, no duplicate Miku, no crowd, no water, no bucket, no rope, no ladder, no debris, no birds, no wings, no halo, no second circle, no floating circle, no circle on the wall, no written characters inside the circle, no letters in the rings, no runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no readable text beyond the word named above, no magic wand, no staff, no floating book, no glowing particles, no sparks, no beam of light, no god rays, no daylight from above, no fog glow, no blood, no wounds, no armour plates, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no motion blur, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like being looked at from above in a place with no other exit: one thin unbroken ring of cyan cut into dry flagstone, a girl standing small at its centre with her face turned straight up, and a ring of rubble closing the picture all the way around her.

She stays vertical: feet a shoulder's width apart, knees faintly bent, back upright, head the highest point of her body. She is not kneeling, not crouching, not pulling against the ring and not turning back. Put nothing in either hand.

Keep them as clean aqua shapes with hard edges, keep them clear of her hands, and never let a tail tip touch the lit line.

seeds.title: CLIFF EDGE
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “CLIFF EDGE”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing at the lip of a sea cliff in strong wind, with a pale weathered rock face dropping away behind her. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the pale stone.

Use a camera at hip height on a normal lens, set on the cliff top about four metres back and angled twenty degrees so the drop falls away to the right and the rock face fills the lower right. Place Miku at approximately thirty-eight percent of the canvas width, full body visible from boots to hair ornaments, occupying about thirty-four percent of the frame height.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Her right hand holds a light anorak closed at the collar, and her left hand is raised at shoulder height, palm open against the wind. Her hair and coat are pushed hard to one side. Keep the pose steady and put nothing else in her hands.

Construct the dominant visual object as the weathered rock face below and beside her: a broad pale cliff of horizontally bedded stone, its upper lip grassed to the very edge, its face split by three vertical gullies and scattered with lichen. Let the face occupy approximately forty-five percent of the canvas area in the lower right, and let it be the brightest large surface in the frame.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The rock is pale grey with ochre lichen and dark wet streaks; the cliff top is short wind-flattened grass with exposed soil at the lip; the sea far below is a flat dark blue with one white breaking line; the sky is a hard pale blue with no cloud structure; the anorak is thin ripstop. Each behaves differently — limestone reads as pale horizontal bands with a fine grain, grass as flattened vertical strokes, the sea as a flat dark field with one bright line, the sky as a graded pale field.

Build a stepped sequence from the cliff top outward. Begin at the bottom left with the grass and one exposed root, then the lip with its crumbling edge, then Miku's boots and her hand, then the rock face with its gullies, then the sea's breaking line, then the empty sky. The sequence must read as a drop, not as a landscape.

Leave one deliberate absence. One gully in the rock face is dry and empty where the other two carry wet streaks: a clean pale channel about a metre wide with no seep, no lichen, no shadow at its base. Keep it just right of her boots so the eye falls from her feet down the one dry line.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: grass, root, crumbling lip. Middle ground: Miku and the rock face's upper third. Background: the lower face, the sea and the sky. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from a low sun off to the left. The sun is the key: hard and warm, raking across the rock face so every bedding plane casts a thin shadow and every gully reads as a dark slot. Add a cool bounce from the sea below, lifting the face's lower third with a blue-grey film. Keep every shadow hard-edged and short, and let the face's top edge blow out to near-white.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the wind. Both tails stream horizontally to the right, the nearer one crossing her shoulder and the farther one whipping past her hip, both reading as one saturated aqua mass against the pale rock. Let the wind press her bangs flat across her brow without hiding her eyes.

Dress Miku in an original cliff-edge costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not outdoor gear. A thin pale anorak worn over a dark thermal top, dark trousers tucked into laced boots, and a narrow strap across her chest. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment.

Use a pale-stone palette with one cool accent and strict area control. seeds.title: RUIN WINDOW
seeds.raw:

Use a camera at her shoulder height on a normal lens, set square to her profile and level with the frame, close enough that her standing figure fills about eighty-five percent of the frame height with a clear margin of wall on both sides. Place her at approximately forty-six percent of the canvas width. Let the window's top edge run out of the frame and its sill cut one straight horizontal line across the lower fifth. Keep the camera level rather than low so the floor stays beneath her boots.

Give Miku exactly one core action: standing still and looking out. Her weight is even on both feet, both knees are straight and locked, no knee is lifted, her shoulders are square to the glass, and her hands hang open at her sides with the fingers relaxed. Her chin is level and her face is turned three-quarters toward the viewer so the black visor reads as one unbroken horizontal band. Keep both arms inside the frame and put nothing in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the window and the figure: one tall grid of twelve equal glass panes in three columns and four rows, one cracked pane with a single spider of hairline fractures, and one narrow vertical shadow cast by the mullion across her dress. Let the grid be the only repeating structure in the frame, and let the cracked pane be its single exception. Keep the sill plain and let the wall on either side stay bare.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. the glass is old plate, faintly grey and dusty so each pane holds one even pale tone with no figure in it; the mullions are dark painted steel with a chipped edge; the black visor is matte woven cloth with no shine; her dress is heavy black cotton with a white scalloped hem and a stiff high collar; her boots are soft black leather to the knee; the floor is pale concrete under a thin even layer of dust; the wall is bare plaster gone grey at the corners. Each behaves differently — glass returns one flat tone and no reflection of a body, painted steel holds a dry grain with one bright worn edge, the visor absorbs all light, cotton reads as a dense matte plane with one crisp white edge, leather shows one narrow highlight, dusty concrete is a soft even field, plaster holds a faint fine grit. Keep the whole frame matte.

Build a stepped sequence across the frame. Begin at the lower left with the dusty concrete and her two boots, then the sill and the hem of her dress, then her hanging right hand and the tall black column of her figure, then the visor and the silver bob, then the mullion shadow crossing her collar, then the cracked pane and the pale glass beyond. The sequence must read as a pause on a long walk, not as a portrait pose, and each step must sit a little higher and a little brighter than the one before.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is no second character, no reflected figure, no mannequin, no display stand, no sign, no price tag, no chair, no plant, no debris and no machine — nothing in the arcade but the window, the dusty floor and her own two boots. Keep the whole right side of the glass bare so the cracked pane is the only break in the grid.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the dusty concrete and the sill. Middle ground: her boots, her hanging hands and the black column of her dress. Background: the glass grid, the pale light beyond it and the cracked pane. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur, and let the brightest value sit behind her so the black visor and collar read as one clean silhouette.

Light the scene from the glass and from nothing else. One cold white side light from the window is the key: it comes in from her right at shoulder height, cuts one hard vertical band across her visor and collar, throws one narrow mullion shadow onto the dusty concrete, and leaves her far side in an even dark tone. Let Miku's extremely long twin tails fall behind both shoulders as she stands. The nearer tail drops along her right arm and stops at her wrist; the farther one hangs straight down into the dark behind her. Let the window's light rim each tail and let the tip near her sleeve catch one cool reflection. Keep both tails clear of the visor's horizontal band.

The final image should feel like one pause on a very long walk: a black-and-white figure standing straight before a wall of pale glass, one cracked pane beside her shoulder, and a whole empty arcade gone quiet behind her.

seeds.title: LAKE STEP
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “LAKE STEP”, shot from slightly above and looking down at Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing upright at the edge of a still lake at golden hour, both her hands lifting the hem of her skirt. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and outfit readable against the pale water.

Use a camera set just above her shoulder height, looking down at her at about fifteen degrees and slightly off her front, so she is seen in three-quarter view from above: she stands on a wide flat quay of wet grey stone at the lake's edge, that stone filling the bottom third of the frame with its joints running away from the lens, and the still lake lying beyond it as a bright band under a high horizon. Place her at approximately fifty percent of the canvas width with her full standing height, head to boots, filling about eighty-five percent of the frame height.

Give her exactly one core action. She stands upright at her full standing height on the wet stone, and both her knees are straight and locked: there is no bend in either leg and no knee is lifted. Her weight is on her right leg, that boot planted flat, and her left heel is raised just clear of the stone so only the toe of that boot touches, with the left ankle in line with the straight left leg. Both hands hold the hem of her skirt at the height of her hips and hold the cloth out to either side in two clean folds, so both legs stay visible from hip to boot. Her arms are empty: nothing is carried in either hand. Her shoulders are level, her chin lifted and her eyes on the camera. She is standing, not kneeling, not crouching and not sitting.

Construct the dominant visual object as the shape her lifted skirt makes against the pale water: two clean triangles of white cloth held out from her hips, with the bright lake showing between and beneath them and her long shadow running back across the wet stone. Let the two folds of skirt be the largest and whitest shapes in the frame after her face.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The stone is wet granite with a dull sheen and dark joints; the lake beyond is a still sheet of pale sky-colour with no chop; the far shore is a low band of matte trees; her blouse is dry cotton with a faint weave, her skirt a crisp pleated cotton that holds a fold, her jacket a heavy wool with a soft nap; her boots are oiled leather with a dull sheen. Each behaves differently: wet stone reflects softly, still water mirrors, cotton absorbs, wool holds one soft highlight, leather takes a small hard specular.

Build a stepped sequence downward from her face. Begin at her eyes meeting the camera, then the red ribbon at her braid, then her level shoulders, then both fists closed on the skirt's hem, then the two white folds of cloth, then both straight legs and the raised left heel, then the wet stone and her long shadow, then the bright lake and the far shore. The sequence must read as one held breath, not as a girl posing.

Leave one deliberate absence. The lake is empty in every direction: no boat, no jetty, no other figure, no birds, no floating petals, no reeds. Nothing in the frame is carried, held or propped: her hands hold only her own skirt, and her only contact with the ground is her two boots on the stone.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the wet stone and her shadow. Middle ground: her boots, both straight legs, the skirt's two folds and her body. Background: the bright lake, the far shore and the pale sky. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

The sun is the warm key: a pale gold rim along her shoulder, her braid, the upper edge of her lifted skirt and the far water, while her front stays in cool shade. The final image should feel like one held breath at the edge of a mirror: a girl standing straight and tall on wet stone, two folds of white skirt held out from her hips, one heel just leaving the ground, and the whole sky lying flat and unbroken behind her.

seeds.raw:

Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable silhouette. Place the hand at approximately thirty percent of the canvas width and her face at seventy percent, the hand occupying about forty percent of the frame height. Let the rail cross behind her arm as one soft diagonal and the street lamps fall away as warm points.

Give her exactly one core action. The shot has already left her: her right arm is still extended forward, dead straight at shoulder height, the elbow locked and the wrist carried through the snap, and her right hand is wide open with the five fingers splayed apart and the thumb flicked up, empty, holding nothing at all. The beam leaves from the flat of that open palm. The recoil has rocked her torso back a few degrees while her shoulders stay square and level. Her chin is lifted and her head is turned a little toward the lens, and both eyes look straight forward out of the frame, calm and steady, never down at her hand. Her hair, her fringe and the hem of her vest are blown back by the shockwave, and her skirt presses to the front of her thighs. Her left arm is flung back beside her hip with the hand loose. Nothing is in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the shot itself: one straight beam of white-blue light leaving her fingertips and running out through the left edge of the frame, its core a hard white line no wider than her arm, its edges feathered by a thin blue halo, and its length broken by two bright knots where the charge bunched. Add a short cone of motion streaks behind the beam's head, a spray of six or seven white sparks thrown off its edges, and one thin curl of smoke twisting off the tip of her thumb. Let the beam occupy the left half of the frame at her hand's height and let her face and open hand stay the second brightest thing in it.

Each behaves differently — chalky steel scatters light, asphalt goes flat, glass emits, cotton absorbs, wool holds one soft highlight, metal takes one hard specular.

Build a stepped sequence that runs from the beam back to her face. Begin at the left edge of the frame with the beam's white core and its spray of sparks, then her splayed open fingers with the thumb still up, then her locked wrist and taut forearm, then the elbow and the square shoulder line, then her profile with both eyes looking forward, then the chipped rail crossing behind her back, then the receding lamps, then the flat dark buildings. The sequence must read as the frame immediately after the shot, not as a girl posing with special effects.

Leave one deliberate absence. The bridge is empty in both directions: no pedestrian, no cyclist, no car on the road below, no lit vending machine, no station entrance. The only things in the frame besides her and her arcs are the lamps and the far windows, and no lettering appears anywhere.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the beam and its sparks, her open splayed hand and the thumb flicked up. Middle ground: her extended forearm, the elbow, her shoulder and her profile. Background: the chipped rail crossing behind her back, the receding lamps, the flat buildings and the night sky. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the shot itself first and from the street lamps second. The beam is the key: it throws a hard white-blue rim along the outer edge of her forearm, the tops of her splayed fingers, the line of her jaw and the near face of the rail, and it makes the sparks read as white dashes. The lamps are a weak warm fill from behind, rimming her hair, her shoulder and the top of the extended arm. Keep the buildings, the sky and the road below at absolute near-black.

Let her hair behave as a third light: it lifts slightly in the static, every edge picking up the arcs' cool glow while the mass stays warm. Keep the fringe clear of her eyes.

Dress her in the Tokiwadai middle-school summer uniform exactly as it reads in the source: a white short-sleeved blouse with a small pointed collar, a tan V-neck vest with brown piping along its edges and a small round school badge on the left chest, a pleated grey skirt to the knee, dark knee socks and brown loafers. Keep the uniform matte and unadorned — no extra straps, no pouch, no ribbon at the throat.

Use a cool night palette with one hot core and strict area control.
