Begin at the bottom edge with the snow and her planted left heel, then the raised right heel hanging beside her left calf, then the crossing point where the right ankle rests on the left knee, then the snow cap of the plinth, then the black train spreading over the stone, then her two hands, then her face and the eyes looking straight into the lens, then the falling snow above her head. Each step must sit a little higher and a little cooler than the one before, and the crossing of the legs must read as the hinge of the whole composition.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is no chair, no bench, no throne, no cushion, no footstool, no carpet, no suitcase, no trolley, no lamp post, no timetable board, no train, no bird, no tree on the platform, no litter and no debris — nothing on the platform but the one plinth, the snow, one leaning sign, the rails and her own two feet, one planted and one raised.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the raised right heel hanging beside her planted calf, and the crossing point at her left knee. Middle ground: the planted left heel, the snow cap of the plinth and the black train. Background: her upright shoulders, her loose hair, the leaning sign and the rusted rail at the far edge. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur, and let the one bright value sit overhead as falling snow rather than on a surface.

Light the platform from the flat white sky and from nothing else. One wide soft cold light comes down through the falling snow, lights the top of her head, both shoulders, the snow cap and the raised sole, and leaves the underside of the plinth and the front of her legs in a dim grey-blue value that still holds shape. Her eyes must stay readable inside that dim value, never a black silhouette, and her straight gaze must stay clear. Never introduce a front fill, never add a second source, never brighten the platform evenly and never let the snow light flare into a sunbeam. Let the snow hold no reflected face and no mirrored body anywhere in it.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails fall behind both shoulders as she sits. The nearer tail drops along her right arm and stops at the snow beside her hip; the farther one hangs straight down the front face of the plinth and ends in the dim below. Let the falling snow break into small pale flecks where it crosses each tail and let the tips stay dark so the silhouette closes. Keep both tails clear of the raised heel and clear of the train's folded edge.

Dress her in one black evening gown cut to the floor: a fitted bodice closed high at the collarbone, narrow shoulder straps, an open back, long elbow-length gloves in matte black, and one train of the same satin that spreads across the snow behind her hips. Her legs wear fine black tights scattered with tiny silver points that hold the cold light as one fine dusting, and one pair of black patent high heels with a slim tapered heel and an open toe. Keep every seam, hem and fastening visible so the cloth reads as real tailoring rather than costume, and keep the train narrow enough that neither heel is hidden by it.

Use a grey-blue-and-snow palette with strict area control. Approximately forty percent of the image is the flat white platform and the falling snow, twenty percent is the pale limestone where the sky light reaches the plinth, sixteen percent is the black satin of the gown, eight percent is the black mesh of the tights with its silver points, six percent is the rusted rail and the leaning sign, five percent is her loose hair, four percent is the snow cap and the drift across her shoulders, and one percent is the bright edge of the raised sole. Keep every bright note in the snow, her hair and the silver points, and let the whole frame stay in cool grey with no warm colour anywhere.

Drive the printed graphic language from the falling snow rather than from decoration. Let one vertical band of cold blue ink run down the frame's right edge from the top to the plinth, printed flat and matte and dissolved at its lower end into a scatter of fine dots. Add one horizontal band of pale grey ink across the snow at the base of the plinth, and let a fine dot field stand in for the snow in the upper third of the frame. Keep every graphic element square to the frame, keep all of them behind the figure rather than over her, and let no dot pattern touch her face.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable words "SILENT SNOW" once, in thin pale gold leaf pressed flat into the fresh snow along the front edge of the plinth, so the letters read as clean gold strokes with a fine raised lip of snow along each edge, spanning about a third of that strip and level with the frame so they read clearly at thumbnail size. Put no lettering on the plinth, the gown, the gloves or her heels, and put no other letters anywhere in the image. Keep the words clear of her planted heel and clear of the train's hem.

Let every surface carry the shift. The snow cap of the plinth is thinner where her hand has rested and thicker at the chipped corner; the satin is pressed flat where her hips rest and creased once where the right ankle crosses the left knee; the patent of the raised heel holds one fine scuff along its sole edge while the planted heel's sole stays clean; the platform concrete holds one long crack under the snow and the sign leans a few degrees off true. Keep the wear physical and directional, all of it running the same way as the falling snow.

Build a second composition through the empty platform. The snow field carries the scene as one even horizontal tone, the rail as one dark line at the far edge, and the flat sky as one pale void that carries no figure, no face and no reflected body. Let that field stay a tone rather than an image, and let it be broken only where the falling snow thickens behind her shoulder.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One narrow silver clasp at her right wrist where the glove meets the cuff, a single thread pulled from the train's hem, one fine bright line along the raised sole edge, and one hairline crack across the stone at her planted left heel. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where use would put it, and keep no more than four such points in the whole frame.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the raised right heel hanging beside her planted calf and the crossing point at her left knee. Second: the planted left heel and the snow-covered platform. Third: the snow cap of the plinth and the black train. Fourth: her upright shoulders and her loose hair. Fifth: the leaning sign, the rusted rail and the flat white sky. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each, and let no layer borrow an edge from the one behind it.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every stone edge and every heel edge, restrained risograph grain in the cold concrete, crisp flat fills in the black satin, and one clean gradient only inside the falling snow. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the slim gleam along the raised sole. Let the snow read as printed dots rather than photographic noise.

No second character, no duplicate figure, no crowd, no passenger, no chair, no bench, no throne, no cushion, no footstool, no suitcase, no trolley, no litter, no extra pair of legs, no third leg, no third heel, no third foot, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no foot resting on the plinth, no both feet on the plinth, no leg folded sideways on the plinth, no skirt covering her shins, no long skirt hiding the raised leg, no skirt across her lap, no fabric between her legs and the camera, no dress covering her knees, no crossed shins, no shin passing horizontally in front of the other, no pair of raised heels, no heel resting on the ground other than the planted left heel, no leg tucked underneath the body, no knee drawn up to the chest, no crouching, no squatting, no kneeling, no standing, no jump, no foot lifted above the knee, no sole turned toward the lens, no camera above her head, no view from above, no overhead shot, no bright sun, no even daylight, no front fill, no second light source, no train, no sceptre, no orb, no crown, no banner, no glyphs, no readable text beyond the words named above, no mirror, no polished reflection, no falling ice, no bird, no wing, no halo, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like a platform where the timetable has stopped mattering: one figure sitting upright on the snow-capped stone, looking level into the lens, one heel planted in the fresh snow and one heel hanging beside the planted calf with the sole facing down, a black train spread over the plinth, and fine snow falling steadily between her face and the lens.

seeds.title: CROWN
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled "CROWN", featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character seen from a low close angle, seated on one carved high-backed throne in a near-black stone hall, looking down at the lens with one boot lifted clear of the floor and resting across the opposite knee, and one pointed gold crown on her head. The low view makes the throne and the crowned figure loom over the viewer. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep the short gold hair, the green eyes, the blue-and-white armoured dress, the single gold crown and the one raised boot readable in the hard light rising from below.

The throne is one tall solid mass of pale carved stone, and the crown is one single object of gold. Its back rises well above her shoulders into one pointed crest and runs out of the top edge of the frame, its seat is broad and flat, and both armrests belong to the same one throne rather than to two chairs. One single pointed gold crown sits squarely on top of her head, its band closed and unbroken, its spire rising clear of her hair. The hall behind holds one bare wall of repeated shallow vertical flutes, most of it falling away into darkness, and nothing else.

Use a low camera placed close to the front edge of the throne, one step above the floor, tilted up about thirty degrees, with a slightly wide lens so the near knee and the lifted boot loom large in the foreground and the tall throne back runs out of the top edge of the tall frame. Set the camera square to the throne on a three-quarter front view so her face, her chest and the fronts of both legs stay open to the low lens. Keep both legs, the planted boot and the raised boot inside the frame, and let the stone floor run as one low thin strip across the bottom edge. Write the low angle as a physical fact rather than a mood: the camera sits a full step below the seat and looks upward at the underside of her jaw, the sole of the raised boot and the carved crest above her. Never place the camera at her eye height and never look down on her.

Give Miku exactly one core action: sitting enthroned with her right leg crossed over her left. Her hips rest fully on the seat, her back touches the tall throne back, and her torso stays upright. Her right ankle lies across her left knee, so her right boot is lifted clear of the floor and hangs in the air with a visible gap of empty air beneath its sole, its toe tipped down toward the low lens and its sole turned partly toward the camera. Her left boot is planted flat on the floor directly beneath her left knee and it is the only boot touching the floor. The crossing point where her right ankle rests on her left knee is the clearest joint in the whole figure: two shins, one passing over the other, one boot raised and one boot planted, with the raised shin running diagonally across the planted shin. Both legs read as two separate legs, neither leg is folded underneath her, and no part of the raised boot touches the floor or the throne. She is seated, not crouching, not squatting, not kneeling and not standing; her weight stays on the throne and neither knee is drawn up toward her chest. Her short gold hair carries one upright strand, her face is turned to the lens, both her eyes are visible and she looks down at the low camera, and one pointed gold crown sits squarely on her head above the hair. Both hands rest open on the two armrests with the fingers relaxed; nothing is held in either hand. Keep both arms inside the frame.

Construct the dominant visual object as the throne, the crown and the crossed legs: one high-backed carved stone throne with a single column of repeating shallow flutes running up its back, one carved vine band along its crest, one pointed gold crown with a single tall central spire, one deep crimson mantle falling from both shoulders, and one pair of legs crossing at the knee with the raised boot hanging in the near foreground. Let the raised boot and the crossing point be the largest and nearest thing in the frame, larger than her hands and larger than the crown. Let the flutes be the only repeating structure in the frame and let the crown's spire be its single exception. Keep the seat plain and let the wall on either side stay bare and dark.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. the throne is pale limestone, matte and faintly gritty so each carved flute holds one even tone; the crown is one solid piece of dull gold with a single bright edge along its spire; the mantle is heavy crimson velvet, dense and light-absorbing; the armoured dress is white panels over deep blue cloth with fine silver trim; her boots are soft dark leather to the knee; the floor is pale stone under one thin even layer of dust; the wall is bare limestone lost in shadow at the corners. Each behaves differently — limestone returns one flat tone, dull gold holds one narrow highlight, velvet reads as a dense matte plane with one crisp folded edge, blue cloth shows a dry woven grain, leather carries one slim gleam along the raised sole, dusty stone is a soft even field, shadowed walls hold a faint fine grit. Keep the whole frame matte and let no surface act as a mirror.

Build a stepped sequence across the frame. Begin at the bottom edge with the thin pale floor and her planted left boot, then the raised right boot hanging in the air with a clear gap beneath its sole, then the crossing point where the right ankle rests on the left knee, then the crimson mantle spreading over the seat, then her two open hands on the armrests, then the short gold hair and the green eyes looking down, then the gold crown and the carved crest running out of the top edge. Each step must sit a little higher and a little darker than the one before, and the crossing of the legs must read as the hinge of the whole composition.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is no second throne, no second crown, no second chair, no attendant, no courtier, no guard, no banner, no flag, no sceptre, no orb, no cushion, no footstool, no carpet, no candle, no plant and no debris — nothing in the hall but the one throne, the thin floor, the dark wall and her own two boots, one planted and one raised. Keep the whole right side of the wall bare so the carved flutes are the only break in the stone.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the raised right boot hanging in the air, its sole toward the lens, and the crossing point at her left knee. Middle ground: the planted left boot, the crimson mantle, her hands and the two armrests. Background: the tall carved throne back running out of the frame, the gold crown and the dark fluted wall. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur, and let the one bright value sit low and from below so the crown and the pale hair read against near-black stone.

Light the scene from one tall side window set low in the wall and from nothing else. One hard cold white light rises from below and slightly to her right: it lifts the underside of her jaw, the sole of the raised boot, the fronts of both knees and the blue panels of her dress from below, throws one long hard shadow up the carved throne back, and leaves everything more than a hand's width from that line in near black. Her eyes must stay readable in the low light, never a black silhouette, and her downward gaze must stay clear. Never introduce a front fill, never add a second source and never brighten the hall evenly. Let the stone hold no reflected face and no mirrored body anywhere in it, and let the dull gold of the crown return one narrow edge rather than a glow.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails fall behind both shoulders as she sits. The nearer tail drops along her right arm and stops at the armrest; the farther one hangs straight down into the dark behind the throne. Let the low window's light rim each tail from below and let the tip near her sleeve catch one cool reflection. Keep both tails clear of the crown's upright spire and clear of the mantle's folded edge.

Dress Miku in her canonical blue-and-white armoured dress, not a gown and not modern clothing. A blue skirt with white panels falling to the knee, a fitted white bodice with silver trim, long white sleeves with one blue cuff at each wrist, and soft dark leather boots to the knee. Add one deep crimson mantle fastened at both shoulders and falling open over the seat and across her lap, wide enough to frame the crossed legs and to leave the raised boot, its sole and the air gap beneath it fully visible. Add one pointed gold crown, a low closed band with a single tall central spire, resting squarely on top of her short gold hair. Keep the silhouette upright, seated and fully supported by the throne, and let the mantle's hem stop above the floor so no fold hides the planted boot or crosses a printed edge.

Use a gold-on-crimson palette with strict area control. Approximately forty-two percent of the image is the near-black shadowed hall and the unlit throne, sixteen percent is the pale limestone where the low light reaches the carved back, eighteen percent is the deep crimson mantle, ten percent is the blue-and-white armoured dress, six percent is her short gold hair, three percent is the dark leather of the two boots, three percent is the thin pale floor strip, and two percent is the gold crown and its one bright edge. Keep every bright note in the crown, the pale hair, the raised sole and the one low light. The dull gold of the crown is the one high-value colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated and let the near-black field do the oppressive work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the throne's own carved marks rather than from decoration. Let one large deep-crimson ink bloom spread across the shadowed wall in the upper right, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular ochre panel across the thin floor strip at the throne's base as a graphic mask, and let one vertical strip of dull gold run down the frame's left edge from top to floor. Keep every graphic element square to the frame, and keep all three behind the figure rather than over her.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word "CROWN" once, in gold leaf stamped across the flat stone panel of the throne back directly behind her shoulders and level with her collar, the leaf chipped where the stone has worn, sized so it spans about half the panel's visible width and reads clearly at thumbnail size. Put no lettering on the dress, the mantle, the crown, the floor or her boots, and put no other letters anywhere in the image. Keep the word level with the frame, inside the visible lower part of the throne back, and clear of the crown's spire.

Let every surface carry the shift. The limestone is worn along the front edge of the seat and bright only where the low light reaches the flutes; the crown's band holds one shallow scratch where a hand would have set it straight; the velvet is pressed flat where her hips rest and creased once where the right ankle crosses the left knee; the silver trim is grey along the lower fold of the skirt; the raised boot's sole is scuffed along one edge and the planted boot's sole is clean; the carved vine band is chipped at its left end. Keep the wear physical and directional, all of it running the same way as the low light.

Build a second composition through the carved wall. The flutes carry the hall as one even field of narrow vertical tones, the vine band as one dark horizontal line, and the tall low window as one pale interruption that carries no figure, no face and no reflected body. Let that field stay a tone rather than an image, and let it be broken only where the long shadow climbs the throne back.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One narrow silver cuff at her right wrist, a single thread pulled from the mantle's hem, one fine bright line along the crown's spire, and one hairline crack across the stone at her planted left boot. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where use would put it, and keep no more than four such points in the whole frame.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the raised right boot hanging in the air and the crossing point at her left knee. Second: the planted left boot and the thin pale floor. Third: the crossed legs, the crimson mantle and her two hands on the armrests. Fourth: the short gold hair, the downward green eyes and the gold crown. Fifth: the carved throne back running out of the top edge and the dark fluted wall. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each, and let no layer borrow an edge from the one behind it.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every carved flute and crown point, restrained risograph grain in the shadowed stone, crisp flat fills in the crimson mantle, and one clean gradient only along the tall window's light. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the crown's one narrow edge. Let the carving read as printed texture rather than photographic noise.

No second character, no duplicate figure, no crowd, no attendant, no courtier, no reflected figure, no mirrored body, no second throne, no second crown, no second chair, no extra pair of legs, no third leg, no third boot, no third foot, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no pair of raised boots, no duplicate boot, no boot resting on the floor other than the planted left boot, no leg tucked underneath the body, no knee drawn up to the chest, no crouching, no squatting, no kneeling, no standing, no perching on the armrest, no jump, no high camera, no view from above, no overhead shot, no level eye-height camera, no camera looking down at her, no bright white hall, no even daylight, no front fill, no second light source, no sceptre, no orb, no banner, no candle, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no readable text beyond the string named above, no mirror, no polished floor reflection, no light wall, no large face in the background, no birds, no wings, no halo, no duplicated crown spire, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like one held breath under a throne: a crowned figure looming over a low lens, looking down, one boot planted on the stone and one boot held in the air across the opposite knee with a gap of air beneath its sole, a crimson mantle spread across the dark seat, and the carved back running out of the top of the frame.

seeds.title: SEVENTH
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “SEVENTH”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing upright behind a long wooden bar in an empty tavern, turned three-quarters back toward the viewer and perfectly still. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her long dark brown hair, her warm brown eyes, the white sleeveless top, the dark short skirt and the dark red boots readable in the bar's one warm light.

The bar is one long plain wooden counter with four equal stools along its near side and one empty stool at the end. Its light is warm pale amber, the brightest value anywhere in the frame, and each stool reads as one hard dark shape rather than as a soft blur.

Use a camera at her chest height on a normal lens, perfectly level and set back a few paces, so she stands at approximately fifty percent of the canvas width at her full standing height with a clear margin of dark wall on both sides. Let the counter's front edge cut one straight horizontal line across the lower third and let one plain dark shelf run behind her. Keep the camera level rather than low so the floor stays beneath her boots.

Give Miku exactly one core action: standing and looking back. Her long dark brown hair falls past her shoulders, her warm brown eyes look straight toward the lens, and both hands hang open at her sides with the fingers relaxed. Both knees are straight and locked, no knee is lifted, her weight is even on both feet, and her shoulders are turned three-quarters toward the viewer. Keep both arms inside the frame, put nothing in either hand, and keep the counter top completely bare.

Construct the dominant visual object as the counter and the stools: one long wooden counter with a straight front edge, four equal dark stools along its near side, and one fifth stool pulled out and empty at the end. Let the stools be the only repeating structure and the empty one its single exception. Keep the shelf behind her as one plain dark plane with no bottles, no glasses and no objects on it.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. the counter is dark varnished oak with a dry grain and one pale worn edge; the stools are dark painted wood with a chipped seat each; the white sleeveless top is dense matte cotton; the dark short skirt is heavy woven cloth; the dark red boots are soft leather; her long dark brown hair holds one fine even strand; the shelf behind is a near-black flat plane; the wall is dark plaster with a faint grain. Each behaves differently — varnished oak takes one narrow warm highlight and one broad matte plane, painted wood absorbs light with one chip, white cotton stays crisp and matte, woven cloth reads as a dense dark plane, leather shows one narrow shine, hair reads as fine parallel marks, the shelf stays a flat void, plaster holds a soft even tone.

Build a stepped sequence across the frame. Begin at the lower left with the nearest dark stool and the counter's front edge, then the second, third and fourth stools, then the empty fifth stool, then her white top and dark skirt behind the counter, then her warm brown eyes and long dark hair, then the plain dark shelf and the wall. The sequence must read as a quiet moment after closing, not as a portrait pose, and each step must sit a little higher and a little paler than the one before.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is no second character, no customer, no glass, no bottle, no cup, no mug, no coaster, no sign, no menu, no clock, no lamp shape and no reflected figure — nothing on the counter and nothing on the shelf. Keep the whole right half of the wall bare so the empty stool is the only break in the row.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the four dark stools and the counter's front edge. Middle ground: the bare counter top, her white top and the dark skirt. Background: her face, the long dark hair, the plain shelf and the dark wall. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur, and let the brightest value sit behind her so the white top reads as one clean shape.

Light the scene from one warm source and from nothing else. A single pale amber light from behind the bar is the key: it rims her dark hair, her shoulders and the counter's worn edge, throws one narrow warm band along the wood, and leaves her face lit only by a soft even return from that same light. Let the four stools fall into a dark even tone and let the frame's near corners stay dark. Never introduce a front fill, never add a ceiling lamp and never add a second source. Keep the shelf one flat dark plane with no glow.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails fall behind both shoulders as she turns. The nearer tail drops along her left arm and stops at her wrist; the farther one hangs straight down into the dark behind her. Let the warm light rim each tail and let the tip near her sleeve catch one pale reflection. Keep both tails clear of the white top so that bright plane stays unbroken.

Dress Miku in her canonical white top and dark skirt, not armour and not a coat. A white sleeveless cotton top with a plain round neck, a dark short skirt falling above the knee, a narrow dark belt, and dark red soft leather boots. Keep the palette strictly white, dark brown, dark red and warm amber, and keep the silhouette long, straight and fully upright. Let the skirt's hem stop above the counter's front edge so the pale wood line never crosses a printed fold.

Use a warm-on-dark palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty-four percent of the image is the dark wall and the plain shelf, twenty-two percent is the four dark stools, eighteen percent is the wooden counter and its warm band, eleven percent is the white sleeveless top, six percent is her long dark brown hair, four percent is the dark skirt and belt, three percent is her face and hands, and two percent is the dark red boots and the empty stool's bright edge. Keep every bright note in the white top and the counter's worn edge. The warm pale amber of the single light is the one high-value colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single value does all the contrast work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the tavern's own marks rather than from decoration. Let one large deep-teal ink bloom spread across the dark wall in the upper right, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular ochre panel across the counter's front edge at her waist as a graphic mask, and let one vertical strip of rust-red run down the frame's left edge from wall to stool. Keep every graphic element square to the frame, and keep all three behind the figure rather than over her.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “SEVENTH” once, in pale paint stencilled across the counter's front edge beneath her hands, the strokes chipped where the varnish has worn, sized so it spans about half the edge's visible width and reads clearly at thumbnail size. Put no lettering on the top, the skirt, the stools or the shelf, and put no other letters anywhere in the image. Keep the word level with the frame and clear of the counter's worn edge.

Let every surface carry the shift. The counter's varnish is worn along one long strip; the nearest stool's seat is chipped at one corner; the empty fifth stool is pulled a hand's width out of line; the white top's hem is faintly frayed at one side; one boot carries a pale scuff at its toe; the belt is flattened where a hand would have rested. Keep the wear physical and directional, all of it running the same way as the counter.

Build a second composition through the dark shelf. The flat plane holds the warm light as one even pale band and the wall as one dark field. It carries no figure, no face, no reflected body and no bottle shape. Let that field stay a tone rather than an image, and let it be broken only where the ink bloom sits in the upper right.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One narrow dark belt at her waist, a single thread pulled from the white top's hem, one fine bright chip in the counter's worn edge, and one hairline crack across the nearest stool's seat. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where use would put it, and keep no more than four such points in the whole frame.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the four dark stools and the counter's front edge. Second: the bare counter top and the empty fifth stool. Third: her white top and the dark skirt. Fourth: her face and the long dark brown hair. Fifth: the plain dark shelf and the wall. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each, and let no layer borrow an edge from the one behind it.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every stool and wood grain, restrained risograph grain in the dark wall, crisp flat fills in the white top, and one clean gradient only along the counter's warm band. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the varnished edge and the eye. Let the wood grain read as printed texture rather than photographic noise.

No second character, no duplicate figure, no crowd, no customer, no glass, no bottle, no cup, no mug, no coaster, no sign, no menu, no clock, no lamp, no reflected figure, no mirrored body, no birds, no wings, no halo, no second bar, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no readable text beyond the string named above, no blood, no wounds, no armour plates, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no lifted knee, no bent knee, no kneeling, no crouching, no jump, no umbrella, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like one quiet moment after closing: a white top behind a bare wooden counter, four dark stools in a row with one pulled out, and a whole tavern gone still around her.

seeds.title: TEMPLE
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “TEMPLE”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing upright at the top of a long stone stair inside an old temple hall, perfectly still with both arms hanging at her sides. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her long gold hair, her pointed ears, her green eyes, the white princess gown with gold trim and the pale gold clasp at her waist readable in the temple's one shaft of light.

The hall is one long perspective of paired stone columns and one round opening high above. Its light is cold white, the brightest value anywhere in the frame, and each column reads as one hard vertical bar rather than as a soft blur.

Use a camera at her chest height on a normal lens, perfectly level and set back down the stair, so she stands at the frame's centre at her full standing height with a clear margin of dark wall on both sides. Place her at approximately fifty percent of the canvas width, occupying about sixty percent of the frame height. Let six stone steps descend toward the lens and let two rows of three columns recede behind her. Keep the camera level rather than low so the steps stay beneath her boots.

Give Miku exactly one core action: standing still at the top of the stair. Her long gold hair falls past her shoulders, one pointed ear shows clearly beside her cheek, her green eyes look straight toward the lens, and both hands hang open at her sides with the fingers relaxed. Both knees are straight and locked, no knee is lifted, her weight is even on both feet, and her shoulders are square to the camera. Keep both arms inside the frame and put nothing in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the stair and the colonnade: six equal stone steps with one shallow worn hollow in the fourth, two rows of three identical square columns, and one broken column at the end of the right row. Let the steps be the only repeating horizontal structure and the columns the only repeating vertical one. Keep one round opening high in the far wall as the single source of light.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. the steps are pale limestone with a dry grain and one worn hollow; the columns are squared pale stone with a chipped corner each; the white princess gown is heavy matte silk with a narrow gold trim; the pale gold clasp at her waist takes one crisp highlight; her long gold hair holds one fine even strand; the far wall is dark rough masonry; the shaft of light is one flat pale wedge with no dust in it. Each behaves differently — limestone returns one hard pale edge and one soft plane, squared stone holds a dry grain with one chip, matte silk stays a broad even plane, gold takes one crisp line, hair reads as fine parallel marks, rough masonry absorbs the light, the shaft stays a printed tone rather than a beam with volume.

Build a stepped sequence across the frame. Begin at the lower left with the nearest step and its worn hollow, then the second and third steps, then her two boots and the hem of the white gown, then her hanging hands and the gold clasp, then her green eyes, pointed ear and gold hair, then the paired columns and the round opening high behind her. The sequence must read as an arrival at the end of a long climb, not as a portrait pose, and each step must sit a little higher and a little paler than the one before.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is no second character, no distant small figure, no statue, no altar, no candle, no torch, no banner, no inscription, no glyph and no offering — nothing in the hall but the six steps, the six columns, the broken one and her own two boots. Keep the whole right side of the far wall bare so the broken column is the only break in the colonnade.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the nearest steps and their worn hollow. Middle ground: her boots, her hanging hands and the white gown. Background: her face, the paired columns, the dark wall and the round opening. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur, and let the brightest value sit high behind her so the gold hair reads as a clean silhouette.

Light the scene from the round opening and from nothing else. One cold white shaft from high in the far wall is the key: it falls as one hard-edged wedge across the top step and her shoulders, rims her gold hair and the gown's gold trim, and leaves her face lit only by a soft even return from that same light. Let the lower steps fall into a dark even tone and let the frame's near corners stay dark. Never introduce a front fill, never add a torch and never add a second source. Let the shaft stay one flat wedge with no dust, no halo and no volumetric haze.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails fall behind both shoulders as she stands. The nearer tail drops along her left arm and stops at her wrist; the farther one hangs straight down into the white gown behind her. Let the shaft's light rim each tail and let the tip near her sleeve catch one pale reflection. Keep both tails clear of the gold clasp so that narrow line stays unbroken.

Dress Miku in her canonical white princess gown, not armour and not a cloak. A long white silk gown with a narrow gold trim at the hem and sleeves, a fitted pale bodice with one pale gold clasp at the waist, soft white sleeves falling to the wrist, and pale leather shoes. Keep the palette strictly white, pale gold and gold hair, and keep the silhouette long, straight and fully upright. Let the gown's hem stop above the top step so the shaft's bright edge never crosses a printed fold.

Use a cold-on-dark palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty-four percent of the image is the dark wall and the shadowed colonnade, twenty-two percent is the pale limestone steps, eighteen percent is the white princess gown, eleven percent is the cold shaft of light, six percent is her gold hair, four percent is the paired columns' lit edges, three percent is her face and hands, and two percent is the gold trim and the waist clasp. Keep every bright note in the shaft and the white gown. The cold white of the shaft is the one high-value colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single value does all the contrast work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the hall's own marks rather than from decoration. Let one large deep-teal ink bloom spread across the dark far wall in the upper right, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular ochre panel across the nearest step at her boots as a graphic mask, and let one vertical strip of rust-red run down the frame's left edge from wall to stair. Keep every graphic element square to the frame, and keep all three behind the figure rather than over her.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “TEMPLE” once, in dark paint stencilled across the stone lintel above the round opening, the strokes chipped where the masonry has worn, sized so it spans about half the lintel's visible width and reads clearly at thumbnail size. Put no lettering on the gown, the steps or the columns, and put no other letters anywhere in the image. Keep the word level with the frame and clear of the opening's bright edge.

Let every surface carry the shift. The fourth step holds one shallow worn hollow; the nearest column is chipped at one corner; the broken column ends in one clean flat cut; the gown's gold trim is flattened at one sleeve; one shoe carries a pale scuff at its toe; the shaft's edge stops in a straight line at the step's nosing. Keep the wear physical and directional, all of it running the same way as the stair.

Build a second composition through the pale steps. The limestone holds the shaft as one even pale wedge and the columns as six dark vertical marks. It carries no figure, no face, no reflected body and no distant small person. Let that field stay a tone rather than an image, and let it be broken only where the ink bloom sits in the upper right.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One pale gold clasp at the waist, a single thread pulled from the gown's gold trim, one fine bright chip in the broken column's cut, and one hairline crack across the nearest step. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where use would put it, and keep no more than four such points in the whole frame.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the nearest steps and their worn hollow. Second: her boots and the gown's hem. Third: her hanging hands and the pale bodice. Fourth: her face, pointed ear and gold hair. Fifth: the paired columns, the dark wall and the round opening. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each, and let no layer borrow an edge from the one behind it.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every step nosing and column chip, restrained risograph grain in the dark wall, crisp flat fills in the pale limestone, and one clean gradient only along the shaft's wedge. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the gold clasp and her eye. Let the masonry read as printed texture rather than photographic noise.

No second character, no duplicate figure, no crowd, no distant small figure, no background person, no statue, no altar, no candle, no torch, no banner, no inscription, no glyphs, no symbols, no readable text beyond the string named above, no blood, no wounds, no armour plates, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no lifted knee, no bent knee, no kneeling, no crouching, no jump, no umbrella, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like the last step of a long climb: a white gown standing straight under one cold shaft of light, six stone steps falling dark toward the lens, and a whole empty hall gone quiet behind her.

seeds.title: BALCONY
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “BALCONY”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing on a small hotel balcony overlooking the sea, both forearms resting on the railing and a white curtain blowing out through the open door behind her. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the pale sea.

Use a camera at chest height on a normal lens, set inside the room's doorway and square to the balcony, so the railing runs level across the middle of the frame, the sea fills the upper half beyond it, and the doorframe closes the sides. Place Miku at approximately fifty percent of the canvas width, visible from her waist up in three-quarter figure, occupying about fifty-six percent of the frame height, with her back to the room and her face turned a quarter toward the water.

Give Miku exactly one core action. She stands with her weight on one hip and both forearms resting on the top of the railing, her hands loosely clasped in front of her, her chin lifted and her head turned a quarter toward the sea. Her eyes come back over her shoulder to the lens, and nothing is in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the balcony itself: a low parapet of painted steel tube in faded white, a floor of small square tiles with a drain slot, a pair of folding chairs stacked against the wall, and a single potted plant with dry leaves at the corner. Let the railing occupy the middle band and let the sea beyond it read as one flat plane ending in a pale line.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The railing tube is painted steel, chalky white with rust at its joints and a worn bright patch where hands have rested; the floor tiles are small and pale with dark grout and a steel drain; the wall is rendered concrete with a stain under the sill; the curtain is thin cotton, sunlit and translucent; the sea is a flat grey-blue plane with a slow swell; the chairs are aluminium with faded webbing. Each behaves differently — chalky paint scatters light, glaze holds a small sheen, concrete goes matte, thin cotton glows, water returns a broad dull reflection.

Build a stepped sequence from the floor upward. Begin with the tiled floor and its drain, then the stacked chairs and the plant's dry leaves, then her forearms and clasped hands on the railing, then the railing's top tube and its worn patch, then her turned face, then the sea's flat plane and its pale horizon, then the sky and the blowing curtain's edge. The sequence must read as a rented room's balcony in the afternoon, not as a resort advertisement.

Leave one deliberate absence. The balcony is otherwise bare: no drinks on the railing, no towels over the rail, no ashtray, no one on the neighbouring balconies within the frame. The only objects besides her are the two stacked chairs, the one plant and the curtain.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the tiled floor, the drain, the stacked chairs. Middle ground: Miku, her forearms, the railing's top tube. Background: the sea, its pale horizon, the sky and the curtain blowing in from the door. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the sea side in the afternoon. The sea and sky are the key: a broad cool wash from in front of her, lifting her face, the front of her blouse and the railing's chalky tube. Add one warm bounce from the tiled floor, which touches her wrists and the underside of her chin, and let the room behind her stay in shade. Keep the doorway's interior at near-black.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the two sources. Both tails lift and stream toward the room, blown by the wind off the water, one clean aqua mass lit cool along its outer curve and warmed at its underside by the floor. Let the ends tangle slightly with the curtain's edge so hair and cloth read as two different weights in the same wind.

Dress Miku in an original balcony costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not resort wear. A loose pale blouse with the sleeves rolled and the collar open over a dark camisole, a dark mid-length skirt below the frame line, and thin bare arms; no jewellery. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment, and keep the silhouette quiet so the railing line reads clearly.

Use a pale-white-and-sea palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty-two percent of the image is the flat sea and its horizon, twenty-two percent is the pale sky and the sunlit curtain, eighteen percent is the chalky railing and its shadow, twelve percent is the tiled floor, eight percent is her pale blouse and dark skirt, five percent is her aqua hair, and three percent is the rust at the railing's joints.

Drive the printed graphic language from the balcony's own tiles rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the tiled floor at the lower left, printed flat and matte, its edge following a grout line. Add a rectangular pale panel on the rendered wall beside the door as a graphic mask at the height of her shoulder, and let one vertical strip of deep oxide red run down that wall aligned to the doorframe. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “BALCONY” once, large, in pale grey paint applied across the flat rendered wall beside the door, spanning about half the wall's width, in heavy condensed capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “ROOM 5” sit on a small enamel plate screwed to the doorframe at hip height. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the salt air. The railing is chalky on its top and rusted at every joint, with one bright patch worn by hands; the tiles are paler where the sun reaches and grey along the drain; the wall has a stain under the sill and a hairline crack beside the door; the chairs' webbing is faded in stripes; the plant's leaves are dry at their tips; her blouse keeps a soft crease across the elbow. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the window glass beside the door. The pane carries the sea as one flat band, the railing as a thin white line and her shoulder as a soft shape, all with a faint double edge where the glass is old. Let the reflection be weaker than the sea itself and stop at the frame's edge.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. Two folding chairs stacked against the wall; one potted plant with dry leaf tips; a steel drain slot set in the tiles; a rusted bracket at the railing's joint; a folded towel on the nearest chair's seat. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a small hotel balcony would actually have it.

Illuminate with the sea's cool wash as the only key and the tiled floor's bounce as the only fill. Let the sea lift her face and the front of her blouse, let the floor warm her wrists and the underside of her chin, and keep the room behind her at absolute black so she reads as a figure standing in a bright rectangle.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the tiled floor and the drain. Second: the stacked chairs and the plant. Third: her forearms and clasped hands on the railing. Fourth: her face and the railing's top tube. Fifth: the sea, its horizon and the sky. Separate them by value steps of roughly eleven percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every tile, railing joint and curtain fold, restrained risograph grain in the shaded room, and the sea kept as one flat clean plane.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no guest on a neighbouring balcony, no drinks, no towels over the rail, no birds, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no laundry on a line, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like a room rented for one afternoon: a chalky railing holding two forearms, a flat sea beyond it, and a curtain blowing out past a girl who has not gone back inside yet.

seeds.title: BREAKWATER
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “BREAKWATER”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing on the crest of a concrete breakwater with both hands pressed to the sides of her head against the wind. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the pale concrete and the grey sea behind her.

Use a camera at chest height on a normal lens, set on the breakwater crest a few paces along from her and square to the walkway, so the crest runs as a hard horizontal line across the middle of the frame and the stacked armour units fall away to the right into the water. Place Miku at approximately thirty-four percent of the canvas width, full figure visible from her boots to her hair ornaments, occupying about fifty-two percent of the frame height, standing on the crest with her weight on her front foot.

Give Miku exactly one core action. She stands braced against a steady onshore wind with both palms pressed flat to the sides of her head, holding her hair back from her face, her elbows lifted and her shoulders drawn up. Her chin is dipped a few degrees into the wind and her eyes come up to the lens. Nothing is held in either hand and no second gesture is added.

Construct the dominant visual object as the armour field: a long slope of interlocking concrete units below the crest on the seaward side, each one a squat four-legged block, stacked three deep and running to the far end of the frame, occupying approximately forty-eight percent of the canvas. Their legs interlock into a lattice of holes, and the outermost row is dark and slick where the swell has reached it.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The blocks are dense grey concrete, their upper faces chalky pale and their lower faces stained near-black by the tide line; the crest walkway is a poured slab with an expansion joint every four metres; a low steel handrail runs along the seaward edge, its galvanised coat worn to bright metal along the top; the water beyond is a flat grey-green swell with no breaking crest; the sky is an even overcast sheet. Each behaves differently — chalky concrete scatters light flatly, wet concrete goes two stops darker, worn galvanising keeps one line, the sea returns a broad dull sheen, and the sky stays perfectly even.

Build a sequence from the crest outward and down. Begin at the walkway's expansion joint under her boots. Move to the low rail and the bright wear along its top, then down over the first row of blocks and the dark tide stain across their faces, then along the interlocking lattice where the rows meet, then out to the outermost blocks and the swell beyond. The sequence must read as a defended shore, not as a pile of rubble.

Leave one deliberate absence. Two blocks in the middle row have been displaced, leaving a clean rectangular void about the width of a door in the lattice, its inner faces pale and newly exposed. Keep that void as the sharpest, emptiest shape in the frame, and let the sea show through it without filling it.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the walkway slab and the bright top of the rail. Middle ground: Miku, the first row of blocks and the tide stain. Background: the armour field running to the frame's right edge, the swell and the even sky above.

Light the scene from a low sun behind the overcast, sitting just above the horizon on her left, so the crest is a bright edge and every block's upper face is lit while its seaward face stays dark. Let her face take the flat light with a soft falloff under the jaw, and keep the sea and sky almost equally bright so the armour field reads as the only textured thing in the frame.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the wind. Both tails are blown out to one side and up, lifted clear of her back and pressed sideways by the same gust that her hands are fighting, so they read as two long aqua flags streaming toward the sea. One strand whips across her cheek and another is caught between her fingers. Keep the hair dense around her head and clearly separated from the concrete.

Dress Miku in an original breakwater costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language. Use a cropped windbreaker in pale grey with a high collar and a single zip, a fitted dark layer beneath, dark trousers cut narrow at the ankle, and low rubber-soled boots with a bright steel eyelet at each lace. Add a thin webbing strap across her chest and a narrow band on her right wrist, and let the wind press the jacket flat against her ribs on one side.

Use a pale concrete-and-grey-sea palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty-four percent of the image is the armour field in a narrow range from chalky pale to tide-black. Twenty-two percent is the even sky. Sixteen percent is the open swell. Twelve percent is the crest walkway. Eight percent is her pale jacket and dark trousers. Five percent is the worn steel rail. Less than three percent is the aqua of her hair and the bright eyelets.

Drive the printed graphic language from the blocks' own lattice rather than from decoration. Let one large slate-blue ink bloom bleed across the first row of blocks at the lower right, printed flat and matte, its edge following the line where two rows interlock. Place two hard-edged slate-blue rectangular colour blocks in the sky, one at the height of her shoulder and one low at the frame's left edge, both square to the frame. Add a halftone dot gradient that gathers in the lattice holes and thins across the crest. Cut several clean white knockout strips along the walkway's expansion joints so the concrete appears to pass through the printed layer.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “BREAKWATER” once, large, in pale grey stencil paint on the crest walkway at her feet, spanning about a third of the walkway's visible width and running along the slab rather than across it, in heavy condensed capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “ARM 07” sit stencilled on the front face of the nearest block below the rail. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the sea's work. The walkway is stained in long streaks that run back from the seaward edge; the rail's galvansing is worn bright in one continuous band at hand height and pitted below it; the blocks are chalky on top, salt-stained at mid height and black at the waterline, with one leg chipped to expose coarse aggregate; a thin line of dried seaweed is caught in the lattice. Keep the wear horizontal and tidal.

Build a second composition through the lattice. Behind the blocks, the swell shows through each hole as a small disc of moving grey, and where two rows meet the holes line up into three continuous tunnels of water. Keep that water a set of flat discs only: no reflection of the sky forms a picture, no second figure appears in it, and no face is mirrored.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. The bright steel eyelet on one boot; the webbing strap across her chest; a chipped leg on the nearest block; a single rusted bolt head on the rail post; the fine salt bloom along the rail's underside. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a breakwater would actually show it.

Illuminate with the low sun as the only key and the overcast as the only fill. Let the crest cut a bright line, let the armour field fall away into even shadow, and keep her face a stop brighter than the concrete behind it so both eyes read at thumbnail size.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the walkway slab and the rail. Second: her boots and the first row of blocks. Third: her braced body and lifted elbows. Fourth: the interlocking lattice and the two missing blocks. Fifth: the outer blocks, the swell and the even sky.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: a crisp cel-shaded figure, concrete rendered with flat planes and dry-brush edges, precise drawing of the lattice geometry, and a restrained risograph grain in the shadows. Keep the drawing exact and the sea flat, with no photographic depth of field.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no reflected or mirrored figure in the water, no fisherman, no boat, no gull, no floating interface, no holograms, no glowing particles, no random letters or numbers, no watermark, no signature, no muddy background, no neon, no rainbow lighting, no face obstruction, no hair covering her eyes, no heavy bloom, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, and no malformed hands. Preserve a strict hierarchy: Miku's face first, her hands at her temples second, the missing blocks third, the armour field fourth, then the rail, typography and even sky.

The final image should feel like a shore built to take a beating: one long field of interlocking blocks, one door-sized gap in the lattice, a bright worn rail, and a girl standing on the crest with both hands fighting her own hair.

seeds.title: DUNE
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “DUNE”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing on the crest of a coastal sand dune at dusk, turned half back toward the camera with the sea far behind her. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the pale sky.

Use a camera at chest height on a normal lens, set on the dune's lee side and slightly below her, so the crest runs diagonally from the lower left to the upper right and the sea closes the horizon as a flat band. Place Miku at approximately thirty-eight percent of the canvas width, full figure visible from bare feet to hair ornaments, occupying about forty-four percent of the frame height, standing on the crest line itself.

Give Miku exactly one core action. She stands with her weight on her front foot and her back heel lifted, one hand shading her brow against the last light and the other holding the hem of her skirt down against the wind. Her chin is lifted, her head turned a quarter toward the sea, and her eyes come back over her shoulder to the lens.

Construct the dominant visual object as the dune's face: a long wind-carved slope of pale sand with three sharp ripple lines running across it, a crest that cuts the sky, and a fringe of dry marram grass on the lee side. Let the dune occupy the lower two thirds and let its crest carry her figure almost as a horizon of its own.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The sand is fine and pale, its surface rippled and its grains catching a low warm light; the crest is looser and softer than the slope; the marram grass is dry, thin and bent all one way; the sea beyond is a flat grey-blue sheet with one bright path of reflected light; the sky is a pale washed orange at the horizon turning grey above. Each behaves differently — sand scatters light finely, loose crest blurs its own edge, grass draws thin dark lines, water returns a broad soft sheen, sky goes flat.

Build a stepped sequence from the lower edge upward. Begin with the rippled slope and its three lines, then her bare feet and the sand they have pressed, then her skirt and her bracing hand, then her turned face under a shading hand, then the crest and its grass, then the sea's flat band and its bright path, then the washed sky. The sequence must read as standing on the top of a dune in the last light, not as a beach snapshot.

Leave one deliberate absence. The dune and the beach below are empty: no other walker on the sand, no umbrella, no towel, no footprints but the few she has just made on the crest. The only objects in the frame besides her are the grass and a single bleached marker post leaning out of the sand.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the rippled slope and one wind-cut hollow. Middle ground: her feet, her skirt, her body on the crest. Background: the sea's flat band, its bright path, the pale horizon and the sky above. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the last low sun behind her right shoulder. The sun is the key: a warm rim along her forearm, the edge of her skirt and the crest line, with the dune's face in soft shadow and the ripples lit only on their seaward sides. Add one weak cool fill from the sky to keep her shaded side readable. Keep the sea and the sky bright but flat, and the troughs of the dune at near-black.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the light. Both tails stream sideways in the wind off the water, one clean aqua mass rimmed warm along its upper edge by the sun and cooled underneath by the sky, so they read as two flags lifted off her back. Let one strand whip across her cheek and another lift clear of her shoulder.

Dress Miku in an original dune-walk costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not beachwear. A pale linen shirt with the sleeves rolled and the collar open, a dark calf-length skirt held down at one side, and bare feet with the sand printed on her ankles; a thin cord at her waist. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment, and keep the silhouette loose so the wind can read in it.

Use a pale sand-and-dusk palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty-six percent of the image is the lit sand face, twenty-two percent is the shaded slope and troughs, sixteen percent is the pale sky, twelve percent is the sea's flat band, eight percent is her pale shirt and dark skirt, four percent is her aqua hair, and two percent is the bright path on the water.

Drive the printed graphic language from the dune's own wind marks rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the shaded slope at the lower left, printed flat and matte, its edge following a ripple line. Add a rectangular pale panel on the sky's lower band as a graphic mask at the height of her shoulder, and let one vertical strip of deep oxide red run up from the crest aligned to the marker post. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “DUNE” once, large, in pale grey paint on the flat weathered face of the bleached marker post leaning out of the sand at her right, spanning about half the post's width, in heavy condensed capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “SHORE ROAD” sit on a small enamel plate nailed below the word. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the wind. The sand's ripples are sharp on their windward side and soft on the lee; the crest spills a thin plume that never quite leaves the ground; the grass is bent and split at its tips; the post is bleached grey with its grain raised and its base half buried; her skirt is pressed flat against one leg and lifted off the other; her ankles carry a fine dusting of sand. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the sea's wet sand. A thin sheet of water left by the tide lies along the beach far below, carrying the sky as one pale strip and the sun as a single warm point, its edge scalloped where the last wave stopped.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A single bleached shell on the crest; one footprint already softened by wind; a coil of dry kelp at the slope's foot; the marker post's iron nail; a folded cloth pressed under a stone. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a coastal dune would actually have it.

Approximately thirty percent of the image is the wet sand mirror, twenty-four percent is the sea and its horizon, twenty percent is the pale sky, twelve percent is the foam line, eight percent is her pale shirt and dark skirt, four percent is her aqua hair, and two percent is the warm rim on the foam.

Drive the printed graphic language from the shore's own posts rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the higher dry sand at the lower left, printed flat and matte, its edge following the tide's last line. Add a rectangular pale panel on the sky's lowest band as a graphic mask at the height of her knee, and let one vertical strip of deep oxide red run up from the sand aligned to a leaning post. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “SURF LINE” once, large, in pale grey paint on the flat weathered face of a leaning timber post driven into the dry sand at her right, spanning about half the post's width, in heavy condensed capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “LOW WATER” sit on a small enamel plate nailed below the word. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the tide. The wet sand is smooth and unmarked except for her own footprints and one thin line of grit; the foam is thicker at its centre and thinner at both ends; the dry sand above the line is rippled and holds a scatter of shell grit; the post is split at its top and bleached grey; her skirt's hem keeps a damp line; her ankles are wet to a sharp edge. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the wet sand. The mirror carries the sky as one pale field, the foam as a bright broken line, and her legs as two dark shapes standing in it, and the reflection runs the whole width of the frame until the sand dries. Let her feet break the mirror into two half-rings.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One strand of kelp left at the foam's edge; a single shell fragment in the dry sand; her own footprints leading back toward the frame's edge; a leaning marker post with a split top; a thin line of grit marking the tide's last reach. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a shoreline would actually have it.

Illuminate with the low sun as the only warm key and the wet sand as the only cool fill. Let the sun light the foam's tops, her arm and her cheek, let the sand keep her legs and chin readable, and keep the sea flat and the sky even so the frame reads as one bright band of water and one dark band of beach.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the wet sand mirror. Second: the foam line and her toes. Third: Miku's gathered skirt and open hand. Fourth: her face and the sea's swell. Fifth: the horizon, the pale sky and the leaning post. Separate them by value steps of roughly eleven percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every foam blob and shell fragment, restrained risograph grain in the wet sand, and the sea kept as one flat clean plane.
