seeds.title: TIDE POOL
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “TIDE POOL”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing ankle-deep at the edge of a rock tide pool in the hour of low tide, her head bent down to look into the water and one fingertip just touching its surface. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the pale sky.

Use a camera at hip height on a normal lens, set on the rock shelf slightly to her right and tilted down about fifteen degrees, so the pool fills the lower two thirds as a dark mirror and the low horizon closes the top. Place Miku at approximately forty-four percent of the canvas width, full figure visible from bare feet to hair ornaments, occupying about sixty percent of the frame height. Let her ankles and their reflection meet at the frame's centre.

Give Miku exactly one core action. She stands with her weight on her back foot and bends forward from the waist, her right arm reaching down so one fingertip just breaks the water's surface, while her left hand gathers the hem of her skirt at her hip to keep it clear of the pool. Her eyes are on the ring her fingertip makes, and nothing else is in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the tide pool itself: an irregular basin about two paces across, scoured into dark basalt, its rim stepped in three ledges and its water perfectly still except for the single ring under her finger. Let the water occupy the lower half of the frame and let the pool's far rim hold a skirt of green weed and three white barnacle scars.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The basalt is wet below the tide line and dry and dusty grey above it, its edges rounded by water; the pool's water is clear to the bottom and dark where the rock deepens; the weed is a low mat of olive green, wet and glossy; the barnacles are chalky white rings; her linen shirt is dry and creased; her bare feet are wet to the ankle only. Each behaves differently — wet stone holds a sheen, still water returns an inverted image, weed carries one soft highlight, chalky shell scatters light, dry linen goes matte.

Build a stepped sequence from the bottom edge upward. Begin at the lowest ledge with its weed and barnacles, then the water's surface and the ring under her finger, then her wet ankles and her bare feet, then the gathered hem and her bent waist, then her lowered face, then the pool's far rim, then the pale horizon. The sequence must read as standing inside a low basin looking down into it, not as a beach panorama.

Leave one deliberate absence. The pool holds one creature only: a single small crab standing still on the sand at its bottom, no shells and no weed drifting on the surface. The whole rock shelf beyond the pool is empty of other figures for as far as the frame reaches.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the near ledge, its weed, the water's surface. Middle ground: Miku's feet and ankles, her bent figure, the ring under her fingertip. Background: the pool's far rim, the flat sea beyond it, the pale horizon and one low cloud. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from a low, overcast sky. The sky is the key: a broad soft wash from the horizon side, laying an even silver light on her back, the crown of her head and the water's surface. Add one weak warm bounce from the wet rock at her feet, which touches only the underside of her jaw, her forearms and the hem she holds. Keep the deepest part of the pool and the near ledge at near-black.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the two sources. Both tails fall forward over her shoulders toward the water, one clean aqua mass silvered along its upper curve by the sky and warmed underneath by the rock's bounce, with the two ends hanging clear of the surface by a hand's width. Let one strand slip across her cheek as she bends.

Dress Miku in an original low-tide costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not beachwear. A loose pale linen shirt with the sleeves rolled to the elbow, a short dark skirt gathered in one hand, and a thin woven belt; her feet are bare and the skirt's hem is turned back once. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment, and keep the silhouette loose enough to read at thumbnail size.

Use a cool grey-green palette with one pale note and strict area control. Approximately thirty-four percent of the image is the dark pool and wet basalt, twenty-two percent is the pale overcast sky and horizon, eighteen percent is her linen shirt and hair, twelve percent is the dry upper rock, eight percent is the olive weed and chalky barnacles, four percent is the water's bright ring, and two percent is the warm bounce on her jaw.

Drive the printed graphic language from the shore's own fittings rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the dry upper rock at the lower left, printed flat and matte, its edge following the tide line. Add a rectangular pale panel on the rock's flat face as a graphic mask at the height of her knee, and let one vertical strip of deep oxide red run down from the panel aligned to a crack. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “TIDE POOL” once, large, in pale grey paint on the flat weathered face of a low timber marker post driven into the rock at her right, spanning about half the post's width, in heavy condensed capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “LOW TIDE” sit on a small brass gauge plate screwed to the post below the word. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the tide. The basalt is dark and slick below the waterline and chalky dry above it, with a salt line marking where the water last stood; the weed lies flat in one direction; each barnacle ring is broken on its seaward side; her feet are wet only to the ankle, the skin matte above it; the gathered hem keeps a damp edge where it has brushed the rock. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the pool's still water. The surface carries her face and shoulders inverted as a soft pale shape, the pale sky as one bright band and the far rim as a dark line, and the ring under her fingertip breaks the whole image into two half-moons. Let the reflection stop exactly at the pool's near rim.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One small crab on the pool's sandy bottom; a coil of dry kelp on the upper rock; a single limpet clinging at the waterline; a folded cloth laid on the dry ledge; a rusted iron ring set into the rock where a boat once moored. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a tide shelf would actually have it.

Illuminate with the flat sky as the only broad key and the wet rock's bounce as the only fill. Let the sky silver her back and the water's surface, let the rock warm only the undersides, and keep the pool's deepest corner at absolute black so the single crab reads as a pale mark on darkness.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the near ledge, its weed, the water's surface. Second: her feet and the ring under her fingertip. Third: her bent figure and gathered hem. Fourth: the pool's far rim and the crab below. Fifth: the flat sea, the pale horizon and its one cloud. Separate them by value steps of roughly eleven percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every barnacle ring and basalt edge, restrained risograph grain in the dark fields, and the water drawn as one flat mirror with a single clean ring.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure on the shelf, no swimmer, no boat, no umbrella, no beach towel with a lounger, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scattered shells, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like the sea has stepped back and left one glass dish on the rock: a single ring spreading under her fingertip, her own face hanging upside down in it, and a crab that has not noticed her yet.

seeds.title: CORRIDOR
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 9:16 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “CORRIDOR”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing at the near end of a long narrow apartment corridor, with a single window at the far end throwing her shadow back toward the camera. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the dim interior.

Use a camera at waist height on a normal lens, set dead centre in the corridor so the walls, the floorboards, the ceiling and the far window all converge on one vertical vanishing line. Place Miku at approximately forty-two percent of the canvas width, seen from behind at three-quarter angle, full body visible from slippers to hair ornaments, occupying about forty-six percent of the frame height, standing about four metres from the window. Let the corridor run to the far window so the composition is a narrow room ending in one bright rectangle.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Her right hand rests flat on a door frame at hip height, and her left hand holds a folded towel against her side. Her head is turned back over her shoulder toward the camera, both eyes visible in the dim light. Keep the pose still, the arms close to her body, and put nothing else in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the corridor itself: a narrow passage with four doors on the left and three on the right, a continuous skirting board, a worn timber floor, a ceiling with one bare pendant lamp unlit, and a single sash window at the far end with a pale curtain half drawn. Let the corridor occupy the whole frame, with the far window as its only bright area.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The walls are painted plaster in a faded off-white, scuffed at hip height along both sides; the doors are four-panel timber painted the same off-white, with brass knobs dulled to brown; the skirting is the same paint, chipped at every corner; the floorboards are narrow softwood, worn pale along the centre path and dark at the edges; the window is a timber sash with old glass; the curtain is thin cotton. Each behaves differently — plaster reads flat and slightly uneven, painted timber holds a soft matte value, brass returns one small dull point, worn boards hold a long pale sheen, glass transmits a bright pale field.

Build a stepped sequence down the corridor. Begin at the bottom edge with the near floorboards and one loose board edge, then the first door frame under her hand, then Miku's figure and her shadow, then the second and third doorways, then the far window's bright rectangle, then the pale curtain. The sequence must read as a passage narrowing toward light, not as a symmetrical pattern.

Leave one deliberate absence. One doorway on the right is missing its door entirely: the frame stands empty with the hinges still screwed in place and a clean pale rectangle on the floor where the door has not swung. Keep the opening about a door's width, placed in the middle distance so the empty frame interrupts the corridor's rhythm of closed panels.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: near floorboards, loose board edge, skirting chip. Middle ground: Miku, the first door frame, her shadow. Background: the middle doorways, the far window and curtain. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the far window only. The window is the key: a flat pale daylight entering from the far end, laying a bright pool on the floor at the corridor's end, a soft rim along every door's far edge, and Miku's long shadow stretching toward the camera. Add a faint cool bounce from the floorboards, lifting the shadow side of the near door frames. Keep the near end of the corridor about two stops darker than the far end, and let the ceiling lamp stay completely unlit.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the corridor's light. The nearer tail falls forward over her shoulder in one clean aqua mass, its far edge catching the window's pale rim; the farther tail drops behind her and merges into the dark near end. Let her shadow on the floor separate the two tails into one clean silhouette.

Dress Miku in an original corridor-night costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not pyjamas. A long pale shirt worn loose over the hips, a dark narrow trouser, soft slippers, and a thin cord at her wrist. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment, and keep the silhouette simple enough to read at thumbnail size.

Use a dim-warm palette with one cool bright accent and strict area control. Approximately forty-eight percent of the image is dim off-white plaster and door paint in shadow, twenty percent is the dark near end and floor edges, fourteen percent is the pale daylight at the far window, eight percent is the worn floor's pale centre path, six percent is Miku's pale shirt and aqua hair, and four percent is the dull brass of the knobs. Keep the daylight the only bright value so the far end reads as the destination.

Drive the printed graphic language from the corridor's own architecture rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the lower left of the floor, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular pale panel behind the door frames as a graphic mask at the height of the knobs, and let one vertical strip of dark shadow run from the ceiling to the floor, aligned to a door frame. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “CORRIDOR” once, in dark paint stencilled across the upper panel of the nearest door, worn through at the middle letters, sized so it spans about two thirds of the door's width. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “4 B” sit on a small brass number plate on the nearest door. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the years. The walls are scuffed in a continuous band at hip height where bags have passed; the door's lower panels are darker from hands; the skirting is chipped at every corner and repainted in two slightly different whites; the floorboards are pale along the centre and dark at the walls, with two nails standing proud; the window's paint has failed along its bottom rail. Keep the wear physical and directional, never a uniform grime.

Build a second composition through the floor. The worn boards carry the far window as one long pale rectangle stretched toward the camera, carry each door's far edge as a thin vertical line, and carry Miku's shadow as a dark shape with two clean tail silhouettes. Let the reflection stretch but never sharpen, since the boards are matte.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A brass knob with its rose plate tarnished in a ring, one small hook on the back of the near door, a folded mat pushed against a threshold, and a cobweb in the far window's upper corner. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where an old apartment corridor would actually have it.

Illuminate with the far window as the only key, pale and cool, plus the floor's weak bounce as a fill. Let the window produce a bright pool at the corridor's end, a pale rim on every far-facing edge, and Miku's long shadow. Let the bounce keep the near door frames readable at about two stops down. Keep the ceiling lamp dead and give it no light of its own.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: floorboards, loose board edge, skirting chip. Second: Miku, her hand on the frame, the towel. Third: the first two doorways and her shadow. Fourth: the middle doorways and the empty frame. Fifth: the far window, the curtain and the daylight pool. Separate them by value steps of roughly eleven percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every door panel and skirting edge, restrained risograph grain in the dark fields, crisp flat fills in the lit areas, and fine chips only at corners. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the brass knobs.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no neighbour in a doorway, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no open doors showing rooms, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like a passage that only exists at night: seven doors and one empty frame, floorboards pale down the middle, and a girl standing four metres from the light with her head turned back as if she had just decided something.

seeds.title: BLACK MEMBRANE
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 9:16 dark futurist installation key visual, shot as a photograph inside a room with no walls rather than a poster, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only figure standing on the water in front of one colossal white membrane. There is nothing behind the scene: the black is empty space itself, depth without any surface, and every object sits directly inside it. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, a slim virtual-singer silhouette, and her original grey-and-teal costume structure. Keep her face, both eyes and both hands fully readable at thumbnail size.

Place Hatsune Miku standing on the water in front of the membrane, offset six percent left of the frame’s midline, three-quarters turned away from the camera with her chin lifted toward the fabric. She occupies about thirteen percent of the canvas height, her weight is settled on one leg with the other slightly forward, and both arms hang loose with her hands open at her sides.

Weave Hatsune Miku’s extremely long aqua twin tails into the cobalt field. Both tails hang down her back as one narrow aqua mass that picks up the blue transmitted through the fabric, near-black against the unlit room and pale aqua where the membrane glows behind them, with one strand drifting forward across her shoulder. Her aqua hair is the only colour note in the whole photograph.

Dress Hatsune Miku in an original dark-room performance costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not sportswear. A close black technical bodysuit with matte panels, one narrow pale seam running the length of each limb, short structured shoulder pieces lifted from the silhouette, and a thin silver clasp at the throat. Keep every material matte so nothing competes with the membrane’s light.

Hang one colossal membrane of white translucent fabric from the crown of the frame: forty metres tall, sixty metres wide, its lower edge stopping two metres above the water. Let air from below press the middle of the membrane outward toward the camera, so the whole surface becomes one slow curve rather than a flat wall, and let the lower third carry eight or nine soft vertical folds that open toward the bottom. It must read as cloth under tension, with weight in the folds and a fine sag between the suspension points.

Light the membrane from behind with one enormous cobalt field: a flat saturated blue plane occupying the entire space beyond the fabric, its edge nowhere visible. The membrane therefore becomes the picture: near-white where it faces the camera, thinning to pale blue along every fold, and going almost transparent where the fabric pulls tight, so the blue passes through as soft transmitted light with no halo and no rays. Keep the blue a body colour rather than an emission, and let it read deepest where the fabric is thickest.

Suspend the membrane from a silver gantry across the top of the frame: eleven machined clamps gripping the upper hem, one horizontal box beam, two diagonal struts, and a short travel rail cropped by the top edge. The gantry must be the only hard geometry in the upper half, and it must be dimmer than the fabric so the eye stays on the cloth.

Build the metal with real reflectance. The clamps, the beam and the struts are cool polished alloy carrying a silver ramp from near-white on their upper faces through two mid greys into a deep blue-grey underneath, with one hard white edge where each box turns and faint anisotropic streaks along the beam. Let the blue field smear along the underside of the beam as one long cold reflection, and let the crinkled upper hem cast a broken silver line onto the fabric below it.

Set the floor as black water meeting the dark on a level horizon at seventy-four percent, owning only the bottom quarter. That water is a heavy, dark, broken surface that returns only the brightest ten percent of the scene: the white lower hem, one soft patch of blue beneath it and one thin bright outline of her figure come back; every fold, every mid tone and every dark area simply disappears. Render what comes back thirty-five percent darker than the fabric, and break it with one long wave running diagonally from the lower right toward the middle left plus two short cross-ripples, so the returned light lies in unequal vertical strokes and never repeats the membrane above.

Use a strict four-value palette and assign the colour by measured area. Black takes thirty-eight percent: the empty room, the space beyond the field, the water and every unlit face. White takes twenty-two percent, and it belongs to the membrane alone, from near-white on the lit belly down to pale blue in the folds. Silver takes fourteen percent: the gantry faces, the clamp edges and the reflection on the water. Cobalt takes twenty-four percent, and it is a deep saturated blue body with a hard white lip where the fabric edge crosses it. Aqua takes two percent, only in her long hair. No warm value appears anywhere in the frame.

Let light come only from the blue field behind the membrane. It stays inside the fabric and inside the metal: it lights the cloth from within, it lights the gantry's upper faces, and it never enters the air as a beam, a fringe or a fog. The gantry stays almost black on its lower faces, her back edge keeps only a thin cold rim, and the water carries a single dull blue column. Refuse every other source and add no atmospheric haze.

Add an abstract instrument language at the margins only: one vertical row of short ticks down the left edge, one hairline circle inscribed at ninety percent of the frame width, four crosshair marks on that circle, and three index dots under the water line. All of it dimmer than the membrane, and none of it touching her.

Separate depth by edge quality, not by focus: the fabric surface softest and largest, her silhouette and the near folds sharp, the gantry sharp with visible metal thickness, the water softest and darkest. Let the room feel eighty metres deep.

Break the composition on both axes. The membrane sits eight percent right of the frame's midline so its left edge enters the frame and its right edge is cropped. The gantry's beam is not level: it drops four percent from left to right. One long fold runs off the bottom of the frame and one clamp hangs loose with its cable slack. Keep the bottom-left corner occupied by a low unlit platform standing in the water, filling about one eighth of the frame, carrying one thin silver edge along its top.

Keep the frame honest as a photograph of one room: no readable text of any kind, one figure only, no visible hands, and nothing floats — the membrane hangs from the gantry, the gantry hangs from the crown, and the water is the only thing that is not solid.

The final image should read as a huge white sail breathing in front of a blue nothing, and it must look like a photograph of a real installation: one forty-metre membrane under tension, eleven machined clamps on a silver beam, a saturated cobalt field behind it, one small singer on black water holding a broken strip of light, five silver values on the metal, soft fabric, hard gantry, deep empty hall, off-centre axis, dark futurist key visual, monumental quiet.

Let the cloth carry its own weight. The membrane is a fine synthetic weave with a faint sheen along every fold, its surface dusted with a thin film of moisture that catches the cobalt behind it; the suspension clamps are machined aluminium with one bright chamfer each; and the water below holds a single long swell that bends the reflection without breaking it. Every mark stays close to the fabric so the room still reads as empty.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Hatsune Miku, no second figure, no reflection that reads as a second person, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text of any kind, no watermark, no signature, no frame, no border.

seeds.title: CORRIDOR AXIS
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 9:16 dark futurist installation key visual, shot as a photograph looking straight down a corridor rather than a poster, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only figure. Camera on the exact centre axis at chest height, fifty millimetre lens, one-point perspective with the vanishing point half a centimetre above the middle of the frame, horizon absolutely level. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, a slim virtual-singer silhouette, and her original grey-and-teal costume structure. Keep her face, both eyes and both hands fully readable at thumbnail size.

Place Hatsune Miku standing at the near mouth of the corridor at thirty percent of the frame depth, centred and facing away from the camera, occupying eighteen percent of the canvas height. Her feet are together, both arms hang straight down, and her head is level so the tails read as two clean shapes against the far square.

Weave Hatsune Miku’s extremely long aqua twin tails into the corridor’s dark. Two long tapered aqua shapes fall from the crown of her head past her hips, each with a clear square tie at the top, dim on the side away from the far square and faintly lit along the other. Her aqua hair is the only colour on the figure.

Dress Hatsune Miku in an original archive-aisle costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language. A fitted dark top with one pale collar chip, a narrow dark tie, a short pleated dark skirt that reads as one small bell, dark thigh-highs and low boots. Keep every value black-on-black so the figure reads as a silhouette with two bright chips.

Refuse a fifth material. The plates are matte black glass with one machined silver edge, the floor is polished black stone under two centimetres of water, the far square is flat cobalt behind a machined silver lip, and her costume is matte dark fabric. Everything that is not an edge stays black.

Let the aisle show only what use leaves: a faint haze of dust on the plate faces nearest the camera, one thin smear on the water where something crossed it long ago, and a single fingerprint on the silver lip at hand height. Nothing is broken and nothing floats.

Build the depth from repetition, not from architecture: hang two hundred black glass plates in eight concentric rectangular rings, each plate eight hundred millimetres square and twelve millimetres thick, all of them facing the camera, each ring smaller than the one in front of it and spaced one and a half metres deeper, so the rings converge on a single square opening at the far end. Let the plates of the nearest two rings be cropped by the left, right and top edges of the frame. Set the plate spacing irregular by a few centimetres per ring so the repetition reads as built rather than generated.

Give every plate one hard silver edge along its top face and one narrow cobalt sliver along its left face, and nothing else: their faces are matte black and swallow light. Let the plates rotate a few degrees each around their vertical axis, alternating left and right, so the tunnel wall reads as a dense stack of thin edges rather than a flat surface.

End the corridor in a single glowing square three metres across, filled with flat cobalt and framed by a machined silver lip one hundred millimetres thick. This square is the only strong light in the frame. Keep its interior absolutely flat, with a single white-hot vertical filament one pixel wide running down its centre and stopping a hand's width short of the bottom lip.

Reflect the corridor in the floor. The floor is polished black stone flooded with two centimetres of water, so the reflection is nearly perfect: the eight rings, the plates, her silhouette and the far square all repeat downward at full length and full colour, and the reflection is the second half of the composition. Break it with a single long wave running diagonally from the lower left to the lower right, no taller than four crests, which turns the reflection into a fan of soft vertical strokes while the square's reflection stays intact as one hard glowing rectangle.

Hold the palette with strict area control. Black holds about eighty-two percent of the frame as the plate faces, the void and the water; silver-white holds ten percent as the plate top edges, the square’s lip and the specular line down the corridor; cobalt holds six percent as the far square and its reflection; and aqua holds two percent, only in her long hair. No hue outside these four appears anywhere in the frame.

Light with the far square alone. It must lay a bright rectangle on the water, draw one thin vertical highlight down the centre of the corridor, and leave every plate face unlit so the tunnel is read entirely through edges. Add only the faintest cool bounce near the frame edges so the nearest plates keep a visible top face, and refuse every other source.

Separate the depth by edge, not by focus: the near plates razor sharp with visible thickness, the middle rings dimmer and narrower in apparent contrast, the far square crisp and flat, and the water carrying every one of them back in a softer register.

seeds.title: FLOODED HALL
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 9:16 dark futurist installation key visual, shot as a photograph of a flooded hall rather than a poster, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only figure standing on a narrow dry ridge among thirteen black glass pipes. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, a slim virtual-singer silhouette, and her original grey-and-teal costume structure. Keep her face, both eyes and both hands fully readable at thumbnail size.

Place Hatsune Miku standing on a narrow dry ridge among the pipes at about forty-five percent of the frame width, three-quarters turned away from the camera and looking up into the cluster, occupying fifteen percent of the canvas height. Her feet are set one behind the other on the ridge, both arms hang loose, and she stays perfectly still so the pipes carry the height.

Weave Hatsune Miku’s extremely long aqua twin tails into the cobalt glow. Two clean tapered aqua shapes fall from the crown of her head past her waist, each with a visible square tie at the top, brightest where the nearest pipe’s light reaches them and almost black at the tips, with one tail doubled inside the water reflection. Her aqua hair is the only character colour.

Dress Hatsune Miku in an original flooded-hall costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not workwear. A fitted black technical top with sealed seams, a pale silver collar chip that stays bright at this scale, tapered dark trousers, short sealed boots, and one narrow cobalt band at each wrist. Keep the values dark and the shapes simple so she reads as a small precise silhouette against the water.

Fill the upper two thirds with a forest of black glass pipes of unequal height, none of them touching, arranged in a loose arc around her. Use thirteen pipes: four very tall ones cropped by the top edge, five medium ones between four and seven metres, four short stubs breaking the water. Diameters vary between six hundred millimetres and one metre eight hundred. Each pipe is a straight cylinder of black glass with a polished lip, a matte outer wall and a faint vertical seam, and every lip is cut at the same flat horizontal angle so the whole cluster shares one level, like the mouths of an instrument.

Open every pipe to the same light: the inner wall of each one glows cobalt from deep inside, brightest at the lip and fading down into black, so the cluster reads as thirteen chimneys of the same fire. In the three nearest pipes the glow spills over the lip and lays a cobalt chip of light on the outer wall; in the far pipes it only outlines the rim. Give the tallest pipe one single white-hot point inside it, low down, so the eye has a place to start.

Give the glass the behaviour of black glass and nothing else: no mirror finish, no rainbow iridescence, no frosted plastic. Its outer wall must catch one long soft vertical reflection of the neighbouring glow, hold the shape of that reflection with a hard edge, and lose the rest to black. The lip must carry a thin bright ring where the polished edge meets the light, and that ring is the only specular allowed on the whole cluster.

Hold the palette with strict area control. Black takes about fifty-two percent of the image: the void, the water, the pipe walls and the unlit half of every cylinder. Silver-white takes eighteen percent for the polished lips, the vertical reflection, the collar chip and the single hard reflection in the water. Cobalt takes twenty-six percent for the thirteen inner walls, the spill chips and the reflected glow. Aqua takes four percent, only in her long hair. No warm value appears anywhere in the frame, and cobalt never becomes a fill colour outside the pipes.

Ring the nearest three pipes with a single elliptical ripple each, concentric and low, so the water shows that something is standing in it. Do not add foam, spray, droplets or splashes.

Keep the background absolute black and give it only a measuring language: a column of short horizontal ticks climbing the left edge, one long hairline arc sweeping across the top third, and four small calibration crosses spaced unevenly through the empty upper right. All of it stays dimmer than the darkest pipe and never crosses the figure.

Hold the colour to four values and assign each a job: black for the void, the water, the pipe walls and the unlit half of every cylinder; silver-white for the polished lips, the vertical reflection, the collar chip and the single hard reflection in the water; cobalt for the thirteen inner walls, the spill chips and the reflected glow; aqua only in her twin tails. Do not let cobalt become a fill colour anywhere outside the pipes.

Light with one system only: the pipes light themselves, and everything else in the frame is lit by them. No sky, no moon, no ceiling lamp, no volumetric shafts, no bloom larger than a couple of millimetres around the brightest lip. Add the faintest cool bounce off the water so her back edge keeps a thin rim, and nothing else.

Separate depth by edge and by value rather than by focus: the ridge and her boots razor sharp, the near pipes sharp with visible glass thickness at the lip, the middle cluster slightly dimmer, the cropped tall pipes at the top reduced to dark silhouettes with one glowing line inside, the water and its smeared reflection softest of all. The whole frame stays quiet, cool and almost silent.

The frame carries no lettering of any kind, no second person, no visible hands, and nothing floats: every pipe rises out of the water, every ripple belongs to a pipe, and the ridge is part of the floor.

The final image should read as a flooded engine room where sound has been turned into light, and it must look like a photograph of a real installation: thirteen black glass pipes of unequal height, thirteen cobalt throats, one figure on the ridge, one soft mirror below, absolute darkness, cold silver lips, measured empty hall, dark futurist key visual, restrained monumental quiet.

Let every pipe carry its own wear. The black glass is flawless at the lip and faintly scuffed below it, with a soft bloom of condensation where the cobalt light spills over the edge; the water holds a thin film of dust that breaks the reflection into two soft bands; her boots leave two small dry arcs on the ridge; and the nearest pipe shows one long hairline seam running its full height. Each mark stays local and quiet so the cluster still reads as thirteen clean cylinders.

Distribute the light evenly across the cluster. Each pipe lip carries the same narrow bright ring, brightest on the three nearest and dimmer as they recede, and the spill chips fall on the outer walls at exactly the height of that ring; the water under the ridge shows one clear vertical smear for every pipe; and the far wall stays pure black with no visible corner. Nothing in the hall is lit except by the tubes themselves.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Hatsune Miku, no second figure, no divers, no fish, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text of any kind, no watermark, no signature, no frame, no border.

seeds.title: HOVER STUDY
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 9:16 dark object study, built as a photograph of one hovering thing in an unlit hall rather than a poster or a diagram, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only figure and the measure of everything in the frame. There is nothing behind it: the black is empty space itself, depth without any surface, and the object sits directly inside it. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, a slim virtual-singer silhouette, and her original grey-and-teal costume structure. Keep her face, both eyes and both hands fully readable at thumbnail size.

Place Hatsune Miku standing on the black water directly beneath the hovering rings, offset a little right of the frame’s midline, three-quarters turned away from the camera with her chin lifted toward the object. She occupies about fourteen percent of the canvas height, her weight settled on one leg, both hands open at her sides.

Weave Hatsune Miku’s extremely long aqua twin tails into the cobalt bloom. Both tails hang down her back in one narrow aqua mass, near-black against the unlit hall and faintly pale where the discs’ light reaches their crown, with one strand drifting free of her shoulder. Her aqua hair is the only cool note on the figure.

Dress Hatsune Miku in an original dark-study costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language. A close black bodysuit with matte panels, one narrow pale seam running the length of each limb, short structured shoulder pieces, and a thin silver clasp at the throat. Keep every material matte so nothing competes with the alloy rings.

Let the metal show only what a workshop leaves: a fine turned finish on every band face, one narrow fillet at each rim, faint handling marks on the nearest ring, and a single torn end where one filament has been cut. Nothing rusts and nothing decorative appears.

Build it from twelve flat rings of pale alloy, none sharing a centre. Scatter their centres across a two-metre field so every ring overlaps at least one other and no two are ever concentric, and give each ring its own tilt between four and thirty degrees on its own axis. Make the bands one hundred millimetres wide and twelve millimetres thick, with a soft irregular wobble in their radii so no ring is a perfect circle. Break three of them: one clean snap with the two halves sitting out of line, one notch torn out with a stepped edge, and one that simply stops in mid-air and ends in a tapered point.

Give every band two faces and one edge line. The face turned toward the camera is polished to near-white and carries a soft sheen; the edge is matte black; and one thin bright line runs round the inner rim of every ring, unbroken except where the ring is broken. Let the white faces catch one single soft light from above left so the cluster reads as a stack of bright bands separated by black gaps.

Cover every band with hairlines that thicken and thin without a scale: some run the full circumference, some stop halfway, some thicken into a short dark bar and then vanish, and several run off the edge of the band and continue into the dark. Let no two bands carry the same interval, and let none of it ever resolve into a readable scale.

Thread the cluster with a loose web of four-millimetre filaments. They cross between rings, curve away from the mass, pass behind one band and come out in front of another, and every one of them ends in the dark, connected to nothing.

Set two solid cobalt discs inside the cluster at different depths: one nine hundred millimetres across and one three hundred, both flush-faced, both with a hard white lip and a slightly denser blue at the core, both holding all of their colour inside their own surface. Let the large one be occluded by two bands and the small one float free in a gap.

Build the metal in five values. Near-white on the lit crown of every band, bright silver on the sheen, two mid greys down the flank, deep blue-grey on the inner rim, and black in every gap. Add one interrupted bright edge where a ring's tilt catches the light and one dull patch where the sheen has worn.

Light it from one soft source above and to the left. That single light draws the silver lines, fills the white faces and leaves every gap between the rings completely black; nothing else in the frame receives any light, and the air between the bands stays empty.

Put her on the machine, because the machine's own geometry leaves her only one option. She sits astride the third band where it tilts down through the lower left: one leg drops on either side of the band, both boots crossed behind it and hooked under its lower edge, her weight settled on the metal rather than hanging from it, her torso turned in toward the cluster, her face lifted into the gap between two rings, and one hand closed around a filament that runs down past her shoulder so she does not slide. A band one hundred millimetres wide and tilted at eighteen degrees can be sat on but never stood on, and the filament is the only thing in reach that can be gripped, so that hand is what keeps her there. Her twin tails hang down past the band and their ends dissolve into the black beneath her.

Keep the space around her and the cluster almost empty, with one enormous arc running behind everything: a hairline curve cropped by both side edges, so far out that it reads as the rim of something larger than the frame. Add four crosshair marks spaced unevenly through the upper right and one row of nine index dots along the bottom edge, all of them dimmer than the object.

Hold the palette with strict area control and assign the colour by measured area. Black takes fifty-six percent: the void, every gap between the rings and the space beneath her. Silver takes twenty-four percent: the band faces, the rims, the filaments and the torn ends. Cobalt takes sixteen percent: the two discs and the faint bloom they cast on the water. Aqua takes four percent, only in her long hair. No warm value appears anywhere in the frame.

Separate depth by edge: the band she sits on, her legs and her silhouette razor sharp with visible band thickness, the middle rings sharp, the far rings dimmer and narrower in value, the arc behind reduced to a hairline. Let the object feel nine metres across and completely silent.

Break the balance on both axes. The cluster's centre sits six percent right of the frame's midline and she sits six percent left of it, so the two never line up; one ring escapes far to the upper left and one drifts low right, and the largest ring is cropped at a different height on each side. Let the lower-left corner stay completely empty black apart from one small cold-grey circle no larger than a coin.

Keep the frame honest as a photograph of one object and one person: no readable text of any kind, one figure only, and nothing floats because nothing is holding anything — the rings simply occupy the dark, the threads end in it, and no part of the machine touches a floor, a wall or a support.

The final image should read as someone who found the one place on an instrument where a body can rest, and it must look like a photograph of a real object rather than an illustration: twelve eccentric alloy rings at twelve different tilts, three of them broken, hairlines that never resolve into a scale, a web of filaments ending in nothing, two solid cobalt discs at different depths, one small figure sitting astride a tilted band with one hand closed around a filament and her legs crossed under the metal, five silver values on every band, one soft raking light, absolute darkness around her, hovering study, dark futurist key visual, quiet found hold.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Hatsune Miku, no second figure, no visible raised hands, no readable text of any kind, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no watermark, no signature, no frame, no border. Every ring stays exactly where it hovers and nothing else moves.

seeds.title: INSTRUMENT ROOM
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 9:16 dark futurist installation key visual, shot as a photograph looking down into a black instrument room rather than a poster, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only figure. There is nothing behind the scene: the black is empty space itself, and every object sits directly inside it. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, a slim virtual-singer silhouette, and her original grey-and-teal costume structure. Keep her face, both eyes and both hands fully readable at thumbnail size.

Place Hatsune Miku standing at the near edge of the stone disc, offset a little left of the frame’s midline, three-quarters turned away from the camera and looking down into the instrument face, occupying about thirteen percent of the canvas height. Her feet are together on the wet stone, both arms hang loose, and she stays the only figure in the room.

Weave Hatsune Miku’s extremely long aqua twin tails into the graduation light. Both tails hang down her back in one narrow aqua mass, near-black against the unlit room and faintly pale along the edge that faces the lit band, with one strand lifting across the water. Her aqua hair is the only cool note on the figure.

Dress Hatsune Miku in an original instrument-room costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language. A close black bodysuit with matte panels, one narrow silver seam down each leg, short structured shoulder pieces, and a thin pale band at the wrist echoing the graduation marks. Keep every material matte so the only gloss belongs to the wet stone.

Let the instrument show only what calibration leaves: a fine polish along the pointer’s track, one oiled collar at the drum hub, faint fingerprints on the white band at hand height, and a single thin scratch across the nearest ten-degree tick.

Build the floor as one enormous instrument face: a black polished stone disc thirty metres across, flooded with two centimetres of water, ringed by a white graduation band one metre wide. Engrave the band with a tick every degree, a longer tick every ten degrees, and a hairline centre line running across the whole disc, and let the white band be worn and slightly chipped at three places so it reads as something used.

Set the pointer across the disc: a silver arm fifteen metres long, one point two metres wide and forty centimetres thick, pivoting on a machined drum three metres across and sixty centimetres tall. Point it at forty-seven degrees, running from the pivot toward the lower right, its far end cropped by the disc's edge. Lift it five centimetres off the water on a hidden shoe so a thin gap runs the whole length of it.

Let the cobalt live in that gap. The pointer's underside carries one continuous cobalt strip, hard-edged and solid, and it throws a flat band of blue down onto the wet stone directly beneath it: a band one and a half metres wide with a crisp edge, brightest under the middle of the arm and stopping dead where the graduation band begins. That band is the only light in the frame, and it stays on the floor.

Give the metal five values. The pointer's top face is cool polished alloy: near-white along its spine, two mid greys on the flats, a deep blue-grey on the chamfer, with one hard white edge where it turns. The pivot drum carries the same ramp plus one ring of bolts and one worn silver band where hands would steady it. The graduation band is cold white with a faint blue cast in its worn areas.

Let the water carry the second picture, but a broken one. It returns only the brightest ten percent: the blue band, the pointer's lit spine, the white graduation band and one thin bright outline of her boots come back, thirty-five percent darker than the real thing, cut into unequal vertical strokes by one long diagonal wave that runs from the lower left to the middle right. Everything else below the surface falls into black.

Hold the palette with strict area control and assign the colour by measured area. Black takes forty-eight percent: the void beyond the disc, the wet stone, the water and every unshadowed gap. Silver takes twenty-four percent: the pointer, the drum, the bolts and the graduation band. White takes eight percent: the freshest printed ticks and the one pale seam on her kit. Cobalt takes fourteen percent: the drum face and the bloom it lays on the water. Aqua takes four percent, only in her long hair, and the last two percent is the faint amber of a single instrument lamp. No other value appears anywhere in the frame.

Light with the strip alone. It should read as a luminous edge rather than a lamp: the whole band on the floor is even, its boundary is hard, and the arm above it is lit from below, so the pointer's underside glows cold and its top face stays a metal surface catching only the ambient. Keep the far half of the disc almost black so the instrument dies away into the dark.

Add an instrument language that stays abstract: a ring of radial index marks inside the graduation band, four crosshair marks at the cardinal points, one hairline arc sweeping behind the disc, and a row of nine index dots under the near edge. None of it becomes text.

Separate depth by edge: her boots, the pivot drum and the near graduation band razor sharp; the pointer sharp with visible thickness along its full length; the far band of the disc softened by distance; the water reduced to a texture. Let the room feel sixty metres wide.

Break the composition on both axes. The disc sits six percent right of the frame's midline, the pointer points at forty-seven degrees rather than along an axis, she stands between the pivot and the graduation band rather than at the centre, and the far edge of the disc is cropped at a different height on each side. Let the lower-left corner hold one low unlit block, one eighth of the frame, with a single silver edge along its top.

Keep the frame honest as a photograph of one instrument: no readable text of any kind, one figure only, and nothing floats — her boots are on the wet stone, the pointer is on its drum, the drum is bolted to the disc.

The final image should read as a reading being taken on a machine the size of a room, and it must look like a photograph of a real instrument: a thirty-metre black stone dial ringed by a white graduation band, one fifteen-metre silver pointer at forty-seven degrees, a hard-edged band of cobalt light thrown down through the gap beneath it, one small figure standing still beside the pivot looking out along the arm, five silver values on the metal, black water holding a broken strip of blue, ceremonial scale, off-axis instrument, dark futurist key visual, quiet measurement.

The final image should read as a giant instrument left running in the dark: one polished stone disc, one white graduation ring, one pointer, one small figure at its edge, and a mirror of black water completing the circle.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Hatsune Miku, no second figure, no visible raised hands, no readable text of any kind, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no watermark, no signature, no frame, no border. Every bolt, tick and pointer stays fixed to the instrument.

seeds.title: MACHINE ROOM
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 9:16 dark futurist installation key visual, shot as a photograph of a real room-sized machine rather than a graphic poster, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only figure. Camera on the horizontal axis of the frame at her knee height, thirty-five millimetre lens, one-point perspective, absolutely level horizon. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, a slim virtual-singer silhouette, and her original grey-and-teal costume structure. Keep her face, both eyes and both hands fully readable at thumbnail size.

Place Hatsune Miku dead centre on the water line, occupying thirteen percent of the canvas height, facing the camera with her arms loose at her sides and her weight settled evenly on both feet. Only the outer third of each tail and the hem of her skirt may sink into the black.

Weave Hatsune Miku’s extremely long aqua twin tails into the machine’s dark. Two clean tapered aqua shapes fall behind her knees, pale where the cobalt sphere reaches them and pure black where they leave its light, the very ends dissolving into the void. Her aqua hair is the only colour on the whole figure.

Dress Hatsune Miku in an original dark-room costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language. A close black bodysuit with matte panels, one thin bright sleeve stripe per arm, a narrow dark tie at the throat, a short pleated dark skirt, and two small silver blocks at the headset. Keep every material matte so nothing competes with the cobalt sphere.

Refuse a fifth material. The rings are brushed stainless steel with a visible directional grain, their edges and hub plates are matte black anodised aluminium, the water is black and perfectly still, and her costume is matte black fabric with one thin bright stripe. Every surface answers only to the cobalt sphere.

Let the metal show only what a workshop leaves: a fine circular polish inside each ring’s bore, one oiled collar at the hub, faint fingerprints on the outer band at hand height, and a single thin scratch across the nearest graduation. Nothing rusts and nothing chips.

Build the picture around one machine and nothing else: three colossal gimbal rings of brushed stainless steel, each about nine metres across, hung so that no two are parallel. The outer ring stands nearly upright and is cropped by the top edge. The middle ring rolls to the left at eighteen degrees and is cropped by the left edge. The inner ring pitches forward at twelve degrees and passes behind her head. Every ring is a flat band one hundred and twenty millimetres wide and fifteen millimetres thick, with a machined outer face that catches a single hard specular line along its top arc and falls to black everywhere else.

Cut the same opening through all three rings: their centres align on one point directly above her head, so the three bands cross into a continuous channel of empty black and the eye reads a tube rather than three circles. Suspend a solid cobalt sphere at that shared centre, nine hundred millimetres across, matte on its upper hemisphere and glowing from within on its lower one, so the sphere holds one single white-hot point at its base where the light leaves it.

Engrave the metal with instrument language only, never with text. Give every ring a vernier graduation on its outer face: one short tick per degree, a longer tick every five degrees, a hairline centre line across the top of each ring, and a thin blade of a pointer riding on the middle ring. Keep the graduations under one pixel at the far edges so they fade into black instead of turning into decoration.

Use exactly three materials and refuse a fourth: brushed stainless steel with a visible directional grain, matte black anodised aluminium on the ring edges and the hub plates, and one black glass surface inside the sphere's collar. Nothing is plastic, nothing is chrome, nothing is painted.

Light the room from one source only: the cobalt sphere. It throws a narrow cyan-white bloom into the empty channel, lays a hard rim along the inner face of whichever band passes closest to it, and leaves the outer bands almost black. Add one very weak cold ambient from above so the top arcs keep a single bluish edge, and stop there. No second lamp, no fill, no fog light, no lens flare, no god ray.

Set the floor as a single plane of still black water that meets the back wall on a hard level horizon at seventy percent of the frame height. The water is a perfect mirror: the three rings, the sphere and the figure are reflected vertically, identical and unbroken, and the reflection carries the same gradations and the same specular line. Disturb it only once, with one narrow ripple band across the bottom eight percent of the frame, no more than three crests wide, which breaks the reflection into soft vertical strokes.

Keep the sky pure black and empty. Add only a faint polar grid above the machine: four hairline circles at unequal radii, one vertical centre line drawn as a row of short ticks, and one horizontal rule at the height of the outer ring's crown. The grid must be dimmer than the reflection and must never cross her body.

Hold the palette with strict area control. Black holds about eighty percent of the frame as the void, the water and the unlit faces; silver-white holds twelve percent as the ring bands and the instrument graduations; cobalt holds six percent as the sphere and its reflected bloom; and aqua holds two percent, only in her long hair. No hue outside these four appears anywhere in the frame.

Keep the four depth layers separated by edge quality: the figure and the sphere razor sharp; the near ring band sharp with a hard grain; the middle band softened a hair by distance; the far band and the polar grid reduced to faint lines. Add the thinnest possible cool haze between the middle and far bands so the machine has air in it, and no haze anywhere near her face.

The final image should read as a silent instrument waiting in a dark hall: three stainless rings crossing into one channel of empty black, a cobalt sphere low behind them, one small figure standing on the water, and a floor that returns all of it perfectly.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Hatsune Miku, no second figure, no visible raised hands, no lettering of any kind, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no watermark, no signature, no frame, no border. Every ring, hub plate and pointer stays bolted to the machine.

The final image should read as a silent instrument waiting in a dark hall, and it must look like a photograph of a physical installation rather than an illustration: monumental steel gimbals, one glowing cobalt sphere, one small singer standing on black water, absolute darkness, cold silver specular, mirrored floor, graduated metal, wide empty hall, dark futurist key visual, restrained industrial scale, quiet engineered precision.

seeds.title: SPIRAL TOWER
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 9:16 dark futurist installation key visual, shot as a photograph inside an unlit tower rather than a poster, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only figure walking up the second turn of a steel spiral ramp. There is nothing behind the scene: the black is empty space itself, and every object sits directly inside it. Put the camera on the water below the ramp at her knee height, thirty-five millimetre lens, looking up along the spiral, so the lowest flight enters the frame at the lower right and climbs toward the upper left with the horizon level at seventy-eight percent of the frame height. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, a slim virtual-singer silhouette, and her original grey-and-teal costume structure. Keep her face, both eyes and both hands fully readable at thumbnail size.

Give her a full chain of movement rather than a pose. Her right boot is planted flat on the tread above, her left boot is still on the tread below with the heel lifted and the sole rolling off the front edge, her knees are flexed, her hips are shifted over the front foot, her torso leans forward eight degrees into the climb, her left hand rests on the outer handrail with the fingers curled over the top rail, her right arm hangs and swings back, and her head is tilted down toward the next tread instead of up at the column. Let the two long aqua twin tails hang behind her shoulders and trail a half beat late, their ends lifting away from her back because she is moving forward; let the pleated skirt swing back against her thighs and the hem break into a shallow wave on the trailing side.

Weave Hatsune Miku’s extremely long aqua twin tails into the column’s light. Both tails fall from the crown of her head in two clean tapered aqua masses, the left one rimmed cobalt where the column reaches it and the right one nearly black, with their ends just clearing the tread she left. Her aqua hair is the only colour on the figure.

Dress Hatsune Miku in an original ramp-climb costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language. A fitted dark technical jacket with sealed seams, tapered dark trousers, low sealed boots with a pale toe cap, and one narrow silver band at the wrist. Keep every material matte so the only gloss in the frame belongs to the column and the water.

Make the contact visible, because that is what sells it. Show the front boot's sole pressed onto the tread's silver anti-slip strip, flattening the reflection there into one small dark patch; show the rear boot's toe still hooked on the tread edge with the tread's lip just catching the light under it; show the handrail's polished top rail brighten where her hand closes on it, and the rail dim again past her fingers. Let one fold of the skirt be caught between her thigh and the rail post.

Build the ramp as something built for walking. Four metres wide, steel, wrapping the column in two and a half turns with a pitch of eleven metres per revolution, so the turns cross the frame as three broad diagonal bands. Cut the walking surface into treads twenty-eight centimetres deep with a raised silver nosing on every step, a diamond tread pattern in the middle, and a handrail on the outer edge carried by posts every two metres. Let the flight she is on run off the right edge of the frame and the flight above crop the top edge.

Give the ramp two faces and the metal real reflectance. The treads are matte black with the silver nosing catching the column's light as a broken dotted line that runs from her boot down to the bottom right corner; the underside of every turn is cool polished alloy carrying a silver ramp from near-white at the outer edge through two mid greys into a deep blue-grey where it curves under. Let each turn lay one long curved silver reflection on the turn below it, and let the handrail read as one continuous bright line that passes behind her hand.

Its light stays on steel. Give it one narrow machined silver collar where the lowest flight is anchored, and let the collar answer with a single hard white line.

She must read as a figure lit by the thing she is walking past, not as a cutout pasted on the ramp.

Set the water far below as a heavy, dark, broken surface meeting the dark on a level horizon at seventy-eight percent, returning only the brightest ten percent of the scene: the cobalt column, the silver collar and the nearest tread nosings come back, thirty-five percent darker than the real thing, cut into unequal vertical strokes by one long diagonal wave. Black takes forty-six percent of the frame: the tower volume, the treads, the shadow side of every turn, the water and the unlit space above. Silver takes fourteen percent: the tread nosings, the handrail and one hard reflection on the water. Cobalt takes thirty-six percent: the central column, the rim it lays on her left side, and the bloom it throws across the near treads. Aqua takes four percent, only in her long hair. All of it dimmer than the metal.

The column stands eight percent right of the frame's midline and the spiral enters from the right, so the left third of the frame stays empty black above the horizon. No additional physical characters, no duplicate Hatsune Miku, no second figure, no other climbers, no readable text of any kind, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no watermark, no signature, no frame, no border. seeds.title: DROPPED BLADE
seeds.raw:
