Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes and twin-tail identity readable in the empty hall. Its weapon is rose quartz: deep rose-pink, translucent, and the only saturated mass anywhere in the frame.

The weapon is one solid mass of rose-quartz glass: translucent, deep rose-pink, lit from within, and it throws pink light onto everything around it.

Use a camera at her chest height on a normal lens, set back far enough that her whole body fits with clear headroom above her hair, square to her so she is centred and the falling sword hangs in the lower right quadrant. Place Miku at approximately forty-two percent of the canvas width, occupying about forty-six percent of the frame height, and keep her head and both boots well inside the frame rather than letting either edge crop her. Let the sword hang a hand's width off the floor, still tilted fifteen degrees, its point already touching the stone so the shadow reads as contact.

Give Miku exactly one core action: letting go. Her right hand is open at hip height with the fingers still spread from the grip, her left hand hangs closed at her side, and her head is turned down toward the sword with her expression flat. Keep her shoulders level, her feet apart, and put nothing in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the falling sword: a straight double-edged longsword with a two-finger-wide blade, a plain crossguard and a wheel pommel, caught in the instant after release so it hangs tilted with its point on the stone and its pommel still in the air. Keep it plain and unadorned. Let the sword occupy the frame's lower right and let its shadow spread under it as a second shape.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. the blade is one solid piece of rose quartz, deep rose-pink and translucent so the whole mass reads as one saturated stone, its interior holding three long fractures, its edges polished, and it lies almost invisible against the pale floor except where the window crosses it; the guard and pommel are blackened iron; the grip is dark leather over cord, still compressed where her hand was; the floor is pale limestone flags worn smooth; the walls are tall and blank, washed in a cool grey; the ceiling is out of frame. Each behaves differently — steel returns one long soft sheen and one hard edge line, blackened iron holds almost nothing, compressed leather shows a fine crease pattern, limestone holds a soft diffuse light and a faint polish where feet pass, the wash on the walls is a flat even field.

Build a stepped sequence across the frame. Begin at the lower right with the sword's point and its shadow, then the sword's blade and pommel in the air, then her open right hand, then her body and turned head, then the pale floor's receding joints, then the blank wall behind her. The sequence must read as a grip that has just failed, not as a weapon being placed down.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is nothing else in the hall — no scabbard falling with it, no belt hanger, no second weapon, no furniture. Keep the floor's whole left half empty and unmarked apart from the joints, so the sword's shadow is the only dark shape on it.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the sword's point and its shadow. Middle ground: Miku, her open hand, the sword's body. Background: the limestone floor's joints, the blank wall, the hall's height. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from a tall window out of frame at the right. The window is the key: a cool broad light that falls across the floor in a long rectangle, catches the blade's edge as one bright line, and lights her open hand from beneath. Let the wall behind sit two values darker than the lit floor and let the hall's height fade to grey. Never introduce a warm source. Let the crystal pass the light rather than return it: one thin saturated magenta line along its thickest edge, and one hard-edged magenta caustic patch thrown onto the limestone beside it.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails hang straight down, settling after the motion. The nearer tail falls across her shoulder as a clean aqua mass with one bright edge, the farther one hangs behind her arm and disappears at her waist. Let the light catch the tips where they pass through the window's rectangle.

Dress Miku in a plain training layer over her canonical palette, not armour. A dark teal wrap top with the sleeves rolled, a black sash at the waist, dark trousers with the hems loose, and soft flat shoes. Keep the palette close to teal-and-black with one pale wrap at her left wrist, and keep the silhouette simple and vertical.

Use a cool neutral palette with strict area control. Approximately forty-two percent of the image is pale limestone floor, twenty-four percent is the blank wall, fourteen percent is the sword and its shadow, eight percent is Miku's clothing, six percent is her aqua hair, four percent is her skin at the hands and face, and two percent is the bright edge and the pale wrist wrap. Keep every warm note out of the image except the crystal. The rose quartz's deep rose-pink tone is the one saturated colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the hall's own floor markings rather than from decoration. Let one large deep-teal ink bloom spread across the blank wall in the upper left, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular black panel across the wall at her shoulder height as a graphic mask, and let one vertical strip of rust-red run down the frame's right edge from top to floor. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “DROPPED BLADE” once, in black paint brushed across the pale floor in the empty left half, the strokes flaking where the limestone is polished, sized so it spans about half the floor's visible width and reads clearly at thumbnail size. Put no lettering on the sword, the wall or her clothing, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The blade's grind is dulled in a band halfway down; the grip's leather holds a deep crease pattern from her fingers; the guard's blacking is worn at one quillon; the limestone is dished in a shallow path where feet pass and holds one hairline crack; the wall's wash is scuffed low down in a long horizontal band. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the limestone floor. The floor carries the sword's shadow as one sharp-edged diagonal with the pommel's shadow separated by a hand's width from the blade's, her own shadow as a soft vertical shape, and the window's rectangle as the only bright field. Never let the floor mirror the blade and never let the two shadows join.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One pale wrist wrap at her left arm, a single bright chip at the blade's edge near the point, one loose limestone flake beside the shadow's edge, and a fine cord end fraying at the sword's grip. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where the moment would put it.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the sword's point and its shadow. Second: the sword's body and pommel. Third: her open hand and hip. Fourth: her torso and turned head. Fifth: the receding floor joints and the blank wall. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every floor joint and blade facet, restrained risograph grain in the wall, crisp flat fills in the lit floor, and one clean gradient only along the blade's sheen. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the blade's edge.

No second character, no duplicate Miku, no crowd, no banners, no flags, no birds, no wings, no halo, no second sword, no scabbard, no additional weapon, no glowing crystal, no neon glow, no self-lit weapon, no rainbow dispersion, no stained glass, no plastic, no glass bottle, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no magical effects, no readable text beyond the string named above, no blood, no wounds, no armour plates, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no sword in her hands, no motion blur, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like the exact frame after a decision: five fingers still spread around nothing, a blade hanging a hand's width from the floor with its point already down, and an empty hall with nothing left to hold.

seeds.title: DRY GARDEN
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “DRY GARDEN”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing on the raked gravel of a Zen rock garden in flat morning light, with a plaster wall and a single pine behind her. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the pale gravel field.

Use a camera at knee height on a normal lens, set at the garden's edge and angled about twenty degrees so the raked lines run diagonally across the lower frame and the wall runs horizontally behind her. Place Miku at approximately fifty-eight percent of the canvas width, full body visible from sandals to hair ornaments, occupying about thirty-four percent of the frame height. Let the gravel fill the left two-thirds as a field of parallel lines, so the composition is pattern interrupted by one standing figure.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Her right hand holds a bamboo rake upright, its tines resting on the gravel beside her, and her left hand is closed loosely at her waist. Her head is turned a quarter toward the stones, both eyes visible. Keep the pose still, the arms clear of her face, and put nothing else in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the raked gravel itself: a field of fine pale granite chips combed into parallel lines that curve around three dark stone groups, with one perfect circle raked around a single standing stone. Let the gravel occupy approximately sixty percent of the canvas area and let the rake lines compress with exact perspective toward the wall.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The gravel is fine, pale grey-white, uniformly graded, with each line holding a bright crest and a soft trough; the stones are dark volcanic rock, wet-looking even when dry, mossed at their bases; the wall is pale ochre plaster with a dark timber base and a tiled coping; the pine is trained into flat tiers with dark needles and pale exposed bark; the rake is bamboo with cord bindings. Each behaves differently — gravel scatters light into a fine even value, dark stone absorbs and holds a single soft sheen, plaster is uniform and matte, pine needles read as dense dark texture, bamboo holds a dry pale line.

Build a stepped sequence across the garden. Begin at the lower left with the rake lines running out of frame, then the first stone group with its moss base, then Miku and her rake, then the circle around the standing stone, then the wall's timber base, then the pine's lowest tier. The sequence must read as a surface organised by hand, not as a decorative pattern.

Leave one deliberate absence. One section of the rake lines has been erased: a smooth crescent about two metres wide where the gravel is flat and unraked, sitting between two stone groups with no explanation. Keep the crescent's edge sharp where the lines stop, and place it just left of Miku's rake so the tool appears to have caused it.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: rake lines, gravel crest, the bamboo tines. Middle ground: Miku, the first stone group, the circle. Background: the wall's base, the pine, the tiled coping. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from a low morning sun at the side. The sun is the key: warm and raking, coming from the left at about fifteen degrees, so every gravel line casts a fine shadow into its own trough and every stone casts a short directional shadow to the right. Add a cool ambient fill from the open sky, keeping the shadows open and blue-grey rather than black. Keep the light's angle low enough that the rake pattern reads as relief.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the garden's order. The nearer tail falls forward in one clean aqua mass over her shoulder, its edge sharp against the pale gravel; the farther tail drops behind her and is cut by the stone group's shadow. Let one strand rest against the rake's shaft without covering the bamboo bindings.

Dress Miku in an original garden-morning costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not a monk's robe. A pale linen wrap top with a wide sleeve, a dark narrow trouser cropped at the ankle, flat sandals, and a thin dark sash tied once at the waist. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment, and keep the silhouette simple enough to read at thumbnail size.

Use a pale-grey and ochre palette with strict area control. Approximately forty-eight percent of the image is pale raked gravel, eighteen percent is the ochre plaster wall, twelve percent is dark volcanic stone, eight percent is the deep green of the pine, six percent is Miku's pale linen and dark trouser, five percent is her aqua hair, and three percent is the morning sun's warm edge. Keep the image almost achromatic apart from her hair and the ochre wall.

Drive the printed graphic language from the garden's own geometry rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the lower right of the gravel, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular pale panel behind the wall as a graphic mask at the height of its timber base, and let one vertical strip of dark stone run from the pine to the gravel, aligned to the wall's timber post. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “DRY GARDEN” once, in dark ink brushed onto a narrow timber board hung on the wall at the left, the strokes slightly uneven, sized so the board spans about a seventh of the canvas width. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “SEVEN STONES” sit on a small stone tablet set into the gravel near the wall base. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the care. The gravel's lines vary in width where the rake has been drawn at slightly different speeds; the stones are dusted pale on their upper faces and dark beneath; the plaster is stained dark at the base where rain splashes; the pine's needles are dense at the tier edges and thin beneath; the bamboo rake's tines are worn shiny at their points. Keep the wear physical and hand-made, never a uniform texture.

Build a second composition through the rake pattern. The parallel lines curve around each stone group in exact contour, so each stone reads twice: once as a dark solid, once as a pale ring of compressed lines around it. Let the circle around the standing stone be the only perfect form in the frame.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A bronze ladle resting on a stone basin at the garden's edge, one fallen pine needle caught across three rake lines, a timber post's iron strap rusted at the bolt, and a small stone lantern half hidden behind the pine. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a temple garden would actually have it.

Let the sun produce a fine shadow in every gravel trough, a short directional shadow to the right of every stone, and a warm edge along Miku's arm and cheek. Let the fill keep the troughs readable as a soft grey rather than black. Keep the wall evenly lit with no shadow across it.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: rake lines, gravel crest, bamboo tines. Second: Miku, her sandals, the rake shaft. Third: the first stone group and the erased crescent. Fourth: the standing stone's circle and the middle stones. Fifth: the wall's timber base, the pine and the tiled coping. Separate them by value steps of roughly eight percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every stone edge and rake line, restrained risograph grain in the shadow fields, crisp flat fills in the pale areas, and fine dust only on upward stone faces. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the bronze ladle.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no gardener in the background, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no blossom, no water feature, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like a surface that is read rather than walked on: a thousand parallel lines bending around seven stones, one crescent erased by the rake still in her hand, and a girl standing at the edge of her own work.

seeds.title: FIRST SNOW

Let the gate occupy the right third and the snow-covered flight fill the space between, so the composition is a figure, a gate and a rising white field.

Her head is tilted slightly back, both eyes visible. Keep the pose still, the arms clear of her face, and put nothing else in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the torii gate itself: two battered vermilion pillars on stone footings, a double lintel, and a small plaque centred beneath the top beam. Let the gate occupy approximately thirty-five percent of the canvas area on the right, cut by the top edge, with its pillars sunk about a hand's depth into the snow.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The gate is painted timber, the vermilion faded and blistered, with snow resting on every upward face and none on the verticals; the pillars' stone footings are grey and lichened; the snow is dry powder over a thin crust, with footprints cutting through the crust to darker layers; the stair's stone steps show as pale horizontal bars; the cedar trunks behind are dark and heavily laden. Each behaves differently — painted timber holds one flat saturated value, snow scatters almost all light and holds only soft blue shadow, stone reads as a hard edge under a soft cap, cedar needles hold a black weight of snow.

Build a stepped sequence up the frame. Begin at the bottom edge with two pairs of footprints cutting through the snow crust, then the umbrella point and its small crater, then Miku's boots, then the gate's near footing with its lichen, then the rising stair where the steps read as pale bars, then the cedar tops against a white sky. The sequence must read as an approach upward, not as a flat field.

Leave one deliberate absence. One of the two footprints trails simply stops: the prints come in from the left, pass Miku, and end cleanly about three metres beyond her with no print returning. Keep the end of the trail about a hand's width from the gate's footing, and keep the snow beyond it untouched.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: snow crust, footprints, umbrella point and crater. Middle ground: Miku, the near footing, the gate's pillar. Background: the rising stair, the cedar trunks, the white sky. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from a flat overcast sky. The snow is the key reflector: an even white light with almost no direction, bouncing up from the ground to lift every underside — Miku's jaw, the gate's lintel, the umbrella — with a cool blue-grey fill. Add a faint warmer patch at the upper left where the cloud is thinner. Keep every shadow soft, blue, and no darker than mid-grey.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the snow light. The nearer tail falls forward over her coat in one clean aqua mass, the only saturated cool in the frame; the farther tail drops behind her back and reads as a dark vertical against the white stair. Let three flakes settle on the near tail and hold their own small highlights.

Dress Miku in an original first-snow costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not winter sportswear. A long padded coat in deep charcoal with a wide collar, the hem falling to mid-calf, cinched once at the waist; a pale scarf wound twice; thick boots laced high; dark gloves. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale accent, and keep the silhouette simple enough to read at thumbnail size.

Use a pale-blue and vermilion palette with strict area control. Approximately fifty percent of the image is snow white and pale sky, sixteen percent is the cool blue-grey of snow shadow, twelve percent is the vermilion gate, eight percent is Miku's charcoal coat, six percent is dark cedar and stone, five percent is her aqua hair, and three percent is the pale scarf. Drive the printed graphic language from the shrine's own order rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the lower left of the snow, printed flat and matte, reading as a deep cool hole in the white. Add a rectangular pale panel behind the gate as a graphic mask at the height of the lower lintel, and let one vertical strip of vermilion run from the lintel to the snow, aligned to the pillar. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “FIRST SNOW” once, in white paint applied across the broad stone face of the torii's lower lintel, worn at the lower strokes, sized so it spans about two thirds of the lintel's visible width. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “STONE 01” sit on a small bronze plate bolted to the near footing. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the weather. The snow lies deepest on the gate's upper faces and the stair's nosings, thinnest on the verticals; the crust is broken in irregular plates where feet have passed; the vermilion is blistered into small scales along the pillar's weather side; the stone footings hold a cap of snow with a clean drip line beneath; the tree branches carry the snow as a black-and-white weight. Keep the accumulation physical and directional, never a uniform blanket.

Build a second composition through the snow surface. The snow between the camera and Miku carries the gate's vermilion as a long soft reflection in its crust, and carries her legs as two dark verticals. Let the reflection break at every footprint edge, so the surface reads as broken crust rather than mirror.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A bronze plaque with no readable text beneath the gate's top beam, one iron snow chain hanging from the lintel, a cedar branch's load bending to the stair, and a small stone lantern half buried at the upper right. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a shrine approach would actually have it.

Let the bounce produce a lift on the gate's lintel underside, on Miku's jaw and on the umbrella's shaft. Keep the sky featureless and slightly brighter than the snow.

Fourth: the rising stair and the cedar trunks. Fifth: the top lintel, the plaque and the white sky. Separate them by value steps of roughly eight percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every gate joint and stair nosing, restrained risograph grain in the blue shadow fields, crisp flat fills in the white areas, and fine blistering only on the gate's weather side. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the bronze.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no visitor on the stair, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text on the plaque, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no birds, no falling lanterns, no scrapbook clutter.

seeds.title: FOG CHRONOMETER
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 premium science-fiction game key visual titled “FOG CHRONOMETER”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character inside an infinite white fog-filled Victorian engine hall. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable silhouette. Keep her face, both eyes, both hands, and her lifting gesture completely unobstructed; allow transformation only on the outer hair tips, cuff edges, skirt hem, and the final third of each twin tail, where the strands may turn into pale glass or thin away into fog.

Place her in the right third of the canvas, standing on a low granite kerb of wet flagstones, shown from the boots to the top of her head and occupying approximately thirty-two percent of the canvas height. Her body turns three-quarters toward the left. Both arms rise in front of her chest to lift a glass cloche: her left hand grips the brass knob at the crown of the dome, her right hand supports the rim from below, and the bell is already two centimetres off its iron base, with fog leaking from the gap. Keep her face, aqua eyes, individual fingers, and the exact lift the sharpest and most legible detail of the whole image.

Place the dominant object across the centre and centre-left: one colossal glass orchid standing beneath that cloche, nearly three quarters of the canvas wide and cropped by the left, lower, and upper edges. The orchid rises from a black cast-iron base of four paw feet and a scrolled bracket. Its eleven petals occupy five distinct material states: three fully polished glass with thick rounded edges, internal bubbles, layered reflections, local magnification and sharp caustic bands; three frosted translucent glass with pale cold veins; three bare silver wireframe ribs; one flaking into thin cobalt fragments; one almost gone, leaving a faint contour inside the dome. The column of the flower is a single hollow glass tube with a visible inner thread of pale aqua light, and condensation gathers on the inside of the cloche in uneven beads.

Build the circular interface behind the flower as a cathedral-scale clock dial rather than a floating panel. The dial stands upright behind the orchid, tilted about fourteen degrees, cropped by the top and left edges, and roughly twice the height of the character. Construct it from an unmarked brass chapter ring carrying only engraved minute ticks and no numerals, a black iron minute track, six offset concentric cobalt rings, thin silver radial spokes, translucent calibration discs, and a glass sub-dial near the four-o'clock position. Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “GREATSWORD FIELD”, a frame built around one colossal amber weapon, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing very small in the long shadow of a colossal sword driven into a dead grass plain. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes and twin-tail identity readable against the deep amber crystal blade and the cold sky.

The weapon is one solid mass of orange amber glass: translucent, warm orange-brown, lit from within, and it throws orange light onto everything around it.

Use a camera at her chest height on a normal lens, set low and level so the horizon sits at the lower third and the sword rises out of frame through the upper right. Place Miku at approximately eighteen percent of the canvas width and eighteen percent of the frame height, standing left of centre with the blade's shadow crossing toward her feet. Let the blade occupy the frame from the lower right to the top left on a shallow diagonal.

Give Miku exactly one core action: looking up. Her chin is lifted and her face is turned toward the blade's rising edge, both arms hanging loose at her sides with the fingers slightly curled, one heel lifted a centimetre off the dirt. Keep the pose still, the shoulders dropped, and put nothing in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the sword: a colossal straight double-edged blade four metres wide at the guard, driven point-first into the ground so only the upper half shows, with a plain crossguard as wide as a road and a grip wrapped in cracked leather that disappears off the top edge. Flatten the whole weapon into hard planes — no ornate fantasy filigree, no studs, no gemstones. Let it occupy the right two thirds of the frame.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. the blade is one solid piece of amber, honey-dark and translucent so the whole mass reads as one saturated stone, its interior holding three long fractures and a drift of fine bubbles, its edges polished but chipped in two places, and it does not emit light of its own — it only bends whatever passes through it; the fuller is a shallow channel holding a line of standing water; the crossguard is pitted iron with chipped black paint; the grip leather is split and pale where hands have worn it; the plain is dead winter grass, ochre and grey, bending one way in the wind; the sky is a flat overcast, no sun disc. Each behaves differently — steel returns one long cold sheen and a bright edge, the water in the fuller mirrors a thin strip of sky, iron swallows light, split leather reads as coarse grain, dead grass breaks into fine dry strokes, overcast sky stays completely matte.

Build a stepped sequence across the frame. Begin at the lower left with the flattened grass and the blade's shadow edge, then Miku's boots and her small dark silhouette, then the grass rising into the middle distance, then the sword's lower blade and the water line in the fuller, then the blade widening upward, then the pale sky behind the crossguard. The sequence must read as an enormous object seen from the ground, not as a prop standing near a person.

Leave one deliberate absence. Halfway up the left edge of the frame a second blade should be visible only as a broken stump: a snapped tang and a ragged fracture face, no blade above it, no debris below. Keep it thin and easy to miss, and place it far behind Miku so the plain reads as a field where something larger once stood.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: dead grass at the bottom edge and the near shadow. Middle ground: Miku, the sword's lower blade, the stump. Background: the plain flattening out, the blade's upper mass, the overcast sky. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from a single overcast source above and slightly behind the blade. The sky is the key: a broad soft light that leaves the blade's front face in cool mid-grey, picks out a bright rim along its left edge, and throws the fuller into a dark line. Let Miku be lit only by the sky, so she reads as a small dark shape with a thin bright edge on her hair and shoulder. Keep the grass in the middle distance one value darker than the foreground, and never introduce a warm light. Let the crystal pass the light rather than return it: one thin saturated amber line where the mass is thickest, and one hard-edged amber caustic patch thrown onto the dead grass beside it.

Lift Miku's extremely long twin tails in the plain's constant wind. Both tails stream to her right and slightly up, the nearer one crossing her back as a clean aqua mass, the farther one thinning into separate strands at its tip. Let the wind also bend the grass the same direction so the whole plain agrees with her hair.

Dress Miku in a plain field coat over her canonical palette, not armour. A long charcoal wool coat worn open over a dark teal high-collar shirt, dark trousers tucked into scuffed boots, a wide belt with one brass buckle, and fingerless gloves. Keep the silhouette narrow and vertical, keep one pale garment at the collar, and make every piece look worn rather than styled.

Use a cold desaturated palette with strict area control. Approximately forty-two percent of the image is overcast sky, twenty-six percent is the blade and crossguard, eighteen percent is dead grass, six percent is the blade's shadow, five percent is Miku's coat, two percent is her aqua hair, and one percent is the brass buckle and the leather grip. Keep every warm note down to the crystal and that single buckle. The amber's honey-dark tone is the one saturated colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the weapon's own markings rather than from decoration. Let one large rust-red ink bloom spread across the sky in the upper left, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular dark panel across the plain at the horizon as a graphic mask, and let one vertical strip of pale grey run down the frame's left edge from the sky to the grass. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “GREATSWORD FIELD” once, cut shallow into the crystal's flat and filled with white paint so the letters read as pale grooves that catch the light, sized so it spans about three quarters of the blade's visible width and reads clearly at thumbnail size.

Let every surface carry the shift. The blade's edge is nicked in three places and rounded by weather; the fuller's water has a scum line at one end; the crossguard's paint is chipped back to bare iron at its corners; the grip leather is split along one seam; the grass is flattened in a wide arc where the blade's shockwave once passed. Keep the wear physical and directional, never a uniform grime.

Build a second composition through the blade's shadow. The shadow lies across the grass as a long soft-edged band, dark enough to read as a shape but never black; the boundary where it crosses Miku's boots stays crisp; the shadow's far end frays into separate grass strokes. Never let the shadow read as a second blade.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One brass rivet at the guard's centre, a single strand of dead grass caught on the blade's lower edge, a thin line of frost along the fuller's water, and one loose thread at Miku's cuff. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where weather would put it.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: grass and the near shadow. Second: Miku and her own shadow. Third: the plain rising and the broken stump. Fourth: the blade's lower half and the water line. Fifth: the blade's upper mass and the sky. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every blade edge and grass blade, restrained risograph grain in the sky, crisp flat fills in the light areas, and one clean gradient only along the blade's sheen. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the blade's edge and the water.

No second character, no duplicate Miku, no crowd, no army, no banners, no flags, no horses, no birds, no wings, no halo, no second sword, no second blade of the same kind, no ornate filigree, no gemstones, no glowing crystal, no neon glow, no self-lit weapon, no rainbow dispersion, no stained glass, no plastic, no glass bottle, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no readable text beyond the string named above, no blood, no wounds, no armour plates, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no weapon in her hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no smoke shaped like objects, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like the plain after a war nobody remembers: one blade too large to be lifted still standing in dead grass, one small figure standing in its shadow looking up, and a second blade broken off at the stump behind her.

seeds.title: HALBERD TOWER
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “HALBERD TOWER”, a frame built around one colossal aquamarine weapon, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing at the base of a stone tower with a colossal halberd leaning against its top, the shaft running diagonally into the sky. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face and twin-tail outline readable against the tower's brick face.

The weapon is one solid mass of aquamarine glass: translucent, cold blue-green, lit from within, and it throws cyan light onto everything around it.

Use a camera at her chest height on a wide lens, set back and to her right so she is seen from three quarters and the tower rises out of frame at the left while the halberd's shaft crosses the upper right. Place Miku at approximately twenty-six percent of the canvas width, occupying about twenty-two percent of the frame height. Let the halberd's head hang above and behind the tower's parapet, its axe blade and spike both visible against the sky.

Give Miku exactly one core action: shading her eyes. Her right forearm is raised across her brow with the hand flat, her left hand on her hip, and her head tipped back to follow the shaft upward. Keep her elbows out, her feet apart, and put nothing in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the halberd: a colossal polearm fifteen metres long, its shaft as thick as a ship's mast, its head combining a broad axe blade, a down-curved hook and a straight spike. Rest it against the tower's parapet so the shaft leans at thirty degrees and the head overhangs the drop. Keep the head plain and forged — no engraving, no cloth, no gilding.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. the shaft and head are one piece of aquamarine, cold blue-green and translucent so the whole mass reads as one saturated stone, its interior holding a column of small voids climbing the length, its axe edge ground flat, and it takes colour only from what passes through; the head is blackened forged iron with a bright ground edge on the axe and a blunt spike; the tower is hand-made brick, uneven and pale, with a stone coping; the ground is dry paving with weeds in the joints; the sky is flat and bright. Each behaves differently — greyed oak shows a hard linear grain and one soft highlight, blackened iron holds almost no sheen except at its edge, brick reads as a fine horizontal grain with mortar joints, stone coping returns a dull flat plane, paving is a matte field with sharp weed strokes, the sky stays completely flat.

Build a stepped sequence up the frame. Begin at the bottom edge with the paving and its weeds, then Miku's boots and her hip, then her raised arm and upturned face, then the tower's brick face rising, then the coping and the leaning shaft, then the halberd's head against the sky. The sequence must read as an object resting against a building, not as a weapon planted beside one.

Leave one deliberate absence. The tower has no door. Its base is solid brick across the full width, with a single small window at the height of the coping and nothing at ground level but a shallow recess where a doorway was once walled up. Keep the recess's brickwork a shade lighter than the wall around it.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: paving and weeds. Middle ground: Miku, the tower's base, the walled recess. Background: the brick face rising, the coping, the leaning shaft and the halberd's head. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from a high sun at the frame's right. The sun is the key: a raking light that puts a hard bright edge along the shaft's upper side, lights the tower's brick face in even warm tone, and leaves the recess in shadow. Let the halberd's head catch one narrow bright line along the axe edge and let Miku be lit from her front right with a short shadow at her feet. Keep the sky blown to near white and never introduce a second source. Let the crystal pass the light rather than return it: one thin saturated cyan line where the mass is thickest, and one hard-edged cyan caustic patch thrown onto the paving beside it.

Lift Miku's extremely long twin tails in the wind that runs along the wall. Both tails stream to her left, the nearer one crossing her raised arm as a clean aqua mass, the farther one flattening against the brick behind her. Let the sun catch each tail's top edge as a warm rim.

Dress Miku in a surveyor's field layer over her canonical palette, not armour. A dark teal short jacket with the collar down, a pale shirt underneath with the sleeves rolled, dark trousers with a leather thigh strap, and scuffed boots. Keep the palette close to teal-and-black with the pale shirt as the only light garment, add one brass clip at her breast pocket, and keep the silhouette simple enough to read at thumbnail size.

Use a warm-on-pale palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty-six percent of the image is brick wall, twenty-two percent is flat sky, sixteen percent is the leaning shaft, ten percent is paving, six percent is the halberd's head, five percent is Miku's clothing, three percent is her aqua hair, and two percent is the stone coping and brass clip. Keep the cool note down to her hair and the crystal alone. The aquamarine's cold blue-green tone is the one saturated colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the tower's own survey marks rather than from decoration. Let one large deep-teal ink bloom spread across the sky in the upper left, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular black panel across the brick's lower band as a graphic mask at her shoulder height, and let one vertical strip of rust-red run down the frame's right edge from sky to paving. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “HALBERD TOWER” once, in black paint brushed across the brick face above her head at the height of the walled recess, the strokes following the mortar joints where they can, sized so it spans about two thirds of the wall's visible width and reads clearly at thumbnail size. Put no lettering on the shaft, the sky or her clothing, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The shaft is checked with three long splits and greyed in the middle where it has leaned for years; the head's blackening has flaked off along the axe's cheek; the brick is spalled around the recess and lime-washed unevenly; the paving is worn hollow where feet have turned; the weeds are dry and broken. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the paving. The paving carries the shaft's shadow as one long hard diagonal, the halberd's head as a small soft patch near the tower's base, and Miku's own shadow with her raised arm. Let the brick wall interrupt the shadow with a sharp vertical edge. Never let the paving mirror the tower.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One brass clip at her breast pocket, a single weed growing from the recess's sill, one lime-wash drip frozen down the brick beside the text, and a thin line of grit on the coping's edge. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where weather would put it.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: paving and weeds. Second: Miku's boots and hip. Third: her raised arm and the walled recess. Fourth: the brick face and the coping. Fifth: the leaning shaft and the halberd's head. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every brick joint and shaft check, restrained risograph grain in the wall, crisp flat fills in the sky, and one clean gradient only along the axe edge. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except that edge.

No second character, no duplicate Miku, no crowd, no guards, no banners, no flags, no birds, no wings, no halo, no second halberd, no additional weapon, no glowing crystal, no neon glow, no self-lit weapon, no rainbow dispersion, no stained glass, no plastic, no glass bottle, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no magical effects, no readable text beyond the string named above, no blood, no wounds, no armour plates, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no weapon in her hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like an inventory of something too big to move: a halberd leaning against a tower that has no door, a girl at its base shading her eyes, and a shaft that keeps going up past everything she can see.

seeds.title: DAM CREST
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 2:3 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “DAM CREST”, a frame built around one long amber crystal sword just cleared from its black sheath, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing on the bare concrete crest of a dam, the drawn blade held high beside her right shoulder and the empty scabbard hanging low from her left hand. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes and twin-tail identity readable against the pale concrete behind her.

The weapon is one solid mass of orange amber glass: translucent, warm orange-brown, lit from within, and it throws orange light onto everything around it.

Use a camera at her chest height on a normal lens, set three quarters to her right and far enough back that her whole figure, the raised blade, the hanging scabbard and the empty crest on both sides all sit inside the frame with air around them. Place Miku at approximately fifty percent of the canvas width, occupying about seventy percent of the frame height from her boots to the crown of her head, and keep her boots well inside the lower edge so nothing of her is cropped. Let the blade's tip reach into the frame's upper right and the scabbard's chape hang into its lower left, so the two objects stretch her silhouette across the whole picture.

Give Miku exactly one core action: having just cleared the blade. Her right arm is raised and carried back beside her right shoulder with the blade angled up and back, so the amber steel sits entirely clear of the sheath line; her left arm is held out from her side at roughly forty-five degrees below the horizontal, gripping the empty black scabbard by its throat so the scabbard cuts across the picture at its own angle instead of continuing the line of the blade. The two objects sit at opposite ends of her body and on crossed lines — bright amber high and rising on her right, black lacquer low and falling to her left — with her whole torso held between them. Her feet are planted a shoulder's width apart with her weight even, her chest open, her chin level and her eyes straight down the lens.

Construct the dominant visual object as two separate objects at opposite ends of her body. The blade is amber crystal, fully drawn and held high on an angle up and back, carrying one raised ridge down its spine, two flat faces and a single visible bevel on each edge with a bright line running its whole length. The scabbard is a black lacquered case as long as her thigh, hanging from her left hand with its brass throat at the top and its chape worn pale at the bottom, and it is visibly empty: a thin dark mouth shows at its throat with nothing inside it. Keep the amber blade and the black scabbard as two completely separate shapes on opposite sides of her silhouette, never touching, never overlapping and never merging into one line.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The blade is one piece of amber, honey-dark and translucent so its whole length reads as one saturated stone, its interior holding a faint cloudy core along the spine and its bevel ground to a hard edge; the scabbard is black lacquer, glossy on its flats and dusty in its seam; the brass throat and chape are dull, polished only where her hand has taken them; the crest is cast concrete, grey-white and porous, with a wet dark band along its seaward lip and a pale worn strip where feet have passed; the parapet rail is galvanised steel gone chalky; the water below is a flat grey sheet read through haze. Each behaves differently — crystal passes light and returns one thin orange line at its bevel, lacquer holds a long clean streak of sky, brass returns one soft warm spot, cast concrete reads as a flat matte field full of pinholes, galvanised steel breaks into a dull dotted line, water dissolves into haze.

Build a stepped sequence down the whole of her body. Begin at the frame's upper right with the amber blade raised beside her shoulder, then down her right arm to the shoulder itself, then across her open chest to her waist, then down her left arm to the black scabbard hanging at her side, then to her boots on the concrete, then out to the crest and the haze. The sequence must read as one finished motion — the blade already out, the sheath already empty — not as a girl holding a sword.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is nothing on the dam to have drawn against: no opponent, no post, no mark, no second figure anywhere along the visible crest. Let the concrete run empty from her to both frame edges, and keep the largest quiet area of the picture on the seaward side, where the crest meets the haze.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: her boots and the worn concrete at their contact. Middle ground: her legs, hips, the hanging black scabbard and the raised amber blade. Background: her torso and head, her twin tails, the crest, the parapet rail and the haze over the water. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from a low sun out of frame at her right, raking along the crest. The sun is the key: a hard warm light that puts one bright line down the blade's lower bevel, a crisp edge on her raised forearm, a rim along her jaw and a thin highlight down the scabbard's lacquered flat. Let the concrete hold the sun as a flat pale field one value below the blade, and let the water below go two values darker than the crest. Keep the sky out of the frame so no second large light source exists. Let the crystal pass the light rather than return it: one thin saturated orange line where the mass is thickest, and one hard-edged orange caustic patch thrown onto the concrete behind her boots.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails swing against her raised arm. The far tail is thrown across her back by the lift of her right shoulder and its end clears her hip; the near tail hangs straight down her front and drags one lock across her collarbone. Keep both tails as clean aqua shapes with hard edges, and route them so neither crosses the amber blade, the black scabbard or her eyes.

Dress Miku in a plain working layer over her canonical palette, not armour. A dark teal sleeveless top under an unbuttoned charcoal work jacket with the sleeves pushed to the elbow, dark trousers with a narrow brass belt, and boots scuffed pale at the toe. Keep every garment matte and unpatterned, so the only glossy surface in her half of the frame is the scabbard.

Use a cold grey field carrying one warm mass, under strict area control. Approximately thirty percent of the image is the pale concrete crest, twenty-four percent is the haze and the water below it, nineteen percent is the black scabbard and the amber blade, twelve percent is Miku's clothing, six percent is the parapet rail, five percent is her aqua hair, two percent is her skin at the hands and jaw, and two percent is the brass throat, the chape and her belt. Keep every warm note down to the crystal and the brass. The amber's honey-dark tone is the one saturated colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the dam's own markings rather than from decoration. Let one large black ink bloom spread across the concrete beside her, its edge breaking along the crest's pinholes, and let a single faded hazard stripe run along the seaward lip where the paint has worn through to bare grey. Keep all printed matter matte and weathered, as if it has stood in the weather for years.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “DAM CREST” once, stencilled in worn white paint across the concrete at her shoulder height, the strokes broken where the aggregate has spalled through, sized so it spans about half the visible width of that concrete face and reads clearly at thumbnail size. Put no lettering on the blade, the scabbard, her clothing or the rail, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The blade's bevel is polished bright and shows one faint thumbprint near its ricasso; the scabbard's lacquer is chipped at its mouth and holds a line of grit in its seam; the chape is worn through to bright brass at one corner; the concrete is pitted and carries a dark damp band along the crest with a pale polished strip where boots have crossed it. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the scabbard's lacquer. The scabbard carries the crest line as one long thin vertical streak, her left hand as a dark shape above it, and the raised blade as a bright diagonal at the picture's other edge. Let the reflection never mirror her face and never extend past the scabbard's own length.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One brass belt keeper, a single bead of water running down the blade's flat until it stops at the bevel, one loose thread at her jacket cuff, and a small chip of concrete lying beside her boot. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where the motion would have put it.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: her boots and the worn concrete at their contact. Second: her legs and the hanging black scabbard. Third: her hips, her belt and her left hand. Fourth: her torso, both shoulders and the raised amber blade. Fifth: her head, the crest, the rail and the haze. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each, with the exposed blade the brightest small area in the frame and the water the darkest.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp controlled edges, deliberate value grouping, no airbrush softness, fine grain in the flat fields, every highlight placed rather than suggested, and the whole image composed so it holds at poster scale and again at thumbnail scale.

No second character, no duplicate Miku, no crowd, no opponent, no birds, no wings, no halo, no second sword, no additional weapon, no second scabbard, no scabbard on her back, no single fused object, no sheath merged with the blade, no sword still inside a sheath, no glowing crystal, no neon glow, no self-lit weapon, no rainbow dispersion, no stained glass, no plastic, no glass bottle, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no magical effects, no readable text beyond the word named above, no blood, no wounds, no armour plates, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no third hand, no cropped hands, no cropped blade, no blade leaving the frame, no rock in frame, no stone block, no waterfall in frame, no turbine house, no vehicle on the crest, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no motion blur, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like the moment after a decision: one amber blade already up beside a shoulder, one black sheath already hanging empty at the other hand, and a kilometre of bare concrete with nothing left on it to cut.

seeds.title: AFTERGLOW
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “AFTERGLOW”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing on a mountain summit at night in a yukata, her back half turned to the camera and her face lifted toward a sky of fireworks opening over the valley below. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the burst light.

Use a camera at shoulder height on a normal lens, set behind and to her left on the summit's flat rock, so the ridge line runs across the lower third, the valley's dark mass fills the middle, and the sky holds the bursts across the upper half. Place Miku at approximately twenty-six percent of the canvas width, full body visible from wooden sandals to hair ornaments, occupying about thirty-four percent of the frame height, small against the drop.

Give Miku exactly one core action. She stands still at the very edge of the flat rock with her weight on her back foot and her hands clasped behind her waist, her chin lifted and her head tipped back so her face turns three quarters to the sky with both eyes open on the bursts. Her yukata's hem and the ends of her obi lift in the wind off the ridge, and nothing is in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the vista itself: four receding ridge lines stepping down into a valley of scattered town lights, a river running through the floor of the valley as one pale thread, and three fireworks open in the sky — one large chrysanthemum burst at the upper right, two smaller ones further left, with a long diagonal of grey smoke trailing away from them. Let the ridges occupy the middle band and the sky the upper half, and let the nearest ridge hold her and the summit's stone marker.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The summit rock is coarse grey stone, dry and wind-polished with lichen in its cracks; the low timber railing is silvered and gapped; the ridges are layered masses of near-black with a faint blue rim on each crest; the valley is a field of small warm points; the river is one cool grey thread; the bursts are clean radiating strokes of white-gold; the sky is deep blue-black; her yukata is printed cotton. Each behaves differently — stone scatters light, silvered timber goes matte, distant ridges absorb into blue, town light emits without texture, cotton moves.

Build a stepped sequence from the bottom edge upward. Begin with the summit rock and its lichen, then her sandals and the lifting hem, then her obi and her clasped hands, then her lifted profile, then the stone marker and the low railing, then the ridges stepping down, then the town lights and the river thread, then the bursts and the smoke, then the flat sky. The sequence must read as standing on a high edge above a whole valley, not as a rooftop.

Leave one deliberate absence. The summit itself is empty: no other walker on the flat rock, no one at the low railing, no tent and no bench. The only people in the frame stand far below on a lower viewing deck cut into the third ridge, where five small dark figures are no taller than her thumb.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the summit rock, its lichen, her sandals, the near post of the low railing. Middle ground: Miku, her obi, the stone marker, the ridge's crest and its wind-bent pine. Background: the four receding ridges, the town lights, the river thread, the bursts and the smoke. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the fireworks and from the town. The bursts are the cool key from in front of her and above: a white-gold wash on her forehead, the tops of her shoulders and the crest of the ridge she stands on. The town is the weak warm fill from below: an amber line along the underside of the railing, her hem and the marker's face. Keep the sky black between the bursts and let the ridges darken as they recede.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the two sources. Both tails stream sideways in the ridge wind, one clean aqua mass silvered along its upper curve by the bursts and warmed at its underside by the town. Let two strands cross her turned cheek and one end lift clear of her shoulder.

Dress Miku in an original summer-festival yukata derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not a generic kimono.
