She holds the round fan up in her right hand by its bamboo handle, the paper face turned flat to the lens and its rim level across her nose bridge, and her left hand rests at her obi with the fingers hooked into the tie. Her eyes look straight over the fan's rim into the lens, both open, the corners slightly narrowed, and nothing else is in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the fan itself: one flat circle of washi paper about two hand-spans across, stretched over a split bamboo frame whose ribs show through the paper as seven pale lines, with a dark lacquered handle and a printed design of a single large wave confined to the lower arc. Let the fan occupy about a quarter of the canvas area at its centre and let its paper be the brightest surface in the frame.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The fan's paper is thick washi, warm and slightly translucent, its fibres visible where the light strikes it edge-on; the ribs are split bamboo, pale and dry; the handle is black lacquer with one worn patch; her yukata is printed cotton; the lantern row behind is warm paper over bamboo, out of the key light; her hair is glossy; the firework is flat clean light. Each behaves differently — washi glows and shows fibres, bamboo holds a dry sheen, lacquer carries one hard specular, cotton goes matte, light emits without texture.

Build a stepped sequence from the bottom edge upward. Begin at the bottom with the fan's handle and her hooked left hand at the obi, then the fan's lower arc and its printed wave, then its rim across her nose, then her eyes and brows above it, then her hair ornaments, then the lantern row behind her shoulders, then the firework's flat disc above. The sequence must read as a face interrupted by a circle, not as a portrait holding a fan.

Leave one deliberate absence. The lane behind her is empty and still: no walkers, no stall fronts lit, no lantern swinging. The only things above her shoulders are the lantern row on its cord and the one firework's flat disc, and nothing crosses the fan's paper but the seven ribs.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the fan's paper, its ribs, its handle and her two hands. Middle ground: her eyes, brows and hair ornaments above the rim, her shoulders in the yukata. Background: the lantern row on its cord, the flat firework disc, the black lane. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the lantern row behind her and from the firework above it. The lanterns are the warm key from behind and slightly above, rimming her hair and the fan's upper edge with amber and leaving her eyes in soft shadow. The firework is the cool fill from high behind her shoulder, laying a thin blue-white line along the fan's paper and the top of her cheekbone. Keep her face's front plane at the darkest value in the frame so the eyes read as the brightest human note.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the two sources. Both tails fall behind her shoulders into the lane, one clean aqua mass rimmed amber at its crown by the lanterns and cold along the outer curve where the firework reaches it. Let one strand fall forward past the fan's handle without crossing the paper.

Dress Miku in an original summer-festival yukata derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not a generic kimono. A cotton yukata whose cloth is deep navy, almost black-blue, carrying small pale morning-glory flowers so the garment reads as a dark ground with light flowers rather than as a pale robe, a wide woven obi in teal and black tied at her back, the collar crossed left over right, one sleeve slipped slightly off the shoulder, her hair ornaments kept, and flat wooden sandals below the frame line. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale print.

Use a warm-paper-and-navy palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty-two percent of the image is the fan's warm paper and its printed wave, twenty-six percent is the dark lane and her shadowed front plane, eighteen percent is her navy yukata, nine percent is her aqua hair, eight percent is the amber lantern field, four percent is the flat firework light, and three percent is the black lacquer handle.

Drive the printed graphic language from the fan's own paper rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the fan's lower arc, printed flat and matte, its edge following the printed wave. Add a rectangular pale panel on the lane's far wall as a graphic mask at the height of her ear, and let one vertical strip of deep indigo run down that wall aligned to a lantern cord. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “ROUND FAN” once, large, in deep indigo ink printed on the fan's paper across its middle band, sitting above the printed wave and below the rim, spanning about two thirds of the fan's width, in heavy condensed capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “UCHIWA” sit on a small paper tag tied to the fan's handle. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the night. The fan's paper holds a soft crease down its centre and a faint water stain at its lower edge; the ribs show pale where the paper has been handled; the handle's lacquer is worn to wood at one point; her obi is flattened where it has been tied since morning; her collar keeps a crease from folding; the lantern row's paper is darker at every rib. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the fan's own translucency. The firework's light passes through the paper as one soft diffused disc with the seven ribs drawn across it as dark lines, so the fan carries the whole sky in reverse. Let that be the only place in the frame where the light comes through a surface rather than off it.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A folded second fan tucked into her obi at the back; one lantern cord knotted twice at the frame's edge; a paper tag tied to the fan's handle with a twist of cord; a wooden sandal showing at the very bottom edge; a single strand of hair caught on the fan's rim. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a festival lane would actually have it.

Illuminate with the lantern row as the only key and the firework as the only cool accent. Let the lanterns rim her hair, her shoulder and the fan's upper edge without reaching her eyes, and let the firework thin the paper from behind and place one cold line along her cheekbone. Keep her face's front plane at near-black so the eyes carry the whole expression.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the fan's paper and its rim. Second: her hands on the handle and at the obi. Third: her eyes, brows and hair ornaments. Fourth: the lantern row and the lane's far wall. Fifth: the flat firework disc and the black sky. Separate them by value steps of roughly ten percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every rib, fibre and flower print, restrained risograph grain in the dark fields, and the printed wave rendered as one flat clean shape with no soft edge.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no crowd in the lane, no vendor, no second fan in her hands, no bag, no umbrella, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no mask, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like a face hidden on purpose: one circle of paper taking the whole sky through it, a row of lanterns rimming her hair, and two eyes above the rim doing all the talking.

seeds.title: GOLD FISH
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “GOLD FISH”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character crouched at the edge of a shallow goldfish tank at a summer festival at night in a yukata, her paper scoop touching the water's surface with one hand and her other hand steadying the tank's rim. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the tank's reflected light.

Use a camera at her crouched eye level on a normal lens, set across the tank and slightly to her left, so the tank's near rim runs level across the lower third and the water's surface fills the middle band, with the stall's dark interior closing the top. Place Miku at approximately forty-eight percent of the canvas width, crouched with her knees together and her figure visible from sandals to hair ornaments, occupying about sixty percent of the frame height. Let the water fill the bottom half and her knees overlap its far edge.

Give Miku exactly one core action. She crouches low with her weight over her heels, her right hand holding a paper scoop by its rim so the paper just touches the water's surface, and her left hand flat on the tank's wooden rim with the fingers spread. Her head is tilted down toward the scoop but her eyes lift to the lens, and the scoop holds no fish yet.

Construct the dominant visual object as the tank as a whole: a shallow wooden tray about two paces wide, its frame worn pale at the rim, its lining a sheet of black vinyl, and the water inside standing an inch deep and perfectly still except where the scoop touches it. Let three goldfish hang in the water at different depths, one bright orange near the surface and two smaller and deeper, and let the tank occupy the lower half of the frame entirely.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The tank frame is worn pale timber, damp and darker at every joint; the water is a black mirror with a faint green cast; the goldfish are lacquer-bright orange with translucent tails; the paper scoop is white washi over a wire hoop, its paper already softened and slightly torn at one edge; her yukata is printed cotton, its hem folded up and tucked at the waist; the stall's interior is dark timber and hanging cloth. Each behaves differently — wet timber darkens and holds a sheen, water returns a broken image, fish carry one small specular, wet paper goes translucent, cotton goes matte.

Build a stepped sequence from the bottom edge upward. Begin at the bottom with the tank's near face and its joints, then the water's black surface and the three fish, then the scoop touching the surface and the ring it makes, then her hands, then her knees and the folded hem, then her lifted eyes, then the stall's dark interior above her head. The sequence must read as a working game being played, not as a still life of a tank.

Leave one deliberate absence. The tank holds only three fish and nothing else: no net but her own paper scoop, no second player's hand at the rim, no coins or tickets on the frame. The stall's counter behind holds one folded towel and an empty tray, and no vendor stands there.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the tank's near rim, its damp joints, the water's black surface. Middle ground: the three fish, the scoop and its ring, her hands, her knees. Background: the stall's dark frame and hanging cloth, one lantern above. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from one lantern hung low over the tank and from the festival's glow behind her. The lantern is the warm key from above and slightly in front: a close amber wash on the water's surface, the backs of her hands, the scoop's wet paper and her forehead. The festival behind is a weak warm fill on her shoulders and the cloth. Keep the stall's interior at near-black so the water reads as a black plate holding three bright fish.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the two sources. Both tails fall forward over her shoulders toward the tank, one clean aqua mass lit warm at its crown and cold in its shadowed underlayer, with the ends resting on her own knees rather than in the water. Let one strand hang clear of her cheek so the profile stays readable.

Dress Miku in an original summer-festival yukata derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not a generic kimono. A cotton yukata whose cloth is deep navy, almost black-blue, carrying small pale morning-glory flowers so the garment reads as a dark ground with light flowers rather than as a pale robe, a wide woven obi in teal and black, the collar crossed left over right, the sleeves tied back with a thin cord at each shoulder so they clear the water, her hair ornaments kept, and flat wooden sandals set side by side on the boards behind her. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale print.

Use a black-water-and-amber palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty percent of the image is the black water and the tank's dark interior, twenty-two percent is the pale worn timber of the rim and frame, twenty percent is her navy yukata, ten percent is the amber lantern wash, eight percent is her aqua hair, six percent is the three orange fish, and four percent is the white paper scoop.

Drive the printed graphic language from the tank's own boards rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the tank's near face at the lower left, printed flat and matte, its edge stopping at a joint. Add a rectangular pale panel on the stall's cloth behind her as a graphic mask at the height of her shoulder, and let one vertical strip of deep indigo run down the cloth aligned to the stall's post. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “GOLD FISH” once, large, in pale cream paint across the flat wooden face of the tank's near frame, spanning about two thirds of its visible width, in heavy condensed capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “POOL” sit on a small tin plate nailed to the frame's corner. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the night and the water. The rim is worn pale where hands have gripped it and dark where it stays wet; the water's surface carries one faint film line at the frame's edge; the scoop's paper is softened, translucent at the hoop and torn at one corner; her sleeve cords are knotted twice; her hem keeps a dark damp line an inch above its fold; the boards behind her hold wet sandal prints. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the water. The surface carries her two hands as dark shapes, the lantern as one warm disc broken by the scoop's ring, and the three fish as bright strokes that ignore the reflection entirely. Let the ring spread as two thin circles rather than one clean disc.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One spare paper scoop lying flat on the frame's edge; a small wooden bowl holding two fish on the boards; a folded towel on the counter behind; a paper ticket pressed under the tin plate; a coil of thin cord hanging from the stall's post. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a goldfish stall would actually have it.

Illuminate with the low lantern as the only key and the festival's glow as the only fill. Let the lantern put one broad warm disc on the water, one hard highlight on the wet paper and a warm edge on her knuckles, and let the fill place a soft band on her shoulders. Keep everything below the waterline at absolute black so the fish read as three bright marks in a void.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the tank's near face and rim. Second: the water surface, the scoop's ring, the near fish. Third: her hands and the two deeper fish. Fourth: her knees, her folded hem, her lifted eyes. Fifth: the stall's dark interior and the lantern. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every board joint and flower print, restrained risograph grain in the dark fields, and the fish rendered as flat clean orange with one small hard highlight each.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no vendor at the stall, no other player, no second hand at the rim, no crowd, no bag, no umbrella, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like the second before the scoop lifts: black water holding three bright fish, a ring spreading from wet paper, and a girl crouched so low that her hair almost touches her own knees.

seeds.title: FOX MASK
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “FOX MASK”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing in front of a festival mask stall at night in a yukata, holding a white fox mask up beside her own face at temple height so that its shadow falls across one cheek. Use a camera at her eye level on a normal lens, set square to the stall and slightly to her right, so the board of hanging masks fills the upper two thirds as a grid and the stall's dark counter closes the bottom. Place Miku at approximately forty-six percent of the canvas width, visible from the obi up in half figure, occupying about sixty-five percent of the frame height. Let the fox mask sit just left of her face at the height of her ear, its printed side turned toward the lens.

Give Miku exactly one core action. She holds the fox mask up in her right hand by its edge, the mask tilted about fifteen degrees, its painted side facing the lens, and her left hand hangs at her side with the fingers loose. Her chin turns a little toward the mask while her eyes stay on the lens, and the mask's shadow crosses the bridge of her nose and one cheek.

Construct the dominant visual object as the mask board: a dark timber frame strung with three rows of festival masks hung on hooks, every one a different face and each painted in its own colours — a red long-nosed goblin, a round-cheeked woman with two black brows, a wide-mouthed comic man, a round-eyed cat, a blue demon, a small white rabbit, a green frog and a dozen more — with two thin horizontal battens dividing the board. Let the board occupy the upper two thirds of the frame, and let every mask face the lens with its own expression so the wall reads as a crowd of painted faces.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The board's frame is dark stained timber with a raised grain; the masks are lacquered papier-mâché, chalky white with red and black painting, each hanging by a thin cord; the fox mask in her hand is the same papier-mâché but newer, its white brighter and its red still sharp; her yukata is printed cotton; the stall's counter below is worn pale timber; the lantern above is warm paper. Each behaves differently — stained timber absorbs, lacquer holds a chalky sheen and one small specular, cotton goes matte, paper glows.

Build a stepped sequence from the bottom edge upward. Begin at the bottom with the counter's worn edge, then the obi and her hanging left hand, then her raised right hand and the fox mask's chin, then her own face beside it, then the rows of masks climbing the board, then the board's top batten and the dark roof above. The sequence must read as standing in front of a wall of faces, not as a portrait holding a prop.

Leave one deliberate absence. Only one face in the frame is unpainted: the fox mask in her raised hand is bare white papier-mâché with its red and black brushwork left half finished at one ear, while every mask on the board behind her carries its own full colours. No price tags hang from the board and no vendor stands behind the counter.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the counter's worn edge and one hook lying loose on it. Middle ground: Miku, her raised hand, the fox mask, her own face beside it. Background: the board of brightly painted masks of many different faces, its battens, the dark roof and one lantern. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from one lantern hung above the board and from the festival behind her. The lantern is the warm key from above and in front: a close amber wash on the fox mask's painted brow, the back of her raised hand, her forehead and the board's upper batten. The festival behind is a weak warm fill on her shoulder and the top of her hair. Keep the board's lower rows and the counter at near-black.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the two sources. One tail falls forward over her raised shoulder so its tip hangs beside the fox mask's ear, the mask's white reflected as a thin cool line along the hair. The other tail drops behind her hip into the dark and is read only by one warm edge. Let one strand fall clear of her cheek so the shadow across her face stays unbroken.

A cotton yukata whose cloth is deep navy, almost black-blue, carrying small pale morning-glory flowers so the garment reads as a dark ground with light flowers rather than as a pale robe, a wide woven obi in teal and black tied at her back, the collar crossed left over right, long open sleeves falling away from the raised wrist, her hair ornaments kept, and flat wooden sandals below the counter line. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale print.

Approximately thirty-four percent of the image is the dark board and its shadow, twenty-four percent is the painted mask field, eighteen percent is her navy yukata, nine percent is her aqua hair, seven percent is the warm lantern wash, five percent is the red painting on the fox mask, and three percent is the worn pale counter.

Drive the printed graphic language from the stall's own paper rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the counter's front face at the lower left, printed flat and matte, its edge stopping at the counter's end. Add a rectangular pale panel on the stall's dark cloth at her left as a graphic mask at the height of her waist, and let one vertical strip of deep red run down the cloth aligned to the board's frame. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “FOX MASK” once, large, in deep red paint applied across the flat paper panel above the board's top batten, spanning about half the panel width, in heavy condensed capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “KITSUNE” sit on a small wooden tag hung from the counter's corner. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the night. The board's frame is worn at the hooks and darker where hands have brushed it; each hanging mask carries a dust line at its chin and a cord frayed where it meets the hook; the fox mask in her hand is newer but keeps one thumbprint in the lacquer at its edge; the counter is rounded and pale at its front; her obi is flattened where it has been tied since morning. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the lacquer of the fox mask. Its glossy brow carries the lantern as one small warm disc and the board's blank masks as a pale band, and the reflection stops at the mask's painted cheek line. Let that one small curved reflection be the only gloss in the frame.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A loose brass hook lying on the counter; a folded cloth on the counter's end; one spare cord coiled and hung from the board's frame; a paper ticket pressed under a hook; a small tin of red paint with its lid off at the counter's far end. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a mask stall would actually have it.

Fourth: the board's lower rows of painted masks and its battens. Fifth: the upper rows, the roof and the lantern. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no vendor behind the counter, no crowd, no second mask in her hands, no bag, no umbrella, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like standing in front of a wall of painted faces: a hundred small expressions hung in rows, one bare white fox lifted beside her cheek, and its shadow lying across her own cheek.

seeds.title: HANABI
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “HANABI”, a first-person view of Hatsune Miku as the only physical character two steps ahead of the camera on a summer festival street at night, walking away from the viewer and turning her head back over her shoulder to look into the lens with a bright open smile, her right hand reaching back to take the viewer's hand, wearing a yukata. Keep her face, her smile, her eyes, her hands and her twin-tail identity readable against the festival light.

Use a camera at her eye level on a normal lens, held by the viewer, so the frame is the viewer's own field of view: her body seen from behind and slightly above, her head turned back so both eyes meet the lens, and the viewer's own right forearm entering from the bottom edge of the frame in the near foreground with its hand closed around hers. Place her at approximately fifty-two percent of the canvas width, the figure from the hem of her yukata up to her hair ornaments filling about seventy percent of the frame height, with her obi sitting at the centre of the frame.

Give her exactly one core action. She walks forward while her torso twists back toward the viewer, her right arm reaching back and down so her hand meets the viewer's hand at the bottom of the frame with the fingers laced, and her left hand holding the front panel of her yukata at the hip. Her chin is dropped toward her shoulder, her eyes look straight into the lens, her mouth is open in a bright smile that lifts both cheeks and shows her upper teeth, and nothing else is in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the festival street itself: two rows of paper lanterns strung on a sagging line overhead, wooden stalls with hanging indigo cloth on both sides, and the packed-earth lane running between them. Let the lantern line occupy the top third in perspective, converging to a vanishing point just behind her head, and let the lane's dark surface fill the bottom third.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The lanterns are washi paper over bamboo ribs, warm and translucent, each with a dark wooden cap; the stall cloth is indigo cotton with a white crest and a raw stitched hem; the lane is packed earth, dark and dry with a scatter of straw; the stall counters are pale worn timber; her yukata is crisp printed cotton; her hair reads as one glossy mass. Each behaves differently — paper glows and shows its ribs, cotton absorbs and goes matte, timber holds a soft sheen, packed earth scatters light, hair carries one long specular.

Build a stepped sequence from the bottom edge upward. Begin with the viewer's forearm and the two joined hands, then the hem of her yukata and her wooden sandals, then the obi, then her turned face, then the lantern line rising to the vanishing point, then the flat night sky holding one small firework. The sequence must read as being pulled forward by the hand, not as a portrait of her.

Leave one deliberate absence. Both rows of stalls are shut for the moment: every counter stands empty with its cloth hanging still and no vendor behind any of them. The lane holds no walker within ten paces, and the only movement close to the lens is the lantern line swaying and the hem of her yukata lifting with her step. Far down the lane, beyond the third lantern, four visitors stand as small dark shapes.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the viewer's forearm, the joined hands, one lantern's near cap. Middle ground: her back, the obi, her turned face, the two rows of stall cloth. Background: the lane's vanishing point with its four distant visitors, the sagging lantern line, the small firework in the sky. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

The lantern line is the warm key: a soft amber wash from above, laying warm light on her shoulders, the back of her yukata and the curve of her turned cheek. The firework is the cool fill from the far end of the street: a faint blue-white pulse on the lantern tops, on the packed earth and along the edge of the viewer's forearm. Keep both sides of the lane at near-black.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the two sources. Both tails fall down her back in one clean aqua mass, warm along their upper curve from the lanterns and cold in their shadowed underlayer, with two strands caught across her turned cheek. Let the ends swing slightly forward with her step and lift clear of the obi.

Dress Miku in an original summer-festival yukata derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not a generic kimono. A cotton yukata whose cloth is deep navy, almost black-blue, carrying small pale morning-glory flowers so the garment reads as a dark ground with light flowers rather than as a pale robe, a wide woven obi in teal and black tied at her back, the collar crossed left over right, long open sleeves, her hair ornaments kept, and flat wooden sandals on bare feet. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale print, and keep the silhouette simple enough to read at thumbnail size.

Use a warm amber-and-navy palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty percent of the image is the dark lane and its shadow, twenty-four percent is the amber lantern field, twenty percent is her navy yukata, twelve percent is the indigo stall cloth, eight percent is her aqua hair, four percent is the cool firework glow, and two percent is the viewer's forearm in the near foreground.

Drive the printed graphic language from the festival's own cloth rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the packed earth at the lower left, printed flat and matte, its edge following a wheel rut. Add a rectangular pale panel on the stall cloth at her right as a graphic mask at the height of her waist, and let one vertical strip of deep indigo run down the cloth aligned to a stall post. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “HANABI” once, large, in pale cream paint on the flat cloth banner of the stall at her right, spanning about half the banner's width, in heavy condensed capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “MATSURI” sit on a narrow cloth strip tied to the nearest stall post at the left edge. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the night. The lantern paper is warm at its middle and darker at every rib; one lantern has a scorched lower edge; the stall counters are worn pale where hands have rested; the indigo cloth holds a crease at each fold; the packed earth keeps her sandal prints and a scatter of trodden straw; the back of her obi is flattened where it has been tied since morning. Keep the wear physical and directional, never a uniform grime.

Build a second composition through a puddle in the lane. The water holds the lantern line as a warm broken band, her sandals as two small shapes, her obi as a dark bar and the firework as one cold point, and the reflection stops at the puddle's near edge. Let her step break the band into dashes rather than one clean line.

Add a rectangular pale panel behind the machine row as a graphic mask at the height of the shaft line, and let one vertical strip of hazard yellow run from the truss to the floor, aligned to a column. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “IDLE WORKS” once, in white stencil letters applied to the near machine frame's side, chipped at the lower strokes, sized so it spans about a fifth of the frame width. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “HALL 2” sit on a small enamel plate bolted to the column at the left. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the shutdown. The machine frames hold a finger-thick film of oil dust that has been wiped once along a hand rail; the floor's oil band is darkest under the third frame and fades in both directions; the steel trusses show rust bloom only where water has run; the brick wall is dark to knee height and pale above; the belt lies in one stiff coil that has held its shape for years. Keep the wear physical and directional, never a uniform grime.

Build a second composition through the light. Each of the four shafts lays a pale parallelogram on the floor that repeats the shape of its broken pane, and each parallelogram carries the shadow of one truss crossing it. Let the third parallelogram pass under Miku's boots, so her shadow cuts the light rather than falling into it.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A brass pressure gauge with a cracked glass face, one wooden-handled valve wheel, a steel step plate worn bright in the centre, and a short chain hanging from the console with its last link hooked. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a machine hall would actually have it.

Illuminate with the four roof shafts as the only key, hard and pale, with a single flat cool ambient filling the rest. Let each shaft produce a hard-edged pool on the floor, a bright rim on any edge it crosses, and a visible cone in the dust. Keep the ambient just bright enough to read the far frames as shapes, and let the doorway stay at absolute black.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: coiled belt, oil band, steel step. Second: Miku, the console, the chain. Third: the first three frames with their shafts. Fourth: frames four and five in silhouette. Fifth: the far doorway and the high window. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every truss and frame edge, restrained risograph grain in the shadows, crisp flat fills in the lit areas, and fine rust flakes only where water would run. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the gauge glass.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no worker in the background, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no birds, no plants, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like a hall that stopped mid-shift and never restarted: four shafts of daylight crossing a row of identical machines, one missing flywheel still bright, and a girl standing with her hand on a console that no longer does anything.

seeds.title: INDIGO DRIFT
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “INDIGO DRIFT”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing inside a working indigo dye workshop at late afternoon. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands, hair ornaments and long twin-tail identity immediately readable against the hanging cloth.

Use a straight-on camera at chest height with a normal lens and almost no perspective distortion, so the cloth reads as a flat field of verticals. Place Miku in the left third of the frame, full body visible from sandals to hair ornaments, occupying approximately thirty percent of the image. She stands on a wet brick floor that catches a low sheen; her weight rests on the right leg and the left foot turns out. Her torso turns three-quarters toward the right side of the image and her head tilts down, both eyes open and clearly visible, following the cloth she is lifting.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Her left hand holds up one corner of a dripping indigo cloth at shoulder height, pinching only the selvedge between thumb and forefinger; her right hand hangs open at her hip with indigo stains across the palm and knuckles. The lifted corner pulls a shallow diagonal crease across the cloth and a single thread of dye runs down to her wrist. Keep the gesture still and the arms away from her face; add no second action and no tool in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as a drying rack of eleven indigo cloths, each five to nine meters long, hung in two staggered rows that fill approximately seventy percent of the canvas. The nearer row begins at the left edge and runs out of the top frame; the farther row is cropped by the right edge. Because they hang at different depths, their overlapping edges create a rhythm of vertical bands and narrow gaps of pale daylight. Let the far cloths pile up on the floor in soft blue-black pools that catch the wet floor's reflection.

Assign materials by zone rather than mixing them evenly. The cloth is hand-woven cotton with visible slub, darker at the wet hem and chalky where it has dried; the rack is oiled cedar with worn brass collars; the floor is wet terracotta with a thin film of standing water; the vats at the back are cracked enamel over cast iron; the wall is lime plaster with flaking edges and old indigo handprints. Each material must show its own behavior — cotton wicks and darkens, cedar dulls under water, brass keeps one sharp highlight, terracotta holds rings of dried dye, enamel shows rust blooming at the chips.

Build a stepped sequence across the eleven cloths. Begin at the left with a cloth only half dipped, its lower third saturated blue-black and its upper part still raw cream. Move right through cloths that grow progressively more uniform, then to cloths where the dye has bled into a soft gradient, then to one cloth that has dried pale and chalky with a crisp tide line. End at the far right with a cloth so faded it is almost grey, its edge fraying into separate threads. The sequence must read as time, not as decoration.

Leave one deliberate absence for the story. The fourth position in the nearer row is an empty gap where a cloth has been taken down; the rack's brass collar is still wet and a single blue drip marks the floor beneath it. Treat that empty interval as the brightest part of the composition, with clean pale daylight showing through and no object placed inside it.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: a cropped wooden vat rim at the lower left and a few loose threads lying on wet brick. Middle ground: Miku, the near row of cloths, and the rack. Background: the far row, the lime wall, one high shuttered window and a low doorway with daylight spilling across the floor.

Light the scene with low late-afternoon daylight entering from the high window at camera right. Let it rake across the cloth so each fold carries a warm edge and a cool shadow; let the wet floor throw a soft reflected glow upward onto the hems; let the lime wall receive a broad even wash. Keep the light physical and directional, with a single soft bounce from the wet floor and no glow, no bloom and no artificial rim light.

Weave Miku’s extremely long twin tails through the hanging cloth. The nearer twin tail falls in front of the second cloth, passes behind the rack post, and reappears between two bands as three separate aqua strands, each edge-lit by the window. The farther twin tail rises behind her shoulder and is partly hidden by a cloth edge. Keep the hair solid and clearly readable around her head, and allow it to separate into strands only where it physically crosses the cloth.

Dress Miku in a working dyer’s costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language. Use a heavy indigo-dyed apron of hand-woven cotton over a fitted pale inner layer, the apron bib fastened with two small brass buttons, one shoulder strap slipped down, wide rolled cuffs dark to the elbow, a short bandana knotted at the back of the neck, and bare forearms marked by dye to the wrist. Add a narrow leather waist tie, a single chalk mark on the apron where a measurement was taken, and three small coral thread tags at the hem. Keep the garment heavy, soaked and specific to the work rather than styled as fashion.

Use a restrained two-family palette. Approximately fifty-four percent of the image is indigo in its full range, from near-black wet cloth to pale chalky dried cloth. Fourteen percent is raw cream and undyed cotton. Twelve percent is wet terracotta and warm brick. Eight percent is pale daylight and lime plaster. Six percent is oiled cedar brown. Four percent is dull brass. Two percent is the single coral accent on the thread tags, and no more than one percent is the aqua of her hair and eyes.

Drive the printed graphic language from Miku’s own palette. Let one large indigo ink bloom spread across the lime wall behind the rack, its edge following the wall’s flaking plaster. Add two hard-edged rectangular resist blocks on the wall where cloths were hung against it, paler than the surrounding plaster. Let a fine halftone of dye spray sit only on the wet floor near the vats. Cut two clean pale knockout strips where daylight passes between cloths. Add rare brass microdots only at the rack collars and apron buttons.

Print the text as physical matter, not floating type. Hang a small hand-lettered paper tag from the rack’s left post, the exact readable words “INDIGO DRIFT” in a narrow brush script, indigo ink on cream paper, slightly warped by damp. Add one smaller tag marked with a batch number. Both tags hang below eye level and overlap a cloth edge so they read as objects in the room.

Let the surfaces show their history. The apron is soaked dark at the hem and dry at the shoulder, with one patch sewn in a different indigo. The floor holds shallow puddles that mirror the cloth in broken vertical bands. The cedar rack has one split board with a nail repair. The iron vat rims show rust crusted in rings. Nothing should look new.

Build a second composition through shadow and reflection. The wet floor mirrors the cloths as broken blue verticals that stop where the floor dries. The window throws a bright trapezoid across the floor and up the left wall, cutting through the reflected cloth. The empty fourth position leaves an unbroken vertical of pale light in both the cloth row and the reflection below it, so the absence repeats twice.

Add only a few luxury details, all at connection points. A narrow brass hook at each collar, one worn leather thimble on the rack post, three coral thread tags, a folded paper pattern pinned to the wall, and a small enamel measuring cup on the vat rim. Keep them subordinate to the cloth and never scattered across the empty gap.

Illuminate with the single high window plus one warm practical hanging lamp at the back right, just lit, adding a small pool of ochre on the far wall without competing with daylight. Keep every shadow soft-edged and physically consistent, and let the brightest area remain the empty fourth position.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the cropped vat rim, loose threads, one puddle edge. Primary middle ground: Miku, her lifted cloth corner and the near rack row. Secondary: the far rack row and the wall behind it. Tertiary: the lime wall, doorway and the hanging lamp. Background: the pale daylight beyond the doorway, held as clean negative space.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a hand-pulled print: crisp drawn linework, watercolor and ink washes with visible wet edges, dry-brush erosion on the cloth folds, soft paper grain across the flat areas, and clean indigo lithograph texture in the shadows. Keep the drawing precise and the paint loose, with no photographic depth of field.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no floating interface, no holograms, no glowing particles, no abstract light streaks, no full-canvas glitch, no random letters or numbers, no watermark, no signature, no muddy background, no neon, no rainbow lighting, no face obstruction, no cloth covering her eyes, and no malformed hands. Preserve a strict hierarchy: Miku’s face and lifted cloth corner first, the near rack row second, the empty fourth position third, the far row and wall fourth, then typography, shadow and pale negative space.

The final image should feel like a workshop where colour is made by hand and time is measured in how wet a cloth still is: eleven lengths of cloth, one missing, one hand lifting a corner, and the whole room held in the single minute before the light leaves the window.

seeds.title: BELL TOWER
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “BELL TOWER”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing on the worn stone steps of a bell tower's spiral stair, one hand on the central newel. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the pale stone.

Use a camera at chest height on a normal lens, set on the flight below her and looking up, so the stair's curve sweeps out of the frame's lower left, the newel rises through the centre, and one narrow window throws a hard wedge of light across the steps. Place Miku at approximately forty-six percent of the canvas width, full figure visible from her shoes to her hair ornaments, occupying about fifty-eight percent of the frame height, standing on the fourth step from the window.

Give Miku exactly one core action. She stands on the step with her weight on her front foot, her right palm flat on the newel's stone and her left arm hanging at her side, her chin lifted toward the light. Her eyes come down along the stair to the lens, and nothing is in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the spiral stair itself: a drum of pale stone steps winding around a solid central newel, each tread worn hollow in its middle and scarred at its nosing, with a rough stone wall on the outer side pierced by one narrow slit window and a rope handrail looped through iron rings. Let the curve carry the eye from the bottom edge up around the newel and let the window's wedge cut it.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The treads are pale limestone, hollowed and slightly polished by feet; the newel is the same stone, darkened to hand height; the outer wall is rough coursed stone with mortar joints; the slit window is a plain opening with a deep splayed reveal; the rope handrail is hemp, dark and frayed; the iron rings are rusted. Each behaves differently — worn limestone holds a soft sheen, rough stone absorbs, a deep reveal traps shadow, rope goes matte and hairy, rust bleeds a warm stain.

Build a stepped sequence winding upward. Begin with the lowest tread and its hollow, then the nosing's scar, then her shoes and her hand on the newel, then her standing figure, then the slit window and its wedge, then the curve of treads above her, then the dark at the stair's top. The sequence must read as climbing a tower that is never used, not as a castle postcard.

Leave one deliberate absence. The tower is empty: no bell rope hanging, no ladder, no dust sheet, no tools, no graffiti, no birds. The only objects in the frame besides her are the stair, the newel, the rope rail and the window's reveal.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the lowest tread and its hollow. Middle ground: her shoes, her hand on the newel, her body. Background: the slit window's wedge, the curving treads above and the dark stairwell. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the slit window alone. The window is the key: a narrow hard wedge of daylight crossing the newel and three treads, catching the side of her face, her forearm and the rope's fibres, while the rest of the drum stays in cool shade. Add one weak bounce from the pale treads, which touches the underside of her chin and the inner faces of the steps. Keep the stair's top and the wall's lower corner at near-black.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the light. Both tails fall across the treads behind her in one clean aqua mass, one band of light crossing their middle where the wedge reaches, the ends pooling on the stone below. Let one strand fall forward across her raised shoulder.

Dress Miku in an original tower-stair costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not medieval dress. A long dark coat worn closed with the collar up over a pale high-necked top, dark trousers and low boots, the coat's hem falling to mid-calf and catching on the steps. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment, and keep the silhouette narrow so the newel's curve reads around her.

Use a pale-stone-and-shadow palette with strict area control. Approximately forty percent of the image is pale limestone in shade, twenty-two percent is the rough outer wall and its joints, fourteen percent is the window's wedge and its bright reveal, twelve percent is her dark coat, six percent is her aqua hair, four percent is the hemp rope, and two percent is the rust of the rings.

Drive the printed graphic language from the stone's own coursing rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the lowest tread at the lower left, printed flat and matte, its edge following the tread's nosing. Add a rectangular pale panel on the outer wall as a graphic mask at the height of her shoulder, and let one vertical strip of deep oxide red run down that wall aligned to a mortar joint. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “BELL TOWER” once, large, in pale grey paint carved into the flat face of the outer wall above her head, spanning about half the wall's visible width, in heavy condensed capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “LEVEL 4” sit on a small brass plate screwed to the newel below her hand. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry centuries of feet. Every tread is hollowed in its middle and scarred at its nosing, one chipped at its outer corner; the newel is darkened and slightly polished to the height of a hand; the outer wall's mortar is eroded in a horizontal band; the rope rail is frayed where it passes each ring and shiny where hands slide; the rings are rusted with a warm stain running down the stone. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the worn treads. Each tread catches the window's wedge as one bright sliver, and the slivers repeat around the curve, diminishing with distance, so the whole stair reads as a spiral of highlights. Let that be the only place in the frame where the light is repeated rather than single.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One iron ring rusted into the stone with its stain; a frayed section of the rope rail; a chipped outer corner on the third tread; a chalk scratch on the newel; a single dry leaf caught at the wall's foot. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where an old tower stair would actually have it.

Illuminate with the slit window as the only key and the treads' bounce as the only fill. Let the wedge light the newel, her face and three treads, let the bounce keep her chin and the step's inner faces readable, and keep the stair's top and the wall's lower corner at absolute black so the drum reads as a dark spiral with one bright cut in it.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the lowest tread and its hollow. Second: her shoes and the tread below them. Third: her hand on the newel and her body. Fourth: the window's wedge and the treads above. Fifth: the dark stairwell and the stone drum's curve. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every tread nosing and mortar joint, restrained risograph grain in the shaded stone, and the light wedge kept as one hard-edged shape.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no bell rope, no ladder, no tools, no birds, no graffiti, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no cobwebs, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like the fourth turn of a climb: stone treads hollowed by feet, one slit of daylight cutting the newel, and a girl standing with her palm flat on the column and her hair spilling down the steps behind her.

seeds.title: BLAST FURNACE
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “BLAST FURNACE”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing on a steel platform halfway up a disused blast furnace, one hand on the handrail. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the rusted steel.

Use a camera at hip height on a normal lens, set on the opposite platform and slightly below her, so the furnace's rusted casing rises on the left, the open grate floor fills the lower band, and a lattice of pipes and stairs closes the right. Place Miku at approximately thirty-four percent of the canvas width, full figure visible from her boots to her hair ornaments, occupying about forty percent of the frame height.

Give Miku exactly one core action. She stands still with her weight on one leg and her right hand closed over the platform's top rail, her left arm hanging loose, her chin turned toward the furnace's casing. Her eyes come back along the platform to the lens, and nothing is in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the furnace body: a huge riveted steel casing about four storeys tall, its surface scaled in rust, broken by two ring girders, a row of tuyère stubs along one band, and a single inspection hatch standing open on its dark interior. Let the casing occupy the frame's left half and let the plate seams run in long horizontals that dwarf her.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The casing is riveted steel plate, scaled in orange rust with dark runs below each seam; the ring girders are heavier steel, painted once in grey now almost gone; the tuyère stubs are short cast nozzles, their mouths black; the platform is open steel grating with a chequered toe board; the stairs are steel with worn treads; the pipes behind are lagged in silver foil gone dull. Each behaves differently — rusted plate scatters light warmly, cast iron goes dull and pitted, open grating reads as a dark mesh, worn treads show bright metal, foil carries a dull sheen.

Build a stepped sequence from the platform upward. Begin with the open grating and the drop beneath it, then her boots on the toe board, then her hand on the rail, then her body against the casing, then the casing's rivet rows and seams, then the ring girders, then the pipe lattice and the pale sky beyond. The sequence must read as standing on a catwalk inside a dead furnace, not as an industrial portrait.

Leave one deliberate absence. The plant is empty of work: no welder's arc, no crane, no scaffolds, no drums, no cable coils on the grating, no graffiti. The only objects in the frame besides her are the casing, the platform, the stairs and the pipes, and the only mark on the grating is the scatter of rust flakes under her boots.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the open grating and the drop below. Middle ground: her boots, her hand on the rail, her body. Background: the casing's rivet rows, the ring girders, the pipe lattice and the pale sky. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the open sky at the plant's top. The sky is the key: a low warm light raking in from the right, throwing a long rust-coloured glow across the casing's plate seams and lighting her shoulder, her cheek and the rail's top edge. Add one cool fill from the pale sky behind her, which keeps the platform's underside and her dark side readable. Keep the furnace's interior hatch and the platform's depth at near-black.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the light. Both tails stream slightly in the draught, one clean aqua mass lit warm along its upper curve by the low light and darker underneath, the ends lifting clear of the rail. Let one strand cross her cheek as she turns.

Dress Miku in an original furnace-catwalk costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not workwear. A dark close-fitting jacket with a high collar and taped seams, dark cargo trousers gathered at the boot tops, a thin harness across the chest and a small respirator hanging at her hip. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale zip line, and keep the silhouette compact against the rust.

Use a rust-and-steel palette with one pale sky and strict area control. Approximately thirty-eight percent of the image is rusted plate, twenty-two percent is the pale sky and its light, sixteen percent is the steel platform and stairs, twelve percent is the pipe lattice, eight percent is her dark kit, and four percent is her aqua hair.

Drive the printed graphic language from the steel's own plate seams rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the casing's lower plate at the left, printed flat and matte, its edge following a seam. Add a rectangular pale panel on the casing's flat face as a graphic mask at the height of her shoulder, and let one vertical strip of deep oxide red run down the plate aligned to a rivet column. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “BLAST FURNACE” once, large, in pale grey paint stencilled across the flat steel face beside the ring girder above her, spanning about half the visible plate width, in heavy stencil capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “NO 1” sit on a small steel plate bolted to the platform's rail post. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry heat and time. The plate is scaled in orange rust with dark runs below each seam and bare grey where a boot has scraped it; the ring girders' paint survives only in patches; the tuyère mouths are black and ringed with soot; the grating is worn bright along the walking line and holds rust flakes in its mesh; the rail is polished at one point where hands rest; the stairs' treads are worn hollow. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the open hatch. Its black interior carries a faint grey bloom of daylight on the inner wall and the silhouette of a tuyère stub, and nothing else — no fire, no glow, no machinery. Let that hatch be the only place in the frame where the subject is a void rather than a surface.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One open inspection hatch with its hinge seized; a row of soot-ringed tuyère stubs; a cable tie hanging from the rail; a rust flake caught in the grating's mesh; a bolted repair patch on the casing with newer rivets. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a dead furnace would actually have it.

Illuminate with the low sky light as the only warm key and the pale sky behind her as the only fill. Let the low light rake the plate seams and rim her shoulder and the rail, let the fill keep the platform's underside readable, and keep the hatch and the platform's depth at absolute black so the casing reads as a warm wall of rust above a dark drop.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the open grating and the drop. Second: her boots and the toe board. Third: her hand on the rail and her body. Fourth: the casing's rivet rows and girders. Fifth: the pipe lattice and the pale sky. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every rivet row, seam and tread, restrained risograph grain in the rust, and the sky kept as one flat clean tone.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no welder, no crane, no scaffolds, no drums, no cable coils, no fire, no sparks, no graffiti, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no vines or weeds, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like a dead furnace at dusk: a wall of scaled rust with its rivets in long rows, a catwalk of open grating, and a girl standing at the rail with one hand on the steel and the whole drop below her boots.

seeds.title: CANTILEVER YARD
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium industrial editorial poster titled “CANTILEVER YARD”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character, a tiny full figure on a narrow maintenance platform near the lower-left third, inside a colossal brutalist cantilever assembly yard seen from ground level through an extreme low-angle wide-angle perspective. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, a slim virtual-singer silhouette, and her original grey-and-teal costume structure. Keep her face, both eyes and both hands fully readable at thumbnail size.

Concentrate the main architectural mass in the upper-right and central areas. Several enormous concrete cantilever platforms project horizontally from a monumental tower on the right, extending far toward the left and beyond the canvas edges. Suspend a gigantic unfinished cylindrical machine beneath the central platform using heavy steel clamps, crane cables and articulated mechanical arms.

Build the assembly yard from weathered concrete slabs, exposed steel trusses, segmented support ribs, maintenance gantries, suspended cages, industrial ladders, narrow walkways, railings, ventilation openings, pulley housings, docking clamps and dense hanging cable bundles. Add two large overhead crane tracks crossing diagonally through the upper portion of the image. Keep believable structural connections, varied platform depths and strong perspective convergence.

Leave a broad area of pale sky and luminous atmospheric haze in the upper-left quadrant. Use this open region to separate the projecting industrial structures and establish clear negative space for the poster identity.

Place Hatsune Miku on a narrow maintenance platform near the lower-left third, shown from behind as a tiny full-body figure occupying less than five percent of the canvas, looking upward toward the suspended cylindrical machine. Her feet are set one behind the other on the grating and both arms hang loose at her sides.

Weave Hatsune Miku’s extremely long aqua twin tails into the light between the cantilevers. Both tails stream toward the centre of the composition, linking the small figure to the suspended machine, pale where the daylight strikes them and almost black at the tips. Her aqua hair remains the only character colour.

Dress Hatsune Miku in an original assembly-yard costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not workwear. A short dark technical jacket with sealed seams, tapered charcoal trousers tucked into low reinforced boots, a narrow printed band across the chest, and a thin alloy clamp detail at one hip. Keep the values dark and the shapes simple so she stays a scale marker rather than a portrait.

Render the physical environment in cement white, cold gray, graphite, charcoal black and muted metallic silver. Strong daylight enters from the upper-left sky, illuminating concrete edges and producing deep shadows beneath the cantilever platforms. Add atmospheric dust, pale mist, concrete seams, scratched steel, surface stains and restrained cinematic grain.

Separate the design into a flat industrial warning layer and a physical signal-light layer.

The flat warning layer uses safety orange, pure white and deep black exclusively. Place one dominant warning composition at the upper-right canvas edge. Construct it from three broad safety-orange diagonal bars, one solid orange rectangular field and two smaller angular orange fragments. Crop the outer ends beyond the top and right edges. Use forty-five-degree cuts, disciplined spacing, worn stencil texture, chipped ink and tactile screen-print grain.

Connect this orange warning composition to the main architecture by aligning its lower edge with the direction of the largest cantilever platform. Let selected orange fragments overlap the silhouette of the platform as flat poster-plane graphics while several smaller orange markings appear as stencil paint on the platform’s structural edge.

Place one restrained black-and-white diagonal caution block on a lower-right concrete beam. Add several small orange maintenance plates to the suspended cylindrical machine and docking clamps. Keep large uninterrupted areas of gray architecture and pale sky between the warning regions.

Yellow is reserved exclusively for physical signal lighting on the gray and black architecture. A gigantic linear conveyor structure stretches diagonally from the upper-left side toward a monumental support tower on the right. The main transport spine contains two parallel steel rails, segmented concrete housings, suspended cargo clamps, mechanical rollers, maintenance decks and a continuous central transfer channel.

Place Hatsune Miku as a tiny full-body figure on a narrow maintenance platform in the lower-left quadrant, shown from behind and looking diagonally upward along the cargo spine toward the support tower on the right. Begin with a dense opaque orange field at the far-right and lower-right edges. Gradually reduce the orange opacity toward the central architecture, revealing the concrete pylon, steel trusses, railings and structural shadows beneath the translucent inner area.

Place a smaller orange outline version of the same cargo-spine emblem beside “SECTOR-03” inside the orange mask. Use identical proportions so both versions clearly belong to the same visual identity.
