seeds.title: CLOISTER
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “CLOISTER”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing at the third arch of a stone monastery cloister, one hand resting on the pier as she looks out into the sunlit courtyard. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the courtyard light.

Use a camera at chest height on a normal lens, set inside the walkway and about three paces off the arcade's axis, so the arches run in perspective down the right of the frame and the courtyard's bright wall closes the far end. Place Miku at approximately forty-four percent of the canvas width, full figure visible from her shoes to her hair ornaments, occupying about fifty-eight percent of the frame height, with her near shoulder in the walkway's shade and her face turned to the light.

Give Miku exactly one core action. She stands still with her weight on her back foot and her right palm flat on the stone pier beside her, her left arm hanging at her side, her head turned three quarters toward the courtyard and her chin level. Both eyes are open toward the light, and nothing is in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the arcade itself: a run of five round-headed arches carried on short coupled columns with worn capitals, a stone bench along the walkway wall, a ribbed stone vault above, and the courtyard's bright wall and one cypress beyond the arches. Let the arches occupy the right half in perspective and let the vault close the top of the frame.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The piers and columns are pale limestone, pitted and grey at their bases; the capitals are carved and softened by hands; the vault is plastered and stained in the corners; the walkway floor is worn flagstone with a polished path down its centre; the bench is the same stone, hollowed slightly; the courtyard beyond is bleached bright. Each behaves differently — limestone scatters light and holds grit in its pores, carved stone takes a soft shadow, plaster goes flat, polished flagstone returns a long dim reflection, sunlit courtyard blows out to near-white.

Build a stepped sequence from the near floor to the far wall. Begin at the bottom with the flagstones and their polished path, then Miku's shoes and the hem of her dress, then her hand on the pier and her hanging arm, then her turned face in the arch's light, then the arches receding and their coupled columns, then the bench and the vault's ribs, then the courtyard's bright wall and its cypress. The sequence must read as standing in a covered walk looking out, not as a church interior.

Leave one deliberate absence. The cloister is empty of other figures: no monk in the walkway, no visitor in the courtyard, no one on the stone bench. The only things in the frame besides the architecture are her, a single fallen leaf on the flagstones and one iron lamp bracket on the wall.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the near flagstones, the polished path, her shoes. Middle ground: Miku, her hand on the pier, the coupled columns and the bench. Background: the receding arches, the vault, the courtyard's bright wall and the cypress. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the courtyard through the arches. The courtyard is the key: hard afternoon sun reflected up off its bleached wall, throwing a bright wash through each arch onto the columns' inner faces and the flagstones' polished path, while the walkway's vault stays in deep shade. Add one weak cool bounce from the shaded wall behind the camera, which keeps her shadow side just readable. Keep the vault's far end at near-black.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the two sources. Both tails fall down her back, one clean aqua mass with a bright band of courtyard light across its middle where an arch frames it and deep shade above and below. Let two strands fall forward over her turned shoulder and catch the light along their edge.

Dress Miku in an original cloister costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not a habit. A long dark coat with a narrow collar worn open over a pale high-necked top, dark trousers and low boots, the coat's hem falling to mid-calf and its fabric matte. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment, and keep the silhouette narrow so the vertical columns read around her.

Use a limestone-and-shade palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty-four percent of the image is shaded stone and vault, twenty-four percent is the sunlit wall and the light thrown through the arches, eighteen percent is the pale flagstone floor, twelve percent is her dark coat, seven percent is her aqua hair, and five percent is the carved capitals' warm faces.

Drive the printed graphic language from the stone's own coursing rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the near flagstones at the lower left, printed flat and matte, its edge following a joint. Add a rectangular pale panel on the walkway wall as a graphic mask at the height of her shoulder, and let one vertical strip of deep oxide red run down the wall aligned to a pier's edge. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “CLOISTER” once, large, in pale grey paint carved into the flat stone lintel above the nearest arch, spanning about half the lintel's width, in heavy condensed capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “WEST WING” sit on a small brass plaque screwed to the wall beside the bench. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry centuries of use. The flagstones are hollowed in the centre of the walking path and gritty at their joints; the columns' bases are grey and pitted by damp; the capitals are softened where hands have touched them; the bench's edge is worn into a shallow curve; the vault's corners hold a dark stain where water has stood; her coat keeps a crease across the elbow from carrying. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the polished flagstones. The stone path carries the arches as a run of bright half-circles repeated and diminishing, the courtyard's wall as one bright band and her own figure as a soft dark shape at the third arch. Let the reflection be dim and long, and stop where the path's polish ends.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One fallen leaf on the flagstones; an iron lamp bracket on the wall, unlit; a shallow stone basin set into the walkway's edge; a worn step at the nearest arch; a small drain slot with grit caught in it. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a monastery walk would actually have it.

Illuminate with the courtyard's reflected sun as the only key and the shaded wall as the only fill. Let the light throw one bright arch-shaped patch on the flagstones beside her and rim the columns' inner faces, let the fill keep her coat's shadow side readable, and keep the vault and the walkway's far end at absolute black.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the near flagstones and the leaf. Second: her shoes and the coat's hem. Third: her hand on the pier and her turned face. Fourth: the coupled columns, the bench and the caps. Fifth: the receding arches, the bright wall and the cypress. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every stone course and carved capital, restrained risograph grain in the shaded vault, and the light patches kept as hard flat shapes with no soft edge.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no monk, no visitor on the bench, no birds, no potted plants, no candles, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like a walk built for shade: five arches running away with the courtyard burning at the end of each, a polished path holding half-circles of light, and a girl standing at the third pier with her palm flat on the stone.

seeds.title: CONVEYOR
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “CONVEYOR”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing beside a stationary coal conveyor inside an elevated enclosed gallery. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the pale steel and the dark rubber belt.

Use a camera at her chest height on a normal lens, set at the gallery's near end and square to the belt run, so the conveyor recedes in one long perspective to a bright rectangular opening at the far end and the gallery's ribs march down both sides. Place Miku at approximately thirty percent of the canvas width, full figure visible from her boots to her hair ornaments, occupying about fifty percent of the frame height, standing on the maintenance walkway with her right palm resting on the belt's side skirt.

Give Miku exactly one core action. She stands with her weight on her back foot, her right hand flat on the top edge of the belt's steel skirt at hip height, and her left arm hanging at her side with the fingers loose. Her shoulders are square to the camera, her chin is lifted and both eyes come straight to the lens. Nothing is held in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the conveyor itself: a wide rubber belt running down the centre of the gallery on a dense row of steel idlers, edged on both sides by a raised skirt and a low handrail, occupying approximately fifty-two percent of the canvas. The belt is empty and motionless, its surface carrying a fine even coal dust, and the idler row reads as one continuous repeating rhythm into the distance.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The belt is heavy black rubber, matte in the middle and slightly polished along two tracking lines; the skirt and handrail are painted steel in a municipal grey-green, chalky and chipped; the idlers are bare steel rollers, bright where the belt has run and rusted at their ends; the gallery's ribs are galvanised lattice with a fine even dust; the walkway is steel grating over a solid channel; the far opening is a bright rectangle of pale daylight. Each behaves differently — rubber swallows light, chalky paint scatters, polished rollers keep thin bright lines, galvanising goes flat grey, grating prints a dark grid, and the opening stays a blown-out rectangle.

Build a sequence down the belt from the near end. Begin at the belt's near edge and its tracking line. Move along the belt's dusty surface to her palm on the skirt, then to the nearest idlers and their bright crowns, then up the gallery's ribs and the handrail, then down the long receding belt to the bright opening at the far end. The sequence must read as a gallery built to carry coal, not as a corridor with a machine in it.

Leave one deliberate absence. Ten metres down the belt, a section of the rubber has been cut out and rolled back, leaving the idler row exposed for about a metre, its rollers bare, bright and motionless under the light. Keep that exposed stretch as the sharpest, emptiest shape in the frame and put nothing on it.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the near belt edge and the walkway grating. Middle ground: Miku, her palm on the skirt and the first five idlers. Background: the long belt run, the exposed idler stretch, the receding ribs and the bright opening at the end.

Light the scene from the bright opening at the far end and from one strip of high windows along the left wall, so the gallery is lit in two directions: a long gradient down the belt toward the opening, and hard diagonal bars across the ribs from the windows. Let her face take the window light from the left with a soft falloff, and keep the belt's black surface the darkest mass in the frame.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the gallery's draught. Both tails are drawn back along the belt's direction, lifted clear of her shoulders and streaming toward the bright opening, so they read as two long aqua lines following the perspective. Keep the hair dense and clearly readable around her head and let it be the only curved, moving shape among the straight steel lines.

Dress Miku in an original conveyor-gallery costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language. Use a short work jacket in pale grey with a high collar and two chest pockets, worn over a dark fitted layer, with dark straight trousers and low laced boots. Add a thin reflective band around one sleeve, a small pass on a lanyard at her chest and a webbing belt with one buckle. Let a fine even film of coal dust sit on her shoulders and the tops of her boots.

Use a grey-and-black palette with one bright note and strict area control. Approximately thirty-two percent of the image is the black rubber belt. Twenty-four percent is painted steel skirt and handrail. Sixteen percent is the bright opening at the far end. Twelve percent is galvanised rib and grating. Eight percent is her pale jacket and dark trousers. Four percent is bare steel idler. Less than four percent is the aqua of her hair and the reflective band.

Drive the printed graphic language from the idler rhythm rather than from decoration. Let one large rust-red ink bloom bleed along the belt's near edge, printed flat and matte, its upper boundary following the tracking line. Place two hard-edged rust-red rectangular colour blocks in the receding space, one at the height of her knee and one high near the opening, both square to the frame so they cut across the perspective. Add a halftone dot gradient that gathers under the belt and dissolves toward the far opening. Cut several clean white knockout strips along the gallery's ribs so the steel appears to pass through the printed layer.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “CONVEYOR” once, large, in pale grey stencil paint on the belt's side skirt at her hip, spanning about a third of the visible skirt and interrupted once by her palm, in heavy condensed capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “CV-3” sit stencilled on the handrail's post beside her. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry its load. The belt is dusted evenly with a faint darker band along both tracking lines; the skirt's paint is chipped in a long horizontal run where the belt has rubbed; the idlers are bright in a narrow crown and rusted at their bearings; the grating holds dust in every square and two clean patches where boots have stood; the ribs carry a fine even film that thickens at their joints. Keep the wear linear and aligned with the belt.

Build a second composition through the exposed idler stretch. Where the rubber has been cut away, the bare rollers print a row of bright horizontal bars that step down toward the opening, each one shorter than the last, so the gap reads as a ladder of light set into the belt. Keep that ladder geometric only: no figure, no shadow of a person, no second silhouette in the opening.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. The pass on her lanyard; the reflective band on her sleeve; one bright crown on a near idler; a single bolt missing from the handrail's post; the clean boot-shaped patches in the grating dust. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a conveyor gallery would actually show it.

Illuminate with the far opening as the only key down the belt and the high windows as the only cross light. Let the belt fall away into one long dark gradient toward the light, let each rib hold a hard diagonal bar, and keep her face a stop above the steel behind it so both eyes read at thumbnail size.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the near belt edge and the grating. Second: her boots and the first idlers. Third: Miku's body and her palm on the skirt. Fourth: the receding belt, the exposed rollers and the ribs. Fifth: the bright rectangular opening at the far end.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: a crisp cel-shaded figure, rubber rendered as a flat black mass with two soft tracking lines, precise technical drawing of the idler rhythm and the ribs, and a restrained risograph grain in the dust. Keep the drawing exact and the belt flat, with no photographic depth of field.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no worker at the far end, no silhouette in the opening, no reflected or mirrored figure, no floating interface, no holograms, no glowing particles, no coal falling, no random letters or numbers, no watermark, no signature, no muddy background, no neon, no rainbow lighting, no face obstruction, no hair covering her eyes, no heavy bloom, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, and no malformed hands. Preserve a strict hierarchy: Miku's face first, her palm on the skirt second, the exposed idler stretch third, the receding belt fourth, then the bright opening, typography and dust.

The final image should feel like a gallery that has stopped carrying anything: one black belt running to a bright rectangle, a row of steel rollers repeating into the distance, a metre of rubber cut away, and a girl standing at the skirt with dust on her shoulders.

seeds.title: CYCLOPEAN SPINE
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 9:16 ultra-premium mixed-media industrial editorial poster titled “CYCLOPEAN SPINE”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character, one tiny full figure standing at the absolute bottom centre on a narrow inspection platform beneath a colossal near-black raw-concrete structural spine. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, a slim virtual-singer silhouette, and her original grey-and-teal costume structure. Keep her face, both eyes and both hands fully readable at thumbnail size.

ARCHITECTURAL SUBJECT:

One colossal near-black raw-concrete structural spine rises slightly off-centre through the entire image and continues far beyond the upper frame. Its lower section narrows into an immense blade-shaped supporting pier; its upper section widens into irregular cantilevered concrete masses, deep overhangs, hollow underside cavities and enormous shadowed voids. The central spine is a single continuous load-bearing mass rather than a conventional tower.

Behind it stand several gigantic pale-gray concrete shell fragments: incomplete cylindrical enclosures, monumental curved walls, immense ring-like structures, partial arches and enormous circular openings. Only fragments of these shells are visible because they extend beyond the top and both sides of the canvas. Their true size and purpose cannot be understood from the image.

Dense asymmetrical black-steel maintenance gantries grow locally from the central concrete spine. Short triangular truss platforms project at different elevations; narrow inspection decks, service cages and stacked scaffolding overlap around the spine. Every platform is visibly anchored into the concrete with bearing plates, deep triangular braces and heavy connection joints. Avoid ordinary long bridges connecting simple buildings.

A huge curved black conduit sweeps upward along the right edge. Heavy bundled power cables descend from the highest gantries. Smaller hoses, cable trays, suspended wires, ladders, rails and narrow service platforms overlap across several depths. Dark foreground pipework enters from both lower corners and partially crops the scene.

The structure has no recognizable façade, no repeated floors, almost no windows and no obvious entrance. It resembles a continental-scale fragment of unknown infrastructure rather than a normal factory or usable building. It feels ancient, futuristic, oppressive, beautiful and impossibly large.

COMPOSITION AND SCALE:

The architecture occupies more than 85 percent of the image. Major structures are cropped by the top and both side edges, implying that the facility continues far beyond the frame. The central dark spine forms the dominant vertical axis, while the pale curved shells form enormous overlapping arcs behind it.

Use at least five clearly separated depth layers:
1. almost-black foreground pipes and cropped steel frames;
2. the tiny human scale figure and foreground platform;
3. the dominant central concrete spine;
4. attached black-steel gantries and hanging cable systems;
5. gigantic pale concrete shells fading into luminous atmospheric haze.

Strong upward perspective, a very low horizon, extreme differences in scale, deep spatial overlap and large areas of structural occlusion. The highest masses disappear into pale fog and overexposed daylight, but their edges remain crisp enough to show their immense form.

FIXED CHARACTER:

At the absolute bottom centre stands one tiny young adult woman on a narrow inspection platform, occupying only 2 to 2.5 percent of the total image height. She is a distant scale marker, never a foreground portrait.

Weave Hatsune Miku’s extremely long aqua twin tails into the backlit haze. GRAPHIC PAPER-WHITE KNOCKOUT:

This paper-white region is an independent two-dimensional print layer, not a physical white object. It is completely flat and matte, with hard clipped edges, no volume, no perspective shading, no highlights, no glow, no reflections, no surface material and no three-dimensional white machinery.

The knockout selectively erases portions of the distant industrial structure into blank warm paper-white. Inside it remain only sparse, fragmented black marks: broken structural contours, several isolated cable lines, a few rectangular holes, partial truss silhouettes and irregular ink fragments. These fragments merely suggest an industrial structure without resolving into a complete readable machine.

Use high-contrast threshold posterization, screen-print knockout, stencil masking, blank paper negative space, clipped two-tone industrial fragments and slightly torn ink boundaries. The transition from realistic shaded architecture to flat paper-white must be abrupt, hard-edged and unmistakably graphic.

The gigantic background concrete shells remain shaded pale-gray concrete with visible curvature, formwork seams and atmospheric depth. They must not turn into pure white. Warm paper-white is reserved for the lower central knockout, typography and selected graphic stripes.

Refined tonal hierarchy, deep blacks, pale concrete, warm paper-white and saturated vermilion-crimson. Fine analog paper grain, restrained ink variation, slight crimson-and-black print misregistration, subtle green-magenta chromatic displacement along selected high-contrast edges, delicate halation around tiny signal lamps and controlled atmospheric bloom.

seeds.title: DEEP SHAFT
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 9:16 ultra-premium industrial editorial poster titled “DEEP SHAFT”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character, a tiny full figure on a small maintenance balcony in the lower-right area of a continental-scale brutalist deep-shaft ore-transfer complex. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, a slim virtual-singer silhouette, and her original grey-and-teal costume structure. Keep her face, both eyes and both hands fully readable at thumbnail size.

Position her on a small maintenance balcony in the lower-right area, occupying approximately four to five percent of the total image height. She stands beside a black steel railing and looks upward through the immense processing shaft. Use a narrow neutral-white rim light to reveal her hair and dress silhouette against the dark structure.

Weave Hatsune Miku’s extremely long aqua twin tails into the shaft’s darkness. Both tails hang straight down her back as one narrow aqua mass, pale where the neutral-white rim light finds their crown and almost black where they pass into the shadow of the cores, with one strand lifting away from her shoulder. Her aqua hair is the only cool saturated note in the whole shaft.

Dress Hatsune Miku in an original shaft-inspection costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not workwear. A dark technical jacket with reflective seams, tapered graphite trousers, low sealed boots, and one narrow teal band across the chest that echoes the schematic marks. Keep the values dark and the shapes simple so she reads as a small precise silhouette against the concrete cores.

Build the entire complex around three continuous reinforced-concrete structural cores. Each core must extend vertically through the image and continue beyond the upper and lower frame edges. The cores should be city-block-wide monolithic walls containing elevator shafts, service stairs, ventilation channels and deeply recessed maintenance floors.

Make every major floor visibly supported. Span three enormous triangulated steel transfer trusses between the concrete cores. Each truss should connect to large recessed bearing seats embedded directly into the cores. Place the processing decks on top of these trusses rather than allowing slabs to float unsupported.

Align the main columns, cores and bearing joints vertically through every visible level. Diagonal braces must meet at clear structural nodes. Do not let braces terminate against arbitrary wall surfaces or thin slab edges. Show thick connection plates, hinge pins, bearing blocks and expansion joints at every major load-transfer point.

Construct several massive ore-processing floors between the cores. Each floor should be hundreds of meters long and tens of meters thick, with visible deep beams beneath it. Crop both ends outside the frame so the viewer cannot see the complete building.

Add two colossal vertical ore silos integrated into the concrete cores. Shape them as deep rectangular or slightly tapered cavities rather than circular tanks. Let their walls continue downward toward unseen foundations. Connect the silos to crusher floors using short, heavily reinforced chutes with visible structural collars.

Suspend enclosed conveyor galleries between processing levels. Support every gallery using triangular steel trusses attached to concrete bearing ledges. The conveyor bridges should enter rectangular openings in the cores at matching floor elevations. Avoid bridges connecting to random locations.

Where large platforms cantilever from a core, show a substantial backspan extending inside the structure. Add upper tension rods or deep triangular brackets connecting the cantilever to the next structural level. Every projecting platform must have an understandable support system.

Route industrial pipes along dedicated service galleries. Support them at regular intervals using brackets attached to beams or core walls. Include flexible expansion joints where pipes cross between separate structures. Do not let pipes penetrate major concrete supports without visible sleeves or reinforced openings.

At the lowest visible section, reveal partial foundation structures: enormous concrete transfer blocks, deep wall extensions and several massive anchor assemblies disappearing below the frame. Do not reveal a complete ground plane, but make it clear that the continuous cores carry the loads downward into unseen foundations.

Establish at least five readable levels of scale:

1. the tiny woman, railings and doors;
2. maintenance platforms and stair towers;
3. conveyor bridges and processing floors;
4. city-block-sized cores, trusses and ore silos;
5. additional distant structural cores fading into the deep shaft atmosphere.

Repeat tiny service doors, ladders, inspection lights and narrow balconies across dozens of levels. These human-scale details should appear as small marks against the immense structural system.

Use raw board-formed concrete with deep construction joints, mineral streaks, soot, chipped edges and large repaired sections. Use matte charcoal steel for trusses, braces, railings and machinery. Keep most architectural masses dark gray and nearly black so their weight remains visually dominant.

Replace the safety-yellow graphic system with oxidized industrial teal and pale cyan-white.

Hold the palette with strict area control. Oxidized teal at about eight percent marks the border panels, structural diagrams, load-path indicators and small architectural markers, and never covers a whole core or processing floor. Pale cyan-white at about seventeen percent carries the inverse-colour masks, schematic cutaways and large negative-space fields. Seventy percent of the frame stays charcoal concrete, graphite steel and deep structural shadow, and the last five percent is small restrained amber work lights. No hue outside this list appears anywhere in the canvas.

Apply pale cyan-white schematic masks only to selected trusses, one partial core face and several conveyor galleries. Use thin oxidized-teal lines to indicate the major load paths: processing deck into transfer truss, transfer truss into bearing seat, bearing seat into continuous concrete core, and concrete core downward toward the foundation.

The load-path graphics should function as elegant technical design elements rather than literal educational arrows. Keep them sparse, geometric and integrated into the poster layout.

Place a narrow oxidized-teal vertical graphic panel along the far-left edge. Cut two broad pale-cyan diagonal bands through it. Add several small teal brackets, alignment lines and structural-node markers around the outer edges.

Use the following exact readable text only:

"ORE TRANSFER"
"LOAD CORE"
"ZONE-12"

Place “ORE TRANSFER” vertically along the left border in a tall condensed outlined typeface. Place “LOAD CORE” horizontally near the lower-left edge over a pale cyan-white field. Place “ZONE-12” as a small pale label inside the upper teal panel. Do not place typography across the main structural cores or the woman.

Illuminate the shaft through narrow overhead openings located far beyond the upper frame. Use cold pale-cyan daylight to reveal the concrete edges and major truss joints. Add restrained amber service lights inside the deepest machinery cavities. Use atmospheric depth only between distant structural layers.

Keep the nearest woman, balcony, bearing joints, concrete seams and truss connections in crisp hard focus. Render clear material grain, straight hair strands, precise railings and clean structural edges. Avoid depth-of-field blur and excessive fog.

Compose the frame so that all three continuous cores, major processing floors and lower foundations extend beyond the image boundaries. The viewer must perceive only a small visible section of a vastly larger industrial system.

Combine structurally legible megastructure engineering, monumental brutalism, deep-mining infrastructure, industrial cathedral architecture, screen-printed technical graphics and premium anime game-poster design. The finished image should feel immense and speculative while remaining believable as a functioning heavy industrial complex.

No floating slabs, no unsupported platforms, no decorative V-shaped supports without foundations, no braces terminating in midair, no random bridges, no pipes passing through structural members without sleeves, no visible ocean, no conventional city skyline, no complete building outline, no spaceship hull and no toy-like modular construction. Do not add another character. Keep the woman’s straight white hair, golden eyes, single black double-bar hair clip on her left temple, flat chest and opaque white spaghetti-strap dress. seeds.title: DRY DOCK
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “DRY DOCK”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing on the floor of a vast empty dry dock, her head tipped back to look up at the rim far above. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the concrete.

Use a camera at hip height on a normal lens, set at the dock's inner end and tilted up about eighteen degrees, so the dock's stepped walls converge on the open sky and a travelling gantry crosses the frame near its top. Place Miku at approximately forty-eight percent of the canvas width, full figure visible from boots to hair ornaments, occupying about twenty-two percent of the frame height, so the structure dwarfs her.

Give Miku exactly one core action. She stands still at the dock's centre line with her feet a shoulder's width apart and both arms hanging loose at her sides, her chin lifted and her head tipped back so her face turns up toward the rim. Nothing is in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the dock's walls: two long stepped concrete walls rising in six horizontal altars each, their surfaces scarred by keel blocks in a double row on the floor, with a travelling gantry of yellow steel spanning the gap high above and two rusted bollards at the near corners. Let the walls occupy the outer two thirds of the frame and let the sky fill the slot between them.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The concrete is grey and streaked, dark where water once stood and pale above the old waterline; the keel blocks are tarred timber, their tops crushed; the gantry is welded steel painted yellow, chalky and rusted at every weld; the bollards are cast iron with rusted rings; the floor is a shallow sheet of rainwater with silt beneath. Each behaves differently — concrete holds one long matte gradient, tarred timber absorbs, painted steel scatters and bleeds rust, cast iron goes dull, standing water returns a broken image.

Build a stepped sequence from the floor upward. Begin with the rainwater and its silt, then her boots and their reflection, then the keel blocks running away in a double row, then the walls' six altars climbing, then the gantry's yellow span, then the rim's edge and the white sky in the slot. The sequence must read as standing at the bottom of a drained dock, not as a construction site.

Leave one deliberate absence. The dock is entirely empty of work: no crane hook hanging, no scaffolding, no oil drums, no pallets, no graffiti, no ship. The only marks on the whole floor are her own footprints in the silt and the double row of keel blocks.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the rainwater, its silt, her boots. Middle ground: the keel blocks, Miku, her reflection. Background: the stepped walls, the gantry, the rim and the white sky. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the sky above the slot. The sky is the key: a broad overcast light falling straight down between the walls, brightest at the rim and fading as it descends, laying a soft wash on the gantry's underside and the top three altars while the dock's floor stays in shade. Add one weak bounce from the water, which touches the underside of her jaw and her palms.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the light. Both tails hang straight down her back in one clean aqua mass, pale where the light reaches their crown and almost black at their ends, the tips just clearing the water. Let one strand lift in the draught between the walls.

Dress Miku in an original dock-floor costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not workwear. A dark technical jacket closed to the throat with taped seams, dark trousers bloused into low boots, and a thin harness strap across the chest. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale zip line, and keep the silhouette compact so she reads as a small dark mark on a huge grey floor.

Use a concrete-grey palette with one yellow note and strict area control. Approximately fifty percent of the image is bare concrete in shade, eighteen percent is the pale sky in the slot, twelve percent is the water and its reflection, nine percent is her dark kit, five percent is the gantry's yellow steel, four percent is the keel blocks, and two percent is the bright rim.

Drive the printed graphic language from the concrete's own formwork rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the water's surface at the lower left, printed flat and matte, its edge following the silt line. Add a rectangular pale panel on the near wall's flat face at the height of her shoulder as a graphic mask, and let one vertical strip of deep oxide red run down that wall aligned to a form-board joint. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “DRY DOCK” once, large, in pale grey paint stencilled across the flat concrete face of the near wall at her right, spanning about half the visible wall width, in heavy stencil capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “DOCK 4” sit on a small steel plate bolted to the nearest bollard. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry decades of water. The concrete is streaked in long vertical runs from the rim, with a dark tide line at the old waterline and pale salt bloom above it; the keel blocks are crushed flat on top and tarred black at their feet; the gantry's yellow paint is chalky and its welds are rusted; the bollards' rings are worn bright at one point; the water carries a film of silt and a thin tideline on the concrete. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the standing water. The water carries the whole dock as an inverted slot of grey bands converging on her boots, the gantry as one yellow line, and the rim as a bright edge, and the reflection is sharper than the concrete above it. Let her own reflection be the only human shape in the lower half.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One rusted ring on the near bollard; a steel ladder stub fixed into the wall at mid-height; a broken keel block showing its timber grain; a coil of cable left on the second altar; a chalk survey mark on the floor beside her boot. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a working dock would actually have it.

Illuminate with the sky in the slot as the only key and the water as the only fill. Let the sky light the rim, the gantry's underside and the upper altars, let the water lift her jaw and her hands, and keep the floor, the lower altars and the frame's corners at absolute black so the dock reads as a grey well with light falling into it.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the water and its silt. Second: her boots and her reflection. Third: the keel blocks running away. Fourth: the stepped walls and the bollards. Fifth: the gantry, the rim and the white sky. Separate them by value steps of roughly thirteen percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every altar edge and weld, restrained risograph grain in the shaded concrete, and the sky kept as one flat clean white.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no workers, no crane hook, no scaffolding, no oil drums, no pallets, no graffiti, no ship, no birds, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no vines or weeds, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like standing at the bottom of a drained sea: two grey walls stepping up to a slot of white sky, one yellow gantry crossing it, and a girl so small on the wet floor that the dock does all the talking.

seeds.title: FREIGHT LIFT

Use a combination of one broad orange field, two long diagonal orange extensions and three narrow transparent cuts. Add three white diagonal openings through the lower section of the mask, allowing the architecture beneath to remain visible. The boundary of the orange area follows the major architectural silhouette and gradually fragments into small stencil-like edges.

The entire main typographic content consists of three elements.

Place the words “MASS TRANSFER” vertically inside the solid section of the upper-left orange mask. Use tall condensed white capitals with clean geometric construction, narrow spacing and several custom forty-five-degree cuts. Extend the title through most of the height of the orange region while keeping it fully contained inside the mask.

Place “SECTOR-12” horizontally inside the translucent lower portion of the orange mask. Use a smaller bold white geometric sans-serif typeface. Add one thin white underline and a short segmented rule beside the sector code.

Place the word “WARNING” in the lower-left quadrant directly over a quiet pale concrete area. Use large charcoal-black condensed capitals. Keep this secondary word separate from the orange mask and align it with the lower edge of the architecture.

Build a peripheral industrial symbol family and distribute it around the outer boundaries of the poster. Construct every symbol from thin white or charcoal linework, broken circles, corner brackets, measurement ticks, split arrows, modular rectangles and forty-five-degree cuts. Keep the symbols compact while giving each one a clear visual function.

Place one custom safety-orange angular emblem in the upper-right corner. Construct it from two mirrored mechanical arrows and one triangular cut, forming a compact industrial logo.

Place one thin white segmented circular icon near the upper-center-right edge. Build it from two incomplete concentric rings, four short radial ticks and one small central square. Align this symbol visually with the circular machinery in the background.

Place a pair of large white corner brackets along the middle-right edge. Use one upper bracket and one lower bracket, connected by a sparse vertical measurement scale. Add five short horizontal ticks between them.

Place a compact black-and-white diagonal caution stripe at the lower-right edge. Use seven evenly spaced diagonal bars contained inside a thin rectangular wireframe. Add a small triangular direction marker above the stripe.

Place a small white coordinate symbol in the bottom-left corner. Combine one L-shaped corner, three short horizontal data bars, two dots and a miniature segmented circle.

Place two small white chevrons near the left-center edge, aligned with the diagonal direction of the orange mask. Place one tiny orange square marker near the upper-left title and one orange triangular marker near the lower-right caution stripe.

Add a thin interrupted line-frame around the canvas perimeter. Use short white corner segments, controlled gaps and small registration ticks. Allow the frame to connect visually with the surrounding symbols while keeping the central architecture open.

The peripheral symbol system has five anchor regions: upper right logo, upper-center-right circular icon, middle-right measurement brackets, lower-right caution stripe and bottom-left coordinate symbol. Their shared stroke thickness, repeated diagonal cuts and consistent spacing create one coherent industrial graphic language.

Warm yellow appears exclusively as physical signal lighting mounted on the gray and black architectural surfaces outside the orange graphic mask. Place narrow yellow light bars beneath suspended platforms, along bridge railings, beside ladder openings and around the central mechanical tower. Add a few tiny yellow indicator lamps on distant platforms. Each light produces a restrained warm reflection on the surrounding concrete and steel.

The orange mask carries the typography, the peripheral line symbols organize the canvas, and the yellow signal lamps guide the eye through the physical depth of the architecture. Keep clear separation between these three functions.

Use opaque and translucent screen-print ink, subtle stencil wear, slight registration offset, clipped geometric masks and tactile paper grain in the flat graphic layer. Use realistic materials, structural depth, atmospheric perspective and cinematic lighting in the scene layer.

Final visual hierarchy: colossal mass-transfer architecture first, tiny Hatsune Miku second, upper-left orange scene-derived mask third, sparse typography inside the mask fourth, distributed peripheral line symbols fifth, yellow architectural signal lights last. The final image feels monumental and cinematic while clearly reading as a sophisticated industrial graphic poster.

Hold the palette with strict area control. Approximately forty-eight percent of the image is pale concrete and cement white, eighteen percent is charcoal-black steel and deep shadow inside the ring structures, twelve percent is the safety-orange mask in the upper-left quadrant, nine percent is the pale sky and atmospheric haze, six percent is muted steel, four percent is Hatsune Miku and her dark kit, two percent is the dark transfer tower, and one percent is the warm yellow signal lighting. No hue outside this list appears anywhere in the canvas.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Hatsune Miku, no second figure, no workers, no vehicles, no birds, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the sparse strings named above, no watermark, no signature, no frame, no border.

seeds.title: MEGA FIELD
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium brutalist industrial editorial poster titled “MEGA FIELD”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character, a tiny full figure at the bottom centre, inside a colossal futuristic industrial megastructure seen from ground level through an extreme low-angle worm’s-eye perspective. The architecture occupies about eighty-five percent of the canvas and extends far beyond the upper and side edges. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, a slim virtual-singer silhouette, and her original grey-and-teal costume structure. Keep her face, both eyes and both hands fully readable at thumbnail size.

Construct the megastructure from monumental weathered concrete towers, enormous cantilevered platforms, suspended maintenance decks, exposed steel trusses, dense scaffolding, heavy structural beams, circular mechanical hubs, turbine-like machinery, industrial pipes, ladders, railings, ventilation openings and long bundles of hanging black cables. Several massive concrete sections bridge across the upper half of the image, creating deep overlapping layers and a dark mechanical canopy.

Place Hatsune Miku as the single tiny full-body character at the bottom centre, occupying less than five percent of the canvas, shown from the back in a calm upright pose and looking upward toward the enormous structure. Her feet are together, both arms hang at her sides, and nothing is in either hand.

Weave Hatsune Miku’s extremely long aqua twin tails into the industrial wind. Both tails flow gently toward one side in one clean aqua sweep, lifted off her back by the draught between the towers, pale where the overcast light catches them and almost black at the tips. Her aqua hair remains the only character colour.

Dress Hatsune Miku in an original survey-crew costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not workwear. A short dark technical jacket with sealed seams, tapered charcoal trousers, low reinforced boots, and a narrow pale band across the chest. Keep the values dark and the shapes simple so she reads as a scale marker rather than a portrait.

Use a pale overcast sky with large soft clouds and bright white atmospheric haze behind the architecture. Strong daylight enters from the upper-right area, creating bright concrete edges, deep charcoal undersides, crisp structural shadows and subtle volumetric rays passing through gaps between the platforms. The environmental palette consists of cement white, cold gray, graphite, charcoal black and muted metallic silver.

Separate the visual language into two independent layers: a flat industrial graphic-design layer and a physical architectural signal-light layer.

The flat graphic-design layer uses safety orange, deep black and pure white exclusively. Build one major orange composition in the upper-left corner: four broad diagonal safety-orange bars with varied lengths, controlled spacing, sharp cut ends and cropped outer edges. Combine these orange bars with several smaller orange rectangles and angular fragments, forming one unified industrial warning emblem. Use worn stencil surfaces, chipped paint, scratched screen-print ink and subtle paper grain.

Add one secondary black-and-white diagonal stripe block near the lower-right edge. Keep this secondary block smaller and quieter than the upper-left orange group. Use a few tiny orange stencil tabs on selected canvas edges and concrete surfaces to connect the poster graphics with the architecture.

Warm yellow appears exclusively as physical signal lighting mounted on the gray and black architectural areas. Place sparse narrow yellow light bars beneath maintenance platforms, along beam joints, beside ladders, around circular machinery and at selected cable junctions. Use a few tiny yellow indicator dots on distant platforms. Each signal light produces a restrained warm halo on the surrounding concrete and metal. Arrange these lights in a subtle repeating rhythm across the structure, allowing them to guide the eye through the architecture. Keep the orange graphic areas visually flat while the yellow signal lamps remain luminous and spatial.

Build a sophisticated multi-level typographic identity system inspired by high-end industrial science-fiction posters. Use typography as an architectural graphic element rather than a single isolated title block.

Place an oversized vertical column of outlined alphanumeric characters along the far-left edge. Rotate the characters ninety degrees, extend them across most of the left side and crop several glyphs beyond the top and bottom edges. Use an ultra-condensed geometric sans-serif typeface with custom cut corners, interrupted strokes and narrow internal spaces. Let portions of these white outline characters overlap the upper-left orange diagonal bars.

Place the main readable title “MEGASTRUCTURE” in the lower-left quadrant using bold solid-white condensed capitals. Directly beneath it, place “WARNING” in a larger hollow outline style. Align both words to a strict left grid and allow the title group to overlap a dark architectural shadow, creating strong white-on-black contrast.

Add the compact code “22A” beneath the title in heavy geometric numerals. Place two orange diagonal warning slashes beside the code. Add a short row of tiny white technical data, serial marks and narrow horizontal rules next to the code. Keep the main title readable while the secondary information functions as precise visual texture.

Create a custom industrial icon family using the same geometric construction language. Build every icon from thick straight strokes, forty-five-degree cuts, triangular corners, split bars, interrupted circles and modular rectangular parts.

Place one large custom white angular emblem in the lower-right corner, partially cropped by the canvas edge. Construct it as an abstract combination of a rotated letterform, infinity-like loop and mechanical warning symbol. Place one small orange triangular sector icon in the upper-right corner. Add several compact white chevrons beside the main title, one striped square symbol near the left margin, a small circular machinery icon, paired alignment arrows and a few narrow barcode-like marks.

Distribute the typography and icons across four controlled anchor areas: the vertical outlined characters on the far left, the main title and code cluster in the lower left, a small triangular icon in the upper right, and the custom angular emblem in the lower right. Connect these anchors with thin white rules, corner brackets, registration marks, small index dots and short measurement ticks.

Use five clear scales of graphic information: enormous cropped outline characters, medium main title, large custom emblem, compact warning codes and extremely small technical marks. Maintain consistent stroke weights, repeated forty-five-degree angles and shared geometric proportions across all letters and symbols. The entire system feels like one designed visual identity rather than separate decorative elements.

Keep most typography and iconography white, use orange only where the graphics intersect the orange warning group, and use black details inside white or orange fields. The yellow signal lights remain confined to the physical architecture, creating a clear distinction between printed graphics and spatial illumination.

Use refined screen-print ink, hard-edged masks, distressed stencil wear, slight registration offset, tactile paper grain and clean vector geometry in the graphic layer. Keep realistic concrete, steel, cables, haze, lighting and depth in the architectural layer.

Final visual hierarchy: colossal industrial architecture first, tiny Hatsune Miku silhouette second, upper-left orange warning emblem third, sophisticated vertical typography and main title system fourth, custom industrial icons fifth, sparse yellow signal lights guiding the eye through the gray architecture. Monumental, severe, mechanical, disciplined, atmospheric and visually precise, combining realistic science-fiction architecture with a premium Japanese industrial graphic-poster identity.

Hold the palette with strict area control. Approximately fifty percent of the image is pale grey and charcoal concrete, sixteen percent is the deep shadow under the cantilevered masses, twelve percent is the safety-orange warning emblem in the upper-left, nine percent is the pale overcast sky, six percent is weathered structural steel, four percent is Hatsune Miku and her dark kit, two percent is the near-black tower core, and one percent is the warm yellow signal lighting. No hue outside this list appears anywhere in the canvas.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Hatsune Miku, no second figure, no workers, no vehicles, no birds, no floating platforms, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the vertical title and the icon system described above, no watermark, no signature, no frame, no border.

seeds.title: MEGAFACTORY
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 9:16 ultra-premium industrial editorial poster titled “MEGAFACTORY”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character, a tiny full figure near the bottom centre of a vast open concrete service plaza, standing outside a colossal brutalist industrial megafactory beneath an overcast sky. The camera stays completely outside the building and the architecture occupies at least eighty-five percent of the image. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, a slim virtual-singer silhouette, and her original grey-and-teal costume structure. Keep her face, both eyes and both hands fully readable at thumbnail size.

Show only the exterior architecture. The building must have a continuous external facade, a clearly grounded foundation and a coherent overall mass. Do not reveal interior floors, open structural shafts, internal atriums, sectional cutaways or indoor bridge systems.

Position her near the bottom center of the outdoor service plaza, occupying approximately four percent of the canvas height. Show her from behind in a calm standing pose, facing the enormous factory. Use a narrow pale rim light to reveal her hair and the edges of her coat. She serves only as a human scale reference.

Weave Hatsune Miku’s extremely long aqua twin tails into the overcast light. Both tails hang straight down her back in one clean aqua mass, pale where the pale rim light finds their crown and almost black against the dark podium behind her, with one strand lifting in the plaza wind. Her aqua hair is the only cool saturated note in the whole frame.

Dress Hatsune Miku in an original plaza-survey costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not workwear. A short dark technical coat with sealed seams, tapered charcoal trousers, low reinforced boots, and one narrow teal band across the back echoing the graphic accent. Keep the values dark so she reads as a tiny silhouette against the pale facade.

Design the factory as a gigantic stepped industrial ziggurat constructed from five increasingly narrow rectangular masses. The lowest podium should be extremely wide and extend beyond both side edges of the frame. Each higher level steps backward, creating enormous exterior terraces and deep shadow lines.

The megafactory should occupy at least eighty-five percent of the image. Crop the uppermost exhaust structures outside the top edge and crop both sides of the lower podium outside the frame. The viewer must understand that the visible facade is only one section of a much larger industrial complex.

Anchor the entire building to a continuous monumental base. Construct the base from a massive reinforced-concrete podium resting directly on bedrock beneath the plaza. Add broad sloped retaining walls and thick vertical foundation piers that visibly continue upward into the facade.

Use twelve colossal vertical concrete buttresses across the front elevation. Every buttress begins at the foundation podium and continues uninterrupted toward the upper factory levels. Gradually taper the buttresses as they rise, making the load path from the upper masses to the ground visually clear.

Between the buttresses, create deep recessed facade bays. Some bays contain enormous matte-black ventilation grilles; others contain narrow rows of tiny maintenance doors, external stair towers and small service balconies. Keep these elements attached to the exterior facade rather than opening into a visible interior.

Place one monumental rectangular service entrance at the center of the lower podium. The entrance should be large enough for heavy industrial equipment, but it remains a dark exterior opening rather than a view into an interior hall. Frame it with thick concrete walls and a massive horizontal lintel.

Above the entrance, add three enormous exterior processing blocks projecting slightly from the facade. Support each block with deep concrete brackets extending continuously into the vertical buttresses. Do not allow them to float or depend on thin decorative supports.

Run several building-scale industrial pipes vertically along the outer facade. Give every pipe visible steel brackets at regular intervals. Route the pipes into reinforced wall penetrations with thick collars and expansion joints. Add two large horizontal pipe galleries across selected terrace levels, supported by exterior trusses attached to the main buttresses.

At the top of the structure, create a group of rectangular exhaust towers and broad ventilation chimneys. Every exhaust tower must rise directly from the upper factory mass. Avoid thin freestanding stacks. Use heavy geometric forms with deep openings and dark internal louvers.

Add one massive exterior gantry crane near the upper-left portion of the facade. Mount the crane on two visible rails integrated into the roof terrace. Include a substantial rear counterweight and a clear support connection. Keep the crane subordinate to the building rather than making it the primary subject.

Use raw board-formed concrete with deep horizontal construction seams, rough aggregate, mineral stains, weathered patches and repaired edges. Combine it with matte charcoal steel, graphite ventilation grilles, dark external staircases and brushed metal pipe collars.

Hold the palette with strict area control. Oxidized industrial teal at about eight percent marks the facade markers, narrow vertical panels, warning bands, external doors and poster-border graphics, and never covers a whole building. Pale cyan-white at about seventeen percent carries the inverse-colour facade masks, large poster fields and simplified technical silhouettes. Seventy percent of the building stays concrete grey, charcoal black and deep shadow, and the remaining five percent is Hatsune Miku, her dark kit and the small amber service lights above the doors. No hue outside this list appears anywhere in the image.

Place a narrow oxidized-teal poster panel along the far-left border. Cut two broad pale-cyan diagonal bands through it. Keep all graphic overlays outside the central factory facade so the architecture remains dominant.

Render only the following exact readable text:

"MEGAFOUNDRY"
"EXTERIOR-12"
"HEAVY INDUSTRY"

Place “MEGAFOUNDRY” vertically along the far-left border in a tall condensed outlined typeface. Place “HEAVY INDUSTRY” near the lower-left corner over a pale cyan-white field. Place “EXTERIOR-12” as a small pale label inside the upper teal panel. Do not place typography across the main facade.

Use a low but not extreme exterior viewpoint from the plaza. Show a narrow strip of concrete ground at the bottom and a narrow band of pale overcast sky around the upper architecture. The building should dominate through physical mass rather than optical distortion.

Illuminate the facade with cold diffused daylight from the upper-left. Create broad architectural shadows beneath the stepped terraces and projecting processing blocks. Use pale atmospheric light only around the highest exhaust towers. Keep the lower facade, woman and service plaza sharply resolved.

Establish scale using repeated exterior details: tiny doors, narrow balconies, hairline railings, small stair flights, service lights and maintenance platforms distributed across dozens of levels. The woman is the smallest element, followed by doors, balconies, processing blocks and finally the entire megafactory.

Combine monumental brutalism, believable heavy-industry architecture, exterior industrial photography, megastructure concept art, screen-printed technical graphics and premium anime game-poster direction. The final image should feel physically grounded, structurally believable, severe, immense and silent.

Absolutely no interior scene, no structural cutaway, no deep shaft, no open atrium, no indoor catwalk maze, no floor seen from underneath, no floating slab, no unsupported bridge, no decorative V-shaped support, no visible ocean, no conventional city skyline, no circular reactor, no spaceship hull and no toy-like modular structure. Do not add another character. Keep the woman’s straight white hair, golden eyes, single black double-bar hair clip on her left temple, flat chest and opaque white spaghetti-strap dress. No random typography, watermark or signature.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Hatsune Miku, no second figure, no workers, no vehicles, no birds, no interior floors, no open structural shafts, no sectional cutaways, no floating interface elements, no readable text of any kind, no watermark, no signature, no frame, no border.

seeds.title: NAVE
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “NAVE”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing alone in the nave of an empty Gothic church, her head tipped back to look up at the vault. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the coloured light.

Use a camera at chest height on a normal lens, set in the centre aisle about six paces behind her and square to the altar, so the two rows of piers converge toward a rose window and the vault closes the top of the frame. Place Miku at approximately forty-eight percent of the canvas width, full figure visible from her shoes to her hair ornaments, occupying about forty-six percent of the frame height, standing on the aisle's centre line.

Give Miku exactly one core action. She stands still with her feet together and both arms hanging at her sides, her chin lifted and her head tipped back so her face turns up toward the vault, both eyes open. Nothing is in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the nave itself: two rows of clustered stone piers running in perspective, each carrying a pointed arch and a shaft up into a ribbed vault, with one tall stained window on the left throwing coloured light across the aisle and a rose window closing the far end. Let the piers occupy the outer thirds and let the vault fill the top quarter.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The piers are pale limestone, their bases dark and their shafts polished by hands; the arches are carved with a roll moulding; the vault is plastered between stone ribs; the floor is a checked pattern of pale and dark marble slabs, worn along the centre line and slightly hollowed; the pews are absent, leaving the whole floor open; the windows are leaded glass in deep reds and blues. Each behaves differently — limestone scatters light and holds grit in its pores, carving takes a soft shadow, marble returns a dim sheen, leaded glass throws coloured patches, plaster goes flat.

Build a stepped sequence from the floor to the vault. Begin with the marble slabs and their worn centre line, then her shoes on the aisle, then her standing figure, then the pier bases and their dark stone, then the pointed arches climbing, then the ribs of the vault, then the coloured window and the rose window beyond. The sequence must read as an empty church between services, not as a cathedral postcard.

Leave one deliberate absence. The church is empty of everything movable: no pews, no chairs, no candles lit, no flowers, no lectern, no people, no kneelers. The only objects in the frame besides her are the piers, the vault, the windows and one stone step before the altar.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the marble floor and its worn line. Middle ground: Miku, the pier bases, the coloured patch of light. Background: the climbing arches, the vault ribs and the rose window. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the tall window on the left plus the rose window at the far end. The side window is the key: it throws three coloured patches — one deep red, one blue, one pale amber — across the aisle and onto the pier faces, catching the side of her face and shoulder. The rose window is a cooler secondary from behind and above, laying a soft glow on the altar end. Keep the pier shadows and the vault's upper corners at near-black.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the two sources. Both tails fall down her back in one clean aqua mass, one band of deep red light crossing it and a blue band below, and the ends resting on the marble. Let one strand catch the amber patch across her cheek.

Dress Miku in an original empty-church costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not liturgical dress. A long dark coat with a narrow collar worn closed over a pale high-necked top, dark trousers and low boots, the coat's hem falling to mid-calf. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment, and keep the silhouette narrow so the piers' verticals read around her.

Use a stone-and-colour palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty-four percent of the image is pale limestone in shade, twenty-two percent is the marble floor, eighteen percent is the vault and its shadow, twelve percent is her dark coat, six percent is her aqua hair, five percent is the coloured window light, and three percent is the rose window's glow.

Drive the printed graphic language from the stone's own coursing rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the marble floor at the lower left, printed flat and matte, its edge stopping at a slab joint. Add a rectangular pale panel on the nearest pier's flat face as a graphic mask at the height of her shoulder, and let one vertical strip of deep oxide red run down that pier aligned to its shaft. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “NAVE” once, large, in pale grey paint carved into the flat face of the nearest pier above her shoulder, spanning about half the pier's width, in heavy condensed capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “WEST” sit on a small brass plaque screwed to the pier below it. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry centuries. The pier bases are dark with damp and their corners chipped; the shafts are polished at the height of a hand; the marble floor is hollowed along the centre line and its joints are wide with grit; the vault's plaster holds a dark stain in one corner; the window's lead came is grey and one pane is cracked; the stone step before the altar is hollowed in two places. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the polished marble. The floor carries the coloured patches as three soft coloured shapes, the piers as long pale verticals and her own figure as a dark shape between them, and the reflection dims as the stone dries toward the walls. Let the marble be the only place in the frame where the coloured light lies flat on a horizontal.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One cracked pane in the side window; a stone step hollowed in two places; a brass plaque with worn lettering on the near pier; a small drain slot in the aisle's centre line; a single dry leaf blown in at the door. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where an old church would actually have it.

Illuminate with the side window as the only warm key and the rose window as the only cool fill. Let the side window lay three coloured patches on the aisle and her shoulder, let the rose window glow at the far end, and keep the pier shadows and the vault's upper corners at absolute black so the nave reads as a tall dim room with colour dropped into it.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the marble floor and its worn line. Second: her shoes and the coloured patches. Third: Miku's figure and her hair. Fourth: the pier bases and the climbing arches. Fifth: the vault ribs, the rose window and the altar end. Separate them by value steps of roughly thirteen percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every stone course and vault rib, restrained risograph grain in the shaded piers, and the coloured light kept as flat clean shapes.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no congregation, no priest, no visitors, no pews, no chairs, no candles lit, no flowers, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no doves, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like a church between two services: two rows of pale piers running to a rose window, three patches of coloured light lying flat on the marble, and a girl standing on the centre line with her face tipped back.

seeds.title: OFFSHORE ARRAY
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium industrial editorial poster titled “OFFSHORE ARRAY”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character, a tiny full figure on a narrow service pier near the lower centre, inside a colossal offshore processing platform rising above a cold pale ocean, seen from a very low service pier through an extreme wide-angle perspective. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, a slim virtual-singer silhouette, and her original grey-and-teal costume structure. Keep her face, both eyes and both hands fully readable at thumbnail size.

Construct the platform entirely from marine high-tech engineering: enormous dark steel support legs, stacked processing decks, dense pipe racks, cylindrical pressure tanks, spherical storage vessels, external stair towers, lattice cranes, suspended maintenance cages, ventilation stacks, pumping stations and long overhead pipelines.

Place the largest processing tower slightly right of center. Extend several massive steel decks horizontally across the upper half of the canvas. Suspend a group of cylindrical tanks beneath the central deck and connect them through articulated pipes, valves and heavy mechanical collars. Add one tall lattice crane leaning diagonally across the upper-left sky.

Use four gigantic offshore support legs descending toward the sea. Connect the legs with diagonal steel braces and narrow maintenance bridges. Let parts of the structure extend beyond the top and side edges, creating overwhelming scale and dense mechanical depth.

Keep an open strip of pale ocean and misty horizon across the lower-left and central background. Add sea fog drifting between the support legs, white steam released from pressure vents and fine salt particles illuminated by daylight.

Place Hatsune Miku as a tiny full-body figure on a narrow service pier near the lower centre, shown from behind and looking upward toward the suspended pressure tanks. She occupies less than five percent of the canvas, her feet are together on the wet grating, both arms hang loose at her sides, and she stays the only human presence above the water.

Weave Hatsune Miku’s extremely long aqua twin tails into the sea wind. Both tails flow out toward the ocean in one clean aqua sweep, lifted slightly off her back by the wind, pale where the overcast daylight catches them and almost black where they cross the dark steel. Her aqua hair remains the only character colour against the cold marine palette.

Dress Hatsune Miku in an original offshore-crew costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not heavy workwear. A short marine-white technical jacket with sealed seams, a dark high-collar top beneath it, tapered grey trousers, pale alloy ankle boots, and one narrow printed rig-band across the chest. Keep the values light against the wet steel so she still reads as herself even at the smallest scale.

Render the physical structure in weathered marine white, galvanized silver, cold gray, graphite and charcoal black. Use bright overcast daylight, silver reflections on wet steel, deep shadows beneath the processing decks and soft volumetric light inside the sea fog. Add chipped marine coating, salt stains, scratched metal, rivets, welded seams and restrained cinematic grain.

Separate the visual identity into a flat industrial warning layer and a physical signal-light layer.

The flat warning layer uses safety orange, pure white and deep black exclusively. Place one dominant safety-orange graphic group along the upper-left canvas edge. Construct it from four broad diagonal bars, one solid rectangular plate and two compact triangular fragments. Crop the group beyond the upper and left edges and align its diagonal direction with the lattice crane.

Use hard forty-five-degree cuts, disciplined spacing, worn stencil texture, chipped screen-print ink and tactile paper grain. Place one smaller black-and-white diagonal caution block near the lower-right edge. Apply several compact orange identification plates to pressure tanks, crane joints and pipe-control housings.

Yellow appears exclusively as physical signal lighting mounted on gray, white and black structural surfaces. Install narrow warm-yellow lamps beneath processing decks, beside stair landings, around pipe junctions and along crane walkways. Place tiny yellow indicator dots around valves and pumping equipment. Each lamp creates a restrained warm reflection on wet steel. Arrange the lights in a path leading from Hatsune Miku toward the central pressure tanks.

Build a sophisticated marine-industrial typography and icon system.

Place enormous outlined characters reading “RIG 06” vertically along the far-right canvas edge. Rotate the characters ninety degrees and use an ultra-condensed geometric sans-serif typeface. Construct the glyphs with interrupted strokes, rectangular counters, angular terminals and narrow internal spaces. Crop several portions beyond the upper and lower edges.

Place the main readable title “OFFSHORE ARRAY” in the upper-left negative space. Use bold condensed solid-white capitals. Place “PROCESSING RIG” beneath it in a larger hollow outline style. Align the title with the orange diagonal warning group.
