seeds.title: PUMP ROOM
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “PUMP ROOM”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing between two rows of large painted pipes in a disused pump room, one hand resting on a valve wheel. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the painted pipework.

Use a camera at chest height on a normal lens, set in the room's doorway and square to the pipe run, so four large pipes march along the left wall in strong perspective, a bank of gauges closes the right, and a concrete floor runs between them. Place Miku at approximately fifty percent of the canvas width, full figure visible from her boots to her hair ornaments, occupying about sixty percent of the frame height, standing in the aisle with her hand on a valve.

Give Miku exactly one core action. She stands with her weight on one hip and her right hand resting on the top of a red valve wheel at waist height, her left hand hanging loose at her side. Her head turns slightly toward the gauges, her eyes come back to the lens, and nothing is in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the pipe run: four steel pipes of stepped diameter, each lagged and painted, running along the wall at four heights, jointed by bolted flanges, with one elbow dropping to the floor and a row of red valve wheels at intervals. Let the pipes occupy the left half in perspective and let the gauges' white faces form a quiet pattern on the right.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The pipes are painted steel in a municipal green, chalky and flaking at every flange; the flanges are bare steel, their bolts rusted; the valve wheels are cast iron painted red, chipped to black iron at their rims; the gauges are enamel dials in brass cases, their glass dusty; the floor is bare concrete with a drainage channel down the middle; the wall is painted the same green to shoulder height and cream above. Each behaves differently — chalky paint scatters, bare steel carries one line, cast iron goes dull at its chips, enamel dials stay bright, concrete scatters dully.

Build a stepped sequence from the floor upward. Begin with the drainage channel and its grating, then her boots on the concrete, then the lowest pipe and its flange, then her hand on the valve wheel, then her body, then the three pipes above her, then the gauges and the two-tone wall. The sequence must read as a plant that has been switched off for years, not as an industrial showroom.

Leave one deliberate absence. The room is empty of work: no tools on the floor, no rag, no oil can, no clipboard, no scaffolding, no one at the gauges. The only objects in the frame besides her are the pipes, the valve wheels, the gauges and the drainage channel.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the drainage channel and its grating. Middle ground: her boots, the lowest pipe, her hand on the valve. Background: the three upper pipes, the gauges and the two-tone wall. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from a high window behind the camera's shoulder. The window is the key: a soft cool light entering from above and behind, laying an even sheen along the top of every pipe and a bright line on the valve wheels' rims, while the undersides of the pipes and the floor between them stay in shade. Add one weak warm bounce from the concrete, which touches her jaw, her forearm and the lowest pipe's underside. Keep the room's far corner and the ceiling at near-black.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the light. Both tails fall down her back in one clean aqua mass with a bright line along their crown and a cool shadow inside, the ends resting against the lowest pipe. Let one strand fall forward over her shoulder beside the valve wheel.

Dress Miku in an original pump-room costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not workwear. A dark boiler suit with the sleeves pushed to the elbow and the collar open at the throat, a pale undershirt showing at the neck, and low work boots; a pair of thin gloves tucked into her waistband. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale note, and keep the silhouette narrow so the pipe perspective reads.

Use a green-pipe-and-grey palette with one red note and strict area control. Approximately thirty-four percent of the image is painted pipework, twenty-two percent is the bare concrete floor and its channel, eighteen percent is the two-tone wall, twelve percent is her dark suit, eight percent is the gauges' white dials, four percent is the red valve wheels, and two percent is her aqua hair.

Drive the printed graphic language from the pipes' own paint rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the concrete floor at the lower left, printed flat and matte, its edge following the drainage channel. Add a rectangular pale panel on the cream upper wall as a graphic mask at the height of her shoulder, and let one vertical strip of deep oxide red run down that wall aligned to a pipe bracket. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “PUMP ROOM” once, large, in pale grey paint stencilled across the flat cream wall above the pipes, spanning about half the wall's width, in heavy stencil capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “LINE 3” sit on a small steel plate bolted to the nearest flange at hip height. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry years of standing. The pipe paint is chalky and flaking in rings around every flange, with rust bleeding below the joints; the flange bolts are rusted to a dull brown; the valve wheels are chipped to black iron at their rims and worn bright where hands turn them; the gauges' glass is dusty and one needle has dropped; the floor's channel is stained and its grating rusted; the wall's green band ends in a hand-painted line. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the gauges' glass. Each dial carries the window's light as one small bright arc and the room as a dark band, and the needles' shadows fall across the white faces. Let the gauges be the only place in the frame where the light is small and round.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One valve wheel chipped at its rim; a pair of thin gloves tucked into her waistband; a rusted bracket holding the top pipe; a drain grating with grit caught in it; a hand-painted line where the green meets the cream. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a real pump room would actually have it.

Illuminate with the high window as the only key and the concrete's bounce as the only fill. Let the window draw one soft sheen along every pipe and a bright line on the wheels' rims, let the bounce keep her jaw and the lowest pipe readable, and keep the room's far corner and the ceiling at absolute black so the pipes read as four lit lines in a dim room.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the drainage channel and its grating. Second: her boots and the lowest pipe. Third: her hand on the valve and her body. Fourth: the three upper pipes and their flanges. Fifth: the gauges and the two-tone wall. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every flange bolt and pipe seam, restrained risograph grain in the shaded floor, and the dials kept as flat white circles with one small bright arc each.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no worker at the gauges, no tools on the floor, no rag, no oil can, no clipboard, no scaffolding, no steam, no leaking water, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no graffiti, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like a plant that stopped years ago: four green pipes marching away with rust bleeding under every flange, one red wheel worn bright where hands turned it, and a girl standing in the aisle with her palm on it.

Construct the letters with rounded rectangular counters, interrupted strokes, circular cutouts and angular terminals. Crop portions beyond the upper and lower canvas edges.

Place the main readable title “MODULAR SKYPORT” in the upper-left negative space. Use bold condensed solid-white capitals. Place “TRANSFER NODE” directly beneath it in a larger hollow outline style. Align both lines with the upper-left orange warning composition.

Add the compact code “NODE 08” beneath the title. Pair it with the readable secondary label “CAPSULE TRANSFER ARRAY”, two thin horizontal rules, a small orange square marker and a short row of technical data.

Create a custom modular icon family from rounded rectangles, capsule silhouettes, broken circles, connection lines and triangular support joints. Every icon shares the same stroke thickness and geometric proportions.

Place one medium transfer-node icon beside “NODE 08”. Construct it from a central circle connected to four rounded capsule shapes through short mechanical arms. Add small numbered index dots around the outer perimeter.

Place one large custom white emblem in the lower-right corner. Combine a capsule outline, circular docking collar and angular letter S into a single geometric mark. Crop part of the emblem beyond the lower and right edges. Place one small orange triangular navigation symbol in the upper-right corner and one compact white elevator icon near the central service spine.

Add corner brackets, paired directional arrows, circular registration marks, short barcode-like lines, modular grid coordinates and small capsule-status pictograms. Connect selected information groups with thin white rules that echo the bridges and cable routes.

Use five information scales: enormous cropped “PORT 08” characters, medium main title, large custom skyport emblem, compact node codes and tiny status markings. Distribute these elements across four controlled anchors: the upper-left title system, vertical characters on the far right, small technical icons around the central spine and the large emblem in the lower right.

Keep typography and icons primarily white. Use orange where symbols intersect the warning composition and black for internal details placed inside white or orange fields. Keep yellow entirely within the luminous signal-light system mounted on the architecture.

Use crisp vector construction, hard masks, distressed stencil wear, subtle print registration offset and tactile screen-print grain in the graphic layer. Use realistic metal, glass, composite panels, atmospheric perspective and bright architectural light in the environmental layer.

Final visual hierarchy: clustered modular skyport architecture first, circular transfer ring second, tiny Hatsune Miku third, upper-left orange warning composition fourth, custom typography and capsule-icon system fifth, sparse yellow signal lights tracing the physical connection nodes last. Lightweight, technological, modular and highly disciplined, combining Japanese Metabolist architecture with a premium industrial graphic-poster identity.

Hold the palette with strict area control. Approximately forty-four percent of the image is pearl-white composite panel, sixteen percent is the pale overcast sky in the upper-left, twelve percent is the safety-orange warning composition, ten percent is graphite and charcoal steel structure, eight percent is lightly tinted smoky glass, six percent is cool silver aluminium, three percent is Hatsune Miku and her pale kit, and one percent is the warm yellow signal lighting. No hue outside this list appears anywhere in the canvas.

seeds.title: SURGE DIVIDE
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium industrial graphic-poster key visual titled “SURGE DIVIDE”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character, a tiny full figure on a narrow gantry near the lower-right third, presenting one colossal counterweighted isolation gate spanning a narrow ocean channel between two immense concrete abutments. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, a slim virtual-singer silhouette, and her original grey-and-teal costume structure. Keep her face, both eyes and both hands fully readable at thumbnail size.

Make the architectural hero one enormous wedge-shaped steel gate blade suspended at a steep diagonal across the composition. Its broad lower edge begins near the right foreground and its tapered upper end disappears beyond the upper-left frame. Construct the blade from overlapping graphite-steel plates, deep longitudinal ribs, recessed pressure cells, thick perimeter seals, and a massive segmented hinge assembly. Support it with four gigantic hydraulic thrust arms attached to the right concrete abutment. Each arm has a visible cylinder, polished piston rod, clevis joint, bearing collar, and triangular load-transfer bracket. Place a tall black chain-lifting tower behind the gate, carrying several parallel chains upward through cropped pulley housings. Let the chains, hydraulic arms, and gate blade create a powerful diagonal mechanical flow across the image.

Frame the moving gate between two battered marine-concrete abutments. The nearer right abutment rises as a broad stepped wall with deep maintenance slots, cantilevered inspection decks, and enormous anchor blocks. The distant left abutment appears through sea mist as a fragmented vertical mass with intake tunnels and narrow connecting rails. Beneath the raised gate, reveal a long horizontal opening toward the pale ocean, with water vapor, suspended spray, and a thin band of distant gray water. Add compact maintenance cages, ladder runs, cable trays, valve clusters, pressure hoses, drainage pipes, and small access bridges directly around the major joints. Keep the diagonal gate blade as the clearest and largest silhouette.

Organize the scene through five spatial layers: cropped wet pipes and a black safety rail in the lower-right foreground; a narrow maintenance gantry carrying the scale-reference character; the vast diagonal gate blade; the hydraulic arms and chain-lifting tower; the distant abutment and ocean fading into luminous fog. Use the rising gate edge as the dominant eye path, with the hydraulic cylinders producing a secondary fan-shaped rhythm. Keep generous pale atmospheric space beneath the gate and around the upper-right edge.

Place Hatsune Miku on the narrow gantry near the lower-right third, occupying approximately three percent of the canvas height, shown from a distant back view facing the suspended gate. Her posture is composed and stationary, both hands resting loose on the handrail, so the physical scale around her does all the talking.

Weave Hatsune Miku’s extremely long aqua twin tails into the wind-driven spray. Both tails stream diagonally upward toward the left, repeating the direction of the gate blade, pale where the low sun rims them and almost black against the wet concrete. Her aqua hair is the sole character colour.

Dress Hatsune Miku in a compact charcoal-grey technical outfit derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language: a fitted jacket with sealed seams, tapered trousers, slim dark boots, and one narrow reflective band across the back. Keep the values dark so she stays a scale reference rather than a portrait.

Use a restrained material palette of weathered marine concrete, graphite structural steel, charcoal rubber seals, blackened chain links, brushed aluminum piston rods, dark wet stone, and slate-gray seawater. Render salt staining, mineral streaks, casting seams, repaired concrete patches, chipped corners, drainage marks, plate welds, bolt rows, bearing grease, chain wear, hydraulic fittings, and restrained wet reflections. Illuminate the environment with cool overcast coastal daylight passing through bright sea fog. Let moisture soften distant layers while the gate’s ribs, hinge, and hydraulic joints retain crisp structural definition.

Hold the palette with strict area control. Approximately forty percent of the image is weathered marine concrete in the two abutments, eighteen percent is the safety-orange warning mask in the lower-left, sixteen percent is the cold sea and the spray, twelve percent is graphite structural steel and the gate blade, six percent is charcoal rubber seals and shadow, four percent is Hatsune Miku and her dark kit, three percent is the wet reflection in the drained basin, and one percent is the warm yellow signal lamps. No hue outside this list appears anywhere in the canvas.

Assign materials by zone rather than mixing them evenly. The abutments are weathered marine concrete, streaked and chipped along the coping; the gate blade is graphite steel with a machined edge and riveted stiffeners; the seals are charcoal rubber; the gantry is dull galvanized steel; and the drained basin is wet dark concrete with a thin film of standing water.

Let the last tide leave its record. The concrete carries a dark waterline and pale salt bloom above it, the gate blade shows one rust run under each rivet, the rubber seals are cracked at the corners, and the drained basin keeps a scatter of wet gravel that catches the light in small points.

Light the scene from the sea side at low sun. The light enters behind the gate blade, so the blade reads as a dark diagonal mass with one bright edge along its top, while the nearer abutment keeps only a raking edge light and the drained basin stays in cool shadow.

Anchor one dominant safety-orange scene-derived warning mask to the lower-left corner, occupying approximately 18% of the canvas. Begin with a dense opaque orange field along the bottom and left edges. Shape its inner contour from the descending underside of the diagonal gate blade and the stepped profile of the distant abutment. Extend one narrow orange wedge upward along the gate perspective, then transition toward the scene through controlled translucent bands. Reveal real plate ribs, structural shadows, chain silhouettes, and mist beneath the translucent orange ink. Form the transition from repeated rectangular pressure-cell cuts and short stepped fragments derived from the gate’s rib spacing. Add two pure-white openings aligned with the gaps between hydraulic brackets and three compact deep-black bars parallel to the gate edge. Treat the mask as a flat screen-printed recoloring of the existing architecture and atmosphere.

The entire visible typographic content consists exclusively of three items. Set the concept title “SURGE DIVIDE” inside the opaque lower-left orange field in large condensed white capitals. Shape the letters with steep diagonal terminals and interrupted crossbars derived from the gate blade and hydraulic brackets. Place the code “LOCK D-31” inside the translucent portion, aligned with the rising gate perspective and accompanied by one short black identification bar. Place the secondary word “HOLD” horizontally on the quiet pale concrete surface near the upper-right edge. Keep the title dominant, the code compact, and the external word isolated.

Create a bespoke emblem derived from the gate’s mechanical section. Reduce the wedge-shaped blade to one bold orange trapezoid, represent the hinge with one black circular joint, express the four thrust arms as three visible white diagonal struts, and place two stepped black water lines beneath the blade. Construct the emblem from eight bold shapes with open internal spacing and repeated diagonal cuts. Position the solid emblem in the quiet upper-right atmospheric area at approximately 7% of the canvas width. Repeat a smaller outline version beside “LOCK D-31” inside the orange mask. Add three short diagonal series stripes beneath the large emblem.

Distribute five compact functional symbol anchors around the outer margins: a simplified side elevation of the inclined gate; a hydraulic-cylinder section glyph; a chain-and-pulley load-path diagram; a stepped water-level scale with brackets and ticks; and one framed black-and-white pressure caution stripe. Use a shared system of diagonal terminals, square joints, trapezoidal enclosures, and consistent stroke weight. Link selected anchors with an interrupted perimeter line that follows the lower and right canvas edges. Keep the central gate silhouette and pale ocean opening as clear visual space.

Reserve warm yellow exclusively for small physical signal lamps mounted on unmasked architecture. Place narrow yellow light bars beneath the maintenance gantry, beside the hinge bearings, around two hydraulic coupling points, and at three ascending positions on the chain-lifting tower. Arrange them as a sparse depth path beginning near Hatsune Miku and rising toward the cropped pulley housings. Give each lamp restrained emitted glow and subtle reflections on damp steel, concrete, or polished piston rods.

Render the safety-orange, pure-white, and deep-black graphic system with crisp vector masks, tactile screen-print grain, slight stencil abrasion, ink absorption, and restrained registration offset. Render concrete, steel, water, fog, spray, illumination, and structural shadows with realistic spatial depth and material response. Establish the final reading order as the colossal diagonal gate first, the lower-left orange scene mask second, the tiny aqua-haired figure third, and the sparse emblem and technical symbols last. The finished poster feels severe, calm, mechanically credible, and unmistakably connected to the same offshore tidal megastructure series.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Hatsune Miku, no second figure, no crew, no vessels, no birds, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the three typographic items named above, no watermark, no signature, no frame, no border.

seeds.title: SUSPENDED GATE
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium industrial editorial poster titled “SUSPENDED GATE”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character, a tiny full figure standing on a narrow platform in the lower-left quadrant, inside a colossal suspended transfer gate viewed from the floor of a monumental brutalist industrial chamber through an extreme low-angle wide-angle perspective. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, a slim virtual-singer silhouette, and her original grey-and-teal costume structure. Keep her face, both eyes and both hands fully readable at thumbnail size.

Two enormous concrete pylons rise from the far left and far right sides of the canvas. A gigantic suspended mechanical gate bridges the pylons across the upper half of the image. The gate contains a huge circular aperture, concentric steel rings, segmented locking mechanisms, heavy support ribs, maintenance decks and several long mechanical arms extending toward the center.

Suspend the central gate from dense black cable bundles, steel trusses and massive overhead rails. Add exposed elevators, narrow walkways, ladders, ventilation openings, maintenance cages, structural braces and industrial pipes. Allow several concrete platforms to project diagonally into the foreground, creating strong depth and layered silhouettes.

Keep a broad opening of pale sky and atmospheric white haze behind the circular gate. Bright daylight passes through the aperture, producing a luminous center surrounded by dark industrial machinery. Use cold cement white, pale gray, graphite, charcoal black and muted steel throughout the architecture.

Place Hatsune Miku as a tiny full-body figure on a narrow maintenance platform in the lower-left quadrant, shown from behind in a calm upright pose, her head tipped back and looking diagonally upward toward the suspended gate. Her figure occupies less than five percent of the canvas and stays the only human presence in the chamber. Nothing is in either hand and her feet stay flat on the platform grating.

Weave Hatsune Miku’s extremely long aqua twin tails into the light falling through the aperture. Both tails hang straight down her back and gather into one clean aqua mass that flows toward the central opening, pale where the daylight reaches their crown and almost black at the tips. Let one strand lift in the draught between the pylons. Her aqua hair remains the only character colour.

Dress Hatsune Miku in an original industrial-observer costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not workwear. A dark technical jacket closed to the throat with taped seams, dark trousers bloused into low boots, one thin harness strap across the chest, and a narrow printed sash that trails toward the platform edge. Keep the silhouette slim and quiet so she still reads as herself even at the smallest scale, and keep the whole outfit subordinate to the architecture.

Organize the poster through three visual layers: the monumental architectural scene, one upper-right orange scene-derived graphic mask carrying the typography, and a structural emblem system derived from the gate itself, supported by a sparse auxiliary interface layer.

Create the primary safety-orange mask in the upper-right quadrant, occupying approximately eighteen percent of the canvas. Derive its silhouette from the suspended gate and the right concrete pylon beneath it. Begin with a dense opaque orange field at the upper-right canvas edge. Gradually reduce the orange opacity toward the center, revealing the gate’s steel framework, circular aperture, cables and structural shadows through the translucent inner area.

Extend two long diagonal orange forms from the upper-right field toward the center. Align their angles with the gate’s mechanical support arms. Cut three narrow white openings through the orange region, allowing the architectural silhouette to continue through the graphic layer. Fragment the inner edge into several small stencil-shaped steps that echo the gate’s locking mechanisms.

The complete typographic content consists of three elements.

Place “SUSPENSION GATE” vertically inside the opaque upper-right orange field. Use tall condensed white capitals with custom cut corners, split horizontal strokes and narrow internal spacing. Keep the title contained inside the orange region and crop its uppermost letter slightly at the canvas edge.

Place “SECTOR-08” horizontally inside the translucent lower portion of the orange mask. Use a smaller bold white geometric typeface. Add one thin underline and three short segmented bars beside the sector code.

Place “TRANSFER” in large charcoal-black condensed capitals over a quiet pale concrete area in the lower-right quadrant. Align it with the lower architectural platform and give it generous surrounding space.

Derive one custom structural emblem directly from the featured architecture. Study the main suspended gate, central circular aperture, vertical support axis and two projecting mechanical platforms, then reduce them into a compact flat geometric symbol.

Construct the emblem around one strong central vertical spine. Add two symmetrical angular arms representing the suspended platforms, one broken hexagonal frame representing the gate structure, and one large downward-pointing arrow representing the vertical transfer route. Add three short diagonal stripes to the upper section of the central spine as a compact industrial identification mark.

Use six to eight bold geometric shapes, forty-five-degree cuts, strong symmetry, clean internal gaps and a clearly readable silhouette. Render the emblem as a solid white screen-printed symbol when placed over a dark architectural area, or safety orange when placed over pale sky or concrete.

Place the structural emblem inside the quietest peripheral corner of the composition, occupying approximately six to eight percent of the canvas width. Give it generous empty space and align it with the nearest canvas edges. Add one short horizontal rule and the compact code “S-08” beneath the emblem.

Repeat a much smaller outline version of the same structural emblem beside the sector code inside the orange mask. The large solid emblem acts as the project identity mark, while the small outline version connects the identity system with the typography.

Keep one sparse auxiliary interface layer so the emblem does not read as a lone sticker: a white segmented circular icon on the left-center edge built from three incomplete rings, six radial ticks and one small offset square, visually aligned with the circular aperture; a vertical measurement system along the far-left edge with two white corner brackets, one thin vertical rule, six short ticks and two small triangular pointers, kept clear of the character; a compact white wireframe elevation of the gate near the bottom center using a rectangular frame, a central circle and four structural lines; a restrained black-and-white diagonal caution stripe inside a thin rectangular frame at the lower-right edge close to “TRANSFER”, with one small orange triangular direction marker above it; one small coordinate symbol in the bottom-left corner beneath Miku’s platform combining an L-shaped corner, three short data bars, a miniature broken circle and two square dots; two small white chevrons near the upper-center edge and one thin crosshair near the right-center margin; and a sparse interrupted white line-frame around the outer perimeter that connects these anchors through controlled gaps and registration ticks, all drawn with consistent line thickness and repeated forty-five-degree cuts.

Every auxiliary symbol stays subordinate to the structural emblem: same line weight, same angular construction, no second logo competing with it, and nothing allowed to enter the quiet negative space reserved for the typography.

Warm yellow appears exclusively as physical signal lighting mounted on the gray and black architecture outside the orange mask. Install narrow yellow light bars beneath the gate, beside locking mechanisms, along maintenance railings and at cable connection points. Add several tiny yellow lamps around the distant platforms. Each signal light creates a restrained warm reflection on nearby concrete and steel.

Arrange the yellow lights in a curved rhythm around the circular aperture, visually guiding the eye toward the bright center. Continue a smaller trail of yellow lamps downward toward Hatsune Miku’s platform, connecting the tiny figure with the suspended gate through light.

Use opaque and translucent screen-print ink, subtle stencil wear, hard-edged masks, slight registration offset and tactile paper grain in the graphic-design layer. Keep realistic concrete, steel, cables, atmospheric depth and cinematic light in the architectural layer.

The emblem preserves the recognizable structural logic of the featured building while functioning as a concise industrial logo, creating a direct relationship between architecture, typography and peripheral graphic design.

Final hierarchy: the colossal suspended gate and luminous circular aperture first, tiny Hatsune Miku second, upper-right orange scene-derived mask third, restrained typography inside the mask fourth, the architecture-derived structural emblem and its small outline repeat fifth, the sparse auxiliary interface symbols sixth, and the yellow architectural signal lights last. Monumental, controlled and mechanical, with a clearly visible premium industrial poster-design layer.

Hold the palette with strict area control. Approximately fifty percent of the image is cold cement white and pale grey concrete, eighteen percent is the safety-orange mask in the upper-right quadrant, twelve percent is the pale sky and atmospheric haze behind the gate, eight percent is charcoal-black machinery and deep shadow, six percent is muted steel, four percent is Hatsune Miku and her dark kit, and two percent is the warm yellow signal lighting. No hue outside this list appears anywhere in the canvas.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Hatsune Miku, no second figure, no workers, no vehicles, no birds, no cranes in silhouette, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the three typographic strings named above, no watermark, no signature, no frame, no border.

seeds.title: SWITCHYARD
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “SWITCHYARD”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing on the gravel between two rows of high-voltage equipment, both hands pushed into her jacket pockets. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the pale steel structures and the flat sky.

Use a camera at her chest height on a normal lens, standing only three metres from her, so she fills the middle of the frame and the nearest steel frame is cut by the top edge just behind her shoulder, with the further rows receding above and past her. Place Miku left of centre, full figure visible from her boots to her hair ornaments, occupying about sixty-two percent of the frame height, standing with her shoulders square to the camera.

Give Miku exactly one core action. She stands with her weight on her right leg and both hands pushed deep into her jacket pockets, her shoulders drawn up against the cold, her chin lifted and her eyes level with the lens. Her elbows are slightly out. Nothing is in her hands and no second gesture is added.

Construct the dominant visual object as the insulator stacks: four tall columns of stacked porcelain discs carrying the busbars, standing on pale steel lattice frames in a receding row, occupying approximately fifty percent of the canvas. Each stack is a vertical rhythm of identical discs, capped with a metal fitting, and behind the front row a second and third row repeat the same rhythm smaller and fainter.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The insulators are glazed porcelain, chalky pale brown with a fine crazing and a dull sheen along each disc's rim; the frames are galvanised lattice, bright at the bolt heads and grey everywhere else; the busbars are aluminium tubes with a soft even bloom; the transformer tanks are painted steel in a faded grey-green with cooling fins standing proud; the yard is washed gravel over bare earth; the sky is a flat pale sheet with one soft band of cloud. Each behaves differently — porcelain keeps a dull edge highlight, galvanising scatters into a chalky grey, aluminium returns one soft cylinder, painted steel holds a flat plane, gravel reads as a fine uniform texture.

Build a sequence from the gravel upward. Begin at the yard's surface with its raked drainage channels. Move up past the concrete pad footings and their rusted anchor bolts, then to her boots on the gravel, then to the nearest insulator stack and its repeating discs, then to the busbars crossing overhead, then to the lattice frames rising out of the top edge. The sequence must read as a working yard at a standstill, not as a sculpture garden.

Leave one deliberate absence. In the second row of stacks, one phase is missing entirely: the frame carries its two neighbours and an empty cross-arm between them, with a bare steel bracket and an unconnected cable end taped back along the arm. Keep that gap as the emptiest shape in the frame and put nothing inside it.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the gravel and her boots. Middle ground: Miku, her hands in her pockets and the nearest insulator stack behind her shoulder. Background: the second and third rows, the transformer tank at her left, and the flat sky.

Light the scene from a low sun at the frame's left, so every insulator disc throws a short shadow onto the one below it and the gravel is raked into long thin shadow lines. Let her face take the light from the side with a clean falloff, and keep the sky a stop brighter than the yard so the structures read as dark rhythms against it.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the wind. Both tails are drawn out to her right and slightly back, lifted clear of her shoulders by a steady crosswind, one of them crossing in front of the nearest insulator stack. Keep the hair dense and clearly readable around her head and let it be the only soft, moving thing among all the rigid verticals.

Dress Miku in an original switchyard costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language. Use a padded work jacket in pale grey with a high collar and two deep pockets, worn over a dark fitted layer, with dark straight trousers and low laced boots. Add a thin reflective band around one sleeve, a small enamel badge at the chest and a webbing belt with one buckle. Keep the jacket boxy so her hands-in-pockets stance reads clearly at thumbnail size.

Use a grey-and-chalk-porcelain palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty percent of the image is washed gravel in a narrow range from pale to shadow. Twenty-four percent is the flat sky. Eighteen percent is galvanised lattice and aluminium busbar. Twelve percent is chalky porcelain insulator. Eight percent is her pale jacket and dark trousers. Four percent is painted transformer steel. Less than four percent is the aqua of her hair and the enamel badge.

Drive the printed graphic language from the insulator rhythm rather than from decoration. Let one large ochre ink bloom bleed up the nearest stack from its base fitting, printed flat and matte, its edge stopping at the third disc. Place two hard-edged ochre rectangular colour blocks in the sky, one at the height of her shoulder and one low at the frame's right, both square to the frame so they cut across the frames' verticals. Add a halftone dot gradient that gathers at the yard's far edge and dissolves toward her feet. Cut several clean white knockout strips along the busbars so the overhead lines appear to pass through the printed layer.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “SWITCHYARD” once, large, in pale grey stencil paint on the flat face of the concrete pad at her feet, spanning about a third of the pad's width, in heavy condensed capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “BAY 6” sit stencilled on the transformer tank's lower flange. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry its weathering. The porcelain is crazed into a fine web and stained at the base of each stack; the galvanising is chalky white in the rain shadow and bright at every bolt head; the transformer's paint is chalky on top and streaked below its fins; the gravel holds rake lines, a few darker wet patches and two tyre tracks; the pad footings are stained by rust bleeding from the anchor bolts. Keep the wear vertical on the steel and horizontal on the ground.

Build a second composition through the repetition of the stacks. The second and third rows repeat the front row's disc rhythm at smaller scale, each slightly fainter and cooler than the one before, so the yard reads as a set of parallel vertical columns rather than as a crowd of objects. Keep that repetition geometric only: no second figure, no worker between the rows, no face hidden behind a stack.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. The enamel badge at her chest; the reflective band on her sleeve; one bright bolt head on the nearest frame; the taped-back cable end on the empty cross-arm; a single rust bleed running down a pad footing. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a switchyard would actually show it.

Illuminate with the low sun as the only key and the flat sky as the only fill. Let each disc cut a short shadow onto the one below, let her face sit a stop warmer than the gravel, and keep the far rows in cool even light so depth comes from scale and value rather than from blur.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the gravel, the rake lines and her boots. Second: the nearest pad footings and the transformer tank. Third: Miku's body and the front insulator row. Fourth: the second row and the empty cross-arm. Fifth: the third row, the fence and the flat sky.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: a crisp cel-shaded figure, porcelain rendered as flat pale drums with one edge highlight, precise technical drawing of the lattice and busbars, and a restrained risograph grain in the shadows. Keep the drawing exact and the sky flat, with no photographic depth of field.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no worker between the rows, no face hidden behind a stack, no reflected or mirrored figure, no floating interface, no holograms, no glowing particles, no sparks, no random letters or numbers, no watermark, no signature, no muddy background, no neon, no rainbow lighting, no face obstruction, no hair covering her eyes, no heavy bloom, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, and no malformed hands. Preserve a strict hierarchy: Miku's face first, her hands in her pockets second, the empty cross-arm third, the insulator rhythm fourth, then the busbars, typography and flat sky.

The final image should feel like a yard standing at zero volts: four columns of pale porcelain repeating into the distance, one cross-arm left empty with its cable taped back, a raked gravel floor, and a girl standing between the rows with both hands in her pockets.

seeds.title: TIDAL PRESSURE
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 9:16 ultra-premium industrial editorial poster titled “TIDAL PRESSURE”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character, a small full figure on a narrow inspection bridge in the lower-middle portion of the image of a colossal brutalist tidal-pressure processing complex. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, a slim virtual-singer silhouette, and her original grey-and-teal costume structure. Keep her face, both eyes and both hands fully readable at thumbnail size.

Design the complex as an immense stepped hydroelectric fortress carved into a deep artificial canyon beside a cold gray sea. Use a high oblique camera angle looking diagonally downward across the facility, revealing dozens of descending industrial terraces and an enormous rectangular pressure basin disappearing into white vapor far below.

Position her on a narrow inspection bridge in the lower-middle portion of the image, slightly right of center. Show her as a clearly readable full-body figure occupying approximately ten to twelve percent of the canvas height. She stands beside a steel railing, facing the vast descending facility while turning her face slightly toward the viewer. A cold rim light reveals her golden eye, black double-bar hair clip, straight white hair and white dress.

Weave Hatsune Miku’s extremely long aqua twin tails into the cold sea light. Both tails fall in two clean aqua masses that reach past her waist, pale where the pearl daylight strikes them and deep turquoise where they cross the charcoal terraces, with one strand lifting in the wind that comes off the basin. Her aqua hair is the only cool saturated note in the whole facility.

Dress Hatsune Miku in an original dam-inspection costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not workwear. A short charcoal technical coat over a fitted grey top, tapered dark trousers, low sealed boots, and a narrow pearl-white band across one arm. Keep the values dark and the shapes simple so she reads as a small precise figure against the descending terraces.

The architecture must be built around massive horizontal and diagonal forms rather than a vertical tower. Construct three gigantic wedge-shaped concrete buttresses extending from the upper-left toward the lower-right. Each buttress should be hundreds of meters wide, with steep sloping faces, deep rectangular openings and enormous hollow chambers cut through the concrete.

Between the buttresses, create a sequence of descending pressure basins, turbine trenches and dry spillway channels. Arrange these levels like an industrial ziggurat, with each terrace stepping farther down into the canyon. Use broad flat concrete planes, sharp sloped retaining walls and repeated rectangular voids to establish brutalist rhythm.

At the upper edge of the complex, place one colossal horizontal processing block spanning almost the entire width of the frame. Give it a long cantilevered underside, rows of narrow maintenance apertures and several deeply recessed ventilation cavities. The structure should resemble an artificial cliff rather than a conventional building.

Add enormous rectangular floodgates embedded into the sloped walls. Some gates remain closed as seamless black steel slabs; others are partially open, revealing dark turbine chambers and narrow streams of white pressurized vapor. Avoid large natural waterfalls. Water should appear only as controlled industrial channels, thin silver flows and mist escaping from mechanical systems.

Connect the terraces using long diagonal conveyor bridges, suspended pipe galleries, narrow service walkways and zigzag stair systems. Add several thick pressure pipes running horizontally through the canyon walls. seeds.title: TIDAL SPINE
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium industrial graphic-poster key visual titled “TIDAL SPINE”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character, a tiny full figure near the lower centre-left, presenting a monumental offshore tidal-pressure exchange station at an impossible infrastructural scale. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, a slim virtual-singer silhouette, and her original grey-and-teal costume structure. Keep her face, both eyes and both hands fully readable at thumbnail size.

Compose the architecture through five clearly readable depths: a cropped foreground railing and wet black conduit; a tiny character on the maintenance causeway; the immense concrete caisson; the overlapping crescent compression ribs and suspended piston; distant intake walls dissolving into sea fog. Keep broad areas of pale pearl-gray sky and luminous mist around the upper-left and lower-left regions. Use the diagonal rise of the causeway, the vertical thrust of the caisson, and the inward sweep of the steel ribs to guide the eye upward. Let the piston and caisson remain the unmistakable central silhouette.

Place Hatsune Miku near the lower centre-left, occupying approximately three percent of the canvas height, shown from a distant three-quarter-back view as a delicate scale reference facing the station. Her posture stays quiet, upright and observant, both arms hanging loose at her sides, so the immense caisson does all the talking.

Weave Hatsune Miku’s extremely long aqua twin tails into the sea wind. Both tails are pulled gently toward the left, echoing the direction of the tidal flow, pale where the low sun catches them and almost black against the bone-white concrete. Her aqua hair is the sole character colour.

Dress Hatsune Miku in a compact charcoal-and-grey technical outfit derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language: a fitted jacket with sealed seams, tapered trousers, slim dark boots, and one narrow pale band at the waist. Keep the values dark so she stays a scale reference rather than a portrait.

Use a restrained physical material palette of bone-white precast concrete, graphite structural steel, deep-black rubber seals, dark brushed metal, weathered aluminum, and slate-gray water. Render concrete casting seams, salt deposits, damp streaks, chipped edges, repaired joints, anchor plates, bolt groups, welded gussets, cable clamps, hydraulic couplings, and wet reflections with realistic material response. Illuminate the scene with soft overcast coastal daylight filtered through pale fog. Let the upper structure fade gently into atmospheric brightness while retaining a strong architectural silhouette. Use restrained reflections on the water and causeway to reinforce depth.

Hold the palette with strict area control. Approximately forty-two percent of the image is bone-white precast concrete in the station and the caisson, eighteen percent is the safety-orange warning mask in the upper-right, sixteen percent is the cold pale sea and horizon mist, twelve percent is graphite structural steel, six percent is deep-black rubber seals and shadow, three percent is Hatsune Miku and her dark kit, two percent is the wet steel reflection, and one percent is the warm yellow signal lamps. No hue outside this list appears anywhere in the canvas.

Assign materials by zone rather than mixing them evenly. The caisson is bone-white precast concrete with crisp chamfered arrises and visible formwork seams; the piston housing is graphite steel with a machined bore and one oiled collar; the seals are deep-black rubber; the causeway is wet basalt block; and the sea is a flat cold plane with no wave detail beyond the smallest ripple.

Let the sea air leave its record. Salt bloom sits in the joint lines of the caisson, the steel collars carry a rust tide mark at the water line, the rubber seals are dusted with dried salt, and the causeway holds a thin film of water that breaks the reflection into a hundred small planes. Every mark follows the water rather than decoration.

Light the scene from the west over the sea. The low sun sits just outside the upper-right mask, raking across the caisson face so the chamfers pick up a thin white edge while the piston housing falls into graphite shadow, and the sea returns a broad flat glare that lifts the lower third without any visible highlight.

Overlay one dominant flat safety-orange scene-derived warning mask from the upper-right corner, occupying approximately 17% of the canvas. Begin with a dense opaque orange field at the outer top and right edges. Shape its sweeping inner boundary directly from the concave curve of the right compression rib, then let it descend along the vertical channel of the concrete caisson. Transition the mask inward through several controlled translucent steps, revealing real steel bracing, concrete texture, cable shadows, and portions of the piston beneath the orange ink. Create a fragmented screen-printed transition using stepped erosion, interrupted rectangular teeth, and small angular breaks derived from hydraulic clamp geometry. Place two pure-white openings inside the mask, aligned precisely with gaps between the compression rib and the caisson. Add a few deep-black identification bars integrated into the opaque orange area. Treat the entire mask as a flat alpha-masked recoloring of the architectural scene.

The entire visible typographic content consists exclusively of three items. Set the concise title “TIDAL SPINE” inside the opaque orange region in large condensed geometric capitals. Give the letters narrow vertical proportions, interrupted horizontal strokes, and curved cuts derived from the caisson channels and crescent ribs. Place the sector code “ARRAY K-07” inside the translucent orange transition, aligned with the rising perspective of a service gantry. Place the secondary word “UPWELL” vertically on a quiet pale concrete surface outside the mask near the lower-right edge. Keep all three items highly legible and spatially concentrated. Support the main title with one white underline and three short black identification bars.

Create a bespoke structural emblem from the pressure station. Reduce the caisson to one tall central white spine, represent the two compression ribs with opposing orange crescents, and express the suspended piston as one compact black capsule between them. Construct the emblem from seven bold geometric shapes with clear internal gaps and repeated curved cuts matching the architecture. Place one solid emblem in the quiet lower-left corner at approximately 7% of the canvas width. Repeat a much smaller outline version beside “ARRAY K-07” inside the orange mask. Add three short diagonal identification stripes beneath the large emblem as a consistent series signature.

Distribute five compact functional symbol anchors around the outer margins: a simplified cross-section of the caisson and piston; a circular pressure-gauge glyph derived from the crescent ribs; a vertical tidal-flow diagram using three stepped arrows; a bracketed measurement scale following the caisson taper; and one framed black-and-white hydraulic caution stripe. Use consistent stroke weight, rounded rectangular terminals, crescent cuts, and 45-degree joints. Connect selected anchors with an interrupted perimeter line and small corner-registration marks. Keep these symbols restrained, edge-based, and subordinate to the architectural scene.

Reserve warm yellow exclusively for small physical signal lamps embedded in unmasked architecture. Mount narrow yellow light bars beneath three service decks, beside two hydraulic collars, at several rail junctions, and around one distant valve chamber. Arrange the lamps as a sparse ascending rhythm leading from the causeway toward the suspended piston. Give each lamp a restrained local glow and a subtle reflection on nearby wet steel or concrete. Keep the luminous yellow spatial, physical, and clearly distinct from the flat safety-orange ink.

Render the orange, pure-white, and deep-black graphic layer with crisp vector construction, hard masks, subtle stencil wear, fine screen-print grain, slight ink absorption, and restrained registration offset. Render the architecture, water, fog, illumination, and structural shadows with realistic depth and tactile material detail. Establish the final reading order as monumental tidal architecture first, the single orange scene mask second, the tiny aqua-haired figure third, and the sparse identity system last. The completed image feels calm, severe, highly designed, structurally coherent, and unmistakably part of a premium industrial megastructure poster series.

The final image should read as one machine standing in a cold sea: a bone-white caisson rising out of flat water, one piston collar catching the last light, a small figure on the causeway with her hair pulled left by the wind, and a single orange mask holding the type. Monumental, tidal and perfectly still.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Hatsune Miku, no second figure, no crew, no vessels, no birds, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the three typographic items named above, no watermark, no signature, no frame, no border.

seeds.title: COOLING TOWER
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “COOLING TOWER”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing at the centre of an abandoned cooling tower's floor, her head tipped back as she looks up at the open circle of sky far above. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the concrete.

Use a camera at hip height on a normal lens, set near the tower's wall and tilted up about twenty degrees, so the concrete shell rises around the frame and the open mouth of the tower sits at the top centre as a bright circle. Place Miku at approximately fifty percent of the canvas width, full figure visible from boots to hair ornaments, occupying about twenty-six percent of the frame height, so the structure dwarfs her.

Give Miku exactly one core action. She stands still at the centre of the floor with her feet a shoulder's width apart and both arms hanging loose at her sides, her chin lifted and her head tipped fully back so her face turns up toward the opening with both eyes open. Nothing is in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the tower's shell: a vast tapered cylinder of poured concrete rising from a plinth of radial piers, its inner face scarred by horizontal form-board lines and vertical pour seams, stained in long dark runoff streaks, with a single band of rusted fixings at mid-height. Let the shell occupy the outer two thirds of the frame and let its rim cut the top edge as a bright ellipse.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The concrete is grey and coarse, dark where water has run and pale where it has dried; the plinth piers are heavier aggregate, their corners chipped; the floor is a shallow sheet of standing water over silt, mirror-flat; the fixings are rusted steel; the opening above is pure overcast white. Each behaves differently — poured concrete holds a matte value with faint sheen, aggregate shows stones, standing water returns a full inverted image, rust bleeds a warm stain, sky emits without texture.

Build a stepped sequence from the floor upward. Begin at the bottom with the standing water and the silt beneath it, then Miku's boots and her reflection, then her standing figure, then the plinth piers and their shadows, then the shell's form-board lines rising, then the rusted fixing band, then the rim and the white sky inside it. The sequence must read as standing inside a vast empty vessel, not as a building exterior.

Leave one deliberate absence. The tower floor is empty: no scaffolding, no machinery, no debris, no graffiti, no puddles breaking the mirror but the one under her feet. The only marks on the whole interior are the concrete's own stains and her own reflection.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the standing water, its silt, her boots. Middle ground: Miku, her reflection, the plinth piers. Background: the rising shell, the rusted band, the rim and the white sky. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the opening above. The sky is the key: a single soft column of overcast light falling down the tower's axis, brightest at the rim and fading as it descends, laying an even grey wash on her shoulders, the crown of her head and the water's surface while the lower shell stays in deep shade. Add one weak bounce from the water, which touches only the underside of her jaw and her palms.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the light. Both tails fall straight down her back in one clean aqua mass, pale where the column of sky reaches their crown and almost black at their ends, the tips just clearing the water. Let one strand lift in the draught that moves through the tower.

Dress Miku in an original tower-floor costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not workwear. A dark technical jacket with a high collar and taped seams, dark trousers tucked into low boots, and a thin harness strap across the chest; the jacket is closed to the throat. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale zip line, and keep the silhouette compact so she reads as a small dark mark in a huge pale room.

Use a concrete-grey palette with one dark figure and strict area control. Approximately fifty-two percent of the image is bare concrete in shade, eighteen percent is the pale sky inside the rim, twelve percent is the lit water and its reflection, nine percent is her dark kit, five percent is her aqua hair, and four percent is the rust band and the warm stains.

Drive the printed graphic language from the concrete's own formwork rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the water's surface at the lower left, printed flat and matte, its edge following the silt line. Add a rectangular pale panel on the shell's flat face at the height of her shoulder as a graphic mask, and let one vertical strip of deep oxide red run down the concrete aligned to a pour seam. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “COOLING TOWER” once, large, in pale grey paint stencilled across the flat concrete face of the plinth at her right, spanning about half the visible plinth width, in heavy stencil capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “UNIT 2” sit on a small steel plate bolted to the plinth's corner. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry decades of weather. The concrete is streaked in long vertical runs from the rim, darker under every form-board joint; the plinth piers are chipped at their corners and stained at their feet; the fixings are rusted with a warm bleed below each one; the water holds a film of silt and a thin tideline on the concrete; her boots keep a wet ring where she stands. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the standing water. The water carries the entire shell as an inverted tunnel of grey bands converging on her boots, the rim as one bright ellipse, and her figure as a small dark shape at its centre. Let the reflection run unbroken to the frame's edge and be sharper than the concrete above it.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A rusted steel ladder stub fixed to the shell at mid-height; one broken pier corner showing aggregate; a thin trickle running down the concrete into the water; a coil of wire left on a pier ledge; a chalk survey mark on the floor beside her boot. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where an abandoned cooling tower would actually have it.

Illuminate with the opening above as the only key and the water as the only fill. Let the sky's column wash the rim and the upper shell, fade to nothing at her waist, and let the water lift only the underside of her jaw and her hands. Keep the lower shell, the plinth's shadowed side and the frame's corners at absolute black so the tower reads as a well of concrete with light falling into it.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the water and its silt. Second: her boots and her reflection. Third: Miku's standing figure. Fourth: the plinth piers and their shadows. Fifth: the rising shell, the rust band and the bright rim. Separate them by value steps of roughly thirteen percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every form-board joint and pier edge, restrained risograph grain in the shaded concrete, and the sky kept as one flat clean white.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no workers, no scaffolding, no machinery, no graffiti, no birds in the opening, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no vines or plants, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like standing at the bottom of an empty well made of concrete: one column of sky falling down the axis, a mirror of silt at her feet, and a girl so small at the centre that the tower does all the talking.

seeds.title: TRANSFER TERMINAL
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 9:16 ultra-premium industrial editorial poster titled “TRANSFER TERMINAL”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character, a tiny full figure on a small projecting observation balcony in the lower-right portion of a continental-scale brutalist mass-transfer terminal. Preserve the immeasurable scale, unbounded architecture, extreme structural weight and sophisticated technical-poster design. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, a slim virtual-singer silhouette, and her original grey-and-teal costume structure. Keep her face, both eyes and both hands fully readable at thumbnail size.

The facility must not resemble one complete building. Construct it as an endless system of city-sized horizontal industrial plates, gigantic V-shaped concrete supports, suspended transfer decks and bottomless structural voids. Every major architectural mass must continue beyond the frame so the viewer cannot understand its full dimensions.

Position her on a small projecting observation balcony in the lower-right portion of the composition, occupying approximately four to five percent of the canvas height. She stands beside a narrow black railing and looks upward toward the suspended transfer decks. Render her as a tiny human scale reference, with a narrow charcoal outline and restrained neutral-white rim light separating her white hair and dress from the distant bone-white atmosphere.

Weave Hatsune Miku’s extremely long aqua twin tails into the terminal’s haze. Both tails hang in one clean aqua mass against the dark concrete, pale where the overhead light reaches their crown and almost black where they cross the shadow beneath the plates, with one strand drifting free. Her aqua hair is the only cool saturated note in the whole frame.

Dress Hatsune Miku in an original transfer-terminal costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not workwear. A dark technical jacket with sealed seams, tapered charcoal trousers, low reinforced boots, and one narrow safety-yellow band across the chest echoing the poster accent. Keep the values dark and the shapes simple so she reads as a tiny scale reference.

Build the primary architecture from four immense horizontal processing plates stacked at different heights. Each plate should be hundreds of meters thick and extend far beyond both side edges of the frame. Offset the plates irregularly so that their dark undersides overlap, creating enormous layered ceilings and deep black architectural shadows.

The lowest visible plate begins below the woman and continues outside the bottom edge. A second plate crosses the middle of the frame at a diagonal. A third plate hangs far above, partially blocking the pale overhead light. The highest plate should appear only as a cropped dark underside entering from the upper edge, implying additional levels beyond the visible composition.

Support these plates using colossal V-shaped and inverted-Y concrete structures. Each support should be wider than a city block, with two sloping legs converging into massive load-transfer joints beneath the horizontal decks. Crop the upper and lower portions of the supports outside the frame so their complete geometry remains impossible to see.

Cut gigantic trapezoidal openings through selected support structures. These voids should be large enough to contain entire industrial districts. Inside the openings, show distant suspended bridges, tiny processing blocks and fine rows of maintenance lights, establishing several additional layers of scale.

Connect the main plates using long enclosed conveyor spines, suspended rail corridors and heavy truss bridges. Some transfer corridors should be thin lines against the giant concrete masses, while others should be thick enough to contain several internal floors. Let selected corridors disappear through deep rectangular apertures in the concrete.

Suspend several enormous rectangular counterweight blocks beneath the upper decks. Attach them using groups of thick steel tension rods and mechanical hinge structures. The counterweights should resemble hanging architectural districts rather than ordinary machinery.

Add wide industrial pipe galleries along the undersides of the plates. Use parallel groups of large graphite pipes, but keep them subordinate to the concrete masses. Some pipes should enter recessed wall cavities; others should bend downward and disappear into the bottomless void.

Establish at least five distinct levels of scale:

1. the tiny woman and railings;
2. maintenance doors, ladders and narrow balconies;
3. multi-level bridges and transfer corridors;
4. city-sized horizontal plates and V-shaped supports;
5. distant plates and structures fading into the upper and lower haze.

Repeat tiny human-scale elements across the architecture. Add narrow stairways, pin-sized doors, hairline railings and small white service lights on dozens of separate levels. These repeated details must make the main structures feel incomprehensibly large.

Do not reveal a conventional floor, roofline, surrounding landscape or horizon. Fill the spaces between structures with pale industrial depth and distant architectural fragments. Additional horizontal plates and supports should continue behind the foreground structures, becoming progressively lighter and less detailed without disappearing into excessive fog.

Use raw board-formed concrete with deep seams, chipped edges, vertical mineral streaks, soot marks and large repaired sections. Combine it with matte charcoal-black steel, graphite machinery cavities and dark truss systems. Avoid smooth spaceship panels or brightly painted building exteriors.

Replace the previous crimson-and-ivory graphic system with safety yellow and muted bone white.

Hold the palette with strict area control. Safety yellow at about eight percent marks the border panels, structural warning bars, diagonal hazard marks and small load-path indicators, and never covers an architectural mass. Muted bone white at about seventeen percent carries the inverse-colour silhouettes, schematic masks and large negative-space fields. Seventy percent of the frame stays raw concrete grey, charcoal black and deep structural shadow, and the remaining five percent is Hatsune Miku, her dark kit and the neutral-white service lights. No hue outside this list appears anywhere in the canvas.

Apply bone-white inverse masks to selected lower transfer bridges and parts of one V-shaped support. Transform these areas into flat screen-printed engineering silhouettes with thin charcoal outlines. The transition between realistic concrete and bone-white schematic rendering should be abrupt, precise and graphic.

Place a large safety-yellow vertical panel along the far-left edge. Cut two broad bone-white diagonal bands through it. Add smaller safety-yellow rectangles, narrow bars and load-direction arrows near selected platform joints. Keep the central architecture mostly free from large flat color fields.

Use the following exact readable text only:

"MASS TRANSFER"
"LOAD PATH"
"ZONE-11"

Place “MASS TRANSFER” vertically along the far-left border in a tall condensed outlined typeface. Place “LOAD PATH” horizontally near the lower-left edge in bold charcoal lettering over a bone-white field. Place “ZONE-11” inside the upper safety-yellow panel in a smaller charcoal stencil typeface. Do not place typography across the woman or central architectural void.

Illuminate the terminal through several narrow overexposed openings far above. Use cold bone-white light to reveal the edges of the horizontal plates and V-shaped supports. Create enormous hard-edged shadows beneath every suspended deck. Add tiny neutral-white service lights across the darker structures as scale indicators.

Keep the nearest balcony, woman, railings and concrete edges in crisp hard focus. Render sharp material grain, clean structural seams, distinct straight hair strands and precise truss geometry. Restrict atmospheric softness to the most distant layers only.

Compose the architecture so that concrete plates, supports, bridges and dark voids cross all four frame edges. The viewer must never see the terminal as a complete object. It should feel like one small visible section of an industrial system extending for many kilometers.

Combine monumental brutalism, continental logistics infrastructure, industrial cathedral design, architectural concept art, screen-printed technical graphics and premium anime game-poster direction. The final image should feel impossibly heavy, ordered, dangerous and silent.

No central tower, no circular reactor, no hydroelectric dam, no visible ocean, no conventional factory hall, no complete building silhouette, no city skyline, no giant vehicle, no spaceship hull, no brightly colored architectural cladding and no toy-like modular structures. Do not add another character. Keep the woman’s straight white hair, golden eyes, single black double-bar hair clip on her left temple, flat chest and opaque white spaghetti-strap dress. No random typography, watermark or signature.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Hatsune Miku, no second figure, no workers, no vehicles, no birds, no floating platforms, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text of any kind, no watermark, no signature, no frame, no border.

seeds.title: VENT SHAFT
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “VENT SHAFT”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing at the bottom of a deep concrete ventilation shaft, one palm flat against the wall. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the pale grey wall.

Use a camera at her hip height on a wide lens, set in one corner of the shaft and tipped steeply up, so the walls converge into a small bright square of sky at the top of the frame and the floor sits low in the composition. Place Miku left of centre, full figure visible from her boots to her hair ornaments, occupying about fifty-two percent of the frame height, standing on a floor of broken concrete with her right palm flat on the wall beside her shoulder.

Give Miku exactly one core action. She stands with her weight on her left foot and her right arm raised so the palm lies flat on the wall at shoulder height, her fingers spread. Her left arm hangs at her side with the fingers loose. Her chin is lifted a few degrees and her face turns toward the lens so both eyes read clearly. Nothing is held in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the shaft itself: four sheer concrete walls rising out of the frame into a small bright square of sky, occupying approximately sixty-eight percent of the canvas. Two opposite walls carry a steel ladder and a cable tray, the other two are bare, and a horizontal construction joint crosses all four at the height of her chest.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The walls are board-formed concrete with vertical grain still printed in it and a chalky pale tone; the construction joint stands a few millimetres proud with a dark shadow line under it; the ladder is galvanised steel, its rungs polished at the centre and rusted at the stiles; the cable tray is a shallow steel channel carrying three dusty cables; the floor is broken concrete and grit with a shallow puddle in one corner; the sky is a flat pale disc. Each behaves differently — board-formed concrete holds fine vertical streaks, the joint cuts one hard line, galvanised rungs keep small bright points, dusty cable stays matte, the puddle returns a broken sheen, and the sky stays a flat square.

Build a sequence from the floor upward. Begin at the broken concrete and the puddle's hard edge. Move up past her boots and the grit caught against the wall, then to her palm on the board-formed face, then up the wall's vertical grain, then to the construction joint and its shadow line, then to the ladder's rungs climbing away, then to the small square of sky at the top. The sequence must read as the bottom of a working shaft, not as a well or a stairwell.

Leave one deliberate absence. Between the construction joint and her head, a rectangular block of the wall's formwork has been left unrendered, a shallow recess one brick deep and two hands wide, its inner face rough and its edges still sharp. Keep that recess as the emptiest shape in the frame and put nothing inside it.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the broken concrete floor and the puddle. Middle ground: Miku, her palm on the wall and the nearest corner. Background: the four walls converging overhead, the ladder and the small bright square of sky.

Light the scene from the open top alone, so a soft even wash falls straight down the shaft and the walls are brightest near the top and dimmest at the floor. Let the light catch the top edge of every joint and the tops of her shoulders, and let her face stay one stop above the wall behind it with both eyes readable. Keep the lower corners near-black.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails against the wall. Both tails fall straight down her back and spread across the floor behind her, one of them trailing into the puddle, so the aqua reads as the only colour in a frame of pale grey. A single strand lifts across her cheek. Keep the hair dense and clearly readable around her head.

Dress Miku in an original shaft costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language. Use a short work jacket in pale grey with a high collar and a single zip, worn over a dark fitted layer, with dark trousers tucked into low laced boots. Add a thin reflective band around one sleeve, a small tag on a cord at her chest and a webbing belt with one buckle. Keep the fit close so the dust on her shoulders reads as a thin even film.

Use a pale concrete palette with one dark note and strict area control. Approximately fifty-eight percent of the image is board-formed concrete in a narrow range from bright to shadow. Sixteen percent is the pale sky. Ten percent is the shadowed lower walls. Eight percent is her pale jacket and dark trousers. Four percent is galvanised ladder and tray. Four percent is the broken floor and puddle. Less than two percent is the aqua of her hair and the reflective band.

Drive the printed graphic language from the wall's vertical grain rather than from decoration. Let one large graphite ink bloom bleed down the wall beside her from the construction joint, printed flat and matte, its edge stopping exactly at the joint. Place two hard-edged graphite rectangular colour blocks, one on the opposite wall at her knee height and one high above her head, both square to the frame so they stay vertical while the walls converge.
