Add a halftone dot gradient that gathers at the floor and dissolves toward the sky. Cut several clean white knockout strips along the wall's vertical grain so the concrete appears to pass through the printed layer.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “VENT SHAFT” once, large, in pale grey stencil paint on the wall at her shoulder height, spanning about a third of that wall's visible width and interrupted once by her raised arm, in heavy condensed capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “S-14” sit stencilled on the cable tray's side below the joint. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry its use. The walls are streaked vertically by years of seepage, with three pale efflorescence blooms at the joint; the ladder's rungs are polished in their centres and its stiles rusted at every fixing; the cable tray carries a fine even dust and one kinked cable; the floor is broken into slabs with grit between them and a shallow puddle holding a grey scum; her boots carry a pale dust line where they meet the trouser cuff. Keep the wear vertical on the walls and horizontal on the floor.

Build a second composition through the shaft's convergence. The four walls repeat the same vertical grain and the same joint line at four different angles, so the frame reads as one square tube narrowing to a point of light, and the puddle holds that small bright square as one broken shape. Keep it a broken square only: no mirrored figure, no second face, no reflected body in the water.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. The tag at her chest; the reflective band on her sleeve; one bright bolt on a ladder fixing; a single kinked cable in the tray; the pale efflorescence at the joint. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a vent shaft would actually show it.

Illuminate with the open top as the only key and the walls' bounce as the only fill. Let the sky be the brightest shape, let every joint hold one thin bright edge, and keep the floor two stops down so the shaft reads as four planes converging on a single point of light.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the broken floor and the puddle. Second: her boots and the grit at the wall. Third: Miku's body and her raised palm. Fourth: the construction joint, the unrendered recess and the ladder. Fifth: the converging walls and the small bright square of sky.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: a crisp cel-shaded figure, concrete rendered as flat planes with fine vertical streaks, exact drawing of the joint and the ladder rhythm, and a restrained risograph grain in the shadows. Keep the drawing exact and the perspective strict, with no photographic depth of field.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no reflected or mirrored figure in the puddle, no floating interface, no holograms, no glowing particles, no volumetric light shafts, no random letters or numbers, no watermark, no signature, no muddy background, no neon, no rainbow lighting, no face obstruction, no hair covering her eyes, no heavy bloom, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, and no malformed hands. Preserve a strict hierarchy: Miku's face first, her palm on the wall second, the unrendered recess third, the joint and ladder fourth, then the square of sky, typography and pale walls.

The final image should feel like the bottom of a hole built for air: four board-formed walls converging on one small bright square, a ladder climbing out of the frame, a shallow recess left unrendered, and a girl standing on broken concrete with one hand on the wall.

seeds.title: WATER TOWER
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “WATER TOWER”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing at the bottom of the inside of an empty water tower, one palm flat on the central riser pipe. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the pale curved wall.

Use a camera at her chest height on a wide lens, set against the wall and tipped back so the cylinder converges overhead into a bright ring of sky and her body stands small against the curve. Place Miku left of centre, full figure visible from her bare feet to her hair ornaments, occupying about forty-eight percent of the frame height, standing on the floor beside the central pipe with her right palm flat against it.

Give Miku exactly one core action. She stands with her weight on her left foot and her right arm bent so the palm lies flat on the riser pipe at shoulder height, her fingers spread. Her left arm hangs at her side with the fingers loose. Her chin is lifted toward the light above and her face turns back down to the lens so both eyes are visible. Nothing is held in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the cylinder itself: a tall round tank interior with a smooth concrete wall curving away on both sides, a narrow ring of open sky at the very top, and a single vertical riser pipe running up the middle of the frame, occupying approximately sixty-two percent of the canvas. Three shallow ring beams break the wall at intervals, and a steel ladder climbs the left side out of the top edge.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The wall is poured concrete with faint horizontal lift lines and a chalky pale tone; the ring beams stand a few centimetres proud and cast a thin shadow above themselves; the riser is painted steel in a faded blue-green, chalky at the joints; the floor is a shallow sheet of standing water over a concrete slab; the sky at the top is a pale even white. Each behaves differently — the curving concrete takes a slow vertical gradient, the beams hold hard shadow lines, painted steel keeps one cold highlight, standing water returns a broken bright sheen, and the sky stays a flat disc.

Build a sequence from the floor upward. Begin at the standing water and the thin ring of light it holds. Move up past her bare feet and the ripples around them, then to her palm on the riser, then up the riser's chalky joints, then to the first ring beam and its shadow, then to the second and third beams compressing overhead, then to the bright disc of sky at the top of the frame. The sequence must read as the inside of a working tank, not as a silo or a well.

Leave one deliberate absence. Two metres above her, a rectangular steel liner panel is missing from the wall, leaving a clean recess the width of her shoulders with its bolt holes bright and empty and the bare concrete showing behind it. Keep that recess as the sharpest, emptiest shape in the frame and put nothing inside it.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the standing water and her bare feet. Middle ground: Miku, the riser pipe and the nearest ring beam. Background: the curving wall, the upper beams and the bright disc of sky above.

Light the scene from the open top alone, so a broad soft wash falls down the cylinder and everything above her is bright while the wall behind her feet goes cool and dim. Let the light catch the top of the riser, the upper faces of each ring beam and the crown of her head, and let her face stay in the soft middle range with both eyes readable. Keep the bottom corners of the frame the darkest part of the image.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails against the curved wall. Both tails fall down her back and spread across the pale concrete behind her, their ends drifting in the standing water, so the aqua reads as the only saturated colour in a frame of pale grey. One strand crosses the riser in front of her palm. Keep the hair dense and clearly readable around her head.

Dress Miku in an original tank-interior costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language. Use a pale shirt with the sleeves rolled to the elbow and the tails left out, worn over a dark fitted layer, with dark trousers rolled at the ankle and bare feet. Add a thin cord at her waist and one small steel tag on a cord at her chest. Let the shirt's hem be damp and darker where the standing water has touched it.

Use a pale concrete-and-water palette with strict area control. Approximately fifty-two percent of the image is curved concrete in a narrow range from bright to cool shadow. Eighteen percent is the bright disc of sky. Twelve percent is the standing water. Eight percent is the painted riser. Six percent is her pale shirt and dark trousers. Less than four percent is the aqua of her hair and the small steel tag.

Drive the printed graphic language from the cylinder's curvature rather than from decoration. Let one large cobalt ink bloom bleed down the wall at her right, printed flat and matte, its lower edge following the waterline. Place two hard-edged cobalt rectangular colour blocks on the wall, one at the height of her shoulder and one high between two ring beams, both square to the frame so they stay vertical while the wall curves. Add a halftone dot gradient that gathers at the floor and dissolves toward the top ring. Cut several clean white knockout strips along the lift lines so the concrete appears to pass through the printed layer.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “WATER TOWER” once, large, in dark paint rolled onto the riser pipe at the height of her hip, running vertically up the pipe so the two words stack, in heavy condensed capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “TANK 2” sit stencilled on the nearest ring beam above her head. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry its service. The wall's lift lines are faint but continuous, with one horizontal damp band two metres up; the ring beams are chipped at their outer edges; the riser's paint is chalky at every joint and worn to metal in a narrow band where hands have gripped; the floor's standing water holds a scatter of grit and a tide ring at the wall; the steel ladder's rungs are polished bright at their centres. Keep the wear concentric and horizontal.

Build a second composition through the standing water. The water holds the bright disc of sky as one broken pale ring that never resolves into a picture, and the riser's lower length breaks that ring into two arcs. Keep it a broken ring only: no mirrored figure, no second face, no reflected body in the water.

Add only a few luxury details, all at contact points. The steel tag at her chest; one bright bolt hole in the missing liner's recess; a single ladder rung polished to a shine; a grit line where the water meets the wall; the pale chalky joint on the riser under her palm. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a tank interior would actually show it.

Illuminate with the open top as the only key and the curved wall's bounce as the only fill. Let the disc of sky be the brightest shape, let each ring beam hold a thin bright edge on its upper face, and keep the wall behind her feet two stops down so the cylinder reads as one tall gradient of light.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the standing water and her feet. Second: the riser's base and the tide ring at the wall. Third: Miku's body and her palm on the pipe. Fourth: the ring beams and the missing liner panel. Fifth: the upper wall, the ladder and the bright disc of sky.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: a crisp cel-shaded figure, concrete rendered as a smooth flat gradient, precise technical drawing of the ring beams and the riser's joints, and a restrained risograph grain in the shadows. Keep the drawing exact and the curve smooth, with no photographic depth of field.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no reflected or mirrored figure in the water, no floating interface, no holograms, no glowing particles, no volumetric light shafts, no random letters or numbers, no watermark, no signature, no muddy background, no neon, no rainbow lighting, no face obstruction, no hair covering her eyes, no heavy bloom, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, and no malformed hands. Preserve a strict hierarchy: Miku's face first, her palm on the riser second, the missing liner third, the ring beams fourth, then the disc of sky, typography and pale wall.

The final image should feel like standing inside a drained tank: one pale cylinder closing overhead into a small bright disc, a riser running up the middle, a bare recess where a panel was taken out, and a girl at the bottom with one hand on the pipe and her chin lifted.

seeds.title: KERB
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “KERB”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character walking along the top of a granite kerb a few minutes after rain, her arms held out to both sides and one foot set in front of the other. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the wet street.

Use a camera at hip height on a normal lens, standing in the road ahead of her and about thirty degrees off her front, so this is a three-quarter front view: her face, both eyes, her chest and the fronts of both legs are open to the lens, her body angled slightly away, the gutter water in the near foreground, and the kerb running as one pale line across the lower third, angling slightly up toward the right of the frame. Place Miku at approximately fifty percent of the canvas width, full body visible from shoes to hair ornaments, occupying about fifty-five percent of the frame height. Let the gutter water fill the bottom quarter and the pale overcast sky fill the top third.

Give Miku exactly one core action. She walks the kerb line heel to toe toward the lens: her front foot is flat on the stone with the toe at the arris, her back heel is lifted with the toe still on the kerb, both arms are held out to the sides at shoulder height with the palms open and turned slightly forward, and her torso stays upright with a small counter-sway at the hips. Her chin is level, her gaze runs along the kerb and toward the camera side, and nothing is in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the kerb itself: a run of grey granite kerb stones with a worn arris, dark mortar joints, one chipped corner and a faded painted line on the road side. Let the kerb occupy the lower third as a single perspective line, its wet top face catching the sky as one pale band, and let its vertical face below hold a dark wet tone with two joints bleeding water.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The kerb is coarse grey granite, dark and saturated on its face, paler on its worn top edge; the gutter water is a mirror holding an oil film and floating grit; the asphalt is dark, coarse and wet except for a drying crown; the sidewalk paving beyond the kerb is pale and damp; the low wall behind is rendered concrete stained at its base; the sky is a flat silver overcast. Each behaves differently — wet granite holds a soft sheen and a bright arris, water returns a broken image, wet asphalt reads as a dark field with one pale matte band, damp paving scatters light, concrete absorbs it.

Build a stepped sequence upward through the frame. Begin at the bottom edge with the gutter water and one floating leaf, then the kerb's vertical face and its joints, then her shoes on the arris, then her spread arms and open palms, then the wet asphalt behind her, then the drying crown of the road, then the flat silver sky. The sequence must read as a street a few minutes after rain, not as a wet street in the middle of a shower.

Leave one deliberate absence. The rain has already stopped and the road's crown is dry: a pale matte band runs down the centre of the asphalt, and the wet surface begins only where the gutter water reaches it. The drying edge is a soft irregular line about two thirds of the way up the road, and nothing in the frame is falling.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the gutter water, its oil film, one floating leaf, the near face of a kerb stone. Middle ground: Miku, her spread arms, her feet on the arris, the painted road line. Background: the damp sidewalk, a low rendered wall, one bare tree, the empty street, the flat sky. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the open overcast sky. The sky is the key: a flat silver wash from above and slightly in front, laying an even light on her face, the pale shirt and the tops of her outstretched forearms, with almost no shadow. Add one weak warm accent from a shop window far behind her right shoulder, which touches only the low wall's edge and one strand of her hair. Let the gutter water return the sky as the brightest band in the lower frame.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the light and into the stride. The nearer tail lifts off her shoulder with the step and swings forward, one clean aqua mass, its underside picking up the pale paving and its outer curve silvered by the sky. The farther tail hangs behind her back, damp, its end darkening where it has brushed the wall. Let one strand lie stuck to her cheek.

Dress Miku in an original after-rain street costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not sportswear. A pale shirt under a short dark jacket worn open, trousers cropped once above the ankle, low canvas shoes with pale soles, and a thin strap across her chest. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment, and keep the arms free and unencumbered so the spread pose reads at thumbnail size.

Use a wet grey-and-teal palette with one pale note and strict area control. Approximately thirty-four percent of the image is wet asphalt and kerb, twenty percent is the pale overcast sky, sixteen percent is the gutter water and its reflection, twelve percent is the damp sidewalk and the low wall, ten percent is Miku's dark jacket and cropped trousers, six percent is her aqua hair, and two percent is the faded painted road line.

Drive the printed graphic language from the street's own markings rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the wet asphalt at the lower right, printed flat and matte, its edge stopping at the gutter water. Add a rectangular pale panel on the low wall behind her as a graphic mask at the height of her shoulder, and let one vertical strip of deep blue run down the wall aligned to a kerb joint. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “KERB” once, large, in deep teal stencil capitals applied across the flat concrete face of the low wall behind her, its baseline just above her hair ornaments, spanning about two thirds of the wall's visible width and staying legible at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “PUDDLE” sit in faded white stencil on the flat vertical face of the kerb stone below her front foot. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the rain that has just passed. The kerb is dark and saturated with a paler drying top edge; its joints hold a line of water; the asphalt reads in two tones, wet below and matte above, with grit gathered in the runoff lines; the wall is stained at its base and pale above; the painted road line is chalky and lifting in patches. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the gutter water. The water carries her legs as two dark shapes broken by ripples, the kerb face as a hard vertical band, the sky as one bright field and the low wall as a pale smear, and the reflection stops at the water's far edge. Let one slow drip from her back sleeve break the surface into a single spreading ring.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One folded leaf floating in the gutter; a bottle cap resting against the kerb face; a drain slot with grit caught across its bars; a faded utility mark stencilled on the kerb; a bicycle leaning against the low wall far behind her, small and out of focus. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a street a few minutes after rain would actually have it.

Illuminate with the flat overcast sky as the only key. Let the sky light every upward face evenly, put one broad soft highlight on the wet kerb's top edge, one on her forearms and one on the paving, and let the shop window add a single weak warm note at the wall's edge. Keep the values compressed and the contrast low, so the street reads silver rather than black.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: gutter water, oil film, floating leaf, kerb face. Second: Miku, her spread arms, her shoes on the arris. Third: the painted road line and the wet asphalt. Fourth: the damp sidewalk and the low wall. Fifth: the bare tree and the flat sky. Separate them by value steps of roughly ten percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every kerb joint and paving slab, restrained risograph grain in the asphalt fields, crisp flat fills in the pale sky, and fine wet-edge detail only along the kerb, the gutter and her shoes.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no pedestrian on the sidewalk, no car, no falling rain, no umbrella, no splash on her clothes, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like the ten minutes after a shower: a dry crown of road, a gutter holding the sky upside down, and a girl walking the kerb line with both arms out as if the whole street were a beam.

seeds.title: KILN SONG
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “KILN SONG”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing at the mouth of a wood-fired kiln during an evening opening. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands, hair ornaments and long twin-tail identity immediately readable against the hot interior.

Use a low three-quarter camera at hip height, tilted slightly upward, with a wide lens and restrained perspective so the kiln mouth reads as a thick architectural ring. Place Miku in the right third, full body visible from boots to hair ornaments, occupying approximately thirty percent of the image. She stands braced with feet apart on packed clay, her weight on the back leg and the front foot angled inward, torso turned toward the kiln and head lowered so both eyes stay visible in three-quarter view, lit from the opening.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Her right hand holds a long iron peel with a single glazed bowl balanced on its flat end, drawing it slowly out of the kiln mouth at chest height; her left hand is raised and open beside her face, palm out, shielding against the heat. The bowl is the brightest object in the frame — its glaze still moving with heat. Keep the pose still and the arms clear of her face; add no second tool and no second action.

Construct the dominant visual object as a wood-fired climbing kiln, a massive stepped masonry mass occupying approximately seventy percent of the canvas, its opening a low arch cropped by the right frame edge and its chimney rising out of the top edge. The brick face is soot-blackened at the mouth and pale with ash higher up, with a row of small spy holes and a collapsed brick at the shoulder. Stacked cordwood fills the lower left, its cut ends facing the camera.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The kiln skin is rough firebrick with slumped mortar and a glassy ash glaze creeping down from the spy holes; the arch mouth is a pale refractory slab cracked in two; the peel is black iron, its shaft scaled with heat; the bowl is celadon glaze over porcelain, its surface wet-looking and alive; the ground is packed red clay dusted with ash; the cordwood is split oak with dry checked ends. Each material must behave differently — brick spalls, ash fuses, iron scales and blisters, glaze flows and pools at the foot ring, ash drifts and holds the shape of boots.

Build a stepped sequence of the fired ware. Begin at the lower left with two bowls still stacked and dull, their glaze matte and unremarkable. Move right toward the mouth through bowls that grow progressively more lustrous: a cup with a fine crackle, then a plate whose glaze has broken into a green pool at one rim, then a tall jar with a long drip that has run past the foot, then the single bowl on the peel with its glaze still fluid and mirror-bright. End with one piece so overfired that its glaze has bubbled and gone rough. The sequence must read as heat across distance, not as decoration.

Leave one deliberate absence. One shelf of the kiln is empty, visible through the widest spy hole as a clean dark rectangle with nothing on it and a thin crescent of pale ash on its front edge. Keep that rectangle as the darkest, quietest shape inside the bright mouth and place no object inside it.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: split cordwood, a pair of heavy gloves dropped on the clay, and the iron peel's shaft crossing the lower-right corner. Middle ground: Miku, the peel, the bowl and the kiln mouth. Background: the stepped brick mass, the chimney, the ash-pale upper wall and a doorway of deep evening blue at the far left.

Light the scene entirely from the kiln opening plus one small hanging work lamp. The mouth is the key: a low orange-white source spilling out across the clay, underlighting Miku's jaw, forearms and the inside of her sleeves, and throwing a long shadow of the peel back across the ground. The lamp adds a small cool-green pool at the far left so the room never goes fully warm. Keep the fire reading as a real contained source with no glow halo and no lens flare.

Weave Miku’s extremely long twin tails against the heat. The nearer twin tail lifts slightly away from her back, passes across the kiln's pale arch, and is cropped by the right frame edge; where it crosses the mouth its edge is burned to a thin bright line. The farther twin tail falls behind her shoulder and stays in shadow. Keep the hair dense and clearly readable at her head, allowing it to thin only where it crosses the hot opening.

Dress Miku in an original kiln-side costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language. Use a heavy ash-grey canvas jacket with the collar turned up, sleeves pushed to the elbow, over a fitted pale inner layer, with a scorched leather apron panel fastened by three iron hooks, a wide waist wrap knotted at the left, thick heat-resistant gloves hanging at her belt, and boots laced to the ankle. Add one charred patch at the right cuff, a fine dusting of ash across both shoulders, and three small coral thread tags at the apron hem. Keep the garment heavy and ash-dulled rather than styled as fashion.

Use a two-temperature palette. Approximately forty-two percent of the image is smoke-black and raw umber brick. Eighteen percent is ash grey and pale bone. Fourteen percent is deep evening blue in the doorway and upper corners. Twelve percent is ember orange. Eight percent is celadon green on the glaze. Four percent is dull iron. Less than two percent is the aqua of her hair and eyes, which must stay the coolest thing in the frame apart from the doorway.

Drive the printed graphic language from Miku’s own palette. Let one large celadon ink bloom spread across the ash-pale brick on the left, its edge following the mortar joints. Add two hard-edged soot rectangles above the mouth where smoke has repeatedly washed. Let a fine halftone of ash speckle live only on the clay floor near the kiln. Cut one clean pale knockout where the work lamp reaches the wall. Add rare iron microdots only along the peel shaft and the apron hooks.

Print the text as physical matter. Fasten a small enamel plate to the kiln's left shoulder with the exact readable words “KILN SONG” in a narrow serif, pale glaze lettering on dark ground, one corner chipped. Add one smaller chalk tally on the arch slab recording a firing count. Both sit flat on the masonry and are partly dusted with ash so they read as objects, not floating type.

Let every surface carry the firing. The brick is dull where it is cold and glassy where ash has fused, with one hairline crack running down from a spy hole. The ground holds boot prints pressed into clay and a drift of ash caught against the cordwood. The peel is scorched in bands. The bowl's glaze pools thick and dark at the foot ring and thins to pale green at the lip. Nothing should look new.

Build a second composition through firelight and shadow. The mouth throws a broad warm trapezoid across the clay and up onto the left cordwood; the peel casts a long thin shadow that crosses it at an angle; the raised hand throws a second, smaller shadow onto her own cheek. Inside the mouth, the empty shelf reads as a dark rectangle framed in orange, so the absence repeats as a shape in light.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A brass caliper on the arch ledge, one small celadon shard used as a test piece, three coral thread tags, a folded firing log with pencil marks, and a single iron hook holding a heat glove. Keep them clustered near the mouth and never scattered across the brick face.

Illuminate with the kiln as key and the hanging lamp as a cool secondary. Keep the brightest value on the bowl on the peel, the second brightest on the ash-pale arch, and let the chimney and the upper brick fall into deep smoke shadow. Every shadow must agree with the single low fire source.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: cordwood ends, dropped gloves, the peel shaft. Primary middle ground: Miku, the peel and the lifted bowl. Secondary: the kiln mouth, arch slab and the row of bowls. Tertiary: the stepped brick mass, spy holes and chimney. Background: the evening-blue doorway, held as clean negative space.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a hand-pulled print: crisp drawn linework, ink and watercolor washes with visible wet edges, dry-brush erosion on the brick and ash, soft paper grain in the flat areas, and clean lithograph texture in the smoke. Keep the drawing precise and the paint loose, with no photographic depth of field.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no floating interface, no holograms, no glowing particles, no abstract light streaks, no full-canvas glitch, no random letters or numbers, no watermark, no signature, no muddy background, no neon, no rainbow lighting, no face obstruction, no smoke covering her eyes, and no malformed hands. Preserve a strict hierarchy: Miku’s face and the lifted bowl first, the kiln mouth second, the row of ware third, the empty shelf fourth, then the brick mass, typography and shadow.

The final image should feel like a room where fire is a material and time is measured in how far a glaze has run: one bowl still moving on the peel, one shelf left empty, and the whole workshop held in the half-minute before the kiln is closed for the night.

seeds.title: KIOSK
seeds.raw:
Create a square 1:1 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “KIOSK”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing inside a small street newspaper kiosk at night, with magazines glowing under a single warm bulb. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the warm interior.

Use a camera at chest height on a normal lens, set outside the kiosk's service window and square to it, so the window frame forms a level rectangle and the interior reads as a shallow lit box. Place Miku at approximately forty-six percent of the canvas width, seen from the waist up, occupying about fifty percent of the frame height. Let the kiosk's counter and window frame fill the lower half.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Her right hand holds a folded newspaper up at chest height, half turned toward the window as if reading a headline aloud, and her left hand rests flat on the counter. Her head is tipped slightly down, both eyes visible above the paper's edge. Keep the pose still, the arms clear of her face, and put nothing else in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the kiosk's magazine wall: three shelves of overlapping magazines and paperbacks, spines out and covers stacked so only their top thirds show, filling the window's back plane edge to edge. Let the wall occupy approximately fifty-five percent of the canvas area, lit from above by one caged bulb.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The magazine covers are coated paper, some curling at the corner, some with a folded return; the shelving is thin steel angle with a grey powder coat; the counter is stained plywood with an aluminium edge strip; the window frame is painted timber, chipped at the sill; the exterior ground is wet pavement; the kiosk's outer skin is painted steel in a faded green. Each behaves differently — coated paper returns a flat bright value with one soft sheen, steel angle reads as thin lines, plywood absorbs, painted timber holds a chalky edge, wet pavement fragments light.

Build a stepped sequence from the counter inward. Begin at the bottom edge with the aluminium counter edge and one coin, then the plywood surface and a rubber stamp, then Miku's hands and the newspaper, then the first magazine shelf, then the overlapping covers of the second and third, then the caged bulb above. The sequence must read as looking into a lit box, not as a flat wall of print.

Leave one deliberate absence. One shelf section stands completely empty: a clean gap of about a forearm's width between two stacks, with the dust line still showing where the magazines used to stand and one wire retainer hanging loose. Keep the gap at eye height on the left of her head so the empty bay reads clearly against the printed wall.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: counter edge, coin, wet pavement below. Middle ground: Miku, the newspaper, her hands. Background: the magazine wall and the caged bulb. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the caged bulb only. The bulb is the key: a small warm source above and slightly in front of her, throwing a hard pool on the counter, a warm wash across the magazine wall, and a bright top light on her hair and shoulders. Add one cool spill from the street behind the camera, giving the window frame's outer face a blue-grey edge. Keep every shadow short and dark, and let the kiosk's corners stay at near-black.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the warm interior. The nearer tail falls forward over her shoulder in one clean aqua mass, its upper curve catching the bulb light; the farther tail is trapped behind her back and reads as a dark vertical against the covers. Let the bulb put one small bright point on her hair ornament.

Dress Miku in an original kiosk-shift costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not a shop apron. A dark short-sleeved shirt with the collar open, a pale knitted vest over it, and a thin cord at her wrist. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment, and keep the silhouette simple enough to read at thumbnail size.

Use a warm-on-dark palette with strict area control. Approximately forty-four percent of the image is warm lamplight on paper, twenty-two percent is deep shadow and dark steel, twelve percent is the plywood counter, ten percent is Miku's dark shirt, six percent is her aqua hair, four percent is the faded green outer skin, and two percent is the cool street spill. Keep the cool value to the frame's outer edge only.

Drive the printed graphic language from the kiosk's own stock rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the lower left of the counter, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular pale panel behind the shelves as a graphic mask at the height of the second shelf, and let one vertical strip of deep red run from the top shelf to the counter, aligned to a shelf upright. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “KIOSK” once, large, in white paint applied across the kiosk's outer fascia board above the window, spanning about half the fascia's width in heavy capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “EVENING” sit on a small enamel plate screwed to the window frame's lower corner. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled; every magazine cover must stay abstract with no letters or numerals of any script.

Let every surface carry the trade. The counter is stained in rings and scuffed at its edge; the aluminium strip is worn bright where hands rest; the magazine covers are curled at the corners and faded along their top edges; the window frame's paint is chipped at the sill; the caged bulb's wire is blackened. Keep the wear physical and directional, never a uniform grime.

Build a second composition through the window glass. The glass carries a faint reversed image of the street behind the camera: one passing light, the kerb line, and a pale rectangle of an opposite window, all at half value and slightly wavy. Let the reflection sit above the magazine wall and never cross the counter.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A brass coin tray with three coins in it, one rubber date stamp on its pad, a paper bag folded flat under the counter's lip, and a short pencil on a string. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a kiosk would actually have it.

Illuminate with the caged bulb as the only key, warm and hard, plus the cool street spill as a weak edge light. Let the bulb produce one pool on the counter, a warm wash on the covers, and a bright top light on her hair and shoulders. Let the spill produce one thin blue edge along the window frame's outer face. Keep the kiosk's interior corners dark and the exterior near-black.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: counter edge, coin tray, wet pavement. Second: Miku, the newspaper, her hands. Third: the first magazine shelf. Fourth: the overlapping covers of the upper shelves. Fifth: the caged bulb and the dark ceiling. Separate them by value steps of roughly ten percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every shelf angle and counter edge, restrained risograph grain in the shadow fields, crisp flat fills in the lit areas, and fine curl only at cover corners. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the aluminium strip.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no customer at the window, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text on any magazine, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no street beyond the frame, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like a lit box in a dark street: three shelves of print under one bulb, one bay standing empty, and a girl reading a headline aloud to nobody.

seeds.title: KNEELING BLADE
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 2:3 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “KNEELING BLADE”, a frame built around one colossal amber weapon, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character kneeling on one knee in the centre of an empty concrete room, both hands stacked on the pommel of a greatsword whose point rests on the wet floor. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes and twin-tail identity readable in the dim room.

The weapon is one solid mass of orange amber glass: translucent, warm orange-brown, lit from within, and it throws orange light onto everything around it.

Use a camera at her chest height on a normal lens, set close and square so her kneeling body fills the lower two thirds and the sword's blade runs vertically through the frame's centre. Place Miku at approximately fifty percent of the canvas width, occupying about fifty percent of the frame height from the floor to her bowed head. Let the sword's pommel sit at her shoulder height and its point be hidden in a shallow film of water on the floor.

Give Miku exactly one core action: holding the sword down. She kneels on her right knee with her left foot planted forward, both hands stacked flat on the pommel with the fingers interlaced, her head bowed so her chin nearly touches her wrists, and her shoulders dropped. Keep her back straight, her gaze down, and let the sword carry her weight rather than the floor.

Construct the dominant visual object as the sword held down: a greatsword with a straight double-edged blade four fingers wide, a plain crossguard a hand and a half across, and a long grip below a wheel pommel. Set it perfectly vertical, its point pressed into the water film, its flat turned slightly off square so one facet catches the room's single light. Keep the weapon bare — no inlay, no wrap around the guard, no ornament on the pommel.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. the blade is one solid piece of amber, honey-dark and translucent so the whole mass reads as one saturated stone, its interior holding three long fractures and a scatter of fine bubbles, its edges polished but chipped, and it lights nothing around it; the crossguard and pommel are blackened iron with the black worn to grey at the corners; the grip is cord-wrapped over leather, greyed and flattened where hands sit; the floor is poured concrete under a two-millimetre film of standing water; the walls are bare concrete with form-board seams; the single high window is a pale rectangle. Each behaves differently — steel returns one long soft sheen, blackened iron holds a dull flatness, cord reads as a fine diagonal grain, the water film mirrors the pale window in a long broken streak, concrete absorbs light into soft values, the window is pure flat white.

Build a stepped sequence from the floor upward. Begin at the bottom edge with the water film and the sword's submerged point, then her planted foot and knee, then her stacked hands and the pommel, then her bowed head and falling twin tails, then the blade rising past her face, then the pale window high on the wall. The sequence must read as a person resting her whole weight on a weapon, not as a person posing beside one.

Leave one deliberate absence. The room has no door and no furniture: four bare walls, one high window, nothing else. Keep the floor entirely clear apart from the water and the sword's point, and let the wall behind her stay unmarked apart from one faint rectangle where a fixture was removed.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the water film and her planted boot. Middle ground: Miku, the sword's lower blade, her stacked hands. Background: the blade rising past her head, the concrete walls, the high window. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the high window only. The window is the key: a narrow cold shaft that falls on the wall opposite and just catches the blade's upper third, her shoulder and the crown of her head. Let the rest of the room sit two values lower, and let the water film return only the window's pale rectangle as a broken vertical streak. Keep every shadow soft-edged and never introduce a second source. Let the crystal pass the light rather than return it: one thin saturated amber line where the mass is thickest, and one hard-edged amber caustic patch thrown onto the water film beside it.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails fall forward over her shoulders as she bows. Both tails drop past her stacked hands and pool on the floor beside her knee, the nearer one lying in the water film as a clean aqua mass, the farther one draped over the blade's lower third. Let the window light catch each tail's upper curve and let the tips darken where they touch the water.

Dress Miku in a plain duelling layer over her canonical palette, not armour. A dark teal fitted jacket worn closed, dark trousers, wrapped calves, and soft soled boots with the left one scuffed at the toe from being planted. Keep the palette close to teal-and-black with one pale under-collar, keep a single brass button at the jacket's throat, and keep the silhouette as narrow as possible so the sword reads larger against her.

Use a cold low-key palette with strict area control. Approximately forty percent of the image is shadowed concrete, twenty-two percent is the blade, fourteen percent is the water film and floor, nine percent is Miku's jacket and trousers, six percent is her aqua hair, five percent is the pale window, three percent is the blackened guard and pommel, and one percent is the brass button. Keep every warm note out of the image entirely. The amber's honey-dark tone is the one saturated colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the room's own stencilling rather than from decoration. Let one large deep-teal ink bloom spread across the wall in the upper left, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular pale panel across the wall at the height of her head as a graphic mask, and let one vertical strip of rust-red run down the frame's right edge from the window to the floor. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “KNEELING BLADE” once, in black paint stencilled across the bare concrete wall directly behind her at the height of her shoulders, the strokes slightly uneven where the wall was patched, sized so it spans about three quarters of the wall's visible width and reads clearly at thumbnail size. Put no lettering on the blade, the water or her clothing, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The blade is peppered with fine pits in its lower third and its edge is rolled in one place; the guard's blacking is worn to a bright grey at both quillons; the grip's cord is flattened and darkened in the exact place her hands sit; the water film holds a faint oil rainbow at its edge; the concrete is patched in two places and the patches have dried a shade lighter. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the water film. The film carries the window as a long broken vertical streak, the blade as a thin dark line running down the middle of that streak, and her knee as a soft dark shape at the frame's lower edge. Let the reflection break at every crack in the concrete and never mirror her body cleanly.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One brass button at her throat, a single drop hanging from the crossguard's lower quillon, a fine crack running from the sword's point toward the frame's corner, and one strand of hair floating on the water film. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where the room would put it.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: water film and her planted boot. Second: her knee and the sword's submerged point. Third: her stacked hands and the pommel. Fourth: her bowed head, her tails and the blade's middle. Fifth: the blade's upper third, the wall and the window. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every blade facet and guard corner, restrained risograph grain in the concrete, crisp flat fills in the window's light, and one clean gradient only along the blade's sheen. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the steel and the water.

No second character, no duplicate Miku, no crowd, no banners, no flags, no birds, no wings, no halo, no second sword, no additional weapon, no glowing crystal, no neon glow, no self-lit weapon, no rainbow dispersion, no stained glass, no plastic, no glass bottle, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no magical effects, no readable text beyond the string named above, no blood, no wounds, no armour plates, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no hand on the blade itself, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like the end of a long wait: a girl on one knee in an empty wet room, both hands stacked on a pommel, and a blade standing vertical in two millimetres of water with her whole weight behind it.

seeds.title: LANTERN TIDE
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “LANTERN TIDE”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing on a stone quay at night while a tide of paper lanterns drifts past on black water. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands, hair ornaments and long twin-tail identity immediately readable against the warm lantern field.

Use a slightly low camera at chest height, angled about twenty degrees off the quay line, with a normal lens so the lantern strings recede in a clean diagonal. Place Miku in the right third, full body visible from sandals to hair ornaments, occupying approximately thirty percent of the image. She stands at the quay's edge with her weight on the right leg, left foot resting on a mooring ring, torso turned a quarter toward the water, head lowered so both eyes stay visible as she looks down at the lanterns.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Her left hand holds a small paper lantern by its wire handle at hip height, just above the water, and her right hand hangs open at her side with the fingers slightly curled. The lantern she holds casts a warm ellipse across her forearm and skirt. Keep the pose still and the arms clear of her face; add no second action and nothing else in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as a tide of two hundred paper lanterns covering the black water, filling approximately seventy percent of the canvas from the lower left corner to the far right edge, where they compress into a bright band beneath a dark pier. Above them, three strings of smaller lanterns cross the frame on a diagonal. Each lantern is a different age — some bright and tight, some sagging and dim, some collapsed and floating on their sides.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The lanterns are ribbed washi paper over bamboo, some oiled and translucent, some waterlogged and opaque; the water is black and slow with a thin skin of reflected light; the quay is grey granite with salt bloom in the joints; the mooring ring is rusted iron; the far pier is dark timber on iron piles; the sky is empty night. Each material behaves differently — paper glows from inside and darkens where it is wet, water doubles every light into a vertical smear, granite holds a cold sheen, iron rusts in flakes, timber swallows light.

Build a stepped sequence across the tide. Begin at the lower left with one lantern half submerged, its paper collapsed and its flame gone. Move right through lanterns that grow progressively brighter and more upright, then to a cluster where three have drifted together and their ribs press against each other, then to one lantern with a torn panel showing its frame, then the far band where they merge into a single warm strip. The sequence must read as drift and decay, not as decoration.

Leave one deliberate absence. One gap in the tide is an empty ring of dark water about a metre across where a lantern has sunk, its wire handle still visible above the surface. Keep that ring as the darkest area inside the bright field and place nothing inside it.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the granite quay edge, the rusted ring and the near lantern. Middle ground: Miku, the tide of lanterns and the low strings above. Background: the dark pier, the far band of lanterns and the blank night sky.

Light the scene entirely from the lanterns plus one distant pier lamp. The lantern field is the key: a warm amber source that underlights everything from below, warmest at the near left and cooling toward the far band. The pier lamp adds one small white point above the water so the night never goes fully monochrome. Keep the light contained inside each paper shell, with no glow halo and no lens flare.

Weave Miku’s extremely long twin tails down against the warm field. The nearer twin tail falls in front of her shoulder, is cropped by the lantern she holds, and reappears below it as two aqua strands lit from beneath; the farther twin tail hangs behind her and stays cool against the amber. Keep the hair dense and readable at her head, allowing it to thin only where it crosses the lantern light.

Dress Miku in an original lantern-night costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language. Use a long dark teal yukata-style wrap with a wide obi tied low at the back, the sleeves falling to mid-forearm, over a pale inner collar, with a narrow woven belt cord and wooden sandals. Add one small coral charm at the obi knot, a folded paper fan tucked at her waist, and three faint water marks at the hem. Keep the garment narrow and vertical with a long clean fall so the silhouette reads against the horizontal tide.

Use a warm-on-black palette. Approximately forty-six percent of the image is black water and deep night. Eighteen percent is lantern amber. Twelve percent is pale washi cream where the paper is thinnest. Eight percent is granite grey. Six percent is dark teal cloth. Five percent is rusted iron brown. Three percent is the cold white of the distant pier lamp. Less than two percent is the aqua of her hair and the coral charm.

Drive the printed graphic language from Miku’s own palette. Let one large aqua ink bloom spread across the black water at the lower right, its edge feathering into the lantern reflections. Add two hard-edged lantern-shaped warm blocks on the quay stones where light has fallen for years. Let a fine halftone of reflected dots sit only in the near water. Cut one clean black knockout where the sunk lantern's ring breaks the reflection. Add rare silver microdots only at the mooring ring and the lantern wires.

Print the text as physical matter. Write the exact readable words “LANTERN TIDE” by hand in dark ink on the paper of the nearest large lantern, the characters following the curve of the ribs and distorted by the fold. Add one smaller ink mark on a second lantern that reads as a maker's stamp rather than words. Both are lit from inside so the ink reads darker than the paper around it.

Let every surface carry the night. The granite is wet at the water line and dry above, with salt bloom in the joints and a dark tide mark. The lanterns are translucent at the top and saturated at the bottom where they touch water. The iron ring has rust flakes standing slightly proud. The water holds a thin film that breaks into skin-like patches near the quay.

Build a second composition through reflection. Every lantern throws a vertical amber smear into the water directly beneath it, and the smears lengthen as the water deepens toward the frame edge. The pier lamp throws one single long white line that crosses the amber field. The empty ring leaves an unbroken black interval in both the lantern row and its reflection, so the absence repeats twice.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A brass hook on the quay, one folded paper fan with a fine rib pattern, a thin silver cord at her obi, three faint water marks, and a single small ink stamp on the nearest lantern. Keep them clustered near hands and the water's edge and never spread across the empty night.

Illuminate with the lantern field as the only key, warm and low, plus the distant pier lamp as a cold accent. Keep her face readable from below, keep the brightest value on the lantern she holds, and let the far band compress into a single warm strip without blooming.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: quay edge, mooring ring, near lantern and near water. Primary middle ground: Miku, the lantern she holds and the first rows of the tide. Secondary: the middle drift and the low strings above. Tertiary: the far band and the pier piles. Background: the blank night sky, held as clean negative space.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a hand-pulled print: crisp drawn linework, ink and watercolor washes with visible wet edges, dry-brush erosion on the granite and paper, soft paper grain in the flat areas, and clean lithograph texture in the dark water. Keep the drawing precise and the paint loose, with no photographic depth of field.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no floating interface, no holograms, no glowing particles, no abstract light streaks, no full-canvas glitch, no random letters or numbers, no watermark, no signature, no muddy background, no neon rainbow lighting, no face obstruction, no lantern covering her eyes, and no malformed hands. Preserve a strict hierarchy: Miku’s face and the lantern she holds first, the near tide second, the middle drift third, the empty ring fourth, then the far band, typography and night.

The final image should feel like a harbour where light is the only thing that floats: two hundred lanterns drifting, one already sunk, one held above the water, and the whole quay held in the minute when the tide turns and nothing moves.

seeds.title: LAST CAR
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 warm editorial poster titled “LAST CAR”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only figure in the carriage of an old wooden-bodied tram at low winter sun. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, a slim virtual-singer silhouette, and her original grey-and-teal costume structure. Keep her face, both eyes, both hands and her full silhouette instantly readable at thumbnail size.

Weave Hatsune Miku’s extremely long aqua twin tails into the low amber sun. Both tails fall over the wine-red seat back in two clean aqua masses, picking up a faint warm rim where the light crosses them and going nearly black in the shadow of the carriage, with one strand sliding down the varnished wood. Her aqua hair is the only cool note in the whole warm car.

Dress Hatsune Miku in an original tram-carriage costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not a slip dress. A fitted chalk-white blouse with a narrow graphite collar, a thin aqua necktie, a short pleated charcoal skirt, dark thigh-highs with a fine seam, and a soft grey coat folded on the seat beside her. Keep the whole outfit warm-neutral so it belongs to the carriage rather than competing with it.

Scene and core image: the last car of an old wooden-bodied tram at low winter sun, seen from the near end in a strict one-point perspective that runs down the aisle to the far door. Five rows of face-to-face seats line both sides, their frames of caramel varnished wood, their cushions in worn wine-red velvet with the pile flattened where people sat. A brass handrail runs the length of the ceiling with leather strap loops hanging from it at even intervals, one of them still swinging a few degrees, catching a thin bright edge. The floor is caramel wood, varnished and worn pale along the aisle, with one folded newspaper on a seat two rows down and one paper ticket lying flat on the boards.

Her position and action: she sits on the right third at a window seat, turned three-quarters toward the camera-left, knees angled into the aisle, her back against the wine-red seat back and her hair spilling over it. Her left palm lies flat on the brass window ledge, fingers spread and fully separated, each fingertip catching the sun; her right hand rests along the top edge of the seat back behind her, relaxed and fully visible. Her face turns toward the light so both gold eyes read clearly, chin slightly lifted, mouth closed and quiet. Both hands stay inside the frame and individually readable. No second gesture and no second prop.

Composition and sight path: keep the vanishing point just right of centre so the aisle leads the eye from the bottom edge to the far door; place her at the right third occupying about thirty percent of the canvas, and let the left window band, the strap loops and the receding seat rows carry the rest. Reading order: her face and eyes, then the hand on the ledge, then the aisle running back, then the destination blind above the far door.

Light: one low winter sun enters through the left windows at a shallow angle, breaking into long warm bars that fall across the seat backs, the aisle boards and her forearm, with visible dust turning in the beams. Her cheek, the crown of her white hair and the near edge of the brass rail take the brightest warm edge; the far end of the carriage falls into deep warm shadow; the windows themselves stay bright and slightly veiled. One light source only, and every shadow stays warm brown rather than grey.

Hold the palette with strict area control. Amber light and warm white daylight account for about thirty percent of the frame, caramel varnished wood for twenty-two percent, wine-red velvet for sixteen percent, warm white cloth for twelve percent, ochre brass for eight percent, graphite for six percent in the dark seams and the strap leather, deep shadow for four percent under the seats, and aqua for two percent in her long hair. No hue outside this list appears anywhere in the carriage.

Texture and material language: varnished caramel wood with worn edges and visible grain along the window frames; wine-red velvet with a flattened pile that scatters a soft matte highlight; brass with a warm narrow specular line and darker tarnish in the joints; leather straps with a crease at the fold and a soft sheen; dust-veiled glass with the faintest warm haze; her slip dress in thin matte white cloth that takes a warm rim at the shoulder and stays opaque everywhere else. Keep every surface close to the eye's real behaviour rather than flat graphic fill.

Second reading inside the scene: the window glass at her shoulder reflects the opposite row of empty seats, doubling the carriage in a softer, lower-contrast image; the sun bars repeat on the floor as a second rhythm; and the strap loops throw small elliptical shadows onto the ceiling.

Typography: set the exact words “LAST CAR” on the destination blind above the far door — a dark amber enamelled metal plate with a rolled brass edge, lit from behind so the letters read as warm-lit cut-outs. Ultra-condensed uppercase sans, cap height about two point six percent of the frame height, centred on the blind, spaced tight, letters crisp and legible, the plate slightly dusty at its lower edge. Keep every other lettering in the image unreadable: the ticket and the newspaper carry only blurred grey marks with no legible words.

Depth: near seat back and one strap loop cropped at the bottom edge; her figure and the window ledge; the middle rows of seats and the brass rail; the far door and the destination blind; the last strip of hazy warm air at the far end. Separate the layers through overlap, edge softness and value contrast rather than blur.

Finish as a polished warm editorial illustration: precise anime-adjacent linework on her face and hands, careful wood and velvet rendering, honest glass reflection, fine print-like grain across the whole plate, a faint warm bloom only in the brightest window corners, and restrained detail density that falls off toward the far end of the carriage.

The final image should read as one quiet held moment: a white-haired woman in a thin slip sits alone in the last car of an old tram, one hand flat on the brass ledge, warm winter sun crossing her cheek and the wine-red seats, leather straps hanging still, a ticket on the worn boards, her reflection doubling in the dusty glass, and the destination blind above the far door reading “LAST CAR”. Her face and both hands stay fully resolved.

Readable text is limited to “LAST CAR”; exactly one figure; both hands complete and inside the frame; no second person; no watermark, signature or logo.

The carriage is built from four materials and nothing else: caramel-varnished wood for the seat frames, window sills and floorboards; worn wine-red velvet for the cushions, its pile flattened in the middle of every seat; ochre brass for the handrail, the strap loops and the window latches; and pale canvas for the ceiling panels. No plastic, no chrome and no modern fittings appear anywhere inside it.

Let the years show at the touch points. The brass rail is polished bright where hands have held it and dull everywhere else, the velvet carries a faint sheen along the seat fronts, the floorboards are worn pale in one path down the aisle, and the window ledge beneath her palm holds a thin film of dust that the low sun catches. Every mark sits exactly where a passenger would have left it.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Hatsune Miku, no second figure, no other passengers, no conductor, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text of any kind, no watermark, no signature, no frame, no border.

seeds.title: LAST TRAIN
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “LAST TRAIN”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character seated alone in an empty subway carriage at the end of the night, with the doors open onto a lit platform behind her. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the cold carriage interior.

Use a low camera placed on the carriage floor at seat height, aimed straight down the aisle with a wide lens so the ceiling line, the seat rows and the floor tiles all converge on one vanishing point behind her. Place Miku in the right third at approximately thirty percent of the canvas width, seated on the near bench facing the camera with her knees together, occupying about forty-five percent of the frame height. Let the open door and the platform occupy the left third, so the composition is a long corridor interrupted by one seated figure.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Both hands hold a folding paper map open on her lap at chest height, her thumbs at the fold, and her head is tilted down so both eyes stay visible above the paper edge. One shoe has slipped half off her heel. Keep the pose still, the arms close to her body, and put nothing else in her hands.

Construct the dominant visual object as the carriage interior itself: two parallel bench rows in faded teal upholstery, a continuous window band above them, a row of steel grab handles hanging from a single polished rail, and a ceiling of parallel light boxes. Let the car occupy the whole frame, with its interior seam lines providing the only geometry.

seeds.title: MOON COURT
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “MOON COURT”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing in a raked gravel courtyard under a full moon. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands, hair ornaments and long twin-tail identity immediately readable in the cool moonlight.

Use a high camera at chest height on the courtyard's diagonal, looking slightly down across the raked gravel, with a normal lens so the raking lines run as clean parallel curves from the lower left toward the upper right. Place Miku in the centre-left, full body visible from sandals to hair ornaments, occupying approximately thirty percent of the image. She stands on the gravel with feet together, weight even, shoulders open to the camera, head raised so both eyes catch the moon.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Her right hand holds a shallow wooden rake with the tines resting on the gravel behind her, and her left hand is lifted to chest height with the palm open and a single pale pebble resting in it. Her gaze is on the pebble, not the viewer. Keep the gesture still and the arms clear of her face; add no second action and nothing else in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as a raked gravel field carrying concentric rings around three standing stones, filling approximately seventy percent of the canvas and cropped by the frame on all four sides. The rings tighten toward the stones and loosen toward the edges; the gravel is pale grey and blue in the moonlight, with the rake lines catching a thin silver highlight on their ridges. Behind the stones, a low plaster wall closes the courtyard, and one pine branch reaches in from the upper right.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The gravel is coarse crushed granite, damp enough to hold a sharp ridge; the stones are weathered grey basalt with lichen in the cracks; the wall is pale lime plaster with a stained base; the pine is dark bark with needle clusters catching rim light; the rake is old wood with a worn handle; the moonlit air is thin and clear. Each material behaves differently — gravel scatters a fine highlight and holds a footprint, basalt interrupts the moon with a hard edge, plaster goes flat and chalky, pine needles split the light into thin strokes.

Build a stepped sequence through the rings. Begin at the lower left with the outermost ring, its ridges soft and half-filled, showing a faint footprint where someone walked. Move inward through rings that grow progressively sharper and cleaner, then to one ring that has been broken and re-raked, its repair visible as a slight change of direction, then to the innermost ring around the largest stone where the gravel is finest and brightest. End at the stone itself, which carries no raking at all.

Leave one deliberate absence. In the second ring there is a clean gap where the rake has not passed: a patch of untouched gravel about the width of a person, its surface flat and matte against the silver ridges. Keep that patch as the only rough area in the composition and place nothing inside it.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the near gravel with one fallen needle and a shallow footprint. Middle ground: Miku, the rake, the three stones and their rings. Background: the low plaster wall, the pine branch and the open night sky above it.

Light the scene with the moon alone as key, high and slightly behind the camera, plus one faint warm spill from a window out of frame at the lower right. The moon gives a cool silver fall across the ridges and a hard shadow under each stone and under Miku. The window spill adds a barely visible ochre on the wall's base so the courtyard never goes fully blue. Keep the light clean, with no halo around the moon and no glow.

Weave Miku’s extremely long twin tails into the raked field. The nearer twin tail falls across her shoulder and its tip lies on the gravel, catching a bright silver edge on the ridge and a thin shadow in the groove. The farther twin tail rises behind her head and its silhouette cuts the moonlit wall. Keep the hair dense and clearly readable at her head, allowing the very tip to separate into strands only where it touches the gravel.

Dress Miku in an original moon-court costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language. Use a long pale robe of heavy matte cloth with a deep overlapping collar, wide sleeves that hang past the wrist, a narrow dark sash tied at the waist, and ankle-length hem that brushes the gravel. Add a folded paper fan tucked at the sash, one small coral cord knot at the collar, and a fine dust of gravel on the hem. Keep the garment wide and calm so the silhouette reads as a single pale vertical against the horizontal rings.

Use a cool silver palette. Approximately forty-eight percent of the image is moonlit gravel, pale grey and blue. Sixteen percent is deep night sky and shadow. Twelve percent is pale plaster wall. Eight percent is dark basalt. Six percent is the matte pale robe. Five percent is pine black-green. Three percent is the faint ochre window spill. Less than two percent is the aqua of her hair and the coral knot.

Drive the printed graphic language from Miku’s own palette. Let one large aqua ink bloom spread across the pale plaster wall behind the stones, its edge following the wall's stained base. Add two hard-edged rectangular shadow blocks on the wall cast by the pine. Let a fine halftone of gravel grain sit only in the near foreground. Cut one clean pale knockout where the moon catches the top of the largest stone. Add rare silver microdots only along the rake tines and the courtyard wall cap.

Print the text as physical matter. Carve the exact readable words “MOON COURT” into a flat stone set level with the gravel at the frame's lower right, the letters cut deep and filled with shadow, half dusted with gravel. Add one smaller carved numeral beside it. Both sit flush with the ground so the text reads as part of the courtyard, not as floating type.

Let the surfaces show time. The gravel holds two shallow footprints and a few scattered needles. The basalt is pitted and lichen-edged, and its shadow is doubled by the low wall behind. The plaster is chalky where it is dry and dark where damp has risen. The pine bark is rough and unlit except at one edge. The moon refuses to make anything shiny.

Build a second composition through shadow. Each stone throws a long hard shadow across the rings, breaking them; Miku and her rake throw their own; the pine branch throws a fine tracery on the wall. The untouched gravel patch stays matte and shadowless inside the silver field, so the absence reads as a hole in the pattern.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A slim brass ferrule where the rake head meets the handle, one folded paper fan with a fine rib pattern, three tiny pebbles placed at the base of the largest stone as an offering, and a thin coral cord at her collar. Keep them clustered near hands and stones and never scattered across the raking.

Illuminate with the moon as key and the window spill as a whisper of warmth at the lower right. Keep the brightest value on the rake ridges and the lifted pebble, keep her face cool and readable, and let the sky fall to a flat deep blue-black with no stars competing.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: near gravel, fallen needle, footprint. Primary middle ground: Miku, the rake, the lifted pebble. Secondary: the three stones and their rings. Tertiary: the low wall and the pine. Background: the night sky, held as clean negative space.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a hand-pulled print: crisp drawn linework, ink and watercolor washes with visible wet edges, dry-brush erosion on the gravel and stone, soft paper grain in the flat areas, and clean lithograph texture in the shadows. Keep the drawing precise and the paint loose, with no photographic depth of field.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no floating interface, no holograms, no glowing particles, no abstract light streaks, no full-canvas glitch, no random letters or numbers, no watermark, no signature, no muddy background, no neon rainbow lighting, no face obstruction, no hair covering her eyes, and no malformed hands. Preserve a strict hierarchy: Miku’s face and the lifted pebble first, the three stones second, the raked rings third, the untouched patch fourth, then the wall, typography and moonlit night.

The final image should feel like a courtyard kept by one person and one tool: three stones in a field of rings, one patch left unraked, one pebble lifted in an open palm, and the whole garden held in the minute when the moon is directly overhead and nothing has yet been disturbed.
