Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “NEON STRIP”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing under a dense stack of projecting shop signs on a narrow Hong Kong street at night, with rain-wet asphalt reflecting every light above her. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the coloured sign field.

Use a camera at chest height on a slightly wide lens, set on the street's centre line and tilted up about twenty degrees so the sign stacks lean inward from both sides and the sky is reduced to a narrow band. Place Miku in the lower left third at approximately thirty-two percent of the canvas width, full body visible from boots to hair ornaments, occupying about thirty percent of the frame height. Let the sign field occupy the upper two-thirds, so the composition is a canyon of light with one figure at its floor.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Her right hand holds a folded umbrella point-down, its tip resting on the wet asphalt, and her left hand is lifted to chest height turning a paper receipt between two fingers. Her head is turned toward the signs, both eyes visible. Keep the pose still, the arms clear of her face, and put nothing else in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the sign stacks themselves: two rows of projecting signs cantilevered from both facades, some horizontal, some vertical, stacked four to six deep and overlapping at every height, each with a metal bracket, a painted face and a light box behind. Let the stacks occupy approximately fifty-five percent of the canvas area and let them converge toward a narrow strip of dark sky at the top centre.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The signs are painted metal and acrylic, some faces faded, some edges chipped, all dusty along their upper rims; the brackets are rusted steel; the facades behind are tiled in small cream and green mosaic, dark with grime at the joints; the street is black asphalt with a continuous water film; the awnings are canvas, sagging between frames; the drain covers are cast iron. Each behaves differently — lit acrylic transmits a saturated flat colour, painted metal returns a dull sheen, mosaic reads as a fine grid with dark joints, wet asphalt breaks every light into vertical fragments, canvas absorbs.

Build a stepped sequence up the frame. Begin at the bottom edge with the wet asphalt holding three long colour streaks, then the near awning's sagging edge and its drip line, then Miku and her umbrella, then the first tier of signs where two boxes overlap, then the upper tiers where they compress into saturated mass, then the narrow sky band. The sequence must read as a street looking up into its own light, not as a wall of advertising.

Leave one deliberate absence. One bracket stands empty: a rusted steel arm projects from the facade with its two mounting bolts still in place and a clean pale rectangle on the tiles where the sign used to hang, but no sign. Keep the bracket about a sign's width, placed in the middle tier directly above Miku's head so the gap interrupts the vertical stack.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: wet asphalt, colour streaks, drain cover. Middle ground: Miku, the umbrella, the near awning. Background: the sign tiers, the mosaic facades, the sky band. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the signs themselves. The signs are the key: dozens of separate saturated sources at every height, each throwing a flat colour onto the wet street beneath it, so the asphalt carries a long red streak, a green streak and a blue streak in parallel. Add one cool white streetlamp above the camera as a weak fill, lifting the tops of Miku's shoulders and the awning's ridge. Keep every colour source hard-edged and flat; this scene has no soft glow anywhere.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the sign light. The nearer tail falls forward in one clean aqua mass that picks up a hard green edge from the sign above her; the farther tail drops behind her shoulder and reads as a dark vertical against a red sign face. Let one strand cross the umbrella's shaft and pick up a warm orange rim.

Dress Miku in an original neon-street costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not tourist clothing. A cropped dark bomber jacket worn open over a pale tee, a short pleated skirt in deep teal, thick socks and chunky trainers, with a small canvas cross-body bag. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment, and keep the silhouette simple enough to read at thumbnail size.

Use a saturated-on-black palette with strict area control. Approximately forty percent of the image is near-black asphalt and shadow, twenty-four percent is the sign field's saturated colour, fourteen percent is the mosaic facades, ten percent is the wet street's colour streaks, six percent is Miku's aqua hair, four percent is the pale awning canvas, and two percent is the dark sky band. Keep black as the ground so every colour reads as emitted rather than reflected.

Drive the printed graphic language from the street's own hardware rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the lower right of the asphalt, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular pale panel behind the near awning as a graphic mask at the height of its ridge, and let one vertical strip of deep red run from a sign face to the street, aligned to a bracket. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “NEON STRIP” once, in white paint applied to the face of the nearest horizontal sign at the left, the corners slightly chipped, sized so it spans about a fifth of that sign's width. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “G / 12” sit on a small enamel plate bolted to the drain cover's frame. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled; every other sign face must stay abstract, with no letters, glyphs or numerals of any script.

Let every surface carry the city. The sign faces are dusty along their top edges and cleaner where rain has reached; the brackets are rusted to a deep orange at every weld; the mosaic tiles are dark in the joints and glossy where water runs; the asphalt is worn pale along two tyre tracks; the awning's canvas sags into three shallow pockets that hold water. Keep the wear physical and directional, never a uniform grime.

Build a second composition through the wet street. The asphalt carries each sign as a long vertical smear broken into short horizontal bands by the water's surface, so the street reads as a second, inverted and compressed version of the sign field. Let every smear stop at the kerb line and never cross it.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A brass shop bell above a doorway at the left, one steel roller shutter half drawn with its slats slightly bent, a plastic crate stacked beside a drain, and a rain chain hanging from an awning corner. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a dense street would actually have it.

Illuminate with the signs as the only key, saturated and hard, plus the cool white streetlamp as a weak fill. Let each sign produce a hard-edged pool of its own colour on the street directly beneath it, and a rim along the nearest edges of the awning and Miku's clothing. Let the streetlamp lift the top surfaces only. Keep the upper sky band at absolute black and give it no glow.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: wet asphalt, colour streaks, drain cover. Second: Miku, the umbrella, her bag. Third: the near awning and its drip line. Fourth: the first two sign tiers. Fifth: the upper tiers and the black sky band. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every bracket and sign edge, restrained risograph grain in the black fields, crisp flat fills in the lit areas, and fine rust only at welds. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the wet street.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no pedestrian in the background, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text on any other sign, no glyphs or numerals of any script beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no vehicles, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like a street that has replaced its sky with signage: hundreds of lit faces stacked four deep, one bracket standing empty, and a girl at the bottom of the canyon holding an umbrella she has not opened.

seeds.title: NIGHT FOLIO
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “NIGHT FOLIO”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing in a private reading room late at night. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands, hair ornaments and long twin-tail identity immediately readable under the lamp.

Use a camera at eye height set back from the table, with a longish normal lens and shallow but honest perspective so the book wall behind her stacks in clean vertical columns. Place Miku in the centre-right, framed from knee up, occupying approximately thirty percent of the image. She stands at the table's end with her hip against it, torso turned three-quarters to the left, head down, both eyes visible and lit from the lamp beside her.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Her left hand holds a large folio open at the spine, keeping it flat against the table with the thumb on the gutter; her right hand lifts one page at the corner, halfway turned. The lifted page casts a thin shadow across the printed columns below. Keep the pose still and the hands clear of her face; add no second action and nothing else in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the book wall itself, thirty or more tall folios and bound runs stacked from floor to ceiling in uneven columns that fill approximately seventy percent of the canvas, cropped by the top and left frame edges. The columns are not tidy: some spines face out, some are stacked flat, one column leans against another, and one gap shows bare wall. In front of them the reading table runs across the lower third, its surface holding the open folio, a lamp and a few loose sheets.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The folios are cloth and calf bindings, some rubbed pale at the corners, some with gold tooling worn to a ghost; the paper is heavy rag stock with visible chain lines; the table is dark walnut with a French-polished sheen broken by cup rings; the lamp is enamel over brass with a green glass shade; the wall behind is plain board; the floor is dark stained timber. Each material behaves differently — cloth fades and frays, gold catches one thin line of light, rag paper holds a soft shadow, walnut reflects the lamp as a long broken streak, enamel chips to show brass.

Build a stepped sequence across the wall. Begin at the lower left with a folio standing open on the floor, its pages splayed. Move up and right through bindings that grow progressively older and more worn, then to one run where all the spines match except a single pale replacement, then to the top right where the cloth has faded to a uniform grey. End with one folio that leans out of line, its spine cracked and its sewing visible. The sequence must read as a collection assembled over decades, not as a set.

Leave one deliberate absence. In the third column a gap about four books wide shows bare board and a faint rectangle of unfaded wall where a set used to stand. Keep that gap as the brightest clean shape on the wall and place nothing inside it.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the table edge, the open folio, the lamp base and two loose sheets. Middle ground: Miku, her hands and the lifted page. Background: the receding columns of bindings, the bare board gap and one tall window at the far left with night behind it.

Light the scene with the single table lamp as key and the window's night as a cold secondary. The lamp throws a warm ellipse across the folio and up onto Miku's hands and jaw; the window adds a thin blue-grey edge to the book columns on the left. Keep the lamp shade from glowing like a bulb — light must come from below its rim, not through it.

Weave Miku’s extremely long twin tails down through the lamplight. The nearer twin tail falls in front of the table edge and is cropped by the open folio, and where it crosses the lamp's ellipse it glows faintly warm; the farther twin tail hangs behind her and merges into the book columns. Keep the hair dense and readable at her head, letting it flatten into shadow only at the far side.

Dress Miku in an original reading-room costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language. Use a long charcoal wool dressing gown over a pale high-necked inner layer, the gown belted loosely at the waist with a narrow cord, sleeves pushed to the forearm, and one shoulder slipping. Add a thin silver reading chain at the collar holding a small loupe, one coral cord at the belt, and three faint paper cuts at the cuff. Keep the garment soft and vertical so the silhouette stays quiet against the dense wall.

Use a warm-dark palette. Approximately forty-two percent of the image is deep walnut brown and shadowed cloth. Eighteen percent is warm lamp amber. Fourteen percent is faded binding cloth in grey, olive and oxblood. Ten percent is rag paper cream. Eight percent is night blue at the window. Four percent is worn gold tooling. Two percent is the green glass shade. Less than two percent is the aqua of her hair and the coral cord.

Drive the printed graphic language from Miku’s own palette. Let one large aqua ink bloom spread across the board wall at the upper right, its edge soaking into the bare wood. Add two hard-edged rectangular blocks of unfaded wall inside the gap. Let a fine halftone of dust sit only in the lamp's beam. Cut one clean pale knockout where the window light crosses the shelf edge. Add rare gold microdots only on the tooling bands and the loupe chain.

Print the text as physical matter. Stamp the exact readable words “NIGHT FOLIO” in gold on the spine of the nearer large folio, tooled flat into the cloth, half worn away at the first letter. Add one smaller accession number in ink inside the front board, visible where the folio lies open. Both sit on the object itself so the text reads as part of the binding.

Let the surfaces carry their use. The walnut has cup rings and a long pale scratch. The folio's cloth is rubbed to the weave at the corners and its gilt is worn to a green ghost. The rag paper is soft at the edges and holds a faint tide line where a page was once damp. The floorboards are dull except where feet have polished them.

Build a second composition through the lamp's beam. The lamp throws a hard-edged cone that lands as an ellipse on the table and climbs the book column behind, and the dust inside the cone reads as a fine diagonal haze. Miku's shadow falls across the folio and stops at the gutter. The unfaded gap in the wall stays bright inside the shadowed field, so the absence reads as a shape made of missing books.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A brass page marker, one small glass inkwell with a fitted stopper, a thin silver chain and loupe, three coral cord ends, and a folded paper slip used as a bookmark. Keep them within reach of the hands and never scattered along the wall.

Illuminate with the lamp as key and the window's cold night as secondary. Keep the brightest value on the lifted page and her hands, keep the second brightest on the unfaded gap, and let the top of the book wall fall into a soft brown dark.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: table edge, open folio, lamp base. Primary middle ground: Miku, her hands and the lifted page. Secondary: the first two book columns and the gap. Tertiary: the receding columns and the window. Background: the dark upper corner, held as clean negative space.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a hand-pulled print: crisp drawn linework, ink and watercolor washes with visible wet edges, dry-brush erosion on the cloth bindings, soft paper grain in the flat areas, and clean lithograph texture in the shadows. Keep the drawing precise and the paint loose, with no photographic depth of field.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no floating interface, no holograms, no glowing particles, no abstract light streaks, no full-canvas glitch, no random letters or numbers, no watermark, no signature, no muddy background, no neon rainbow lighting, no face obstruction, no book covering her eyes, and no malformed hands. Preserve a strict hierarchy: Miku’s face and hands first, the lifted page second, the book columns third, the empty gap fourth, then the lamp, typography and warm darkness.

The final image should feel like a room kept for one reader: thirty bindings deep, one set missing, one page caught mid-turn, and the whole library held in the minute after midnight when the lamp is the only thing still awake.

seeds.title: SPELL IN THE VOID
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “SPELL IN THE VOID”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character hovering alone above a night sea of clouds, her body upright in the air with a long staff raised in one hand and a bright circular magic array open in the air in front of her. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the cold array light and the dark sky behind her.

Use a camera lifted level with her chest on a slightly wide lens, square to her body, so she stands vertical in the frame and the cloud sea lies flat and far below her feet. Place her at approximately fifty percent of the canvas width, seen from the thighs up, occupying about fifty-four percent of the frame height. Let the cloud tops fill the bottom third and dissolve into the star field at the horizon rather than end in a hard line.

Give Miku exactly one core action: casting. She is turned three-quarters toward the viewer with her chest and hips squared to the circle, her weight pushed forward in the air as if she has just released the spell. Her right arm is raised and out, gripping the staff at its middle so the crystal head rides above her shoulder and the shaft points down across her body; her left hand is thrust forward at chest height, palm open and fingers spread, the fingertips almost touching the circle's inner rim. Let visible threads of cold light run from the crystal and from her open palm into the circle's centre, so the eye reads that light as leaving her body and arriving at the array. Keep her legs together with one knee faintly bent and both feet clear of every surface, so the pose reads as flight rather than as a jump. Keep the arms clear of her face, and put nothing else in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the magic circle itself: a perfect luminous ring two and a half times her shoulder width, hanging in the air just in front of her chest and belly, parallel to her body and facing the viewer almost flat, tipped only about ten degrees. Build it from three concentric rings of different thickness, a ring of twelve short radial dashes spaced evenly between them, and a faint hexagonal lattice filling the inner disc, brightest at the rim and dimmer toward the centre, where one small hard core of white light sits like a struck match. Let the circle's lower arc pass in front of her open hand and its upper arc cut across her collarbone, so it plainly belongs to her gesture instead of floating behind her.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The staff shaft is dark oiled hardwood with a brass ferrule at each end and a rough crystal head; the circle is pure emitted light with a soft edge and no visible surface; the cloud sea is cold water vapour with no hard edges and no surface detail smaller than a hand; her cloak is heavy charcoal wool that folds in broad planes; her tunic is matte fine weave. Each behaves differently — oiled wood holds one long soft highlight and a warm rim, brass returns a small hard specular, the crystal scatters its own pale light, the circle washes everything within a metre in cold cyan, cloud swallows light and returns it as a soft gradient, wool diffuses the rim light into a broad dull sheen, fine weave stays flat.

Build a stepped sequence from the bottom edge upward. Begin with the lit cloud tops beneath her, then the folded edge where the cloud surface breaks into shadow, then her boots and legs, then the circle, then her torso and raised arm, then the star field above her head. The sequence must read as a figure suspended over open sky, not as a figure standing on anything.

Leave one deliberate absence. In the cloud sea below her right side, one broad patch has collapsed into a dark hollow: no lit tops, no colour, only a deep blue-black well where the cloud surface folds inward and downward. Keep it wide and shallow, place it clearly inside the frame, and let the circle's light stop short of its rim.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the lit cloud tops at the bottom edge and the dark hollow. Middle ground: Miku, the staff, the circle. Background: the receding cloud bank, the horizon haze, the star field. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from two sources only. The magic circle is the key: a cold cyan-green light that starts at the small white core in its middle and throws her front, her hands, the staff and the cloud tops immediately beneath her, with a bright inner falloff and a thin bright rim along her sleeve, jaw and cloak edge. The star field is the faint secondary: a very weak cool fill from above that keeps her shoulders and the far cloud tops just above black. Keep the space between the lit zone and the horizon near-black, and never introduce a third source.

Lift Miku's extremely long twin tails with the same updraft that holds her in the air. Both tails stream upward and back rather than falling: the nearer one crossing behind her shoulder as a clean aqua mass with its tip curling, the farther one opening above the staff. Let the light catch each tail's outer edge as a cool rim and let a few strands separate against the dark sky.

Dress Miku in an original void-mage costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not a generic wizard robe. A dark teal fitted tunic with a high collar and a long split skirt over dark leggings, a wide black sash at the waist, one pale inner sleeve on the left arm only, fingerless gloves, buckled ankle boots, and a heavy charcoal cloak that flares wide behind her like a sail. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment, and keep the silhouette simple enough to read at thumbnail size.

Use a cold-on-black palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty-eight percent of the image is deep night sky fading to black at the edges, eighteen percent is cloud tops in cold grey-blue, sixteen percent is the cyan circle and its spill, nine percent is Miku's aqua hair, eight percent is her charcoal cloak, five percent is her teal tunic, four percent is her pale inner sleeve, and two percent is the brass and crystal of the staff. Keep the warm values down to the brass alone.

Drive the printed graphic language from the cloak rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the dark sky in the upper left, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular pale panel across the far cloud bank as a graphic mask at the horizon, and let one vertical strip of deep red run down the frame's right edge from the cloak's hem. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “SPELL IN THE VOID” once, in white paint applied across the full width of the cloak's outer face where the fabric flares wide behind her, the strokes slightly uneven where the cloth folds, sized so it spans about four fifths of the cloak's visible width and reads clearly at thumbnail size. Keep the string unbroken and correctly spelled, put no lettering and no symbols anywhere on the circle, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry its own wear. The cloak's hem is frayed in two places and creased along its folds; the leather boots are scuffed at the toe caps; the staff's brass ferrules are scratched bright at their edges; the cloud tops carry faint internal striations where the wind combs them. Keep the wear physical and directional, never a uniform grime.

Build a second composition through the cloud surface rather than through a reflection. The lit cloud tops beneath her carry the circle's light as one broad soft halo, brightest directly under its rim and fading outward in even steps; the cloak's shadow falls downward as a single soft column; the dark hollow swallows light without returning any. Never produce a mirrored second figure anywhere in the cloud.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A brass hook on the staff's upper ferrule, a small drift of fine light dust falling from the circle's lower rim, one loose thread at the cloak's shoulder seam, and a single bright specular on the crystal's facet. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where it would naturally occur.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the lit cloud tops and the dark hollow. Second: the near cloud bank. Third: Miku's boots, her cloak's lower edge. Fourth: Miku, the staff, the circle. Fifth: the far cloud bank, the horizon haze, the star field. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every staff fitting and cloak fold, restrained risograph grain in the dark sky, crisp flat fills in the lit areas, and one clean gradient only inside the circle's light. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the brass and the crystal.

No second character, no duplicate Miku, no crowd, no city, no skyline, no street, no market, no stalls, no awnings, no lanterns, no buildings, no vehicles, no birds, no wings, no feathers, no halo, no second magic circle, no circle behind her, no circle off to one side, no runes, no glyphs, no symbols of any kind, no letters on the circle, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the string named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no staff held in two hands, no arm hidden behind the circle, no mirrored figure in the cloud, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no smoke shaped like objects, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like one held breath above a cloud sea at night: a single figure suspended with her hair streaming upward, one cold circle of light turning in front of her, a dark hollow in the cloud where the light refuses to reach, and nothing else in the sky.

seeds.title: NORTH LIGHT
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “NORTH LIGHT”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing in deep snow before a small timber cabin, with a green aurora band arching across the sky above the roof. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the cold field.

Use a camera at knee height on a normal lens, set low in the snow about eight metres from the cabin, tilted up about ten degrees so the roof line sits below the aurora and the snowfield fills the lower third. Place Miku in the left third at approximately thirty percent of the canvas width, full body visible from boots to hair ornaments, occupying about thirty-two percent of the frame height. Let the cabin occupy the right third and the aurora the whole upper band.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Her right hand holds a storm lantern down at hip height, its handle hooked on two fingers, and her left hand is pushed into her coat pocket at the wrist. Her breath is visible as a small pale plume. Keep the pose still, the arms close to her body, and put nothing else in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the cabin itself: a small timber structure of vertical boards with a pitched roof, one lit square window, a stone chimney and a low door with a snow-crusted frame. Let the cabin occupy approximately thirty percent of the canvas area on the right, cut by the right edge, with a drift banked against its windward wall.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The cabin's boards are weathered spruce, silvered on the exposed faces and dark where snow sits; the roof is corrugated metal under a thick even load; the window is a single pane with a warm interior behind a curtain; the chimney is dry-laid stone with mortar missing in two joints; the snow is dry and wind-packed with a hard crust that holds footprints only where it is broken; the aurora is a soft band of green with a paler lower edge. Each behaves differently — silvered timber reads as vertical strokes, snow scatters all light and holds blue shadow, the window is the only saturated warm rectangle, the aurora emits without illuminating anything.

Build a stepped sequence from the foreground inward. Begin at the bottom edge with broken crust and one deep boot print, then the drift's windward edge with its fine spindrift lip, then Miku and her lantern, then the cabin's near corner and its snow bank, then the lit window, then the roofline and the aurora band. The sequence must read as a figure standing in a field looking at a light, not as a landscape postcard.

Leave one deliberate absence. The cabin's window is only half lit: the curtain is drawn across its left two-thirds, leaving a narrow bright vertical strip on the right with the dark room behind it. Keep the strip about a hand's width and place it so the bright strip falls directly behind Miku's shoulder, giving her hair a pale outline.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: broken crust, boot print, lantern light on snow. Middle ground: Miku, the drift, the cabin's near corner. Background: the lit window, the roofline, the aurora band. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the aurora and the window only. The aurora is a weak cool key: a green-grey wash across the whole field that lifts every upward face of snow and leaves every vertical in shadow. The window is a small warm key: a saturated rectangle throwing a narrow trapezoid of warm light onto the snow in front of it and a warm edge along the cabin's boards. Add Miku's lantern as a third, tiny warm source, lighting her coat's lower half and a small circle of snow at her boots. Keep the three sources strictly separate in reach.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the cold light. The nearer tail falls forward in one clean aqua mass that reads almost luminous against the snow, picking up the aurora's green along its outer edge; the farther tail drops behind her and is cut by the window's warm light into a pale band. Let a few flakes settle on the near shoulder and hold their own small highlights.

Dress Miku in an original deep-winter costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not ski wear. A long quilted parka in deep charcoal with a wide furless collar, cinched once at the waist, over dark trousers tucked into high felt boots; a pale knitted band across her brow; thick mittens. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale accent, and keep the silhouette simple enough to read at thumbnail size.

Use a cold-green palette with two small warm accents and strict area control. Approximately fifty-two percent of the image is snow white and pale blue shadow, sixteen percent is the green aurora band, twelve percent is the near-black sky above it, eight percent is silvered timber, six percent is Miku's charcoal parka and aqua hair, four percent is the warm window light, and two percent is the lantern's small glow. Keep the warm values small and separate so the cold stays dominant.

Drive the printed graphic language from the snow's own surface rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the lower left of the snowfield, printed flat and matte, reading as a cold hole in the white. Add a rectangular pale panel behind the cabin as a graphic mask at the height of the window, and let one vertical strip of deep green run from the aurora to the drift, aligned to the cabin's corner. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “NORTH LIGHT” once, in white paint stencilled on a low board nailed to the cabin's near wall, worn away at the lower strokes, sized so the board spans about an eighth of the canvas width. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “62° N” sit on a small enamel plate bolted to the door frame. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the cold. The snow's crust is broken only along the path her boots have taken; the drift's windward face is scalloped into shallow waves; the cabin's boards are silvered where exposed and dark where sheltered; the window's pane holds a frost fern in its lower corner; the chimney carries a thin cap of snow with one dark seam. Keep the wear physical and directional, never a uniform texture.

Build a second composition through the snow. The snowfield carries the aurora as a broad pale green wash, the cabin as a dark mass with one warm rectangle, and the lantern as a small warm point with a long soft halo. Let the reflections stay diffuse and never mirror, since the snow is matte.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A brass lantern hook worn bright, one split log frozen to the drift, a steel door latch with frost on its spring, and a short length of chain hanging from the chimney's cleanout. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a cabin would actually have it.

Illuminate with the aurora as the weak cool key, the window as the small warm key, and the lantern as the tiny third source. Let the aurora lift every upward snow face and leave the verticals dark. Let the window lay one warm trapezoid on the snow and one warm rim along the boards. Let the lantern produce a small circle of snow light at her boots and a warm edge on her coat's lower half. Keep the sky above the aurora at absolute black.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: broken crust, boot print, lantern circle. Second: Miku, her boots, the drift's lip. Third: the cabin's near corner and snow bank. Fourth: the window, the boards, the chimney. Fifth: the roofline, the aurora band, the black sky. Separate them by value steps of roughly ten percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every board and roof edge, restrained risograph grain in the cold shadow fields, crisp flat fills in the white areas, and fine frost only in the window's corner. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the lantern's glass.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no skier in the background, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no stars, no trees, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like the coldest hour of a northern night: green arching over a silvered roof, one narrow strip of window still lit, and a girl standing in broken crust with a lantern she has not yet raised.

seeds.title: ONE MORE TURN
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 chalk-light editorial poster titled “ONE MORE TURN”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only figure on the plate, standing on the tread of a chalk spiral stair inside a chalk well. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, a slim virtual-singer silhouette, and her original grey-and-teal costume structure. Keep her face, both eyes, both hands and her full silhouette instantly readable at thumbnail size.

Weave Hatsune Miku’s extremely long aqua twin tails into the chalk dust. Both tails hang down her back in one clean aqua mass, pale where the low chalk light catches their crown and almost black at the tips, the ends gathering on the tread beside her, with one strand lifting in the draught that rises through the well. Her aqua hair is the only cool saturated note in the whole plate.

Dress Hatsune Miku in an original chalk-well costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not a slip dress. A fitted chalk-white sleeveless top with graphite trim, a narrow aqua necktie, detached translucent sleeves, a pleated skirt with a thin graphite waistband, and dark thigh-highs with fine seams. Keep the outfit chalk-matte and quiet so it belongs to the stair rather than competing with it.

Set the camera at the bottom of a chalk well, wide lens, looking almost straight up along the spiral so the whole stair rises away from the lens and crops at the top edge. Place her on the left third, standing on a tread about two metres above the well floor, occupying about twenty-eight percent of the canvas, seen slightly from below and behind in a clear three-quarter turn: she leans her shoulder toward the parapet and looks back down along the stair, chin lowered, so her face and both gold eyes stay fully visible.

Give her exactly one core action: her right palm lies flat on the parapet's top edge, fingers spread and fully separated, each fingertip pressing the chalk with its own small contact shadow; her left hand hangs loose at her side with the fingertips just resting on the hem of her slip dress. Both hands stay inside the frame and individually readable, five fingers each. No second gesture and no second prop.

Construct the dominant object as one colossal chalk spiral stair turning inside a chalk shaft: a single continuous helical flight, its treads cantilevered from the well wall, its parapet a smooth chalk band that winds upward and is cropped by the top border, the whole structure occupying about seventy-two percent of the canvas. The spiral is the only geometry in the frame; nothing else is stacked into it.

Let the chalk be matte, arid and porous: chisel arrises holding a hairline of warm light on every nosing, fine shrinkage cracks radiating from the tread anchors, dry bloom where pigment has dried, chalk dust gathered in every recess and along the parapet, corners eroded into soft white powder, and shadow absorbed into the surface instead of reflected off it.

Give the stair eleven visible treads and make their surfaces carry one pigment story that runs downward with gravity: a fresh deep-amber pool near the top where a jar has spilled; a caramel film sliding over the next nosings; a dried ochre ring where the film stopped; a chalk bloom dusting the dried ring; a pale ghost of a ring on the next treads; and finally bare chalk with only a faint amber halo left in the grain. Change material, not clutter, along that path, and space the states unevenly so the rhythm never becomes a ladder.

Treat the pigment as a real material in four states: a wet glossy pool with a pinched edge and one sharp specular line; a caramel film that thins as it runs; a dried ring with a darker rim and a pale interior; and dry ochre dust that stains the chalk grain and turns salmon where chalk dust has settled into it. The pigment never glows and never becomes a graphic splash.

Build the parapet from chalk with one glazed ivory ceramic cap running along its top edge: hard clean silhouette, pearl-white glaze with a cool half-tone where the light falls away, unglazed bisque on its hidden face, and one clean crack lifted a millimetre at a joint. Set one small wine-red enamel seal into the cap at the joint nearest her hand, and space brushed stainless balusters every few treads, each carrying a narrow compressed reflection of the chalk and one hairline welding bead.

Lay one folded sheet of vellum on a tread two levels below her, translucent where pigment has soaked through into a soft halo with visible fibre, opaque dry white where it has not, its corner lifted by the stair's draft. It is the only paper in the frame.

Let her white hair organise the left edge: waist-length, falling straight and thick, holding one warm amber rim along the crown and a few loose strands lifted at the nape by the rising air, cropped once by the left border, its last third dissolving into fine halftone. Keep the hair solid and unmistakable and keep her head silhouette completely clean against the pale well wall.

Rebuild the slip dress as a material study: thin chalk-white silk with a narrow strap and a soft bias fall, translucent only in the last hand-width above the hem where the warm light passes through, opaque over the chest and hips, one asymmetric tide line of dried ochre staining the hem, and a hairline seam catching the light along the ribs. Keep the silhouette modest and quiet.

Build the environment with three anchors and nothing else: the curved chalk well wall with one deep blind recess, the ochre spill's slow path, and a shallow chalk shelf at the very bottom holding a film of amber-tinted water that mirrors one tread upside down. Reserve about twenty-six percent of the canvas as quiet pale chalk in the upper left, carrying only wall texture, one engraved arc and drifting dust.

Hold the palette with strict area control. About fifty-eight percent of the plate is chalk white and ivory across the well, the stair, the silk and the paper; seventeen percent is amber and ochre in the pigment, the seal light and the reflected shelf; eight percent is caramel brown in the stair’s varnished treads; seven percent is graphite in the thin contours and the shadow between treads; five percent is aqua in her hair and the necktie; three percent is cobalt in the deep shadow at the well’s mouth; and two percent is the warm white highlight along the parapet’s top edge. No hue outside this list appears anywhere on the plate.

Add the printed devices of an editorial plate: one pale chalk-white wash spreading from the upper left and stopping at a hard edge against the parapet; one hard-edged wine-red block at the right border; ochre halftone dots that thin outward from the spill into the quiet field; a paper-white knockout strip through the bottom border; a puff of chalk bloom lifting off the parapet; and a one-pixel registration shift on the ochre only.

Keep the interface engraved and non-linguistic: centimetre ticks along the parapet's inner face, bracket corners where the spiral turns, one dot column beside the shelf, and three hairlines that follow the tread arrises. Every mark is cut into physical chalk and catches thin shadow, and every mark belongs to the object it is cut into.

Control occlusion with explicit masks. A translucent chalk wash may cover the lower-left wall and the bottom border; a paper-white knockout may erase the far well wall at the top edge; masks may cut the outer hair, the dress hem, the shadowed hip and the peripheral stair, and they stay clear of her face, both eyes, both hands and the readable title.

Keep the disruption peripheral and one-directional: along the right border, cut three narrow vertical slices through the stair and shift them a few pixels with thin amber seams; erode the topmost tread into loose chalk; reduce the two farthest treads to halftone dots and one bare outline. Her face, her hands, the parapet contact and the near treads stay on a completely clean, fully resolved field.

Set the title into the architecture as a stepped line of type. Cut the exact words “ONE MORE TURN” into the parapet's inner face so each letter sits one tread higher than the last, the baseline climbing with the stair: uppercase, narrow grotesque, wide letterspacing, cap height about three percent of the canvas height, letters recessed and filled with flat amber enamel with a hairline chalk highlight along the top of each stroke. One baluster crosses one letter once and every letter stays fully legible. Add one small label “LOWER WELL” in small condensed capitals cut into the wall at the lower right. Nothing else on the plate spells anything.

Light the scene with one warm late shaft entering through an oculus far above the frame and falling down one side of the well: a broad soft wedge that grazes the parapet, passes over her hair and shoulder, and lands on the treads, carrying visible chalk dust. The rest of the chalk stays luminous and almost shadowless, the pigment holds the only saturated colour in the picture, and there is no second light source.

Build a second composition beneath the first: the spiral lays one long continuous shadow on the well wall that reads as a counter-spiral turning the opposite way; every tread drops one soft ochre ring onto the tread below; and the shelf's film reverses a single tread upside down.

Maintain five clear depth layers. Foreground: the cropped near tread and one baluster at the bottom edge, plus loose chalk dust. Character layer: her face, both hands and the parapet contact. Primary structure: the spiral stair with its parapet and ceramic cap. Secondary: the pigment states, the balusters and the folded sheet. Background: the well wall, the blind recess and the quiet chalk at the top. Separate the layers through overlap, line weight, edge softness and value contrast.

Render the image as an exceptionally polished chalk-light editorial poster: refined anime linework on her face and hands, chalk-matte plaster, glazed ceramic, dried ochre pigment, thin silk, vellum paper, brushed silver, printed halftone, fine paper grain and a one-pixel overprint shift. Give the finest linework to her eyes and fingers, the crispest edges to the parapet cap and the tread noses, the softest transitions to the chalk bloom and the dried rings, and the quietest surface to the upper-left wall.

The final image should read as one figure paused in a chalk stairwell: a white-haired woman in a thin white slip leans on a chalk parapet and looks back down a spiral of chalk treads that carry a single amber spill drying into the stone, one ceramic cap with a wine-red seal, a stepped line of amber letters climbing beside her, warm light from an oculus above with dust in it, and a counter-spiral of shadow on the wall. Read order: her face and both gold eyes first, the hand on the parapet second, the climbing spiral third, the pigment path fourth, the title fifth, the quiet wall last.

Readable text is limited to “ONE MORE TURN” and one small “LOWER WELL” label; exactly one figure; both hands complete and inside the frame; no second person; no watermark, signature or logo.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Hatsune Miku, no second figure, no second gesture, no second prop, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the title named above, no watermark, no signature, no frame, no border.

seeds.title: ORGANON
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 premium editorial key visual titled "ORGANON", featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing in front of one continuous pure-white wall. Preserve her canonical identity exactly: luminous aqua eyes with a fine dark lash line, aqua bangs cut as a soft fringe, extremely long aqua twin tails tied high with black-and-aqua square ornaments, a silver headset with a thin microphone arm, slim youthful anime proportions, and an unmistakable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, both eyes, both palms and the two points where the palms meet the plaster completely readable; the outer third of each twin tail, the skirt hem and the wall beyond her may be cut or erased.

Set the camera dead frontal at her chest height with a forty-millimetre feel and a very slight upward tilt, so the wall closes the top of the frame and the floor enters as a narrow band at the bottom. Place her exactly on the vertical centre line, weight on her left leg, right knee slightly bent, feet bare and parallel, chin lifted, eyes travelling up to the highest jar. She fills about thirty-four percent of the canvas height. She wears one plain white technical dress with a single cobalt panel at the hip, thin aqua seam lines and a short sleeve, and stands in front of the wall, touching only the plaster.

Dress Miku in an original ceremonial costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, with a fitted pearl-white bodice, layered cobalt enamel panels, precise graphite seams and three small aqua fasteners. Keep the costume light and editorial, and let one narrow printed sash overlap the shadow of the main structure.

The single action: both palms press flat against the wall at hip height, fingers spread, arms straight and relaxed, and she looks up along the wall above her own head. Her fingertips press the chalky surface just enough to pale it, and two faint hand-shaped prints sit a centimetre outside her palms where she has already shifted. That one beat carries the whole pose: two flat palms, spread fingers, one upward gaze.

Drive the graphic language from Miku's own palette. Use one large cobalt ink bloom spreading from the base of the nearest structure across the floor plane, two hard-edged royal-blue rectangular color blocks, translucent aqua stains on glass surfaces, and rare champagne-gold microdots on structural joints.

Build the whole picture on one dominant structure: a continuous matte white wall taking about seventy percent of the canvas, its top edge running beyond the frame, its side edges running out of frame. Nine small slabs protrude from it — thin cantilevered shelves about twenty by sixteen centimetres, four centimetres thick, sleeved straight out of the plaster with a crumbled chalky lip where the wall breaks around each one. They are scattered rather than gridded: every slab takes its own height, its own setback and its own spacing, the gaps opening from four centimetres to half a metre, and the whole set drifts upward from the lower left toward the upper right.

Seven of the nine slabs carry glass jars, and every jar is the same size: twenty-six centimetres tall, straight-sided, six-millimetre walls, a flat ground base, a brushed silver screw lid with a small etched numeral, and one narrow vellum label pasted at eye height. Inside each jar one human organ hangs suspended in clear preserving fluid — a heart with its aorta tied off and its coronary tree injected coral; a pair of lungs with every lobe separated; a kidney cut in half so one flat face shows the pale pelvis and the fine calyces; a brain with tight convolutions; a single eye with the optic nerve coiled behind it; one hand with the fingers gently curled and the nails in pearl; and a second kidney, whole and slightly smaller than the rest.

Make the glass and the fluid do visible optical work. Each jar carries a doubled contour on its far wall, a green-white edge where the wall thickness turns, a magnified strip of whatever stands behind it, a bright elliptical meniscus at the fluid surface, and a few slow motes held in the liquid. Each jar rests on a small wet crescent and throws a hard caustic ring onto its slab plus a soft caustic crescent up the wall behind it. The specimens are wax-injected: matte pearl-ivory surfaces, fine coral vein networks branching across the outside of each organ, one incision closed with white thread, and on the sectioned kidney a flat cut face that reads as one clean plane, wax all the way through. Add a few loose thread ends, one hairline crack in a lid, and one label lifting at its corner.

Give the seven jars a visible progression instead of seven copies. The nearest is filled to the brim with a tight bright meniscus; the next has dropped a hand's width and left a dry tide line across the glass; the third is half full with its label cockled and lifting; the fourth holds its organ low with cloud at the bottom; the fifth is full, clean and complete; the sixth has lost its label and keeps a pale rectangle of clean glass; the seventh, at the top right, is bone dry, its organ resting on the glass floor with the thread loosened. The two empty slabs keep one faint wet ring.

Anchor the wall in architecture and hold the whole space to a single plane. It meets the floor in a recessed four-centimetre shadow gap that draws one dark horizontal line across the bottom of the frame, and the floor is a pale matte slab carrying one long soft shadow of her body and one narrow caustic band. Where the raking light crosses the plaster, show the material honestly: fine aggregate under the surface, open pores, a chalky dust bloom at each shelf lip, and one hairline crack that starts at the top edge and dies out above the third jar.

Allocate colour by area and keep the picture almost white: sixty-six percent clean white plaster and pale floor, ten percent cool grey-lilac inside the recesses, under the slabs and in the shadow gap, eight percent pale rose-coral inside the specimens with one percent of it saturated, six percent aqua-green in the glass thickness, the fluid and the meniscus, five percent aqua in her hair and seams, three percent cobalt on the hip panel, the headset and the shoe line, one percent champagne silver on the seven lids and their etched numerals. Every white surface inside a caustic takes the caustic's own colour; everything outside stays neutral white.

Set one word into the plaster as part of the building. "ORGANON" is debossed three millimetres into the wall in an ultra-thin high-contrast serif, set horizontally at the height of the top shelf across about eighty percent of the frame width, its left end running off the left edge. Its value is the groove itself: a bright lower lip, a dark upper lip, and a shadow line between them where the raking light enters. Where a jar stands in front of it the letters are magnified and doubled through the glass, and at the far right, where the wall begins to erase, the last three letters lose their groove and flatten. The only other type is "07", small, etched into the upper lip of the shadow gap at the lower left, with one thin coral bar lying under the numerals. Three tiny aqua registration dots sit on the plaster beside three separate slabs, small enough to read as handling marks.

Let the caustics build a second anatomy. Each jar throws an enlarged soft-edged organ silhouette onto the wall behind and slightly to its right and up, in pale aqua and faint rose light — the heart's outline a hand-span wide, the brain a soft cloud, the eye a bright ring around one dark pupil. The nine slabs throw nine short dark bars at a slight diagonal. Together they make a light drawing of the collection larger than the objects themselves, and that drawing sets the wall's rhythm while the jars stay quiet objects on their slabs.

Run her twin tails as two long aqua paths that interact with the wall. The left tail falls across the shadow gap and picks up one caustic crescent at its tip; the right tail drops past two slabs, passes in front of the third jar and takes a magnified strip of its label on the inside of the hair. Close to the head both tails keep full opaque aqua volume and their tie ornaments, so her identity survives at any glance; the last third of each tail thins into a flat aqua line that the wall starts to erase.

Restrict all erasure to the outer region and let it climb in one direction. From the upper right corner inward the wall loses texture first, then the shelf shadows, then two labels, then two jars, which flatten into pure aqua silhouettes, then one whole slab, which vanishes and leaves a glass ring and a wet circle on white. Under her palms the plaster is fully resolved; beside her cheek the wall is the cleanest surface in the picture. Erasure stops at her silhouette.

Light from a large soft source high on the left, almost shadowless, plus one hard raking beam from the left edge travelling across the wall at a shallow angle. That beam draws the embossed word, the pores, the chalky shelf lips and the meniscus lines; it dies out before the right edge, which is why the right side flattens to white. Add one cool rim along her left shoulder, jaw and forearm lines, and a very slight aqua spill from the nearest jar onto her right palm.

Separate five depth layers by edge quality and value, each layer sharp in its own register: the half-cropped nearest slab and its jar at the lower left, close and crisp; her body, her upturned face and the two palm contacts, the sharpest of all; the middle ring of three jars; the far jars and the caustic anatomy, softer and cooler; and the wall going textureless toward the top and the right. Render as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional anime editorial key visual with real optical glass, chalky mineral plaster, wax specimens and architectural photography discipline. Read it in this order: her upturned face first, the two palm prints second, the seven jars third, the light anatomy fourth, the white space last. Structural constraints: no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no second person in the frame, no extra fingers, and nothing floats — every jar rests on its slab.

No additional figures or hands, no duplicate portrait, no second face, no floating interface elements, no readable text beyond the intended typography, no watermark.

seeds.title: PAPER FESTIVAL
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “PAPER FESTIVAL”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing on a night street strung with rows of paper lanterns. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands, hair ornaments and long twin-tail identity immediately readable against the lantern rows.

Use a camera at chest height in the middle of the street, one-point perspective so the lantern strings converge toward a dark vanishing slot at the centre, with a normal lens and mild exaggeration of the string curve. Place Miku in the left third, full body visible from sandals to hair ornaments, occupying approximately thirty percent of the image. She stands with her weight on the right leg, left toe turned out, shoulders open, chin lifted so both eyes catch the warm light from above.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Her right hand reaches up to touch the lowest lantern on the nearest string, fingertips just under its rim, and her left hand holds the corner of a folded paper charm against her chest. The lantern she touches swings slightly and its light spills across her forearm and cheek. Keep the gesture still and the arms clear of her face; add no second action and nothing else in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as forty rows of paper lanterns receding down the street, filling approximately seventy percent of the canvas from the top edge to the vanishing point and cropped left and right. Each string is a fine dark cable carrying eight to twelve barrel lanterns, and the rows overlap so the far ones compress into stacked bands of warm light. Beneath them, low wooden stall fronts line both sides of the street, shuttered and mostly dark.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The lanterns are ribbed washi paper over bamboo, painted with simple marks and closed with a dark cap at each end; the cables are thin tarred rope; the stall fronts are aged cedar with paper signs pasted and half torn; the street is packed earth and stone with a damp sheen; the far air is full of thin smoke. Each material behaves differently — paper glows and holds a visible rib shadow, rope reads as a single dark line, cedar dries grey and splits, damp earth doubles every light as a short vertical smear, smoke softens distance without greying the near field.

Build a stepped sequence down the street. Begin at the near left with a lantern whose paper has torn along one rib, its frame showing. Move down the rows through lanterns that grow progressively smaller and more uniform, then to one string where two lanterns have been extinguished, then to the far bands where individual lanterns are no longer separable and the light becomes a single texture. The sequence must read as distance and as the accumulation of many small repairs.

Leave one deliberate absence. On the nearest string, the fourth position is an empty hook with no lantern, only the short rope loop and a soot mark where the paper once hung. Keep that gap as a clean dark interval inside the bright row and place nothing inside it.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the damp street, a fallen paper charm and the base of the nearest stall. Middle ground: Miku, the lantern she touches and the first three strings. Background: the receding rows, the dark stall fronts and the vanishing slot of night sky at the centre.

Light the scene with the lantern field as the only key, warm and overhead, plus one small cold spill from a shuttered stall at the far right. The lanterns light Miku from above and slightly behind, modelling her shoulders and the top of her hair, and leave her face in a soft warm shadow she lifts into by tilting her chin. Keep every lantern contained, with no glow halo and no lens flare.

Weave Miku’s extremely long twin tails through the warm rows. The nearer twin tail rises past the nearest string and one lantern is partly hidden behind it; its outer strands catch a bright warm rim. The farther twin tail falls behind her shoulder into cooler shadow. Keep the hair dense and readable at her head, allowing it to separate only where it crosses a lantern edge.

Dress Miku in an original festival-night costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language. Use a short dark indigo wrap jacket with a wide sleeve and a double-breasted front over a pale under-robe, a narrow woven belt with a small knot at the front, a knee-length pleated skirt, and wooden sandals with dark thongs. Add one paper charm tucked into the belt, a fine silver hairpin at the temple, three tiny coral stitches at the cuff, and a faint soot mark on one shoulder. Keep the garment short and graphic so the vertical figure reads against the horizontal lantern rows.

Use a warm-on-dark palette. Approximately forty-four percent of the image is black night and deep indigo cloth. Twenty percent is lantern amber. Fourteen percent is pale washi cream. Eight percent is aged cedar brown. Six percent is damp street grey. Four percent is the dark rope line. Two percent is the cold spill at the far right. Less than two percent is the aqua of her hair and the coral stitches.

Drive the printed graphic language from Miku’s own palette. Let one large aqua ink bloom spread across the damp street at the lower right, its edge following the puddle line. Add two hard-edged lantern-shaped warm blocks on the cedar stall fronts where years of light have fallen. Let a fine halftone of reflected lantern dots sit only in the near street. Cut one clean black knockout where the empty hook breaks the bright row. Add rare silver microdots only on the cables' knots and the hairpin.

Print the text as physical matter. Paste a paper strip to the nearest stall front bearing the exact readable words “PAPER FESTIVAL” in a narrow brush script, dark ink on cream paper, one corner lifting and one edge darkened by damp. Add one smaller strip with a maker's mark beneath it. Both are pasted flat and overlapped by the stall's frame so they read as objects, not as floating type.

Let every surface show the festival's age. The cedar is split and grey, its paste stains darker where old strips were removed. The lanterns are clean and glowing at the top and smoke-darkened near their caps. The street is damp with a few flattened paper scraps. The ropes sag slightly between their knots. Nothing should look new except the lantern Miku is touching.

Build a second composition through reflection and the rows themselves. Every lantern throws a short vertical amber smear into the damp street, and the smears lengthen toward the foreground. The rows converge into a second, inverted set of bands in the wet ground. The empty hook leaves an unbroken dark interval in both the string and its reflection, so the absence repeats twice.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A brass hook at the end of the nearest string, one folded paper charm with a fine printed edge, a thin silver hairpin, three coral stitches, and a small enamel token tied to her belt. Keep them clustered near her hands and the near lantern and never scattered across the night.

Illuminate with the lantern field as key and the far cold spill as a single accent. Keep the brightest value on the lantern she touches, the second brightest on the nearest rows, and let the far street compress into a warm haze that never becomes a flat orange wash.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: damp street, fallen charm, stall base. Primary middle ground: Miku, the touched lantern and the first three strings. Secondary: the middle rows and the shuttered stalls. Tertiary: the far bands and the smoke. Background: the dark vanishing slot, held as clean negative space.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a hand-pulled print: crisp drawn linework, ink and watercolor washes with visible wet edges, dry-brush erosion on the cedar and paper, soft paper grain in the flat areas, and clean lithograph texture in the smoke. Keep the drawing precise and the paint loose, with no photographic depth of field.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no floating interface, no holograms, no glowing particles, no abstract light streaks, no full-canvas glitch, no random letters or numbers, no watermark, no signature, no muddy background, no neon rainbow lighting, no face obstruction, no lantern covering her eyes, and no malformed hands. Preserve a strict hierarchy: Miku’s face and the touched lantern first, the near three strings second, the receding rows third, the empty hook fourth, then the stalls, typography and night.

The final image should feel like a street prepared for a crowd that has not arrived: forty rows of paper light, one hook empty, one hand lifting a lantern to check it, and the whole festival held in the minute before the first visitor turns the corner.

seeds.title: PARKADE
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “PARKADE”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing between two rows of concrete columns on an empty upper deck of a multi-storey car park at night. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the pale concrete.

Use a camera at chest height on a slightly wide lens, set on the deck's centre line so the columns repeat in perspective and the painted bay lines converge behind her. Place Miku at approximately forty-two percent of the canvas width, full body visible from boots to hair ornaments, occupying about thirty-six percent of the frame height.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Her right hand holds a paper parking ticket up at chest height, and her left hand rests flat on a column's corner. Her head is turned toward the ramp, both eyes visible. Keep the pose steady and put nothing else in her hands.

Construct the dominant visual object as the concrete column: a square column about a metre across, painted white to shoulder height with a grey band above, standing in the near middle ground. Let the columns occupy approximately thirty percent of the canvas area through repetition, and let the near column's flat lit face be the brightest large surface in the frame.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The concrete is painted white with a soft roller texture, chipped at the corners and marked by a red band at knee height; the deck is grey concrete with painted bay lines and oil stains; the ceiling is the same concrete with exposed ribs; the far wall is open to the night; the columns' paint is scuffed by tyres. Each behaves differently — painted concrete holds a flat pale value with a soft texture, oil stains read as dark irregular patches, painted lines are worn and chalky, the open side is absolute black.

Build a stepped sequence down the deck.
