seeds.title: PRIMARY MIRROR
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium futuristic anime game key visual titled “PRIMARY MIRROR”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character inside a pure white optical chamber. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, a slim virtual-singer silhouette, and her original grey-and-teal costume structure. Keep her face, both eyes and both hands fully readable at thumbnail size.

Place her in the left third of the frame at a low camera slightly below hip height, looking up and to the right, standing on a narrow white gantry walkway whose front edge is cropped by the bottom border. She occupies about thirty percent of the canvas height. Her body is turned three-quarters away from the camera, torso twisted back toward the mirror above her, head tipped up, both boots planted on the gantry with the weight on her right leg and the left heel lifted a little. Keep her head silhouette against the white plate, her pressing hand and her boot contact lines the three sharpest details of the left frame.

Give her one single action: her left arm reaches up and forward, palm flat against the underside of one loose hexagonal mirror segment high in the dish, pressing it back into its empty socket; her right hand grips the gantry rail behind her hip. The palm-to-socket distance is about one forearm, and their contact is the emotional center of the image. Do not add a second gesture, a second prop or a second point of contact.

Build the dominant object as a colossal concave primary mirror: an array of hundreds of hexagonal segments forming one shallow white dish that occupies seventy-five percent of the canvas, cropped hard by the top and right frame edges. See it from its lower-left inner side at a shallow angle, so the dish curves away upward and its rim sweeps from the lower left to the upper right. Its outer support ring is cropped on three sides. It has no visible ground, no column and no smoke; its scale is expressed by the size of the single unsocketed segment beside her palm and by the slow curvature of the dish.

Organize the segment field into eight concentric rings around a dark central bore. From the bore outward: mirrors of mirror-polished aluminum that read almost black with one hard specular hairline each; then pearl-white ceramic segments with matte faces and thin chipped edges; then segments in cobalt enamel with wet gloss and a little dust; then frosted acrylic segments whose light bleeds through the seam; then vellum segments printed with hairline halftone grids; then segments reduced to graphite linework; and at the outermost cropped ring, segments that are pure white voids with only a bracket outline left. Every ring must be distinguishable by material behavior, never by colour alone.

Let the materials show visible consequences: polished aluminum returns a double outline and a hard sharp reflection of the rim; ceramic holds a hard edge, a shallow relief and one small chipped corner; cobalt enamel pools light into a wet oval; frosted acrylic blurs whatever passes behind it and deforms the seam; vellum shows paper fiber and absorbs a faint ink bloom where it is engraved; graphite dust settles in the grooves; the halftone dots grow coarser toward the cropped edge.

Hold the loose segment in the exact state of the action: a hexagon about one and a half metres across, tipped roughly twelve degrees out of the dish plane, its lower edge already seated in the socket while the upper edge is still lifting free, four of its six edges catching light, a thin cobalt gap ring leaking pale aqua light around the side that has not yet closed, and one hairline shadow travelling across her palm. The already seated segments around it show perfect hairline seams and no thickness at all.

Support the dish with a white space frame behind it: radial trusses, a lattice of square-section ribs, two actuator pistons in front of the near rim and one behind it, and six thin tension cables crossing diagonally in front of the segment field. Make at least three clear front-behind interleavings: a cable passing in front of her shoulder and behind a piston; a truss passing behind the dish rim and in front of the white void; the tipped segment passing in front of a cable and behind her forearm. Nothing overlaps her face, eyes or the contact point.

Let the twin tails run the only curved lines through the dish: the first tail lifts toward the pressing hand and its last third thickens as it crosses the mirror surface, gaining one displaced ghost contour that reappears two segments to the right, shifted and slightly magnified, and never a complete copy of her body; the second tail falls across the gantry edge and is cropped by the bottom border. Keep the hair solid and unmistakable for the first two thirds of its length, and never let a reflection duplicate her figure.

Dress her in a white-and-cobalt optics suit derived from her virtual-singer design language: a fitted high-collar bodice with aqua luminous seams, a mirror-polished ceramic chest plate cut as one large hexagon, a short asymmetrical white skirt of layered plates over a translucent cyan underlayer, detached sleeves with thin black calibration lines, dark thigh-highs with cobalt edge panels, a narrow silver belt with one small coral bead, and soft dust on the boot soles. The costume reads as clean-room instrumentation while keeping her canonical proportions and aqua identity colour.

Keep a disciplined negative space: the entire lower-left corner, the band above her head and a vertical strip along the left border stay almost pure white plate with nothing in them, together about thirty percent of the frame. Let the detail density climb from that quiet corner toward the socket, and again from the socket toward the cropped top-right ring.

Use a strict pearl white, cobalt, aqua, graphite and silver palette. Approximately sixty-two percent is pearl white, chalk white and pale silver on the dish, the plate and the void; fourteen percent is cobalt and deep ultramarine in the seam shadows, the bore and the enamel ring; twelve percent is aqua and icy cyan in the hair, the light leak and the index arc; eight percent is graphite and black in the segment outlines and the bore; three percent is mirror silver on the polished ring; and no more than one percent is warm coral at the single belt bead and one small marker. Keep every large field flat and cool, and let the coral read as the only warm note in a white machine.

Scatter character-palette ink only where it explains structure: one broad translucent aqua wash across the lower skirt and the gantry edge, two hard-edged cobalt rectangles sitting on the cropped right segments like printed swatches, one white knockout strip cutting through the outermost vellum ring, a halftone dot field that thins toward the socket, a few graphite splatter dots near the tipped segment, and one tiny coral dot beside the belt bead. All of it obeys her colour identity and none of it touches her face.

Engrave the interface into the structure itself: five concentric index grooves on the ceramic support ring, ninety-six radial ticks between the second and third grooves, one continuous aqua index arc running along the fourth, a small bracket-and-corner frame around the empty socket, and three one-pixel dots on the gantry rail. Every mark is machined into a physical surface with a thin shadow on its lower side. No floating panels, no holographic cards, no free-floating HUD.

Protect the centre. Masks may cut the outer hair tips, sleeve cuffs, skirt hem, boot shadows, gantry edge, cropped segments and the outer ring; they stay completely clear of her face, both eyes, both hands, the pressing palm, the socket gap and the light leak. Where the lower twin tail crosses a cobalt mask, convert it into a white inverse silhouette with one aqua outline; where a cable crosses the frosted ring, let the segment seams bend and magnify slightly behind it.

Confine the glitch to the outermost cropped ring and the top-right corner: four narrow horizontal slices shifted a few pixels with thin cyan edges at the seams, one segment replaced by cobalt rectangular pixels fading into halftone, one short white knockout erasing a bracket half way, and one misregistered cyan plate offset from its ceramic base. Keep the dish centre, the socket, the light leak, the gantry and her body on a completely clean field.

Add restrained luxury only at joints: hairline silver screws in the segment corners, one row of tiny ceramic beads along the support ring, two polished hinges on the gantry rail, a thin copper inlay around the bore, and a single droplet of coolant hanging from the lowest piston. Each of these appears once and stays smaller than her hand.

Build the second composition from light rather than reflection: the dish focuses a pale aqua caustic that lands as a thin bright ellipse across the white plate behind her and continues as a hairline along one truss, so the brightest shape in the frame is an empty ring of light rather than a copy of the character. Let her shadow fall long and soft toward the lower right, crossed once by the caustic ellipse, and let the loose segment throw a hexagonal shadow onto her forearm.

Set readable typography only twice: the title “PRIMARY MIRROR” machined as voids into the white ceramic support ring along its upper-right sweep, in a wide uppercase sans serif with generous letter spacing and one cable crossing three of the letters; and a small vellum label riveted to the gantry rail at the right of her boots reading “SEG 09 · F/0.9”. All other marks stay non-linguistic: ticks, brackets, dots, hairlines, grooves.

Light the chamber with one huge diffuse white source from an unseen opening high above and behind the dish, so segment faces stay luminous and their camera-away edges hold soft cobalt shadow. Add one narrow aqua beam escaping sideways through the unclosed socket gap, throwing a faint cool pool onto her palm, wrist and collar; a continuous silver specular hairline along the polished ring; and a weak bounce from the white plate that lifts the underside of her chin and skirt. Shadows stay thin, cool and clean so the white chamber reads as light rather than grey.

Maintain five distinct depth layers. Foreground: the cropped gantry edge, one large segment corner entering from the lower right, and three fine dust motes. Primary middle ground: Hatsune Miku, her pressing palm, her head silhouette and the tipped segment, all with the sharpest contours. Secondary middle ground: the socket gap, the light leak, the near trusses and the cables crossing her shoulder. Tertiary: the ceramic and cobalt segment rings with their engraved index grooves. Background: the outer vellum ring, the cropped glitch corner, the pale caustic ellipse and the empty white chamber. Separate the layers with overlap, line weight, edge softness and value contrast rather than with fog.

Render as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional anime editorial key visual combining crisp character linework, machined white architecture, hard-surface mirror shading, precise engraved interface geometry, selective photobashing, subtle halftone on the outer rings, fine paper grain on the vellum segments, clean vector edges and a restrained dry-brush erode at the cropped glitch corner. Give the finest linework to her hand and profile, the hardest edge to the ceramic segments, the widest graphic rhythm to the segment rings and the quietest surface to the white void.

The final image must read in one glance as: a small singer on a white gantry presses the last hexagon back into a colossal concave mirror that fills the sky, a thin line of aqua light escapes the seam, the mirror answers with a ring of focused light on the empty plate, and the machine becomes able to see. Character first, her pressing hand second, the colossal dish third, the engraved interface fourth, the white negative space fifth. One Hatsune Miku only, no second figure and no full-body reflection; face, eyes and both hands fully visible; readable text limited to “PRIMARY MIRROR” and “SEG 09 · F/0.9”.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Hatsune Miku, no second figure, no reflection that reads as a second person, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the title named above, no watermark, no signature, no frame, no border.

seeds.title: QUIET BROADCAST
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 chalk-light editorial poster titled “QUIET BROADCAST”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only figure, seated on the rim of a shallow chalk basin inside a colossal chalk aperture. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, a slim virtual-singer silhouette, and her original grey-and-teal costume structure. Keep her face, both eyes, both hands and her full silhouette instantly readable at thumbnail size.

Weave Hatsune Miku’s extremely long aqua twin tails into the chalk light. Both tails fall from the crown of her head in two clean aqua masses that reach past her waist and pool against the basin rim, pale where the light strikes them and deep aqua where they cross the chalk, with one strand lifting across the aperture. Her aqua hair is the only cool saturated note in the whole plate.

Dress Hatsune Miku in an original broadcast-basin costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language. A chalk-white sleeveless top with graphite trim, a narrow aqua necktie, detached translucent sleeves with fine seams, a pleated chalk skirt held by a thin graphite band, and dark thigh-highs with a single pale edge. Keep the whole outfit chalk-matte and precise so it reads as part of the plate’s design rather than as costume drama.

Seat her on the rim of a shallow chalk basin slightly right of centre, at about sixty percent of the canvas width, in a clear three-quarter profile turned toward the left, knees drawn up, shoulders relaxed, head lowered and eyes half open looking down into her own hands. She occupies about thirty-three percent of the canvas. Use a wide lens at her seated eye level with a very slight upward tilt, so the colossal aperture behind her reads as monumental and her body stays human scale.

Give her exactly one core action: both hands are cupped together on her knee around one small chalk cube, thumbs meeting over its top face, all five fingers of each hand visible and separated, the fingertips pressing the cube's edges. From that cube a narrow cone of flat shards lifts away toward the upper left. Nothing else moves.

Construct the dominant object as one colossal circular oculus cut straight through a chalk wall: a single aperture about fifty-eight percent of the canvas height, its centre at roughly sixty-eight percent width and thirty-four percent height, cropped by the right border, the wall around it one metre thick with a machined chalk arris and a cut face showing chalk aggregate where the edge has broken. The aperture opens onto pale morning sky with fine suspended dust, so it reads as a hole punched in a monument rather than as a moon.

Let the chalk be matte, arid and porous: chisel arrises holding a hairline of light, fine shrinkage cracks running out from the aperture, dry bloom where moisture has left the stone, chalk dust gathered in every recess and along the rim, corners eroded into soft white powder, and shadow absorbed into the surface rather than reflected.

Dress the aperture's inner lip with one glazed chalk-ivory ceramic band: hard clean silhouette, pearl-white glaze with a cool half-tone where the light falls away, unglazed bisque on its hidden face, and one clean crack lifted a millimetre at the seam. Keep the rest of the wall bare chalk with nothing applied to it.

Engrave four hairline orbital arcs across the wall, each about 0.3pt, each carrying small spheres. Five spheres sit along the longest arc as the only repeated element, changing state from the far side to the near side: a solid pearl-ceramic sphere; a sphere swallowed by chalk bloom; a sphere split by one hairline crack; a half-translucent vellum sphere; and a bare silver wireframe with nothing inside. Space them unevenly so the arc never becomes a bead necklace.

Build the shard stream from nine flat pieces leaving her cupped hands toward the upper left, and let the material decay along that one path: solid glazed ceramic at the hands, chalk-dusted ceramic, pieces printed with coarse 65-line halftone, translucent vellum cards, a bare 0.5pt outline, and finally chalk dust at the outer end. The stream widens into a shallow cone and its pieces stay flat, thin and printed, never glowing.

Lay one long translucent vellum ribbon across the lower left, drifting and folded once on itself, its printed hatch doubling through the overlap and its free end lifting above the basin rim. Where it crosses the wall it transmits a soft pale shadow; where it crosses an orbital arc, the arc bends and magnifies slightly beneath it.

Let her twin tails organise the composition: the upper tail sweeps toward the aperture and is magnified once through the vellum ribbon before ending as three separated aqua contours; the lower tail falls along the basin rim and is cropped by the bottom border, dissolving into halftone in its last third. Keep the hair solid and unmistakable for its first two thirds and keep her head silhouette clean against the white field.

Rebuild the costume as a material study while keeping its logic: the sleeveless top is chalk-white woven cloth with crisp graphite trim and a hard small collar; the necktie is a flat aqua enamel strip with one engraved line; the detached sleeves are matte graphite with a cut edge; the pleated skirt is a chalk-white enamel sheet whose hem dissolves into halftone; the thighhighs are cool pale grey with one hairline aqua edge; the boots are graphite lacquer with a thin silver rim.

Build the environment with three architectural anchors and nothing else: the chalk wall with its single aperture, one vertical slot of pale light cut clean through the wall at the far right border, and the shallow chalk basin whose still water film mirrors the aperture as a second, softer disc. Leave about twenty-six percent of the canvas as quiet chalk in the upper left, carrying only chalk texture, one engraved arc and drifting dust.

Hold the palette with strict area control. About sixty-one percent of the plate is chalk white and ivory across the wall, the ribbon, the cloth and the printed pieces; fourteen percent is aqua in her long hair, the necktie and one enamel edge; twelve percent is cobalt and deep blue in the aperture shadow and the pigment; six percent is graphite in the thin contours and the seams; four percent is warm paper tone in the shards lifting from the cube; two percent is silver on the small metal fittings; and one percent is a single amber accent at the basin lip. No hue outside this list appears anywhere on the plate.

Add the graphic devices of a printed poster: one pale chalk-white wash spreading from the lower left and stopping at a hard edge beneath the ribbon; one hard-edged cobalt block behind the aperture's lower rim; aqua halftone dots that thin outward from the shard stream into the quiet upper-left field; one paper-white knockout strip through the bottom border; a puff of chalk bloom drifting off the rim; and a one-pixel registration shift on the cobalt only.

Keep the interface engraved and non-linguistic: centimetre ticks along the aperture rim, bracket corners where the wall turns, one dot column beside the basin rim, and three hairlines that follow the orbital arcs. Every mark is cut into physical chalk and catches thin shadow, and every mark belongs to the object it is cut into.

Control occlusion with explicit masks. A translucent chalk wash may cover the lower-left ribbon field, the farthest shards and the bottom border; a paper-white knockout may erase the far wall at the top-left corner; masks and knockout edges may cut the outer twin tails, the trailing hair, the skirt hem and the peripheral wall, and they stay clear of her face, her eyes, both cupped hands, the small cube and the fully readable title.

Keep the disruption peripheral and one-directional: along the right border, cut four narrow vertical slices through the wall and shift them a few pixels with thin aqua seams; erode the aperture's upper-left rim into loose chalk; reduce the farthest three shards to halftone dots and one outline. Her face, her hands, the cube and the near side of the aperture stay on a completely clean, fully resolved field.

Set the title into the architecture. Cut the exact words “QUIET BROADCAST” into the outer face of the aperture rim so the baseline follows the rim's curve, sweeping over her head from about ten o'clock to two o'clock: uppercase, narrow grotesque, wide letterspacing, cap height about three percent of the canvas height, letters recessed and filled with flat graphite enamel with a hairline chalk highlight along the top of each stroke. One engraved orbital arc crosses the first letter and the upper twin tail crosses one letter near the end; every letter stays fully legible. Add one small label “CHALK / SIGNAL” in small condensed capitals cut into the wall at the lower left. Nothing else on the plate spells anything.

Light the scene with clear morning air entering only through the aperture: a broad soft crescent of daylight falls on the wall beside her shoulder and on the basin rim, carrying visible chalk dust, while the surrounding chalk stays luminous and almost shadowless. Give her hair one narrow specular line, the shards one thin glint each at their leading edge, and the ceramic sphere nearest the aperture one small hard highlight. There is no second light source.

Build a second composition beneath the first: the basin's water film reverses the aperture as a smaller, softer disc with its own faint ceramic rim; the shards lay thin parallel shadows on the wall; and the aperture's rim throws one long crescent shadow that runs opposite to the orbital arcs.

Maintain five clear depth layers. Foreground: the cropped basin rim and two large shards at the bottom edge. Character layer: her face, both hands, the small cube and the cupped contact. Primary structure: the aperture with its ceramic lip and the wall around it. Secondary: the orbital arcs, the five spheres and the ribbon. Background: the pale sky inside the aperture, the halftone field and the quiet upper-left chalk. Separate the layers through overlap, line weight, edge softness and value contrast.

Render the image as an exceptionally polished chalk-light editorial poster: refined anime linework on her face and hands, chalk-matte plaster, glazed ceramic, vellum paper, flat aqua enamel, printed halftone, fine paper grain and a one-pixel overprint shift. Give the finest linework to her eyes and her cupped fingers, the crispest edges to the aperture lip and the shards, the softest transitions to the chalk bloom, and the quietest surface to the upper-left field.

The final image should read as one quiet transmission inside a chalk monument: a singer seated on a basin rim cups a small chalk cube while a shallow cone of printed shards lifts away toward the empty white field, a colossal aperture opens behind her head onto morning sky, five ceramic spheres decay along one engraved arc, a vellum ribbon drifts across the lower left, the title curves over her head along the rim, and everything stays chalk, aqua, cobalt and graphite. Read order: her face and eyes first, the cupped hands second, the aperture third, the shard stream fourth, the title fifth, the quiet field last.

Readable text is limited to “QUIET BROADCAST” and one small “CHALK / SIGNAL” label; one Hatsune Miku only; both hands complete and cupped in frame; no second figure; no watermark, signature or logo.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Hatsune Miku, no second figure, no second gesture, no second prop, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the title named above, no watermark, no signature, no frame, no border.

seeds.title: RAIN MART
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “RAIN MART”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing inside the doorway of a small late-night convenience store while rain falls on an empty street behind her. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and long twin-tail identity readable against the cold fluorescent interior.

Use a slightly high camera at eye level, set just outside the storefront and angled about ten degrees off the door axis, with a normal lens so the doorway frames her cleanly and the street recedes to the left. Place Miku in the right third at approximately thirty-four percent of the canvas width, cropped at mid-thigh by the bottom edge, her body turned three-quarters toward the camera. Leave the left two-thirds for the wet street and the store's reflection, so the composition reads as a wide interior-exterior window rather than a portrait.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Her right hand rests on the aluminium door frame at shoulder height, holding the door a hand's width open, and her left hand hangs at her side holding a clear plastic umbrella by its curved handle, its tip touching the wet step. Water runs off the umbrella onto the concrete. Keep the pose still, the arms clear of her face, and put nothing else in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the storefront itself: one wide plate-glass window and a glass door, together spanning approximately sixty percent of the canvas width, framed in dull aluminium that has been repainted twice. Behind the glass, stack shelving in three horizontal bands from waist height to the ceiling, filled edge to edge with small packages. Keep the glass mostly transparent so the interior reads as depth, and let only the lower corner fog where her breath and the warm air meet it.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The glass is thin, slightly warped, and holds a fine film of rain; the aluminium frame is scratched to a soft grey and cold to look at; the interior floor is cream vinyl tile with a dark grout grid, polished by decades of feet; the shelving is powder-coated steel the colour of old paper; the street is black asphalt with a thin water film; the kerb is cast concrete with a chipped nose. Each behaves differently — glass transmits and fogs, aluminium dulls the highlight, vinyl reflects the ceiling tubes as long soft bars, asphalt breaks every reflection into a thousand vertical fragments.

Build a stepped sequence from the foreground outward. Begin at the bottom edge with one shallow puddle holding a broken rectangle of the store's ceiling light, then the wet step with a drain channel and a floating cigarette end, then the near shelving band with its price rail, then the middle band where a row of chilled bottles glows from behind, then the far interior where the light falls off into a dark stockroom doorway. The sequence must read as depth through a shop, not as a flat lit box.

Leave one deliberate absence. One shelf slot in the middle band sits empty, its price label still clipped in place, showing a clean rectangle of bare backing board. Keep it about the width of two packages and place it just left of Miku's shoulder, so the eye finds the gap before it finds the goods.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the wet step, the drain, the umbrella tip and its drip line. Middle ground: Miku in the doorway and the first two shelving bands. Background: the rear of the shop, a closed stockroom door, and beyond the glass the opposite side of the street with one shuttered shopfront and a leaning utility pole. Keep all three separated by value, not by blur.

Light the scene entirely from the store plus one street lamp. The ceiling tubes are the key: cold white, flat, running parallel to the glass, throwing an even wash across the shelves and a hard falloff at the doorway threshold. The street lamp is sodium amber, positioned high and off-frame left, laying a low warm band across the wet asphalt that never reaches the shop floor. Let the two colour temperatures meet exactly at the door frame and not blend.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the interior light. The nearer tail falls in front of the shelving in a single clean aqua mass, catching a cold highlight along its outer edge; the farther tail passes behind the door frame and darkens into the stockroom shadow. Let two strands of the near tail hang past the door edge into the rain, where they catch the amber lamp and read slightly warmer than the rest of her hair.

Dress Miku in an original late-shift costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not a uniform copy. A cropped off-white work jacket with a wide flat collar and two patch pockets, worn open over a dark ribbed top; a short pleated skirt in charcoal with a thin aqua hem line; knee socks; low canvas shoes wet at the toe. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one off-white garment, and keep the silhouette clean enough to read at thumbnail size.

Use a cold-on-warm palette with strict area control. Approximately forty-two percent of the image is cold white and pale grey interior light, twenty-four percent is near-black asphalt and shadow, fourteen percent is the pale cream of shelving and tile, ten percent is sodium amber in the street reflection, six percent is Miku's aqua hair and hem, and four percent is small red and green packaging accents. Keep the amber strictly outside the glass.

Drive the printed graphic language from the shop itself rather than from decoration. Let one large cyan ink bloom spread across the lower left of the glass where condensation has gathered, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular pale panel behind the shelving as a graphic mask, and let one vertical strip of packaging colour run from the middle band to the ceiling, aligned to the shelving uprights. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “RAIN MART” once, in white vinyl lettering applied to the inside of the glass at the upper left of the window, slightly peeling at the final corner, sized so it spans about a fifth of the window width. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “OPEN 24H” sit on a small illuminated panel beside the door, dimmed. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the rain. The glass holds fine droplets in the upper half and larger running beads near the bottom, with one long streak where a bead has travelled; the aluminium frame traps water in its lower channel; the step is dark where it is wet and pale where it has dried; the puddle holds a skin of oil at its edge; the asphalt shows tyre tracks pressed into the film. Keep the wetness physical and gradual, never a uniform glitter.

Build a second composition through reflection. The wet asphalt carries the store's lit window as one long vertical smear broken by the kerb line, doubling the shelving bands into soft horizontal bars, and carrying Miku's silhouette as a dark shape with one aqua edge. Let the reflection extend further left than the window itself, so the street becomes the larger half of the picture in reflected form.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A stainless door handle worn bright where hands have gripped it, one small brass bell above the door on a coiled spring, a folded cardboard carton stacked beside the drain, and a thin rubber mat inside the threshold with its ribs flattened. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a shop would actually have it.

Illuminate with two sources only: the ceiling tubes inside, cold and even, and the sodium lamp outside, warm and low. Let the tubes produce one clean reflection on the vinyl floor and a soft top light on Miku's hair and shoulders. Let the lamp produce a thin rim along the wet umbrella and the outer edge of her skirt where she crosses the threshold. Keep the space between them dark.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: puddle, drain, wet step, umbrella tip. Second: Miku's near leg and the door frame. Third: the first shelving band and its packages. Fourth: the refrigerated band with its glow and the empty slot. Fifth: the stockroom doorway and the reflected street. Separate them by value steps of roughly ten percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every frame edge, restrained risograph grain in the shadows, crisp flat fills in the lit areas, and fine scratch marks on the metal only where hands would touch. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except water.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no background person, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no neon signage in Japanese or any other script, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no volumetric god rays, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like the last hour of a shift in a city that has already gone quiet: cold light spilling onto wet asphalt, shelves holding more product than customers, one umbrella dripping onto the step, and a girl standing in the doorway deciding whether to leave.

seeds.title: RAIN PLATFORM
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “RAIN PLATFORM”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing alone on an empty railway platform under a corrugated rain canopy at night. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands, hair ornaments and long twin-tail identity immediately readable through the rain.

Use a one-point perspective camera placed on the platform centre line at shoulder height, with a normal lens, so the canopy ribs and the platform edge converge cleanly toward a vanishing point just left of centre. Place Miku in the left third, full body visible from shoes to hair ornaments, occupying approximately twenty-eight percent of the image. She stands with her weight on the left leg, right heel lifted slightly, shoulders squared to the camera but head turned a little toward the tracks so both eyes read in three-quarter view.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Her right hand holds a transparent umbrella tilted back over her shoulder so the canopy is caught between her fingers and the ribs, and her left hand is closed loosely around the strap of a small bag at her hip. Rain runs off the umbrella's edge in one continuous broken line behind her. Keep the pose still and the hands clear of her face; add no second action and nothing in the other hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the rain canopy itself, a long corrugated steel roof carried on eleven riveted iron ribs that fill approximately seventy percent of the canvas, its near end cropped by the top frame edge and its far end shrinking to a dark slot at the vanishing point. Beneath it, the platform edge runs a single hard white line into the distance. Beyond the edge, the tracks and the far embankment dissolve into rain.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The canopy underside is galvanised steel with condensation beading and long rust stains running along the rivet lines; the ribs are painted iron with chipped edges showing black beneath; the platform is wet concrete with a scored anti-slip strip and shallow standing water; the yellow safety line is worn paint with grit pressed into it; the umbrella is clear vinyl with a steel shaft; the rain itself is bright threads against dark. Each material behaves differently — steel beads and streaks, paint chips and powders, concrete darkens and reflects, vinyl transmits and scatters, water gathers in the low side of every slab.

Build a stepped sequence along the platform. Begin in the near foreground with a bench whose paint has blistered and peeled into a pale map. Move along the platform through a vending machine glowing softly, then a hanging sign whose face is half fogged, then a column with a faded poster, then the far platform lamp reduced to a single bright point. End at the vanishing point where the canopy and platform edge close together and everything becomes a dark slot. The sequence must read as distance, not as a row of props.

Leave one deliberate absence. One bay of the canopy is missing a light fixture: only the bracket and a short length of cut cable remain, and the floor beneath it is the darkest patch on the platform. Keep that dark bay as the quiet centre of the composition and place nothing inside it.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the wet platform edge, a puddle breaking the yellow line, and the near bench leg. Middle ground: Miku, her umbrella and the rain falling around her. Background: the receding ribs, the vending machine glow, the sign, the far lamp and the dark slot of the vanishing point.

Light the scene with three practical sources only. A cold blue-white strip light runs along the canopy underside in broken segments; a warm vending machine throws a soft rectangle across the wet concrete; and one distant platform lamp gives a small halo lost in rain. Let the strip light rim the ribs and glaze the puddles, let the vending glow warm her right side, and keep everything beyond twenty metres falling into wet blue darkness. No glow bloom, no lens flare.

Weave Miku’s extremely long twin tails through the rain. The nearer twin tail hangs in front of her shoulder, collects a few bright droplets along its length, and is cropped by her bag strap; the farther twin tail swings behind her and catches the strip light as a broken aqua line. Keep the hair dense and readable at her head, allowing droplets to sit on the surface rather than dissolving it.

Dress Miku in an original platform-night costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language. seeds.title: RESONANCE CATHEDRAL
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 premium science-fiction game key visual titled “RESONANCE CATHEDRAL”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character inside an infinite pure-white resonance cathedral. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, a slim virtual-singer silhouette, and her original grey-and-teal costume structure. Position Hatsune Miku in the right third of the canvas, standing on a narrow floating white plinth, shown from the boots to the top of her head and occupying approximately thirty-two percent of the canvas height. Her body turns three-quarters toward the left. Both arms extend forward and slightly downward with the palms open and lifted, as though she is conducting a bloom that is already larger than herself. Her left hand sits higher than her right, and the gap between her palms forms the exact center of the composition. Keep her face, aqua eyes, individual fingers, and that two-handed conducting gesture the sharpest and most legible detail of the entire image.

Place the dominant object in the center-left: one colossal glass crown flower opening upward, nearly half the canvas wide and cropped slightly by the left and lower edges. Three petals are fully polished glass with thick rounded edges, internal bubbles, layered reflections, local magnification, and sharp caustic bands. Three are frosted translucent ceramic-glass with pale cyan veins running through the interior. Three remain silver wireframe structures with visible radial ribs. The final two are breaking apart into cobalt rectangular fragments and hovering cubic dust. The flower's hollow center holds a single black glass sphere wrapped in a thin ring of warm pale gold light, the smallest and most saturated point in the whole image.

Surround the flower with two enormous mechanical wings that sweep downward and leftward from Miku's back, wrapping the bloom like a protective shell instead of spreading like wings. The upper wing climbs from her shoulder blades toward the upper-left corner, built from polished white ceramic feather blades, cobalt edge panels, black hinge joints, and thin silver hydraulic rails. Build a colossal circular HUD behind the flower and slightly behind Miku, tilted into a steep ellipse that reads as a standing instrument seen from below. Keep the ring's interior mostly empty white so the flower and Miku's silhouette both sit inside clean negative space rather than inside interface clutter. The pale-gold arc should end precisely beneath the black sphere at the flower's core.

Arrange six repeated diagnostic portraits of the same Hatsune Miku inside the left segment of the ring, hanging like narrow film strips between cobalt support bars. Each strip is a different stage of the same scan: the first holds one aqua eye and bangs in clean cobalt line art; the second holds a three-quarter face in pale blue halftone; the third holds a profile cut by horizontal scan bands; the fourth holds only a hair ornament and an ear; the fifth is almost entirely white knockout with a faint cyan contour; the sixth dissolves into square pixels at its lower edge. Extend the environment as a pure-white abstract cathedral without walls, corners, sky, landscape, or realistic architecture. Add only a few large geometric anchors: a tall cobalt rectangle entering from the far-left edge behind the wing, a thin black horizontal slab floating beneath the flower, two frosted translucent panels near the upper center, a low white step system descending from her plinth, and a single narrow silver rail crossing the entire width behind the HUD. Keep at least thirty-five percent clean white negative space, concentrated across the upper-right quadrant and the far-right margin beside her.

Use a strict white, cobalt, aqua, graphite, and pale-gold visual system. Approximately sixty-four percent of the image is pure white, pearl white, and pale silver; eighteen percent is cobalt blue and deep ultramarine; eleven percent is aqua and icy cyan; six percent is graphite and black; no more than one percent is warm pale gold. Reserve the gold exclusively for the ring inside the flower core, one HUD progress arc, and a single fastener on her sleeve. Hold every large field flat and cool, and let the gold function as a needle of warmth inside an otherwise white and blue image.

Develop the blue-white interface as architecture rather than decoration. Use large cobalt arcs and rectangles as primary anchors, black rails and silver construction lines as secondary structure, and tiny cyan dots, brackets, crosshair marks, waveform fragments, and grid segments as tertiary detail. Align every interface mark with the circular HUD, the wing hinges, the plinth, or the floor-step grid. Drive a controlled glitch system vertically down the left edge rather than horizontally across the middle. Vertical scan columns, rectangular cobalt masks, white erased blocks, cyan channel offsets, pixel clusters, halftone erosion, photocopy grain, and narrow black slit bars descend from the upper-left border, climb the outer wing, pass through the film-strip portraits, and stop before reaching the flower's gold core. Concentrate the strongest disruption at the left and bottom borders, then let it thin out toward the center. Keep her face, hands, and the conducting gesture on a completely clean vertical band.

Let her extremely long twin tails carry two distinct paths through the composition. The upper tail rises behind her head, crosses one gap in the HUD ring, and returns as a pale aqua glass ribbon drifting into the upper-right white space. The lower tail sweeps forward beneath her arms, wraps once around the crown flower's outer petal, is magnified and doubled inside that petal, then reappears as three separated cyan contours descending toward the lower center. Keep the hair solid and clearly recognizable for the first two thirds of its length, and let only the final sections turn translucent or break into fragments.

Dress her in a white-and-graphite resonance attendant suit derived from her familiar virtual-singer design language: a fitted sleeveless bodice with aqua luminous seams, an asymmetrical white skirt built from layered ceramic plates and translucent cyan fabric, detached sleeves with fine black calibration lines, dark thigh-high elements with cobalt edge panels, narrow silver connectors at the shoulder blades, and three small fasteners, one of them pale gold. Apply multiple graphic mask layers with strict protection zones. Place one broad translucent cyan mask across the lower skirt and plinth, one white knockout bar through the fourth portrait strip, and several cobalt rectangles along the vertical glitch columns at the left edge. Place “RESONANCE 09 / BLOOM” in small condensed type beneath the HUD's outer ring on the right side of the flower. Place one outlined “39” emblem inside a white square near the lowest step. Keep every other interface mark non-linguistic: bars, dots, brackets, waveforms, calibration ticks, and abstract grid fragments only.

Light the scene with broad, nearly shadowless white architectural illumination from above, a concentrated aqua glow rising from inside the crown flower, and a narrow cool rim along her bangs, shoulders, wing joints, and upper twin tail. Let the polished petals cast cyan caustics across her open palms, sleeve edges, and the floating plinth. Allow the black sphere to absorb nearby light while its gold ring stays razor sharp. Render the image as a refined high-end two-dimensional anime key visual combining crisp character linework, pure-white editorial negative space, cobalt screen-print planes, polished glass rendering, precise interface geometry, selective photobashing, halftone portrait fragments, subtle paper grain, clean vector edges, fine silver technical lines, and restrained dry-brush erosion. Give the finest linework to her face and hands, the richest optical detail to the polished petals and black core, the largest graphic rhythm to the HUD rings and downward wing sweep, and the quietest texture to the white background.

The final image should feel like a quiet coronation of glass: Hatsune Miku conducts an enormous crown flower with open palms while her mechanical wings fold downward around it, a tilted circular instrument measures the bloom, six narrow portrait strips record her own scan in sequence, and a vertical glitch tide descends along the far-left edge without touching her. Pure-white abstract technology cathedral, monumental tilted circular HUD, downward-sweeping asymmetric mechanical wings, colossal glass crown flower with a black gold-ringed core, repeated Miku diagnostic film strips, blue-white interface architecture, disciplined vertical glitch collage, generous negative space, tight color hierarchy, sophisticated anime presentation, premium Krea 2 game key visual, extremely polished detail, and a completely original spatial composition.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Hatsune Miku, no second figure, no second virtual singer, no realistic human interpretation, no reflection that reads as a second person, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the title named above, no watermark, no signature, no frame, no border.

seeds.title: REVERSE GRIP
seeds.raw:

Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes and twin-tail identity readable in the low light.

The weapon is one solid mass of orange amber glass: translucent, warm orange-brown, lit from within, and it throws orange light onto everything around it.

Use a camera at her eye height on a short lens, set close and slightly to her left so her raised right forearm is nearest the viewer and the dagger's blade points down past her hip. Place Miku at approximately forty-six percent of the canvas width, occupying about seventy-two percent of the frame height from her waist to the top of her head. Let the dagger's point sit just inside the frame's lower right and its pommel beside her elbow.

Give Miku exactly one core action: holding the blade back. Her right elbow is bent tight against her ribs with the forearm angled across her body, the dagger gripped so the blade runs back along the underside of her forearm with the point past her wrist, and her left hand is closed at her sternum. Keep her chin down, her gaze level at the viewer, and put nothing in her left hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the forearm and dagger: a short single-edged dagger with a blade four inches long, a plain bolster and a cord-wrapped handle, held point-down along the inside of her forearm so the edge faces outward. Keep the weapon plain — no guard spikes, no jewelled pommel, no engraving. Let the blade catch the only strong light in the frame and let her forearm read as the shape that hides it.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. the blade is one short piece of amber, honey-dark and translucent so the whole mass reads as one saturated stone, its interior holding a single long fracture and three small voids, its edge ground sharp, and it stays almost invisible until the lamp crosses it; the bolster is plain iron; the handle is black cord over wood; her forearm is bare skin with one old flat scar; her sleeve is matte dark wool, pushed to the elbow; the wall behind is damp plaster with a wide damp band at shoulder height. Each behaves differently — blued steel holds almost nothing except at its bevel, iron returns one small dull point, cord reads as a fine diagonal grain, skin holds a soft subsurface glow and one tight specular at the wrist bone, wool absorbs, damp plaster reads as a darker slick field.

Build a stepped sequence across the frame. Begin at the lower right with the dagger's point, then her wrist and gripped hand, then her raised forearm crossing her chest, then her shoulder and collar, then her face and level gaze, then the damp wall above her head. The sequence must read as a weapon held out of sight rather than displayed.

Leave one deliberate absence. Her left hand is empty and closed against her chest, and there is no sheath, no second blade, no holster anywhere on her. Keep her left forearm and the space below it entirely bare, so the missing second weapon becomes the calmest area of the frame.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the dagger's point and her wrist. Middle ground: her forearm, hand and chest. Background: her shoulder, jaw, eyes and the damp wall. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from a single low lamp at the frame's right, below her shoulder. The lamp is the key: a warm narrow light that catches the blade's bevel as one hard line, rims her forearm and the edge of her jaw, and leaves the left side of her face almost black. Let the damp wall show one broad soft reflection of that lamp and let everything outside it fall to near black. Never introduce a fill. Let the crystal pass the light rather than return it: one thin saturated amber line where the mass is thickest, and one hard-edged amber caustic patch thrown onto the damp plaster beside it.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails fall forward over her raised arm. The nearer tail drops across her forearm and hangs past her wrist, half hiding the blade's handle; the farther one falls behind her shoulder into the dark. Let the lamp catch one narrow streak down the nearer tail and let its tip curl at the frame's lower edge.

Dress Miku in a close-fitting dark layer over her canonical palette, not armour. A dark teal high-collar top with the right sleeve pushed to the elbow, a black chest strap, and a narrow belt at the frame's bottom edge. Keep the palette close to teal-and-black with one pale inner collar as the only light garment, and keep the silhouette narrow enough that her forearm dominates.

Use a warm-on-black palette with strict area control. Approximately forty-four percent of the image is near-black shadow, twenty percent is damp plaster, fourteen percent is her clothing, eight percent is her forearm and hand, six percent is her aqua hair, four percent is her face, three percent is the blade and bolster, and one percent is the pale inner collar. Keep the cold notes only in her hair and the crystal. The amber's honey-dark tone is the one saturated colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the wall's own stain rather than from decoration. Let one large deep-teal ink bloom spread across the wall's upper left, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular black panel across the wall's lower band as a graphic mask at her chest height, and let one vertical strip of rust-red run down the frame's right edge from lamp to bottom. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “REVERSE GRIP” once, in white paint stencilled on the damp plaster behind her head, the strokes running slightly where the wall is wet, sized so it spans about three quarters of the wall's visible width and reads clearly at thumbnail size. Put no lettering on the blade, her skin or her clothing, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The blade's bluing is rubbed pale along its spine; the bolster is dented where it has been struck; the cord handle is polished and flattened at the grip point; her forearm carries one flat old scar and a fresh red line where the pommel presses; her sleeve is creased hard at the elbow; the plaster's damp band has a tide mark with a fringe of bloom. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the damp plaster. The wall carries her shoulder and jaw as a soft dark shape, the lamp's reflection as one broad vertical smear, and the blade's bevel as a single bright horizontal tick. Never let the wall mirror her face and never produce a second blade.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One old scar across her forearm, a single bright chip on the bolster's edge, one drop of water tracking down the plaster beside her head, and a fine cord end fraying at the handle's end. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where use would put it.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the dagger's point and her wrist. Second: her gripped hand and raised forearm. Third: her chest, collar and left hand. Fourth: her jaw, mouth and eyes. Fifth: the damp wall and the dark above her. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every cord wrap and plaster seam, restrained risograph grain in the darkness, crisp flat fills in the lit plaster, and one clean gradient only along the blade's bevel. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except that bevel and her eye.

No second character, no duplicate Miku, no crowd, no banners, no flags, no birds, no wings, no halo, no scabbard, no second dagger, no additional weapon, no glowing crystal, no neon glow, no self-lit weapon, no rainbow dispersion, no stained glass, no plastic, no glass bottle, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no magical effects, no readable text beyond the string named above, no blood, no wounds, no armour plates, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no weapon in her left hand, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like a knife kept out of sight: a blade laid back along a forearm, one hand closed at the chest, and a face that has already decided something the hands are not showing.

seeds.title: RIVER BEND
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “RIVER BEND”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing on a shingle bar in the middle of a wide river, with a concrete road bridge crossing behind her. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the pale water.

Use a camera at hip height on a normal lens, set low on the shingle and square to the river so the water runs level across the frame and the bridge spans the upper third. Place Miku at approximately thirty-four percent of the canvas width, full body visible from boots to hair ornaments, occupying about thirty-four percent of the frame height.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Her right hand holds a long stick with a net bag at hip height, its hoop dipping into the shallows, and her left hand shades her eyes at brow height. Her head is turned toward the bridge, both eyes visible. Keep the pose steady and put nothing else in her hands.

Construct the dominant visual object as the bridge's near pier: a broad rectangular concrete pier rising from the water about thirty metres upstream, weathered to a pale grey, with a rusted steel bearing at its top and a waterline stain at its base. Let the pier occupy approximately twenty-two percent of the canvas area, and let its flat face be the brightest large surface in the frame.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The concrete is pale grey with form-board lines and dark streaking below the deck joints; the deck above is a plain parapet of the same concrete; the river is green-grey and moving, with a fine chop in the middle and flat water in the lee of the shingle; the shingle is flat grey stones, wet at the edge; the far bank is a dark treeline. Each behaves differently — concrete holds a flat pale value with fine form lines, moving water breaks light into short horizontal dashes, still water returns a soft inverted image, wet shingle holds a thin sheen.

Build a stepped sequence from the shingle outward. Begin at the bottom edge with wet shingle and one driftwood stick, then the shallows with their clear bed, then Miku's boots and her net, then the moving middle water, then the pier's waterline stain, then the parapet and the far treeline. The sequence must read as standing in a current, not as a riverside view.

Leave one deliberate absence. The pier's waterline stain stops short on one face: the dark band runs the full width of the upstream face but ends abruptly about a hand's width from the downstream corner, leaving a clean pale strip where the water has never reached. Keep the strip at the height of Miku's knee so the eye finds the one clean edge on an otherwise stained pier.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: wet shingle, driftwood, shallows. Middle ground: Miku, her net, the moving water. Background: the pier, the parapet, the far treeline. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from an overcast sky. The sky is the key: a flat pale grey light from above, even and directionless, laying a soft wash on the concrete and a dull skin on the water. Add one faint warm break in the cloud at the upper left, giving the parapet's top edge a thin warm line and nothing else. Keep every shadow open and pale.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the river light. The nearer tail falls forward over the shingle in one clean aqua mass, the only saturated colour in the frame; the farther tail drops behind her and is doubled faintly in the still water at the shingle's lee. Let two strands lift slightly in the current's wind.

Dress Miku in an original river-bend costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not fishing gear. A thin dark rain jacket worn open over a pale top, dark shorts, and rubber wading boots laced high. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment.

Use a grey-green palette with one saturated accent and strict area control. Approximately thirty-six percent of the image is moving green-grey water, twenty-two percent is overcast sky, eighteen percent is pale concrete, twelve percent is grey shingle, eight percent is the dark far treeline, and four percent is Miku's dark jacket and aqua hair.

Drive the printed graphic language from the water's own motion rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the lower right of the moving water, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular pale panel behind the pier as a graphic mask at the height of its bearing, and let one vertical strip of dark green run from the parapet to the shingle, aligned to the pier's edge.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “RIVER BEND” once, large, in dark grey paint applied across the broad flat face of the concrete pier, spanning about two thirds of the pier's visible width, in heavy square capitals that read clearly at thumbnail size against the pale concrete. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “CH 320” sit on a small steel plate bolted to the parapet above her. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the water. The concrete is streaked dark below every deck joint and stained at the waterline; the parapet's top is pale and clean; the shingle is darker at the water's edge and dry above; the driftwood is bleached and smooth; the far treeline is a flat dark mass with no detail. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the water. The lee water carries the pier inverted as a pale soft rectangle, the parapet as a thin line, and Miku's silhouette as a dark shape with one aqua edge. The moving water carries nothing but short horizontal dashes of sky.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One bleached driftwood branch, a rusted steel reinforcing bar exposed at the pier's base, a coil of green line at her feet, and a small stone cairn on the shingle. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a river bar would actually have it.

Illuminate with the overcast sky as the only key, even and pale, plus the water's dull bounce as a weak fill. Let the sky produce a flat even wash on the concrete and a dull skin on the water. Let the bounce lift the underside of her jaw and her net. Keep the far treeline at its darkest and give the frame no directional shadow beyond her own.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: shingle, driftwood, shallows. Second: Miku, her net, her boots. Third: the moving middle water. Fourth: the pier and its stain. Fifth: the parapet, the treeline and the sky. Separate them by value steps of roughly nine percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every form-board line and shingle edge, restrained risograph grain in the water, crisp flat fills in the concrete and sky, and fine streaking only below deck joints.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no angler on the far bank, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no boats, no birds, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like standing in the middle of a current: pale concrete holding one clean strip against a stained face, water running short dashes of sky, and a girl with a net in the shallows looking up at a bridge she will not climb.

Both hands hold a length of laundry line at shoulder height, pulled taut between her right fist and a bracket bolted to the tank leg, with three small garments already pegged to it, lifting slightly in the wind. Let the tank occupy approximately forty-five percent of the canvas area in the upper left, cut by the top edge, and let its legs cross the skyline behind Miku without touching her head.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The tank shell is riveted steel painted a faded municipal green, rusting in vertical streaks below every rivet line; the legs are heavier section steel with bolted feet on timber pads; the roof deck is bitumen felt with gravel pressed into it, patched in three places; the parapet is cast concrete with a chipped coping; the laundry line is plastic-coated wire with the coating cracked at every bend; the far towers are dark glass and steel with scattered lit windows. Each behaves differently — painted steel holds a dull matte value, rust bleeds downward, bitumen swallows light, concrete holds a cold sheen, glass repeats a hundred small points.

Build a stepped sequence from the deck upward. Begin at the bottom edge with the gravel and one shallow puddle holding a slice of tower light, then the parapet coping with a rusted anchor eye, then Miku and the laundry line, then the tank legs and their bolted feet, then the tank body with its ladder and vent, then the skyline behind. The sequence must read as a climb from ground to structure, not as a flat backdrop.

One of the tank's four legs has no foot plate: the bolted flange ends in air about a hand's width above the felt, with clean bolt holes and a pale unpainted rectangle on the deck where the pad used to sit. Keep the gap clearly visible between the leg and the deck so the structure appears to stand on three points.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: gravel, puddle, parapet coping, one dropped clothes peg. Middle ground: Miku, the laundry line, the tank legs, the ladder's lower rungs. Background: the tank body and the tower lights beyond the parapet. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

The towers are the key: a cool blue-green wash from the right, broken into many small sources, laying a low rim along Miku's hair and shoulder and a pale edge on the tank's right flank. Add one warm window behind her at parapet height, throwing a small amber patch across the deck gravel and the near leg. Keep the sky itself almost black and give it no glow.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the rooftop wind. The nearer tail lifts across the laundry line, its aqua reading bright against the dark tank; the farther tail falls behind the parapet and is cut off by the coping. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment, and keep the silhouette simple enough to read at thumbnail size.

Use a blue-on-black palette with one warm accent and strict area control. Approximately fifty percent of the image is deep navy and near-black night, eighteen percent is faded municipal green tank, twelve percent is dark bitumen and gravel, eight percent is the pale blue-green city rim, five percent is Miku's aqua hair, four percent is the small amber window patch, and three percent is pale concrete coping. Drive the printed graphic language from the rooftop's own hardware rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the lower left of the deck where the puddle sits, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular pale panel behind the tank legs as a graphic mask at the height of the parapet, and let one vertical strip of rust orange run from the tank lid to the deck, aligned to a rivet line. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “ROOF TANK” once, in white stencil letters painted on the tank shell's near face, the lower strokes flaking, sized so it spans about a third of the tank's visible width. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “LOT 7” sit on a small enamel plate bolted to the parapet at the left. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the city air. The tank shows vertical rust streaks that begin at rivets and end in a soft stain; the deck felt is dark where water pools and pale where it has dried around the gravel; the coping is stained black along its lower face; the laundry line's coating is cracked at every bend; the garments hold one damp crease each. Keep the wear physical and directional, never a uniform grime.

Build a second composition through reflection. The deck puddle carries the tank's lit right flank as one long vertical smear, the amber window as a small round point, and Miku's silhouette as a dark shape with a single aqua edge. Let the puddle stop dead at the gravel and never reach the parapet.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A brass padlock hanging open on the ladder's lowest rung, one steel access hatch with a worn handle, a coiled rope tied off at the parapet anchor, and a small thermometer strapped to a tank leg. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a rooftop would actually have it.

Illuminate with the city as the only key, cool and broken, plus the single amber window as a small secondary. Let the city produce a thin rim along every right-facing edge — Miku's shoulder, the tank's flank, the coping — and a dim wash across the deck. Let the amber produce one small patch on the gravel and a warm edge on the near leg. Keep the sky free of any glow and the tank's left side at near-black.

Fourth: the tank body with its stencil and streaks. Fifth: the tower lights and the black sky. Separate them by value steps of roughly ten percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every rivet and ladder rung, restrained risograph grain in the night fields, crisp flat fills in the lit areas, and fine rust flakes only where water would run. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the puddle.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no rooftop couple, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no neon signage in any script, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no birds, no satellites, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like a rooftop that belongs to the building rather than to the city: a tank standing on three feet, a line of washing lifting in the wind, and a girl holding it taut while the towers burn cold behind her.

seeds.title: SALT TIDE ARCHIVE

Keep the upper-left 30% of the frame as empty white air, broken only by a faint salt haze and the tip of one distant architectural block at the far right, well behind the carousel.

Hold the palette to percentages: pearl white 62%, cobalt and ultramarine 14%, aqua and cyan 10%, graphite and matte black 6%, silver 6%, coral 1%, with the coral reserved for the collar bead and one contact highlight.

Drive all graphic color by the character palette: one cobalt ink bloom spreading behind the carousel at mid height, two hard-edged aqua rectangles lying flat on the salt floor, one translucent aqua stain bleeding across a glass bay, a halftone dot gradient that thickens toward the fourth bay, a white knockout where the key light strikes the brass ring, and a sparse field of coral microdots around the lifted vial.

Etch the interface into the structure itself: engraved tick marks and bracket glyphs on the brass ring, a bar-graph band on the front rail, and small numbered stamps on each cradle — no floating HUD, no detached panels.

Escalate glitch only from the far-right edge inward: misregistration, halftone slippage and white knockout grow across the last three bays and stop before the character's side; the center of the frame stays optically clean.

Place luxury micro-ornament only at joints: a silver chain looping from the ring to the nearest bracket, a champagne-gold filigree seam on one enamel panel, ceramic beads at the cradle pins, three suspended droplets under the lifted vial, and one vellum tag tied to the front rail.

IX — 09:41" bottom left at 0.9% height in the same face; no other readable text anywhere.

seeds.title: EMPTY CLASS
seeds.raw:

Use a camera at her seated eye level on a normal lens, set in the aisle and square to the window wall, so five rows of desks run in perspective toward the far wall and the window's light falls across them in long bands. Place Miku at approximately thirty-two percent of the canvas width, seated on the desk's near corner with her full figure visible from shoes to hair ornaments, occupying about fifty-five percent of the frame height. Let the desk rows fill the middle and right of the frame.

Give Miku exactly one core action. She sits on the desk's front edge with her weight on one hip, both feet hanging clear of the floor, her right hand flat on the desk beside her and her left hand resting on her own knee. Her shoulders stay level, her chin lifts a little, and her eyes come to the lens over the room's empty rows.

Construct the dominant visual object as the desk rows themselves: five rows of pale steel-framed desks with timber tops, each chair pushed in at a slightly different angle, all of them empty, with the window's light lying across them as long diagonal bands. Let the rows occupy the middle half of the frame and let the far wall carry a blackboard and a notice board.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The desk tops are varnished timber, dulled in the centre where elbows rest; the steel frames are pale grey with chipped paint at the feet; the chairs are the same steel with bent plywood seats; the floor is worn timber strip, pale along the aisle; the blackboard is a flat dark green with a grey ghost of erased chalk; the windows are plain sashes with thin curtains. Each behaves differently — varnish holds a low sheen, chipped steel shows bright metal, plywood goes matte, worn floor scatters light, chalkboard absorbs almost everything.

Build a stepped sequence from the near desk to the far wall. Begin with Miku's desk and her hand on it, then her shoes hanging free and the chair beside her, then the second and third rows running away, then the aisle's worn line, then the blackboard and its erased ghost, then the window's bands and the pale sky outside. The sequence must read as a room emptied ten minutes ago, not as a classroom during a lesson.

Leave one deliberate absence. Every desk in the frame is empty and every chair is pushed in: no bags on the floor, no books left open, no one at the blackboard. The only objects besides the furniture are a single chalk stub in the blackboard's tray and one chair pulled out slightly further than the rest.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: her desk, her hand, the chair beside it. Middle ground: the rows of desks and the aisle. Background: the blackboard, the notice board, the window wall and the pale sky. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the window wall on the right. The windows are the key: long afternoon bands of warm light falling diagonally across the desks and the floor, leaving the aisles between them in cool shade. Add one weak cool fill from the corridor door behind the camera so her shaded side keeps detail. Keep the far corner and the ceiling at near-black.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the light. Both tails fall behind her over the desk's edge, one clean aqua mass with two warm bands of sun laid across it and deep shade between them, the ends hanging into the shadow of the desk row behind. Let one strand fall forward over her near shoulder and cross the light.

Dress Miku in an original after-school costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not a school uniform.
