Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment, and keep the silhouette simple enough to read at thumbnail size.

Use a warm-wood-and-shade palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty percent of the image is the shaded classroom and its ceiling, twenty-four percent is the sunlit desk rows and floor, eighteen percent is her dark jacket and skirt, twelve percent is the blackboard wall, eight percent is her aqua hair, five percent is the window's pale sky, and three percent is the bright chalk tray.

Drive the printed graphic language from the classroom's own boards rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the near floor at the lower left, printed flat and matte, its edge following a floorboard joint. Add a rectangular pale panel on the blackboard's lower corner as a graphic mask at the height of her knee, and let one vertical strip of deep oxide red run down the far wall aligned to a window edge. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “EMPTY CLASS” once, large, in pale chalk white across the flat face of the notice board on the far wall, spanning about half the board's width, in heavy condensed capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “ROOM 3” sit on a small enamel plate screwed to the corridor door's frame at the frame's left edge. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the term. The desk tops are dulled in one oval per desk where elbows and books have rested; the steel frames are chipped at the feet and bright where shoes have rubbed them; the floor is worn pale along the aisle and darker under the desks; the blackboard holds a grey ghost and one clean swipe; the curtains are faded along their folds. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the varnished desk tops. Each top carries the window's bands as two bright strips and the far chairs as small dark shapes, repeated down the rows and diminishing with distance. Let the reflection be shallower than the blackboard wall and stop at each desk's back edge.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One chalk stub in the tray; a chair pulled out a hand's width further than the rest; a clock above the blackboard with its hands at ten past four; a rolled map on a shelf bracket; a pencil on the floor under the third desk. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a classroom would actually have it.

Let the bands lay warm light across her arm, the varnished tops and the aisle's edge, let the fill keep her shadow side just readable, and keep the ceiling and the far corner at absolute black so the room reads as a box of light and dust.

seeds.title: COURT
seeds.raw:

Approximately thirty-four percent of the image is the asphalt and its paint, twenty-two percent is the pale dusk sky beyond the fence, sixteen percent is the fence and its shadow, twelve percent is her dark jacket and hair, eight percent is the concrete kerb, five percent is the hoop's pole and backboard, and three percent is the ball's scuffed side.

Place Miku at approximately forty percent of the canvas width, full figure visible from shoes to hair ornaments, occupying about forty-six percent of the frame height, small against the hangar of the hall.

Approximately thirty percent of the image is the tiered stand and its shade, twenty-six percent is the empty pale-green water, eighteen percent is the pale far wall and its panels, ten percent is the dark roof grid, eight percent is her dark clothing, five percent is her aqua hair, and three percent is the painted aisle numbers.

Set the exact readable word “POOL STAND” once, large, in pale grey paint stencilled across the flat concrete face of the second tier's riser at her right, spanning about half the riser's visible length, in heavy condensed capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size. The nosings are polished in a continuous band and one corner is chipped; the risers are stained darker at their feet; the steel frame is chipped to bare metal at every joint; the aisle numbers are worn thin at their edges; the water's surface holds one faint tideline on the tiled wall; the handrail is bright where hands have slid; her shoes are scuffed at the toe. Let the clerestory wash the water and the nosings, let the bounce lift her jaw and forearms, and keep the roof grid and the stand's far end at absolute black so the tiers read as four pale lines stepping down to bright water.

seeds.title: STAIRS
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “STAIRS”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing on the half-landing of a school stairwell, one hand on the rail, looking up the next flight. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the pale stairwell.

Use a camera at her eye level on a normal lens, set on the flight below and square to the landing, so the next flight climbs out of the top of the frame, the rail cuts a diagonal across the middle, and a tall window throws light down the well. Place Miku at approximately forty-eight percent of the canvas width, full figure visible from her shoes to her hair ornaments, occupying about sixty percent of the frame height, standing on the landing's outer corner.

Give Miku exactly one core action. She stands with her weight on her back foot and her right hand closed around the steel rail at hip height, her left arm hanging at her side, her chin lifted to look up the next flight. Her eyes come back down to the lens, and nothing is in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the stairwell itself: two flights of bare concrete steps meeting at a half-landing, a steel rail with its vertical balusters on the outer edge, a painted dado along the wall at shoulder height, and a tall window on the landing's far wall throwing a bright wedge down the well. Let the steps occupy the lower half in perspective and let the rail lead the eye upward.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The steps are bare concrete, their nosings polished by feet and one chipped; the landing is the same concrete with a painted edge line; the rail is painted steel, chalky at its joints and bright where hands slide; the wall is painted cream, marked at shoulder height by years of bags; the window is a plain steel frame with wire glass; the floor below is speckled terrazzo. Each behaves differently — concrete scatters light and polishes at wear points, chalky paint scatters more, steel carries one long highlight, wire glass breaks the light into a faint grid, terrazzo shows small stones.

Build a stepped sequence from the bottom upward. Begin with the terrazzo floor and the first step's worn nosing, then her shoes on the landing, then her hand on the rail, then her lifted chin, then the flight climbing out of frame, then the window's bright wedge and the dado, then the dark underside of the flight above. The sequence must read as a stairwell at the end of the day, not as an architectural study.

Leave one deliberate absence. The stairwell is empty above and below her: no student on either flight, no bag left on a step, no notice on the wall, no mop and bucket on the landing. The only objects in the frame besides her are the rail, the window and one fire hose reel box set into the wall.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the terrazzo floor and the first step. Middle ground: her shoes, her hand on the rail, her body. Background: the climbing flight, the window's wedge, the dado and the dark underside above. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the landing window. The window is the key: a hard afternoon wedge falling across the landing and the lower steps, catching the rail's top tube and lighting the side of her face and shoulder, while the upper flight stays in cool shade. Add one weak fill from the terrazzo floor, which touches the underside of her chin and the hem of her skirt. Keep the well's top and the stair's underside at near-black.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the light. One tail falls forward over her shoulder into the window's wedge, one clean aqua mass lit bright along its upper curve and dark beneath; the other drops behind her onto the landing as a cooler vertical. Let the ends rest against the rail's balusters.

Dress Miku in an original end-of-day costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not a school uniform. A dark short jacket worn open over a pale shirt, a pleated mid-length skirt in deep teal, dark socks and low shoes, with a thin strap across her chest. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment, and keep the silhouette narrow so the rail's diagonal reads.

Use a concrete-and-cream palette with one bright wedge and strict area control. Approximately thirty-four percent of the image is the bare concrete and its shade, twenty-four percent is the cream wall and dado, sixteen percent is the window's bright wedge and wire glass, twelve percent is her dark jacket and skirt, eight percent is her aqua hair, four percent is the steel rail, and two percent is the painted edge line.

Drive the printed graphic language from the stairwell's own paint rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the landing's concrete at the lower left, printed flat and matte, its edge following the painted line. Add a rectangular pale panel on the wall beside the window as a graphic mask at the height of her shoulder, and let one vertical strip of deep oxide red run down the wall aligned to the window's frame. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “STAIRS” once, large, in dark grey paint applied across the flat cream wall above the dado, spanning about half the wall's visible width, in heavy condensed capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “FLOOR 3” sit on a small enamel plate screwed to the wall beside the hose reel box. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry years of feet. The steps' nosings are polished in a band and chipped at one corner; the landing's painted edge line is worn through in the middle; the rail is bright where hands slide and chalky at its joints; the wall is marked across its middle by bag straps and one patch is repainted; the wire glass holds dust in its mesh; the terrazzo is dull along the path to the stairs. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the polished nosings. Each step carries the window's wedge as one bright line and the rail as a thin dark diagonal, repeating smaller as the flight climbs, so the whole staircase reads as a series of stacked highlights. Let that be the only place in the frame where the light is broken into steps.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One fire hose reel box set into the wall with a brass hinge; a chipped nosing on the third step; a bolted repair plate on the rail's joint; one dry leaf caught in a corner of the landing; a chalk mark on the wall at the height of a shoulder. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a real school stairwell would actually have it.

Illuminate with the window as the only key and the terrazzo's bounce as the only fill. Let the wedge light the rail and the side of her face, let the bounce keep her jaw and hem readable, and keep the upper flight and the stair's underside at absolute black so the well reads as a shaft of light with a girl standing in it.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the terrazzo floor and the first step. Second: her shoes and the landing's edge. Third: her hand on the rail and her body. Fourth: the climbing flight and the dado. Fifth: the window's wedge and the dark underside above. Separate them by value steps of roughly eleven percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every step nosing and baluster, restrained risograph grain in the shaded flight, and the light wedge kept as one hard-edged shape.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no student on either flight, no bag on a step, no notice, no mop and bucket, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no graffiti, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like a stairwell that has just emptied: two flights of concrete meeting at a landing, one hard wedge of afternoon light, and a girl with her hand on the rail looking up at the next floor.

seeds.title: SCYTHE GATE
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “SCYTHE GATE”, a frame built around one colossal garnet weapon, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing in the opening of an arch formed by two colossal scythe blades leaning toward each other. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face and twin-tail outline readable against the bright field beyond the arch.

The weapon is one solid mass of garnet glass: translucent, dark crimson, lit from within, and it throws red light onto everything around it.

Use a camera at her waist height on a wide lens, set square to the arch so the two blades frame her symmetrically and the field beyond glows between them. Place Miku at approximately fifty percent of the canvas width, standing at the arch's threshold, occupying about thirty percent of the frame height. Let the two blade tips cross just above her head, close enough to read as a gate and not as a ceiling.

Give Miku exactly one core action: looking back. Her body is turned toward the field beyond, but her head and shoulders are rotated back over her left arm toward the viewer, one hand lifted to the strap of her pack. Keep her feet planted, her weight on the back leg, and put nothing in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the two scythe blades: each a curved blade four metres along its edge, mounted on a shaft as thick as a mast, leaning inward at about thirty degrees so the two edges nearly touch at the top of the frame. Keep them bare — no cloth wraps, no chains, no ornament. Let each blade rise from its own corner of the lower frame and let the gap between them be exactly her width.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. both blades and shafts are garnet, dark crimson and translucent so the whole mass reads as one saturated stone, their interiors holding long fractures that follow the curve, their edges ground but never polished, and they hold no light of their own; the shafts are tarred timber, split at their bases and bound with three iron straps each; the ground inside the arch is packed earth with a scatter of straw; the field beyond is tall pale grass under flat light; the near foreground is shadowed dirt. Each behaves differently — pitted iron breaks its highlight into speckles, the worn bevel returns one continuous bright line, tarred timber absorbs light and shows only a soft top edge, packed earth reads as a matte plane, the field beyond goes nearly white, shadowed dirt holds a fine grit.

Build a stepped sequence through the arch. Begin at the bottom edge with the shadowed dirt and one fallen straw, then Miku's boots and the packed threshold, then her body with her head turned back, then the two shafts converging, then the blade curves crossing above her, then the white field beyond. The sequence must read as a doorway made of weapons, not as two props arranged around a figure.

Leave one deliberate absence. Both scythes have lost the snath collar that should join blade to shaft: at each joint the blade sits in an empty socket, its tang visible, held only by a single bolt. Keep both sockets at the same height so the symmetry reads as damage rather than design.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: shadowed dirt and fallen straw. Middle ground: Miku, the packed threshold, the shafts' lower halves. Background: the blade curves, the crossing tips, the white field. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the field behind the arch. The field is the key: a flat bright light that blows out to near white, wraps the two blade edges in a thin bright line, and leaves the arch's inner faces in deep shade. Let Miku be rimmed on her shoulders, hair and jaw by that same bright field while her front stays in shadow, one value above the dirt. Keep the near foreground darkest and never introduce a light from the viewer's side. Let the crystal pass the light rather than return it: one thin saturated crimson line where the mass is thickest, and one hard-edged crimson caustic patch thrown onto the packed earth beside it.

Lift Miku's extremely long twin tails in the wind that comes through the arch. Both tails stream toward the field, the nearer one crossing her turned shoulder as a clean aqua mass, the farther one caught between the two shafts. Let the bright field rim each tail's edge and let a few strands blow across her face.

Dress Miku in a long travelling coat over her canonical palette, not armour. A charcoal wool coat worn open over a dark teal high-collar shirt, dark trousers tucked into wrapped boots, a wide leather strap across her chest for a pack, and one pale scarf. Keep the palette close to teal-and-black with the pale scarf as the only light garment, and keep the silhouette narrow enough to read at thumbnail size.

Use a high-contrast palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty percent of the image is the bright field, twenty-six percent is the shadowed arch interior, eighteen percent is the two blades, ten percent is the shafts, seven percent is packed earth, five percent is Miku's coat, three percent is her aqua hair, and one percent is the worn bevel's bright line. Keep every warm note out except the crystal, which is the only warm mass in the frame. The garnet's dark crimson tone is the one saturated colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the gate's own boundary markers rather than from decoration. Let one large rust-red ink bloom spread across the bright field in the upper right, printed flat and matte so it reads as a stain on the light. Add a rectangular dark panel across the dirt at the arch's base as a graphic mask, and let one vertical strip of black run down the frame's left edge from blade to ground. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “SCYTHE GATE” once, cut shallow into the inner face of the left crystal shaft and filled with white paint so the letters read as pale grooves, sized so it spans about two thirds of the shaft's visible width and reads clearly at thumbnail size.

Let every surface carry the shift. The blades are pitted in a wide band along their backs and bright only at the bevel; the sockets are worn oval where the tang has worked; the shafts are split at their bases and tarred over the splits; the packed threshold is polished by feet and holds a shallow dip; the straw is broken and grey. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the bright field. The field carries the two blades as soft dark silhouettes, their tips meeting as a single dark point, and Miku as a dark shape with a bright edge. Let the field never mirror the arch cleanly and never produce a second figure.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One brass bolt at the left socket, a single strand of straw caught in the right shaft's split, a small stone set upright in the threshold, and one fold of her scarf lifting free. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where use would put it.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: shadowed dirt and straw. Second: Miku's boots and the threshold. Third: her body and the shafts' lower halves. Fourth: the blade curves and the sockets. Fifth: the crossing tips and the white field. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every blade curve and iron strap, restrained risograph grain in the shadowed arch, crisp flat fills in the bright field, and one clean gradient only along the worn bevels. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except those bevels.

No second character, no duplicate Miku, no crowd, no army, no banners, no flags, no birds, no wings, no halo, no second pair of scythes, no additional weapon, no glowing crystal, no neon glow, no self-lit weapon, no rainbow dispersion, no stained glass, no plastic, no glass bottle, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no magical effects, no readable text beyond the string named above, no blood, no wounds, no armour plates, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no weapon in her hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like a door that was never meant to be a door: two scythes leaning until their tips almost meet, a girl standing in the gap already turning to look back, and a field so bright behind her that it has no detail left.

seeds.title: EAVE
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “EAVE”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing at the prayer front of a small Japanese shrine while it rains steadily outside, her right hand stretched out past the drip line with the palm turned up to catch the falling water, her left arm hanging loose at her side. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the grey rain.

Use a camera at chest height on a normal lens, set square to the prayer front so the eave runs level across the top of the frame, the offering box sits level at the bottom and the stone courses stay horizontal, with no tilt and no wide-angle spread. Place Miku at approximately forty-four percent of the canvas width, full body visible from shoes to hair ornaments, occupying about fifty percent of the frame height. Let the eave, the sacred rope and the bell fill the upper third, and let the wet stone step fill the bottom fifth.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Her right arm is raised and pushed straight out past the eave line at shoulder height, the palm turned up and the fingers slightly cupped, with three drops still in the air above the palm and one bead already sitting in the hollow of it. Her left arm hangs at her side with the fingers relaxed and the palm turned in, well clear of the hanging rope. Her weight is on her back foot, her body turns a quarter toward the camera, her chin lifts slightly toward the rain, and both eyes are visible. Keep her right forearm clear of her face and put nothing else in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the prayer front itself: a deep overhanging timber eave carried on exposed rafter ends and finished with courses of dark glazed clay tiles whose lower edge is a single row of round tile ends, and beneath it the three things a visitor faces — a straw sacred rope thick as a forearm strung taut between the two columns with four folded white paper streamers hanging from it, a cast bronze bell the width of her shoulder hanging from the centre bay, and its thick red-and-white braided rope falling straight down to the wooden offering box. Let the eave occupy approximately twenty-six percent of the canvas area across the top, the rope and bell the right fifth, and the offering box the bottom eighth.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The tiles are dark glazed clay, each course holding a bead line of water; the rafter ends are weathered timber, silvered on the cut faces and black where the rain reaches; the sacred rope is coarse twisted straw, pale and dry under the eave with one damp dark patch; the paper streamers are folded white paper, limp in the wet air; the bell is cast bronze, green in its casting pits and bright along the rim where hands have pulled; the offering box is dark stained timber with a slotted lid; the wall behind is coursed granite, grey and coarse, wet to knee height; the flagstones under the eave are pale and dry. Each behaves differently — glazed clay carries a hard specular bead, timber absorbs and darkens, straw scatters light, paper goes translucent at its fold, bronze holds one warm specular, dry stone scatters light.

Build a stepped sequence downward through the frame. Begin at the top edge with the row of round tile ends, then the rafter ends, then the sacred rope with its four streamers, then the bronze bell, then the red-and-white rope, then Miku's reaching hand and her hanging arm, then her body, then the pale dry flagstone band at her feet, then the offering box, then the wet courtyard beyond. The sequence must read as standing at the front of a shrine looking out into the rain, not as a temple exterior.

Leave one deliberate absence. Under the eave the flagstones are dry in a straight band that ends exactly where the drip line falls, pale and faintly dusty, and beyond that line every stone is dark, saturated and puddled. The boundary is one clean edge running the full width of the frame at her ankles, and the falling water strikes outside it only.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the offering box's slotted lid and one coin resting on it, the pale dry flagstone band, the near face of a column. Middle ground: Miku, her reaching arm, the drops above her palm, her left arm hanging at her side. Background: the rain curtain, a vermilion torii standing in the courtyard beyond the drip line seen through the rain, the shrine's low stone wall, the far roof. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the overcast sky beyond the eave. The sky is the key: a flat cool wash from the courtyard side, slightly above her eye line, laying an even silver light on her chest, the front of her thigh and the outer edge of her extended forearm. Add one small warm source inside the shelter, a bronze lantern hanging from the eave at her left, which touches the timber, the underside of the tiles, the dry straw of the sacred rope and the polished lower rim of the bell. Keep the courtyard beyond the drip line two stops brighter than the interior.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the two sources. The nearer tail falls forward inside the dry zone, one clean aqua mass lit warm along the lantern side and cool along its outer curve. The farther tail passes the drip line, takes a scatter of beads along its length, and darkens toward its dripping end. Let one strand lie damp against her cheek.

Dress Miku in an original shrine-visit rain costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not shrine-maiden dress. A short dark waterproof coat worn open over a pale high-collared top, a narrow pleated skirt, thin dark tights and low boots, with the right sleeve pushed to the elbow and visibly darkened where the rain has soaked it. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment, and keep the silhouette simple enough to read at thumbnail size.

Use a cool grey-green palette with warm accents and strict area control. Approximately thirty-two percent of the image is wet grey stone and courtyard, twenty-two percent is the dark timber eave and its shadow, sixteen percent is the bright rain curtain and overcast sky beyond, twelve percent is Miku's dark coat and her aqua hair, eight percent is the pale dry flagstone band, six percent is the warm lantern wash on the timber and the straw, and four percent is the vermilion torii and the warm bronze of the bell.

Drive the printed graphic language from the shrine's own fittings rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the dry flagstones under the eave, printed flat and matte, its edge stopping at the drip line. Add a rectangular pale panel on the shrine wall behind her as a graphic mask at the height of her shoulder, and let one vertical strip of deep oxide red run down the wall aligned to the column's edge. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “EAVE” once, large, in pale grey paint applied across the flat plaster face of the shrine wall above her extended arm, spanning about two thirds of the visible wall width, in heavy condensed capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “SIDE SHRINE” sit on a small enamel plate screwed to the timber column at hip height. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the weather. The tiles hold a bead line along each course and a dark runnel below one broken tile; the rafter ends are black where water has reached and silver where it has not; the sacred rope's straw is dry and roughened under the eave except where one damp strand has darkened; the streamers hang limp and one has taken a grey water mark at its fold; the bell is green in its pits and bright along the rim where hands have pulled; the rope's fibres stand up where it is dry and lie flat where it is damp; the granite is dark to knee height with a tide line; the dry band keeps a film of dust and two fallen leaves. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the courtyard puddle. The water outside the drip line carries the eave as a black band, the bell rope as one pale vertical line, the torii as a broken vermilion stroke, the rain as short vertical dashes and the lantern as one warm point, and the image stops at the puddle's near edge. Let the falling drops break every reflection into dashes rather than one clean shape.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. The bell rope's knotted grip and its looped end hanging free at shoulder height; the bell's dark clapper visible inside its mouth; the offering box's slotted lid with one coin lying on it; a stone water basin with a bamboo spout standing just outside the drip line; a pair of wooden sandals set neatly on the dry step. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a shrine front would actually have it.

Illuminate with the flat overcast sky as the only broad key and the bronze lantern as the only warm accent. Let the sky silver the courtyard, the torii and the outer edge of her extended arm, let the lantern warm the timber, the straw rope and one cheek, and let the rain read as bright vertical threads against the dark interior. Keep everything deeper inside the eave at near-black except what the lantern reaches.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: offering box lid, dry flagstone band, column face. Second: Miku, her reaching hand, the drops, her hand on the rope. Third: the drip line and the near courtyard stones. Fourth: the rain curtain and the torii. Fifth: the shrine's low wall and its far roof. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every tile end, straw strand and stone course, restrained risograph grain in the dark interior, crisp flat fills in the lit bands, and fine water detail only along the drip line and her extended forearm.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no worshipper at the offering box, no hand touching the bell rope, no hand pulling the rope, no swinging bell, no shrine maiden, no priest or monk in the courtyard, no umbrella, no hood over her head, no second hand reaching out, no falling rain inside the dry band, no wet floor under the eave, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no rows of lanterns, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like the first minute of a downpour at a shrine's prayer front: the sacred rope hanging still, the bell quiet above the offering box, a wall of grey water one step away, and a girl with one hand out to catch it and the other hanging loose at her side.

seeds.title: SHIELD WALL
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “SHIELD WALL”, a frame built around one colossal rose-quartz weapon, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character sitting on the sand at the base of a colossal shield driven upright into the ground. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face and twin-tail outline readable against the shield's painted face. Its weapon is rose quartz: deep rose-pink, translucent, and the only saturated mass anywhere in the frame.

The weapon is one solid mass of rose-quartz glass: translucent, deep rose-pink, lit from within, and it throws pink light onto everything around it.

Use a camera at her seated eye level on a normal lens, set square to the shield so its face reads flat and its lower edge cuts the frame at the sand line. Place Miku at approximately twenty-eight percent of the canvas width, sitting with her back against the shield's lower left corner, occupying about twenty-four percent of the frame height. Let the shield occupy the right two thirds of the frame and rise slightly out of the top edge.

Give Miku exactly one core action: resting. She sits with her knees drawn up and her shoulders against the shield face, one forearm laid across her knees, the other hand flat on the sand beside her hip, her head tipped back against the metal. Keep her eyes half closed, her jaw slack, and put nothing in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the shield: a colossal tower shield four metres wide and six tall, driven a forearm's depth into the sand so its pointed lower edge is buried, its face dished outward, its rim banded in riveted iron. Keep its surface plain apart from paint: one broad field of faded teal, a horizontal band of chipped white, and a single deep dent where something struck it. Let it fill the frame's right side as a flat wall.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. the shield's face is a single slab of rose quartz, deep rose-pink and translucent so the whole mass reads as one saturated stone, its interior holding a wide fan of hairline cracks, its rim banded in iron, and it stays matte until the sun cuts its edge; the rim is riveted iron, blackened and rusted in the seams; the dent is bare bright metal where the paint has broken away; the sand is fine dry dune sand, rippled and pale; the sky behind is a flat bleached haze. Begin at the bottom edge with the rippled sand and the shield's buried point, then Miku's boots and the sand she has pushed into a ridge, then her seated body, then the shield's painted field and its dent, then the white band, then the bleached sky at the top. The sequence must read as a wall she is leaning on, not as a prop beside a sitting figure.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: rippled sand and her pushed ridge. Middle ground: Miku, the shield's lower field, the buried point. Background: the shield's upper field, the white band, the bleached sky. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

The sun is the key: it throws the shield's face into flat shade, rims its top edge and the rivet band in white, and lights the sand in a broad bright field. Let Miku sit in the shield's shadow so her face is lit only by bounce from the sand, one value above the sand's own shade. Keep the sky blown out to near white and never introduce a second source. Let the crystal pass the light rather than return it: one thin saturated magenta line along its thickest edge, and one hard-edged magenta caustic patch thrown onto the sand beside it.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails spread on the sand beside her. The nearer tail loops across her drawn-up knee and lies in the sand as a clean aqua mass; the farther one falls behind her shoulder and is cut off by the shield's edge. Let the sun catch the tail lying on the sand as a bright top edge and let a few strands stick to the metal behind her.

Dress Miku in a traveller's light layer over her canonical palette, not armour. A dark teal sleeveless tunic with a high collar, loose sand-coloured trousers gathered at the ankle, a wide cloth sash at the waist, and worn boots with the soles half sanded through. Keep the palette close to teal-and-black with one pale garment, keep one brass clasp at the sash, and keep the silhouette simple enough to read at thumbnail size.

Use a bleached high-key palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty-four percent of the image is the shield's painted field, twenty-two percent is bright sand, fifteen percent is the bleached sky, ten percent is the shield's shadowed lower edge, eight percent is the iron rim, five percent is Miku's clothing, three percent is her aqua hair, two percent is the bare dent, and one percent is the brass clasp. Keep every cool note down to her hair and the teal paint. The rose quartz's deep rose-pink tone is the one saturated colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the shield's own paintwork rather than from decoration. Let one large rust-red ink bloom spread across the sky in the upper left, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular dark panel across the far sand at the horizon as a graphic mask, and let one vertical strip of deep teal run down the frame's left edge from sky to sand. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “SHIELD WALL” once, cut shallow across the crystal shield's face and filled with white paint so the letters read as pale grooves with the caustic passing through them, sized so it spans about three quarters of the shield's visible width and reads clearly at thumbnail size.

Let every surface carry the shift. The shield's paint is blistered in a wide patch and gone along one plank seam; the rim's rivets are set unevenly, two of them replaced with square-headed ones; the white band is worn through to wood along its lower edge; the sand holds a wind-combed ripple and a scatter of grit on the shield's buried point; the dent's edges are rolled and bright. Build a second composition through the shield's shadow. The shadow lies on the sand as one large soft-edged block, darkest against the shield's base and fraying at its far edge; Miku's own shadow sits inside it as a slightly darker shape; the sand ridge she pushed catches a bright rim. One brass clasp at her sash, a single grain of sand caught on the shield's buried point, one loose rivet sitting in the sand below the empty holes, and a thin line of dust settled along the white band's lip. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where weather would put it.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: rippled sand and her ridge. Second: Miku's boots and lower legs. Third: her seated body and the shield's buried edge. Fourth: the shield's painted field and the dent. Fifth: the white band and the bleached sky. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every rivet and plank seam, restrained risograph grain in the shadowed sand, crisp flat fills in the lit sand, and one clean gradient only along the shield's top rim. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the dent and the rim.

No second character, no duplicate Miku, no crowd, no army, no spears, no banners, no flags, no birds, no wings, no halo, no second shield, no additional weapon, no glowing crystal, no neon glow, no self-lit weapon, no rainbow dispersion, no stained glass, no plastic, no glass bottle, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no readable text beyond the string named above, no blood, no wounds, no armour on her body, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no weapon in her hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter.

seeds.title: SHOULDER GUARD
seeds.raw:

Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes and twin-tail identity readable against the flat wall behind her.

The weapon is one solid mass of amethyst glass: translucent, deep violet, lit from within, and it throws violet light onto everything around it.

Use a camera at her shoulder height on a normal lens, set square to her right side so her profile reads cleanly and the sword's blade points away into the frame's upper left. Place Miku at approximately forty-eight percent of the canvas width, occupying about sixty percent of the frame height from her boots to the blade's tip. Let her right hand rest on the grip at her shoulder and the blade extend behind her head out of the top edge.

Give Miku exactly one core action: carrying the sword at rest. Her right hand grips the sword just below the guard with the wrist bent so the blade lies along her shoulder, her left hand hangs at her side with the fingers loosely curled, and her head is turned forward in profile with the chin level. Keep her weight on her back foot, her shoulders squared, and put nothing in her left hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the sword on the shoulder: a straight double-edged longsword with a blade two fingers wide, a simple crossguard, and a wheel pommel, its flat lying against her sleeve so the edge faces up. Keep it plain and unadorned — no inlay, no etched fuller, no wrapped guard. Let the blade occupy the frame's upper left as a long diagonal and her arm occupy the lower right.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. the blade is one solid piece of amethyst, deep violet and translucent so the whole mass reads as one saturated stone, its interior holding a fine web of cracks near the guard, its edges polished, and it returns no light except where the wall's light passes through; the guard and pommel are blackened iron worn to grey at the corners; the grip is dark leather over cord; her jacket is a heavy matte wool with a visible twill; the wall behind is flat painted board, pale and unmarked; the floor is dark stone. Each behaves differently — steel returns one long narrow sheen along its flat, blackened iron holds a dull flatness, leather reads as a fine grain with a low polish, wool absorbs light completely, painted board stays a flat even field, dark stone holds a weak diffuse reflection.

Build a stepped sequence across the frame. Begin at the bottom edge with the dark stone floor, then her boots and the trailing hem of her jacket, then her hip and the hanging left hand, then her torso in profile and the right hand at the guard, then her face and the blade along her shoulder, then the blade's tip leaving the frame. The sequence must read as an object carried with the ease of long habit, not as a weapon being presented.

Leave one deliberate absence. Her left side carries nothing at all — no scabbard, no belt hanger, no second blade, no pack. Keep that whole vertical strip of the frame as her body against empty wall, so the missing sheath is the largest unbroken area of the image.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: dark stone and the hem of her jacket. Middle ground: her boots, hips and hanging hand. Background: her profile, the hand at the guard, the blade along her shoulder and the flat wall. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from a hard side light at the frame's left. The light is the key: it runs down her profile, picks out the blade's edge as one unbroken bright line, and lights the wall behind her in an even pale tone while leaving her back and the wall's right side darker. Let her shadow fall across the wall as a soft dark shape with the blade's line still bright inside it. Never introduce a front fill. Let the crystal pass the light rather than return it: one thin saturated violet line along its thickest edge, and one hard-edged violet caustic patch thrown onto the dark stone beside it.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails hang straight down her back, pulled slightly back by her posture. The nearer tail falls across her spine as a clean aqua mass with one bright top edge, the farther one hangs behind her shoulder and is partly hidden by the blade. Let the side light rim both tails and let a few strands separate against the pale wall.

Dress Miku in a long coat over her canonical palette, not armour. A well-worn heavy coat in dark teal with a wide collar turned up, a black shirt underneath, dark trousers tucked into tall boots, and a narrow belt with one iron ring. Keep the palette close to teal-and-black with a single pale cuff at her left wrist, and keep the silhouette long and vertical so the blade reads against it.

Use a narrow cold palette with strict area control. Approximately forty percent of the image is the pale painted wall, twenty-two percent is her coat and trousers, sixteen percent is the blade, eight percent is the dark stone floor, six percent is her aqua hair, five percent is the guard and pommel, two percent is her skin at the profile and hand, and one percent is the iron ring and the bright edge. Keep every warm note down to the crystal and the iron ring. The amethyst's deep violet tone is the one saturated colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the wall's own paint rather than from decoration. Let one large deep-teal ink bloom spread across the wall's upper right, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular black panel across the wall's lower band at her knee height as a graphic mask, and let one vertical strip of rust-red run down the frame's right edge from top to bottom. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “SHOULDER GUARD” once, in black paint brushed across the pale wall at the height of her shoulder, the strokes slightly uneven where the board has absorbed unevenly, sized so it spans about four fifths of the wall's visible width and reads clearly at thumbnail size. Put no lettering on the blade, her coat or the floor, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The blade's flat is hazed in a band where it meets her sleeve; the guard's blacking is worn bright on its upper face from resting against cloth; the grip's leather is compressed and pale where her hand sits; her coat's shoulder is creased in a permanent fold from the weight; the wall's paint is scuffed at hip height along one long band. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the pale wall. The wall carries her profile as a soft dark shape, the blade as a thin bright diagonal crossing it, and her hanging hand as a small dark note at the frame's lower right. Never let the wall's shadow mirror her face and never produce a second blade.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One iron ring at her belt, a single thread pulled from the coat's shoulder seam, a fine nick in the blade's edge near the guard, and one buckle strap hanging loose at her boot. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where use would put it.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: dark stone and her jacket's hem. Second: her boots and hanging hand. Third: her hip, belt and torso. Fourth: her profile, hand at the guard and the blade's near half. Fifth: the blade's far half and the pale wall. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every coat seam and blade facet, restrained risograph grain in the wall, crisp flat fills in the lit areas, and one clean gradient only along the blade. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the blade's edge.

No second character, no duplicate Miku, no crowd, no banners, no flags, no birds, no wings, no halo, no scabbard, no second sword, no additional weapon, no glowing crystal, no neon glow, no self-lit weapon, no rainbow dispersion, no stained glass, no plastic, no glass bottle, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no magical effects, no readable text beyond the string named above, no blood, no wounds, no armour plates, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no weapon in her left hand, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like the walk home after a long day: a blade laid along a shoulder out of habit, a coat creased permanently at that shoulder, and a girl in profile against a wall that has her shadow printed on it.

seeds.title: SKYWALK
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “SKYWALK”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character walking straight at the lens along a pedestrian footbridge above a six-lane road at night, facing the camera full on with her right hand riding the top rail as she goes, with traffic light streaming below and a wall of lit towers behind her. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the city light.

Use a camera at chest height on a normal lens, tracking backwards in front of her and facing her, so she walks toward the lens and is seen entirely from the front: her face looks into the camera, her chest and the fronts of both thighs are turned to it, and the deck streams away under her feet. The railing enters at the left edge of the frame at hip height and ends at her right hand. Place Miku at approximately fifty percent of the canvas width, full body visible from boots to hair ornaments, occupying about fifty-eight percent of the frame height. Let the traffic below the railing fill the left third and the lit tower wall fill the right third behind her shoulder.

Give Miku exactly one core action. She walks toward the lens with her front foot planted and her back heel lifting; her right hand holds the top rail at hip height with the fingers curled over it and the elbow slightly bent; her left arm hangs at her side. Her shoulders stay level, her chin stays level, and her eyes look straight into the camera. Keep both arms clear of her face and put nothing in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the bridge railing itself: a painted steel top rail, a mid rail, and vertical infill bars at even spacing, entering at the lower left corner and running to a vanishing point just right of her waist. Let the railing and its shadow occupy approximately thirty percent of the canvas area across the lower half, and let the traffic below pass behind it as unbroken light.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The railing is painted steel in a municipal grey, worn to bright metal in one hand patch exactly under her palm; the deck is cast concrete with an anti-slip coating and a painted edge line running to the vanishing point; the traffic below is a river of red and white light with no vehicle shapes; the tower wall behind is glass and steel with a hundred small lit windows; the sky above is flat near-black. Each behaves differently — painted steel holds a soft sheen and one bright patch, concrete is flat and slightly pitted, the light emits without texture, glass towers read as a field of points, sky absorbs everything.

Build a stepped sequence from the bottom edge upward. Begin at the bottom with the painted edge line and the deck's transverse joints, then her boots mid-stride, then her hand on the top rail, then the traffic light beyond the railing on the left, then the tower field behind her right shoulder, then the flat black sky. The sequence must read as height above motion crossed at walking pace, not as a city panorama.

Leave one deliberate absence. One section of the railing's vertical infill is missing: about four bars have been removed between two posts, leaving a clear opening with the two cut ends still showing their bright metal and a temporary mesh panel leaning against the far post. Keep the opening about a shoulder's width and place it about two strides beyond her on the railing, so the traffic below shows through it without blur.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: deck, painted edge line, the nearest three railing bars. Middle ground: Miku, her hand on the rail, her swinging arm, the missing infill. Background: traffic light, tower wall, black sky. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the road below and the towers behind. The traffic is the warm key from below left: a broad amber and red wash rising through the railing, laying a warm underside on her jaw, chin, the front of her coat and the leading edge of her forward thigh. The towers are the cool key from behind: a blue-white field of small points giving a cold rim along her shoulders, her hair and the rail's top edge. Keep the two washes separate and let the top of the frame stay black.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the two light sources and into the stride. The nearer tail swings forward over her left shoulder with the step, one clean aqua mass, warm underneath from the traffic and cold along its upper curve. The farther tail trails behind her right hip, cut by the railing into one dark vertical, its end lifting slightly with her pace. Let the cool rim pick out both outer curves.

Dress Miku in an original overpass-night costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not streetwear. A short dark windbreaker worn open over a pale top, a narrow skirt, thick tights and boots, with the collar turned up and the hem lifting slightly with the stride. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment, and keep the silhouette simple enough to read at thumbnail size.

Use a warm-on-black palette with a cool rim and strict area control. Approximately forty percent of the image is near-black sky and shadow, twenty-two percent is the traffic's warm light field, sixteen percent is municipal grey railing and concrete, ten percent is the cool tower points, eight percent is Miku's dark windbreaker and aqua hair, and four percent is the painted edge line. Keep the cool values at the edges only.

Drive the printed graphic language from the bridge's own hardware rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the lower left of the deck, printed flat and matte, its edge following the painted line. Add a rectangular pale panel on the parapet behind the railing as a graphic mask at the height of the mid rail, and let one vertical strip of deep red run from the traffic field up to the deck aligned to a railing post. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “SKYWALK” once, large, in pale grey paint applied across the flat steel panel of the overhead gantry that spans the bridge's far end behind her, its lower edge just above her hair ornaments, spanning about half the panel width, in heavy condensed capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “LANE 3” sit on a small enamel plate bolted to the nearest post at the left edge of the frame. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the city. The top rail is worn bright only under her palm and dull everywhere else; the deck's anti-slip coating is polished along the walking line; the parapet carries a grey film of exhaust that is darker at its lower edge; the posts hold a rust line at their base; the tower glass reflects nothing at this height. Keep the wear physical and directional, never a uniform grime.

Build a second composition through the traffic. The light below reads as a second horizon: long red bands running one way and white bands the other, compressed by speed into unbroken lines, with the dark gaps between lanes as the only structure, and the perspective of the railing cutting across them. Let the bands never resolve into vehicles.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A brass bolt cap worn bright on the top rail; one steel drainage slot at the deck edge; a laminated notice strapped to a post with no readable text; a coiled cable tie hanging from the mid rail. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a footbridge would actually have it.

Illuminate with the traffic as the warm key from below left and the towers as the cool rim from behind. Let the traffic produce a broad amber wash on every downward face, a warm stripe on the deck edge and a glow on the underside of the railing; let the towers produce one cold rim along her shoulders, hair and the rail's top edge. Keep the sky at absolute black with no gradient.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: deck, edge line, the nearest railing bars. Second: Miku, her hand on the rail, her swinging arm. Third: the missing infill and the traffic beyond it. Fourth: the mid-distance towers. Fifth: the flat black sky. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every railing bar and parapet edge, restrained risograph grain in the dark fields, crisp flat fills in the lit areas, and fine rust only at the post bases. Keep the whole image matte, with no glossy highlight anywhere except the hand-worn patch under her palm.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no pedestrian on the bridge, no umbrella, no bag, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable signage on any tower, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no birds, no aircraft, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like a bridge crossed at walking pace: an open railing running away to the left, one panel of bars torn out, and a girl coming straight at the lens with one hand riding the rail as if she were counting the posts.

seeds.title: SOLITARY TREE
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “SOLITARY TREE”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing in a snowfield beside a single bare tree, with a flat white horizon behind her. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the white.

Use a camera at knee height on a normal lens, set about six metres from her and square to the horizon, so the snowfield fills the lower two thirds as a wide plane and the horizon cuts the frame at her shoulders. Place Miku at approximately forty-four percent of the canvas width, full body visible from boots to hair ornaments, occupying about thirty percent of the frame height.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Her right hand rests flat on the tree's trunk at chest height, and her left hand hangs at her side holding a folded fur hat. Her head is turned toward the horizon, both eyes visible. Keep the pose steady and put nothing else in her hands.

Construct the dominant visual object as the snow surface itself: an unbroken field of wind-packed snow running from the bottom edge to the horizon, marked by long low drifts, boot tracks, and the tree's single hard shadow. Let the snow occupy approximately sixty percent of the canvas area and be the brightest large surface by far.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The snow is wind-packed with a fine crust, blue in every hollow and almost white on every crest; the tree is bare black hardwood with rough bark and three main limbs; the sky is a flat pale grey with no cloud structure; Miku's coat is dark wool; her boots are dark rubber. Each behaves differently — snow scatters all light and holds only blue shadow, bark absorbs and reads as a black vertical, the sky is a clean graded field, wool holds a flat dark value.

Build a stepped sequence from the near snow to the horizon. Begin at the bottom edge with the crust and one set of boot prints, then the tree's shadow running to the right, then Miku's boots and their small crater, then her hand on the trunk, then the drifts flattening with distance, then the horizon line. The sequence must read as distance across a surface, not as a landscape.

Leave one deliberate absence. The tree's shadow runs unbroken to the right except for one section: a clean gap about a metre long where the shadow simply stops and resumes, leaving a bright unmarked band of snow in the middle of the dark stripe. Keep the gap just right of her boots so the shadow reads as damaged rather than natural.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: crust, boot prints, shadow. Middle ground: Miku, the trunk, her crater. Background: the drifts and the horizon. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from a low sun at the far left, behind thin cloud. The sun is the key: warm but heavily diffused, so the snow's crests go nearly white and its hollows go a deep blue, and the tree's shadow runs long and hard-edged to the right. Add the snow's own bounce as a strong cool fill, lifting every underside. Keep the sky brighter than the snow's hollows and darker than its crests.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the white field. The nearer tail falls straight down in one clean aqua mass, the only saturated colour within a hundred metres; the farther tail is cut by the trunk into two dark segments. Let the snow's blue bounce tint the underside of both tails.

Dress Miku in an original snowfield costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not expedition gear. A long dark wool coat with a wide collar, cinched once at the waist, over dark trousers and high laced boots, with a pale scarf wound twice. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale accent.

Use a white-and-blue palette with one dark anchor and one saturated accent. Approximately sixty-two percent of the image is snow white and its blue hollows, sixteen percent is the flat pale sky, ten percent is the tree's black silhouette and shadow, six percent is Miku's dark coat, four percent is her aqua hair, and two percent is the pale scarf.

Drive the printed graphic language from the snow's own relief rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the lower left of the snowfield, printed flat and matte, reading as a cold hole in the white. Add a rectangular pale panel behind the tree as a graphic mask at the height of its lowest limb, and let one vertical strip of deep blue run from the horizon to the bottom edge, aligned to the trunk.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “SOLITARY TREE” once, large, in dark blue paint applied across the broad flat snow surface in the middle distance, spanning about a third of the canvas width, laid out as if stamped into the crust, in heavy square capitals that read clearly at thumbnail size against the white. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “N 68” sit on a small steel plate bolted to the trunk at her hand's height. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the wind. The crust is sculpted into low sastrugi running one way; the boot prints break through it to a darker layer; the tree's bark is split vertically on its weather side; the drifts flatten with distance; her coat hem is stiff with frost. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the shadows. The tree's shadow and Miku's short crater shadow are the only dark marks on the field, both hard-edged and both running right, so the snow reads as a surface receiving two objects rather than as an empty plane.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A short length of rope coiled at the trunk's base, one frozen puddle showing a pale disc of ice, a steel thermos standing in the snow beside her boots, and a small cairn of three stones half buried. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a snowfield would actually have one.

Illuminate with the diffused low sun as the key, warm-white and weak, plus the snow's strong cool bounce as a fill. Let the sun produce long hard shadows to the right and bright crests on every drift. Let the bounce lift the underside of her jaw, the tree's lower limbs and the shadow's inner edge. Keep the sky as a flat field with no gradient cast on the snow.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: crust, boot prints, shadow. Second: Miku, the trunk, her crater. Third: the middle drifts and the painted word. Fourth: the far field flattening. Fifth: the horizon and sky. Separate them by value steps of roughly eight percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every sastrugi crest and bark split, restrained risograph grain in the blue hollows, crisp flat fills in the white, and fine frost only on her hem.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no skier, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no birds, no buildings, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like the quietest place a person can stand: a white field holding two long shadows, one shadow interrupted by nothing at all, and a girl with her palm on a trunk that is the only vertical for a hundred metres.

seeds.title: SPEAR POINT
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 2:3 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “SPEAR POINT”, a frame built around one long aquamarine spear levelled straight at the lens, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing squarely behind it with her eyes fixed on the camera and the point pushed forward until it almost touches the glass. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes and twin-tail identity readable on either side of the shaft.

The weapon is one solid mass of aquamarine glass: translucent, cold blue-green, lit from within, and it throws cyan light onto everything around it.

Use a camera at her chest height on a wide lens, set a little to her right and tilted up only slightly, so the whole spear runs on one steep diagonal from its butt at the frame's upper right down to its point at the frame's lower left, and both ends stay inside the picture. The point sits only a hand's width from the glass and reads as a flattened faceted mass about one sixth of the canvas width; the shaft thins steadily as it recedes, and its butt shows as a small capped end just above her rear wrist. Place Miku at approximately fifty-eight percent of the canvas width, standing upright at her full height with both boots on the floor and her whole figure from boots to the crown of her head inside the frame, occupying about seventy-two percent of the frame height, so no part of her body is hidden behind the shaft. Let her eyes look down the whole length of the shaft at the viewer.

Give Miku exactly one core action: levelling the spear at the viewer. Both hands are on the shaft at its middle, far back from the point and nowhere near the head: her rear hand grips it a hand's width below the butt cap so that cap stays visible behind her wrist, and her forward hand grips it a forearm further down toward the point, so the point stands a full arm's length beyond her forward hand and much closer to the lens than either hand. She stands on both feet at her full standing height, her boots a shoulder's width apart, both knees straight but not locked, her weight even across both soles and her hips level — she is standing tall, not crouching, not kneeling and not squatting. Keep her chin slightly down, her eyes following the shaft toward the camera, and nothing else in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the spear's point, because the point faces the lens and the shaft only recedes behind it. The blade is a socketed leaf of aquamarine about a hand and a half long, ground with two straight edges and a visible bevel on each, a raised central spine running its full length, and a dull bronze collar at its socket. Since the flat faces the viewer, show it as two bright converging bevel lines with the spine as one central ridge between them, and let the shaft behind it read as a short series of narrowing ellipses rather than as a length. Keep it rigorously plain — no tassel, no binding bands, no inlay.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The blade and the first shaft section are aquamarine, cold blue-green and translucent so the whole near mass reads as one saturated stone, the blade's interior holding a faint spiral and two small flattened voids, its edges ground to a visible bevel, and the whole weapon passes light rather than making it; the socket collar is dull bronze, pitted around its rim; the further shaft sections lose colour through the mist and read as flat grey-green ellipses; the walls are damp stone with a wet tide line at knee height; the air holds a thin cold mist. Each behaves differently — crystal returns one thin saturated line at each bevel and lets the rest pass through, bronze absorbs almost everything it receives, each foreshortened shaft section goes one step flatter than the last, damp stone holds soft value steps, mist dissolves every edge it crosses and leaves the furthest shaft section reading as a smudge.

Build a stepped sequence from the point back to her face. Begin at the frame's lower left with the faceted point pushed past the edge, then the bronze collar and the first shaft section, then the second section narrowing toward her two hands, then both her grips, then her squared shoulders and her lowered chin, then her head and the dark hall behind her. The sequence must read as one object travelling out of the picture toward the viewer, each step larger than the last as it nears the lens, not as a figure holding a stick beside her.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is no opponent anywhere inside the picture and no one else in the hall. The point is not aimed at anything the frame contains — it is aimed out through the viewer's side of the picture plane, so the only thing it threatens is whoever is holding the camera. Keep the hall behind her empty all the way to its walls: no figure, no door, no object she could have levelled the blade at.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the blade's flat face and the bronze collar, both nearer to the lens than her hands. Middle ground: the three shortening shaft sections, her supporting hand and her squared shoulders. Background: her head and twin tails, the damp wall and the misted hall. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur, and never let anything behind her climb above the blade face in contrast.

Light the scene from a single cold lamp high behind her. The lamp is the key: a hard narrow light that rims her shoulders, her jaw and the shaft's upper edge in white, and falls away without reaching her front. Let the flagstone catch one bright pool at the frame's lower right where the butt has split it, and let her front sit two values under. Keep the mist glowing faintly where the light passes through it and never introduce a front light. Let the crystal pass the light rather than return it: one thin saturated cyan line where the mass is thickest, and one hard-edged cyan caustic patch thrown onto the cracked flagstone beside it.

Lift Miku's extremely long twin tails with the effort of the brace. Both tails pull back and slightly up from her shoulders, the nearer one crossing her spine as a clean aqua mass, the farther one whipping out past the shaft. Let the back light rim each tail in a hard white edge and let a few strands separate against the dark.

Dress Miku in a bracing rig over her canonical palette, not armour. A dark teal fitted jacket with the sleeves cut at the elbow, a wide leather belt with two brass keepers, dark trousers with reinforced knees, wrapped calves and flat soled boots with the toes scuffed white. Keep the palette close to teal-and-black with one pale shirt collar, and keep the silhouette compact so the diagonal of the spear dominates.

Use a cold low-key palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty-two percent of the image is the dark hall and its mist, twenty-four percent is the foreshortened shaft, sixteen percent is the pale blade face at the centre, ten percent is Miku's clothing, six percent is her aqua hair, five percent is the damp wall, four percent is her skin at the hands and jaw, and three percent is the brass keepers and the bronze socket collar. Keep every warm note down to the crystal, the bronze and the brass. The aquamarine's cold blue-green tone is the one saturated colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the hall's own markings rather than from decoration. Let one large rust-red ink bloom spread across the dark upper left, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular pale panel across the wall at the height of her shoulder as a graphic mask, and let one vertical strip of deep teal run down the frame's right edge from the mist to the stone. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “SPEAR POINT” once, cut shallow into the flat of the crystal point below the central spine and filled with white paint so the letters read as pale grooves running across the blade face, sized so it spans about two thirds of the blade's visible width and reads clearly at thumbnail size. Put no lettering on the shaft, her hands or her clothing, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The blade's bevels are polished bright along their two converging lines and hazed in one band where a thumb has passed over them; the bronze collar is worn to a shine on its left side and green in its pits; the shaft's second section carries one shallow gouge; the wall's tide line is darker and slick where the mist collects. Keep the wear physical and directional, and keep every trace of it behind the blade.

Build a second composition across the wet wall behind her. The wall carries the blade's outline as one soft vertical smear, her squared shoulders as a dark horizontal band, and the mist as a pale field between them. Let that smear never resolve into a second figure and never mirror her face.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. Two brass keepers at her belt, one thin bead of water running down the bronze collar, a single loose hair caught on the shaft where her fingers have passed it, and a small scuff of white on her boot toe. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where the weapon would put it.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the blade's flat face and the bronze collar. Second: the three foreshortened shaft sections. Third: her hands and her squared shoulders. Fourth: her head, her lowered chin and the twin tails. Fifth: the damp wall, the mist and the dark hall. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each, with the blade face the brightest thing in the frame and the hall behind her the darkest.
