Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every shaft dent and fracture line, restrained risograph grain in the dark hall, crisp flat fills in the lit pool, and one clean gradient only along the shaft's highlight. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the blade and the wet stone.

No second character, no duplicate Miku, no opponent, no crowd, no banners, no flags, no birds, no wings, no halo, no second spear, no additional weapon, no spear lying across the frame, no spear parallel to the lens plane, no full-length shaft seen in profile, no blade seen edge-on, no short stub of a shaft, no spear butt in frame, no glowing crystal, no neon glow, no self-lit weapon, no rainbow dispersion, no stained glass, no plastic, no glass bottle, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no magical effects, no readable text beyond the word named above, no blood, no wounds, no armour plates, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no third hand, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no motion blur, no scrapbook clutter, no spear standing upright, no vertical spear, no hands crossed on the shaft, no hand on the spear head, no spear butt on the ground, no spear planted in the floor.

The final image should feel like being pinned by the picture itself: a faceted point hanging a hand's width from the glass, two bright bevel lines converging on nothing, a girl squared up behind it with her eyes on you, and an empty hall behind her with no one left to point it at.

seeds.title: SPEAR THROUGH CLOUDS
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “SPEAR THROUGH CLOUDS”, a frame built around one colossal rose-quartz weapon, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing on a narrow stone ledge high above a cloud sea, a colossal spear driven down through the cloud layer at a steep diagonal toward her. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face and twin-tail silhouette readable against the white cloud and the dark shaft. Its weapon is rose quartz: deep rose-pink, translucent, and the only saturated mass anywhere in the frame.

The weapon is one solid mass of rose-quartz glass: translucent, deep rose-pink, lit from within, and it throws pink light onto everything around it.

Use a camera at her shoulder height on a wide lens, set behind and left of her so she is seen from three quarters and the spear's shaft crosses the frame from the upper left down to the lower right. Place Miku at approximately twenty-two percent of the canvas width, standing at the frame's lower left on the ledge. Let the spear's tip stop about a metre above the cloud surface, and let the shaft continue out of frame at the top.

Give Miku exactly one core action: reaching up. Her right arm is lifted toward the descending tip, fingers open and not yet touching it, while her left hand grips the ledge's stone lip at her hip. Keep her feet planted with the front foot braced, her knees slightly bent, and put nothing in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the spear: a colossal shaft three hand-spans thick, made of dark oiled ash bound at intervals with blackened iron collars, ending in a leaf-shaped blade the size of a small boat. Keep the weapon plain and functional — no banners, no tassels, no engraving. Let the shaft occupy the whole upper left quadrant and the blade hang in the centre of the frame.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. the shaft and blade are one piece of rose quartz, deep rose-pink and translucent so the whole mass reads as one saturated stone, the shaft's interior holding a long spiral crack and the blade's holding a cloud of tiny voids, its surfaces ground flat but never polished, and it throws no light of its own; the iron collars are blackened and pitted with rust in their seams; the blade is pale steel with a coarse grinding pattern and a blunt, chipped point; the ledge is coarse granite with a wet dark line where the cloud mist settles; the cloud sea is cold water vapour with no hard edges; the sky above is a flat pale grey. Each behaves differently — oiled ash holds one soft highlight along its ridge, iron returns almost nothing, dull steel spreads its highlight across a wide face, wet granite reads as a dark mirror strip, cloud swallows light into a soft gradient, flat sky stays completely matte.

Build a stepped sequence along the shaft. Begin at the lower right with the cloud surface and the blade's shadow, then the blade itself, then the shaft rising through the frame with its collars spaced unevenly, then Miku's raised arm and upturned face, then the ledge's granite edge, then the pale sky. The sequence must read as a weapon far too large for the figure, not as a normal spear held at an odd angle.

Leave one deliberate absence. Where the shaft passes through the cloud layer, one collar is missing: the shaft there is bare, lighter, and shows a ring of four empty bolt holes. Keep the gap small and high in the frame, and place it so the eye finds it only after following the shaft upward.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the granite ledge and Miku's boots. Middle ground: Miku, the blade, the near cloud tops. Background: the shaft's upper mass, the far cloud bank, the pale sky. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from a single diffuse source above the cloud layer. The sky is the key: a cool even light that puts a soft top highlight on the shaft's ridge, a pale flat sheen on the blade, and a thin bright edge on Miku's hair and raised forearm. Let the cloud beneath act as a reflector that lifts the underside of her chin and the blade's lower face by one value. Keep the ledge's front face in shadow, and never introduce a warm source. Let the crystal pass the light rather than return it: one thin saturated magenta line along its thickest edge, and one hard-edged magenta caustic patch thrown onto the cloud tops beside it.

Lift Miku's extremely long twin tails in the hard updraft that rises off the cloud. Both tails stream upward and outward, the nearer one lifting past her shoulder as a clean aqua mass, the farther one breaking into separate strands against the pale sky. Let the tips catch the sky light as a cool rim.

Dress Miku in a light climbing rig over her canonical palette, not armour. A fitted dark teal jacket with a high collar, a short charcoal half-cape pinned at one shoulder, dark trousers with wrapped calves, and flat soled boots with visible stitching. Keep the palette close to teal-and-black with one pale garment at the collar, and keep the silhouette narrow enough to read at thumbnail size.

Use a cold high-key palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty percent of the image is pale sky, twenty-four percent is cloud, twenty-two percent is the spear's shaft, ten percent is the blade, six percent is the granite ledge, four percent is Miku's jacket, three percent is her aqua hair, and one percent is the iron collars' rust. Keep every warm note down to the crystal and that rust. The rose quartz's deep rose-pink tone is the one saturated colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the weapon's supply markings rather than from decoration. Let one large black ink bloom spread across the pale sky in the upper right, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular ochre panel across the far cloud bank as a graphic mask, and let one vertical strip of dark grey run down the frame's right edge from sky to cloud. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “SPEAR THROUGH CLOUDS” once, cut shallow along the crystal shaft's upper third and filled with white paint so the letters read as pale grooves, sized so it spans about four fifths of the shaft's visible length and reads clearly at thumbnail size.

Let every surface carry the shift. The shaft's oil is worn pale where it has been handled; one collar sits a centimetre out of line; the blade's edge is rolled over in two places rather than sharpened; the granite ledge is chipped at its lip and holds a shallow puddle; the cloud has a faint internal grain where the wind combs it. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the cloud surface. The cloud carries the spear's shadow as one long soft band running away from the viewer, the blade's shadow darker at its centre and fraying at the edges, and Miku's own shadow as a small soft patch at the ledge lip. Never let the cloud mirror the spear or produce a second blade.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One brass pin at the nearest collar, a single strand of fibre caught on the blade's chipped point, one hairline crack across the granite lip, and a thin line of mist curling over the ledge edge. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where weather would put it.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: granite and Miku's boots. Second: Miku and her raised arm. Third: the blade and the near cloud tops. Fourth: the shaft's mid-section and its collars. Fifth: the shaft's upper mass and the pale sky. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every collar and blade facet, restrained risograph grain in the sky, crisp flat fills in the cloud, and one clean gradient only along the shaft's ridge. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the blade's ground face.

No second character, no duplicate Miku, no crowd, no army, no banners, no flags, no birds, no wings, no halo, no second spear, no additional weapon, no glowing crystal, no neon glow, no self-lit weapon, no rainbow dispersion, no stained glass, no plastic, no glass bottle, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no magical effects, no readable text beyond the string named above, no blood, no wounds, no armour plates, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no weapon in her hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no motion blur, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like the moment before a hand closes on something it should not touch: a spear driven down out of a white sky, a girl on a granite lip reaching up without yet touching it, and a single missing collar on the shaft above her.

seeds.title: SPIN CYCLE
seeds.raw:
Create a square 1:1 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “SPIN CYCLE”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character sitting on a plastic chair inside a self-service laundrette at night, surrounded by six running washing machines. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the pale tiled interior.

Use a camera at seated eye height on a slightly wide lens, set square to the back wall so the machine row reads as a level band across the frame and the tile grid stays true. Place Miku in the lower left at approximately thirty-four percent of the canvas width, seated with her knees together and her feet flat, occupying about fifty percent of the frame height. Let the machine row fill the upper right, so the square reads as one seated figure against a wall of light.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Both hands hold a paper laundry ticket open at chest height, and her head is tilted down so both eyes stay visible above the paper. One socked foot has slipped half out of a canvas shoe on the floor. Keep the pose still, the arms close to her body, and put nothing else in her hands.

Construct the dominant visual object as the machine row: six front-loading washers in a single band, each with a circular glass door, a chrome ring, and a small digital panel above. Let the row occupy approximately fifty-five percent of the canvas area, with the nearest machine cut by the right edge and the farthest compressed by perspective.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The machine fronts are enamel-painted steel in a faded cream, chipped at every corner; the door rings are chrome, dulled to a soft grey with fine scratches; the drum glass is thick, slightly blue-green, and covered on the inside with running water; the floor tiles are small cream hexagons with dark grout, one broken corner; the plastic chair is moulded polyethylene, scuffed white; the wall is glazed brick. Each behaves differently — enamel holds a flat hard value, chrome draws one thin bright arc, glass transmits a moving pattern, tile reflects the ceiling as a soft grid, plastic takes a dull sheen.

Build a stepped sequence along the row. Begin at the lower right with the nearest machine's drum holding a red garment turning over, then the second drum with pale linen pressed to the glass, then the middle drums where the motion blurs into a soft field, then the fifth drum standing empty and dark, then the far machine with its light brown-out. The sequence must read as a row of separate machines, not as a single glowing wall.

Leave one deliberate absence. One drum among the six stands completely empty and unlit, its door ajar about a hand's width, its chrome ring reflecting nothing, its interior a black circle. Keep it the fifth from the near edge, and place it directly behind Miku's head at a slight offset so the black circle frames her hair without covering it.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: hexagon tile floor, one broken tile corner, Miku's shoe and socked foot. Middle ground: Miku, the plastic chair, the ticket, the first two machines. Background: the middle and far machines, the glazed brick wall, and the ceiling's fluorescent tray. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the ceiling tray only. One long fluorescent diffuser runs across the upper frame parallel to the machine row, throwing a flat cold white wash on every machine front, a soft grid reflection on the tile floor, and a pale rim on Miku's hair and shoulders. Add the drum interiors as six small secondary sources, each a soft circular glow that spills a coloured wash onto the floor in front of its machine. Keep those spills distinct and unsmiling.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the seating geometry. The nearer tail falls over the chair's back edge in one clean aqua mass, catching the ceiling light along its upper curve; the farther tail drops straight down behind the chair and pools slightly on the tile. Let one strand rest against her near arm and pick up a faint red bounce from the nearest drum.

Dress Miku in an original laundrette-night costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not pyjamas. An oversized pale sweatshirt with the sleeves pushed to the elbow, dark shorts, thick socks and canvas shoes, with her hair ornaments catching the ceiling light. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment, and keep the silhouette simple enough to read at thumbnail size.

Use a cream-and-cyan palette with one red accent and strict area control. Approximately forty percent of the image is pale cream enamel and tile, twenty-two percent is cold white ceiling light, fourteen percent is dark shadow under the chairs and between machines, ten percent is the soft grey of chrome and grout, six percent is Miku's aqua hair, five percent is the red garment inside the nearest drum, and three percent is a small blue bounce from a far drum. Keep that red confined to the one drum and nowhere else in the room.

Drive the printed graphic language from the laundrette's own surfaces rather than from decoration. Let one large aqua ink bloom spread across the lower right of the tile floor, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular pale panel behind the machine row as a graphic mask at the height of the control panels, and let one vertical strip of red run from a drum's spill to the floor, aligned to a tile grout line. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “SPIN CYCLE” once, in dark blue vinyl lettering applied to the glazed brick wall above the middle machines, slightly lifting at the final letter, sized so it spans about a quarter of the wall's visible width. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “MACHINE 5 ONLY” sit on a small laminated card taped to the empty drum's door. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry use. The tiles are worn pale along the walking path and dark in the grout; every machine front is chipped at the corner nearest a door; the chrome rings are scratched in one direction from years of wiping; the plastic chair has a scuff at each foot; the wall bricks hold a faint grey film at hand height. Keep the wear physical and directional, never a uniform grime.

Build a second composition through reflection. The tile floor repeats the six drum glows as six soft coloured ovals, repeats the ceiling tray as one long pale band, and carries Miku's chair and legs as a dark shape. Let the reflections stop dead at the grout lines so the floor reads as tile rather than mirror.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A chrome coin slot with a worn brass trim, one wire laundry basket on castors, a folded paper notice taped at eye height with no readable words, and a steel mop bucket in the far corner. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a laundrette would actually have it.

Illuminate with the ceiling tray as the only key, cold and even, plus the drum glows as small secondaries. Let the tray produce one continuous highlight along every machine top, a soft grid on the floor, and a pale rim on Miku's hair. Let each drum produce one circular spill of its own colour on the floor, brightest at the near machine and weakest at the far. Keep the corners of the room darker than the centre band.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: hexagon tile, broken corner, shoe and socked foot. Second: Miku, the chair, the ticket. Third: the first two machines and their spills. Fourth: the middle machines and the empty dark drum. Fifth: the far machine, the glazed brick wall and the ceiling tray. Separate them by value steps of roughly ten percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every machine edge and tile line, restrained risograph grain in the shadow fields, crisp flat fills in the lit areas, and fine chips only where doors have struck. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the chrome rings.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no attendant, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no suds or foam outside the drums, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like the only lit room on the street: six drums turning, one standing dark and open, and a girl reading a ticket as if it were the timetable of her own evening.

seeds.title: STACK ROOM
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “STACK ROOM”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing in the aisle of a closed-stack archive, with ceiling lights running away in perspective above her. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the warm paper-brown depth.

Use a camera at chest height on a normal lens, set dead centre in the aisle so both shelf walls converge symmetrically and the ceiling lights form a receding line above her head. Place Miku at approximately forty-six percent of the canvas width, full body visible from shoes to hair ornaments, occupying about forty percent of the frame height. Let the aisle run past her to a distant reading table, so the composition is a corridor with one figure in the middle third.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Her right hand draws one thin volume halfway out of the shelf at chest height, and her left hand holds a short pencil between two fingers at her side. Her head is turned toward the pulled book, so only one eye and the edge of her mouth are visible. Keep the pose still, the arms clear of her face, and put nothing else in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the shelving walls themselves: two continuous ranks of steel shelving from floor to just below the ceiling, each rank divided into seven horizontal bays and each bay packed with volumes of every height, spine outward, leaning where they are thin. Let the shelving occupy approximately seventy percent of the canvas area, with the far bays compressing into a single warm brown value.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The shelf uprights are pale grey powder-coated steel with the paint worn to metal at every shelf lip; the volumes are buckram and paper of every age, some with gold tooling dulled to brown, some with torn spines showing binder board; the aisle floor is linoleum, dark green, polished in a continuous band along the centre; the ceiling is a grid of acoustic tiles with two fluorescent battens per bay; the distant table is oak. Each behaves differently — steel holds a hard edge, cloth spine absorbs, paper edge catches a thin light line, linoleum reflects the battens as long soft bars.

Build a stepped sequence down the aisle. Begin at the bottom edge with the linoleum's worn centre band, then the nearest shelf base with a kick plate and one book lying flat on the floor, then Miku and the volume she is drawing, then the middle bays where spines compress into texture, then the far table with its lamp, then the ceiling's vanishing line. The sequence must read as depth through stored knowledge, not as a wall of books.

Leave one deliberate absence. One complete shelf bay, about chest height on her left, stands entirely empty: no volumes, no bookends, only a clean dust line along the shelf lip and four small screw holes where a divider used to be. Keep the bay exactly one shelf wide, placed directly opposite her shoulder so the empty rectangle balances her figure.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: worn linoleum, kick plate, the book lying flat. Middle ground: Miku, the pulled volume, the near bays. Background: the receding bays, the reading table with its lamp, and the ceiling line. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the ceiling only. The battens are the key: warm white, evenly spaced, each throwing a soft pool onto the shelf tops and a narrow falloff down each bay face, so every vertical run of spines goes bright at the top and dark at the base. Add one small warm task lamp on the distant table as a second point. Keep the aisle floor's centre band the brightest horizontal in the frame.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the shelving. The nearer tail falls forward across the shelf face in one clean aqua mass, catching the batten light along its upper curve and shadowing the spines behind it; the farther tail is trapped between her back and the opposite shelf and reads as a dark vertical. Let one strand rest on the pulled volume's top edge.

Dress Miku in an original archive-shift costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not a librarian uniform copy. A slate-grey long cardigan over a pale shirt, a dark narrow skirt, opaque tights and low lace-up shoes, with a thin canvas satchel strap crossing one shoulder. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment, and keep the silhouette simple enough to read at thumbnail size.

Use a warm-brown-on-green palette with strict area control. Approximately forty-two percent of the image is warm paper brown and ochre spine tone, twenty-two percent is deep shadow between volumes, twelve percent is pale grey steel, ten percent is dark green linoleum, six percent is warm-white ceiling light, four percent is Miku's aqua hair, and four percent is the small amber table lamp. Keep the ceiling light cooler than the paper so the two temperatures stay separate.

Drive the printed graphic language from the archive's own order rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the lower right of the aisle floor, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular pale panel behind the shelving as a graphic mask at the height of the fourth bay, and let one vertical strip of rust orange run from the ceiling to the floor, aligned to a shelf upright. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “STACK ROOM” once, in white paint applied across the timber header board that runs the full width above the upper shelf bays, the letters slightly uneven, sized so it spans about half the board's visible length. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “B 12” sit on a small brass holder clipped to the shelf lip near her hand. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the years. The linoleum is worn pale along the centre band and dark at the shelf bases; each shelf lip shows a bright line where hands grip and dust gathers behind it; the volume tops are grey with dust except where one has been recently pulled; the ceiling tiles are stained in the corners; the shelf uprights hold fingerprints in a soft sheen. Keep the wear physical and directional, never a uniform grime.

Build a second composition through repetition. The ceiling battens repeat as bright rectangles down the frame, and the shelf bays repeat as dark verticals beneath them, so the two rhythms cross. Let Miku's silhouette break both: her hair interrupts one batten's reflection on the floor, and her shoulder cuts one bay's edge.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A brass label holder with a blank card, one leather bookmark hanging from a spine, a small step stool folded against the shelf base, and a steel book trolley with two volumes on it. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where an archive would actually have it.

Illuminate with the ceiling battens as the only key, warm and even, plus the distant task lamp as a small secondary. Let the battens produce one soft highlight down each shelf top and one pale reflection on the linoleum's centre band. Let the lamp produce a small amber pool on the table and a thin rim on the far chair back. Keep the far aisle darker than the centre so depth reads by value.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: linoleum band, kick plate, fallen book. Second: Miku, the pulled volume, the near bay. Third: the middle bays with their spine texture. Fourth: the far bays compressing to a single value. Fifth: the reading table, lamp and ceiling vanishing line. Separate them by value steps of roughly ten percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every shelf lip, restrained risograph grain in the brown fields, crisp flat fills in the lit areas, and fine dust lines only where surfaces are horizontal. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the brass.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no reader at the far table, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text on any spine or card, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no floating books, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like a room built entirely of stored paper: warm light on a thousand spines, one empty bay holding its shape, and a girl drawing out a single volume as if the whole floor were waiting for her to choose.

seeds.title: STILL LAKE
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “STILL LAKE”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing at the edge of a mountain lake before sunrise, with a pale limestone wall rising across the water behind her. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the pale water.

Use a camera at hip height on a normal lens, set on the shingle shore and square to the water so the far wall runs level across the frame and the lake fills the middle third. Place Miku at approximately twenty-eight percent of the canvas width, full body visible from boots to hair ornaments, occupying about thirty percent of the frame height. Let the pale limestone wall occupy the upper right and the still water the centre, so the composition is a figure, a mirror and a wall.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Her right hand holds a flat stone at hip height, thumb along its edge, ready to skim, and her left hand hangs open at her side. Her head is turned toward the far wall, both eyes visible in profile. Keep the pose still and put nothing else in her hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the limestone wall across the water: a broad pale cliff face about two hundred metres away, banded in three horizontal strata, with a broken talus slope at its base and a thin line of surviving pines along its top. Let the wall occupy approximately thirty percent of the canvas area in the upper right, and let it be the brightest large surface in the frame.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The water is black-green and perfectly still, holding a full mirror of the wall; the shore is flat grey shingle with wet stones at the waterline; the wall is pale limestone with horizontal bedding planes and dark streaks where water seeps; the pines are dark and small; the sky above is a flat pre-dawn grey; the far talus is a soft grey slope. Each behaves differently — still water returns a perfect inverted image with a slight vertical smear, wet shingle holds a thin sheen, limestone reads as pale horizontal bands, pines are near-black silhouettes.

Build a stepped sequence from the shore outward. Begin at the bottom edge with the wet shingle and one skimming stone, then the still water's black edge, then the inverted wall in the water, then Miku's boots and her hand, then the real wall with its strata, then the pines and the flat sky. The sequence must read as two halves of one world, not as a landscape photograph.

Leave one deliberate absence. The inverted wall in the water carries a missing band: one horizontal stratum visible in the real cliff has no counterpart in the reflection, leaving a smooth gap of unbroken water about a metre tall. Keep the gap at the height of Miku's shoulders so the eye passes from the real wall to her face to the missing band.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: wet shingle, skimming stone, water's edge. Middle ground: Miku and the still water. Background: the limestone wall, the talus, the pines. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the pre-dawn sky only. The sky is the key: a flat, cool, even grey that lights the wall evenly and leaves the water's mirror almost as bright as the stone itself. Add one faint warmer band low in the sky behind the pines, giving the wall's top edge a barely warm line. Keep every shadow open and colourless; this hour has no directional light.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the still air. The nearer tail falls straight down in one clean aqua mass, the only saturated colour in the frame; the farther tail drops behind her and is doubled faintly in the water. Let the tips touch the shingle, since there is no wind.

Dress Miku in an original lake-dawn costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not hiking gear. A long charcoal parka worn open over a pale knit, dark trousers tucked into short rubber boots, and a thin scarf hanging loose. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment, and keep the silhouette simple enough to read at thumbnail size.

Use a pale-grey palette with one saturated accent and strict area control. Approximately thirty-eight percent of the image is pale limestone and its inverted reflection, twenty-four percent is black-green still water, sixteen percent is flat pre-dawn sky, ten percent is grey shingle, six percent is Miku's charcoal parka, four percent is near-black pine, and two percent is her aqua hair. Keep the aqua the only saturated value so the whole frame reads as a cold monochrome.

Drive the printed graphic language from the stone's own bedding rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the lower left of the water, printed flat and matte, reading as a dark hole in the mirror. Add a rectangular pale panel behind the wall as a graphic mask at the height of the middle stratum, and let one vertical strip of dark green run from the water's edge to the shingle, aligned to a bedding joint.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “STILL LAKE” once, large, in dark charcoal paint applied across the broad flat face of the limestone wall's middle stratum, spanning about a third of the wall's visible width, in heavy square serif capitals that read clearly at thumbnail size against the pale stone. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “ELEV 1240” sit on a small steel plate bolted to a boulder at the shore. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the hour. The shingle is wet in a band at the waterline and dry above; the wall carries dark seep streaks running down from its top edge; the water's surface has one long ripple from a rising fish; the boulder's steel plate is fogged; Miku's boots hold a wet ring at their soles. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the water. The mirror carries the wall inverted with its strata intact except for the missing band, carries the pines as a dark inverted line, and carries Miku's silhouette as a dark shape with one aqua edge. Let the reflection be almost but not exactly as bright as the stone.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One flat skimming stone already in her palm, a rusted iron mooring ring set into a shore boulder, a folded canvas tarp weighted with stones, and a thin line of dead pine needles at the water's edge. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a lake shore would actually have it.

Illuminate with the flat pre-dawn sky as the only key, cool and even, plus the wall's bounce off the water as a weak secondary. Let the sky produce an even wash on the wall's face and a pale skin on the water. Let the bounce lift Miku's jaw and hands very slightly. Keep the frame free of any directional shadow except her own soft contact shadow.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: shingle, skimming stone, water's edge. Second: Miku and her reflection. Third: the near water's black field. Fourth: the inverted wall and the missing band. Fifth: the real wall, the talus and the pines. Separate them by value steps of roughly eight percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every bedding plane, restrained risograph grain in the dark water, crisp flat fills in the pale stone, and fine seep streaks only on the wall.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no boat, no fisherman, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no birds, no clouds, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like the last hour before the mountain wakes: a wall of pale stone standing in its own reflection, one stratum missing from the mirror, and a girl holding a flat stone she has not yet thrown.

seeds.title: MARKET RING
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “MARKET RING”, a frame built around one luminous ring drawn on the wet paving of an empty night market after the stalls have closed, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing upright at the exact centre of that ring with both knees straight and locked. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes and twin-tail identity readable in the ring's coloured light.

The ring is one continuous line of light drawn on a single flat plane, and it is complete. Its light is saturated violet, the most saturated colour anywhere in the frame, and each segment reads as a lit bar rather than as white paint.

Use a camera at her chest height on a normal lens, perfectly level and set back a few paces, so she stands at the frame's centre at her full standing height with her boots on the paving inside the innermost ring. Place her at approximately fifty percent of the canvas width, occupying about seventy percent of the frame height. Let the outer ring run past both side edges of the frame and let the closed shutters of the stalls cut one straight horizontal line across the upper third. Keep the camera level rather than low, so the paving stays under her feet instead of rising behind her.

Give Miku exactly one core action: holding the ring open. She stands on both feet with her knees straight and her weight even, her right arm extended forward and down with the palm turned toward the ring's centre directly between her boots, and her left arm hangs at her side. Her right hand sits in the near foreground between the lens and her chest so the ring's centre comes closer to the lens than her face does. Her eyes look down at that centre. Keep both knees straight, no knee lifted, and keep her shoulders square to the camera. It is a magic circle, drawn and lit, and nothing else.

Construct the dominant visual object as the ring and nothing else. Build it from three concentric rings of unequal weight, twelve short radial dashes spaced evenly between the middle and outer rings, and four segmented arcs that stop short of closing. Keep every line the same width, keep the ring flat on the paving, and keep its centre exactly between her two boots. Let the ring be the only long curved object in the frame and let the shutters be the only straight one. There is one saturated violet light source and one ring; there is no second ring, no floating ring and no ring on any wall.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. the ring is a groove of light cut into the wet paving, violet and saturated so the whole line reads as one lit bar, with a short hard bleed onto the stone beside it; the paving is wet granite with a shallow grey sheen and a fine cut joint every three paces; the shutters are ribbed steel painted a flat dark green, each rib casting one thin shadow; her clothing is matte wool; the stall frames are bare tubular steel; the air is a cool dark grey with no visible rain. Each behaves differently — the lit groove returns one hard violet edge and one soft bleed, wet granite holds one even tone without a figure in it, ribbed steel reads as a long repeat of equal stripes, wool absorbs everything, tubular steel gives one narrow dull highlight, the air stays a flat dark field with no streak.

Build a stepped sequence across the frame. Begin at the lower left with the outer ring crossing the wet paving, then a radial dash and a cut joint, then her left boot and the innermost ring, then her right palm and the ring's centre, then her lowered face and falling hair, then the closed shutters behind her. The sequence must read as one held moment after the market has gone, not as a performance, and each step must sit a little higher and a little darker than the one before.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is no stall, no crate, no signboard, no lantern, no awning, no chair, no discarded paper, no vehicle and no passer-by — nothing on the paving but the ring and her two boots. Keep the whole right half of the shutters bare so the violet bleed is the only mark on them. Let the far end of the lane hold one even dark tone and nothing more.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the wet paving and the near arc of the outer ring. Middle ground: her boots, the ring's centre and her extended palm. Background: her lowered face, the tubular frames and the closed shutters. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur, and let the darkest value sit behind her head so the hair reads as a clean silhouette.

Light the scene from the ring and from nothing else. The lit line is the only source: a saturated violet light that sits in the groove, throws one short hard bleed onto the wet paving beside it, climbs her right palm and forearm, and leaves her face lit only by that same return. Let the shutters catch one narrow band of it and let the frame's near corners fall dark. Never introduce a front fill, never add a street lamp and never add a second source. Let the crystal-clear groove pass the light rather than scatter it: one thin saturated violet line along each segment and one hard-edged violet patch on the stone beside her right boot.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails hang behind both shoulders as she stands. The nearer tail falls along her right arm and its tip stops a hand's width above her extended palm; the farther one drops straight down into the dark behind her. Let the ring's light rim each tail and let the tip near her palm catch one cool reflection. Keep both tails clear of the ring's centre so the lit groove stays unbroken at the point her eyes follow.

Dress Miku in a loose outdoor layer over her canonical palette, not armour. A dark teal wrap jacket worn open with the sleeves pushed to the elbow, a black undershirt, dark loose trousers, and two soft boots planted flat on the wet stone. Keep the palette close to teal-and-black with one pale cuff at her right wrist, and keep the silhouette long, straight and fully upright. Let the jacket's hem stop above the outer ring so the lit groove never crosses a printed fold.

Use a violet-on-dark palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty-four percent of the image is the dark lane and the closed shutters, twenty-two percent is the wet paving, eighteen percent is the ring and its bleed, nine percent is her clothing, seven percent is the stall frames and the air, five percent is her aqua hair, four percent is her face and hands, and one percent is the pale cuff and the boot's bright rim. Keep every saturated note in the ring. The violet tone is the one saturated colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the shutters' own marks rather than from decoration. Let one large deep-teal ink bloom spread across the dark shutters in the upper right, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular ochre panel across the paving at her left boot as a graphic mask, and let one vertical strip of rust-red run down the frame's left edge from shutters to paving. Keep every graphic element square to the frame, and keep all three behind the figure rather than over her.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “MARKET RING” once, in white paint stencilled across the shutters above her head, the strokes chipped where the steel has rusted, sized so it spans about half the shutters' visible width and reads clearly at thumbnail size. Put no lettering on the ring, the paving or her clothing, and put no other letters anywhere in the image. Keep the word level with the frame and clear of the shutters' horizontal rib line.

Let every surface carry the shift. The ring's groove is bright along its whole length and hazed only where her boot shades it; the paving's sheen stops in a straight line where the shutters' shadow begins; the shutters' paint is worn along one rib and chipped at one corner; the tubular frames carry one dull rubbed patch where a hand would have held them; the handle of her jacket is frayed at one cuff; the granite's joint is polished in a shallow hollow. Keep the wear physical and directional, all of it running the same way as the lane.

Build a second composition through the wet paving. The stone holds the ring as one even violet tone spread flat beneath her boots, and it holds the shutters as one dark horizontal band. It carries no figure, no face and no reflected body. Let that tone stay a tone rather than an image, and let it be broken only where her two boots meet the innermost ring.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One pale cuff at her right wrist, a single fine bright nick in the ring's outermost arc where a dash meets it, one hairline crack across the paving at her left boot, and one bead of water held at a shutter's lower rib above her shoulder. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where use would put it, and keep no more than four such points in the whole frame.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the wet paving and the near arc of the outer ring. Second: her boots and the innermost ring. Third: her extended palm and the ring's centre. Fourth: her lowered face and falling tails. Fifth: the tubular frames and the closed shutters. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each, and let no layer borrow an edge from the one behind it.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every ring segment and paving joint, restrained risograph grain in the dark lane, crisp flat fills in the lit stone, and one clean gradient only along the ring's bleed. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the lit groove and her eye. Let the wet paving read as a printed tone rather than photographic noise.

No second character, no duplicate Miku, no crowd, no stall, no crate, no signboard, no lantern, no awning, no chair, no vehicle, no passer-by, no birds, no wings, no halo, no second circle, no floating circle, no circle on the wall, no closed ring of white paint, no lattice, no grid, no glyphs, no symbols, no written characters inside the circle, no script of any kind, no engraved letters, no glowing runes, no magical effects beyond the one ring, no continuous wall of light, no light cage, no blood, no wounds, no armour plates, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no lifted knee, no bent knee, no kneeling, no crouching, no jump, no mirrored figure in the paving, no reflected face, no puddle carrying a second body, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like one held moment after closing time: a single violet ring flat on the wet paving, a girl standing straight at its centre with one palm turned down toward it, and a whole lane of shutters gone quiet behind her.

seeds.title: SHEATHING
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 2:3 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “SHEATHING”, a frame built around one long amber crystal sword being guided back into a black sheath, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing upright under the deep eave of a narrow service lane while rain falls steadily beyond the eave line, both knees straight and locked. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes and twin-tail identity readable in the eave's hard light.

The weapon is one solid mass of amber crystal: translucent, warm honey, lit from within, and it throws one amber line onto the granite beside her boot.

Use a camera at chest height on a short lens, set square to her body and level with her jaw, close enough that the sword and sheath run as one diagonal through the frame's middle and her head fills the upper third. Place Miku at approximately fifty percent of the canvas width, occupying about eighty-five percent of the frame height at full standing height from boot to crown. Let the sheath's chape sit just inside the lower left and the sword's pommel just inside the upper right. Let the eave's edge cut one straight horizontal line across the top tenth of the frame, and keep a clear margin of wall on both sides of her.

Give Miku exactly one core action: sheathing the sword. Both hands work close together on the same one sword, her right hand gripping the cord-wrapped handle and guiding the point down into the sheath's mouth, her left hand steadying the sheath at its throat, and the blade is still half visible between them. Her shoulders are square to the camera, her elbows are bent and held in front of her chest, and her eyes look down at the sheath's mouth. Keep her standing at full height with both knees straight, no knee lifted, and her weight even on both feet, with both boots flat on the stone.

Construct the dominant visual object as one sword and one sheath: a single-edged blade two fingers wide and three feet long, its amber crystal flat turned toward the viewer, sinking into a plain black sheath with one iron throat and one iron chape, and no engraving anywhere. Let the gap between her two hands be the only opening in the frame's centre, and let the visible half of the blade be the only warm surface in the whole picture.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. the blade is one piece of amber crystal, translucent and warm so the whole exposed half reads as one saturated mass, its interior holding a fine web of cracks that catch the lane light, its edge polished and one nick deep; the sheath is black lacquer over wood, matte and unmarked; the throat and chape are pitted iron; the handle is dark cord over ray skin; her clothing is matte wool; the paving is wet granite; the eave above is dark timber with a square-cut edge; the rain beyond the eave line is one even grey veil. Each behaves differently — crystal passes one thin saturated amber line and one hard-edged caustic onto the stone, lacquer absorbs everything, pitted iron holds a dull grain, cord shows a fine diagonal, wool reads as a dry soft plane, wet granite returns one shallow tone, timber shows a long straight grain, the rain reads as a flat printed veil with no individual streak.

Build a stepped sequence across the frame. Begin at the lower left with the wet granite and her two boots, then the sheath's iron chape, then her left hand at the sheath's throat, then the exposed amber half of the blade, then her right hand on the handle, then her lowered face and falling hair, then the eave's dark edge. The sequence must read as the last motion of a long day, not as a display of a weapon, and each step must sit a little higher and a little brighter than the one before.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is no umbrella, no parasol, no second weapon, no scabbard stand, no signboard, no crate, no stall and no passer-by — nothing in the lane beside her but the wet stone. Keep the whole right half of the paving bare so the amber caustic is the only mark on it. Let the rain beyond the eave line occupy one narrow band at the frame's right edge and nothing more.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the wet granite and her boots. Middle ground: the sheath, her two hands and the exposed blade. Background: her face, the dark wall and the eave's edge. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur, and let the wall behind her stay one even dark plane so her silhouette reads clean from crown to boot.

Light the scene from the lane's open mouth. One hard wedge of grey daylight is the key: it comes in under the eave from her left at shoulder height, cuts a straight bright band across her two hands and the exposed blade, and leaves her face lit only by the crystal's amber return. Let the wet granite catch one narrow band of that light and let the frame's near corners fall dark. Never introduce a front fill. Let the crystal pass the light rather than return it: one thin saturated amber line where the mass is thickest, and one hard-edged amber caustic patch thrown onto the stone beside her right boot. Keep one hard light, one soft return and no third source, and let the rain band stay a single even grey tone.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails hang behind both shoulders as she stands. The nearer tail falls along her left arm and its tip rests against the sheath's upper third; the farther one drops straight down into the dark behind her. Let the lane light rim each tail and let the tip near the lacquer catch one warm reflection. Keep both tails clear of the blade's diagonal so the sword stays the only long straight line in the frame.

Dress Miku in a loose outdoor layer over her canonical palette, not armour. A dark teal wrap jacket worn open with the sleeves pushed to the elbow, a black undershirt, dark loose trousers, and two soft boots planted flat on the wet stone. Keep the palette close to teal-and-black with one pale cuff at her right wrist, and keep the silhouette long, straight and fully upright. Let the jacket's hem stop above the sheath so the black lacquer never crosses a printed fold.

Use a warm-on-dark palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty-four percent of the image is the dark wall and the eave's shadow, twenty-two percent is the wet granite, eighteen percent is the black sheath and the exposed blade together, nine percent is her clothing, seven percent is the rain band and the lane beyond, five percent is her aqua hair, four percent is her face and hands, and one percent is the pale cuff and the iron throat's bright rim. Keep every warm note in the crystal. The amber's honey tone is the one saturated colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the lane's own marks rather than from decoration. Let one large deep-teal ink bloom spread across the dark wall in the upper right, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular ochre panel across the wet granite at her boots as a graphic mask, and let one vertical strip of rust-red run down the frame's left edge from the eave to the paving. Keep every graphic element square to the frame, and keep all three behind the figure rather than over her.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “SHEATHING” once, in white paint stencilled across the eave's timber soffit above her head, the strokes chipped where the grain has split, sized so it spans about half the soffit's visible width and reads clearly at thumbnail size. Put no lettering on the blade, the sheath, the paving or her clothing, and put no other letters anywhere in the image. Keep the word level with the frame and clear of the eave's cut edge.

Let every surface carry the shift. The blade's polish is hazed in a band along its lower third and bright only at the edge; the lacquer is rubbed flat where her left thumb sits and chipped at the chape; the iron throat's blacking is gone at both ends; the handle's cord is flattened under her right palm; the granite's nosing is polished in a shallow hollow and chipped at one corner; the eave's cut edge is fretted where rain has run off it. Keep the wear physical and directional, all of it running the same way as the blade's descent.

Build a second composition through the polished crystal. The exposed half carries the lane as one dark vertical band, her two hands as two soft dark shapes, and the sheath's mouth as one pale hard interruption. Never let the crystal mirror her face and never let the reflection extend past the visible half. Let that band stay a tone rather than an image, and let it be broken only where the blade enters the lacquer.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. seeds.title: STUCK IN GROUND
seeds.raw:

Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face and twin-tail outline readable against the low grey field.

The weapon is one solid mass of orange amber glass: translucent, warm orange-brown, lit from within, and it throws orange light onto everything around it.

Use a camera at her kneeling eye level on a normal lens, set square to her so the sword stands vertical at the frame's right and her body fills the left two thirds. Place Miku at approximately thirty-eight percent of the canvas width, occupying about forty-four percent of the frame height. Let the sword's guard sit at her shoulder height and its blade disappear into the mud at the frame's bottom edge.

Give Miku exactly one core action: pulling herself up. Her right hand grips the pommel from above with the knuckles white, her left hand presses flat into the mud beside her knee for balance, and her head is lifted toward the horizon. Keep her back straightening, one knee still down, and put nothing else in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the driven sword: a straight double-edged blade three fingers wide, sunk to three quarters of its length, with a plain crossguard, a wheel pommel and a grip wrapped in dark cord. Keep it plain and unadorned. Let it stand perfectly vertical and let the mud hold it in a raised collar of displaced earth.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. the blade is one solid piece of amber, honey-dark and translucent so the whole mass reads as one saturated stone, its interior holding three long fractures and a scatter of bubbles, its edges polished and chipped, and it passes the flat sky without making light; the guard and pommel are blackened iron; the grip's cord is dark and swollen with damp; the mud is black-brown silt holding a film of standing water in its hollows; the field behind is dead grass flattened by weather; the sky is a flat pale ceiling of cloud. Each behaves differently — dull steel holds a broad weak sheen, blackened iron returns nothing, wet cord reads as a dark coarse grain, mud holds a soft glossy skin where water sits and a matte crust where it does not, flattened grass is a fine broken texture, the cloud ceiling is completely flat.

Build a stepped sequence up the frame. Begin at the bottom edge with the mud's raised collar and the blade entering it, then her pressing hand, then her kneeling knee and boot, then her torso and gripping arm, then her lifted face and hair, then the flat field and the cloud ceiling. The sequence must read as a person using a planted object to stand, not as someone posing beside a sword.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is nothing else planted in the field — no second sword, no stakes, no markers, no boot prints leading away. Keep the middle distance completely smooth and unmarked, so the mud's single disturbed patch is the only evidence of an event.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the mud's raised collar and the blade's entry point. Middle ground: her pressing hand, her knee and her boot. Background: her torso, the gripping arm, her lifted face, the flat field and the cloud ceiling. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the overcast sky alone. The sky is the key: a flat even grey light with no direction that leaves the steel one value above the mud, her coat one value below the field, and the water in the mud hollows as small pale mirrors. Let the far field fade one value lighter toward the horizon and never introduce a sun or a warm source. Let the crystal pass the light rather than return it: one thin saturated amber line where the mass is thickest, and one hard-edged amber caustic patch thrown onto the mud beside it.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails hang forward over her shoulders as she lifts her head. The nearer tail drops across her pressing arm and its tip lies in the mud as a clean aqua mass with mud on its last two inches; the farther one falls behind her gripping shoulder. Let the flat light make her hair the only saturated note in the frame.

Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “STUCK IN GROUND” once, in white paint stencilled across the mud's flat foreground to the left of the blade, the strokes broken by the silt's grain, sized so it spans about a third of the mud's visible width and reads clearly at thumbnail size. Put no lettering on the blade, the field or her clothing, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The blade's grind is hazed above the mudline and bright only along one edge; a rust bloom has started at the guard's underside; the mud's crust has cracked in a wide ring around the blade and holds two boot-shaped depressions near her knee; the field grass is flattened in one direction only; her coat's hem is caked to the height of her boot. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the water in the mud.

No second character, no duplicate Miku, no crowd, no banners, no flags, no birds, no wings, no halo, no second sword, no scabbard, no additional weapon, no glowing crystal, no neon glow, no self-lit weapon, no rainbow dispersion, no stained glass, no plastic, no glass bottle, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no magical effects, no readable text beyond the string named above, no blood, no wounds, no armour plates, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no weapon in her left hand, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter.
