seeds.title: SUMMIT NIGHT
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 9:16 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “SUMMIT NIGHT”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing beside a small dome tent on a mountain summit at night, with the Milky Way arching over the ridge behind her. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the dark.

Use a camera at chest height on a normal lens, set about three metres from the tent and slightly off axis so the tent's lit wall fills the lower right and the ridge line crosses the frame above her head. Place Miku at approximately forty percent of the canvas width, full body visible from boots to hair ornaments, occupying about thirty percent of the frame height.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Her right hand holds a small lantern down at hip height, its light making a soft pool on the rock, and her left hand rests on the tent's guy line at shoulder height. Her head is tipped back toward the sky, both eyes visible. Keep the pose steady and put nothing else in her hands.

Construct the dominant visual object as the lit tent wall: a dome tent's near wall of pale ripstop nylon about two metres wide, lit from inside so it glows, with one dark guy line crossing it and a rolled flap at its base. Let the tent occupy approximately thirty percent of the canvas area in the lower right and be the brightest large surface in the frame.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The tent is pale ripstop that diffuses its interior light into a soft even glow; the rock is dark slate scree with a fine broken surface; the sky is near-black with a bright band of stars and a pale dust lane; the ridge is a hard black silhouette; her lantern is a small warm glass cylinder; the guy line is thin dark cord. Each behaves differently — ripstop glows rather than reflects, slate reads as dark faceted texture, stars are small hard points, the ridge absorbs everything, the lantern is the only warm source.

Build a stepped sequence from the scree upward. Begin at the bottom edge with dark scree and her lantern's pool, then the tent's rolled flap, then its glowing wall, then Miku's silhouette and her hand on the guy line, then the ridge, then the star field. The sequence must read as a small warm volume under a large cold one.

Leave one deliberate absence. The tent's glowing wall carries one dark panel: a rectangular section about two hand widths across where the ripstop has been patched with a darker material, and no light passes through it. Keep the patch at her shoulder height so the glowing wall holds one unlit rectangle.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: scree, lantern pool, flap. Middle ground: Miku, the tent wall, the guy line. Background: the ridge and the star field. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from inside the tent only. The tent is the key: a soft warm glow that lights the rock in front of it, rims Miku's near side, and leaves everything above the tent at near-black. Add her lantern as a second small warm pool at her feet. Keep the sky free of any glow, and let the stars be small and hard rather than blooming.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the two warm sources. The nearer tail falls forward and is rimmed warm along its tent-facing edge; the farther tail drops into the black and reads as a dark shape only. Let the lantern put one small point on the tip of the near tail.

Dress Miku in an original summit-night costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not climbing gear. A dark insulated jacket worn open over a pale layer, dark trousers and boots, with a thin beanie pushed back on her head. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale layer.

Use a warm-on-black palette with strict area control. Approximately fifty-six percent of the image is near-black sky and rock shadow, eighteen percent is the glowing tent wall, twelve percent is dark slate scree, eight percent is the star field's pale band, four percent is Miku's dark jacket, and two percent is her aqua hair and the lantern's warm pool.

Drive the printed graphic language from the sky's own banding rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the lower left of the scree, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular pale panel behind the tent as a graphic mask at the height of the guy line, and let one vertical strip of deep blue run from the ridge to the bottom edge, aligned to the tent's pole.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “SUMMIT NIGHT” once, large, in dark charcoal paint applied across the broad glowing face of the tent's near wall, spanning about two thirds of the wall's width, its strokes reading as if brushed onto the fabric, in heavy square capitals that stay legible at thumbnail size even against the glow. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “3180 M” sit on a small steel plate bolted to the tent's pole. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the altitude. The scree is dry and loose with frost forming in its gaps; the tent's fabric is creased from packing and its flap is rolled tight; the guy line is taut and dark; the ridge is a clean silhouette with one jagged notch; the lantern's glass is fogged at its base. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the star field. A dense pale band runs diagonally from the lower left to the upper right with a darker dust lane through its middle, and the ridge cuts it cleanly at the frame's lower edge. Let the stars never brighten near the tent.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A coil of guy line pegged at the tent's corner, one steel carabiner clipped to the pole, a thermos standing in the scree, and a small cairn of three stones at the frame's left. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a summit camp would actually have it.

Illuminate with the tent's interior glow as the only key, warm and soft, plus the lantern as a small second pool. Let the glow produce a warm wash on the scree in front of the tent and a rim along Miku's near side and hair. Let the lantern light only her boots and the rock at her feet. Keep the sky and the ridge at absolute black apart from the stars.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: scree, lantern pool, flap. Second: Miku, the tent wall, the guy line. Third: the tent's dark patch. Fourth: the ridge line. Fifth: the star field and its dust lane. Separate them by value steps of roughly fourteen percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every scree facet and tent seam, restrained risograph grain in the black fields, crisp flat fills in the glowing nylon, and fine frost only in the scree gaps.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no climber on the ridge, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no campfire, no moon, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like the highest quiet a person can stand in: one glowing dome holding a single dark patch, a ridge cutting a band of stars, and a girl with her head tipped back and a lantern she has forgotten she is holding.

seeds.title: THREAD BINDERY
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “THREAD BINDERY”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing at a bookbinding bench in a narrow craft workshop before dawn. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands, hair ornaments and long twin-tail identity immediately readable above the work surface.

Use a high three-quarter camera from the left, looking slightly down at the bench, with a normal lens and mild foreshortening that keeps the bench receding cleanly toward the right side of the frame. Place Miku in the right third, framed from mid-thigh up, occupying approximately thirty-two percent of the image. She leans forward over the bench with both elbows near the front edge, her weight on the left forearm, her head low and tilted so both eyes read clearly in three-quarter view.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Her left hand holds a folded quire open at the spine while her right hand draws a needle and waxed thread through the centre fold, the needle entering at the middle station and exiting two centimetres lower. The thread is pulled taut and leaves one bright line across the fold. Keep both hands over the paper and away from her face; add no second action, no tool swap and no gesture toward the viewer.

Construct the dominant visual object as a wall of stacked paper quires and standing signatures, forty or more, rising from the bench to above the top frame edge in approximately seventy percent of the canvas. They are stacked in uneven columns with visible gaps, their fore-edges showing the layered page lines. Some quires stand on end and lean; some lie flat and overflow the bench edge. Behind them, a press with two iron screws anchors the left side, and above, a hanging rail carries drying signatures clipped in a row.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The paper is unbleached laid stock with visible chain lines and a soft deckled fore-edge; the thread is waxed linen, dull and slightly stiff; the press is blackened cast iron with polished wear at the handles; the bench is scarred beech; the wall is bare board with old paste stains; the drying rail is thin steel with small brass clips. Each material behaves differently — paper absorbs and curls at a wet corner, waxed thread stays rigid and catches one hard highlight, iron holds a cold grey sheen and bleeds rust where the paste touched it, beech shows compressed dents and raised grain.

Build a stepped sequence of the forty quires. Begin at the lower left with a fresh, bright, untouched quire, its pages perfectly aligned. Move upward and right through quires that grow progressively more handled: edges darkened by thumbing, one corner dog-eared, then a quire with a visible repair strip pasted across the spine, then one that has swollen with damp and no longer closes flat. End at the top right with a quire so old its paper has turned buff and its thread has broken loose and hangs free. The sequence must read as wear across time rather than as random damage.

Leave one deliberate absence. One slot in the second column is empty, the space exactly the size of a removed quire, with a fine rectangle of clean board showing where dust never settled. Keep that clean rectangle as the sharpest, brightest shape on the wall and place nothing inside it.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the bench edge with a bone folder, a small pot of paste and a loose coil of waxed thread. Middle ground: Miku, her hands at the spine, the open quire and the nearest stacks. Background: the receding columns of quires, the iron press, the board wall and a high narrow window with the first grey light.

Light the scene with a single cool window at the upper left, raking almost horizontally so it catches the fore-edges of the quires and leaves the front of each stack in shadow. Let a small warm task lamp on the bench add one pool of amber at the work point and a second, smaller shadow under her hands. Keep the two lights physically separate, warm against cool, with no glow and no artificial edge light.

Weave Miku’s extremely long twin tails down through the stacks. The nearer twin tail spills over the bench edge, hangs between two columns of quires, and reappears on the far side as three separate aqua strands that catch the window light. The farther twin tail falls behind her shoulder and is partly occluded by the tallest stack. Keep the hair dense and clearly readable around her head, allowing separation only where it physically passes between paper.

Dress Miku in a binder’s work costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language. Use a pale linen smock with a high buttoned collar and a crossed back strap, over dark narrow trousers, with wide cuffs turned back twice and a leather apron panel across the front fastened by three bone toggles. Add a thimble on the middle finger of the right hand, a short pencil behind her ear, one paste-stiffened patch at the left hip, and three small coral thread ends caught in the cuff. Keep the garment loose where she leans and tight where it is tied, so the folds follow her posture.

Use a restricted warm-neutral palette. Approximately forty-six percent of the image is unbleached paper cream and buff. Sixteen percent is bench and board brown. Twelve percent is shadowed umber. Ten percent is cool grey window light. Eight percent is blackened iron. Five percent is waxed linen off-white. Two percent is amber lamp light, and no more than one percent is the aqua of her hair and the coral of the thread ends.

Drive the printed graphic language from Miku’s own palette. Let one large aqua ink bloom spread across the board wall behind the tallest stack, its edge soaking into the raw wood. Add two hard-edged rectangular paste blocks on the wall where paper was pressed against it, paler than the surrounding board. Let a fine halftone dust gradient sit only along the bench edge. Cut one clean pale knockout strip where the window light crosses the wall. Add rare brass microdots exactly at the drying-rail clips and the press screws.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable words “THREAD BINDERY” in a small wood-type label pasted to the spine of the tallest standing quire, dark ink on cream paper, set slightly crooked and beginning to lift at one corner. Add one smaller hand-numbered tag tied to the press handle. Both sit at the level of the paper and are partly overlapped by a page edge so they read as objects, not floating type.

Let the surfaces carry their history. The bench has a pale ring where a paste pot stood for years, a scatter of pin holes near the front edge, and one deep gouge filled with dark paste. The iron press has a bright band worn by hands and rust freckles in the recesses. The paper is clean only where it has been protected and softly grey at every exposed edge. Nothing should look new and nothing should look randomly damaged.

Build a second composition through shadow and edge-light. The window throws a clear parallelogram across the wall and the tops of the stacks, stopping sharply against the tallest column. The task lamp throws a second, smaller pool on the bench that overlaps the first, and the two together pick out the fore-edges of the front quires as a stair of fine horizontal lines. The empty slot stays a clean bright rectangle inside the shadowed field.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A brass rule lying along the bench edge, one small glass paste pot with a fitted lid, three coral thread ends, a folded paper pattern with pin marks, and a single bone folder with a polished tip. Keep them clustered at the bench and never spread across the stacks.

Illuminate with the cool window as the key and the small amber lamp as a warm secondary. Let the lamp light her hands and the open quire, let the window light the paper edges, and let the space between them fall into a soft umber shadow. Keep the brightest value on the empty slot and on her hands, and keep every shadow edge physically consistent.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the bench edge, bone folder, paste pot and thread coil. Primary middle ground: Miku, her hands, the open quire and the nearest stacks. Secondary: the middle columns of quires and the iron press. Tertiary: the board wall, the drying rail and the window. Background: the darkest corner of the room, held as clean negative space.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a hand-pulled print: crisp drawn linework, watercolor and ink washes with visible wet edges, dry-brush erosion on the board and bench, soft paper grain across the flat areas, and clean lithograph texture in the shadows. Keep the drawing precise and the paint loose, with no photographic depth of field.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no floating interface, no holograms, no glowing particles, no abstract light streaks, no full-canvas glitch, no random letters or numbers, no watermark, no signature, no muddy background, no neon, no rainbow lighting, no face obstruction, no paper covering her eyes, and no malformed hands. Preserve a strict hierarchy: Miku’s face and her hands at the spine first, the open quire second, the columns of paper third, the empty slot fourth, then the press, typography and shadow.

The final image should feel like a room where books are made one quire at a time: forty signatures stacked past the frame, one missing, one needle caught mid-stitch, and the whole workshop held in the grey minute before the lamp is needed and after the window is enough.

seeds.title: TIDAL FLAT
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “TIDAL FLAT”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing on a wet sand flat at low tide, with the receding water line running diagonally behind her. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the pale wet sand.

Use a camera at knee height on a normal lens, set low on the flat and angled about fifteen degrees so the water line runs diagonally and the sky occupies only the top eighth. Place Miku at approximately fifty-two percent of the canvas width, full body visible from boots to hair ornaments, occupying about thirty-two percent of the frame height.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Both hands hold a shallow basket at hip height, one handle in each fist, with three shells already in it, and her head is tipped down toward the sand, both eyes visible under her bangs. Keep the pose steady and put nothing else in her hands.

Construct the dominant visual object as the wet sand flat: an enormous plane of pale grey-brown sand running from the bottom edge to the horizon, mirror-wet in its lower half, drying in a fine pattern of pale ridges in its upper half, with the last water standing in shallow sheets. Let the flat occupy approximately seventy percent of the canvas area and be the brightest large surface in the frame.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The wet sand is a thin water film over packed grains, holding a soft mirror of the sky; the drying sand is broken into pale polygonal ridges; the remaining water is a shallow sheet with no depth; the far water line is a hard dark edge; the sky is a flat pale grey; Miku's boots are dark rubber. Each behaves differently — wet sand returns a diffuse inverted image, dry ridges scatter light, shallow water holds one bright band, the far line is a hard edge, sky is a clean field.

Build a stepped sequence from the near sand to the water line. Begin at the bottom edge with the mirror-wet sand and one shell, then Miku's boots and their reflections, then her basket, then the drying ridges with their polygonal pattern, then the last shallow sheet, then the hard water line. The sequence must read as a surface receding into itself, not as a beach.

Leave one deliberate absence. One patch of sand among the drying ridges is completely smooth and unbroken: about two metres across, with no ridges and no wet film, sitting pale and featureless between two ridged areas. Keep it just right of her boots so the eye finds the one blank plane on a patterned surface.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: wet sand, shell, boots. Middle ground: Miku, the basket, the ridges. Background: the shallow sheet and the water line. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from a flat overcast sky. The sky is the key: an even pale light from above with almost no direction, so the wet sand mirrors it evenly, the ridges show only a thin shadow in their troughs, and Miku casts a soft small shadow at her feet. Add one faint warm band low in the sky, tinting the far water line slightly. Keep every shadow soft and pale.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the flat's light. The nearer tail falls forward over her basket in one clean aqua mass, the only saturated colour in the frame; the farther tail drops behind her and is doubled softly in the wet sand. Let the tips hang without touching the surface.

Dress Miku in an original tidal-flat costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not beachwear. A dark short jacket over a pale top, dark rolled trousers and high rubber boots, with a thin cord at her wrist. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment.

Use a pale sand palette with one saturated accent and strict area control. Approximately fifty-eight percent of the image is wet and drying sand in pale grey-brown, eighteen percent is the shallow water sheet, twelve percent is the flat overcast sky, six percent is Miku's dark jacket and boots, four percent is her aqua hair, and two percent is the basket's woven cane.

Drive the printed graphic language from the sand's own drying pattern rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the lower left of the wet sand, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular pale panel behind the flat as a graphic mask at the height of the water line, and let one vertical strip of deep grey-brown run from the sky to the bottom edge, aligned to the water line's direction.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “TIDAL FLAT” once, large, in dark grey paint stamped into the drying sand's broad pale patch, spanning about a third of the canvas width, its edges slightly soft where the sand has crept, in heavy square capitals that read clearly at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “LOW 0.4” sit on a small steel plate driven into the sand beside her boots. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the tide. The wet sand is mirror-smooth and holds one long streak where water has drained; the drying sand is broken into pale polygons with fine dry grains at their crests; the shallow sheet holds a thin bright band at its edge; the far water line is hard and dark; her boots are muddied to the ankle. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the wet sand. The mirror carries the sky as a broad pale field, Miku's figure as a dark soft shape with one aqua edge, and her basket as a small dark oval. Let the reflection weaken as the sand dries so the upper half of the flat holds almost nothing.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One ribbed shell and one spiral shell in her basket, a rusted steel marker post standing at the water line, a coil of rope half sunk in the wet sand, and a small pale crab hole with a fresh pellet beside it. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a tidal flat would actually have them.

Illuminate with the flat overcast sky as the only key, even and pale, plus the wet sand's mirror as a weak secondary bounce. Let the sky produce an even wash on the ridges and a soft small shadow at her feet. Let the mirror lift the underside of her jaw and basket. Keep the far water line as the darkest value in the frame.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: wet sand, shell, boots. Second: Miku, the basket, her reflection. Third: the drying ridges and the blank patch. Fourth: the shallow sheet. Fifth: the hard water line and the sky. Separate them by value steps of roughly seven percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every ridge polygon, restrained risograph grain in the wet fields, crisp flat fills in the pale sand, and fine mud only at her boots.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no other beachcomber, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no seabirds, no boats, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like a sea that has stepped back to show its floor: an enormous pale plane holding a weak mirror, one blank patch among a thousand polygons, and a girl standing with a basket of two shells as if the whole tide were hers to walk.

seeds.title: TIP DOWN
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 2:3 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “TIP DOWN”, a frame built around one colossal amber weapon, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing with her forehead against a wall, a longsword hanging from her right hand with its point resting on the floor. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes and twin-tail identity readable in the corridor's half light.

The weapon is one solid mass of orange amber glass: translucent, warm orange-brown, lit from within, and it throws orange light onto everything around it.

Use a camera at her chest height on a short lens, set close and slightly behind her left shoulder so the back of her head and her drooping arm are nearest the viewer and the wall fills the frame's right side. Place Miku at approximately forty-six percent of the canvas width, occupying about seventy percent of the frame height. Let her forehead touch the wall at the frame's upper right and the sword's point touch the floor at the lower left.

Give Miku exactly one core action: resting her head on the wall. Her forehead and the bridge of her nose press against the plaster, her right arm hangs straight down with the sword gripped loosely so the blade stands vertical on its point, and her left hand hangs open at her side. Keep her shoulders collapsed forward, her knees slightly bent, and put nothing in her left hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the sword hanging from her hand: a straight single-handed sword with a blade two fingers wide, a short crossguard and a round pommel, held at its grip near the guard so the blade drops vertically and its point bears on the floor. Keep it plain — no fuller engraving, no wrapped guard, no pommel jewel. Let it read as dead weight rather than as a held weapon.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. the blade is one piece of amber, honey-dark and translucent so the whole mass reads as one saturated stone, its interior holding a long fracture running its length and a scatter of small voids, its point blunted, and it makes no light of its own; the guard and pommel are blackened iron, worn to bright metal at the pommel's end; the grip is cord over leather, dark with sweat; the wall is painted plaster with a fine orange-peel texture and one long scuff at shoulder height; the floor is dark tile with a thin layer of dust. Each behaves differently — dull steel holds a broad weak sheen and nothing sharp, blackened iron returns a single small point at the pommel, cord reads as a fine diagonal grain, plaster holds a soft matte field with a faint texture, dark tile holds a weak reflection of the blade's lower third.

Build a stepped sequence down the frame. Begin at the upper right with her forehead against the plaster, then her hair falling forward, then her shoulder and arm hanging, then her hand and the sword's grip, then the blade's vertical length, then its point on the dark tile. The sequence must read as exhaustion held upright by a wall, not as a pose.

Leave one deliberate absence. She has no scabbard, no belt, no pack and no second weapon — nothing at all on her but her clothes. Keep the floor and the wall's lower half completely empty so the only vertical line in the frame is the blade.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the dark tile and the blade's point. Middle ground: her hanging arm, hand and the sword's grip. Background: her shoulders, the back of her head and the plaster wall. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from a single dim lamp above and behind her. The lamp is the key: a weak warm light that grazes the plaster, picks out her hair's outer strands, and leaves her face in shadow against the wall. Let the blade's lower half catch only a thin grey reflection of the tile and let the corridor behind her fall to near black. Never introduce a second source. Let the crystal pass the light rather than return it: one thin saturated amber line where the mass is thickest, and one hard-edged amber caustic patch thrown onto the dark tile beside it.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails fall forward over her shoulders and down past her arms. Both tails hang almost straight, the nearer one crossing her hanging arm as a clean aqua mass with a single warm rim from the lamp, the farther one disappearing along her back into the dark. Let the tips hang motionless with one strand separated.

Dress Miku in a worn coat over her canonical palette, not armour. A long dark teal coat hanging open, a black high-collar shirt beneath, dark trousers, and boots that have lost their shape. Keep the palette close to teal-and-black with one pale shirt collar, and let the coat's weight pull it straight so her shoulders read as sagging.

Use a warm-on-black palette with strict area control. Approximately forty-six percent of the image is shadowed corridor, twenty-four percent is the painted plaster, twelve percent is her coat, seven percent is the blade, five percent is her aqua hair, three percent is the dark tile, two percent is her hand and wrist, and one percent is the pale collar and the pommel's bright end. Keep every cold note in her hair and the crystal. The amber's honey-dark tone is the one saturated colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the corridor's own paint rather than from decoration. Let one large black ink bloom spread across the shadowed left side, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular deep-teal panel across the plaster at her shoulder height as a graphic mask, and let one vertical strip of rust-red run down the frame's left edge from top to bottom. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “TIP DOWN” once, in white paint stencilled across the plaster beside her head at the height of her ear, the strokes slightly blurred where the plaster's texture breaks them, sized so it spans about half the wall's visible width and reads clearly at thumbnail size. Put no lettering on the blade, the floor or her clothing, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The blade's lower half carries a grey bloom that stops in a clean line where the dust ends; the pommel's end is worn bright and slightly flattened; the grip's cord is dark and compressed in the exact place her fingers sit; the plaster's scuff is a long horizontal band at shoulder height from years of the same gesture; the tile is dusty except in a narrow path. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the dark tile. The tile carries the blade's lower third as one thin weak reflection, her boots as two soft dark shapes, and the pommel as a single small bright point. Never let the tile mirror her body and never extend the blade's reflection past its point.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One pale shirt collar showing at her neck, a single strand of hair stuck to the plaster beside her forehead, a fine crack running from the tile's path toward the wall, and one loose cord end at the grip. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where exhaustion would put it.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the dark tile and blade's point. Second: her hand and the grip. Third: her hanging arm and the blade's middle. Fourth: her shoulders and the back of her head. Fifth: the plaster wall and the dark corridor. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every coat fold and plaster seam, restrained risograph grain in the darkness, crisp flat fills in the lit plaster, and one clean gradient only along the blade's bloom. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the pommel.

No second character, no duplicate Miku, no crowd, no banners, no flags, no birds, no wings, no halo, no scabbard, no second sword, no additional weapon, no glowing crystal, no neon glow, no self-lit weapon, no rainbow dispersion, no stained glass, no plastic, no glass bottle, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no magical effects, no readable text beyond the string named above, no blood, no wounds, no armour plates, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no weapon in her left hand, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like the minute after everything has been spent: a forehead pressed to plaster, a sword standing on its point because her hand has stopped lifting it, and a corridor with no door in sight.

seeds.title: UNDERPASS
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 2:3 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “UNDERPASS”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing in the middle of a tiled pedestrian underpass at night, with the tunnel running away behind her in both directions. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the pale tile.

Use a camera at chest height on a slightly wide lens, set on the tunnel's centre line so the tiled walls, the ceiling strip and the floor all converge on one point behind her. Place Miku at approximately forty-eight percent of the canvas width, full body visible from shoes to hair ornaments, occupying about forty-four percent of the frame height. Let the tunnel run twelve metres behind her and close with a dark stair mouth, so the composition is a corridor with one figure at its centre.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Her right hand holds a folded newspaper against her hip, and her left hand is lifted to shoulder height, palm flat against the tile as if checking its temperature. Her head is turned a quarter toward the wall, both eyes visible. Keep the pose still, the arms clear of her face, and put nothing else in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the underpass itself: a rectangular tunnel of glazed white tile on both walls and the ceiling, a continuous painted dado at hip height, a floor of grey terrazzo, a steel drainage channel along both edges, and a strip of fluorescent battens down the centre of the ceiling. Let the tunnel occupy the whole frame, narrowing to a dark stair mouth at the far end.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The wall tile is glazed white, cracked in three places, with grout darkened by damp; the dado is painted a municipal green, chipped along its top edge; the ceiling tile is the same white, stained in rings where water has dried; the floor is grey terrazzo with pale chips, worn smooth in a continuous band down the centre; the drainage channel is cast iron with a rusted grate; the far stair is bare concrete. Each behaves differently — glazed tile holds one long highlight per batten, painted dado absorbs, terrazzo returns a dull sheen, cast iron reads as dark slots, concrete is flat and dry.

Build a stepped sequence down the tunnel. Begin at the bottom edge with the terrazzo's worn band and one cigarette end, then the drainage grate and its rust, then Miku's shoes and her hand on the tile, then the first batten's reflection on the wall, then the middle battens repeating, then the far stair's dark mouth. The sequence must read as a passage underground, not as a wall of tile.

Leave one deliberate absence. One wall panel has been removed: a rectangle of bare grey backing board about two tiles wide, with the tile edges cut clean and the backing still holding four dried adhesive pads, sits at shoulder height. Keep it on the right wall just behind her hand so the gap interrupts the tiled field at the point where she is touching it.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: terrazzo, cigarette end, drainage grate. Middle ground: Miku, her hand on the wall, the missing panel. Background: the receding battens, the far stair mouth. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the ceiling battens only. Each batten is a separate cool white source, so the tunnel is lit in repeating bands: a bright stripe along the wall at batten height, a pale pool on the floor beneath each, and shadow between bands. Add one warm spill from the stair mouth behind her, giving the far end a brown-orange edge. Keep the two temperatures separate and let the wall's reflections stay cool.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the tiled geometry. The nearer tail falls forward over her shoulder in one clean aqua mass, catching a bright stripe of batten light along its upper curve; the farther tail drops behind her back and is cut by a band of shadow into two values. Let the tails reflect faintly in the glazed tile beside her, duller and one tone warmer.

Dress Miku in an original underpass-night costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not streetwear. A dark cropped jacket worn open over a pale high-necked top, a narrow skirt, opaque tights and low boots, with a thin canvas bag across one shoulder. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment, and keep the silhouette simple enough to read at thumbnail size.

Use a cold-white palette with one warm accent and strict area control. Approximately forty-eight percent of the image is glazed white tile and its reflections, twenty percent is the cool shadow between battens, twelve percent is grey terrazzo, eight percent is the municipal green dado, six percent is Miku's dark jacket and aqua hair, four percent is the far warm stair spill, and two percent is the rusted grate. Keep the warm value confined to the far end.

Drive the printed graphic language from the tunnel's own markings rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the lower right of the floor, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular pale panel behind the wall as a graphic mask at the height of the missing tile, and let one vertical strip of municipal green run from the ceiling to the floor, aligned to a grout line. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “UNDERPASS” once, large, in dark green paint stencilled across the wall's painted dado band on the left side, spanning about two thirds of the visible dado length, in heavy condensed capitals that read clearly at thumbnail size. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “EXIT B” sit on a small enamel plate bolted to the wall beside the missing panel. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the damp. The tile grout is darker in a band at floor level and pale above; the dado is chipped in one continuous line where trolleys strike; the ceiling holds three water rings; the terrazzo is worn smooth down the centre and dull at the walls; the grate's slots hold a fine silt. Keep the wear physical and directional, never a uniform grime.

Build a second composition through reflection. The glazed wall carries Miku's figure as a pale ghost at half strength, the battens as bright vertical dashes, and the missing panel as a flat grey rectangle with no reflection at all. Let the reflection stop dead at the dado line.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A steel handrail bracket bolted through the tile, one small ceramic tile patch of a slightly different white, a folded newspaper wedged behind the drainage grate, and a short length of cable clipped along the ceiling. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where an underpass would actually have it.

Illuminate with the ceiling battens as the only key, cool and banded, plus the stair mouth's warm spill as a small secondary. Let each batten produce one bright stripe on the wall and one pale pool on the floor. Let the stair spill produce a warm edge along the far wall and a brown cast on the far floor. Keep the middle of the tunnel the brightest zone and the far mouth the warmest.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: terrazzo, cigarette end, grate. Second: Miku, her hand, her bag. Third: the missing panel and the near battens. Fourth: the middle battens repeating. Fifth: the far stair mouth and its warm spill. Separate them by value steps of roughly ten percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every grout line and grate slot, restrained risograph grain in the shadow bands, crisp flat fills in the lit areas, and fine silt only in the grate. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the glazed tile.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no passer-by, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable advertising panels, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no graffiti, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like a passage that belongs to the city's plumbing rather than its streets: a thousand white tiles repeating, one panel missing, and a girl standing with her palm flat against the wall as if testing whether the night were solid.

seeds.title: BELL
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “BELL”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing alone beside one row of empty desks in a classroom after school, seen from a level camera at the back of the room, with the desks making one flat grid of pale rectangles. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Her back is three-quarters to the camera, her head is level, and both twin tails hang quiet down her back.

The room is one flat interior with one wide window band across the upper third: three rows of pale desk lids set square to the frame at shortening intervals, one dark aisle running straight up the middle, one flat pale window band with four vertical mullions, and one dark board strip along the left edge. There is no chair stack, no bag, no book, no lettering on the board and no second figure. Every desk edge runs dead level and the aisle's two edges converge on one single point, so the picture reads as one measured grid of pale rectangles.

Use a level camera set about one metre above the floor, tilted up no more than three degrees, so the nearest desk row is broad at the bottom edge and the far rows compress into thin bars. Set the lens wide enough that the whole window band runs from edge to edge. Never angle the camera into a dutch tilt, never look down at the desks from above, and never let the window band tilt.

Give Miku exactly one core action: standing in the aisle beside the middle desk row with her feet together, one hand resting flat on the nearest desk lid and the other holding the strap of her bag at her shoulder, her head turned a quarter toward the window band. She is not sitting, not writing, not walking and not turning back toward the camera. Her whole figure stands clear of the desk edges.

Construct the dominant visual object as the desk grid against the dark floor: twelve flat pale rectangles in three rows, each row shorter and narrower than the one in front of it, with one crisp dark edge along every near side. Let the window band be the second structure, one wide pale field with four vertical mullions. Her figure is the third, one compact dark vertical in the aisle. Keep all three quiet so the bright window band stays the single light thing.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The desk lids are flat pale laminate with one fine even grain; the floor is one flat warm grey field with no board joint drawn; the window band is one flat pale value with no outside view; the board strip is one flat dark green-black; her coat is heavy charcoal wool. Each behaves differently: laminate returns one even pale value, the floor one warm mid tone, the window one pale flat, and wool one dense matte mass. seeds.title: CABLE
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “CABLE”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing on the walkway of one cable-stayed bridge at night, seen from a low camera at the deck's edge looking up along the tower, with the bridge's stay cables fanning from one point at the tower's top down to the deck as one radial field of bright lines. She stands at the walkway rail with her body turned three-quarters away, her head lifted toward the tower, and both twin tails hanging down her back.

The bridge is one single span, not a harbour and not a waterfront: one straight deck running out of the frame at the bottom, one single tower rising out of the top edge, exactly nine stay cables fanning down the near side of that tower, and one parapet rail running along the deck beside her. There is no second tower and no second cable plane. The tower rises dead centre in the frame, the nine cables radiate from one small anchor block at its top, and the deck's parapet runs as one straight horizontal across the bottom third.

Use a tall camera set at rail height on the walkway, tilted up about thirty-five degrees so the tower's shaft fills the frame's middle and its top runs out of the upper edge. Set the lens wide enough that the two nearest cables are cropped by the side rules and the deck's parapet crosses the bottom third at a slight upward angle. Never look down at the deck from above, never shoot the bridge from the shore, and never let the tower lean off the centre line.

Give Miku exactly one core action: standing still at the parapet with both hands resting flat on its top rail, her body turned three-quarters away from the camera, her head lifted toward the tower's top. She is not leaning over the rail, not walking, not holding a phone and not turning to the camera. Her weight is even on both feet, her shoulders stay level with the parapet, and her chin is lifted so the underside of her jaw catches the city light from below.

Construct the dominant visual object as the cable fan: one tower of pale concrete split into two legs by one narrow central gap, one anchor block at its top, and nine bright steel cables running from that block down to nine separate points along the parapet, each cable a single straight line at its own angle so the nine together read as one measured fan. Let the fan be the largest structure in the picture and let the figure be one small vertical standing at the parapet. The nine cables are the only diagonal lines in the frame and the parapet is its only horizontal; keep every other surface flat and quiet.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The tower is pale poured concrete, matte and faintly mottled, lit only along its left face; the cables are thick steel strands in a smooth dark grey sheath, each carrying one thin bright edge along its upper side; the deck is dark asphalt; the parapet is pale concrete with one dull steel top rail; the city behind is a flat field of small lights; the water below is a single dark plane. Each behaves differently: concrete returns one flat pale tone, the cable sheaths hold one narrow specular line each, asphalt is a near-black even field, steel is a dull grey with a hard highlight, and the city is a pointillist field of tiny lights rather than a skyline of buildings. Keep the whole frame matte and never let the water act as a mirror.

Build a radial composition instead of a stepped one: one anchor block at the top, nine lines running out and down from it, one parapet crossing the bottom third, and one deck below. Begin at the top edge with the tower's shaft running out of frame, then the anchor block, then the nine cables fanning outward at widening angles, then her standing figure against the parapet, then the parapet's rail, and end at the dark deck along the bottom edge. Every cable must start at the same point and end at its own separate point on the rail, so the picture reads as one measured fan rather than as scattered wires.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is no car, no truck, no bus, no motorcycle, no cyclist, no pedestrian, no second figure, no lamp post, no sign, no camera housing, no maintenance platform, no scaffold, no crane, no boat, no ferry, no bird and no floating debris anywhere in the frame. Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the parapet's top rail and her two hands resting flat on it, both dark. Middle ground: her standing figure, the nine cables running down to their anchor points, and the deck behind her. Background: the tower's shaft filling the frame's middle, the city's field of small lights on both sides of it, and the dark water below the deck. Separate them by value rather than by blur: the rail and her hands stay near black, the tower holds the palest value, and the city sits one step below the cables. Let her dark figure read as a clean silhouette against the lit tower.

Light the scene from the city and the bridge's own lamps and from nothing else. There is no moon, no sky glow and no light from the camera side. Her face turned up toward the tower must stay readable, her coat must stay a clean dark mass, and her hair must keep one cool edge where the city light reaches it. Never add a second light, never brighten the sky, never let the water glow and never spill the amber across the whole deck.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails hang down her back as she stands. Both lengths drop past her waist and end below her coat's hem, and the city's low amber rims each tail along its lower edge so both read as dark ribbons with one warm line beneath. Keep both tails inside her silhouette, clear of her hands on the rail, and let the nearer tail cross in front of the farther one by a hand's width so the two read as two separate lengths.

Dress Miku in a dark charcoal wool coat that reaches below her knees, worn open over a black knit top and dark straight trousers, with short black leather boots and a narrow dark scarf at her throat. The coat's collar stands at the back of her neck, its hem hangs clear of the deck, and its shoulders stay square as she leans her hands on the rail. Keep the outfit unpatterned and keep her only warm note to a thin brass zip at the coat's front, so her figure stays one dark mass against the pale tower.

Use an amber-on-black palette with strict area control. Keep every saturated note in the city's points and along the cable rims, keep the water near black, and let the tower's pale face be the one large light value in the frame.

Drive the printed graphic language from the cable fan rather than from decoration. Let each cable print as one straight flat grey line with a single crisp bright edge, and let the nine together print as one radial figure whose angles widen evenly from top to bottom. Add one wide horizontal band of flat amber across the city's light field behind her, and let one thin vertical strip of pale grey run down the frame's left edge from the sky to the water line. Keep every graphic element square to the frame and keep all three behind the figure rather than over her.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “CABLE” once, stencilled flat in pale paint across the dark bridge deck in the clear near foreground of the lower third, well in front of her boots and with nothing crossing the letters, the letters set square to the frame, each letter as tall as her boot, and the whole word spanning about a third of the frame's width so it reads clearly even at thumbnail size. Let the letters read as flat pale marks lying on the deck with one crisp edge and no cable or railing over them. Put no lettering on the parapet, the cables, the towers or her coat, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The parapet's top rail is polished pale in one short stretch where hands rest; the tower's left face holds one long vertical water stain; the lowest cable's sheath is scuffed where it meets its anchor; the deck's asphalt is worn smoother along one walking line; and her boot toes are scuffed pale. Keep the wear directional and small, all of it running with the bridge's own lines rather than across them.

Build a second composition through the city lights. Let the light field read as one flat band of small amber points laid on a grid of dark streets, denser at its lower edge and thinning toward the sky, with each point a solid square rather than a glow. Let that field stay a texture rather than a skyline, with no building shapes drawn into it, no windows and no logos, and let it be broken only where the tower's shaft and the nine cables cross in front of it.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One thin brass zip at her coat's front, one fine bright edge along the nearest cable's anchor, one small chip on the parapet's top corner, and one loose thread at her coat's cuff. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where use would put it, and keep no more than four such points in the whole frame.

Maintain five readable depth layers. First: the parapet's rail and her hands on it, near black. Second: her standing figure and her two hanging tails. Third: the nine cables running down to the rail and the deck behind her. Fourth: the tower's shaft and its anchor block at the top. Fifth: the amber city field and the pale sky above. Separate them by value steps of roughly thirteen percent each, and let no layer borrow an edge from the one behind it.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp flat concrete planes with precisely printed edges, nine straight cable lines each carrying one hard bright edge, a pointillist amber city field, restrained risograph grain only in the dark deck and the water, and one soft gradient only inside the sky band. Keep the whole image matte; no glow around the city points, no reflected bridge in the water, no lens flare and no bloom.

The final image should feel like standing under a bridge that is holding its own weight in the dark: one pale tower rising out of the frame, nine steel cables fanning down from a single anchor to a single rail, a black deck underfoot, a field of amber city points behind, and one small figure at the rail with her chin lifted and the word CABLE stencilled on the concrete beside her.
