Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Her body faces away from the camera and only her head turns, so the frame shows her back, one shoulder line and the near side of her face at once.

The crossing is one single intersection, not a street scene and not a plaza: exactly four crosswalks meeting at one square of asphalt, each crosswalk built from a set of broad flat white bars of equal width and equal spacing, and four corner poles carrying the only light fixtures in the frame. There is no fifth road and no stray stripe. The bars of the two nearest crosswalks run toward the camera and the bars of the two far ones run away from it, so the four sets meet at one shared geometry in the middle of the frame and their edges converge on the point where she stands.

Use a wide camera set at chest height on the centre line of the near crosswalk, absolutely level, with no tilt and no dutch angle, so the white bars run as straight horizontals across the bottom of the frame and the far crosswalks compress into two narrowing fields above them. Set the lens wide enough that the nearest bars are cropped by the left and right frame rules. Never look down at the crossing, never tilt up into the signs, and never let the camera leave the centre line.

Give Miku exactly one core action: standing still on the middle bar of the near crosswalk with her back to the camera and her head turned back over her right shoulder, both boots planted flat on the wet asphalt, her arms hanging at her sides, her chin lifted slightly. She is not walking, not stepping, not turning her whole body and not looking away. Her head turns only far enough for one aqua eye and the edge of her cheek to be visible past her shoulder, and her twin tails swing a little toward the turn without leaving her back.

Construct the dominant visual object as the crossing's own geometry: one square of wet black asphalt, four sets of white bars meeting at its centre, four corner poles of equal height standing at the corners of the frame, and one single signal head on each pole. Let the white bars be the largest and flattest thing in the picture and let the figure be a small dark vertical standing on them. The repeated bars are the only repeating structure in the frame; the four signal heads are its single interruption. Keep every bar the same width and the same spacing, and keep the asphalt free of arrows, lane markings, manholes, drains, painted symbols and tyre marks.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The asphalt is wet black tarmac, matte and slightly rough, holding flat colour instead of any reflection; the bars are thick matte white road paint, worn thin at their edges; the poles are dark grey painted steel with a faint orange rust at the base; the two light panels behind are flat solid colour from edge to edge with no frame, no image and no lettering; her coat is dark navy wool; her scarf is deep red. Each behaves differently: asphalt returns one flat black field with no sheen and no mirrored figure, paint holds one even white with a soft grey edge, steel holds one narrow vertical highlight, acrylic is a single flat glowing plane, wool is a dense matte mass, and the scarf is the one warm note. Keep the whole frame matte and never let the wet ground act as a mirror.

Build a radiating sequence from the centre out instead of a stepped one. Begin at her boots standing on the middle bar, then the two bars nearest the camera cropped by the bottom edge, then the bars behind her narrowing toward the far side, then the two far crosswalks compressing into fields of short white dashes, then the four corner poles standing at the frame's corners, and end at the flat dark wall of signs above. Every interval must shorten as it moves away from her, so the picture reads as one measured spread outward and not as a scatter of stripes.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is no car, no taxi, no bus, no bicycle, no scooter, no pedestrian, no second figure, no crowd, no dog, no bird, no traffic cone, no barrier, no vending machine, no shop front at ground level, no crossing guard, no puddle with a reflection of her, and no umbrella anywhere in the frame. Nothing stands on the asphalt but her. Keep the whole far side of the crossing completely empty so the white bars run out of the frame with nothing standing on them.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the two nearest white bars cropped by the bottom edge and the wet black asphalt between them, both near black and near white with nothing in between. Middle ground: the small standing figure with one eye visible past her shoulder and the bars spreading out from her boots. Background: the two far crosswalks as compressed fields of dashes, the four corner poles, and the two tall flat light panels standing above them. Separate them by value rather than by blur: the near bars are the brightest white in the frame, the far dashes fall to a dull grey, and the signs sit behind everything as one saturated band of colour.

Light the crossing from two tall flat light panels standing behind it and from nothing else. One panel is solid magenta and stands on the right behind her shoulder, one is solid cyan and stands on the left; each is a plain flat rectangle of colour with no lettering, no image and no frame, and each is the only source in its half of the frame. There is no sun, no moon, no daylight, no street lamp above the frame and no key light from the camera side. The magenta panel washes the right ends of the white bars and the right side of her coat, the cyan panel washes the left ends and the left side, and the middle of every bar where the two washes meet stays a clean neutral white. The four signal heads hold their own small coloured faces. The lower half of the frame stays close to black and white with only those two flat washes over it. Her back must stay a dark shape against the coloured band, her turned face must keep both the eye and the cheek readable, and the red scarf must be the only warm value in the lower half. Never add a front fill, never brighten the asphalt evenly and never let the signs flare into a bloom.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails hang down her back as she stands. Both lengths fall past her waist and end below her coat's hem, and the turn of her head swings the nearer tail outward so it breaks her shoulder line on the right. Let the magenta wash behind her rim each tail along its outer edge and keep the aqua reading as one clean cool note against the warm band. Keep both tails inside the frame, clear of the scarf's hanging end and clear of her arms.

Dress Miku in a long dark navy wool coat worn open over a short pleated skirt and dark tights, with a deep red scarf wrapped once at her neck and one end hanging down her back, and short dark leather boots with a low heel. The coat's shoulders stay square across her back, its hem stays clear of the ground, and the scarf's fringe hangs free so its silhouette reads against the white bars. Keep the outfit unpatterned so the only colour in her figure is the scarf, and let her dark mass sit as one solid vertical against the flat white paint.

Use a magenta-on-black palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty-eight percent of the image is the wet black asphalt holding flat colour, sixteen percent is the matte white bars, fourteen percent is the flat magenta wash from the signs, twelve percent is the flat cyan wash on the left, twelve percent is her dark coat and tights with her hair and her one visible eye, and eight percent is the grey steel of the four poles. Keep every saturated note in the sign band and the signal heads, keep the lower half close to black and white only, and let the red scarf be the one warm exception.

Drive the printed graphic language from the crossing's own stripes rather than from decoration. Let the four sets of bars print as one flat geometric figure, each bar a solid rectangle with a crisply printed edge and no gradient inside it, and let the bars crop hard at the frame's edges rather than fading out. Add one wide horizontal band of flat cyan across the far crosswalks as a graphic mask, and let one thin vertical strip of magenta run down the frame's right edge from the top to the asphalt. Keep every graphic element square to the frame and keep all three behind or beside the figure rather than over her.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “CROSSING” once, in flat white paint stamped across the two nearest bars in the lower third of the frame, the letters set square to the frame and sized so they span about a third of the frame's width and read clearly at thumbnail size. Let the letters sit as paint on paint, slightly worn at the edges where tyres would pass. Put no lettering on her coat, her scarf, the poles, the signs or the asphalt beyond that one word, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The white bars are worn thin along their centre where tyres cross them, the asphalt holds one faint dry patch near the left corner pole, the steel poles are rusted at their bases, the acrylic signs are scratched in one long diagonal on the right, and her boots are scuffed pale at the toes. Keep the wear directional and small, all of it running along the crossing's own lines rather than across them.

Build a second composition through the two panels. The magenta panel and the cyan panel stand as two large flat rectangles of pure colour behind the crossing, each one even from edge to edge, their inner edges running straight down the frame and their tops running out of the top edge, so the two of them close the background as two walls of colour rather than as a city. Let them stay two tones rather than two scenes, with no lettering, no figures, no windows and no interiors inside either of them, and let each be broken only where one corner pole crosses in front of it.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One narrow silver buckle on the scarf's pin, one fine bright edge along the nearest white bar's worn lip, one thin line of dried water at the edge of the asphalt, and one loose thread at her coat's hem. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where use would put it, and keep no more than four such points in the whole frame.

Maintain five readable depth layers. First: the two nearest white bars and the asphalt between them, near black and near white. Second: the small standing figure and her red scarf on the middle bar. Third: the bars spreading away from her boots and the two far crosswalks. Fourth: the four corner poles standing at the frame's corners. Fifth: the flat lit sign band above. Separate them by value steps of roughly thirteen percent each, and let no layer borrow an edge from the one behind it.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp flat white bars with precisely printed edges, clean flat magenta and cyan washes, restrained risograph grain only in the black asphalt, and no gradient anywhere except one soft falloff inside the nearest signal head. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlight on the ground, no reflected figure, no bloom on the signs, and let the only soft edge in the picture be the rim of her hair.

No second character, no duplicate figure, no crowd, no pedestrian, no reflected figure, no mirrored body, no reflection of her in the wet asphalt, no puddle holding her shape, no face in the signs, no large face in the background, no third crosswalk, no diagonal stripes, no arrows, no lane markings, no painted symbols, no manhole, no drain, no tyre marks, no car, no taxi, no bus, no bicycle, no scooter, no cart, no vehicle of any kind, no traffic cone, no barrier, no vending machine, no street furniture, no shop front at ground level, no umbrella, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no readable text beyond the string named above, no sunlight, no moon, no daylight, no long cast shadow across the bars, no lit shop windows, no building facade with windows, no neon tube signage, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no photographic depth of field, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter, no drop shadow under the figure.

The final image should feel like the moment a city holds its breath: four sets of white bars meeting under one small figure with her head turned back, two flat washes of magenta and cyan standing behind her as walls of colour, and the word CROSSING painted straight across the bars at her feet.

seeds.title: DUNE
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “DUNE”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character sitting on the crest of one sand dune at sunset, seen from a level camera square to the ridge, with the dunes making five wide flat bands of warm colour under one pale sun disc. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Her body is side-on to the camera, her chin is level, and both twin tails hang quiet down her back.

The desert is one flat field of five wide horizontal bands: five dune crests of slightly different warm value crossing the full width of the frame at measured intervals, one pale sun disc sitting exactly on the highest crest, one flat pale orange sky above it, and one narrow dark foreground band at the bottom. There is no ripple drawn, no plant, no rock, no camel and no second figure. Every crest runs dead level and the horizon stays dead level, so the picture reads as one measured stack of warm bands under one circle.

Use a level camera set about one metre above the sand, its sensor exactly parallel to the dune crests, so all five bands stay horizontal and the sun disc stays a true circle. Set the lens wide enough that the whole sky and the foreground band fit inside the frame. Never angle the camera, never let the bands converge, and never tilt the frame.

Give Miku exactly one core action: seated on the near crest with her knees together and both hands braced flat on the sand behind her hips, her chin level and her head turned a quarter toward the sun. She is not standing, not walking, not lying down and not turning back toward the camera. Her whole figure sits inside the foreground band and no crest cuts across her at the waist.

Construct the dominant visual object as the five dune bands against the pale sky: five wide flat warm rectangles of slightly different value, each with one crisp upper edge and one softer lower edge, each shallower than the one in front of it. Let the sun disc be the second structure, one flat pale circle with one hard edge. The foreground band is the third, one narrow dark bar. Keep all three quiet so the single circle stays the loud thing.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The sand is flat matte warm ochre with no grain, no ripple and no sparkle; the five bands are five stepped warm tones with no gradient inside them; the sun disc is one flat pale cream with no halo and no glow; the sky is one flat pale orange; her coat is heavy charcoal wool. Each behaves differently: sand returns one even warm value, the bands five stepped flats, the disc one clean pale circle, and wool one dense matte mass. Keep the whole frame matte and let no sand shine.

Build a receding sequence instead of a stepped one. Begin at the bottom edge with the narrow dark foreground band and the stencilled word, then the nearest and widest dune crest and her seated figure, then the second and third crests at shortening intervals, then the fourth and fifth crests, and end at the pale sun disc and the flat orange sky. Every band must be shallower than the one in front of it, so the picture reads as one measured recession across a single plane.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is no ripple line, no plant, no cactus, no rock, no camel, no footprint, no track, no cloud, no second figure, no bird, no halo around the sun and no cast shadow of a person. Nothing stands in the frame but her. Keep the whole right third of the sky empty so the flat warm field carries that side alone.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the narrow dark band, the stencilled word, the nearest crest and her seated figure. Middle ground: the second and third dune bands and her braced hands. Background: the fourth and fifth bands, the pale sun disc and the flat orange sky. Separate them by value rather than by blur: the foreground holds one deep warm dark, the near dunes one mid ochre, the far dunes a paler ochre, and the sky the brightest warm value. Let her dark coat cut a clean vertical into the pale distance.

Light the desert from the low sun disc and the flat sky and from nothing else. The sky holds one even pale orange value from edge to edge, the sun disc stays one flat pale circle with no halo, and every dune band keeps its own stepped warm value with one narrow cool edge along each crest. There is no ray, no glare, no sparkle on the sand, no hard cast shadow and no glow around the disc. Her face is turned away so only the edge of her cheek is visible, her coat must stay distinct from the foreground band, and the bands must stay flat colour fields rather than a gradient. Never brighten the near sand, never add a second light, and never let the sun bloom.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails hang quiet down her back without lifting, the nearer one a shade darker than the farther one, so they read as two still vertical lines against the horizontal bands. Let the flat field behind her make both tails read as dark aqua ribbons with one cool edge, keep their tips well inside the frame, and keep them clear of her arms.

Dress Miku in a heavy charcoal wool coat that reaches below her knees, worn closed with the collar turned up, over dark straight trousers tucked into short dark leather boots with pale rubber soles. The coat hangs still in the still air, the collar stands at the back of her neck, and the sleeves pull straight at her sides. Keep the outfit unpatterned so the five dune bands stays the only broad structure in the frame.

Use a ochre-on-cream palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty-eight percent of the image is the five warm dune bands, twenty-four percent is the flat pale orange sky, fourteen percent is her dark charcoal coat and boots, eleven percent is the narrow dark foreground band, nine percent is the pale sun disc, and four percent is the cool edges along the crests. Keep the cream disc the only pale note in the entire frame, keep the sand free of any blue cast, and let the five bands and the single circle do all the work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the dune bands rather than from decoration. Let the five bands print as five wide flat warm horizontal rectangles of stepped value with one crisp upper edge each, and let the foreground print as one narrow dark bar along the bottom. Add one wide horizontal strip of flat pale orange across the upper third, and let one thin vertical strip of warm white run down the frame's right edge from the sky to the foreground. Keep every graphic element square to the frame except the disc, and keep all of them behind or under the figure rather than over her.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “DUNE” once, stencilled flat in deep charcoal across the nearest warm dune band in the clear near foreground of the lower third, well in front of her boots and with nothing crossing the letters, the letters set square to the frame, each letter as tall as her boot, and the whole word spanning about a third of the frame's width so it reads clearly even at thumbnail size. Let the letters read as flat marks lying on the surface with one crisp edge and no shadow over them. Put no lettering on the upper bands, the sun disc, the sky or the foreground band or her coat, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The sand under her braced hands is pressed into two small flatter ovals; the nearest crest holds one fine pale line; one band has a slightly uneven edge; and her boots carry a thin rim of sand at their soles. Keep the wear directional and small, all of it running with the frame's main lines rather than across them.

Build a second composition through the sky. Let the sky read as one flat pale orange field with a single slightly paler band just above the highest crest, banded rather than graded, with no cloud drawn into it and no halo around the sun. Let that field stay a tone rather than an image, with no birds and no distant hills, and let it be broken only where her head and the sun disc cut into it.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One small wooden toggle at the coat's collar, one fine stitch line along the shoulder seam, one tiny scuff on her rear boot's heel, and one loose thread at the coat hem. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where use would put it, and keep no more than four such points in the whole frame.

Maintain five readable depth layers. First: the narrow dark foreground band, the stencilled word and the nearest crest along the bottom edge. Second: her seated figure, her braced hands and the second band. Third: the third band. Fourth: the fourth and fifth bands. Fifth: the pale sun disc and the flat orange sky. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each, and let no layer borrow an edge from the one behind it.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp flat planes with precisely printed edges, a clean hard contour on the figure, restrained risograph grain only in the shadowed fields, and no gradient anywhere except the faint lift at the horizon. Keep the whole image matte; no glare, no sparkle, no lens flare and no bloom.

Exclude every failure mode explicitly: no second figure, no extra limb, no extra twin tail, no floating foot, no mirrored duplicate, no visible shaft or beam of light in the air, no sun disc, no cloud shapes, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no readable text beyond the string named above, no ripple line, no plant, no footprint, no halo around the sun, no cloud, no gradient in the sky, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no photographic depth of field, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter, no drop shadow under the figure.

Close on one quiet fact. The whole picture is five flat warm dune bands, one pale sun circle, one small seated figure and one word stencilled across the near sand. Everything else has been removed so the single measured structure can carry the frame alone.

seeds.title: SHARED

Both figures have their backs to the camera, both heads are level, and Miku's twin tails hang quiet down her back on the left of the pair.

The street is one flat pale plane with one wide dark umbrella circle sitting in the upper middle: one even wet pavement field from the bottom edge to a dead-level far edge, one big flat dark circle for the umbrella canopy with eight short ribs, one pale wall of fine vertical rain behind it, and two small dark figures standing side by side beneath it. There is no building, no sign, no car and no puddle reflection. The far edge is dead level across the whole frame and every rain line runs dead vertical, so the picture reads as one circle over one vertical field over one horizontal plane.

Use a level camera set about one metre above the pavement, tilted up no more than three degrees, so the umbrella sits in the upper third and the two figures fit fully beneath it. Set the lens wide enough that both figures and the whole canopy stay inside the frame. Never look down at the street from above, never crop the umbrella, and never let the far edge tilt.

Give the pair exactly one core action: walking away side by side, both of them holding the same umbrella handle between them with one hand each, their shoulders almost touching and their steps matched. They are not facing each other, not embracing, not turning back and not holding separate umbrellas. Both figures stand fully on the pavement with both feet visible, and the single handle is the one contact point that joins them.

Construct the dominant visual object as the umbrella circle against the rain field: one wide flat dark disc with eight short ribs meeting at one centre point, one clean hard outer edge, and one straight thin handle running down from its centre into the pair's joined hands. Let the two figures be the second structure, two compact dark verticals of equal height standing close together. The rain lines are the third, one even field of fine pale vertical strokes. Keep all three quiet so the single circle stays the loud thing.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The canopy is flat matte near-black fabric with no shine and no wet highlight; the rain is one flat pale grey field of fine vertical strokes with no droplet drawn; the pavement is one flat pale wet grey with no mirror sheen and no reflected figure; the handle is one thin dark line; both coats are heavy charcoal wool. Each behaves differently: fabric returns one flat dark disc, rain one pale field, pavement one even grey, and wool one dense matte mass. Keep the whole frame matte and let no surface reflect either figure.

Build a receding sequence instead of a stepped one. Begin at the bottom edge with the nearest wet pavement and the stencilled word, then the two pairs of boots, then the two figures and their joined hands on the single handle, then the canopy's near rim, then its eight ribs, and end at the flat pale rain field and the dead-level far edge. Every rib must be shorter than the one in front of it, so the picture reads as one measured recession across a single plane.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is no second umbrella, no third figure, no building, no sign, no car, no lamp, no puddle, no reflected or mirrored image of either figure, no bird, no bench, no bin, no tree and no cast shadow of a person. Nothing stands in the frame but her. Keep the whole left third of the rain field empty so the pale vertical strokes carry that side alone.

Middle ground: the two pairs of boots, the two figures, their joined hands and the single handle. Background: the canopy rim, the eight ribs, the pale rain field and the level far edge. Separate them by value rather than by blur: the pavement holds one pale grey, the two coats one deep dark, the canopy one near-black, and the rain the lightest field. Let the two dark verticals read clearly beneath the disc.

Light the street with one flat overcast sky and from nothing else. The overcast fills the scene evenly so the pavement holds one pale value from edge to edge and the rain field stays one even grey, while the canopy keeps one flat near-black value with one narrow cool edge along its rim. There is no sun, no lamp, no glow, no sparkle on the wet ground and no hard cast shadow. Both faces are turned away, both coats must stay distinct from the canopy, and the rain must stay a flat field of strokes rather than a haze. Never brighten the near pavement, never add a second light, and never let the street reflect a figure.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails hang quiet down Miku's back without lifting, both lengths falling on the left of the pair so they read as two still vertical lines beside her companion. Let the flat field behind her make both tails read as dark aqua ribbons with one cool edge, keep their tips well inside the frame, and keep them clear of her arms.

Dress Miku in a heavy charcoal wool coat that reaches below her knees, worn closed with the collar turned up, over dark straight trousers tucked into short dark leather boots with pale rubber soles. The coat hangs still in the still air, the collar stands at the back of her neck, and the sleeves pull straight at her sides. Use a pale-on-black palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty-eight percent of the image is the flat pale rain field, twenty-four percent is the flat pale wet pavement, fourteen percent is the wide near-black umbrella canopy, ten percent is the two dark charcoal coats and boots, nine percent is the thin handle and the eight ribs, and five percent is the cool edge along the canopy rim. Keep the canopy the only dark mass in the upper half, keep the pavement free of any blue cast, and let the single circle and the two small verticals do all the work.

Let the rain read as one flat pale grey field with a single slightly cooler band just above the far edge, banded rather than graded, with no cloud, no building and no droplet drawn into it. seeds.title: TILT
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “TILT”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing in one narrow night alley, seen from a level camera square to the walls, with two tall dark wall bars closing into a flat pale slot at the far end. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Her back is to the camera, her head is level, and both twin tails hang quiet down her back.

The alley is one tall rectangle: two wide flat dark wall bars along the left and right edges, one narrow pale slot of light at the far end, one flat dark paving field running from the bottom edge to that slot, and one thin pale strip of sky along the top edge. There is no window, no door, no pipe, no sign and no second figure. Both walls stand dead vertical and the paving's two edges converge on one single point, so the picture reads as one measured perspective between two flat bars without any tilt in the frame.

Use a level camera set about one metre above the paving, with its sensor exactly parallel to the walls, so both wall edges stay dead vertical from top to bottom. Set the lens wide enough that the pale slot sits in the upper third. Never angle the camera into a dutch tilt, never look down at the paving from above, and never let the horizon or the wall edges lean.

Separate them by value rather than by blur: the aisle holds one dark grey, the seat one pale value, the glass one near-black, and the streaks the brightest notes. Let her compact figure read clearly against the seat.

Light the carriage from the six window streaks and from nothing else. The streaks hold one flat pale value with no glow around them, the seat keeps one even pale value, and the rest of the carriage stays in one deep dark value. There is no ceiling lamp, no station light, no motion blur, no reflection in the glass and no hard cast shadow. One cheek must read clearly, her coat must stay distinct from the glass, and the streaks must stay flat bars rather than a glowing rush. Never brighten the near aisle, never add a second light, and never let the streaks bloom.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails fall quiet along the seat back without lifting, the nearer one a shade darker than the farther one, so they read as two still vertical lines against the pale seat band. Let the flat field behind her make both tails read as dark aqua ribbons with one cool edge, keep their tips well inside the frame, and keep them clear of her arms.

Dress Miku in a heavy charcoal wool coat that reaches below her knees, worn closed with the collar turned up, over dark straight trousers tucked into short dark leather boots with pale rubber soles. The coat hangs still in the still air, the collar stands at the back of her neck, and the sleeves pull straight at her sides. Keep the outfit unpatterned so the six pale window streaks stays the only broad structure in the frame.

Use a dark-on-streak palette with strict area control. Approximately forty-two percent of the image is the flat near-black window glass, twenty percent is the six pale horizontal streaks, fourteen percent is the pale seat band, ten percent is her dark charcoal coat and boots, nine percent is the dark aisle strip, and five percent is the two dark window mullions. Keep the streaks the only bright note in the entire frame, keep the seat free of any yellow cast, and let the six rules and the dark glass do all the work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the streaks rather than from decoration. Let the streaks print as six wide flat pale horizontal bars of equal length with one crisp edge each, and let the two mullions print as two crisp dark vertical bars crossing them. Add one narrow horizontal strip of pale white across the lower third for the seat, and let one thin vertical strip of deep grey run down the frame's right edge from the window to the aisle. Keep every graphic element square to the frame and keep all of them behind or under the figure rather than over her.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “LAST” once, stencilled flat in pale white across the dark aisle strip in the clear near foreground of the lower third, well in front of her boots and with nothing crossing the letters, the letters set square to the frame, each letter as tall as her boot, and the whole word spanning about a third of the frame's width so it reads clearly even at thumbnail size. Let the letters read as flat marks lying on the surface with one crisp edge and no shadow over them. Put no lettering on the window streaks, the seat band, the mullions or the glass or her coat, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The aisle under her boots is worn smooth in one small oval; the seat's near edge holds one fine dark line; one streak has a slightly uneven end; and her boots carry a thin rim of dust at their soles. Keep the wear directional and small, all of it running with the frame's main lines rather than across them.

Build a second composition through the glass. Let the glass read as one flat near-black field with a single slightly paler strip just above the seat, banded rather than detailed, with no outside view, no station, no tunnel and no reflection drawn into it. Let that field stay a tone rather than an image, with no silhouette, and let it be broken only where the six streaks and the two mullions cross it.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One small wooden toggle at the coat's collar, one fine stitch line along the shoulder seam, one tiny scuff on her rear boot's heel, and one loose thread at the coat hem. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where use would put it, and keep no more than four such points in the whole frame.

Maintain five readable depth layers. First: the dark aisle and the stencilled word along the bottom edge. Second: the seat's near edge and her boots. Third: her seated figure, her folded hands and the seat band. Fourth: the first through fourth streaks and the two mullions. Fifth: the fifth and sixth streaks and the window's top edge. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each, and let no layer borrow an edge from the one behind it.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp flat planes with precisely printed edges, a clean hard contour on the figure, restrained risograph grain only in the shadowed fields, and no gradient anywhere except the faint lift at the horizon. Keep the whole image matte; no glare, no sparkle, no lens flare and no bloom.

Exclude every failure mode explicitly: no second figure, no extra limb, no extra twin tail, no floating foot, no mirrored duplicate, no visible shaft or beam of light in the air, no sun disc, no cloud shapes, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no readable text beyond the string named above, no other passenger, no advertising panel, no hanging strap, no reflection, no station sign, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no photographic depth of field, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter, no drop shadow under the figure.

Close on one quiet fact. The whole picture is one flat dark window, six pale horizontal streaks, one narrow pale seat, one small seated figure and one word stencilled across the near aisle. Everything else has been removed so the single measured structure can carry the frame alone.

seeds.title: LAMP
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “LAMP”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character seated at one long reading table at night, seen from a high camera almost directly above, with a single pale circle of lamplight lying flat on the dark table. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Her head is turned a little toward the lamp, one cheek reads clearly, and both twin tails spill off the chair onto the dark floor.

The table is one wide flat dark rectangle seen from directly above: one pale circle of lamplight sitting at its centre, one small dark lamp base at the circle's edge, one open pale book rectangle inside the circle, and two dark shelf bands running dead vertical along the left and right edges. There is no second lamp, no chair stack, no window and no other reader. Every edge runs parallel to a frame edge, so the picture reads as one pale circle inside one dark rectangle.

Use a camera set directly above the table, its sensor exactly parallel to its surface, so the lamplight circle stays a true circle and both shelf bands stay parallel. Set the lens wide enough to hold the whole table and both shelf bands. Never angle the camera, never let the shelf lines converge, and never tilt the frame.

Give Miku exactly one core action: seated square to the table with both forearms resting flat on its surface, one hand holding the edge of the open book and the other lying beside the lamp base, her knees together under the table and both boots flat on the floor. She is not standing, not writing, not turning a page and not turning back toward the camera. Her whole figure stays outside the pale circle's far half.

Construct the dominant visual object as the pale lamplight circle against the dark table: one flat even pale disc with one hard clean edge, one small dark lamp base breaking its rim, and one pale book rectangle lying inside it. Let the shelf bands be the second structure, two tall dark bars. Her figure is the third, one compact dark shape at the near edge. Keep all three quiet so the single circle stays the loud thing.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The lamplight is one flat matte pale value with no gradient, no halo and no glow; the table is one flat dark walnut field with a fine even grain; the book is one flat pale rectangle with no lettering on its pages; the shelf bands are one flat near-black with no book spines drawn; her coat is heavy charcoal wool. Each behaves differently: the disc returns one even pale value, walnut one deep dark, the book one pale flat, and wool one dense matte mass. Keep the whole frame matte and let no lamp bloom.

Build a receding sequence instead of a stepped one. Begin at the bottom edge with the near table edge and the stencilled word, then her boots and the chair, then the near half of the dark table and her seated figure, then the pale circle and the book, then the far half of the table and the lamp base, and end at the two shelf bands and the dark top edge. Every band must be shallower than the one in front of it, so the picture reads as one measured stack upward across a single flat frame.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is no second lamp, no second reader, no chair stack, no window, no book spine detail, no lettering on the pages, no cup, no clock, no poster, no reflected image and no cast shadow of a person. Nothing stands in the frame but her. Keep the whole upper left of the dark table empty so the two shelf bands carry that corner alone.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the near table edge, the chair and the stencilled word. Middle ground: her boots, her seated figure, her forearms and the near half of the table. Background: the pale circle, the book, the lamp base and the two dark shelf bands. Separate them by value rather than by blur: the table holds one deep dark, her coat a shade lighter, the book one pale value, and the circle the brightest note. Let her two hands read clearly at the circle's edge.

Light the table from the single lamp and from nothing else. The lamp throws one flat pale circle onto the table with one hard edge and leaves everything outside it in one even deep dark value, with one narrow cool edge along the book's spine. There is no halo, no glow around the circle, no second light, no window light and no hard cast shadow of a person. One cheek must read clearly, her coat must stay distinct from the table, and the circle must stay a flat disc rather than a glow. Never brighten the near table, never add a second light, and never let the lamp bloom.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails spill off the chair onto the dark floor in two wide soft curves, the nearer one ending lower than the farther one, so they answer the hard edge of the pale circle. Let the flat field behind her make both tails read as dark aqua ribbons with one cool edge, keep their tips well inside the frame, and keep them clear of her arms.

Dress Miku in a heavy charcoal wool coat that reaches below her knees, worn closed with the collar turned up, over dark straight trousers tucked into short dark leather boots with pale rubber soles. The coat hangs still in the still air, the collar stands at the back of her neck, and the sleeves pull straight at her sides. Keep the outfit unpatterned so the single pale circle stays the only broad structure in the frame.

Use a dark-on-pale palette with strict area control. Approximately forty-four percent of the image is the flat dark walnut table, twenty percent is the two near-black shelf bands, fourteen percent is the pale lamplight circle, ten percent is her dark charcoal coat and boots, eight percent is the pale book rectangle, and four percent is the small dark lamp base. Keep the circle the only bright note in the entire frame, keep the table free of any blue cast, and let the single disc and the two dark bars do all the work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the circle rather than from decoration. Let the circle print as one flat pale disc with one crisp edge, and let the two shelf bands print as two tall flat dark bars running the full height of the frame. Add one narrow horizontal strip of deep dark across the table's near edge, and let one thin vertical strip of warm white run down the frame's right edge from top to bottom. Keep every graphic element square to the frame except the disc, and keep all of them behind or under the figure rather than over her.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “LAMP” once, stencilled flat in pale white across the dark table near edge in the clear near foreground of the lower third, well in front of her boots and with nothing crossing the letters, the letters set square to the frame, each letter as tall as her boot, and the whole word spanning about a third of the frame's width so it reads clearly even at thumbnail size. Let the letters read as flat marks lying on the surface with one crisp edge and no shadow over them. Put no lettering on the lamplight circle, the book, the lamp base or the shelf bands or her coat, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The floor under her boots is worn smooth in one small oval; the table's near edge holds one fine pale line; one corner of the book rectangle is slightly uneven; and her boots carry a thin rim of dust at their soles. Keep the wear directional and small, all of it running with the frame's main lines rather than across them.

Build a second composition through the shelf bands. Let the two bands read as one flat near-black tone with a single slightly paler line along each inner edge, banded rather than detailed, with no book spine, no shelf division and no object drawn into them. Let those bands stay tones rather than images, with no titles and no shadows, and let them be broken only where the far table edge meets them.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One small wooden toggle at the coat's collar, one fine stitch line along the shoulder seam, one tiny scuff on her rear boot's heel, and one loose thread at the coat hem. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where use would put it, and keep no more than four such points in the whole frame.

Maintain five readable depth layers. First: the near table edge, the chair and the stencilled word along the bottom edge. Second: her boots and the near half of the dark table. Third: her seated figure, her forearms and the circle's near edge. Fourth: the pale book, the lamp base and the circle's far edge. Fifth: the far table, the two dark shelf bands and the top edge. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each, and let no layer borrow an edge from the one behind it.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp flat planes with precisely printed edges, a clean hard contour on the figure, restrained risograph grain only in the shadowed fields, and no gradient anywhere except the faint lift at the horizon. Keep the whole image matte; no glare, no sparkle, no lens flare and no bloom.

Exclude every failure mode explicitly: no second figure, no extra limb, no extra twin tail, no floating foot, no mirrored duplicate, no visible shaft or beam of light in the air, no sun disc, no cloud shapes, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no readable text beyond the string named above, no second lamp, no second reader, no lettering on the pages, no window, no halo, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no photographic depth of field, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter, no drop shadow under the figure.

Close on one quiet fact. The whole picture is one flat dark table, one pale circle of lamplight, one small seated figure and one word stencilled across the near edge. Everything else has been removed so the single measured structure can carry the frame alone.

seeds.title: LIFT
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “LIFT”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing alone inside one small elevator car, seen from a camera fixed high in the car's upper corner and angled down so the floor reads as a full plane and the walls close in on all four sides. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. She stands in the middle of the floor with her head tilted up toward the corner lens, and her twin tails hang straight down past her hips.

The car is one single closed box, not a corridor and not a lobby: one flat floor, two side walls, one back wall carrying the closed doors, and one ceiling panel above with its own light. There is no opening, no window and no second door. Every surface is square to every other, so the frame reads as one measured cube seen from one corner, and the ceiling light sits exactly above the floor's centre.

Use a camera set high in the car's top corner, about thirty centimetres below the ceiling, angled down at roughly forty-five degrees, with the lens wide enough that the two side walls converge toward the bottom corners and the floor fills the lower two thirds of the frame. Tilt no further than that, and never put the camera at her eye height, never look up at the ceiling and never let a wall run out of square. The result must read as one sealed box observed from one fixed point.

Give Miku exactly one core action: standing still in the centre of the floor with both boots together, her arms hanging at her sides, her head tilted up and her eyes fixed on the corner lens. She is not pressing a button, not leaning on a wall, not holding a phone and not turning. Her weight is even on both feet, her shoulders stay square to the back wall, and her chin is lifted just enough that the underside of her jaw catches the ceiling light. Let her stand no taller than two thirds of the frame's height so the floor in front of her keeps a wide empty band.

Construct the dominant visual object as the car itself: one flat floor of brushed metal panels with three visible seams, four walls meeting at four hard vertical corners, one ceiling panel of frosted white plastic with a thin dark frame, and one closed door pair on the back wall with a single vertical seam down its middle. Let the box's geometry be the largest thing in the picture and let the figure be one narrow vertical standing inside it. The three floor seams are the only lines crossing the floor and the door's centre seam is the only line breaking the back wall; keep every other surface blank.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The floor is brushed stainless steel with a fine horizontal grain, matte rather than polished, and never reflective; the walls are the same brushed steel in a slightly darker tone with one narrow brighter band at waist height; the door is a third tone, marginally greener; the ceiling panel is frosted plastic glowing from behind its own edge; the trim is dark anodised aluminium; her coat is heavy black wool. Each behaves differently: brushed steel returns one even tone with a faint directional grain and no reflected figure, the trim holds one narrow hard highlight, the frosted panel is a single flat luminous plane, and wool is a dense matte mass. Keep the whole frame matte and never let any metal surface act as a mirror.

Build a converging composition instead of a stepped one: four walls running in toward the floor, one ceiling plane at the top edge, and the floor opening out toward the bottom. Begin at the top edge with the ceiling panel and its dark frame, then the two upper wall corners converging, then the back wall with its closed doors, then her standing figure at the floor's centre, then the three floor seams running toward the bottom corners, and end at the near floor edge cropped by the bottom rule. Every line must run toward one of the four corners so the box reads as one sealed volume rather than a flat diagram.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is no button panel, no handrail, no mirror, no floor indicator above the door, no emergency phone, no inspection certificate, no poster, no advertisement screen, no camera dome, no vent grille, no second light, no bag, no suitcase, no umbrella, no second figure, no reflection of her in any wall and no door that is open. Keep the whole floor empty around her boots so the metal plane carries the lower third alone.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the near floor edge cropped by the bottom rule and the first floor seam, both slightly darker. Middle ground: her standing figure with her head tilted up and the three floor seams running out from her boots. Background: the back wall with its closed door pair and the two side walls converging. Separate them by value rather than by blur: the near floor holds the brightest value under the ceiling light, the walls fall one step darker, and the door is a shade darker again. Let her black coat read as the darkest mass in the frame.

Light the car from the ceiling panel and from nothing else. One flat cold white light sits directly above the floor's centre, so the floor holds one broad even pool of light with its brightest point under her feet and its edges falling off toward the four corners; the walls catch that light only along their upper thirds and go dark at the bottom; and the door's centre seam is the one hard line the light does not soften. Her face must stay fully readable as she looks up, with the light catching her jaw and her bangs from above, and her coat must stay a clean dark shape without a single highlight. Never add a second light, never put a glow around the panel and never let the metal show a reflected ceiling.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails hang straight down behind her shoulders as she stands. Both lengths drop past her waist and end below her coat's hem, and the ceiling light rims the top of her head and the crown of each tail so both read as dark columns with one pale top edge. Keep both tails clear of her arms and clear of the floor seams, and let the gap between the two tails be the only break in her silhouette.

Dress Miku in a heavy black wool coat that reaches below her knees, worn closed and belted once at the waist, over dark trousers and short black leather boots. The coat's shoulders stay square, its hem hangs level just above her boots, and the belt gives her silhouette one horizontal break at the waist. Keep the outfit completely unpatterned and completely black except for one small dull steel buckle, so her figure reads as one solid dark column against the pale floor.

Use a steel-on-black palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty-eight percent of the image is the brushed steel of the walls and floor, twenty-two percent is the darkest shadow in the four bottom corners and in her coat, sixteen percent is the pale pool of light on the floor under her, twelve percent is her figure and hair where the light touches it, eight percent is the frosted ceiling panel, and four percent is the one narrow bright band along the walls at waist height. Keep every bright note below the ceiling light, keep the corners near black, and let the metal never shine.

Drive the printed graphic language from the box's seams rather than from decoration. Let the floor print as one flat grey plane divided by two straight seams into three even bands, and let each wall print as one flat rectangle of a slightly different grey so the four planes read as four tones rather than as one texture. Add one wide horizontal band of flat pale grey across the back wall above the doors, and let one thin vertical strip of near white run down the frame's left edge from the ceiling to the floor. Keep every graphic element square to the frame and keep all three behind the figure rather than over her.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “LIFT” once, stencilled flat in dark grey across the pale metal floor in the clear near foreground of the lower third, well in front of her boots and with nothing crossing the letters, the letters set square to the frame, each letter as tall as her boot, and the whole word spanning about a third of the frame's width so it reads clearly even at thumbnail size. Let the letters read as flat dark marks lying on the floor with one crisp edge and no reflection over them. Put no lettering on the walls, the ceiling, the indicator or her coat, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The floor's centre is polished smoother in one broad oval where feet stand; the wall's waist band is scuffed in one short streak near the left corner; the door's bottom edge is scratched in two fine parallel lines; the ceiling panel has one faint grey smudge near its frame; and her boot soles are scuffed pale at the toes. Keep the wear directional and small, all of it running with the grain of the metal rather than across it.

Build a second composition through the door. Let the closed door pair read as one flat panel split by one straight vertical seam, with a thin shadow line running down that seam from the top edge to the floor, and let the two halves sit at two very slightly different values so the split reads as a line rather than a gap. Let that panel stay a tone rather than a scene, with no window cut into it, no indicator lit above it and no light coming through the seam, and let it be broken only where her head and her hair cross in front of it.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One dull steel belt buckle at her waist, one fine bright edge along the ceiling panel's frame, one small scuff on the floor's middle seam, and one loose thread at her coat's cuff. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where use would put it, and keep no more than four such points in the whole frame.

Maintain five readable depth layers. First: the near floor edge and the first seam along the bottom rule. Second: her boots and the pale pool of light under her feet. Third: her standing figure and her two hanging tails. Fourth: the back wall with its closed doors and the three floor seams running away. Fifth: the ceiling panel and the four converging upper corners. Separate them by value steps of roughly thirteen percent each, and let no layer borrow an edge from the one behind it.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp flat metal planes with precisely printed seams, one clean hard contour on her coat, restrained risograph grain only in the darkest corners, and no gradient anywhere except the soft pool of light on the floor. Keep the whole image matte; no metal sheen, no reflected figure, no bloom around the panel and no lens flare.

No second character, no duplicate figure, no reflection of her in any wall or floor, no mirrored body, no face in the metal, no large face in the ceiling, no open door, no second door, no window, no button panel, no handrail, no mirror, no floor indicator, no emergency phone, no certificate, no poster, no advertisement screen, no camera dome, no vent grille, no second light, no bag, no suitcase, no umbrella, no crowd, no animal, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no readable text beyond the string named above, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no photographic depth of field, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter, no drop shadow under the figure.

The final image should feel like four seconds alone in a sealed metal box: one pale pool of light on a brushed floor, a black figure standing dead centre with her chin lifted to the corner lens, four walls converging into darkness, and the word LIFT stencilled on the metal at her feet.

seeds.title: BEACON
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “BEACON”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing at the edge of one tall sea cliff, seen from the side at a level camera, with one white lighthouse tower standing behind her on the cliff top and the whole right half of the frame left open to a flat grey sea. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Her body is in profile to the camera, her head is turned slightly toward the horizon, and the wind pushes both twin tails out behind her.

The cliff is one single vertical mass, not a coastline and not a beach: one flat headland of dark rock running out of the frame at the left, one sheer face dropping out of the bottom edge, one even top surface where she stands, and one white tower planted on that surface a little behind her. There is no second rock, no second building and no path leading away. The tower is the only vertical structure in the frame and the sea's horizon is its only horizontal line, so everything in the picture is measured between those two.

Use a wide camera set at her shoulder height on the cliff top, absolutely level, with no tilt and no dutch angle, so the horizon cuts the frame a little below its middle and the tower rises straight up through the right third of the picture. Set the lens wide enough that the near cliff edge is cropped by the bottom and left rules and the tower's gallery sits just below the top edge. Never look up at the tower from below, never look down at the sea from above, and never let the horizon tilt.

Give Miku exactly one core action: standing still at the cliff's outer edge in profile to the camera, both boots on the rock, her weight on her back foot, her head turned toward the horizon, both hands pushed into the pockets of her coat. She is not leaning over the edge, not sitting, not holding a rail and not looking at the camera. The wind lifts the lower half of her coat and both twin tails out behind her in one direction, and the hem of the coat snaps clear of her legs so her silhouette stays open.

Construct the dominant visual object as the tower: one tapered white cylinder standing on the cliff top, one narrow vertical band of dark glass running up its seaward face, one projecting gallery ring near its top, one glass lamp room above the gallery with a dark metal cap, and one low white service hut at its base. Let the tower be the tallest and whitest thing in the frame, let its taper narrow by about a third from base to gallery, and let the lamp room be the only warm-coloured point in the whole picture. The tower's vertical edge is the only perfectly straight line in the frame and the horizon is the only other one.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The tower is thick white lime render over stone, matte and slightly uneven, chalked pale where wind has dried it; the gallery and cap are dark painted iron, dull and finely pitted; the glass is old and slightly wavy; the cliff is dark basalt in flat angular planes with one pale lichen crust along its upper lip; the sea is a flat opaque grey-green with a fine directional chop; the sky is a flat pale overcast with no cloud shapes drawn in it. Each behaves differently: render returns one flat white with a soft chalky edge, iron holds one narrow dark highlight, basalt is a set of hard flat facets, and the sea is a single even field broken only by short pale wave crests. Keep the whole frame matte and never let the sea act as a mirror.

Build a two-part composition instead of a receding one: one vertical tower on the left and one flat open sea on the right. Begin at the bottom edge with the cliff's near lip and her boots, then her standing profile with the wind in her coat, then the tower's base and the low hut, then the tower's shaft and its dark glass band, then the gallery ring and the lamp room, and end at the flat overcast sky above. Every element must sit either against the tower or against the sea, never between them, so the picture reads as one mass and one void meeting at her silhouette.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is no boat, no ship, no sail, no buoy, no gull, no bird, no cloud, no sun, no moon, no rain, no wave breaking over the cliff, no fence, no railing, no bench, no sign, no lighthouse keeper, no second figure, no path, no grass tuft, no flowers and no debris on the cliff top. Nothing stands on the headland but the tower and her. Keep the sea completely empty from the horizon down to the bottom right corner so the void carries the whole right half alone.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the near cliff lip cropped by the bottom edge and one band of pale lichen along its upper edge, both dark. Middle ground: her standing profile and the tower's base with its low hut. Background: the tower's shaft, gallery and lamp room against the flat sky, and the empty sea running to the horizon. Separate them by value rather than by blur: the cliff stays the darkest value, the tower the lightest, and the sea holds one even mid grey-green. Let her dark coat read as a clean silhouette against the pale sea.

Light the scene from a flat overcast sky and from one faint break on the left, and let the lamp room hold the only warm light. The overcast does the general work and fills the frame evenly, so the tower's seaward face reads a shade lighter than its landward face and the sea holds one broad paler band running out from the cliff. One faint break in the upper left makes the sky's left half slightly brighter than its right and puts a soft edge along the cliff's upper lip. The lamp room holds one small warm amber glow behind its glass, bright enough to read as the only warm point but never flaring. Her face and her coat must stay readable against the pale sea, and her hair must keep a clear cool edge. Never add a sun, never add a shaft of light, never brighten the sea into white and never let the amber spill onto the tower.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails stream out behind her in the wind. Both lengths lift away from her back and run to the left of the frame in two long clean curves, the nearer one crossing above the farther one, and the pale sea behind them makes both read as dark ribbons with one cool highlight along their upper edges. Keep both tails clear of her pockets, clear of the tower's base and clear of the cliff edge, and let their tips stop well inside the frame.

Dress Miku in a heavy charcoal wool coat that reaches below her knees, worn closed with both hands pushed into its side pockets, over a dark knit collar and dark straight trousers, with short black leather boots. The coat's shoulders stay square, its hem lifts in the wind so its lower edge reads as one clean angled line, and the fabric falls in three broad folds down her back. Her face is turned away from the camera and only the edge of one cheek is visible.

There is no third row and no stray tree. The path between them is one pale dirt lane running straight away from the camera to one single vanishing point placed a little left of the frame's centre, where the two rows converge and the light comes through. Everything in the frame obeys that one corridor: the trunk intervals narrow toward the vanishing point, the gold canopy narrows with them, and the far end of the lane is the brightest and the emptiest part of the picture.

Use a wide camera set at chest height on the centre line of the lane, absolutely level, with no tilt up or down and no dutch angle, so the two rows of trunks stand as two vertical columns of equal weight and the lane's vanishing point sits on the horizon line. Set the lens wide enough that the nearest trunks on both sides are cropped by the left and right frame rules and the far end of the avenue compresses into one narrow bright slot. Never look down the avenue from above, never look up into the canopy, and never let the camera leave the centre line.

Give Miku exactly one core action: standing still in the middle of the lane, both boots planted flat on the dirt, her body turned away from the camera, her head level, her arms hanging at her sides, and one small school satchel held in her right hand. Nothing else happens in the frame. She is not walking, not turning, not reaching and not sitting. Her weight is even on both feet and her shoulders stay square to the vanishing point. Let the distance between her and the camera be large enough that her head sits no higher than one fifth of the frame's height, standing in the middle third of the lane with empty path ahead of her and empty path behind her.

Construct the dominant visual object as the avenue's gold tunnel: two receding rows of trunks, one continuous arch of leaves meeting overhead, one pale lane tapering to a single point, and one bright open slot at the far end where the lane leaves the frame. Keep both rows unbroken from the bottom edge to the vanishing point, and keep the lane free of benches, lamps, fences, signs, bins and bicycles.

Build a receding sequence instead of a stepped one. Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp flat foliage plates with thin contour edges, precise vertical trunk edges, restrained risograph grain in the shaded dirt, clean flat fills in the lane, and one soft gradient only inside the far slot. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere, and let the light rays read as flat pale wedges rather than as lens effects.

Her back is to the camera, her hands are pushed into her coat pockets, and the nearer twin tail swings slightly out from her shoulder where the wind lifts it.

Use a wide camera set at chest height two paces behind her, absolutely level, with no tilt and no dutch angle, so the parapet reads as one straight horizontal line across the frame and the city's grid compresses into a shallow band that runs from the parapet down to the bottom edge. Set the lens wide enough that the water tank's near leg is cropped by the right frame rule and the stair hut's wall is cropped by the left. Never look down over the parapet from above, never tilt up into the sky, and never let the horizon sit anywhere but on the parapet line.

Give Miku exactly one core action: standing still at the parapet with her back to the camera, both boots on the deck, both hands pushed into the pockets of her coat, her shoulders slightly raised, her head level and her chin a little lifted toward the towers. She is not leaning on the parapet, not sitting on it, not turning and not pointing. Her weight is even on both feet, her elbows stay close to her body so the coat's silhouette stays square, and the wind pushes the coat's right hem and the nearer tail out to the right while the rest of her stays still.

Construct the dominant visual object as the city grid below the parapet: one flat plane of small warm lights arranged on two crossed sets of lines, the long lines running nearly parallel to the parapet and the short ones running away from it, so the whole lower band of the frame reads as a single drawn mesh of dots and streets. Let that mesh be the largest thing in the picture and let the figure be one narrow vertical standing on the parapet line. The mesh is the only repeating structure in the frame; the four towers above it are its only vertical interruption. Keep the mesh square to the frame so its lines neither fan nor curve.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The deck is dark asphalt with a fine gravel grain; the parapet is poured concrete, grey and matte, chipped along its top edge; the water tank is galvanised steel held on four square legs; the stair hut is painted brick; the towers are flat glass and dark steel; her coat is heavy charcoal wool. Leave one deliberate absence. Nothing stands above the parapet but the four towers and nothing stands on the deck but her. Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the near deck's asphalt cropped by the bottom edge and her two boots standing on it, both near black. Separate them by value rather than by blur: the deck and her coat stay near black, the parapet holds the one mid grey, and the mesh is the only lit field in the frame. Her head and shoulders must stay readable as a clean dark shape against the sky and the lower rim of her coat must keep one thin warm line. seeds.title: SLIT
seeds.raw:

Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Her back is three-quarters to the camera, her head is level, and both twin tails hang quiet down her back.

The hall is one deep closed interior with four flat walls, one high ceiling off the top edge and one dark stone floor: one narrow pale slot cut through the roof at the far end, one long sharp-edged bright band lying on the floor directly beneath it and running toward the bottom edge, two dark side walls with flat peeling plaster, and one dark end wall. There is no window, no open door, no side opening and no second skylight. The bright band has two dead straight parallel edges and its far end sits exactly under the slot, so the picture reads as one measured piece of light lying flat on a surface rather than as a beam hanging in the air.

Use a level camera set about one metre above the floor, tilted up no more than six degrees, so the bright band runs from the bottom edge into the depth of the hall and the roof slot sits in the upper third. Set the lens wide enough that the two dark side walls hold the left and right thirds of the frame. Never look down at the floor from above, never tilt past the ceiling, and never let the band's two edges converge into a wide wedge.

Give Miku exactly one core action: standing at the near end of the bright band with both boots just outside its left edge, one hand raised to shield her eyes as she looks down the band toward the far wall, her body turned three-quarters away from the camera. She is not walking, not kneeling, not reaching up toward the slot and not turning back toward the camera. Her weight is even on both boots, her chin is level, and her whole figure stands clear of the band so no bright edge cuts across her.

Construct the dominant visual object as the bright floor band against the dark hall: one long flat pale rectangle with two hard parallel edges, one crisp far end directly beneath the roof slot, and one slightly softer near end at the bottom edge. Let the roof slot be the second structure, one short thin pale bar with two hard ends. The peeling plaster patches on the side walls are the third, four flat irregular shapes of a slightly paler grey. Keep all three quiet so the floor band stays the single light thing.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The floor is dark worn stone, matte and faintly granular, with one flat pale value only where the band falls; the walls are dark grey plaster with flat peeling patches and exposed brick in one small area; the roof is one flat near-black plane; the slot is one flat pale bar with no glow around it; her coat is heavy charcoal wool; her boots are dark leather over a pale rubber sole. Each behaves differently: stone returns one dark even value, the lit band one clean pale flat, plaster one dark grey mass, and wool one dense matte mass. Keep the whole frame matte and let no surface shine.

Build a receding sequence instead of a stepped one. Begin at the bottom edge with the nearest and widest part of the bright band and the incised word, then her boots and her standing figure just outside it, then the band's middle length, then the plaster patches on both side walls at shortening intervals, then the band's crisp far end, then the dark end wall, and end at the thin pale roof slot. Every plaster patch must be smaller than the one in front of it, so the picture reads as one measured recession into a single closed room.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is no window, no open door, no side opening, no second skylight, no skylight grid, no column, no arch, no pew, no chair, no rubble pile, no fallen beam, no hanging cloth, no torch, no lamp, no second figure and no visible shaft, ray or beam of light hanging in the air anywhere in the hall. Nothing stands in the band but the light itself. Keep the whole left half of the frame dark and empty from the bottom edge to the end wall.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the near end of the bright band, the dark stone beside it and the incised word. Middle ground: her boots, her standing figure and the band's middle length. Background: the plaster patches, the band's crisp far end, the dark end wall and the thin roof slot. Separate them by value rather than by blur: the near stone holds one deep dark, the band one clean pale value, the walls one mid grey, and the roof the darkest value. Let her dark coat cut a clean vertical against the pale band.

Light the hall from the one narrow roof slot and from nothing else. The slot sends one flat pale band down onto the floor, with two razor-straight edges running its whole length, and leaves the air on both sides of it dark and clear; one thin pale rim sits along the near lip of the slot and one faint cool bounce lifts the lower part of the end wall. There is no volumetric column in the air, no visible shaft, no dust motes, no haze, no glow around the slot, no lens flare and no hard cast shadow of her across the band. Her face is turned away so only the edge of her cheek is visible, her coat must stay readable as a dark mass, and the band must stay a flat pale rectangle rather than a glowing beam. Never brighten the side walls, never add a second light, and never let the slot bloom.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails hang quiet down her back. Both lengths fall from her shoulders to below her coat hem without lifting, the nearer one a shade darker than the farther one, so they read as two still vertical lines against the dark wall. Let the pale floor band beside her make both tails read as dark aqua ribbons with one cool edge, keep their tips well inside the frame, and keep them clear of her raised hand.

Dress Miku in a heavy charcoal wool coat that reaches below her knees, worn closed with the collar turned up, over dark straight trousers tucked into short dark leather boots with pale rubber soles. The coat hangs still in the closed air, the collar stands at the back of her neck, and one sleeve pulls taut where her hand is raised to shield her eyes. Keep the outfit unpatterned so the bright floor band stays the only light structure in the frame.

Use a dark-on-pale palette with strict area control. Approximately forty-two percent of the image is the two dark side walls and the roof, twenty-two percent is the dark stone floor, sixteen percent is the long pale floor band, nine percent is her dark charcoal coat and boots, seven percent is the four flat peeling plaster patches, and four percent is the thin pale roof slot. Keep the exposed brick the only warm note in the entire frame, keep the band free of any yellow cast, and let the dark room and the single pale rectangle do all the work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the band rather than from decoration. Let the band print as one long flat pale rectangle with two crisp parallel edges and one hard far end, and let the four plaster patches print as four flat irregular shapes of one even pale grey. Add one thin horizontal bar of flat pale white across the upper third for the roof slot, and let one narrow vertical strip of deep grey run down the frame's left edge from the roof to the floor. Keep every graphic element square to the frame and keep all of them behind or under the figure rather than over her.

Print the text as physical matter.
