Let the letters sit well in front of her boots, with nothing crossing them, and read as exposed lighter stone with edges softened where the surface has worn. Put no lettering on the bright band, the walls, the roof slot or her coat, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The stone under her boots is worn smooth in one small oval; the band's near end holds one fine crisp line where the light stops; her boots carry a thin rim of stone dust at their soles; one plaster patch has a slightly uneven edge; and the end wall holds one faint cool smudge where the bounce light dies. Keep the wear directional and small, all of it running with the band rather than across it.

Build a second composition through the roof. Let the roof read as one flat near-black plane with a single thin pale bar cut into it, banded rather than detailed, with no beam drawn into the air beneath it and no rafters. Let that plane stay a tone rather than an image, with no hanging object and no second opening, and let it be broken only where the pale slot crosses it.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where use would put it, and keep no more than four such points in the whole frame.

Maintain five readable depth layers. First: the band's near end, the dark stone and the incised word along the bottom edge. Second: her boots and her standing figure just outside the band. Third: the band's middle length and the nearest plaster patches. Fourth: the band's crisp far end and the far plaster patches. Fifth: the dark end wall, the roof plane and the thin pale slot. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each, and let no layer borrow an edge from the one behind it.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp flat dark planes with a precisely printed pale rectangle, a clean hard contour on the figure, restrained risograph grain only in the plaster and the stone, and no gradient anywhere, including inside the bright band. Keep the whole image matte; no haze, no glow, no bloom, no lens flare and no visible beam in the air.

Exclude every failure mode explicitly: no volumetric light column, no visible shaft or beam of light in the air, no dust motes, no haze, no second figure, no extra limb, no extra twin tail, no floating foot, no window, no open door, no side opening, no skylight grid, no wide open roof, no second light source, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no readable text beyond the string named above, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no photographic depth of field, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter, no drop shadow under the figure.

Close on one quiet fact. The whole picture is one closed dark room, one long pale rectangle lying flat on its floor, one thin pale slot in the roof, one small dark figure and one word cut into the near stone. Everything else has been removed so the single flat band of light can carry the frame alone.

Every trunk stands dead vertical and the path's two edges converge on one single point, so the picture reads as a piece of measured perspective under one flat band.

Use a level camera set about one metre above the path, tilted up no more than three degrees, so the nearest trunks run out of both side edges and the far pair compresses into two thin lines. Leave one deliberate absence. Let Miku's extremely long twin tails swing out on the turn, both lengths arcing out to the right of the frame at two different heights so they answer the petal drift behind them. Let the flat field behind her make both tails read as dark aqua ribbons with one cool edge, keep their tips well inside the frame, and keep them clear of her arms.

The coat hangs still in the still air, the collar stands at the back of her neck, and the sleeves pull straight at her sides. Use a pale-on-charcoal palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty-six percent of the image is the flat pale canopy band, twenty-four percent is the two dark files of trunks, sixteen percent is the dark earth path, eleven percent is her dark charcoal coat and boots, nine percent is the loose petal drift, and four percent is the bright pale slot at the vanishing point. Keep the pink-white the only warm note in the entire frame, keep the trunks free of any white or papery bark, and let the dark verticals and the single pale band do all the work.

Let every surface carry the shift. The earth under her forward boot is scuffed into one small darker oval; the nearest trunk holds one fine pale line along its shaded edge; one petal has a slightly uneven edge; and her boots carry a thin rim of dry soil at their soles. Keep the wear directional and small, all of it running with the frame's main lines rather than across them.

Build a second composition through the canopy. Let the canopy read as one flat pale pink-white band with a single slightly warmer strip along its lower edge, banded rather than detailed, with no individual blossom, no branch and no sky hole drawn into it. Let that band stay a tone rather than an image, with no birds and no sun disc, and let it be broken only where the nearest trunk pair runs out of the frame.

seeds.title: PETAL
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “PETAL”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing at the foot of one stone stairway in a shrine precinct, seen from behind at a low camera, with four vermilion torii ranked up the stairs above her and the whole approach built as one narrowing corridor of red frames. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Her back is to the camera, her head is lifted toward the gates, and her twin tails hang down her back with pale petals caught in the nearer one.

The approach is one single corridor, not a garden and not a courtyard: exactly four torii standing one behind the other up the stairway, each smaller than the one below it, their pillars planted in pairs on either side of one straight run of stone steps. There is no fifth gate and no side path. Every gate is square to the stairway and centred on the same axis, so the four openings stack into one receding rectangle inside the frame, and the topmost gate's crossbeam sits just below the top edge of the picture.

Use a tall camera set at chest height at the foot of the stairway, on the exact centre line, level with a slight upward tilt of about eight degrees so the four gates stack upward and the stairs compress into one banded climb. Set the lens wide enough that the nearest gate's pillars are cropped by the left and right frame rules and its crossbeam runs above the top edge. Never look down the stairs from above, never stand off to one side, and never let the gates lean out of alignment.

Give Miku exactly one core action: standing still on the first step with her back to the camera, both boots planted on the stone, her head lifted toward the gates, her arms hanging at her sides and one narrow paper charm held in her right hand. She is not climbing, not bowing, not praying, not turning and not reaching up. Her weight is even on both feet, her shoulders stay square to the corridor's axis, and her figure occupies roughly the middle third of the frame's height with clear stone steps above her and clear paving below her.

Construct the dominant visual object as the four gates: four identical vermilion torii of decreasing size, each built from two upright pillars, one straight crossbeam and one short lintel above it, all of them standing on the same axis so their openings frame one another into a single narrowing aperture. Let the gates be the largest and most saturated thing in the picture and let the figure be one small dark vertical standing inside the lowest opening. The four crossbeams are the only horizontal structures in the frame and the eight pillars are its only vertical repeat; keep both perfectly square so the corridor reads as one measured system rather than as scattered architecture.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The gates are painted vermilion timber, matte and slightly chalked, with black painted bases on each pillar; the steps are pale grey granite, worn smooth in the middle and rough at the edges; the flanking trees are dense dark cherry canopy with pale blossom; the lanterns on either side are grey stone with one carved face; her clothing is a pale summer kimono. Each behaves differently: vermilion returns one flat saturated red with a chalky matte surface, black bases hold one narrow vertical highlight, granite is a soft grey field with fine speckle, canopy is a dense dark mass, stone lanterns are a lighter dry grey, and her kimono is a flat pale plane with a printed pattern. Keep the whole frame matte and let no surface act as a mirror.

Build a vertical sequence up the axis instead of a receding one. Begin at the bottom edge with the pale paving and her two boots, then the lowest gate's black pillar bases, then its crossbeam crossing above her head, then the second and third gates stacked at shortening intervals, then the fourth gate's lintel, and end at the narrow strip of pale sky above it. Every gate must sit a little higher and a little smaller than the one below it, and every opening must sit exactly inside the one beneath it, so the picture reads as one measured climb.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is no priest, no visitor, no second figure, no couple, no child, no dog, no cat, no bird, no offering box, no bell rope, no ema rack, no fortune slips, no shop, no stall, no bench, no bicycle, no car, no fence, no signboard and no fallen gate anywhere in the precinct. Nothing stands on the steps but her. Keep every step clean and empty from the bottom edge up to the topmost gate so the eye climbs the full corridor without interruption.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the pale paving along the bottom edge and the two nearest pillar bases cropped by the side rules, both slightly darker than the steps. Middle ground: the small standing figure, the lowest gate's opening and the first four steps. Background: the second and third gates stacking upward, the dense cherry canopy on both sides, and the fourth gate's lintel against the pale sky. Separate them by value rather than by blur: the foreground paving holds a mid grey, the middle steps are the palest stone in the frame, and the canopy falls to near black. Let her pale kimono read as a soft light shape inside the dark corridor.

Light the precinct with a soft overcast sky and one faint side break, and with nothing else. The sky above the topmost gate is a flat pale warm white and it does the general work, filling the corridor evenly and lifting the pale stone steps into one continuous light band; one slightly brighter break comes in from the upper left, so the left face of each gate's pillar reads a shade lighter than its right face and the left canopy holds a faint separation from the right. There is no visible sun, no hard shadow and no dramatic shaft. Her kimono must stay readable as a pale shape against the dark canopy, her hair must keep a clear edge, and the vermilion must stay saturated without glowing. Never add a second light, never let the sky go blue, and never darken the steps into shadow.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails fall straight down her back as she stands. Both lengths drop past her waist and end below her obi, and the nearer one is crossed by two pale petals caught where the hair turns, so one small pale note sits inside the dark mass. Let the flat sky rim each tail along its outer edge without turning them bright. Keep both tails inside her silhouette, clear of the charm in her hand and clear of the stairway's steps.

Dress Miku in a pale summer kimono of flat off-white cloth printed with one small repeating pattern of dark blue waves, worn with a wide deep indigo obi tied at her back, a thin red cord at the collar, and pale wooden sandals on bare feet. The kimono's sleeves hang long and square at her sides, its hem stops just above the sandals so her ankles read, and the obi's knot sits flat against her back so its shape breaks her silhouette at the waist. Keep the printed pattern small and even so the garment stays one pale plane at thumbnail size, and keep the only saturated colour in her figure to the red cord at her collar.

Every edge runs parallel to a frame edge, so the picture reads as a measured layout of flat rectangles rather than as an interior with depth.

Use a camera set directly above the rug, its sensor exactly parallel to the floor, so the sofa's long edges stay parallel from top to bottom and the rug reads as one clean rectangle. Set the lens wide enough to hold the whole sofa and the whole rug without cutting either. Never angle the camera, never let the floor lines converge, and never tilt the frame.

Give Miku exactly one core action: curled on her side on the sofa with her knees drawn together and her feet tucked under the hem of her coat, one arm folded under her cheek and the other resting along the sofa's back cushion. She is not standing, not walking, not sitting upright and not reaching toward the table. Her head rests on the cushion at the left end, her knees point toward the lower edge, and her whole figure fits inside the sofa's long rectangle.

Construct the dominant visual object as the sofa's dark rectangle against the pale rug: one long flat charcoal block with a single lighter cushion seam running its length, one narrow back rail along its upper edge, and one small shadow band where it meets the rug. Let the rug be the second structure, one pale field with three wide horizontal bands of slightly different tone. Her curled figure is the single soft shape inside the hard geometry. Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. Keep the whole frame matte and let no surface reflect the room.

Build a receding sequence instead of a stepped one. Begin at the bottom edge with the bare floor strip and the indented word, then the rug's first and second bands, then the table square, then the sofa's near edge and her tucked feet, then her curled body and folded arm, then the back rail and the third rug band, and end at the bare floor strip along the top edge. Every band must be shallower than the one in front of it, so the picture reads as one measured stack of flat fields from bottom to top.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is no cushion pile, no blanket, no book, no cup, no remote, no lamp, no plant, no picture frame, no window, no wall, no door, no second chair, no pet, no second figure and no cast shadow of a person anywhere in the room. Separate them by value rather than by blur: the floor holds one warm mid grey, the rug one pale value, the sofa one deep dark, and her coat a shade lighter than the upholstery. Let the two soft curves of her knees and tails read against the rug.

The light fills the scene evenly so the rug holds one pale value from edge to edge, the sofa's top plane stays a shade lighter than its front face, and one narrow soft band of shadow sits where the sofa meets the rug. Let Miku's extremely long twin tails spill off the sofa edge onto the rug. Exclude every failure mode explicitly: no second figure, no extra limb, no extra twin tail, no floating foot, no second sofa, no window, no wall, no visible ceiling lamp, no cast shadow of a person, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no readable text beyond the string named above, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no photographic depth of field, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter, no drop shadow under the figure.

Close on one quiet fact. The whole picture is one pale rug, one long dark rectangle, one small curled figure and one word pressed into the pile, seen from directly above so nothing in the room has a perspective line. Everything else has been removed so the flat layout can carry the frame alone.

seeds.title: STEPS

Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “STEPS”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing on one landing and looking back down a stairwell, seen from a low camera below her, with the stair flights making four flat diagonal bands climbing out of the frame. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Her body faces up the next flight while her head turns back over her shoulder toward the camera, so one cheek and both aqua eyes read clearly, and both twin tails swing out on the turn.

The stairwell is one tall shaft: four flat pale stair flights crossing the frame as wide diagonal bands at four different heights, one dark vertical wall strip between each pair, one narrow pale landing at the middle, and one flat dark ceiling band at the top. There is no window, no door, no railing detail and no second figure. Every stair edge runs parallel within its own flight and the four bands sit at measured intervals, so the picture reads as one stack of diagonals inside one tall rectangle.

Use a low camera set about half a metre above the lower landing, tilted up about twenty-five degrees, so the four flights climb steeply and the ceiling band sits at the top edge. Set the lens wide enough that all four bands stay inside the frame. Never look down the shaft from above, never tilt past the ceiling, and never let the wall strips converge into a single point.

Give Miku exactly one core action: standing on the middle landing with her feet together, one hand resting on the wall and her head turned back over her left shoulder toward the camera. She is not climbing, not sitting, not leaning over a railing and not facing the camera with her whole body. Her weight is even on both boots and her whole figure fits inside the pale landing band.

Construct the dominant visual object as the four stair flights against the dark shaft: four wide flat pale diagonal bands, each with one crisp upper edge and one softer lower edge, each a little shorter than the one below it. Let the three wall strips be the second structure, three tall dark vertical bars. The landing is the third, one narrow pale horizontal bar. Keep all three quiet so the four diagonals stay the loud thing.

The stair treads are flat pale concrete, matte and slightly granular; the wall strips are one flat cool dark grey with no window and no door; the landing is one flat pale field; the ceiling band is one flat near-black; her coat is heavy charcoal wool. Each behaves differently: concrete returns one even pale value, the walls one cool dark, the landing one pale flat, and wool one dense matte mass. Keep the whole frame matte and let no surface shine.

Build a receding sequence instead of a stepped one. Begin at the bottom edge with the lowest and widest stair flight and the stencilled word, then the first wall strip, then the second flight and the middle landing, then her boots and her turning figure, then the third flight, then the second and third wall strips, then the fourth flight, and end at the dark ceiling band. Every flight must be shorter than the one below it, so the picture reads as one measured recession up a single shaft.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is no window, no door, no railing detail, no handrail, no lamp, no sign, no second figure, no plant, no bag, no visible shaft of light and no cast shadow of a person. Let the flat field behind her make both tails read as dark aqua ribbons with one cool edge, keep their tips well inside the frame, and keep them clear of her arms.

Let the ceiling read as one flat near-black band with a single slightly paler strip along its lower edge, banded rather than detailed, with no fixture, no lamp and no vent drawn into it. Let that band stay a tone rather than an image, with no hanging object, and let it be broken only where the upper wall strips meet it.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One small wooden toggle at the coat's collar, one fine stitch line along the shoulder seam, one tiny scuff on her rear boot's heel, and one loose thread at the coat hem. Third: her boots, her turning figure and the third flight. Fourth: the second and third wall strips and the fourth flight. Fifth: the dark ceiling band and the upper shaft. seeds.title: TORII
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “TORII”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing directly beneath one single enormous torii gate at night, seen from a very low camera so the gate's two pillars rise past both side rules and its double crossbeam fills the top of the frame. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. She stands small at the foot of the gate with her back to the camera and her head lifted, and her twin tails hang down her back into the dark.

The shrine approach is one single threshold, not a corridor and not a precinct: one wide torii standing on two stone plinths, one short run of three stone steps beneath it, and one narrow strip of night sky visible above the top beam. There is no second gate, no lantern row and no fence. The gate is enormous relative to her: its pillars are wider than her shoulders, its lower beam sits at three times her height, and its two ends run out of the left and right frame rules, so the gate reads as a frame she has walked into rather than an object she stands beside.

Use a tall camera set about one metre above the ground on the gate's centre line, tilted up about forty degrees, so the two pillars converge very slightly toward the top of the frame and the two crossbeams cross in front of the night sky. Set the lens wide enough that both pillars are cropped by the side rules and the lower beam runs across the frame's upper third. Never look down at her from above, never stand outside the gate and never let the gate lean off centre.

Give Miku exactly one core action: standing still just inside the gate's threshold, on the top of the three steps, with both boots together, her arms hanging at her sides, her head lifted toward the lower beam. She is not bowing, not clapping, not climbing, not turning and not holding anything. Her weight is even on both feet, her shoulders stay square to the gate, and her chin is lifted enough that her throat catches the warm light from the two lanterns.

Construct the dominant visual object as the gate itself: two round vermilion pillars standing on two square stone plinths, one straight lower beam passing across both pillars, one shorter upper lintel above it, two black metal caps at the pillars' tops, and one narrow strip of night sky visible above the lintel. Let the gate's dark opening be the largest shape in the picture and let the figure be one small vertical standing inside it. The gate's two verticals and two horizontals are the only structural lines in the frame; keep every other surface flat and quiet.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The pillars and both beams are painted vermilion timber, matte and slightly chalked at the edges, with black paint at the bases of the plinths; the plinths and the three steps are pale grey granite, matte and worn; the two lanterns hanging from the lower beam are paper over a wooden frame, glowing warm from inside; the ground beyond the steps is dark gravel; the sky is a flat night blue-black with a fine scatter of small stars. Each behaves differently: vermilion returns one flat saturated red with a chalky edge, black plinth bases hold one narrow highlight, the granite is a soft grey field with fine speckle, the paper lanterns are two flat luminous planes, and the gravel is a near-black even field. Keep the whole frame matte and never let any surface act as a mirror.

Build a framing composition instead of a receding one: one gate, one threshold, one sky slot. Begin at the bottom edge with the first stone step and her two boots, then the second and third steps, then the two plinths and the base of each pillar, then the gate's dark opening around her, then the lower beam and the two hanging lanterns, and end at the upper lintel and the narrow strip of night sky. Everything must frame her rather than lead away from her, so the picture reads as one threshold rather than a corridor.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is no second gate, no gate behind hers, no stone lantern row, no offering box, no bell rope, no ema rack, no fortune slips, no stall, no shop, no fence, no rope barrier, no sign, no bench, no priest, no visitor, no second figure, no animal, no bird and no fallen leaf on the steps. Nothing stands between the two pillars but her. Keep the dark opening completely empty around her silhouette so it reads as one clean shape.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the first stone step along the bottom edge and her two boots on the third step, both dark. Middle ground: her small standing figure with her head lifted, and the two lanterns' warm light falling on the steps. Background: the two vermilion pillars rising past the side rules, the lower beam crossing above her, and the narrow strip of night sky at the top. Separate them by value rather than by blur: the steps fall to a mid grey, the pillars hold the one saturated red, and the night sky is the darkest value. Let her pale-lit face read as one small warm note inside the gate's dark opening.

Light the threshold from the two hanging lanterns and from nothing else. Two paper lanterns hang from the lower beam at equal distances from the gate's centre, each throwing one soft warm pool of light down onto the granite steps and onto the inner faces of the two pillars, so the gate's opening stays dark from the beam upward and the steps stay pale from below. The rest of the frame holds only a faint blue night value, and the sky above the lintel is a flat dark field with small stars. Her face, lifted toward the beam, must keep both eyes and the line of her jaw readable in that warm light, her hair must keep a cool edge against the dark, and her coat must stay one dark mass with only its shoulders warmed. Never add a third light, never brighten the gravel, and never let the lanterns flare or bloom.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails hang down her back into the gate's shadow. Both lengths drop past her waist and disappear below her coat's hem, and only the upper halves catch the lanterns' warm light so each reads as a dark column with one warm top edge. Keep both tails inside the gate's opening, clear of her arms and clear of the steps, and let the gap between them stay the only break in her silhouette.

Dress Miku in a pale summer kimono of flat off-white cloth printed with one small repeating pattern of dark blue waves, worn with a wide deep indigo obi tied at her back, a thin red cord at the collar, and pale wooden sandals on bare feet. The kimono's sleeves hang long and square at her sides, its hem stops just above the sandals so her ankles read, and the obi's knot sits flat against her back so its shape breaks her silhouette at the waist. Keep the printed pattern small and even so the garment stays one pale plane at thumbnail size.

Use a vermilion-on-night palette with strict area control. Approximately twenty-eight percent of the image is the flat night sky and the dark opening between the pillars, twenty-six percent is the flat vermilion of the gate's four members, sixteen percent is the pale granite of the plinths and the three steps, fourteen percent is the warm light from the two lanterns falling on the steps and the pillar faces, ten percent is her pale kimono and dark hair, and six percent is the fine scatter of stars in the sky. Keep every saturated note inside the gate's vermilion, keep the steps' warm pool as the only soft light in the frame, and let the night do the framing.

Drive the printed graphic language from the gate's own frame rather than from decoration. Let the gate print as two flat vermilion columns crossed by two flat vermilion bars, each edge crisp and each surface one unbroken tone, and let the dark opening between them print as one flat near-black rectangle. Add one wide horizontal band of flat blue-black across the sky above the lintel, and let one thin vertical strip of pale grey run down the frame's right edge behind the right pillar. Keep every graphic element square to the frame and keep all three behind the figure rather than over her.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “TORII” once, stencilled flat in pale paint across the flat stone landing in the clear near foreground of the lower third, well in front of the first step and her sandals and with nothing crossing the letters, the letters set square to the frame, each letter as tall as her boot, and the whole word spanning about a third of the frame's width so it reads clearly even at thumbnail size. Let the letters read as flat pale marks lying on the stone with one crisp edge and no shadow over them. Put no lettering on the steps, the gate, the lanterns or her coat, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The vermilion is chalked pale along the outer edge of the lower beam; the black plinth bases are scuffed at their corners; the third step is worn smooth in a shallow dish at its centre; the lantern paper is creased once near its top ring; and her sandals are dark at the heel. Keep the wear directional and small, all of it running with the gate's own lines rather than across them.

Build a second composition through the night sky. Let it read as one flat dark blue-black field with a fine scatter of small stars, denser toward the top edge and thinner toward the lintel, with each star a solid point rather than a glow. Let that field stay a texture rather than a sky, with no cloud, no moon, no milky band and no aircraft, and let it be broken only where the upper lintel crosses it near the top edge.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One thin red cord tied at her collar, one fine bright edge along the nearest plinth's worn corner, one small brass ring at the top of the nearer lantern, and one loose thread at her kimono's cuff. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where use would put it, and keep no more than four such points in the whole frame.

Maintain five readable depth layers. First: the first stone step and her two sandals, near black. Second: the second and third steps with the lanterns' warm pool on them. Third: her small standing figure with her head lifted. Fourth: the two plinths and the pillars rising past the side rules.
