Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “SILL”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character sitting on one wide window sill in winter, seen from a level camera square to the glass, with the window making one tall grid of pale rectangles above four flat bands of snow. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Her back is three-quarters to the camera, her head is level, and both twin tails hang quiet down her back.

The window is one tall rectangle: two vertical and three horizontal mullions dividing it into six pale panes, four wide flat white snow bands showing through the lower half at measured intervals, one flat pale grey sky above them, one wide dark sill band across the bottom, and one narrow dark frame at the top. There is no roof, no building, no tree, no blanket, no reflection in the glass and no second figure. Every mullion stays square to the frame and every snow band runs dead level, so the picture reads as one measured grid above one stack of white bars.

Use a level camera set about one metre above the sill, its sensor exactly parallel to the glass, so all six panes keep equal size and the snow bands stay horizontal. Set the lens wide enough that the whole window and the whole sill fit inside the frame. Never angle the camera, never let the mullions converge, and never tilt the frame.

Give Miku exactly one core action: seated on the sill with her knees together, both hands resting flat on its top edge and her head turned a quarter toward the left of the frame. She is not wrapping a blanket, not leaning on the glass, not looking down at roofs and not turning back toward the camera. Her weight is even on both boots and her whole figure fits inside the dark sill band.

Construct the dominant visual object as the six pale panes against the dark sill: six flat pale rectangles of equal size with one crisp dark mullion between each, and four wide flat white snow bands of slightly different value crossing the lower panes. Let the sill be the second structure, one wide flat dark bar. The sky band is the third, one flat pale grey field. Keep all three quiet so the grid stays the single measured thing.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The panes are one flat matte pale grey with no outside detail and no gradient; the snow bands are four flat white tones with no sparkle and no drawn drift; the mullions are dark painted wood with one fine matte edge; the sill is one flat dark field; her coat is heavy charcoal wool. Each behaves differently: panes return one even pale value, snow four stepped white flats, mullions one dark line, and wool one dense matte mass. Keep the whole frame matte and let no glass reflect a figure.

Build a receding sequence instead of a stepped one. Begin at the bottom edge with the dark sill band and the stencilled word, then her boots and her seated figure, then the lowest snow band, then the second and third snow bands at shortening intervals, then the fourth band, and end at the six pale panes, the mullions and the pale grey sky. Every band must be shallower than the one in front of it, so the picture reads as one measured stack upward across a single tall frame.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is no roof, no building, no tree, no blanket, no cushion, no cup, no reflection in the glass, no mirrored image of her, no snowflake, no second figure, no sun disc and no cast shadow of a person. Nothing stands in the frame but her. Keep the whole upper right of the window empty of any object so the six pale panes carry that corner alone.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the dark sill band, the stencilled word and her boots. Middle ground: her seated figure, her resting hands and the lowest snow band. Background: the second through fourth snow bands, the six pale panes, the mullions and the pale grey sky. Separate them by value rather than by blur: the sill holds one deep dark, the snow four stepped white values, the panes one pale grey, and her coat the deepest dark. Let her compact figure read clearly inside the dark sill band.

Light the room from one flat pale winter sky behind the window and from nothing else. The sky fills all six panes with one even pale grey value and all four snow bands with their stepped white values, while the sill stays one deep dark band with one narrow cool edge along her shoulders. There is no sun disc, no lamp, no glare, no sparkle on the snow, no reflection in the glass and no hard cast shadow. Her face is turned away so only the edge of her cheek is visible, her coat must stay distinct from the sill, and the snow bands must stay flat white fields rather than a glowing view. Never brighten the near sill, never add a second light, and never let the window bloom.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails hang quiet down her back without lifting, the nearer one a shade darker than the farther one, so they read as two still vertical lines inside the dark sill band. Let the flat field behind her make both tails read as dark aqua ribbons with one cool edge, keep their tips well inside the frame, and keep them clear of her arms.

Dress Miku in a heavy charcoal wool coat that reaches below her knees, worn closed with the collar turned up, over dark straight trousers tucked into short dark leather boots with pale rubber soles. The coat hangs still in the still air, the collar stands at the back of her neck, and the sleeves pull straight at her sides. Keep the outfit unpatterned so the six-pane window grid stays the only broad structure in the frame.

Use a white-on-dark palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty-six percent of the image is the four flat white snow bands, twenty-six percent is the six pale grey window panes, fourteen percent is her dark charcoal coat and boots, eleven percent is the wide dark sill band, nine percent is the dark mullions and top frame, and four percent is the narrow cool edge along her shoulders. Keep the snow the only bright note in the entire frame, keep the sill free of any warm cast, and let the six panes and the four white bars do all the work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the window grid rather than from decoration. Let the window print as six flat pale rectangles of equal size separated by crisp dark mullions, and let the snow print as four wide flat white horizontal bands of stepped value across the lower panes. Add one wide horizontal strip of flat deep dark across the bottom edge for the sill, and let one thin vertical strip of warm white run down the frame's right edge from the sky to the sill. Keep every graphic element square to the frame and keep all of them behind or under the figure rather than over her.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “SILL” once, stencilled flat in pale white across the dark sill band in the clear near foreground of the lower third, well in front of her boots and with nothing crossing the letters, the letters set square to the frame, each letter as tall as her boot, and the whole word spanning about a third of the frame's width so it reads clearly even at thumbnail size. Let the letters read as flat marks lying on the surface with one crisp edge and no shadow over them. Put no lettering on the window panes, the snow bands, the mullions or the sky or her coat, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The sill under her boots is worn smooth in one small oval; the sill's upper edge holds one fine pale line; one snow band has a slightly uneven boundary; and her boots carry a thin rim of dust at their soles. Keep the wear directional and small, all of it running with the frame's main lines rather than across them.

Build a second composition through the top frame. Let the frame read as one flat dark band with a single slightly paler line along its lower edge, banded rather than detailed, with no fixture, no curtain and no hanging object drawn into it. Let that band stay a tone rather than an image, with no lamp, and let it be broken only where the two vertical mullions meet it.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One small wooden toggle at the coat's collar, one fine stitch line along the shoulder seam, one tiny scuff on her rear boot's heel, and one loose thread at the coat hem. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where use would put it, and keep no more than four such points in the whole frame.

Maintain five readable depth layers. First: the dark sill band, the stencilled word and her boots along the bottom edge. Second: her seated figure, her resting hands and the lowest snow band. Third: the second and third snow bands. Fourth: the fourth snow band and the six pale panes. Fifth: the mullions, the pale grey sky and the top frame. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each, and let no layer borrow an edge from the one behind it.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp flat planes with precisely printed edges, a clean hard contour on the figure, restrained risograph grain only in the shadowed fields, and no gradient anywhere except the faint lift at the horizon. Keep the whole image matte; no glare, no sparkle, no lens flare and no bloom.

Exclude every failure mode explicitly: no second figure, no extra limb, no extra twin tail, no floating foot, no mirrored duplicate, no visible shaft or beam of light in the air, no sun disc, no cloud shapes, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no readable text beyond the string named above, no roof, no building, no blanket, no reflection, no mirrored duplicate, no snowflake, no sun disc, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no photographic depth of field, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter, no drop shadow under the figure.

Close on one quiet fact. The whole picture is one flat dark sill, a six-pane pale window, four white bands of snow, one small seated figure and one word stencilled across the near sill. Everything else has been removed so the single measured structure can carry the frame alone.

seeds.title: WATERLINE
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 premium experimental anime editorial poster titled “WATERLINE”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only living figure inside a colossal chalk-white swimming hall at first light. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long turquoise twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments at the base of each tail, slim virtual-singer proportions, and a silhouette that reads as Hatsune Miku at a single glance. Keep her face, both eyes and both hands fully readable at thumbnail size.

Build the camera as a true split-level poster. The lens housing sits a few centimetres above the water surface, so one clean horizontal waterline runs edge to edge across the entire canvas at about forty-eight percent from the top edge. Everything above it is dry morning air, chalk architecture and Hatsune Miku; everything below it is water, turquoise glazed tile and one calm inverted reflection seen through that water at a shallow downward angle. The two halves share the same vanishing axis and the same tile module, so the split reads as a single architecture cut by a liquid horizon rather than as a collage of two pictures. Keep the waterline one crisp line carrying a soft scalloped meniscus along every tile junction.

Place Hatsune Miku in the left third, turned into a clear three-quarter profile that faces the water and slightly toward the open right side of the frame, medium full figure with her whole body readable from the top of her head to her bare feet, occupying about thirty percent of the canvas area. Her near hand reaches down and rests flat on the chalk-white coping exactly where the deck meets the water: four fingers lie together, the thumb spreads, the fingertips touch the tile edge without pressing into it, and the hand is anatomically exact with five clear fingers, defined knuckles, a drawn wrist bone and a clean thumb-to-forearm line. Her far arm hangs relaxed behind her hip, and her head turns down toward the waterline.

Weave Hatsune Miku’s extremely long turquoise twin tails into the water and the chalk. Both tails fall from the crown of her head in two clean aqua masses that reach past her waist, pale where the morning light strikes them and deep turquoise where they cross the chalk, with one strand lifting across the waterline and doubling inside the reflection. Her aqua hair remains the only character colour.

Dress her in one competition swimsuit that keeps her colour identity and her original neckline logic. Chalk-white matte panel fabric across chest and back, a pale-aqua graduated side panel that deepens toward the hip, a thin cobalt enamel piping tracing the V line of her canonical collar from shoulder to sternum and then running down the flank like a tile grout line, narrow shoulder straps, one small black-and-magenta square clasp quoting her hair ornament on the near strap, a low athletic back crossed by a single hairline silver tension strap, and a modest competitive hip cut that follows the body naturally. The fabric stays dry and chalk-matte, with a soft dusty sheen at the hem, one damp patch only where her supporting hand has touched water, and a hairline aqua luminous seam catching the window light along the ribs.

Let her twin tails organise the left edge of the frame. The upper tail falls behind her shoulder toward the deck and is cropped once by the left border; the lower tail hangs past her hip, stays solid and unmistakable for its first two thirds, and its final third turns into three separated cyan contours. Where that tail approaches the waterline region, its echo appears inside the water as a faint magnified aqua shape displaced a few pixels from the real tail, so the hair itself tests the water surface without breaking it.

Construct the dominant object as the hall itself: one colossal rectangular swimming basin carved from a single block of chalk. Pale chalk-white cast plaster forms the walls, the coping, the blind arched recesses and the colonnade of seven square piers along the far wall; this whole chamber fills about seventy-five percent of the canvas and is cropped by the left, right and top borders so it feels larger than the poster. Chalk surfaces are matte and porous, with crisp chiseled arrises, hairline shrinkage cracks, a fine bloom of chalk dust along the coping, and soft shadow absorption in place of hard specular glare. The architecture is delivered by volume alone — mass, arris, blind recess and window band — with every surface left as bare chalk and nothing applied on top of it.

Set the single readable line of type into the architecture. A horizontal band of pale chalk-white glazed tiles, about four percent of the canvas height, sits exactly on the waterline and runs from border to border. Into that band the exact word “WATERLINE” is inlaid as cobalt enamel letters: uppercase, narrow grotesque, wide letterspacing, cap height about two and a half percent of the canvas height, the letters flush with the tile face, each one beveled so a hairline highlight catches its upper edge and a thin shadow sits beneath its lower edge. The word begins just right of Miku's hip at roughly thirty-two percent of the width and runs to about ninety percent, interrupted once where the chrome ladder upright crosses the final letters. Immediately below the waterline the same letters continue as a darker cobalt refracted echo, inverted, magnified once, displaced a few pixels, and dissolving into the tile shadow within the first metre of water, so the title reads simultaneously as chalk architecture and as a submerged reflection.

Build the underwater half as pure tile geometry. Glazed turquoise ceramic tiles of one square module cover the pool wall and floor, laid in an exact grid with hairline pale-grey grout, small bevels catching a cool edge light, three chipped corners and one replaced ivory tile breaking the rhythm, a wet gloss that darkens toward cobalt at the deep end, and pearl-white glazed coping above. The grid compresses with perspective toward the far end until the tile lines become a dense blue band, and that band is the second rhythm balancing the right side of the frame.

Hang one stainless lane cable across the open right water and turn it into a stage sequence. Nine floats sit along the cable at even spacing, each about one fortieth of the canvas width, changing state from left to right: solid pearl ceramic, chalk-bloomed ceramic, ceramic with a hairline crack, half-translucent acrylic, frosted glass, clear glass with two internal bubbles, an outlined glass shell alone, a chalk-dust ghost of the former float, and finally a bare empty span of cable. This sequence is the only repeated element in the poster and must read as a slow material decay rather than as decoration.

Use real supporting structure and interleave it twice. A mirror-polished chrome ladder stands at the right third, its upright crossing the waterline and its rungs holding compressed reflections of the tiles; behind it the lane cable passes, and behind that the far colonnade. In front of Miku, her own hand lies over the title band and over the far tile grid, so the front-to-back order is unambiguous: hand, then band, then water, then far wall. Every edge that crosses another edge carries a clean occlusion and a drawn contact shadow.

Keep the water glassy and almost still: two faint concentric ripple rings only, one where the lane cable enters the surface and one thin drift line at the far end, an unbroken mirror face everywhere between them. The surface refracts what lies behind it, pinching the tile grid by a few pixels along every grout line, bending the chrome ladder's underwater shaft, magnifying the final letters of the title, and holding one calm inverted reflection of Miku directly beneath her — a soft-edged, low-contrast, faceless silhouette in cobalt-aqua that dismantles downward into tile shadow and never reads as a second person. Caustics stay thin and netlike, a lattice of pale aqua light lying on the pool floor, running opposite to the colonnade's rhythm so the water owns a composition of its own.

Reserve quiet space on the right. The open water, the empty far wall above the colonnade and the clean band above the title hold about thirty percent of the frame as low-density air, and detail thins from her face and hand outward toward the right border and the top edge.

Hold the palette with strict area control. About sixty percent of the image is chalk white, ivory and pearl across plaster, tiles, deck and letter faces; fifteen percent is pale aqua and turquoise in the water, the tile grid and the hair; thirteen percent is cobalt and deep ultramarine in the letter inlay, the deep-end tiles, the refracted title and the water shadow; six percent is graphite in the thinnest contours and the ladder’s darker edges; five percent is silver on the chrome, the straps and the hairline highlights; and no more than one percent is magenta-coral at the square clasp and the two microdots on her hair ornaments. Every large field stays flat and cool, and the cobalt title is the only saturated note in the whole poster.

Add the graphic devices that belong to a printed poster. One broad translucent pale-aqua wash spreads across the lower-left water corner and stops at a hard edge before the ladder; two hard-edged cobalt rectangles sit along the right tile crust like overprint blocks; a translucent turquoise stain bleeds behind the ladder; cyan halftone dots grow in density from the centre of the tile grid toward the far blue band; a pearl-white knockout strip runs through the bottom border and two chalk-white knockouts erase parts of the far recesses; a puff of chalk bloom drifts off the coping into the window beam; the cobalt letters carry a one-pixel registration shift against their own aqua shadow.

Keep the interface engraved and non-linguistic. Centimetre calibration ticks run along the chalk coping, bracket corners mark both ends of the title band, one dot column sits beside the drain grate, three hairlines follow the tile grout at the deep end, and a single short bar marks the ladder's waterline crossing. Every mark is cut into a physical surface and catches thin shadow, and every mark belongs to the object it is cut into, reading as a groove, a bracket or a tick.

Control occlusion with explicit masks. A translucent aqua mask may cover the lower-left water corner, the outer twin tail, the far tiles, two floats, the bottom border and the right tile crust; a pearl-white knockout may erase the far recesses and the bottom strip. Masks stay clear of her face, her eyes, the complete hand, the swimsuit silhouette, the contacting fingertips and the fully readable word.

Let the glitch stay at the perimeter and escalate in one direction. Starting at the far end of the pool and the right border, cut four narrow horizontal slices through the tile band and shift them a few pixels sideways with thin aqua seams; replace the two furthest floats with cobalt rectangular pixels and a pale halftone fade; erase two short bands of the far chalk wall into pure white; stair-step the ripple line into one-pixel cyan steps at the extreme right. Her body, her hand, the coping she touches and the first six letters of the title stay on a clean, undisrupted field.

Place luxury micro-detail only at connections: silver links at the ladder rungs, one chipped porcelain tile resting on the coping, three suspended air bubbles under the meniscus, chalk dust caught on the coping edge, a hairline silver bead on the ankle tie, and a single wet highlight on the thumb where it touches the water.

Light the hall with low clear morning sun through a band of high clerestory windows: one broad shaft crosses the far wall, breaks into the window's mullion rhythm across the plaster, and lands on the water at the right third carrying visible chalk dust. Her face receives near-shadowless chalk-white illumination with a cool aqua bounce from the pool under her jaw and along her shoulder, a water highlight lifting the underside of her chin, thin cool shadows beneath her feet, and a narrow specular line running down each twin tail. Every shadow stays thin, cool and chalky so the room remains luminous rather than grey.

Maintain five distinct depth layers. Foreground: the cropped underwater tile corner at the bottom border, one large float edge, the meniscus line and a few dust motes on the deck. Character layer: Miku's face, her complete hand, the swimsuit silhouette and the exact contact point. Primary structure: the chalk basin, the title band, the chrome ladder. Secondary: the lane cable with its nine-float decay, the colonnade and the blind recesses. Background: the far blue tile band, the caustic net, the inverted reflection and the empty chalk air. Separate the layers through overlap, line weight, edge softness and value contrast rather than through blur.

Render the image as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional anime editorial poster combining precise anime linework, chalk-matte plaster surfaces, hard glazed ceramic geometry, translucent water refraction, cobalt enamel inlay, chrome reflection, restrained halftone, fine paper grain, one-pixel overprint misregistration and hairline silver detailing. Give the finest linework to her profile, her eyes and the five fingers of her supporting hand; the crispest edges to the tile grid and the letter inlay; the softest transitions to the refracted title and the inverted reflection; and the quietest surface to the chalk air on the right.

The final image should read as one voice in a chalk room at first light: a singer in a chalk-white and aqua swimsuit stands at the edge of a colossal turquoise basin, one hand resting on the tile band where the word “WATERLINE” is inlaid, a single horizontal waterline cutting the poster into architecture above and reflection below, nine floats decaying along a stainless cable, thin caustics and one calm inverted silhouette under the surface, morning light through high windows, print grain and restrained halftone on the surface, a tight cool palette with one magenta note, and complete clarity on her face, her eyes and her hand.

Readable text is limited to “WATERLINE”; one Hatsune Miku only; both her hands stay complete, unobstructed and anatomically correct; no watermark, signature or logo.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Hatsune Miku, no second figure, no swimmer in the water, no lane ropes, no spectators, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text beyond the single word inlaid in the tile band, no watermark, no signature, no frame, no border.

seeds.title: WHEAT FIELD
seeds.raw:
Create a wide 16:9 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “WHEAT FIELD”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character standing in a ripe wheat field in late afternoon wind, with a white timber barn behind her on the right. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the gold.

Use a camera at waist height on a normal lens, set inside the field about five metres from the barn and angled so the barn's wall fills the right third and the wheat runs to the horizon on the left. Place Miku at approximately forty-two percent of the canvas width, full body visible from boots to hair ornaments, occupying about thirty-two percent of the frame height.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Both hands hold a bundle of cut wheat at hip height, stems bundled in one fist, and her head is turned toward the barn, both eyes visible. Her hair and the wheat are pushed the same way by the wind. Keep the pose steady and put nothing else in her hands.

Construct the dominant visual object as the barn's wall: a broad side wall of vertical white-painted boards with a sliding door, a small square window, and a stone footing at its base. Let the wall occupy approximately thirty percent of the canvas area on the right and be the brightest large surface in the frame.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The boards are white-painted pine, the paint chalky and flaking at the lower courses; the sliding door is the same boards on rusted steel track; the stone footing is grey fieldstone with pale mortar; the wheat is dense ripe gold with pale awns; the sky is a flat pale blue; the field's far edge is a dark treeline. Each behaves differently — chalky paint holds a flat pale value and reads as vertical stripes, fieldstone reads as irregular blocks, ripe wheat scatters light into a fine even field with individual awns catching a bright line, the sky is a clean graded field.

Build a stepped sequence from the field inward. Begin at the bottom edge with the wheat's near stalks and one fallen sheaf, then Miku's boots and her bundled stems, then the middle field running to the treeline, then the barn's footing, then its wall and sliding door, then the sky. The sequence must read as standing inside a crop, not as a farm postcard.

Leave one deliberate absence. One board in the wall's middle course is missing: a clean dark slot about a board's width, with the two cut ends showing raw pine and the darkness behind reading as empty interior. Keep the slot at her shoulder height so the bright wall carries one unexplained vertical gap.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: wheat stalks, fallen sheaf, boots. Middle ground: Miku, the field, the barn's footing. Background: the wall, the door, the sky and treeline. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from a low sun at the left. The sun is the key: warm and raking, so every wheat awn catches a bright line and the barn wall goes warm white where it faces the light and cool grey on its shadowed return. Add the field's own bounce as a warm fill under her jaw. Keep the shadows long and warm, and let the sky stay cooler than the wall.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the wind. Both tails stream to the right, the nearer one crossing her shoulder and the farther one trailing into the wheat, both reading as one saturated aqua mass against the gold. Let the wind press her bangs aside without hiding her eyes.

Dress Miku in an original harvest costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not farm wear. A dark blue work shirt with the sleeves rolled, a pale canvas apron tied at the waist, dark trousers and short boots. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment.

Use a gold-and-white palette with one cool accent and strict area control. Approximately thirty-eight percent of the image is ripe wheat gold, twenty-two percent is the pale sky, eighteen percent is the chalky white wall, ten percent is the dark treeline, six percent is Miku's dark shirt and apron, four percent is her aqua hair, and two percent is the grey fieldstone.

Drive the printed graphic language from the barn's own boards rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the lower left of the wheat, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular pale panel behind the wall as a graphic mask at the height of the window, and let one vertical strip of deep gold run from the sky to the field, aligned to a board joint.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “WHEAT FIELD” once, large, in dark charcoal paint applied across the broad flat face of the barn's sliding door, spanning about two thirds of the door's width, in heavy condensed capitals that read clearly at thumbnail size against the white boards. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “LOT 12” sit on a small enamel plate screwed beside the window. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the season. The paint is chalky and flaking at the lower courses; the door's track is rusted and its rollers worn bright; the footing's mortar is missing in two joints; the wheat is heavy-headed and bent one way; the field's stubble shows between the stalks. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the field. The wheat runs in wind waves from the near edge to the treeline, three broad bands of light and shade crossing the whole frame, and the barn's shadow falls across the nearest band as one long cool wedge. Let the waves never break into individual pattern.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A rusted sickle hung on a nail beside the door, one twine-tied sheaf leaning on the footing, a steel bucket on its side in the stubble, and a short length of rope looped on the door's handle. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where a barn would actually have it.

Illuminate with the low sun at the left as the only key, plus the field's warm bounce as a fill. Let the sun produce long shadows to the right, a warm white on the lit wall and a bright edge on every awn. Let the bounce lift the underside of her jaw and the bundle in her hands. Keep the sky flat and slightly cooler than anything lit.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: near stalks, fallen sheaf, boots. Second: Miku, the bundle, her apron. Third: the middle field and its wind waves. Fourth: the barn's footing, wall and door. Fifth: the treeline and the sky. Separate them by value steps of roughly nine percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every board joint and wheat awn, restrained risograph grain in the shadow bands, crisp flat fills in the gold and white, and fine flaking only at the wall's lower courses.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no farmer, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable text on any sack or sign, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no birds, no machinery, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like the last hour of a harvest day: gold running in three wind waves to a dark treeline, a white wall holding one missing board, and a girl standing with a bundle of cut stems she has not yet tied.

seeds.title: WINDOW SEAT
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 9:16 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “WINDOW SEAT”, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character sitting on the deep sill of a rain-covered window in a small apartment, with the evening street running wet beyond the glass. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes, hands and twin-tail identity readable against the pale interior.

Use a camera at seated eye height on a normal lens, set inside the room about two metres back and square to the window so the frame's verticals align with the window reveal. The window is one undivided sheet of glass in a plain steel frame, from the sill up past the top of the frame, with no crossbars, no sash and no glazing bars at all. Place Miku at approximately fifty-two percent of the canvas width, seated on the sill with her knees drawn up, her whole figure, both knees, both shins, both shoes and the entire hem of her skirt kept inside the right half of the pane, and her shoulder a hand's width clear of the reveal's edge. Let the window occupy the upper two-thirds and the radiator and floor the lower third.

Give Miku exactly one core action. Both hands hold a chipped ceramic mug against her knees, and her forehead rests lightly against the cold glass so her breath makes one small clear patch on it, while the rest of her face stays a finger's width clear of the pane, both knees and both shins stay inside the right half of the pane, and both shoes hang clear of the glass by a hand's width. Her eyes are half closed. Keep the pose still, the arms wrapped loosely, and put nothing else in her hands.

Construct the dominant visual object as the window itself: a full-height opening closed by one undivided sheet of glass in a plain dark steel frame, a deep painted sill at its foot, and a cast-iron radiator beneath with its pipe entering the wall at the corner. The glass carries no divisions of any kind, so the only straight lines in the window are its outer frame and its sill. Let the window occupy approximately sixty percent of the canvas area and let the street beyond read only as blurred colour and rain. Keep all of the timber work behind her in depth, so no frame member crosses her face, her shoulder or her knees, and let the glass plane sit clear of her shoes by a hand's width.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. The glass is old and slightly wavy, covered on the outside with running rain and on the inside with one clear breath patch; the timber sash is painted off-white, cracked at the meeting rail; the sill is the same paint, worn to bare wood along its front edge; the radiator is cast iron with a ribbed face; the floor is worn linoleum in a dull pattern; the mug is glazed stoneware with a chipped rim. Each behaves differently — wet glass refracts everything behind it, painted timber holds a flat matte value, cast iron reads as repeated vertical ribs, linoleum returns a dull sheen, glaze holds one small hard highlight.

Build a stepped sequence from the room outward. Begin at the bottom edge with the lino's worn pattern and one slipper, then the radiator's ribs and its pipe, then the sill's bare edge, then Miku's knees and the mug, then her breath patch and half-closed eyes, then the lower rail and the running rain, then the street's blurred colour. The sequence must read as sitting inside looking out through weather, not as a portrait against a window.

Leave one deliberate absence. One pane of the window has no rain at all: the upper right pane is completely dry and clear, showing a sharp slice of the street beyond while every other pane runs with water. Keep it exactly one pane in size and place it above her head so the sharp rectangle interrupts the blurred field.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: lino, slipper, radiator ribs. Middle ground: Miku, the sill, the mug. Background: the rain-covered panes and the blurred street. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the street and one interior lamp. The street is the cool key: a blue-grey wash through wet glass, broken into a soft colour field by the rain, laying a cool cast on Miku's face, mug and knees. The lamp is a small warm source behind and above the camera, giving a thin warm rim along her shoulder, hair and the sill's front edge. Keep the two strictly separated: cool from outside, warm only on edges.

Weave Miku's extremely long twin tails into the window light. The nearer tail falls forward over her shoulder and pools on the sill in one clean aqua mass, catching the street's cool wash along its upper curve; the farther tail drops down behind her back and disappears behind the reveal as a darker vertical. Let one strand rest against the breath patch without clearing it.

Dress Miku in an original rain-evening costume derived from her recognizable virtual-singer design language, not pyjamas. An oversized grey knit worn long over the hips with the sleeves pulled over her hands, thick socks, and a thin chain at her ankle. Keep the palette close to her canonical teal-and-black with one pale garment, and keep the silhouette simple enough to read at thumbnail size.

Use a cool-grey palette with one warm accent and strict area control. Approximately forty-four percent of the image is rain-blurred blue-grey street, twenty percent is the pale off-white frame and reveal, fourteen percent is the dark radiator and floor, eight percent is Miku's grey knit, six percent is her aqua hair, four percent is the blurred warm points in the street, and four percent is the small warm rim from the lamp. Keep the warm values small and only at edges.

Drive the printed graphic language from the window's own geometry rather than from decoration. Let one large teal ink bloom spread across the lower right of the sill, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular pale panel behind the radiator as a graphic mask at the height of its top edge, and let one vertical strip of deep blue run from the top rail to the sill, aligned to the centre of the pane. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “WINDOW SEAT” once, in white paint stencilled across the painted wall panel below the window, worn at the middle letters, sized so it spans about half the panel's width. Let a second, much smaller exact readable line “3 F” sit on a small enamel plate screwed to the reveal above her shoulder. Keep both strings unbroken and correctly spelled, and put no other letters anywhere.

Let every surface carry the damp. The glass's rain runs in uneven channels, thicker at the bottom and broken where the frame's putty has failed; the sill's paint is worn to bare wood in a band the width of a forearm; the radiator's ribs hold dust in their valleys and one pale chalk mark; the lino is dull along the path feet take; the mug's chip is dark at its edge. Keep the wear physical and directional, never a uniform grime.

Build a second composition through the wet glass. The glass carries the street as a soft field of blurred colour bars — a red sign, a white lamp, a green awning — all pulled into vertical streaks by the running water, and carries Miku's silhouette as a pale ghost from the room's lamp behind her. Let the two overlap without either becoming sharp.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. A brass sash latch worn bright at the thumb, one small crack in the reveal's plaster, a folded newspaper wedged between radiator and wall, and a steel mug hook screwed into the sill's underside. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where an apartment window would actually have it.

Illuminate with the street as the cool key, plus the interior lamp as a thin warm rim. Let the street produce a blue-grey wash across her face, hands and knees, and a soft colour field in the glass. Let the lamp produce one warm edge along her shoulder, her hair and the sill's front face. Keep the room's interior darker than the street so the window reads as the source.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: lino, slipper, radiator ribs. Second: Miku, the sill, the mug. Third: the breath patch and the lower rail. Fourth: the rain-covered pane with the street's blurred bars. Fifth: the far lamps and the dark building opposite. Separate them by value steps of roughly ten percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every frame member and radiator rib, restrained risograph grain in the shadow fields, crisp flat fills in the lit areas, and fine chips only on the mug's rim. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the glaze and the brass.

No additional physical characters, no duplicate Miku, no second figure, no passer-by in the street, no frame member crossing her body, no timber dividing the glass, no shoe or toe touching the glass, no skirt hem crossing the sill's edge, no floating interface elements, no holographic panels, no readable signage in the street, no readable text beyond the two strings named above, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like an evening spent against cold glass: rain running down every pane but one, a breath patch slowly shrinking, and a girl holding a mug she has stopped drinking from while the street blurs past her forehead.

seeds.title: WIPING EDGE
seeds.raw:
Create a tall 3:4 ultra-premium editorial key visual titled “WIPING EDGE”, a frame built around one colossal aquamarine weapon, featuring Hatsune Miku as the only physical character sitting on a stone step with a long blade across her knees, drawing a cloth along its edge. Preserve her unmistakable canonical identity: luminous aqua eyes, straight aqua bangs, extremely long aqua twin tails, black-and-magenta square hair ornaments, youthful anime facial structure, slim proportions, and a clearly recognizable Hatsune Miku silhouette. Keep her face, eyes and twin-tail identity readable in the door's low light.

The weapon is one solid mass of aquamarine glass: translucent, cold blue-green, lit from within, and it throws cyan light onto everything around it.

Use a camera at her seated eye level on a short lens, set close and slightly above so the blade across her knees runs horizontally through the frame's middle and her bowed head fills the upper third. Place Miku at approximately forty-eight percent of the canvas width, occupying about seventy percent of the frame height. Let the blade's tip pass the frame's right edge and its guard sit just inside the left.

Give Miku exactly one core action: wiping the edge. Her left hand holds the blade steady across her knees with the fingers wrapped under the flat, her right hand draws a folded cloth along the edge from guard to tip at about halfway, and her head is bowed so her eyes follow the cloth. Keep her wrists relaxed, her shoulders forward, and put nothing else in either hand.

Construct the dominant visual object as the blade and cloth: a single-edged sword two fingers wide and three feet long, laid flat across her thighs with its edge turned toward the viewer, and a folded grey cloth pinched in her right hand with one corner dragging behind the stroke. Keep the sword plain — one iron guard, one cord-wrapped handle, no engraving. Let the cloth be the only soft thing in the frame.

Assign materials by zone instead of mixing them evenly. the blade is one piece of aquamarine, cold blue-green and translucent so the whole mass reads as one saturated stone, its interior holding a fine web of cracks that catch the doorway light, its edge polished and one nick deep, and it stays dark except where light crosses it; the cloth is coarse grey linen, frayed at one corner and dark where it has been used; the guard is pitted iron; the handle is dark cord over ray skin; her clothing is matte wool; the step is worn granite; the doorway behind is a dark rectangle with a stone frame. Each behaves differently — steel returns one narrow hard light and one broad soft one, linen reads as a coarse weave with soft folds, pitted iron holds a dull grain, cord shows a fine diagonal, wool absorbs everything, worn granite is a soft matte plane with a faint polish on its nosing, the doorway is a near-black void.

Build a stepped sequence across the frame. Begin at the lower left with the granite step and her knee, then her thigh and the blade's flat, then her two hands and the cloth at mid-stroke, then her bowed face with its lowered lids, then her shoulder and falling hair, then the dark doorway. The sequence must read as a habit performed in a doorway, not as a display of a weapon.

Leave one deliberate absence. There is no scabbard, no sheath cloth, no oil flask and no whetstone — nothing on the step beside her but her own boot. Keep the step's whole right end bare so the cloth's trailing corner is the only object beyond the blade.

Build real foreground, middle ground and background. Foreground: the granite step and her knee. Middle ground: the blade's flat, her hands and the cloth. Background: her bowed head, her shoulder, the dark doorway. Separate them by value and edge, not by blur.

Light the scene from the doorway's far side. The doorway is the key: a low raking light that comes through it from behind and to her left, rims her hair, shoulder and the blade's upper edge, and leaves her face lit only by the blade's reflection. Let the granite step catch a narrow band of that light and let the frame's near corners fall dark. Never introduce a front fill. Let the crystal pass the light rather than return it: one thin saturated cyan line where the mass is thickest, and one hard-edged cyan caustic patch thrown onto the granite step beside it.

Let Miku's extremely long twin tails fall forward over both shoulders as she bows. The nearer tail drops across her left arm and lies along the blade's flat, its tip curled just short of the cloth; the farther one hangs behind her shoulder into the dark. Let the doorway's light rim each tail and let the tip on the steel catch one cool reflection.

Dress Miku in a loose indoor layer over her canonical palette, not armour. A dark teal wrap jacket worn open with the sleeves pushed to the elbow, a black undershirt, dark loose trousers, and one bare foot with the other still in a soft boot. Keep the palette close to teal-and-black with one pale cuff at her right wrist, and keep the silhouette soft and seated.

Use a warm-on-dark palette with strict area control. Approximately thirty-four percent of the image is the dark doorway and its shadow, twenty-two percent is the granite step, eighteen percent is the blade, nine percent is her clothing, seven percent is the cloth, five percent is her aqua hair, four percent is her face and hands, and one percent is the pale cuff and the guard's bright rim. Keep every cold note in her hair and the crystal. The aquamarine's cold blue-green tone is the one saturated colour in the entire frame and must read at a glance even at thumbnail size; keep every other surface desaturated so that single hue does all the colour work.

Drive the printed graphic language from the doorframe's own marks rather than from decoration. Let one large deep-teal ink bloom spread across the dark doorway in the upper right, printed flat and matte. Add a rectangular ochre panel across the granite at her knee as a graphic mask, and let one vertical strip of rust-red run down the frame's left edge from top to step. Keep every graphic element square to the frame.

Print the text as physical matter. Set the exact readable word “WIPING EDGE” once, in white paint stencilled across the stone doorframe beside her head, the strokes chipped where the stone has spalled, sized so it spans about half the doorframe's visible width and reads clearly at thumbnail size. Put no lettering on the blade, the cloth, the step or her clothing, and put no other letters anywhere in the image.

Let every surface carry the shift. The blade's polish is hazed in a band along its lower third and bright only at the edge; the cloth is dark along one folded edge and frayed at its corner; the guard's blacking is gone at both ends; the handle's cord is flattened where her left fingers sit; the granite's nosing is polished in a shallow hollow and chipped at one corner. Keep the wear physical and directional.

Build a second composition through the polished blade. The steel carries the doorway as one dark vertical band, her hands as two soft dark shapes, and the cloth as a pale soft smear that interrupts the reflection. Never let the blade mirror her face and never let the reflection extend past its tip.

Add only a few luxury details, all at working points. One pale cuff at her right wrist, a single thread pulled from the cloth's corner, a fine bright nick in the blade's edge just ahead of the stroke, and one hairline crack across the step's front face. Keep each detail small, plausible and placed where use would put it.

Maintain five readable depth layers. Foreground: the granite step and her knee. Second: the blade's flat and her left hand. Third: her right hand and the cloth at mid-stroke. Fourth: her bowed face and falling tails. Fifth: her shoulder and the dark doorway. Separate them by value steps of roughly twelve percent each.

Render the result as an exceptionally polished two-dimensional editorial illustration that reads like a screen print with photographic discipline: crisp cel-shaded figure, precise thin contours on every blade facet and stone chip, restrained risograph grain in the dark doorway, crisp flat fills in the lit granite, and one clean gradient only along the exposed edge. Keep the whole image matte; no glossy highlights anywhere except the steel and her eye.

No second character, no duplicate Miku, no crowd, no banners, no flags, no birds, no wings, no halo, no scabbard, no second blade, no whetstone, no oil flask, no additional weapon, no glowing crystal, no neon glow, no self-lit weapon, no rainbow dispersion, no stained glass, no plastic, no glass bottle, no glowing runes, no glyphs, no symbols, no magical effects, no readable text beyond the string named above, no blood, no wounds, no armour plates, no duplicate face, no extra limbs, no malformed hands, no cropped title, no photographic depth of field, no lens flare, no chromatic aberration, no heavy bloom, no 3D render, no painterly brushwork, no scrapbook clutter.

The final image should feel like a chore done in a doorway: a blade laid flat across two knees, a grey cloth halfway along the edge, and a girl looking down at the steel as if it were the only thing in the building worth cleaning.
